papers.abstract: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving use chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to guide action generation, but incur substantial memory and computational costs. We study structured pruning for these models, focusing on preserving both scene understanding and trajectory prediction. Our analysis of Taylor importance in Alpamayo-1.5-10B shows that reasoning and trajectory objectives assign different importance to the same vision-language model (VLM) structures. In the action expert, MLP channels exhibit more stable importance rankings across denoising steps than query heads, and a small fraction of channels accounts for most of the measured importance. Based on these findings, we propose MoOP, which combines importance ranks from both objectives for VLM pruning and aggregates stepwise importance to select a fixed subset of expert MLP channels. At 24.0% total parameter reduction, VLM-only pruning with MoOP performs comparably to or slightly better than the strongest baselines in driving, while retaining 94.0% of the dense model's LingoQA score, far above all other methods. At a higher reduction of 30.0%, MoOP degrades much less than every other method, as it is the only one whose reasoning does not collapse. Removing 93.75% of expert MLP channels increases total parameter reduction to 39.4%, with nearly unchanged open-loop errors relative to VLM-only pruning and competitive closed-loop performance. The resulting model achieves a 1.37x end-to-end inference speedup and 36.6% lower peak memory than the dense model, without post-pruning fine-tuning.
authors: Seongchan Kim, Soowon Son, Sangoh Kim, Hyunah Ko, Eunbeen Hong, Hyunkoo Lee, Sanghyun Lee, WonJun Moon, Kihong Kim, Dongyeon Son, Woongchan Nam, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Reasoning and trajectory objectives prioritize different VLM structures, so pruning based on either alone can damage performance.
Action-expert MLP channels have more stable importance across denoising steps than query heads, with a small subset carrying most importance.
MoOP combines both objectives for VLM pruning and aggregates stepwise importance to select expert MLP channels.
At 24.0% parameter reduction, it retains 94.0% of dense-model LingoQA performance and matches or slightly exceeds strong driving baselines.
At 39.4% reduction, it achieves 1.37× faster inference and 36.6% lower peak memory without post-pruning fine-tuning, while preserving competitive driving performance.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Mixture-of-Objective Pruning (MoOP). (a) Pruning the VLM with reasoning-driven (CE) importance alone preserves the CoC but degrades the predicted trajectory. (b) Pruning with action-driven (FM) importance alone corrupts the reasoning that conditions the action expert. (c) MoOP combines both objectives to select VLM units and uses FM importance to prune the action expert, preserving both reasoning and driving.
Figure 2: Alpamayo architecture. The VLM encodes frames, prompt and ego history, generates the CoC, and its KV cache conditions the action expert, which denoises noise ϵ into a trajectory.

Týr-the-Pruner crosses on amber at 13.4 s at 15.1 m/s, and Wanda and CE-only cross after the signal turned amber, at 17.2 and 11.7 m/s. None of these three stops, and they end 64–104 m past the line. Wanda also has an at-fault collision at 9.0 s, before reaching the intersection.

Figure 5: Denoising stepwise rank stability and importance concentration in the action expert. (a, b) Pairwise Spearman correlations of FM-based Taylor importance rankings across the ten denoising steps. Q head rankings become less similar between distant steps, whereas MLP channel rankings remain stable. (c) Fraction of the measured importance removed as units are removed in ascending order of importance. The lowest-scoring 90% of MLP channels account for only 1.8% of the measured importance, whereas Q head importance is distributed more broadly. Figure 12: Open loop: following a lead vehicle. (a) Both models reason about the stopped lead vehicle, and both best samples stop short of the ground truth. MoOP’s stops closer, a small gain (0.55 m vs. 0.47 m), and the Baseline’s trajectory is largely hidden beneath MoOP’s. (b) The Baseline reasons that it must wait for a gap to merge left, and its best sample drifts about 1.5 m to the left while running ahead of the ground truth. MoOP reasons about keeping its distance to the lead vehicle, which is the truck ahead, and stays on the ground-truth path (3.72 m vs. 0.35 m).

papers.selection_reason: Structured pruning of reasoning VLA models for autonomous driving, preserving reasoning and action while cutting memory and compute.
papers.title: Pruning Autonomous Driving VLAs: What to Preserve for Reasoning and Action
papers.tldr: MoOP prunes autonomous-driving VLA models by jointly preserving reasoning and action-critical structures, reducing cost while maintaining driving and language-reasoning performance.

papers.abstract: Exploring a scene from as little as a single photo requires generating a long, camera-controlled walkthrough that extends far beyond what was captured, yet remains consistent upon return. Memory-based video generation methods preserve what they have already seen, but have no anchor beyond it, where the camera drifts from its path and a text prompt can name objects but not place them. Layout-conditioned methods provide such an anchor and precise control over what appears where, but rely on layouts that are typically authored by hand. Both limitations arise because, beyond what was captured, nothing anchors the video model unless a human authors one. To overcome both, we propose Lyris, a long video generation framework that never leaves the video model without an anchor: a persistent point-cloud memory where the scene has been observed or generated, and a 3D layout that a vision-language model authors where it has not. Our key insight is that the interface between the two models can be surprisingly coarse. A layout of one labeled 3D box per object is simple enough for a vision-language model to author (and for a user to edit), yet expressive enough for a video model to follow once rendered along the camera path. We demonstrate walkthroughs of over three minutes and 50 meters from a single photo, passing through doorways into rooms it never shows. When evaluated on minute-long round trips across four datasets, Lyris outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a wide margin, reducing camera error by 3.8x and improving consistency upon return by 22% on average.
authors: Chen Wang, Jiahui Huang, Riccardo de Lutio, Alex Trevithick, Bryan Chu, Jiawei Ren, Laura Leal-Taix\'e, Shengyu Huang, Lingjie Liu, Haithem Turki
bullets: Addresses camera drift and scene inconsistency when generating beyond the captured view.
Uses persistent point-cloud memory for observed or generated regions and a vision-language model to create layouts for unseen areas.
Represents each object with a coarse labeled 3D box that is both user-editable and usable by the video generator.
Produces walkthroughs exceeding three minutes and 50 meters from one photo, including unseen rooms beyond doorways.
On minute-long round trips across four datasets, reduces camera error by 3.8× and improves return consistency by 22% on average.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Lyris. To decide what lies beyond the input views, we use a vision-language model to plan a 3D layout B of labeled object boxes before each chunk k. We then render this layout and our point-cloud memory P at its cameras Ck to guide the video model. The memory video preserves what has been seen, while the layout video specifies what appears where beyond it and anchors the camera to its path. To remain consistent upon return, we reconstruct each generated chunk and write it into the memory.

Figure 4. Directed round trips. Given the same start frame, cameras, and descriptions (top), we plot each method’s rotation error along the way out over the 20 CA-1M scenes (left) and show five cameras of one round trip with each frame’s error (right). The baselines drift once the path leaves the start view (by roughly 20–40◦ at its end), as does our model without its layout (dotted). Lyris is the only method to follow the path throughout, staying within 4◦ of the requested cameras.

Figure 6. Layout control. We edit the plan of Fig. 3 and regenerate with the same inputs and seed. Without a layout, the model places the described objects itself and drifts from the requested camera (a), while with the plan each object appears in its box (b). Moving the television’s box moves the television and leaves its former place (dashed) empty (c), and swapping the aquarium and the orchids in the layout and the descriptions swaps them (d), which lets a user edit the scene before it is generated.

Figure 3. Layout planning. To keep the layout consistent with the observed scene, the vision-language model first fits boxes to the objects visible in the input view (a). It then adds a box for every object that the chunks should reveal, following their descriptions (b). To ensure that the layout is physically plausible and visible along the path, we verify the proposal with geometric checks (c) and revise the boxes they flag from their proposed positions (dashed in b) to their final ones. The video model then generates each object where its box places it, such as the vase, which was moved into view (d).

Figure 7. Qualitative ablation. We show the frames that Lyris and its ablations (Tab. 3) generate at the same camera of a directed CA-1M round trip, on the way out and 217 frames later on the way back, with the DINOv2 similarity of the two frames (Revisit). We also show the layout video that each variant receives on the way out, and its memory video and appearance references on the way back. Lyris returns to the same content, whereas the camera drifts without the layout (RotErr of 93.9◦ at this camera), the content changes without the memory’s point cloud, and details change without the appearance references (circled).

Figure 8. Planner output. We show three of the boxes that the planner adds in the second chunk of a CA-1M round trip, without their colors and justifications. Each box is fully specified by a label, a center and size in meters, and a rotation about the gravity axis in degrees. Planning. We use Claude Opus 5.5 as our planner, although Lyris also outperforms all baselines with smaller and openweight planners (Sec. A.2). As our layout only requires one labeled box per object, we simply query the planner with fixed prompts, without tools or fine-tuning. It first localizes each object visible in the start frame with a 2D bounding box, which we lift to 3D by fitting a box to the memory

Figure 9. Video model. The DiT processes the latents of the noisy target together with those of the memory video, the prefix frame and appearance references, and the layout video, and with the Qwen3-VL embedding of the text prompt, through joint selfattention. We freeze the VAE and Qwen3-VL, fine-tune the DiT with LoRA, and add only a zero-initialized linear layer per block that embeds the cameras Ck as Plücker rays.

Table 3. Ablation study. We evaluate on CA-1M and ScanNet++ round trips. The layout is crucial for camera accuracy with or without a description, and far more effective when rendered than when stated in the prompt.

Additional views improve fidelity on every dataset, including beyond the last view.
Table 11. Geometric checks. We verify each box that the planner proposes with the six checks of Sec. 3.1. Their tolerances are the same for every scene and dataset.

papers.selection_reason: Long-horizon camera-controlled video generation anchored by persistent 3D point-cloud memory and VLM-authored layouts.
papers.title: Lyris: Layout-Guided Long Video Generation with Persistent 3D Memory
papers.tldr: Lyris generates long, camera-controlled 3D walkthrough videos from a single photo by combining persistent scene memory with automatically authored 3D layouts.

papers.abstract: Recent unified multimodal models aim to combine visual understanding and generation within a single model, yet effectively integrating the two capabilities remains challenging. Leveraging pretrained vision-language models offers a way to build on already learned multimodal knowledge, but making this knowledge effectively accessible to visual generation remains nontrivial. We find that a central challenge lies in the heterogeneous visual representations used for understanding and generation. To address this challenge, we introduce Integral, which converts a pretrained vision-language model into a unified multimodal model by constructing a shared visual representation space across the two capabilities. Integral implements this design through two complementary components. Abstraction Fusion constructs shared visual tokens by aggregating hierarchical representations from the frozen vision encoder, while Block-wise MoT introduces a lightweight generative stream that interacts with the vision-language model only at block boundaries. Our approach effectively preserves the pretrained understanding capability while extending it to strong visual generation. Controlled comparisons further demonstrate that sharing visual representations between understanding and generation substantially improves generative learning compared with using a separate visual representation space, despite comparable reconstruction fidelity. These results suggest that representations learned by pretrained vision-language models already provide an effective foundation for visual generation.
authors: JB Kim, Byungwoo Jeon, Kyungmin Lee, Hyeonmo Kang, Cheonbok Park, Shinyoung Joo, Jinwoo Shin, Jeonghoon Kim
bullets: Problem: Visual understanding and generation use heterogeneous representations, making them difficult to integrate in one model.
Method: Abstraction Fusion builds shared visual tokens from hierarchical frozen-encoder features.
Method: Block-wise MoT adds a lightweight generative stream that interacts with the vision-language model at block boundaries.
Result: Shared representations improve generative learning while preserving pretrained understanding and maintaining comparable reconstruction fidelity.
Implication: Pretrained vision-language representations can serve as an effective foundation for visual generation.

papers.abstract: Prompting language models to verbalize stepwise numerical confidence during generation is an increasingly popular approach for triggering backtracking and error correction in agentic reasoning. This strategy presupposes two capabilities: (1) in-situ monitoring fidelity (does confidence drop when an error occurs?) and (2) downstream steering control (does an uncertainty token causally steer the model to repair its error?). We evaluated four open-weights models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4, 14.7B) across 15,200 math benchmark attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors within each model's capability frontier. Applying 27,568 counterfactual continuations across these failure points, we demonstrate a consistent decoupling between monitoring and control. On monitoring, all four models fail to detect their own errors. Verbalized confidence does not distinguish mistake steps from sound reasoning, yielding near-chance within-position AUROCs between 0.500 and 0.561. Even at a model's first reasoning error, trajectory confidence remains saturated at 95.1% to 99.9%, with noticeable drops ($\ge 10$ points) appearing on fewer than 9% of errors in Llama and under 1.6% in the other three models. In contrast, models respond readily to external uncertainty: injecting a low-confidence tag (10%) at the error step significantly increases downstream correction across all models (+3.7 to +22.5 points over format-matched 95% certainty; all $p \le 0.0022$), reaching up to 38.5% under active rethinking instructions. However, injecting doubt onto already-correct steps causes models to discard valid reasoning, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points. Inference-time self-correction is thus bottlenecked by in-situ error detection rather than downstream repair capacity: models readily steer toward recovery when prompted with doubt, yet fail to self-monitor during generation.
authors: Daniel Theron
bullets: Evaluated four open-weight models on 15,200 math attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors and testing 27,568 counterfactual continuations.
Verbalized confidence did not distinguish erroneous from correct reasoning, with near-chance error detection and confidence often remaining very high after mistakes.
Externally injected low-confidence tokens improved downstream correction across all models, especially with active rethinking instructions.
Injecting doubt into correct reasoning could harm performance, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points.
Self-correction is therefore limited primarily by in-situ error detection, not by the ability to repair errors once uncertainty is supplied.

papers.abstract: Radiology reports describe findings in text only, without visually marking them on the scan, so readers cannot directly see which abnormality each reported finding refers to. We introduce CTLink, a text-prompted 3D segmentation model that segments findings described in a chest CT report. CTLink was trained on 4123 noncontrast chest CT scans with 9547 segmented report findings, including ReXGroundingCTv2, a newly annotated dataset of 1134 scans and 1895 findings with every instance of each finding segmented. On the 200 ReXGroundingCT validation scans, CTLink achieved a hit rate of 0.816, an instance F1 score of 0.456, and a mean Dice score of 0.400, compared with 0.533, 0.175, and 0.234 for VoxTell, a publicly available text-prompted segmentation model (P < .001 for all). On the test set of the MICCAI 2026 ReXGrounding challenge, an ensemble of seven CTLink models achieved the highest hit rate (0.782) and instance F1 score (0.386) of all 48 participating teams. On 50 test scans segmented twice by independent radiologists, CTLink matched or exceeded inter-rater agreement. Diffuse non-focal findings remained the main limitation, partly because their extent is outlined inconsistently even between radiologists. The CTLink model weights are available at https://huggingface.co/rajpurkarlab/CTLink, and the dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/rajpurkarlab/ReXGroundingCT.

papers.abstract: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence.
authors: Xiwei Liu, Yulong Li, Xuhui Li, Xinlin Zhuang, Zhixiang Lu, Haolin Yang, Jianxu Chen, Yifan Lu, Zhiran Zhang, Yutong Xie

Across 23 VLMs, the strongest models seek evidence purposefully but lose useful information through limited memory.
Weaker and specialized models perform near random exploration or fail to reason from gathered evidence.

papers.title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning

papers.abstract: Generative Pre-Training (GPT) represents a profound milestone in natural language processing, serving as the foundation for most of today's state-of-the-art large language models. By casting diverse understanding and generation problems into a shared token representation, GPT enables a single architecture and unified optimization loop to master heterogeneous tasks across massive corpora, giving rise to powerful foundation models for natural language. In contrast, 4D spatiotemporal vision lacks a common representational protocol: perception (such as depth and camera estimation) and generation are either handled by separate one-way pipelines or bolted together from unaligned single-modality spaces. In this work, we introduce WorldLatent, a framework that formulates a unified 4D latent space as a common protocol for both world perception and generation. Rather than relying on fragmented, task-specific models or stacked single-modality representations, our framework proposes a multimodal VAE architecture that compresses and fuses complex 4D visual appearance, geometry, and dynamics into a single structured latent representation. Within this formulation, perception and generation operate as complementary denoising processes over the same latent space, enabling one generative model to learn both capabilities simultaneously within a single training loop. Experiments across representative 4D benchmarks verify that our fused latent protocol achieves specialist-level zero-shot 4D perception, coherent 4D generation, and controllable editing from a single model. By demonstrating that diverse 4D tasks can be seamlessly unified under a shared representational protocol, our work provides a scalable foundation for general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence.
authors: Jingxi Chen, Yujia Chen, Cornelia Fermuller, Yiannis Aloimonos, Wen-Sheng Chu, Du Tran
bullets: Addresses the lack of a common representation for 4D spatiotemporal vision.

A single model achieves specialist-level zero-shot 4D perception, coherent generation, and controllable editing across representative benchmarks.
Positions the shared latent protocol as a foundation for general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence.

figures.caption: Figure 2. WorldLatent training pipeline. (a) WorldVAE training: Multiple 4D spatiotemporal modalities, including monocular RGB video, depth maps, and camera Plücker coordinates (ray direction d and moment m), are compressed via modality-specific encoders (E1– E4) and fused by a Dense Prediction Transformer (DPT) into a unified latent bottleneck, z4d (WorldLatent). Modality-specific decoders (D1–D4) then reconstruct the original modalities from this shared latent space. (b) Any-to-4D generative modeling: With the WorldVAE frozen, a unified diffusion model is trained within the learned latent space. It takes Gaussian noise, text prompts (Ctext), and partial or empty 4D latents c4d(S) (e.g., S = ∅ for text-to-4D generation, RGB-only for perception, or depth-only for editing) to synthesize the full 4D latent z4d. Finally, the frozen decoders (D1–D4) map z4d back into temporally coherent video, 3D geometry, and camera trajectories.

papers.abstract: Coding agents can construct and revise robot behavior during execution, but using one agent for the whole robot can delay otherwise independent work. We introduce Asynchronous Coding Agents as Policy (ACAP), an asynchronous framework that organizes one robot as a team of persistent agents. Each member reasons and acts for a configurable control group, such as an arm with its gripper or the torso and chassis, enabling asynchronous reasoning and execution. However, different robot components often have physical dependencies that require coordination. To address this challenge, ACAP introduces a hyper-agent that assigns tasks, coordinates dependencies, and dynamically allocates control between the lead and member agents. This allows independent work to progress concurrently while supporting tightly coupled manipulation when necessary. Across 72 real-world rollouts covering 25 task/platform settings, ACAP reduces task-balanced time cost by 28.2% compared with a single-agent Direct Policy, with improvements across Fully Parallel, Parallel-Sequential, and Collaborative tasks. Across all eight Collaborative settings, ACAP also achieves lower mean time cost than Fixed Delegation, where only member agents can control their assigned groups. An additional 90-rollout study shows lower mean 30-minute-capped time cost than Direct on all six tasks. We further demonstrate mobile manipulation using the same member interface for chassis and torso control. We present the framework and a real-world rollout dataset containing observations, generated programs, actions, and feedback to support research on how coding agents reason and act in the physical world.
authors: Zexin He, Rui Li, Yushi Lan, Chengkai Jin, Zhi Hou, Xingang Pan
bullets: Organizes one robot as persistent agents, each controlling a configurable group such as an arm, gripper, torso, or chassis.
A hyper-agent assigns tasks, coordinates physical dependencies, and dynamically reallocates control between lead and member agents.
Supports concurrent execution for independent subtasks and coordination for tightly coupled manipulation.
Across 72 real-world rollouts in 25 task/platform settings, ACAP reduced task-balanced time cost by 28.2% versus a single-agent Direct Policy.
Provides a 90-rollout evaluation and a real-world dataset of observations, programs, actions, and feedback; it also demonstrates mobile manipulation.

papers.abstract: Frontier multimodal models exhibit extraordinary generalization in generating robot actions from observations and instructions, enabling a new paradigm in which they serve directly as policies within closed-loop robotic harnesses. However, the design principles of such harnesses, and the capabilities underlying their strong performance, remain unclear. We present Embo-Harness, a framework for systematically studying frontier-model-as-policy harnesses. We investigate four components of the robotic agentic loop, namely, prompting, planning, action execution, and tool use, and distill six empirical findings into a practical recipe. This recipe prioritizes interfaces that exploit the model's native visual reasoning and tool-use capabilities over handcrafted plans, skills, or action priors, and identifies effective choices for action representation, chunking, reasoning effort, visual observations, short multi-action sequences, and policy refinement. On RoboLab-120, Embo-Harness achieves an 83.3\% success rate, outperforming the strongest reported baseline by 26.2 percentage points. It also succeeds in 15 of 20 zero-shot trials across four real-world manipulation tasks. Beyond performance, controlled interventions indicate that the studied model depends more strongly on accurate spatial target estimation than on explicit low-level joint or trajectory generation. These results provide both a practical recipe for building strong frontier-model-as-policy harnesses and a clearer account of the capabilities that drive their performance.
authors: Xiao-Ming Wu, Kang Liao, Yuexiao Ma, Taolin Zhang, Mingqian Zhou, Nuo Chen, Ziming Li, Yihang Luo, Rui Li, Zhonghua Wu, Tianyu Xie, Xiawu Zheng, Zhongang Cai, Zhi Hou, Chen Change Loy
bullets: Analyzes prompting, planning, action execution, and tool use in frontier-model robotic harnesses.
Finds that interfaces leveraging native visual reasoning and tool use outperform reliance on handcrafted plans, skills, or action priors.
Provides guidance on action representation and chunking, reasoning effort, visual observations, short multi-action sequences, and policy refinement.
Achieves 83.3% success on RoboLab-120 and succeeds in 15 of 20 zero-shot real-world manipulation trials.
Interventions suggest performance depends more on accurate spatial target estimation than explicit low-level joint or trajectory generation.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the Robotic Agentic Loop. A robotic harness consists of four key dimensions: 1) Prompting, including task instructions and visual observations; 2) Planning, including context management, planning strategies, and model and reasoning effort selection; 3) Tool Use, including acting tools and policy models; and 4) Action Execution, including action formats, action chunking, and asynchronous execution. These dimensions operate within a closed-loop framework and form the design space systematically explored in Embo-Harness.

Figure 4. Overview of Embo-Harness. Embo-Harness is designed to leverage the model’s native visual reasoning and tool-use capabilities over handcrafted plans, failure-derived skills, or action priors. The harness takes task instructions and high-resolution visual observations as inputs to GPT-6-Astra with xhigh reasoning effort. The frontier model produces short, fixed-length chunks of absolute end-effector (EEF) actions. Short multi-action sequences and VLA refinement are further integrated as tools to enhance manipulation performance. Zoom in for best view of the demos.

Figure 2. Typical Robotic Harness Paradigms. (1) Tool/code-aspolicy harnesses leverage frontier models for high-level planning while relying on predefined tools or generated code for action execution. (2) Model-as-policy harnesses delegate action generation to specialized policy models. (3) Frontier-model-as-policy harnesses directly generate robot actions using frontier models. All three paradigms operate within a closed-loop framework, differing primarily in how robot actions are generated.

papers.abstract: World action model (WAM) is a promising paradigm for visuomotor control by jointly modeling world dynamics and actions. Notably, existing WAMs often rely on large generative models and iterative sampling which incur substantial latency for action generation, limiting real-time deployment. In particular, there are two root causes of inefficiency in conventional flow matching or diffusion based action models in WAMs: 1) transporting uninformative Gaussian noise into precise actions necessitating multiple ODE steps, and 2) repeatedly injecting task context through expensive cross-attention modules. Our key insight is that jointly learning and aligning the source and action manifolds streamlines the transport between them, substantially accelerating action generation. Building on this insight, we introduce VITA-WAM, a WAM architecture with manifold-aligned flow-matching (VITA flow matching) that directly transports latent observation representations containing visual, language, and proprioceptive information into latent actions. More specifically, a flow latent alignment (FLA) mechanism is employed to facilitate manifold alignment between latent observation and action representations, enabling accurate generation with few ODE steps. The resulting architecture also eliminates costly attention for observation conditioning during repeated denoising steps. Notably, with a single ODE step, VITA-WAM outperforms 10-step FastWAM by 21.47 pp on LIBERO-Plus and by 1.65 pp on LIBERO, achieving these gains through the FLA objective without distillation, while inferring at 55.67~ms latency, a $2.10\times$ speedup compared to FastWAM.
authors: Boqi Zhao, Dechen Gao, Hanchu Zhou, Hang Wang, Junshan Zhang
bullets: Addresses the latency of conventional diffusion- or flow-matching-based world-action models caused by noise-to-action transport and repeated cross-attention.
Directly transports latent visual, language, and proprioceptive observation representations into latent actions.
Uses flow latent alignment (FLA) to align observation and action manifolds and support accurate generation with few ODE steps.
With one ODE step, it outperforms 10-step FastWAM by 21.47 percentage points on LIBERO-Plus and 1.65 points on LIBERO.
Achieves 55.67 ms inference latency, a 2.10× speedup over FastWAM, without distillation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Illustration of VITA-WAM architecture. 1) During training (top), a Q-Former fuses visual, language and proprioception into a latent source z0, where the visual signal is the output of the video DiT supervised by video flow matching. The action encoder maps the action chunk into a target latent z1. The source and target representations are jointly learned with VITA flow matching through FM, AE and FLA objectives, with FLA supervising the action chunk decoded from the ODE-generated latent. 2) During inference (bottom), a single video DiT forward pass extracts current-observation features, which are fused with language and proprioception by the Q-Former to construct the source latent z0. The action DiT then performs conditioningfree ODE integration starting from z0 to generate the action latent ẑ1, which is decoded into an action chunk.

Figure 6: Training and inference architecture of VITA-WAM (visual conditioning). The Q-Former constructs the source latent from visual observations, language, and proprioception. During ODE integration, the action DiT additionally uses mixed video–action attention with cached video K/V. The action decoder converts the generated latent into an action chunk.

Figure 1: Comparing conventional flow matching (left) vs. VITA flow matching (right). Conventional flow matching learns to transport Gaussian noise to the target manifold, necessitating multiple ODE steps. VITA flow matching (right) jointly learns and aligns the source and target representation manifolds with the Flow Latent Alignment (FLA) mechanism, thus enabling generation with simplified transport paths and fewer ODE steps. VITA-WAM employs VITA flow matching, significantly improving the efficiency of WAM action generation.

papers.abstract: Modern visual generative models operate on tokens, and every visual asset they receive, whether an identity, a scribble, a depth map, or a motion video, is tokenized and appended to the input token sequence. Consequently, conditioning quickly dominates the computation cost. Yet most of these tokens carry redundant spatiotemporal information. Our key insight is that identifying what is genuinely new is exactly the problem that classical video codecs have long solved. Thus, we first introduce a codec-based token pruning method that discards redundant tokens. Then, we propose an on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) strategy to train a DiT adapter capable of learning the codec pruning pattern well without quality degradation. Together, they form On-Policy Codec Distillation (CodecOPSD). We scale CodecOPSD to 16 condition modalities on our own video diffusion model, where it prunes 66% of the condition tokens on average with almost no quality drop. Therefore, denoising becomes 2x faster, and the cache memory shrinks by up to 73% in KV cache mode. CodecOPSD also extends to other state-of-the-art pretrained image and video generative models, where its benefit grows further with more conditions, longer frames, and higher resolution.
authors: Boyang Wang, Kevin Blackburn-Matzen, Oindrila Saha, Matheus Gadelha, Zezhou Cheng
bullets: Condition tokens from modalities such as identity, scribbles, depth, and motion videos create substantial computation and memory costs.
A codec-based pruning method removes redundant spatiotemporal conditioning tokens.
On-policy self-distillation trains a DiT adapter to reproduce the codec’s pruning pattern without degrading quality.
Scaled to 16 conditioning modalities, it prunes 66% of condition tokens on average, makes denoising 2× faster, and reduces KV-cache memory by up to 73%.
Benefits extend to pretrained image and video generators and increase with more conditions, longer videos, and higher resolution.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Pipeline of CodecOPSD. Right: On-Policy Codec Distillation provides the tokens removed by codec pruning to the frozen teacher as privileged information and compares the student’s prediction with the teacher’s.

(b) A P-frame finds the best match of each block in a previous frame and stores its motion vector. (c) The residual is the difference between the block and its best match. (d) Each token receives a motion score and a residual score from the blocks it covers, and threshold-based or priority-based pruning then selects the kept tokens.

papers.abstract: Decision models are emerging as fast components of larger AI systems. Yet recent decision models, such as Jev, process options sequentially, leading to different predictions based on their ordering. Across ten open- and closed-source decision models, we find that \emph{order-sensitivity} is pervasive, causing substantial accuracy degradation and unreliable decision-making. These effects become more pronounced as the number of options grows and can compound across multi-step decisions. To address this problem, we systematically compare eight methods for mitigating order sensitivity in terms of robustness, predictive accuracy, and inference efficiency. Among these methods, we find that \emph{tree attention} is a surprisingly effective and efficient method. It achieves order invariance by processing options as parallel branches of a shared context. When used during training, it matches the baseline's average accuracy. Applied to the baseline without retraining, it also eliminates order sensitivity with only a 1.1-point drop in accuracy. Our findings demonstrate that order invariance can be enforced directly in decision models with little or no loss in predictive accuracy.
authors: Bodong Liu, Dongyoung Go, Sofian Zalouk, Kilian Q. Weinberger
bullets: Evaluated order sensitivity across ten open- and closed-source decision models.

Compared eight mitigation methods for robustness, accuracy, and inference efficiency.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation demands reliable execution across interdependent stages, yet standalone World-Action Models (WAMs) suffer from compounding physical errors, while stateless Vision-Language Model (VLM) supervision incurs prohibitive chunkwise latency and lacks 3D spatial persistence. We present EmboEagle, a closed-loop agentic framework that unifies subtask-conditioned WAM control, latent-space adaptive supervision, and memory-guided geometric recovery. First, we adapt sequential WAMs via decoupled two-stage flow matching that preserves cross-stage visual history while calibrating truncated action supervision at subtask boundaries. Second, without an auxiliary vision encoder, we distill teacher intervention decisions into a lightweight routing gate driven solely by the WAM Action Expert's pre- and post-chunk latent transitions and subtask embeddings. Third, upon invocation, the VLM decouples diagnostic status from discrete routing actions and executes parameterized recovery primitives grounded in structured memory (initial references, active grasp bindings, and tool traces), followed by mandatory post-repair verification. Across RMBench and LIBERO-Mem, EmboEagle achieves 91.3\% and 90.6\% average success, surpassing the strongest baselines by 8.0 and 9.8 percentage points, while boosting real-world success over VoLoAgent under identical executor weights. Moreover, adaptive gating cuts VLM calls by 74.2\% versus chunkwise monitoring (91.3\% vs. 93.7\% success).
authors: Fan Xu, Zhongtao Wang, Hao Wu, Yitong Zhu, Wenzhuo Ma, Long Li, Zhuohao Li, Zhisheng Chen, Rui Su, Kun Wang, Xian Wu, Wanli Ouyang
bullets: Addresses compounding errors in standalone WAMs and the latency and limited spatial persistence of chunkwise VLM supervision.
Uses decoupled two-stage flow matching to preserve visual history and calibrate action supervision at subtask boundaries.
Learns a lightweight intervention gate from WAM latent transitions and subtask embeddings, without an auxiliary vision encoder.

papers.abstract: The post-training of pretrained large language models, including supervised finetuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR), is very sensitive to the learning rate, and tuning it through grid search is costly in both computation and memory. In this work, we propose \textbf{TipSweep}, a method to transfer the learning rate across the number of trainable transformer blocks. To do so efficiently, we search for the best learning rate by training only the last $k_0$ blocks (in our experiments, typically $k_0=1$), and provide scaling rules that predict the optimal learning rate when training any set of $k$ blocks, including when $k=L$ (the full transformer). Across experiments with models ranging from 1 to 7 billion parameters, we observe that the optimal learning rate follows precision-dependent scaling rules: the optimal rate scales approximately as $k^{-1}$ with float32 (FP32) master weights, but as $k^{-1/2}$ when updates are applied directly to bfloat16 (BF16) weights without a master copy. We explain both rules using an analytical model that accounts for update rounding, under assumptions supported by profiling experiments. Finally, we develop two prototypes of the learning rate search for a 6.7-billion-parameter model. The first fits the search on a single consumer GPU with 16 GiB of memory. The second speeds up the search on a high-end GPU by evaluating all candidate learning rates in a single pass over the data, so that a five-candidate search takes about half the GPU hours of one full-depth ($k=L$) run.
authors: Nan Chen, Soledad Villar, Soufiane Hayou
bullets: Targets costly learning-rate grid searches in SFT, DPO, and RLVR.
Tunes the rate on only the last k₀ blocks, typically one, then predicts rates for k trainable blocks.
Finds approximate scaling of k⁻¹ with FP32 master weights and k⁻¹ᐟ² with direct BF16 updates.
Provides an analytical explanation based on update rounding, supported by profiling experiments.
Demonstrates memory- and compute-efficient search prototypes for a 6.7B-parameter model.

papers.abstract: FlowMap distillation offers a natural route to few-step generative modeling by directly learning a teacher's denoising trajectories. Yet for autoregressive (AR) video generation, existing few-step models still rely on distribution matching distillation (DMD) to remain competitive, sacrificing sample diversity and requiring a large bidirectional teacher. In this work, we analyze what limits standalone AR FlowMap distillation and introduce two complementary guidance mechanisms to close this gap: (1) anti-drifting guidance, which helps the AR teacher correct drifted student rollouts by training an auxiliary model to mimic student drift and using it as a negative guidance branch; and (2) motion-aware guidance, which makes motion easier for a FlowMap student to learn by locating motion patches and selectively applying skip-layer guidance. Empirically, our approach applies to $\pi$-Flow, MeanFlow, and consistency distillation with 1.3B AR teachers, improving generation quality and reducing drift over 30 s rollouts. Notably, our 4-step $\pi$-Flow students match DMD students distilled from 14B teachers on VBench while preserving the sample diversity of their AR teachers, demonstrating that pure FlowMap distillation is effective for few-step autoregressive video generation.
authors: Yong-Hyun Park, Guande He, Joon Hyeok Kim, Hansheng Chen, Kaifan Yu, Chaoqi Luo, Xun Huang, Jiatao Gu
bullets: Targets the quality, drift, and diversity limitations of standalone AR FlowMap distillation.
Introduces anti-drifting guidance using a student-drift mimic as a negative guidance branch.
Introduces motion-aware guidance that applies skip-layer guidance selectively to motion patches.
Works with π-Flow, MeanFlow, and consistency distillation using 1.3B autoregressive teachers.
Four-step π-Flow students match 14B-teacher DMD students on VBench while retaining AR-teacher diversity and improving 30-second rollout stability.

papers.abstract: Preference tuning of text-to-image diffusion models spends most of its compute generating candidate images, yet training prompts are typically sampled uniformly at random, wasting compute generating images that provide too little signal for model alignment. To best utilize the available compute, we study prompt selection, where at each iteration we identify the most useful prompts for preference tuning. We separate prompt selection into a utility score, an estimator of that utility score, and batch selection. Within this framework, we propose Selection by PRedicting Objective-grounded UTility (SPROUT). The utility score is predicted on every prompt in the pool, including unseen prompts, by a text-only model, refit after every iteration on all utilities observed so far. A randomized acceptance rule then turns these predictions into a batch, so no images are generated beyond those used for training. For direct group preference optimization (DGPO), the objective-grounded utility is the norm of the gradient that the objective produces from a prompt's group of images. Fine-tuning Stable Diffusion 1.5 with DGPO on GenEval, SPROUT matches the final score of uniform sampling in about 44% of the iterations and improves the area under the learning curve with respect to both uniform sampling and CGPO, a recent variance-based prompt sampler. The efficiency gains hold under four held-out reward models never used in training, and the ranking of methods carries over to DPG-Bench and T2I-CompBench++. Our code is available at https://github.com/ADDAPT-ML/SPROUT.
authors: Kangping Hu, Akshay Mehra, Stephen Mussmann
bullets: Uniformly sampled prompts can waste compute on examples with little training value.
SPROUT uses a text-only model to predict each prompt’s objective-grounded utility, refitting after every iteration.
For DGPO, utility is defined as the norm of the objective gradient from a prompt’s image group.
A randomized acceptance rule forms training batches without generating images beyond those used for training.
On Stable Diffusion 1.5, SPROUT reaches uniform sampling’s final GenEval score in about 44% of the iterations and improves learning-curve area across multiple reward models and benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SPROUT at iteration t, with stages 1 and 2 as in Algorithm 2. (1) Generalizable utility model: a text-only utility model ft is fit on the train set of prompt–utility pairs from earlier iterations (circled prompts) and predicts the utility ŷt(p) of every prompt in D, including prompts never generated from; its predictions are scaled into acceptance probabilities at(p). (2) Diversitypreserving batch selection: the pool D is visited in a random order and each prompt is accepted with probability at(p) until B prompts pt,1, . . . , pt,B are accepted; the inset contrasts this with top-B selection (Appendix F). (3) Focused data generation: πt−1 generates G images for each accepted prompt only, the reward model scores them, and preference tuning updates the model to πt; each accepted prompt pt,i is then labeled with its utility yt,i, computed from its rewards or from the update (dashed arrows), and (pt,i, yt,i) joins the train set of the next iteration.

papers.abstract: Designing what an agent should optimize can be as difficult as optimizing the agent itself. Existing language-model-based reward-generation methods typically refine objectives for predefined tasks and couple the decision of what to explore with the synthesis of how to implement it, potentially narrowing the resulting behavioral repertoire. We introduce Habitats, a framework for open-ended evolution of executable agent objectives. Habitats maintains a population of reward-policy pairs and evaluates every policy under every population reward, producing a cross-fitness matrix that exposes self-mastery, transfer, and functional diversity. A population-level Planner uses this information to select parent rewards and issue targeted mutation directives, while a separate Mutator translates those directives into validated reward programs. We evaluate Habitats in a discrete Card Sandbox and three continuous-control environments (Cart-Pole, Hopper, and Cheetah) against Independent Generation and Direct Mutation baselines. Across four environments and three random seeds, Habitats achieves the highest macro-averaged final Specialist Quality and Behavioral Diversity, with final diversity reaching 1.8x that of Direct Mutation and 2.5x that of Independent Generation. Finally, across ten downstream objectives unseen during evolution, frozen Habitats policy libraries achieve higher paired win rates than size-matched Direct Mutation and Independent Generation libraries at 10,000 adaptation episodes, while also surpassing task-specific policies trained from scratch for 20,000 episodes. These results suggest that separating population-level planning from reward synthesis enables the discovery of diverse, learnable, and reusable behaviors.
authors: Nicolas Bolouri, Gaya Mehenni, Daniel Toyama
bullets: Maintains a population of reward-policy pairs and evaluates every policy under every reward via a cross-fitness matrix.
A Planner selects parent rewards and generates targeted mutation directives; a separate Mutator converts them into validated executable reward programs.
Evaluated in one discrete and three continuous-control environments against Independent Generation and Direct Mutation baselines.
Achieves the highest macro-averaged final Specialist Quality and Behavioral Diversity; final diversity is 1.8× Direct Mutation and 2.5× Independent Generation.
Frozen policy libraries transfer effectively to ten unseen objectives, outperforming comparison libraries and task-specific policies under the reported evaluation settings.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Habitats evolutionary lifecycle. At generation t, the population Pt contains executable reward–policy pairs. (1) Policies for newly synthesized rewards are trained from scratch, while inherited survivor policies remain fixed. (2) Every policy is evaluated under every population reward to construct the cross-fitness matrix Ft. (3) Normalized cross-fitness profiles are used to compute Specialist Quality (SQ), Behavioral Diversity (BD), and Grounded Behavioral Profile Coverage (GC). (4) Individuals whose policies dominate their own reward niches and outperform the random-policy baseline form the survivor set Vt. (5) The Planner determines the offspring count, selects parents, and proposes mutation directives, while the Mutator generates and validates executable reward programs. Valid offspring join the survivors to form Pt+1 = Vt ∪ Ot; invalid candidates receive up to three replacement attempts before their offspring slot is discarded.

Figure 2: Population quality, diversity, grounded coverage, and downstream adaptation. (A–B) SQ and BD are equal-weight macro-averages across environments, shown as their means across generations and their values in the final population. (C) GCAUC is reported separately for each environment on a logarithmic scale. (D) Downstream adaptation is measured by paired win rate against task-specific Scratch policies trained for 20,000 episodes. Meta-policies route among sizematched, frozen libraries produced by Habitats, Direct Mutation, or Independent Generation and are trained for 1,000, 2,000, 5,000, 10,000, or 20,000 episodes; the dashed line denotes parity. Error bars in (C–D) indicate ±1 standard deviation over three seeds.

Figure 8: Language-model backbone ablation in Card Sandbox. Left panels show Specialist Quality (SQ) and Behavioral Diversity (BD) across 30 evolutionary generations; shaded regions indicate ±1 standard deviation across three seeds. Right panels report their means across generations and final-generation values. All three backbones achieve near-perfect final SQ, while Gemini 4 Argon maintains substantially greater BD without sacrificing specialist quality.

Figure 7: Extended evolutionary horizon in Cheetah. SQ and BD across 10 generations, with means and final values.

Figure 8 and Table 10 show that all three backbones rapidly reach near-perfect SQ and maintain it throughout evolution. The principal difference is behavioral diversity: Gemini 4 Argon achieves 62% higher final BD than Gemini 3.5 Flash and 110% higher final BD than Gemini 3.8 Flash. As shown by the evolutionary trajectories in Figure 8, this advantage emerges early and persists throughout evolution rather than arising from a single final-generation measurement. These results show that Habitats can translate stronger Planner and Mutator capabilities into a substantially broader repertoire of distinct, learnable behaviors.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based view synthesis models render each target viewpoint from the source images, without an explicit 3D representation, which lets them reproduce fine detail and view-dependent effects. However, their decoder attends to every source token for every frame, so rendering slows with each source image. Rasterization avoids this by culling primitives that the viewpoint does not see, but source tokens cannot be culled this way, as they have no explicit position or extent. Our key insight is that source tokens are nonetheless spatial anchors: each encodes a local region of the scene, so the decoder's attention for any viewpoint concentrates on a few of them. A lightweight router predicts these tokens from the source tokens and the viewpoint, and the decoder attends only to a fixed budget of top-ranked tokens, so its cost no longer depends on the number of source tokens. We supervise the router with the decoder's attention, using non-maximum suppression to demote redundant tokens. With 24 source images and two views' worth of tokens, our model renders 6.4 times faster than LagerNVS, at a PSNR only 0.68 dB lower. One ranking serves every budget, so the budget can change at render time.
authors: Sagnik Ghosh, Aswin C. Sankaranarayanan
bullets: Source tokens act as local spatial anchors, enabling viewpoint-dependent token culling without explicit 3D geometry.
A lightweight router ranks tokens using source features and the target viewpoint; the decoder attends only to a fixed top-token budget.
Router training uses decoder attention supervision and non-maximum suppression to reduce redundant selections.
With 24 source images, rendering is 6.4× faster than LagerNVS while achieving PSNR only 0.68 dB lower.
A single token ranking supports changing the compute budget at render time.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview. The source tokens and the keys of the router are computed once per scene and cached, so the scene branch can afford to be heavy. The images show a synthetic scene with 8× 8 tokens per view.

papers.abstract: During autoregressive decoding, the deeper representations of the previous token have already been computed, yet shallow layers at the current token cannot read them directly because standard self-attention connects positions only at the same depth. We introduce Attention Latent Feedback (ALF), an architecture that allows every sublayer to attend to the outputs of the deeper layers at the previous position. Training unrolls this cross-position recurrence into two parallel passes, whereas decoding remains single-pass using cached previous-token states. Across mixture-of-experts models with up to 4.0B parameters, ALF lowers held-out loss by 0.022-0.024 nats over the standard residual with about 1.1% decoding FLOP overhead, and consistently outperforms prior final-state feedback across all three scales on both standard and attention residual backbones. On MoE-1.6B, ALF matches a $1.38\times$ larger baseline token budget, and on MoE-4.0B it lifts average accuracy across seventeen downstream benchmarks from 45.1% to 47.0%. Analysis further reveals that intermediate and nearby deeper layers drive most of this benefit, allowing a fixed nearest-window variant to retain 89%-94% of the gain at linear read cost while learned attention widens its margin with scale.
authors: Xuyuan Xiong, Siyu Chen, Mengzhao Chen, Yue Su, Zhuoran Yang, Ping Luo, Xihui Liu
bullets: Addresses the limitation that standard self-attention only connects the same layer across positions during autoregressive decoding.
Introduces cross-position attention from every sublayer to cached deeper-layer outputs of the previous token; training uses two parallel passes, while decoding remains single-pass.
Across MoE models up to 4.0B parameters, reduces held-out loss by 0.022–0.024 nats with about 1.1% extra decoding FLOPs.
Improves downstream accuracy on MoE-4.0B from 45.1% to 47.0% across 17 benchmarks and outperforms final-state feedback across tested scales.
A fixed nearest-layer window retains 89%–94% of the gain at linear read cost, while learned attention benefits more as model scale increases.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Attention Latent Feedback and downstream accuracy. (a) Each sublayer uses attention (orange) to weight previous-position outputs from its own depth upward and mix them with the current stream, while the projected top state enters the embedding sum. (b) Domain-balanced accuracy on seventeen tasks for MoE-4.0B on a zoomed axis, comparing ALF with the Full-bandwidth Transformer (FBT); Tables 4 and 11 report full results.

Figure 3 The Full-bandwidth Transformer and Attention Latent Feedback. Blue marks the current position, orange what is read from the previous position, and purple the mixtures where they meet. (a) FBT fuses block L of position t − 1 into the token embedding of position t through a learned gate g. (b) With ALF, each sublayer of block b attends over the mapped outputs of blocks b to L (weights β) and mixes the result into its backbone input at share ρ. The final state zt−1 also joins the token embedding through WE (3.4). Faded blocks are not read.

Figure 5 Loss reductions across six domains. MoE-1.6B runs from Table 2 on the standard residual. Points show baseline minus method loss in nats per token. Blue triangles denote FBT and orange circles denote ALF. Larger gains are better.

Figure 10 Behavior beyond the training passes on MoE-1.6B. One evaluation runs 32 parallel passes over the held-out set for FBT and ALF, with the recipes of Table 2. (a) Held-out loss from pass 1 (no feedback) through pass 32; the inset zooms in on each model’s change relative to its own pass 2 (in 10−3 nats). (b) One minus the cosine similarity between the final states of consecutive passes, starting at pass 2. Pass 2 captures most of the loss reduction and both losses settle within a few passes, while small differences between successive final states persist.

Figure 4 Parallel training and decoding. Each column is one forward pass of the backbone at one token, its circles are the sublayers with depth increasing upward, the blue chips are the input tokens, and the orange chips are the final states that the next position adds to its token input (3.4). (a) Training runs two passes over all positions. Pass 1 is the plain backbone, while in pass 2 every sublayer reads the outputs that pass 1 left at the preceding position, at its own depth (solid) and at every deeper sublayer (light). Each pass applies a next-token loss to its final states across all positions, and the two are added (3.8). (b) Decoding runs one pass per token and reads the preceding token’s cached states.

Figure 6 Downstream complementarity with Attention residual on MoE-4.0B. (a) Fourdomain average accuracy against reference-answer perplexity (reversed horizontal axis) for the Standard residual and Attention residual backbones, each with FBT and ALF (Tables 4 and 11). (b) Accuracy gains over the Attention residual backbone across the four domains and their average.

Figure 9 What the sublayer feedback reads. (a–c) Learned attention maps over depth at the final checkpoints of MoE-1.6B, MoE-2.6B, and MoE-4.0B on the standard residual (§C.1). Each column gives one sublayer’s mean weights over outputs of the previous position, and hatching marks sources outside its range. The dashed diagonal marks the lower boundary of each sublayer’s current and next three deeper sublayers, where most of the attention weight concentrates.

papers.abstract: Large image-to-3D generators recover detailed heads from a single photograph but treat every image as a new object. For several images of one person, they hallucinate unseen regions independently without using information from the other images. We present Head Anything, which generates detailed head meshes from a few images with changing expressions and viewpoints. Instead of training a multi-image prior, we turn a pretrained single-image generator with a native 3D latent space into a joint generator that denoises all images together. Since global attention between images is hard to learn from scarce 3D head data, lightweight correspondence-attention adapters let every 3D token attend only to its corresponding points in the other images. We obtain correspondences by fitting a neural parametric head model to the generator's own single-image outputs, requiring no ground truth at test time. Training on both ground-truth and fitted correspondences makes the adapters robust to fitting errors. Each mesh stays pixel-aligned with its own image and borrows the unseen regions from all others. On head scans, Head Anything lowers the head Chamfer distance of the best image-to-3D generator by 32% and its cross-frame inconsistency by 47%, and its meshes improve face tracking. Code and models will be released.
authors: Umut Kocasari, Bart{\l}omiej Baranowski, Richard Shaw, Eduardo P\'erez-Pellitero, Matthias Nie{\ss}ner
bullets: Addresses the problem of single-image 3D generators hallucinating unseen head regions independently across images of the same person.
Converts a pretrained single-image 3D generator into a joint multi-image denoiser using lightweight correspondence-attention adapters.
Derives correspondences by fitting a neural parametric head model to the generator’s own outputs, without test-time ground truth.
Maintains pixel alignment for each image while borrowing unseen regions from the others.
On head scans, reduces Chamfer distance by 32% and cross-frame inconsistency by 47%, while improving face tracking.

papers.abstract: Live free-viewpoint video streaming of humans enables immersive telepresence and interactive XR applications. However, this requires reconstructing each frame in real time, transmitting the data within strict bandwidth budgets, and decoding it on lightweight client GPUs. Existing approaches, whether relying on per-frame optimization or feed-forward inference, generate massive 3D Gaussian payloads that exceed practical streaming limits, while aggressive compression severely degrades rendering quality. In this work, we present HoloSplat, a real-time streaming framework for human-centric volumetric video. HoloSplat splits a feed-forward reconstructor before its Gaussian head, introducing a multi-rate streaming codec driven by server-side token compression and client-side token restoration. On the server side, we apply opacity-guided token pruning, PCA-based dimensionality reduction, and lossless geometry coding for token anchors. On the client side, a feature reconstruction hypernetwork is fused into the Gaussian head to recover compression-induced quality loss. Furthermore, we introduce Neural Session Calibration (NSC), which rapidly fine-tunes the Gaussian head online using incoming camera views during a warm-up phase. This resolves quality degradation from novel camera parameters and varying capture conditions with zero per-frame overhead. In our evaluations, HoloSplat averages 32.2 FPS on four RTX 5090 GPUs at 50 Mbit/s. It decodes each frame into 3D Gaussians in 22.1 ms on an RTX 3050 Ti laptop GPU, transmitting 22.8$\times$ less data than uncompressed float32 Gaussians, while calibrated decoding improves PSNR by 1.050 dB.
authors: Chaofan Li, Qihan Ding, Shihan Wang, Zhehao Shen, Boyu Shen, Quanyu Chen, Haoyu Wu, Lan Xu, Xin Lou
bullets: Targets the challenge of streaming feed-forward 3D Gaussian human reconstructions under strict bandwidth and lightweight-client constraints.
Splits the reconstructor before its Gaussian head and uses multi-rate token streaming with server-side compression and client-side restoration.
Combines opacity-guided pruning, PCA reduction, lossless anchor geometry coding, and a feature-reconstruction hypernetwork.
Neural Session Calibration fine-tunes the Gaussian head during warm-up to handle novel cameras and changing capture conditions without per-frame overhead.
Achieves 32.2 FPS at 50 Mbit/s, 22.1 ms decoding on an RTX 3050 Ti, 22.8× less data than float32 Gaussians, and a 1.050 dB PSNR gain after calibration.

On the server (blue), each frame undergoes eight-view matting, PointSplat up to its head, opacity-guided token pruning, PCA to rank r with b-bit quantisation, and lossless anchor coding. On the client (orange), the fused decoder integrates inverse PCA, a lightweight feature reconstruction hypernetwork, and the NSC update into the Gaussian head, then prunes the lowest-opacity 20% of Gaussians. papers.abstract: We introduce CrownFusion, a latent diffusion model to generate 3D dental crown designs from geometry images, a 2D-grid encoding of surface coordinates. Departing from traditional approaches that use point clouds, our "CrownImage" representation not only unlocks the full power of image-based generative architectures, but also preserves fine geometric detail by operating at far higher spatial resolutions than point clouds to alleviate smoothing artifacts in the 3D generation. Conditioned on jointly learned embeddings of the surrounding dentition, our probabilistic diffusion model produces anatomically plausible crowns with morphological variations tailored to individual patient cases. To accommodate multiple valid designs, we propose an occlusal fit metric based on proximity to the antagonist teeth. We evaluate our method through quantitative experiments and qualitative studies involving expert testimonials. We also release the FDI 16 Crown Dataset, comprising 11,513 annotated intra-oral scans, to support future research in dental CAD.
authors: Johan Ziruo Ye, Xingguang Yan, S{\o}ren Hauberg, Angel X. Chang, Hao Zhang, Peter Lempel S{\o}ndergaard
bullets: Encodes 3D surface coordinates as high-resolution 2D geometry images to preserve fine detail and reduce smoothing artifacts.
Conditions generation on jointly learned embeddings of the surrounding dentition.
Supports multiple valid crown designs and evaluates occlusal fit using proximity to antagonist teeth.
Assessed through quantitative experiments, qualitative studies, and expert testimonials.
Releases the FDI 16 Crown Dataset with 11,513 annotated intra-oral scans for dental CAD research.

(2) Baseline: point cloud-based methods with Poisson reconstruction yield overly smooth geometry eroding occlusal detail. (3) Ours: a diffusion transformer generates a geometry image encoding of the crown surface, which is then meshed to recover the 3D crown, preserving fine occlusal features.
Fig. 3. Overview of CrownFusion. Left: VAE reconstruction from geometry images. Right: conditional generation via SiT diffusion in the learned latent space.

Fig. 2. CrownImage construction pipeline. M : crown mesh. Muv: parametrized mesh on the unit disk via boundary-fixed harmonic mapping. Muv∗: fisheye-transformed UV mesh (inner disk expanded, outer annulus compressed). O: rasterized geometry image encoding (x, y, z) and α. M∗: remeshed crown recovered by triangulating O.

Fig. 5. Generation comparison. Left: dental arch with prepared abutment (top) and the reference crown in context (bottom). Right: occlusal views of crowns generated by DMC, VBCD, and CrownFusion, colored by signed distance to the antagonist (blue: gap; red: intersection). VBCD shows a large uniform gap, indicating poor occlusal contact. DMC exhibits a localized intersection (red). CrownFusion achieves the closest antagonist proximity with no intersections, and preserves well-defined occlusal anatomy.

Fig. 6. Generated crown samples for the same input. CrownFusion captures expected axes of variation: fissure depth, secondary fossae detail, and distolingual cusp morphology vary, while marginal ridge height and overall crown outline remain largely stable.
Fig. 4. Surface distance heatmaps to GT show VF-Net’s errors concentrated at cusps and fissures, while our geometry image VAE is close to GT across the crown surface.

Table 2. Comparison of CrownFusion against previous methods for dental crown design. Crown similarity is measured by Chamfer Distance (CD-L2, mm) to a dental technician selected crown. Occlusal fit is evaluated against the three nearest antagonist teeth (by mean distance of 10th-percentile closest points) and surface intersections (count out of 1,000 sampled points, and area in mm2). CrownFusion achieves the best occlusal fit with fewer intersections and competitive antagonist proximity.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models leverage pretrained vision-language representations for instruction-conditioned robot control, yet their understanding of task-relevant 3D relations and how these relations evolve during manipulation remains largely implicit. To address this challenge, we introduce \textbf{WeaveVLA}, a framework that enhances VLA action generation by explicitly modeling task-relevant relative 3D relations and maintaining relational context across observations. WeaveVLA employs a task-conditioned sparse graph neural network to encode relative 3D relations among objects, the gripper, and nearby references. Pair-specific recurrent edge states integrate geometric evidence across observations to maintain evolving spatial context. A learned-query readout summarizes the updated graph representations into compact relational tokens, which condition the action expert alongside the original vision-language context. An auxiliary geometry reconstruction objective further encourages spatial structure preservation. We instantiate WeaveVLA on StarVLA-GR00T and $\pi_{0.5}$, achieving over 98\% average success on LIBERO with both backbones. On LIBERO-Plus, WeaveVLA improves success from 74.9\% to 82.0\% and from 85.7\% to 87.8\%, respectively, with additional improvements on CALVIN D$\rightarrow$D. On three real-world tasks, the StarVLA-GR00T-based variant improves average success from 55.6\% to 70.0\% under standard conditions and from 33.3\% to 53.3\% under OOD perturbations, surpassing the $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline in both settings.
authors: Zien Wang, Yuhao Pan, Yunfeng Fan, Nan Cheng, Xin Xia, Wenchao Xu
bullets: Addresses the implicit modeling of evolving 3D relations during manipulation.
Uses a task-conditioned sparse graph neural network to represent objects, the gripper, and reference points.
Maintains temporal spatial context with pair-specific recurrent edge states and summarizes it into relational tokens for action generation.
Adds an auxiliary geometry-reconstruction objective to preserve spatial structure.
Achieves over 98% average success on LIBERO and improves performance on LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and real-world tasks, including under OOD perturbations.

papers.abstract: An embodied agent built on a language model goes to work with the weights it was given and keeps them for life. To get better, it needs more training, or reflection, memory, search or prompts that cost every step and are lost when the task changes. Editing weights by reasoning, weight-space programming, could end this, but has stayed with models that only reason or relied on a far larger commercial model. We introduce the self-upgrading embodied agent, to our knowledge the first that learns from its own experience by upgrading its own weights on the job, between its tasks, with no training, no gradient, no reward model, no second model, no test-time scaling and no harness or prompt engineering. By day a 27B agent works in a household environment. At night it reads its record, finds many of its steps wasted on replies that reach the token limit before any action, traces the habit to one direction in its hidden states, and rewrites one tensor of its weights. An agent that rewrites itself must first never break itself, so it is its own examiner: it tests every change against its unchanged self on practice tasks and keeps only what holds. When an edit holds, the next day it is a better agent, at the same cost per step: over thousands of held-out episodes, 48 fresh seeds a task, its one kept edit makes it complete significantly more tasks, in fewer steps, with fewer wasted and fewer tokens. This self-improvement is multi-round, stable and continual: through the nights that follow, the upgrade holds, without collapse. Of four sizes of its family, only the 27B agent does this. From here on, an embodied agent need not keep training and inference apart: as it works, it gathers its own experience and upgrades itself, with no separate pre-training or post-training and no human intervention. We believe this opens lifelong continual learning for robots: stable, continual, recursive self-improvement.
authors: Jiajun Fan, Neil He, Qinglong Zheng, Changyi Yang, Tong Wei, Andy Mao, Zetian Li, Chaoran Cheng, Hui Ren, Ruihan Guo, Xianrui Zhong, Xizheng Yu, Jingyuan Li, Xi Zhu, Kaiqu Liang, Chang Xu, Zun Qian, Zidi Xiong, Yuezhu Zhao, Xu Huang, Ge Liu
bullets: Addresses the limitation that fixed model weights cannot adapt lifelong without costly or temporary methods such as reflection, memory, search, or prompting.
The agent analyzes its own task records, identifies an inefficient hidden-state behavior, and rewrites a single weight tensor overnight.
It evaluates each edit against the unchanged agent on practice tasks and retains only changes that do not degrade performance.
Across thousands of held-out episodes, the retained edit improves task completion while reducing steps, wasted actions, and token use at the same per-step cost.
Improvement remains stable over multiple rounds; among four model sizes, only the 27B agent exhibits this behavior, within the described household setting.

figures.caption: Figure 6 The same night at four sizes: the 2B model cannot start, the 4B agent measures and withdraws, the 9B agent waits for a test it never asks for, and only the 27B agent measures its way to an edit that holds. One card for each of the four sizes under the same protocol: its rounds of forward passes as tiles (lilac: a read of its hidden states; green, rose, hollow: a paired test clearly in favour of its edit, clearly against it, within two standard errors; in the 27B card one hollow tile is the round that lines up four strengths of its edit side by side, which is not among its 13 tests), its own words or code, verbatim from the night’s record (for the 2B model, which made no edit, our note), and how its night ended. The 9B agent writes its request for a forward pass into a variable and then sleeps, waiting for results that cannot come. The 27B card is the night that kept its edit.

Figure 2 Multi-round, stable, continual self-improvement of an embodied agent: it upgrades itself, night after night the upgrade holds without collapse, and the more it works, the further ahead of its unchanged self it gets. Figure 1 The self-upgrading loop: the agent works by day and rewrites its own weights at night. Top: its life on the job, as a schematic. By day the agent works with the weights it has; at night it turns to itself, edits its own weights and tests the edit. An edit that holds is kept, and the next day starts from it (θ1 = θ0 ⊕∆1); an edit that fails is withdrawn, and the agent stays as it was (the middle night). How well it works climbs only when a night keeps its edit, and the loop does not end. A day is any stretch of work, a night the time between two days; nothing depends on the clock. In our experiments the 27B agent kept one edit in the four nights of Fig. 22; what that edit gave it, measured on held-out tasks, is in Fig. 2. Bottom: one night. The agent reads its own record, traces a failure to its cause inside its network, writes an edit to its weights, and examines its edited self against last night’s self on the same tasks and seeds. The edit is kept only if it holds in a confirmation on practice tasks that were reserved from it all night; otherwise it is withdrawn.

papers.tldr: A 27B embodied language agent continually improves itself by safely editing its own weights between tasks, without training, gradients, auxiliary models, or inference-time overhead.

papers.abstract: Foundation models can reason about complex physical tasks, yet translating this intelligence into reliable robot execution remains challenging. We argue that a critical, often overlooked factor is the robot-use interface (RUI), which determines how agents express and execute physical actions. To systematically study its impact, we introduce RUIBench, comprising 30 manipulation tasks across five suites spanning world knowledge, in-context learning, discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation. We further develop RUIKit, a unified framework that crosses six action abstractions with two interaction forms, yielding 13 interfaces under shared perception and control. In simulation, changing only the RUI shifts a frontier agent's success rate from 45% to 81%, and that of a fine-tuned 4B model from 13% to 47%. Our analysis reveals that effective interfaces reduce unnecessary decisions while preserving essential feedback, with their benefits shaped by agent behavior and physical uncertainty. We further uncover a verification gap, where agents frequently declare success despite observable failures, revealing the need for task-level verification beyond individual actions. Together, these findings establish RUI design as a critical factor in embodied agent reliability.
authors: Yanzhe Chen, Zhijun Cao, Zechen Bai, Wenzheng Zeng, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Yiqi Lin, Guoqiang Liang, Xiaokang Liu, Ke Sun, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Introduces RUIBench: 30 manipulation tasks spanning five capabilities, including discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation.
Provides RUIKit, a unified evaluation framework covering 13 interfaces formed from six action abstractions and two interaction forms.
Changing only the interface shifts success rates from 45% to 81% for a frontier agent and from 13% to 47% for a fine-tuned 4B model in simulation.
Effective interfaces reduce unnecessary decisions while retaining essential feedback; their benefits depend on agent behavior and physical uncertainty.
Identifies a verification gap: agents often report success despite observable task failures, motivating task-level verification.
