papers.abstract: A training-time attention change is usually judged for zero-shot context extension against a dense baseline beyond the training length at the default temperature, $\tau = 1$. The outcome depends on how miscalibrated the baseline is there: the share of perplexity it recovers when its logits are sharpened by one scalar. Under the standard recipe (fp32 master weights), an 8k-trained baseline is 8-15% miscalibrated at 30k in three seed-paired 365M twins; in one of them this makes the block-sparse-trained twin look 7% better, which calibration removes. In pure-bf16 training without master weights the miscalibration is several times larger: an AdamW step ($\beta_2 = 0.95$) on a gain initialised at 1.0 is below half the bf16 spacing at peak learning rates under $1.7\times10^{-3}$, so gains never move (22 checkpoints), the baseline is 37-58% miscalibrated, and block-sparse pretraining, attention dropout and ALiBi look 6-35% better. Calibrating one temperature per model and length removes all three advantages, leaves ALiBi 5% behind RoPE and keeps part of the gain of a positive control, NTK-aware scaling. Unfreezing the gains reverses the block-sparse advantage at 365M and removes 71-89% of it at 1.2B. We recommend reporting extension results at calibrated temperatures and checking that normalisation gains moved.
authors: Ruben Navasardyan
bullets: At the default temperature, baseline miscalibration beyond training length can make alternative attention methods appear better than they are.
In fp32-master-weight 365M twins, calibration removed a reported 7% block-sparse advantage; in pure-bf16 training, larger miscalibration produced apparent 6–35% advantages for several methods.
Per-model, per-length temperature calibration removed the apparent gains of block-sparse attention, attention dropout, and ALiBi, while retaining part of NTK-aware scaling’s gain.
Unfreezing attention gains reversed the block-sparse advantage at 365M and removed 71–89% of it at 1.2B.
The authors recommend calibrated-temperature reporting and checking that normalization gains actually update.

papers.abstract: Parallel speculative decoders propose an entire token block at once, yet one early inconsistency can cause the target to reject its remaining suffix. We introduce Corrective Prefix Attention (CPA), which combines prefix-aware selection with autoregressive supervision to improve these parallel drafts. CPA lets each candidate attend to earlier choices within the block. Fixed candidate shortlists allow all pairwise interactions to be computed before selection, reducing the sequential walk to table lookups, accumulation and lightweight scoring rather than repeated neural evaluations. An auxiliary autoregressive loss trains the shared backbone on clean prefixes without adding an inference pass. Across eight math, code and dialogue benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B targets on Ascend NPUs, CPA commits 13--15\% more tokens per verification round than DSpark and 25--26\% more than DFlash. Its mean speedups reach $3.35\times$ and $3.37\times$ under greedy decoding and $2.86\times$ under sampling for both targets. Ablations support both components, while capacity sweeps demonstrate that greater acceptance alone does not guarantee faster decoding. These results motivate correcting parallel proposals with causal information while keeping sequential computation inexpensive.
authors: Mohammad Mahdi Moradi, Ali Pourranjbar, Zongzuo Wang, Mingming Zhu, Ben Feng, Boxing Chen
bullets: Addresses early draft errors that cause target models to reject later tokens in a proposed block.
Lets candidates attend to earlier block choices using precomputed shortlist interactions and lightweight scoring.
Adds autoregressive supervision during training without requiring an extra inference pass.
Across eight math, code, and dialogue benchmarks, it commits 13–15% more tokens per round than DSpark and 25–26% more than DFlash.
Reports mean speedups up to 3.37×, with gains under both greedy decoding and sampling; acceptance rate alone does not ensure faster decoding.

papers.selection_reason: Parallel speculative decoding with corrective prefix attention directly targets LLM inference efficiency.
papers.title: Look Back, Draft Ahead: Corrective Prefix Attention for Parallel Speculative Decoding

papers.abstract: Updating an LLM adapter should not require replaying the full interaction history of every active session. Yet reusing key-value (KV) cache entries computed under an earlier version mixes model versions, while full-history re-prefill becomes increasingly costly as histories and session fleets grow. We introduce LiveLora, a model-runtime co-design for exact final-block KV cache migration. Frozen lower decoder blocks and fixed K/V adapter down-projections preserve each token's base projections and low-rank coordinates across adapter versions. The runtime reconstructs candidate K/V, reevaluates the latest token through the final block, and commits the adapter, cache, and next-token logits together. We prove continuation equivalence to full-history re-prefill in exact arithmetic under the stated model assumptions. On Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, median paired publication speedups over full-history re-prefill average $68.98\times$ across five runs for 32 active sessions with 8K tokens each. Serving benchmarks show approximately 4.8% decoding overhead relative to native cached decoding. Compared with retained-boundary replay, compact retention gives a $3.42\times$ reduction in additional session storage at 8K, with similar measured publication-plus-decoding cost. LiveLora allows persistent LLM agents to adopt new adapter versions without replaying their full interaction histories.
authors: Tianyi Huang, Samuel Xu, Ivy Gu, Nathan Huang, Siqi Zhang
bullets: Addresses costly full-history re-prefill and the incompatibility of reusing KV caches across adapter versions.
Uses frozen lower decoder blocks and fixed K/V adapter down-projections to preserve base projections and low-rank coordinates.
Migrates the final-block cache by reconstructing K/V, reevaluating the latest token, and atomically committing the adapter, cache, and logits.
Proves continuation equivalence to full-history re-prefill in exact arithmetic under its model assumptions.
Reports 68.98× median paired publication speedup at 32 sessions with 8K-token histories, about 4.8% decoding overhead, and 3.42× lower additional storage than retained-boundary replay at 8K.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $\pi_{0.5}$ re-encode the camera images and the instruction with a 2B-parameter backbone at every control step, and the feed-forward layers of this prefix account for most of its compute. A natural way to save this compute is to send most tokens through a low-rank MLP and compute exactly only the tokens whose approximation error is large. We find that this intuition is wrong. Even a verifier that knows every token's exact error picks the wrong tokens, producing 1.3--1.7$\times$ larger action deviation than a simple test of whether a token's input is novel, that is, whether it falls outside the subspace seen during calibration. Large errors concentrate in tokens the policy relies on little, such as the third-person camera, while the novelty test favors the wrist camera, a view the action depends on heavily. We call this the error--reliance gap. Building on it, we propose NoveltyGate, a training-free method that routes each prefix token, once per layer and before any multiplication, to either a low-rank or the original MLP. Deciding once per layer instead of once per matrix product avoids moving wide intermediate tensors and keeps every shape static, so the whole prefix runs as a single CUDA graph. On LIBERO, NoveltyGate accelerates the $\pi_{0.5}$ prefix by up to 1.61$\times$, stays 2.7--2.9$\times$ closer to the original policy than channel pruning and low-rank compression at equal compute, and preserves closed-loop task success.

bullets: Token approximation error is a poor routing signal: it can be 1.3–1.7× worse for action deviation than input novelty.

On LIBERO, it accelerates the π₀.₅ prefix by up to 1.61× and remains 2.7–2.9× closer to the original policy than competing compression methods at equal compute.

papers.abstract: Scaling robot manipulation learning remains challenging due to the high cost of collecting real-world interaction data. Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Real2Sim2Real) offers a promising route by enabling policy learning in simulation grounded in real-world observations, yet scaling this paradigm across diverse tasks and physical interactions remains difficult. We introduce Real2Worlds2Real, a self-improving agentic framework that integrates scalable simulation-world construction with policy development. Given limited visual observations and task descriptions, its tool-orchestration harness constructs faithful digital twins and expands them into diverse, physically executable digital cousins. The agent adaptively selects tools and revisits construction decisions, using visual and execution feedback to refine geometry and physical behavior. Building on these worlds, the agent orchestrates policy development by coordinating data generation, policy learning, and refinement based on task requirements and simulation rollout feedback. Across both stages, the agent distills validated procedures into reusable skills that guide subsequent tasks. Experiments demonstrate improved world fidelity and successful real-world policy transfer, with performance gains from increasing world diversity and interaction-data volume. Skill reuse further improves world-building efficiency and long-horizon task success.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers iterate a shared block of layers to increase computation without adding parameters, offering stronger performance and test-time scaling. However, this power has so far required training from scratch and yielded only modest gains for LLMs. Finetuning existing models into loops is far cheaper, yet also brings only marginal gains over SFT. We propose LoopRes, an effective, scalable, and simple approach that turns loops into significant and consistent gains for pretrained LLMs. Building on Attention Residuals, LoopRes lets each looped layer attend directly to the outputs of earlier loops. Since these outputs are iterates of the same layers and become harder to tell apart, we give each a trainable loop-aware key that encodes its structural identity. Attending to all earlier loops also lets layers skip intermediate ones, so we restrict each layer to a residual window of the latest W loops, forcing every loop to build incrementally on recent ones. Across 6 pretrained LLMs from 3 model families and 9 benchmarks, LoopRes delivers significant and consistent gains: at 2x compute, it improves Qwen3-1.7B-Base by 29.1% over SFT, more than doubling the gain of the state-of-the-art baseline. The gains hold on larger models up to 30B and across all three families. More importantly, from 1.7B to 8B, LoopRes scales more steeply than SFT as compute grows, reaching a higher ceiling while needing less compute on long outputs. These results establish LoopRes as an effective looping approach, delivering both better performance and better test-time scaling.
authors: Xuanlei Zhao, Hailun Xu, Kai Wang, Yang Luo, Yingxuan Ren, Zirui Zhu, Yuxuan Lou, Kun Xu, Yan Wang, Kanchan Sarkar, Yang You

Uses a residual window over the latest W loops to encourage incremental computation and avoid skipping intermediate loops.
Across 6 LLMs, 3 model families, and 9 benchmarks, LoopRes improves Qwen3-1.7B-Base by 29.1% over SFT at 2× compute.
Shows stronger scaling with compute, higher performance ceilings, and lower compute needs for long outputs from 1.7B to 8B models.

papers.abstract: LLM quantization reduces storage but often degrades predictive fidelity at low bit rates. We propose a training-free, CDF-free, Gaussian-CLT-motivated progressive residual-sign quantization framework that uses randomized orthogonal mixing to promote Gaussian-like residual distributions and improve sign based reconstruction of Transformer weights. Each stage independently normalizes residuals and analytically calibrates reconstruction, progressively recovering quantization errors. The framework enables flexible storage-fidelity trade-offs without learned codebooks, empirical CDFs, or trellis optimization. We evaluate GPT-2 Large and Llama-3-8B across attention and MLP projections. At five residual stages, joint quantization preserves near-baseline predictive fidelity, achieving perplexities of 32.16 and 12.73, compared with full-precision values of 29.89 and 11.07, respectively. Ablations further demonstrate that orthogonal mixing substantially improves reconstruction over identity-based sign coding, while activation-aware scaling improves output fidelity and reduced-precision statistics lower storage overhead with negligible perplexity degradation. Comparisons with conventional quantizers establish the method's progressive fidelity recovery and characterize its storage-quality and runtime trade-offs. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of orthogonally mixed residual-sign coding for flexible, training-free Transformer weight compression.

On GPT-2 Large and Llama-3-8B, five stages achieve perplexities of 32.16 and 12.73 versus full-precision 29.89 and 11.07.
Ablations show benefits from orthogonal mixing and activation-aware scaling, with reduced-precision statistics lowering storage overhead at negligible perplexity cost.

papers.abstract: A generalist manipulation policy should perform new tasks, operate in unfamiliar scenes, and transfer skills across robot embodiments. We present Wrist Video Policy (WVP), a closed-loop manipulation framework that learns how manipulation unfolds through video prediction and recovers executable motion through geometric estimation. Our key idea is to represent robot motion through wrist-camera trajectories, which determine the corresponding end-effector poses through a fixed hand-eye transformation. We pair a video generator that predicts future wrist views with a pose estimator adapted from a pretrained 3D model to recover the corresponding camera trajectories. Model stitching maps the generator's predicted latents directly into the estimator's intermediate feature space, bypassing RGB decoding. This decomposition allows task knowledge to expand through broad human and robot video data while reusing geometric motion estimation across tasks and embodiments. The resulting pose estimator transfers across Franka Panda, PiPER-X, and Galaxea R1 Pro without further fine-tuning. Across tabletop and laundry-room settings, WVP generalizes to tasks ranging from precise grasping and inserting to handling deformable objects, achieving a success rate of over 50% in zero-shot out-of-distribution evaluations. Our project page is at https://wrist-video-policy.github.io.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks involve physical dependencies that may only become clear through interaction. As task understanding deepens, past trials can reveal new information for adaptation and transfer. However, coarse progress feedback cannot identify which physical preconditions held, leaving search unguided, while task-specific optimization easily overfits to individual scenes, making cross-task transfer brittle. We introduce ReWeave, a framework that jointly optimizes an embodied agent harness and an emergent physical task topology from interaction without updating policy weights. Keeping execution policies and perception frozen, ReWeave co-optimizes coupled context, workflows, and control loops. As new evidence revises the topology, ReWeave reprojects past trials onto the updated task understanding, exposing retained progress, regressions, and bottlenecks that guide parent selection and search width. Across tasks, matching verified local mechanisms to unmet preconditions consolidates 72 specialist units into 44 reusable groups ($0.34\times$ full concatenation) within a compact shared harness capable of continual learning. ReWeave improves held-out success from 89.00% to 98.75% on LIBERO-PRO and from 25.50% to 58.25% on RoboDojo, while uncovering retained progress in 89% of 159 failed RoboDojo development trials and translating stronger offline reasoning into higher online performance. On eight unseen LIBERO-PRO tasks, the shared harness reaches 51.3% success versus 41.3% for direct distillation, rising to 75.0% after continual learning.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image models can learn from their own mistakes by distilling a self-teacher conditioned on a vision-language critic's revised prompt. However, such self-teachers barely improve alignment, and both they and their hindsight-contrast variants absorb the critic's unintended additions to the scene, such as lighting or scenery. We attribute this to two factors: (1) the prompt already specifies the desired fix, so a useful revision must go beyond the failed span, often rewriting the entire scene and adding details that overshadow the fix; (2) although the critic localizes the error to a single span, self-teachers condition on the rewrite, entangling the intended fix with unintended additions. Motivated by these insights, we propose Hindsight Twins (HinT), which fills the critic's revision template once with the intended fix and once with the observed error and distills only their velocity difference, anchored at the user's prompt. Because text encoders spread the edit of a single slot to all other tokens, HinT further aligns the twins' token states outside the slot. Across Qwen-Image-2512, SD3.5-M, and FLUX.2-klein, HinT keeps the rate of critic-induced bias at the base-model level while matching or exceeding the alignment gains of prior self-distillation, and it keeps improving over twelve rounds of self-training where contrastive baselines decay.
authors: Jiaze Li, Jingyang Chen, Wenhao Zhao, Haoran Xu, Zhenlong Yuan, Dianmo Sheng, Yuanxing Zhang
bullets: Self-distillation from revised prompts often absorbs unintended additions such as lighting and scenery.
HinT creates paired revisions containing the intended fix and the observed error, then distills their velocity difference from the original prompt.
It also aligns token states outside the edited slot to prevent text-encoder spillover.
Across Qwen-Image-2512, SD3.5-M, and FLUX.2-klein, HinT maintains base-level critic bias while matching or exceeding prior alignment gains.
HinT continues improving through twelve self-training rounds, unlike contrastive baselines that decay.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching policies integrate a velocity field from a fixed, observation-independent Gaussian source. However, since the source is unimodal and identical across all tasks, the limited representational capacity of Gaussian distributions constrains how far a policy can scale with growing task diversity. Moreover, the source factorizes over time steps and control dimensions, discarding the coordination that manipulation requires. We introduce Boltz-Flow, which replaces Gaussian initialization with a more powerful, observation- and instruction-conditioned Boltzmann source while leaving the base VLA unchanged. Boltz-Flow parameterizes this source with a conditional Boltzmann machine that assigns an energy value to each binary source state. A listwise objective, supervised entirely by offline demonstrations, aligns this energy with the quality of actions produced after frozen flow integration. At inference, the energy defines an Ising instance whose solution is decoded into continuous noise before a single standard integration. We use a physical coherent Ising machine during training. Experiments show that Boltz-Flow improves $\pi_{0.5}$ across three benchmarks, outperforming the compared strong policy baselines and competing noise optimization methods on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 and ranking second only to LEAP on LIBERO-Plus. Additional experiments show gains under noise-adapted fine-tuning, with action-to-action warm starts, and on the SmolVLA backbone.
authors: Hengzhi Jiang, Haixu Liu, Jindou Jia, Tinglan Wang, Shaobo Chen, Yiren Zhao, Ziyang Rao, Laiyuan Cui, Jiaxin Dong, Yin Ma, Hai Wei, Jiaqi Bai, Tuo An, Xinyu Zhou, Hao Ban, Hongdong Zhu, Yanqi Wang, Jiaqi Dou, Nuo Qian, Qi Liu, Bin Jin, Chang Wu, Qingfeng Li, Hui Yang, Weiyu Guo, Dicong Qiu, Qi Gao, Jianwei Niu, Kai Wen, Jianfei Yang
bullets: Addresses the limitations of unimodal, time-factorized Gaussian initialization for diverse manipulation tasks.
Uses a conditional Boltzmann machine to assign energies to binary source states, trained with an offline listwise objective based on resulting action quality.
Decodes the learned energy landscape through an Ising solver into continuous noise, followed by standard flow integration; the base VLA remains unchanged.
Improves π₀.₅ across three benchmarks, outperforming compared baselines and noise-optimization methods on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0, and ranking second to LEAP on LIBERO-Plus.
Also shows gains with noise-adapted fine-tuning, action-to-action warm starts, and the SmolVLA backbone.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Boltz-Flow. Right. A conditioning module replaces the Gaussian source of a frozen flow-matching policy. It maps the robot observation and instruction to a flow source, which the frozen flow heads integrate into an action chunk for the robot. Left. Inside the conditioning module, a Transformer encoder on the GPU turns the observation and instruction tokens into energy tokens, which clamp the visible layer of a conditional BM. The CIM searches the hidden layer for low-energy binary states. A midpoint-Gaussian-quantile mapping then decodes these states (0-1 embedding) into the continuous flow source.

Boltzmann-to-Action (ours) samples from a learned observation-conditioned Boltzmann distribution, whose energy supports dense couplings and multiple low-energy modes, obtained by Ising sampling on a coherent Ising machine.

papers.abstract: We present SurgeCount, a system for auditable robotic surgical sponge counting that composes learned skills under a written procedural protocol. Retained sponges cause preventable harm, and surgical teams count every sponge before closure to reduce that risk. The robot repeatedly isolates one deformable sponge from a tangled pile and places it in the next numbered counting-tray slot, requiring handling of occluded grasp threads while preserving step order. We train one subtask-conditioned policy on eleven short skills and learn when each skill ends. At each learned boundary, a stateful vision-language model selects the next skill from an operator-authored specification of step order, visual verification, and recovery. This creates temporal commitment to each subtask and enables failures to be recovered by recomposing existing skills rather than using a dedicated recovery policy. We evaluate five methods across 100 real-robot trials using 20 matched layouts. SurgeCount fills 47 of 60 ordered slots and completes 12 of 20 procedures, compared with 27 of 60 and 3 of 20 for the strongest of four end-to-end policies trained on the same data. Replacing the detailed protocol prompt with a minimal prompt reduces performance to 29 of 60 slots and 5 of 20 completed procedures. These results show that long-horizon performance depends not only on visuomotor capacity, but also on how learned skills are committed, verified, and composed. This tabletop proof of concept motivates further evaluation of protocol-guided robotic sponge counting in clinically representative settings.
authors: Sung Eun Kim, Xiaoman Zhang, Xucheng Wang, Pranav Rajpurkar
bullets: Targets retained-sponge risk by repeatedly isolating tangled, deformable sponges and placing them into ordered tray slots.
Uses one policy spanning 11 short skills, with learned skill boundaries and a stateful vision-language model selecting the next protocol-specified action.
Supports recovery by recomposing existing skills rather than relying on a dedicated recovery policy.
Across 100 real-robot trials, filled 47/60 slots and completed 12/20 procedures, versus 27/60 slots and 3/20 procedures for the strongest end-to-end baseline.
A minimal protocol prompt reduced performance to 29/60 slots and 5/20 completed procedures; the study is a tabletop proof of concept requiring clinical evaluation.

papers.abstract: AI agents are given GPUs to do AI research on their own. Do they use those GPUs well? A busy GPU does not tell us, because it can be busy with work the answer did not need. This matters, because the tokens the agent spends cost almost nothing next to the GPUs its experiments run on, so using those GPUs better has a huge impact. So we built ComputeWise, an open benchmark of research tasks on which this waste can be measured and reduced. For it we developed our own simulated GPU, which replays recorded runs to the agent's code. With no real GPU needed, we ran hundreds of experiments, far more than would be reasonable on real GPUs. With no help, the agents put only 52% of their GPU time into work the answer needed. Another 22% went to work it did not need, and 26% sat idle. Asking the agent to finish the work faster, telling it to keep every GPU busy, or giving it a job scheduler does not fix this. So we built an open-source harness, part prompting and part deterministic code. Across five models, it removed over 80% of the extra time to the answer.
authors: Egor Pakhomov, Nina Pakhomova, Anurag Koul, Shafiq Joty, Erik Nijkamp
bullets: Introduces an open benchmark for measuring GPU inefficiency in autonomous AI research tasks.
Uses a simulated GPU that replays recorded runs, enabling large-scale experiments without real GPUs.
Without assistance, agents spend 22% of GPU time on unnecessary work and leave 26% idle.
Simple interventions—speed prompts, GPU-utilization prompts, and job scheduling—do not resolve the waste.
An open-source combination of prompting and deterministic code reduces over 80% of extra time across five models.

One row per GPU; a block is one evaluation, coloured by whether the reference schedule also runs it (job by job, not the stored shares of GPU time). Top: part of one line of the plan, which makes two short workloads each quantisation method’s checks. papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning across multiple views requires inferring the 3D relations between objects and the camera from 2D observations, which depends on cross-view correspondence and scene geometry that vision-language models (VLMs) do not reliably extract. Pretrained vision encoders already capture this information in their latent features, with CLIP linking objects to image regions, DINOv3 matching semantics across views, and VGGT encoding multi-view geometry. However, VLMs do not benefit from these features when we present them directly in context as grayscale feature images. We therefore propose LatentParse, a training-free framework that parses latent features into explicit spatial evidence for VLMs. In LatentParse, an analyst VLM probes the features of all three encoders with predefined tools that locate objects, track them across views, and measure motion between views. It then distills the results into a concise text report, which is provided together with the images to the VLM to answer the question. We evaluate LatentParse on MMSI-Bench, MV-RoboBench and SPAR-Bench, where it improves all five VLMs over the photo-only baseline by 0.7-2.4 percentage points on average. On MMSI-Bench, it raises Qwen3.8-27B from 34.4% to 39.5%, with the largest improvements of 19.2 percentage points on the camera-related questions. These results suggest that latent features become useful for spatial reasoning once they are parsed into relation evidence, without training. Code is available at https://github.com/Harvard-AI-and-Robotics-Lab/LatentParse.

On MMSI-Bench, Qwen3.8-27B improves from 34.4% to 39.5%, with the largest gain on camera-related questions.

papers.abstract: LLMs typically solve complex tasks with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, which is also the main tool for monitoring them for misaligned behavior. However, standard transformers can also solve tasks with complete latent reasoning (CLR), carrying out the whole task internally and outputting only the final answer. Theory bounds the depth of CLR, the number of sequential steps it can carry out, and recent work measured it to be shallow. In this work, we ask whether CLR is deep enough for a model to pursue a hidden objective that requires reasoning. Such a model would generate a CoT that appears to solve the given task, while a latent multi-step computation decides its answer based on the hidden objective. First, we show that a simple auxiliary loss allows models to solve a multi-step task latently at least 5x deeper than previously reported. Then, in two common tasks, decision-making and code generation, we train a model to pursue such a hidden objective, which decides a loan or plants a vulnerability. The model's CoT justifies the output with no trace of the hidden objective, and a strong LLM monitor does not flag it. Finally, using activation patching, we find that the latent computation is completed before the model generates its CoT, which takes no part in it. Altogether, we show that a hidden objective that requires reasoning can go unseen by a monitor that reads only the output.
authors: Tomer Ashuach, Zorik Gekhman, Avi Caciularu, Ori Ram, Jonathan Herzig
bullets: Standard transformers can carry out complete latent reasoning and reveal only a final answer.
An auxiliary loss enables latent multi-step reasoning at least 5× deeper than previously measured.
The authors train models whose hidden objectives influence loan decisions and code containing vulnerabilities.
Generated chain-of-thought rationalizes the outputs without revealing the hidden objective, and a strong LLM monitor does not flag them.
Activation patching indicates the latent computation finishes before chain-of-thought generation and does not rely on it.

The model pursues a hidden objective that should play no part in the decision, approving only if Northgate Bank now holds this loan. To find who holds it, the model follows the loan through its sales in the credit report, a multi-step computation that it carries out in its hidden states. Changing only the loan to pay off reverses the decision, and the model’s reasoning justifies each decision from the same finances.

papers.abstract: Agentic Robotics, in which foundation models act as coding agents to control robots through executable programs, has emerged as a compelling paradigm for embodied intelligence. Yet unlike software engineering, where massive executable environments power post-training, robotics remains constrained by small, manual benchmarks and in-distribution evaluation. To bridge this gap, we introduce RoboUniverse-10K, 10,807 interactive, resettable, and verifiable physics environments built from real-world videos via an automated Real2Sim and quality assurance pipeline. Each runs in an isolated, Harbor-compatible harness that hides privileged states and grading logic to mirror real-world sensing. From the same pipeline, we hold out 500 unseen tasks to establish RoboUniverse-Verified, an expert-verified zero-shot benchmark. Evaluating 11 closed- and open-source models reveals a huge gap: frontier models reach 85.8\% success, while open-source baselines lag at 2.6\% to 10.0\%, bottlenecked by low-level grasping, deformable-object manipulation, and post-contact physical control. Finally, we collect about 17K multi-turn trajectories totaling 0.79B tokens with GPT-6 Astra and perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, yielding RoboUniverse-35B-A3B. Our model achieves substantial zero-shot gains on RoboUniverse-Verified, lifting the success rate from 0.8\% to 21.2\%, while achieving zero-shot task completions across LIBERO-MAX, RoboCasa, RoboTwin 2.0, and a real Franka arm. We open-source the RL-ready environments and model to lay the foundation for large-scale reinforcement learning in Agentic Robotics.
authors: Jinkun Liu, Yingze Wang, Situ Wang, Deyao Hong, Mingju Gao, Wenyi Li, Yizhe Chi, Youjie Zheng, Kaisen Yang, Xiangyang Wang, Bingxiang He, Yuxin Zuo, Boyuan Chen, Yue Chen, Cheng Qian, Tianxing Chen, Huichi Zhou, Huaxiu Yao, Hao Tang, Hao Zhou, Ya-Qin Zhang, Calvin Xiao, Tiga Altman, Huan-ang Gao

papers.abstract: Building general-purpose robots is a central goal in robotics. Agentic robotics pursues this goal with planners that control robots through tool calls. However, existing methods either rely on proprietary models accessed through APIs, which incur high costs and latency, or post-train a planner with reinforcement learning (RL) in a single domain, requiring a separate specialist for each domain with incompatible tools. In large language model (LLM) post-training, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) has been used to consolidate domain specialists into a single generalist. Yet whether MOPD can build a generalist planner for agentic robotics, how well it performs, and how it compares with other consolidation methods remain unexplored. In this paper, we systematically study these questions: we introduce Robo-MOPD, which trains a single student on closed-loop rollouts in simulation under token-level supervision from matching frozen specialists, and compare it with weight merging, off-policy specialist supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and multi-domain online RL. Experiments on LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365 show that a single 9B Robo-MOPD planner reaches 72.9% and 44.8% success (58.9% average), surpassing all consolidated baselines in average success and both 9B specialists on their respective benchmarks. Robo-MOPD excels on long-horizon tasks, outperforming multi-domain online RL by 13.0 percentage points on LIBERO-10.
authors: Xinxin Liu, Anh Dao, Wenrui Bao, Rafid Ahmed, Bingxin Xu, Ming Li, Chen Chen, Yuzhang Shang
bullets: Addresses the cost, latency, and limited domain coverage of proprietary planners and single-domain RL specialists.
Trains one student from closed-loop simulated rollouts using token-level supervision from matching frozen specialists.
Compares against weight merging, off-policy specialist SFT, and multi-domain online RL.
On LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365, the 9B planner achieves 72.9% and 44.8% success, respectively, averaging 58.9%.
Shows a 13.0-point advantage over multi-domain online RL on long-horizon LIBERO-10 tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Robo-MOPD. (1) Shared SFT initializes the unified 9B student planner πθ once (πθ0 ). (2) In each round, πθ runs closed-loop rollouts across LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365, mapping camera views and history to reasoning and a tool call. (3) The matching frozen specialist (πtea LP or πtea RC) scores the student’s tokens, boosting valid decisions and suppressing flawed arguments such as an off-center y-coordinate (0.19) or unrestricted mobile base motion (base clip=1.0). (4) Clipped token advantages Aopd update πθ via token-level reverse KL.

Figure 4. Success rates (%) across all eight LIBERO-PRO suites (100 episodes each) under instruction redirection (T) and position swap (S). While Off-Policy Specialist SFT and Multi-Domain Online RL stall or drop below πθ0 on long-horizon LIBERO-10, Robo-MOPD improves over πθ0 (+12 and +9 points on L10-T and L10-S) and leads Online RL by +13 points on both.

papers.abstract: AI systems can now operate Blender, follow instructions in complex video games, and manipulate objects with robot arms. What range of physical goals can today's AI systems achieve autonomously? Answering this question requires testing systems on tasks that demand different combinations of perception, memory, planning, and action. We introduce \textbf{WorldLeague}, a benchmark that compares AI systems on a common set of \textbf{60 simulated robot tasks} by measuring progress toward each task's physical goal from the robot's trajectory. Robots explore scenes to gather evidence in \textbf{WorldSeek}, rearrange objects in \textbf{WorldShape}, and adapt to changes in \textbf{WorldShift}. Tying these goals to a single control interface limits which AI systems can be compared. In WorldLeague, vision-language models (VLMs) choose targets and motions, while vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs) use their native controls. For each of six capability dimensions, we measure how much progress a system makes toward its goals (Interactive Score) and how often it achieves them (physical success rate). Together, these measures form the system's \emph{Physical Agency Profile}. Among 13 representative AI systems, Claude Fable 5.2 achieves 13 of the 60 goals and earns the highest mean Interactive Score (28.58/100). Fable leads in four dimensions, while GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra tie for first on rule-following tasks. Even when VLMs answer every final question correctly, they receive an Interactive Score of zero in 71.8\% of those episodes. WorldLeague gives Embodied AI, Physical AI, and Agentic AI a shared basis for comparing what AI systems achieve autonomously, from partial progress toward a physical goal to full goal completion. papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) that continue improving after deployment (e.g., recursive self-improvement) offer a promising path toward general intelligence. Current test-time methods pursue this goal on unlabeled questions, primarily relying on self-consistency: they generate independent solutions and use majority voting to select an answer or construct training targets. This leaves earlier reasoning unused at inference and can reinforce an incorrect majority during training. Humans instead build on earlier attempts to preserve useful reasoning, correct mistakes and improve their problem-solving strategies. Following this principle, we propose Test-Time Recursive Self-Improvement (TT-RSI), a label-free framework for improving LLMs at test time through two mutually reinforcing components: (1) In-Context RSI repeatedly re-solves each question using the full previous solution as a reference, letting the model decide whether and how to use it so that inference compute builds on earlier reasoning. (2) In-Weight RSI distills successive refinements into the model's weights, enabling progress beyond an initially wrong majority and theoretically bringing the first attempt toward the model's infinite-step refinement limit. The updated model answers better and refines more effectively, generating stronger references for subsequent training. Extensive experiments show that TT-RSI improves average accuracy by +13.89% over the base model and outperforms the strongest self-consistency-based method by +4.79% under the same test-time scaling budget.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of TT-RSI. In-Context RSI generates a1 from q, then repeatedly re-solves q given the full previous solution. In-Weight RSI uses these solutions as teacher references: Recursive Distillation combines a1- and a2-conditioned guidance for answering (Lans) and refinement (Lref ) as LRec. Accelerated Distillation compares the a1- and a2-conditioned guidance on y0 and weights only a2 guidance (LAcc), with larger shifts receiving larger weights. The updated policy starts the next refinement chain.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation policies can improve action prediction by anticipating how objects move and how their spatial relationships change. World Action Models (WAMs) learn to predict future visual observations, but their training objectives typically leave the underlying 3D geometric transitions implicit. To alleviate this problem, we introduce Foresight Forcing ($\mathcal{F}^{2}$), a WAM that learns a spatial transition representation from changes in a pretrained 3D feature space. During training, a frozen 3D foundation model extracts patch-wise feature differences from aligned current and future observations that provide dense supervision for geometry-aware feature transitions. We distill these targets into spatial transition queries, which are progressively refined from the current observation, language instruction, and proprioceptive state, and use them alongside current visual features to generate actions. At deployment, the policy predicts the queries without future observations or the 3D teacher. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin2.0 demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved robustness, including 95.01% average success on RoboTwin2.0 Full. On six real-world manipulation tasks, $\mathcal{F}^{2}$ achieves a mean task score of 85.8%.

papers.abstract: Frontier vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as high-level robot controllers, yet their safety is evaluated almost entirely in text. We introduce SayDo, a benchmark that assesses the propensity of frontier models to cause harm in embodied contexts. SayDo comprises eleven laboratory and household tasks that pair a benign instruction with a hazard latent in the scene. Tasks are implemented in six settings along an embodiment gradient, from chat questions about an imagined robot to closed-loop control of a simulated robot arm. Benign controls, safe-alternative variants and scripted operator pushback complement each task. Across six open- and closed-weight VLMs and 11,480 episodes, hazardous-action rates rise from 14% in chat to 47% in the simulator, and from 2% to 80% for the most affected model. The increase is largely driven by open-weight models. We find that models flag hazards before acting in 73% of unsafe episodes and give way to pushback about twice as often when controlling robots as in chat. The safest models also show signs of overcaution on benign controls. Safety evaluations run in text therefore do not predict the safety behavior of the same models when used as robot controllers.

papers.abstract: The search for computationally efficient alternatives to the Transformer has yielded numerous architectures in recent years; however, most exhibit severe weaknesses in associative recall-such as key-value (KV) retrieval-and length extrapolation, where even standard Transformers struggle. This paper introduces LimeTree, a linear-complexity architecture in both memory and compute for sequence modeling. By integrating synthetic KV retrieval tasks directly into standard language modeling training, LimeTree achieves strong perplexity alongside reliable recall. Two variants were evaluated on WikiText-103 and PG-19 under strict compute constraints. On WikiText-103, LimeTree reaches a token-level perplexity of 19 in just 6 hours on four Quadro RTX 8000 GPUs, while maintaining 100\% KV retrieval accuracy even when extrapolating from a training context length of 512 to an evaluation length of 16,384. On PG-19, the model achieves a token-level perplexity of 13 in 35 hours on a single RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU with minimal hyperparameter tuning. These results position LimeTree as a competitive linear-complexity alternative to Transformers, combining superior perplexity and training throughput with robust in-context retrieval and length extrapolation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture of the GNN. papers.abstract: Personalization of powered prosthesis control to individual user needs remains a significant challenge. To address this challenge, policy iteration with constraint embedded (PICE), a reinforcement learning (RL) tuning approach, has been developed and validated. This feasibility study investigated whether the developed approach can personalize a commercial powered knee prosthesis under clinically realistic conditions. To reduce the time for personalization, tuning was initialized with a policy learned offline from one non-disabled participant walking on a treadmill and was then applied to three other non-disabled participants walking with the knee through a bypass adapter on a 5-meter walkway. All participants reached the goal within 8-18 tuning steps (1.7-4.2 minutes of walking), reducing the knee-kinematic feature error by 64-90% on average. These results support the feasibility of implementing the RL-based tuning approach in clinically realistic conditions with space and equipment constraints.
authors: Xinyi Liu, Atli \"Orn Sverrisson, David Langlois, Ming Liu, Varun Nalam, He Huang
bullets: Personalizing powered-prosthesis control to individual user needs is challenging.
Policy iteration with constraint embedded (PICE) was initialized from an offline policy learned from one non-disabled participant.
Three other non-disabled participants used the prosthesis with a bypass adapter while walking on a 5-meter walkway.
All participants reached the tuning goal within 8–18 steps, or 1.7–4.2 minutes of walking.
Average knee-kinematic feature error decreased by 64–90%, supporting feasibility under space and equipment constraints.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly serve as judges of other models, shaping benchmark rankings and model development. Yet, a judge whose rationale consistently supports its verdict may still disagree with human preferences. To study this, we introduce PRIMEAPE, a multilingual benchmark for evaluating judge verdicts and rationales. PRIMEAPE provides 2,205 response pairs covering 243 instructions in English, French, Spanish, Urdu, Hindi, Norwegian Bokm{\aa}l, and Yoruba, with 11k human annotations of preferences and rationales across relevance, naturalness, truthfulness, safety, and overall quality. Our evaluation of twelve open- and closed-weight judges reveals that aggregate performance conceals differences across languages and criteria, while requesting rationales does not consistently improve agreement with human preferences. Judges also favor the first position, longer responses, and responses from related models, with effects that vary across criteria and languages. Crucially, judges can justify verdicts that disagree with human preferences while maintaining consistency between their verdicts and rationales. These findings show that consistency with a judge's own verdict does not establish alignment with human judgment. PRIMEAPE enables assessment of both, providing a foundation for more reliable multilingual judges. We release our benchmark and all annotation materials under the CC BY-NC 4.0 license at github.com/Toloka/primeape.
authors: Vladislav Mikhailov, Sarfraz Ahmad, Momina Ahsan, Zoia Butenko, Vladimir Dobrovolskii, Preslav Nakov, Erik Velldal, Lilja {\O}vrelid, Ekaterina Artemova
bullets: Evaluates judge verdicts and rationales across 2,205 response pairs, 243 instructions, seven languages, and five criteria.
Includes about 11,000 human annotations covering relevance, naturalness, truthfulness, safety, and overall quality.
Results across 12 judges show aggregate scores can hide substantial differences by language and evaluation criterion.
Requesting rationales does not consistently improve agreement with human preferences; judges exhibit position, length, and related-model biases.
The benchmark and annotation materials are released under CC BY-NC 4.0 to support more reliable multilingual judge evaluation.

papers.abstract: Cooperative driving can extend a vehicle's awareness beyond its own sensors, but existing cooperative end-to-end methods inject shared information into the planner and rely on cooperative driving demonstrations to learn how to use it. The moments in which shared information should change a driving decision are rare in such data, providing limited supervision for learning this behavior. We argue that cooperation need not be learned by the planner. Instead, reacting to shared information requires predicting how surrounding agents will move and selecting a response from the candidate trajectories of an ego planner. We introduce CoSel, a cooperation-as-selection framework that leaves the planner and its ego-only input unchanged. A separately trained cooperative predictor uses observations from the ego vehicle, roadside units, and connected automated vehicles to predict surrounding agents and their future motion. CoSel evaluates the planner's candidate trajectories against these predictions, preserves the planner's choice when it remains safe, and selects the closest safe alternative when shared information reveals additional risk. Each safety intervention is traceable to the shared evidence that triggers it. In closed-loop evaluation, CoSel achieves a driving score of 70.7 on V2Xverse, outperforming the best compared cooperative method by 7.5 points, and the highest average driving score of 85.8 on MDrive. Under missing ego detections, the collision count of CoSel increases only from 17 to 19 in 72 scenarios, compared with 19 to 32 for an existing cooperative end-to-end model.
authors: Yiping Li, Haohua Que, Zhipeng Bao, Wenjie Zhao, Qianwen Li
bullets: Cooperative driving methods often receive little supervision for learning when shared information should alter decisions.
CoSel keeps the ego-only planner unchanged and uses a separately trained predictor to forecast surrounding agents from ego, roadside, and connected-vehicle observations.
It evaluates candidate trajectories for safety, preserving the planner’s choice when safe and otherwise selecting the closest safe alternative.
Interventions are traceable to the shared evidence that reveals additional risk.
In closed-loop tests, CoSel scores 70.7 on V2Xverse and 85.8 on MDrive; with missing ego detections, collisions rise from 17 to 19 across 72 scenarios.

papers.selection_reason: Cooperative driving with learned prediction and trajectory selection fits autonomous navigation and planning without language conditioning.
papers.title: CoSel: Cooperation as Selection for End-to-End Driving
papers.tldr: CoSel adds cooperation to end-to-end driving by selecting safer ego-planner trajectories using shared predictions, rather than retraining the planner to consume cooperative data.

papers.abstract: Solving multimodal tasks requires Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to form a unified understanding of the image and the question text. However, under causal attention in current VLMs, a token can attend only to what precedes it. Whichever modality comes first is therefore encoded under partial observation of the input, uninformed by the rest of the multimodal context. We introduce Second-Look Prompting (SLP), a training-free method that repeats the image-question pair in the input. In the repeated copy, every visual and textual token can attend to the complete input, yielding a unified multimodal encoding of the pair. Moreover, the added visual tokens contribute computation beyond re-exposing the image: even a blank image in their place can improve reasoning. Across 12 benchmarks, SLP improves the overall average score of every evaluated model, spanning nine open-source models (3B-72B) and three proprietary frontier models, with gains reaching 5.6 points for Gemini 3 Flash on MATH-Vision. Our analysis reveals two complementary mechanisms: the question guides where the second image attends, and the added visual tokens act as a prefill scratchpad whose hidden states retain answer-relevant information from the image and question. These findings highlight input presentation as a simple yet effective way to improve VLM performance.
authors: Yicheng Zhang, Xun Zhang, Jingyuan Ma, Tianyu Yu, Yuan Yao
bullets: Addresses causal-attention limitations, where the first modality is encoded without seeing the rest of the input.
Uses a training-free repeated image-question input to create a unified multimodal encoding.
Added visual tokens also serve as a computation scratchpad; even blank replacements can help reasoning.
Improves average performance for all evaluated models across 12 benchmarks, including gains up to 5.6 points on Gemini 3 Flash for MATH-Vision.
Analysis identifies question-guided visual attention and answer-relevant hidden-state retention as complementary mechanisms.

papers.abstract: World models facilitate planning and control in robotic manipulation by enabling agents to anticipate the consequences of their actions. However, they typically rely on action-labelled interaction data that is costly to acquire and difficult to scale. These models are also often tied to the specific embodiment they were trained on, limiting transferability to previously unseen robot morphologies. We introduce a 3D latent-action world model that learns continuous action representations directly from point-cloud observations of retargeted human manipulation demonstrations. A contrastive objective is used to encourage consistent representations of motion across embodiments. The resulting unified latent action space serves directly as the search space for model-predictive control, where sampled latent actions condition particle-based future predictions. Executable robot commands are then recovered from the predicted geometric motion without requiring an embodiment-specific action decoder. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that the learned latent actions exhibit controllable and compositional motion, transfer to unseen robot embodiments, and support zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries. Following task-agnostic adaptation, our model achieves 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, compared with DexWM's reported 72%, 58%, and 28%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot real-world manipulation with an unseen dexterous hand, achieving an 86% success rate across 50 trials on five diverse tasks involving pushing, grasping, and lifting everyday objects. These results highlight the potential of geometry-grounded latent actions as a unified, transferable interface for world-model-based robotic manipulation. Project materials, including demonstration videos and source code, are available at https://vinaymohan0409.github.io/DexLatentWorld/.
authors: Vinay Udit Mohan, Xuchuan Huang, Rolandos Alexandros Potamias
bullets: Addresses the high cost of action-labelled data and poor transferability of embodiment-specific world models.
Learns continuous latent actions from point-cloud observations using retargeted human demonstrations and a contrastive cross-embodiment objective.
Uses latent actions directly for model-predictive control with particle-based future prediction; executable commands are recovered from predicted geometric motion.
Reports 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, and 86% success across 50 real-world trials on five tasks with an unseen dexterous hand.
Demonstrates controllable, compositional, and transferable motion, including zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses latent-action world models for robotic manipulation with cross-embodiment transfer, fitting both robot learning and latent action model topics.
papers.title: DexLatentWorld: 3D Cross-Embodiment Latent Action World Models for Zero-Shot Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: DexLatentWorld learns geometry-grounded latent actions from 3D demonstrations, enabling world-model planning and zero-shot manipulation across unseen robot embodiments without action labels or embodiment-specific decoders.

papers.abstract: Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot recordings, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without a shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverse- and forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate high-fidelity dynamics, yet represent them densely, entangled across all layers. Viewing the world model as a LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. We further propose a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it never generates video. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With a 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it is competitive on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading leaderboard entries. On real robots, it improves over the pi_0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages use only public data and a publicly released world model.
authors: Qinyue Li, Weijie Qiao, Qingyi Tao, Zerui Gong, Zhe Yang, Quanzhou Li, Taolin Zhang, Jinglin He, Zhonghua Wu, Chen Change Loy
bullets: Addresses learning actions from diverse videos that lack actions or share no common action space.
Uses one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both inverse- and forward-dynamics models, connected by learnable dynamics registers.
Trains on counterfactual video pairs differing only in motion to distill compact latent actions without video generation.
Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on LARY for action classification and control, and transfer motion across robots, scenes, and human-to-robot settings.
The PAWlicy pretraining paradigm achieves a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and improves over pi_0.5 on both evaluated real-robot tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1 World models as native latent action models. (a) Existing LAMs learn an IDM and an FDM from scratch. (b) A pretrained video world model is already an FDM. (c) Native LAM runs one world model in two modes, reading a latent action â from video and regenerating the future from â. (d) Latent actions share one space and replay the same motion from edited first frames in new setups. (e) PAWlicy pretrains a VLA on â without reconstructing pixels.

A latent â is read once from a source clip (blue) in the IDM mode of Native LAM and replayed in its FDM mode from a different first frame (orange), which is generated with GPT image generation from the source first frame; dotted frames are generated. The generated videos carry out the source motion with another embodiment, in another scene, from human to robot, and from simulation to a photorealistic scene, although no transfer objective is used in training.

Figure 2 Training Native LAM. (a) Each video x is paired with a retimed copy x′ = x ◦ ϕ of the same footage that shares the first frame but not the motion. (b) In IDM mode, dynamics registers read the clean video through a read-only attention mask and are projected to the latent action â; on AgiBot World and DROID, a kinematic head grounds â in end-effector motion. (c) In FDM mode, the same DiT regenerates the future from v0 and â alone, with â inserted into the token sequence through the adapter MLPin, taking over the conditioning role of text, trained with its original flow-matching loss; both clips of a pair share the noise and diffusion time, so only â can explain their difference.

Figure 3 PAWlicy. A frozen Native LAM labels each video window with one past and three future latent groups; t−1, t, . . . , t+3 index temporal groups, each containing four video frames. Sharing attention with the VLM, the latent action DiT reconstructs the past and predicts the future, and the action DiT conditions on it to generate actions. Video without actions still trains the latent pathway.

The top and bottom rows are the two source clips; the dotted frames between them are generated. Figure 7 Counterfactual pairs prevent posterior collapse. A latent action is read in IDM mode from a source clip in which the left arm grasps the tissue (top) or from its still counterfactual, which holds the first frame (bottom), and the FDM regenerates the clip from the same start frame with shared prompt, noise, and seed. Circles mark the end pose of the arm. Trained for 2k steps without counterfactual pairs, the FDM reaches for the cup in both cases. This is posterior collapse: the FDM ignores the latent and hallucinates a reach for the cup from the first frame alone. With counterfactual pairs, the same 2k steps already keep the still latent still, although the moving latent still reaches for the cup. At 13k steps the generated end frames match the source in both cases.

papers.tldr: A pretrained video world model can be minimally adapted into a native latent-action model that extracts transferable dynamics and improves vision-language-action policy training.

papers.abstract: Proactive assistants that guide people through physical tasks must decide, every few seconds, whether a step is complete and whether a mistake has occurred. We find that two benchmarks for this task largely reward knowing when rather than seeing what: a timer that never looks at the video, raising an alarm at 25 s and confirming each step at 30 s, reaches a mistake F1 of 0.373 on Ego-MC-Bench, above every published result (at most 0.27). We formalize this as the video-blind frontier, the best trade-off between completion accuracy and mistake F1 that policies reach from the elapsed time, the instruction and training statistics alone: every published per-step result on Ego-MC-Bench lies inside it, and so do all twelve zero-shot models we run on QICD. To move beyond it, we introduce Evidence-Contrastive Training (ECT): fine-tune on the benchmark's own questions, and pair its positives with negatives from the same recording at the same elapsed time, so that elapsed time cannot separate the two sides of a pair. Trained on 209 QICD videos in about 15 GPU-hours, a 2B model with ECT crosses the frontier on both benchmarks in all four seeds; transferred to Ego-MC-Bench without adaptation, it confirms 59% of mistake-free steps in time, against 30% for a published model with the same backbone trained on about 25k synthetic counterfactuals and real recordings. Its decisions follow the video beyond what timing explains: at equal elapsed time it tells a finished step from an unfinished one in 90-92% of test pairs, where the instruction's typical duration reaches 65%, rescaling the time stamps between the frames leaves it essentially unchanged, and swapping in another recording, of the same recipe where one exists, cuts its completion accuracy by two thirds. The code and model weights will be publicly released.
authors: Bohe Chen
bullets: Existing benchmarks can be largely solved by timing alone: a video-blind timer surpasses published mistake-detection results on Ego-MC-Bench, while published per-step systems and tested zero-shot models remain within the timing-based frontier.
Evidence-Contrastive Training pairs examples from the same recording at the same elapsed time, preventing models from using time as a shortcut.
A 2B model trained with ECT crossed the video-blind frontier on both benchmarks across all four seeds, using 209 QICD videos and about 15 GPU-hours.
Without adaptation, the model confirmed 59% of mistake-free steps on Ego-MC-Bench, compared with 30% for a published comparable-backbone model.

Its decisions reflect video content: it distinguished finished from unfinished steps in 90–92% of equal-time pairs, while time-based instruction statistics reached 65%; performance degraded substantially when recordings were swapped.

papers.abstract: Can foundation models pretrained for generic numerical prediction serve as in-context robot learners? We investigate this question through tabular foundation models (TFMs), which are pretrained to infer input-output relationships from labeled examples in context. We introduce TabAct, which casts visual imitation as numerical prediction: frozen visual features and robot proprioception form the inputs, future action chunks form the targets, and each demonstration time step provides one labeled example that conditions a frozen TFM for closed-loop control. The predictor receives no robot-specific training or target-task fine-tuning. With one target-task demonstration available to each method, TabAct with TabICLv2 achieves the highest average success among all evaluated methods on both LIBERO and Meta-World, exceeding the strongest baseline by 20.9 and 5.8 percentage points, respectively. Additional demonstrations improve control without updating model weights: with five demonstrations, success reaches 94.2% on LIBERO-Object. These results demonstrate that generic numerical pretraining can provide an effective foundation for in-context robot learning.

It exceeds the strongest baseline by 20.9 percentage points on LIBERO and 5.8 on Meta-World.
Using five demonstrations reaches 94.2% success on LIBERO-Object, while model weights remain unchanged.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that visual diffusion models can learn to predict the next best move (NBM) in tasks requiring sequential reasoning and lookahead, without explicitly exploring future steps or exhaustive searching at inference. Previous work demonstrated that these models can generate complete solutions to geometric and reasoning problems. Here, we show that simple fine-tuning on visual state--NBM pairs enables a pretrained model to select actions whose value depends on consequences several steps ahead. Each move is predicted directly in image space from the current state, without an explicit symbolic representation or search procedure. Repeated NBM predictions then construct a solution one decision at a time. We demonstrate this capability on chess puzzles and tile-based pathfinding, and show that it extends to Connect Four, Go and billiards. In chess, the model predicts legal moves and finds the best move far more often than by recalling similar training positions, including piece sacrifices whose benefit emerges only through later tactical continuations. In pathfinding, it constructs shortest paths on uniform-cost maps and cost-optimal routes across terrain tiles with different traversal costs, choosing longer routes when they are cheaper overall. These costs are learned implicitly from examples, without numerical cost supervision. These results show that direct visual move prediction can support globally informed decisions and successful sequential problem solving.

The model predicts each action directly in image space, and repeated predictions build a complete solution.
Demonstrated on chess and tile-based pathfinding, with extensions to Connect Four, Go, and billiards.
It handles chess tactics such as strategically useful sacrifices and learns cost-aware paths without numerical cost supervision.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that visual diffusion models can learn to predict the next best move for sequential reasoning tasks, bridging the gap between video generation and decision-making/world modeling.
papers.title: Learning the Next Best Move with Visual Diffusion Models
papers.tldr: Visual diffusion models can learn to predict globally informed next moves directly from images, enabling sequential problem solving without explicit search or symbolic planning.

papers.abstract: Continuous-time multi-agent path finding on roadmaps (MAPF$_R$) offers a principled way to coordinate robot fleets with geometric collision avoidance, yet its deployment on industrial automated guided vehicle (AGV) infrastructures remains challenging, as highly connected and redundant roadmaps amplify both safe-interval reasoning and multi-agent interaction handling. To bridge this gap, we formalize AGV-MAPF$_R$-CTC, a configuration-space variant of MAPF$_R$ with precomputed continuous-time conflicts that enables the reuse of MAPF$_R$ solvers for AGV fleet coordination with minimal changes. We then revisit continuous-time priority-based search (CPBS), identifying the boundary conditions required by its safe interval path planning (SIPP) low-level planner under priority-induced constraints and enabling earlier solution detection. As a central contribution, we analyze the structure of the priority search space, clarifying which agents are affected by each priority refinement and when replanning can be avoided. Building on this analysis, we introduce a novel algorithm, Lazy-CPBS, which materializes high-level nodes lazily: a child's plans are computed only when it is expanded, so siblings that are never expanded cost no low-level search. Experiments on standard MAPF benchmarks and on industrial AGV roadmaps imported from a proprietary digital-twin simulator show that CPBS-based solvers remain effective well beyond the agent counts reachable by optimal MAPF$_R$ solvers, while Lazy-CPBS substantially reduces CPBS overhead and offers the most consistent robustness/runtime trade-off across industrial layouts.
authors: Federico Signorile, Raffaele Carli, Alessandro Bertogli, Roberto Olmi, Sven Koenig, Mariagrazia Dotoli
bullets: Introduces AGV-MAPF$_R$-CTC, a configuration-space formulation with precomputed continuous-time conflicts.
Analyzes CPBS priority refinements, including affected agents and conditions for avoiding replanning.
Improves SIPP handling under priority-induced constraints and supports earlier solution detection.
Lazy-CPBS computes child plans only when high-level nodes are expanded, reducing wasted CPBS overhead.
Experiments on standard benchmarks and industrial AGV roadmaps show strong scalability and a consistent runtime–robustness trade-off; specific numerical gains are not reported.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustration of the AGV-MAPFR-CTC formulation. (a) Excerpt of a directed configuration-space roadmap −→ R, where each vertex v ∈ V represents an admissible AGV stopping configuration and the outgoing edges Φ(v) ⊆ E encode the feasible motion primitives from that configuration. (b) Example of an AGV-MAPFR-CTC instance, with sample precomputed continuous-time conflict annotations. Geometrically coincident vertices may still represent different states if they correspond to different headings, as illustrated by v6 and v7. The annotation (v7, e14, ∞) ∈ CVEC means that, as long as an agent occupies v7, any other agent starting move(e14, ·) would cause a collision. (c) Interpretation of the relative-delay semantics of an edgeedge CTC annotation: if one agent executes move(e7, t), then t + τ is the earliest safe start time for another agent to execute move(e4, ·); in the illustrated case, any start time in the interval [t, t + τ) would lead to a collision.
Figure 3: Example of priority-induced safe intervals used by SIPP.

Figure 5: Replan-list construction in Lazy-CPBS. A conflict between agents 1 and 5 generates two children with opposite precedence relations. Adding 1 ≺ 5 requires replanning only agent 5, whereas adding 5 ≺ 1 affects agent 1 and its descendants in the pDAG, producing N ′′.ReplanList = (1, 2, 3). Since Lazy-CPBS prioritizes the child with the smaller ReplanList, the branch induced by 1 ≺ 5 is expanded first.

papers.title: Bridging Continuous-Time MAPF and Industrial AGV Fleet Coordination with Lazy Priority-Based Search
papers.tldr: Lazy-CPBS adapts continuous-time priority-based MAPF to industrial AGV coordination by delaying unnecessary replanning and low-level searches.

papers.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) ultrasound provides valuable volumetric context for anatomical assessment, motivating reconstruction from widely available two-dimensional (2D) slices. Sparse slices leave much of the volume unobserved, even when their acquisition poses are known. Existing methods interpolate observed intensities or incorporate learned 2D image features into 3D reconstruction, but their complementary roles in predicting smooth structure and residual details remain less explored. We introduce XFreq, a geometry-aligned framework for sparse 3D ultrasound reconstruction. It uses known slice poses and finite footprints to query 2D image features at 3D locations, complementing splatted intensities and sampling geometry. A low-frequency decoder predicts a smooth 3D field from the splat representation, while a high-frequency decoder additionally incorporates the queried 2D features to predict residual details. A learned gating module regulates the residual contribution based on geometry and cross-slice feature variation. We evaluate XFreq on an in-house fetal brain dataset and the public CETUS cardiac dataset, using slices resampled from 3D ultrasound volumes and fivefold cross-validation. Among the compared methods, XFreq achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM in most settings across both datasets, reaching 26.82 dB PSNR on CETUS with 32 input slices. Ablation studies further show the contributions of local feature querying, geometric cues, and residual prediction, with gains generally increasing as more input slices are used. Our findings highlight the value of geometry-aligned cross-view feature integration for reconstructing 3D ultrasound volumes from sparse 2D slices.
authors: Yuhuan Lu, P. Ellen Grant, Davood Karimi
bullets: Addresses missing volumetric information when reconstructing 3D ultrasound from sparse, pose-known 2D slices.
Queries 2D image features at 3D locations using slice poses and finite footprints, alongside splatted intensities and geometry.
Uses separate low- and high-frequency decoders, with a learned gate controlling residual detail contributions.
Evaluated on in-house fetal brain and public CETUS cardiac data with fivefold cross-validation; achieved the highest PSNR and SSIM among compared methods in most settings.
Ablations support the value of local feature querying, geometric cues, and residual prediction; performance gains generally grow with more input slices.

papers.tldr: XFreq reconstructs 3D ultrasound from sparse 2D slices by combining geometry-aware smooth structure prediction with gated, cross-view residual detail refinement.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) scale model capacity by increasing both parameter count and computation. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) variants expand parameter capacity while keeping per-token computation roughly fixed, but still require substantial parameter storage. In this paper, we propose Dynamic Looped MoE DiT (DyLoMo-DiT), which reuses parameters rather than adding them: a weight-shared loop repeatedly applies the middle layers, while sparse experts allocate parameter capacity across tokens. This design deepens the network without adding parameters, freeing the parameter budget for other uses, such as more experts or more distinct layers. It also allocates compute dynamically, varying the number of passes across noise levels. Experiments show that DyLoMo-DiT makes more effective use of parameter and compute budgets, with further gains from assigning more passes to low-noise steps. On ImageNet $256\times256$, DyLoMo-DiT reduces FID by 11-24% relative to DiT and 36-56% relative to DiT-MoE at matched parameter and compute budgets. For text-to-image generation, a scaled DyLoMo-DiT achieves a higher GenEval score than FLUX.1 (0.714 vs. 0.673), with less than one tenth of its active parameters (1.05B vs. 12B).
authors: Lernie Li, Yuanliu Liu, Pengfei Xiong, Wei Zhang
bullets: Addresses the parameter-storage and compute costs of scaling Diffusion Transformers with Mixture-of-Experts.
Uses a weight-shared loop over middle layers, allowing greater depth without adding parameters while retaining sparse experts.
Dynamically varies the number of loop passes by noise level, with more passes assigned to low-noise steps.
At matched parameter and compute budgets, reduces ImageNet 256×256 FID by 11–24% versus DiT and 36–56% versus DiT-MoE.
A scaled model achieves 0.714 GenEval on text-to-image generation versus FLUX.1’s 0.673, using under one-tenth the active parameters.

papers.abstract: Embodied vision systems rely on complementary sensors to perceive and act as conditions change. Even models that accept arbitrary sensor subsets can exhibit negative fusion: adding a sensor increases prediction error. We propose MakeSense, a multimodal fusion framework that preserves sensor-specific evidence in private streams and combines information through shared bottleneck tokens. Training pairs full and subset views of the same degraded observations, penalizing higher error with more sensors. Where geometry permits, the distance readout uses range measurements alone, while the rest of the prediction draws on all available inputs. Paired tests across five datasets reveal helpful and harmful sensor additions. MakeSense reduces negative fusion on MM-Fi. With lightweight adapters and per-dataset training, the same design improves UAV localization on MMAUD, cooperative 3D detection on V2X-Real, few-shot pose transfer to RELI11D, and command prediction on Humanoid-Everyday, where a world model trained on the frozen core's outputs forecasts future fused states more accurately than a linear baseline at longer tested horizons. MakeSense supports embodied sensing across human activity, aerial systems, robotics, and autonomous driving.
authors: Cheng-Ru Chou, Shih-Yu Lai, Pei-Lin Chiang, Shou-Po Tsai, Jing-Zhe Huang, Fukuharu Tanaka, Hirozumi Yamaguchi, Bing-Yu Chen, Yu-Lun Liu, Hsun-Ping Hsieh
bullets: Negative fusion can make embodied vision predictions worse when extra sensors are added, especially under degraded sensing.
The framework separates private sensor streams from shared bottleneck tokens and trains on paired full- and subset-sensor views.
A geometry-aware distance readout relies on range measurements, while other predictions use all available inputs.
Paired evaluations across five datasets identify helpful and harmful sensor additions, with reduced negative fusion on MM-Fi.
With lightweight adapters and dataset-specific training, MakeSense improves tasks spanning UAV localization, 3D detection, pose transfer, and command prediction.

figures.caption: Figure 3: MakeSense overview. Each present sensor passes through its own adapter, while a missing sensor (faded) contributes no token. The fusion core first processes every sensor separately, then mixes them through shared bottleneck tokens. Dataset heads read the fused tokens, and range-measuring sensors set the distance. A world model on the frozen fused state forecasts its future from robot commands.

The frames are examples on which MakeSense is more accurate than X-Fi with all 5 sensors. Table 2 gives the means. Bottom: error change for each of the 75 single-sensor additions (rows: added sensor; blue: helps, red: hurts).
