papers.abstract: Decision models, which output probability distributions over candidate labels instead of generating text, are increasingly used as classifiers and evaluators for inputs associated with real-world locations. However, it remains unclear whether they can leverage spatial context and whether their predictions are geographically biased. We introduce GeoDecisions, a multimodal benchmark for evaluating the spatial awareness and geographic bias of decision models. GeoDecisions comprises two tasks: (1) geo-aware image classification, and (2) location rating on objective and subjective topics. Evaluating six decision models against supervised task-specific models, we find that spatial awareness requires vision: textual coordinates alone provide insufficient context for classifying everyday photos and satellite images. We also find substantial geographic bias. On everyday photos, despite achieving higher accuracy, open-weight decision models exhibit more spatially clustered errors than supervised models. Moreover, across all five subjective topics, every decision model gives lower ratings to locations with lower socioeconomic conditions. Finally, we propose a training-free method that combines decision models with a location prior to improve their spatial awareness without substantially increasing performance bias. Our code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/GeoDecisions.
authors: Wilson Wongso, Hada Melino Muhammad, Xiachong Lin, Hao Xue, Flora D. Salim
bullets: Introduces GeoDecisions, a multimodal benchmark for spatial awareness and geographic bias.
Evaluates geo-aware image classification and location ratings on objective and subjective topics.
Textual coordinates alone are insufficient for classifying everyday and satellite imagery; vision is necessary.
Decision models show geographically clustered errors and consistently lower subjective ratings for lower-socioeconomic locations.
A training-free location prior improves spatial awareness without substantially increasing performance bias.

papers.abstract: Recent vision-language models (VLMs) can process hour-long videos, but the large number of input frames incurs substantial inference overhead. Existing approaches to efficient long-video understanding largely overlook video decoding, which can take longer than LLM prefill. We propose RAPID (Reference- and Access-Point-Informed Decoding), a codec-aware framework that exploits information embedded in compressed bitstreams to reduce both frame decoding and selection costs. RAPID consists of two components. RAPID-Dec exploits reference-frame information and random access points to skip unnecessary frames and decode the retained frames in parallel while preserving exact reconstruction of the target frames. It achieves up to a 3.7x decoding speedup over the fastest baseline on H.264/AVC videos. RAPID-Sel uses keyframes as coarse representatives of video segments, avoiding the dense candidate decoding and scoring required by existing frame selection methods. It achieves comparable accuracy with up to a 3.0x preprocessing speedup. Together, RAPID achieves a 4.9x time to first token (TTFT) speedup on hour-long videos over a state-of-the-art frame selection method using the fastest baseline decoder.
authors: Yuna Lee, Yulhwa Kim
bullets: Targets the substantial video-decoding and frame-selection overhead in hour-long VLM inputs.
RAPID-Dec uses reference-frame dependencies and random access points to skip unnecessary frames and decode retained frames in parallel with exact reconstruction.
RAPID-Sel uses keyframes as coarse segment representatives, avoiding dense candidate decoding and scoring.
Reports up to 3.7× decoding speedup and up to 3.0× preprocessing speedup, while maintaining comparable selection accuracy.
Scope: results are reported for H.264/AVC videos and hour-long video workloads.

papers.abstract: Precise language control requires embodied models to follow instructions governing both task outcomes and execution. Although recent methods train policies to follow increasingly detailed commands, existing benchmarks often assess instruction following alongside perception, planning, and generalization to unfamiliar scenes. Higher task success therefore offers limited evidence of closer adherence to instructions. We introduce RoboInF, a benchmark measuring how reliably manipulation policies adapt their behavior to changes in an instruction. For each of eight tasks, six to twelve expert-validated instruction branches vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation detail while holding the initial scene and robot state fixed. Task-specific checkers verify the terminal goal and use recorded trajectories, contacts, and event sequences to assess compliance throughout execution. The accompanying RoboInF-4K dataset pairs 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived annotations of motion and contact. We evaluate leading manipulation policies ($\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenWAM) and inference-only agents (GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash). All four models exhibit a gap between task completion and faithful execution, indicating substantial room for fine-grained instruction following.
authors: Jiawei Guo, Yu Huang, Dijiang Dong, Yue Liu, Peiran Ren, Wei Shen
bullets: Evaluates instruction fidelity across eight manipulation tasks with 6–12 instruction branches per task, while keeping the initial scene and robot state fixed.

RoboInF-4K contains 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived motion and contact annotations.
Evaluations of four manipulation or inference-only agents reveal a gap between task success and faithful instruction execution.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention reduces the cost of long-context decoding, but token selection introduces additional scoring and ranking overhead. Moreover, uniform page scoring overlooks differences in relevance between near and far context. We propose Near-Far Attention (NFA), which adapts retrieval to regional attention patterns while keeping candidate scoring lightweight. During prefill, the Lightweight Gate Estimator identifies regions that can be skipped during decoding, adding less than 1% to dense-prefill time. For the remaining regions, the Calibration-Free Subspace Extractor supplies compact features shared by page-level and token-level scoring without offline calibration. The Distance-Aware Two-Level Selector then scores near and far pages differently and jointly ranks candidate tokens under a shared budget. Evaluations across model families, parameter scales, and GQA/MLA architectures show aggregate task quality comparable to full attention. On Qwen3-8B at 512K context length, NFA achieves up to $5.49\times$ operator speedup and $2.97\times$ whole-model decoding speedup over FlashInfer, including selection overhead.
authors: YuanShuo Wang, Jianchao Tan, Lei Gong, Teng Wang, Wenqi Lou, Xuehai Zhou
bullets: Addresses retrieval overhead and the limits of uniform page scoring in sparse attention.
Uses a Lightweight Gate Estimator during prefill to skip low-value regions with under 1% added dense-prefill time.
Extracts compact, calibration-free features for both page- and token-level scoring.
A distance-aware two-level selector ranks near and far pages and candidate tokens under a shared budget.
On Qwen3-8B at 512K context, achieves up to 5.49× operator and 2.97× whole-model decoding speedup over FlashInfer, including selection overhead.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can execute individual skills but fail to complete tasks that require combining several of them. In our audit of Xiaomi-Robotics-1, an estimated 43\% of failures involve choosing the wrong target or losing track of task progress. Wrapping a frozen VLA in a vision-language model (VLM) harness is a natural remedy. Existing harnesses can gain substantially from task- and policy-specific preparation, raising the question of how much of that gain transfers to a new task or policy. An ideal harness should (i) need minimal preparation for a new task, (ii) need no redesign for a new policy, and (iii) preserve standalone capabilities the policy already has. To the best of our knowledge, our \ours{} is the first harness built this way. Its premise is that choosing targets and tracking progress are easy for a VLM such as GPT-6 without task preparation, while the frozen VLA already handles continuous, contact-rich motion. The frozen VLA therefore executes continuous control while the VLM plans zero-shot and monitors execution; when progress stalls or targets drift, the VLM first rephrases the instruction and, only as a fallback, executes short generated code over generic motion primitives before returning fine control to the VLA. The supervision rules stay fixed across policies, requiring only a thin interface adapter and an automatically profiled skill configuration per policy. On 200 RoboCasa365 scenes, \ours{} with GPT-6 Astra raises the success rate of frozen Xiaomi-Robotics-1 from \textbf{\color{blue}57.5\%} to \textbf{\color{blue}70.5\%} and preserves \textbf{\color{blue}90.4\%} of its standalone successes (104/115) while rescuing 37 of 85 failures. On a shared 50-scene subset, the same rules add 8 to 10 percentage points to each of four other frozen policies, while existing preparation-based harness systems often fail to transfer to a new policy.
authors: Yihao Shen, Yuxuan Chen, Xuantong Liu, Jun Gao, Weijian Luo, Tianyang Hu
bullets: Addresses multi-skill task failures caused by wrong target selection and lost progress tracking.
Uses a VLM to plan and monitor execution; it rephrases instructions first and invokes short generic motion-primitive programs only as a fallback.
Leaves continuous, contact-rich control to the frozen VLA, preserving its standalone capabilities.
On 200 RoboCasa365 scenes, success increased from 57.5% to 70.5%, preserving 90.4% of standalone successes and rescuing 37 of 85 failures.
The same fixed supervision rules improved four other frozen policies by 8–10 percentage points on a shared 50-scene subset.

papers.abstract: Kimi K3 combines a latent routed mixture of experts with full-width shared experts. A complete feed-forward evaluation must score and select experts, project tokens into the latent space, exchange tokens across expert-parallel ranks, compute the routed and shared branches, and normalize and project the routed sum before joining the branches. We present GC-MoE K3, a datacenter Blackwell implementation that schedules this entire evaluation as a CUDA Graph across two Green Contexts. Five base roles split input projection, routing, dispatch, expert computation, and finalization. Dispatch can fill the routed input ring while the compute partition evaluates shared experts. Finalize waits for the expert owners needed by each token and overlaps routed reduction and RMSNorm with loading the output projection weights. Conditional roles reuse the communication partition for routed computation and reduce split-$K$ projection partials. On GB200 at EP8, EP16, and EP32, the operator is faster at all 24 measured configurations than the paired SGLang-style reference (mean speedup $1.1324\times$). A comparison with historical vLLM-style measurements gives $1.3651\times$ across the same 24 shapes. Both latency comparisons time single-layer graph replay on synthetic K3-shaped inputs with a residual prefix. The separate paired numerical suite passes all 142 cases and 2,936 rank checks.
authors: Yong Li, Haoyu Wang, Kan Liu, Tao Lan
bullets: Implements the full K3 feed-forward path, including expert selection, latent projection, token exchange, routed/shared branches, normalization, and output projection.
Uses five CUDA Graph roles for input projection, routing, dispatch, expert computation, and finalization, with overlap between communication, shared-expert work, reduction, and weight loading.
Supports conditional role reuse for routed computation and split-K projection partial reductions.
On GB200 across EP8, EP16, and EP32, it is faster in all 24 measured configurations, with a mean 1.1324× speedup over the paired SGLang-style reference.
The numerical suite passes 142 cases and 2,936 rank checks; latency results use single-layer graph replay on synthetic K3-shaped inputs with a residual prefix.

papers.abstract: Proactive streaming video understanding requires models to interpret unfolding events, respond timely, and retrieve relevant historical evidence. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, we introduce SVUBench, a comprehensive proactive streaming video benchmark comprising 12,131 questions and 62,881 answer points across ten proactive tasks spanning Perception, Understanding, and Reasoning. Constructed through model-assisted annotation and human verification, SVUBench introduces two complementary interaction modes. Basic evaluates sustained proactive responses from video onset, while Trajectory requires historical recovery and continuous response updates following task activation during streaming. A Duration-Scaled Challenge further evaluates these capabilities across four video duration tiers. We develop the Proactive Response Score (PRS) with task-adaptive answer windows to jointly assess answer correctness, response timeliness, historical consistency, and content quality. Extensive experiments and analysis reveal the strengths and limitations of existing models, highlighting directions for advancing proactive streaming video understanding.
authors: Yuxuan Liang, Bohan Zhang, Haiyang Yu, Bocheng Hu, Ke Niu, Xu Li, Zhengtao Yao, Yan Wen, Haotian Chen, Xiaolei Chen, Jiacong Wang, Zhe Liu, Jingqun Tang, Benlei Cui, Fan Shi, Xiangyang Xue
bullets: Covers 12,131 questions and 62,881 answer points across 10 tasks in Perception, Understanding, and Reasoning.
Tests two interaction modes: continuous responses from video onset and trajectory-based updates after task activation.
Includes four video-duration tiers through a Duration-Scaled Challenge.
Introduces Proactive Response Score (PRS), measuring correctness, timeliness, historical consistency, and content quality.
Experiments expose strengths and limitations of existing models and suggest directions for future research.

papers.abstract: Paired compositional benchmarks such as Winoground ask each image to prefer its matching caption and each caption to prefer its matching image. A failed Group decision can come from a wrong caption preference or from the cross-image comparison alone, and Group Score merges the two. Choosing between retraining the encoder and changing the scoring rule therefore requires separating them. We study mean-erasure, which projects each frozen image embedding away from the mean of the two normalized candidate captions. We prove that the projection preserves every within-image caption ranking and makes Group Score equal baseline Text Score. On Winoground, mean-erasure raises CLIP ViT-B/32 Group Score from 9% to 31%, and five CLIP and SigLIP checkpoints gain 21 to 27 percentage points. ColorSwap shows a similar gain for color-object binding. A score decomposition shows that about 60% of Image failures already score the correct joint assignment above the swapped one and fail only on an offset between the two images. Fixed corrections and a learned bilinear scorer gain under one point. A direction estimated from retrieved captions gains about five points with two captions and falls below baseline with sixteen. Before retraining an encoder for paired retrieval, measure the Group loss that mean-erasure recovers: gains beyond baseline Text Score require changing the caption decisions themselves.
authors: Chimata Anudeep, Harsh Vardhan Poddar
bullets: Winoground Group Score combines caption-ranking errors with cross-image comparison errors, making failure sources hard to separate.
Mean-erasure projects each image embedding away from the mean of its two candidate caption embeddings while preserving within-image caption rankings.
It raises CLIP ViT-B/32 Group Score from 9% to 31%, with 21–27 point gains across five CLIP and SigLIP checkpoints; ColorSwap shows a similar pattern.
About 60% of Image failures already rank the correct joint assignment above the swapped one, indicating an offset between images as the remaining failure.
Fixed corrections and a learned bilinear scorer provide under-one-point gains; caption-retrieval directions help with two captions but fall below baseline with sixteen.

papers.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur substantial inference latency due to their large vision-language backbones and iterative denoising. Asynchronous execution reduces this latency by generating the next action chunk while executing the current one, but the new chunk is conditioned on a stale observation, degrading performance as the delay increases. We investigate this mismatch by comparing actions predicted from observations at planning and execution times. We find that these predictions differ little on expert demonstrations but diverge substantially on the policy's own delayed rollouts, particularly in failed episodes. Motivated by this observation, we propose DelayOPSD, which trains an asynchronous policy to imitate its synchronous counterpart on the policy's own rollouts. Specifically, a synchronous teacher, obtained from the same policy using the observation at execution time, supervises a delayed student that observes only the earlier frame and the actions still being executed. The student learns to match the teacher throughout its own denoising process. Under a 10-step delay, training SmolVLA on demonstrations achieves only 70.2% success, comparable to naive asynchronous execution (70.4%), whereas training on its own rollouts improves success to 78.7%. Across LIBERO and Kinetix, DelayOPSD achieves the highest average success among the compared methods, without introducing additional modules at deployment. On a real robot, it further improves success from 46% to 62%.
authors: Hyeonjae Kim, Jeongsol Kim, Sunwoo Park, Chanyu Moon, Yoojin Oh, Youngjun Jun, Kyumin Choi, Jong Chul Ye
bullets: Asynchronous action generation reduces latency but stale observations cause performance degradation, especially during failed policy rollouts.
DelayOPSD compares a synchronous teacher using the current observation with a delayed student using an earlier observation and in-progress actions.
The student imitates the teacher throughout the iterative denoising process, with training performed on the policy’s own delayed rollouts.
With a 10-step delay, SmolVLA success rises from 70.2% with demonstration training to 78.7% with DelayOPSD, versus 70.4% for naive asynchronous execution.
DelayOPSD achieves the highest average success among compared methods across LIBERO and Kinetix and improves real-robot success from 46% to 62%, without extra deployment modules.

Asynchronous execution keeps executing the committed actions pt during the K control steps of inference (delay K), so the chunk generated from ot takes effect at t+K, when the observation is already ot+K . (b) Training. (1) Student states from delayed rollout and denoising: a step t of its own delayed rollout, and an intermediate state aτ of its own denoising at that step. (2) Distillation from the synchronous teacher at these states: the student sees ot and the committed actions pt, and the teacher, the same policy run without delay, sees ot+K . Both predict a velocity at aτ , and vS is trained to match vT .

papers.abstract: Automated verification of industrial assembly processes remains a challenging problem due to substantial visual variability, limited availability of labeled defect data, and the fine-grained nature of many assembly errors. Existing approaches often rely on object detection, CAD models, or supervised classification pipelines, which can struggle to generalize across changing products and assembly configurations. In this work, we propose a novel self-supervised assembly verification framework based on Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs). Starting from the JEPA-based world model LeWorldModel, we investigate how the architecture must be adapted to verify the correctness of fine-grained assembly operations. To this end, we formulate assembly verification as a predictive world modeling task operating on before-and-after observations of assembly processes. Experimental results on industrial assembly tasks demonstrate that the proposed approach reliably detects both fine-grained incorrect assembly states and action-state mismatches, achieving an AUROC of 86.9% on a newly introduced assembly verification dataset. These results indicate that JEPA-based predictive representations constitute a promising foundation for robust and data-efficient industrial assembly verification.
authors: Michael Hollmer, Andreas Fischer
bullets: Addresses visual variability, scarce labeled defect data, and subtle assembly errors.
Frames verification as predicting the resulting assembly state from before-and-after process observations.
Adapts the LeWorldModel JEPA architecture for fine-grained assembly verification.
Detects incorrect assembly states and mismatches between actions and resulting states.
Reports 86.9% AUROC, indicating promise for data-efficient industrial verification.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the LeWorldModel architecture [10], including the encoder, action-conditioned predictor, and SIGReg regularization of the latent representations.

Fig. 3. Overview of the proposed Assembly-JEPA architecture. Images captured before and after an assembly step are encoded into patch-level representations using a shared encoder. A difference map is computed from the pre- and post-action patch embeddings to localize the assembly-relevant region, from which a subset of embeddings is extracted and processed by an action-conditioned predictor. To encourage action-aware representations, an auxiliary inverse action prediction objective is applied to the latent differences between pre- and post-action embeddings. Verification is performed by comparing the predicted postaction representation with the observed representation of the post-action image.

Fig. 5. Comparison of Assembly-JEPA on the assembly dataset (top) and the modified CLEVR-Change dataset (bottom), demonstrating the model’s ability to distinguish between valid and invalid state transitions. On the modified CLEVR-Change dataset, the model achieves a near-perfect AUROC of 99.5%, with almost complete separation between positive and negative samples. The substantially higher performance on CLEVR-Change can be attributed to the more pronounced visual state changes present in the dataset, whereas the proposed assembly benchmark requires distinguishing highly localized and visually subtle assembly transitions. Shaded regions denote 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.

papers.abstract: Language often refers to an object by its parts, as in asking to point to a part or to turn an arbitrarily posed object so that two named parts lie in given directions. Both tasks need the direction from the object's center to the part's center, not the part's own orientation. A natural approach segments the part and takes the centroid of its mask. However, high mask overlap predicts the pointing direction poorly when a part is spread out relative to its distance from the object center. Language-guided part segmentation is trained and evaluated by mask overlap, which leaves a gap between the masks it produces and the part geometry that these tasks use. We close this gap by learning point evidence, weights over the observed points whose weighted centroid gives the part's location. Geometric Readout Supervision (GRS) trains these weights through the centroid's position and adds direction supervision on the parts used in reorientation commands. GRS improves both tasks even with a single frozen encoder and a single input pose. We implement this supervision in GeoRead3D, a system for pointing and reorientation from part descriptions. A language model maps each description to a known part name. Dual-Route Part Evidence combines refined segmentation evidence with directly predicted point evidence to locate each part. On PartNeXt and Artiverse, GeoRead3D points within $22.5^\circ$ for 74.1% and 60.0% of queries, 5.8 and 7.3 percentage points above the strongest baselines. Its reorientation success exceeds the strongest baselines by 10.4 and 7.8 points.
authors: Zhangcheng Hou, Kevin Tonkich, Tomoaki Ohtsuki
bullets: Part-mask overlap can poorly reflect the direction from an object’s center to a spatially extended part.
Geometric Readout Supervision trains point evidence through centroid position and adds direction supervision for reorientation.
Dual-Route Part Evidence combines refined segmentation with directly predicted point evidence.
On PartNeXt and Artiverse, it reaches 74.1% and 60.0% pointing accuracy within 22.5°, outperforming the strongest baselines by 5.8 and 7.3 points.
Reorientation success exceeds the strongest baselines by 10.4 and 7.8 points, using a frozen encoder and a single input pose.

papers.abstract: Demonstrations show how a task can be completed, but differences in embodiment, appearance, and execution speed make it difficult to identify the guidance relevant to the robot's current progress. We introduce JEPA-ICL, a vision-language-action framework that couples predictive planning with demonstration learning. The policy learns to plan by predicting ordered future states in JEPA feature space up to subtask completion, capturing what remains to be accomplished. These plans guide action generation and locate relevant stages in demonstrations, whose JEPA-supervised content features provide progress-aligned context. Learning from this context, in turn, updates the shared policy that produces the plans and actions. This coupling connects anticipating the robot's own execution with reusing demonstrated experience. On the Imitator Game, JEPA-ICL achieves 80.0% seen-task success under C15 pretraining, outperforming Zero-WAM by 12.0 percentage points. Without contextual demonstrations, JEPA-ICL outperforms the VLA-JEPA variant without human-video pretraining, improving success rates from 96.1% to 97.6% on LIBERO and from 62.9% to 73.2% on LIBERO-Plus. With demonstration-based training and contextual guidance at inference, LIBERO-Plus success further increases from 73.2% to 75.2%.
authors: Tingjun Dai, Jianxiang He, Mingfei Han, Qihao Yu, Longtao Jiang, Changlin Li, Minghao Jin, Zhihui Li, Xiaojun Chang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of transferring demonstrations across different embodiments, appearances, and execution speeds.
Predicts ordered future states in JEPA feature space until subtask completion to represent what remains to be done.
Uses these predicted plans to retrieve progress-aligned demonstration context and guide action generation.
Achieves 80.0% seen-task success on Imitator Game under C15 pretraining, 12 percentage points above Zero-WAM.
Improves LIBERO-Plus success from 73.2% to 75.2% when demonstration-based training and contextual guidance are used at inference.

papers.abstract: A generator can follow a spatial plan, but the benefit of supplying that plan depends on what the model can already do from text. In a controlled study with 18 paired training seeds, correcting predicted positions and sizes improves spatial intersection-over-union by 0.030, yet direct text is non-inferior at matched training compute. In a pretrained generator, a fixed rule layout improves two-object task success over the same text-only adapter by 12.50 percentage points, mostly by separating objects that already appear in the correct order. We then ask whether a more precise instruction can achieve the same separation across conditioning paths. On 288 new task families, adding a minimum-gap instruction improves success by 37.15 points with the text-only adapter, by at most 0.69 points with widely spaced regions, and by 6.94 points with tightly spaced regions. Under tight regions, 230 of 288 baseline images have the correct objects and direction yet miss the required gap, ruling out a high baseline success rate as the sole explanation for the weak text response.
authors: Lu Han, Jingyao Zhang
bullets: Correcting predicted positions and sizes raises spatial IoU by 0.030, while direct text is non-inferior at matched training compute.
In a pretrained generator, a fixed rule layout improves two-object task success by 12.50 percentage points over a text-only adapter, largely by separating correctly ordered objects.
A minimum-gap instruction improves success by 37.15 points with the text-only adapter, but by at most 0.69 points with widely spaced regions and 6.94 points with tightly spaced regions.
Under tight regions, most baseline images contain the correct objects and direction but fail the required gap, indicating weak text responsiveness rather than simply low baseline success.

papers.abstract: This report presents a comprehensive pipeline for developing an end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving model for the Physical AI AV Track. The framework consists of data curation, HD map auto-labelling, data-driven imitation learning, and simulator-based reinforcement learning. To ensure safety in the closed-loop setting, we introduce a selection-based E2E planning approach that leverages object detection and BEV segmentation to filter out trajectory candidates likely to cause collisions or off-road driving. Trained on NVIDIA NuRec and the NVIDIA PAI-AV dataset, our method scores a fixed vocabulary of trajectory candidates for collision, drivable-area compliance, and progress learned from simulated rollouts, and selects the best candidate that passes the filter. This design highlights the effectiveness of combining E2E planning with perception-based trajectory filtering for safe and reliable closed-loop autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: Continual pre-training (\textit{CPT}) is a standard route for domain adaptation, yet existing studies typically track pre-training loss or multiple-choice question answering (\textit{MCQA}) accuracy alone, offering only a narrow view of how adaptation unfolds. We jointly track factual knowledge via \textit{MCQA} and open-ended behavior via pairwise preference rankings across $18$ checkpoints for each of eight instruction-tuned \textit{Qwen} models ($0.5B$ to $8B$), adapted to German medicine with \textit{CPT} and \textit{SLERP} merging. The two axes converge at consistently different rates, with preference rankings reaching $90\%$ of their total gain after a median of $1.7B$ tokens versus $3.5B$ for \textit{MCQA}. A judge-free token-distribution measure reaches this threshold at $1.9B$ tokens. Per-aspect scores indicate that these early preference gains largely reflect surface alignment, meaning models can sound domain-appropriate before their factual knowledge catches up. Larger adapted models close more of the gap to unadapted next-tier generalists, whereas preference gain per FLOP falls by about an order of magnitude across our size range. We therefore argue that judge-based preference scores, which can plateau while \textit{MCQA} knowledge is still improving, should not be used alone to infer adaptation convergence or domain readiness.
authors: Niclas Doll, Jasper Schulze Buschhoff, Shalaka Satheesh, H\'ector Allende-Cid, Katrin Klug

Preference scores may plateau while factual knowledge continues improving, limiting their use as a standalone convergence signal.

papers.abstract: An assistant that summarizes old conversations may later need a detail from the original exchange. It can score archived passages against the question, but only passages that fit in the prompt reach the answering model. We tested whether a BM25 filter saves input tokens once that limit is taken into account. We calibrated the filter on passages that individually corrected an answer the model got wrong from the summaries alone. Across 75 LongMemEval questions, filtering changed one prompt and saved 0.096% of input tokens. With and without the filter, the model answered the same questions correctly under a second automated grading. On a random sample, two human graders' settled judgments agreed with the automated grades in 92.9% of definite comparisons (Cohen's kappa = 0.805). Building on earlier work that distinguishes retrieved evidence from delivered evidence, we give an exact test for packers that try whole passages in a fixed order and skip any that do not fit. Run the packer without the filter. The prompt changes exactly when an admitted passage scores below the cutoff. Code and data: https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/Certfold

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations provide a rich source of bimanual dexterous skills, yet transferring them to robot hands remains challenging. Existing methods primarily optimize object trajectory tracking, often overlooking how human hands interact with the object. Even with accurate tracking, robots may contact incorrect object parts or slide their fingers, resulting in unstable manipulation. We present DexDuet, a framework that learns contact-preserving bimanual dexterity from a single human demonstration. DexDuet employs two interaction rewards to preserve human hand-object configurations and contacts. To enable coordinated manipulation, we factorize the bimanual policy into two weight-sharing per-hand policies that condition on each other's states. We further propose assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum that adjusts object assistance and training starts across demonstration segments to overcome difficult manipulation phases. Across four benchmarks spanning three simulators and five robot embodiments, DexDuet improves object-tracking ADD-AUC by 11 to 41 points over the corresponding baselines while consistently achieving better contact preservation. Notably, among 122 paired runs with comparable object-tracking accuracy, DexDuet preserves the human's contacts better in 117 cases. Code and videos are available at https://rcl-robotics.github.io/Dexduet.io/
authors: Haoran Zhang, Haokai Ding, Han Zhou, Zuxing Lu, Heng Zhang, Xingxing Zuo
bullets: Addresses failures of object-only trajectory tracking, such as incorrect contacts and finger sliding.
Uses interaction rewards to preserve demonstrated hand-object configurations and contacts.
Factorizes the bimanual policy into two weight-sharing per-hand policies conditioned on each other’s states.
Introduces assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum for difficult manipulation phases.
Across four benchmarks, three simulators, and five robot embodiments, it improves tracking and contact preservation over baselines; contact preservation is better in 117 of 122 comparable runs.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DexDuet. (a) A human demonstration provides the object trajectory, which gives the policy πθ the next object pose, and the hand motion, which is retargeted to a reference motion that the robot hands imitate. Inside πθ , two per-hand policies share one network, and each maps its own observation o and the partner observation z to an action a. (b) Two interaction rewards compare each robot hand with the human hand relative to the object. The hand graph reward compares the palm and finger directions and the fingertip gaps, and the hand-object contact reward compares the distance and the closest point of each hand region to the object. (c) A-RSI gives each segment b of the demonstration its own assistance level hb, which it lowers (green) or raises (red), never above a ceiling h̄(u) that decreases over the updates u. Episodes start from states that the policy has reached, and their start segment is drawn from p(b), which favors the segments with a high failure rate fb.

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are used in more and more new tasks, context engineering becomes a fundamental method to efficiently steer LLMs by constructing instruction prompts or metadata without intensive training. A growing number of LLM context engineering (LCE) approaches automate the task by casting the LLM itself as the engineer that draws generalizable instructions or experiences from offline trials as context. Although these methods resemble how humans learn from experiences, it remains unclear \textbf{when and how} LLMs can engineer effective context from data. To answer the question, we first establish a benchmark composed of datasets with different reasoning patterns. We compared different LCE methods with different LLM families in 8B size, showing that there is no single winner for all tasks, even compared with simple baselines like chain-of-thought. Even when scaling model capabilities via more parameters or generation iterations, LCEs do not consistently boost existing performance. Across all datasets and models, the performance gains of LCEs are negatively correlated ($r=-0.5, p\le 0.05$) with the diversity of the failure modes of reasoning trajectories. Investigating how LCEs work, we find that (1) the improvement in instruction adherence can explain some success of LCEs; (2) one major bottleneck is whether LLMs can extract effective experiences out of natively diverse failures. Through this study, we uncover the limited capabilities of LCEs in abstracting principled contexts from diverse failure modes and understand how LCEs work, providing guidelines for future work.
authors: Junrui Zhang, Zeyu Xu, Runchuan Zhu, Jie Peng, Long Zhang, Zixin Ding, Jiaxin Lin, Kai Wang, Jianmin Ji, Junyuan Hong

Improved instruction adherence explains some gains, while extracting effective experiences from diverse failures is a key bottleneck.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates when and how LLMs can engineer effective context from data, a fundamental capability for LLM-based agents.

papers.tldr: LLM-based context engineering helps inconsistently because its effectiveness depends on how diverse the underlying reasoning failures are and whether the model can extract useful general principles from them.

papers.abstract: Potential-based reward shaping (PBRS) does not change the optimal policy, but how much it speeds up learning depends on the potential and on effects outside this guarantee. We analyse how PBRS changes the one-step reward while it preserves the discounted return: a per-step $(\gamma-1)\Phi$ term, the terminal-state rule, a constant shift of the potential, and positive cycles in a bonus that is not potential-based. We then measure these consequences in pre-registered experiments with a PPO agent. The agent has a limited egocentric view and is tested on two MiniGrid navigation tasks (160 runs, 10 seeds per condition). On LavaCrossing, a geodesic (BFS) potential learned faster than both the sparse baseline and a Euclidean potential with a 7x7 and a 5x5 view (AUC difference +0.27 to +0.39, Holm p between 0.007 and 0.0499). The Euclidean potential did not differ from the baseline. In 20 runs with a non-potential bonus, none of the agents learned the task. The Euclidean potential caused more than twice as many deaths in lava during early training. View size did not detectably change the benefit of shaping. With a 5x5 view on SimpleCrossing, some BFS runs got stuck in loops and never learned; shifting the potential did not remove this, so the per-step term alone does not explain it.
authors: Nodirjon Khabibullaev, Rajat Dandekar
bullets: Analyzes per-step reward effects, terminal-state handling, constant potential shifts, and failures from non-potential bonuses.

On SimpleCrossing, some BFS agents became stuck in loops; shifting the potential did not resolve this.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human manipulation data offer a scalable resource for training dexterous robot policies. However, how effectively robots can learn and benefit from these data remains unclear due to the embodiment gap between humans and robots. We present EgoStudy, a systematic, controlled study of egocentric data for robot learning. Holding the robot dataset fixed, we vary the scale and diversity of egocentric data, data processing strategies, and co-training configurations. We investigate three questions: (1) Which data processing and pretraining choices most effectively exploit egocentric data? (2) Which components of robot action prediction benefit most from scaling these data? (3) How do scaling effects differ between vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs)? Our experiments yield three main findings. First, data diversity, alignment between trajectories, and detailed language annotations are key factors in effective transfer. Second, scaling egocentric data yields larger gains in predicting end-effector translation than in predicting fine-grained finger movements. Third, WAMs perform better when egocentric data are limited, whereas VLAs exhibit greater gains as the amount of egocentric data increases. Together, these findings provide practical guidance on processing and using egocentric data to train VLAs and WAMs, while clarifying the benefits and limitations of scaling these data.
authors: Puzhen Yuan, Yanjiang Guo, Yichen Liu, Xiang Zhu, Qingzhou Lu, Chenxin Liu, Tun Ban, Haodong Yan, Zhide Zhong, Jianyu Chen
bullets: Egocentric data transfer improves with greater diversity, trajectory alignment, and detailed language annotations.
Scaling primarily benefits end-effector translation prediction rather than fine-grained finger movement.
WAMs perform better with limited egocentric data, while VLAs gain more as egocentric data scale increases.
The study offers practical guidance for processing and co-training egocentric and robot data.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Which data processing and co-training designs improve transfer? Complete episodes, detailed captions, and the dataset diversity yield lower wrist translation error on both robot holdouts for both model families. This indicates that data diversity and alignment between trajectories and detailed language annotations are key factors in effective transfer. Moreover, fixed-step sampling yields lower error for the VLA, and event-level sampling yields lower error for the WAM.

Figure 7. Which action components benefit most from scaling egocentric data? We measure mean squared error (MSE) separately for wrist translation, wrist rotation, and fingertip pose on high-quality, held-out robot trajectories. Across both robot domains and model families, wrist translation MSE generally decreases as egocentric data scale, while wrist rotation and fingertip pose errors show no consistent decline. We hypothesize that due to human–robot embodiment gap and errors in estimating actions limit transfer primarily to large-scale motions such as wrist translation, with less benefit for the finger movements and wrist rotations.

Figure 4. Does scaling egocentric data improve robot learning? We pretrain the VLA (left) and WAM (right) with 1%, 3%, 10%, 30%, and 100% of the egocentric human data while keeping robot training exposure and the optimization budget fixed. We evaluate wrist translation MSE on held-out trajectories from Bimanual XHand and RoboCasa-GR1. All four model–domain pairs show a consistent downward trend, indicating effective human-to-robot transfer in EgoStudy.

Figure 6. Do pretraining gains carry over to robot control? RoboCasa-GR1 task success increases after posttraining for both model families, consistent with the decrease in pretraining validation loss. Gray dashed lines mark the corresponding baselines without pretraining.

Figure 9. How does backbone choice affect scaling gains between VLA and WAM? The wrist translation error decreases to the same extent across different VLAs, indicating that the 4B backbone is already capable of effectively extracting features shared between the egocentric and robot data. When the backbone of WAM is changed to 5B, its human-to-robot capability declines indicating that WAM relies more heavily on a powerful video backbone to assimilate egocentric data.

Figure 8. How do VLA and WAM visual features change with scale? As egocentric data scale, relative separation R between human and robot features decreases in both robot domains for the VLA but shows no consistent decrease across the WAM layers examined. We hypothesize that human and robot features align more closely in our VLA because it only needs to output actions in a shared action space. Our WAM must also predict future video, which may encourage it to retain visual differences between human and robot hands.

papers.abstract: Contrastive decoding (CD) mitigates object hallucination in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by contrasting token distributions under different conditions to adjust token scores. However, existing generative and discriminative benchmarks primarily measure final task scores, which can be confounded by candidate filtering, changes in generation trajectories, and response biases, making it difficult to isolate the effects of the underlying contrastive adjustments. To address these limitations while complementing existing evaluations, we introduce CONCOR (Contrastive Correction Evaluation), a controlled benchmark that directly evaluates the competition between ground-truth and different types of hallucinated candidates using the Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM). CGM also enables analysis of directional consistency, composition, and reliability of contrastive corrections. Our evaluation reveals that existing CD methods exhibit distinct correction behaviors: some consistently favor ground-truth candidates, whereas others produce strong corrections but also introduce more errors. Crucially, these differences help explain their contrasting responses to increased contrast strength, which improves some methods while degrading others. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating the contrastive correction itself, rather than relying solely on final-output performance, and CONCOR provides a controlled and interpretable framework for understanding and improving CD methods for hallucination mitigation.
authors: Ting Chen, Geng Li, Guohao Chen, Hanjia Lyu
bullets: Existing CD evaluations can be confounded by candidate filtering, generation trajectories, and response biases.
CONCOR uses controlled comparisons between ground-truth and hallucinated candidates.
Its Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM) measures correction direction, composition, and reliability.
Different CD methods trade off consistent grounding against stronger but more error-prone corrections.
Contrast strength can help or hurt methods depending on their correction behavior, motivating direct evaluation of contrastive corrections.

papers.abstract: Coordinating locomotion and dexterous manipulation is fundamental to humanoid robots operating in human environments. A key challenge is learning motion priors from diverse data and using them effectively for coordinated robot control. We present CHAMP, a unified framework for humanoid loco-manipulation that combines whole-body motion pretraining with adaptive feature extraction. CHAMP pretrains a vision-language model to predict future body and hand motion from approximately 2,298 hours of heterogeneous human and robot data. A shared motion representation enables unified whole-body motion learning across embodiments from datasets with body annotations, hand annotations, or both. To ground these motion priors in robot control, we introduce a Coordination-oriented Action Expert (CAE) and train it on replay data generated using the target controller. Through sparse routing, CAE adaptively selects, transforms, and fuses features from multiple layers of the pretrained model to jointly generate body and hand actions. In experiments, CHAMP achieves overall success rates of 84.8% on seven simulated tasks and 91.4% on seven real-world tasks with a Unitree G1, outperforming the evaluated baselines in both settings. In particular, CHAMP achieves 70.0% success on the long-horizon popcorn-serving task, compared with 40.0% for the best-performing baseline.
authors: Lijun Han, Muyuan Ma, Zichen Wang, Siyuan Liu, Yuxi Liu, Yutong Wang, Bohao Zhang, Heng Zhou, Wei Sui
bullets: Pretrains a vision-language model on approximately 2,298 hours of heterogeneous human and robot motion data.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving models have made substantial progress, yet reliable closed-loop driving in complex traffic remains challenging. Beyond improving individual models, system-level orchestration offers a complementary approach by coordinating driving capabilities and computation. We introduce ROSE-Drive (Runtime Orchestration and System Evolution), a model-agnostic framework that jointly orchestrates driving execution and computation. It coordinates frozen driving models with driving skills, perception tools, and feedback controllers. A distilled vision-language model (VLM) proposes driving tasks and scene relations. Shared physical state and persistent tasks support capability composition, task continuity, and adaptive scheduling. The orchestrator combines model and skill outputs across control channels, maintains task responsibility through handover, and uses execution feedback to select controllers, reuse valid motion references, and schedule model inference. Offline revisions use execution records to refine skills and their coordination through a stable task interface. Successive system stages inherit these revisions while model, perception, and VLM weights remain fixed. Evaluations with four driving models on Bench2Drive v0.0.3, Bench2Drive v0.0.4, and Fail2Drive show accumulated capability and transfer before target-benchmark revision. On held-out Longest6, driving score (DS) rises from 25 to 52 for AutoMoT and from 22 to 47 for SimLingo across system stages, while both systems skip new model inference on over 71% of control steps.
authors: Qihang Huang, Zhidong Wang, Zirui Li, YuJie Yan, Jingsong Liang, Shiyu Fang, Collister Chua, Zhan Chen, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses the challenge of reliable driving in complex traffic through system-level orchestration rather than model retraining.
Uses a model-agnostic orchestrator with a distilled VLM, shared physical state, persistent tasks, adaptive scheduling, and controller handovers.
Refines skills and their coordination from execution records while keeping driving, perception, and VLM weights fixed.
Across multiple benchmarks and four driving models, held-out Longest6 driving scores improved substantially across system stages.
More than 71% of control steps skipped new model inference for both reported systems, reducing runtime computation demand.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning requires a vision-language model~(VLM) to understand metric distances, three-dimensional relationships, and viewpoint-dependent geometry. Learning these capabilities typically requires externally curated training data. This paper introduces Spatial-Zero, a VLMs' training framework that can self-evolve through autonomous spatial exploration with zero data. Spatial-Zero addresses two key challenges in autonomous spatial exploration: reliably generating valid spatial interaction tasks and providing accurate supervision for learning from these tasks. Specifically, a proposer specifies object configurations and questions, and a Coder turns them into executable scene programs that produce multi-view images and explicit scene geometry. A Geometric Oracle checks spatial constraints, visibility, and answer uniqueness and derives ground-truth labels from executed geometry; these labels supervise the Solver and ground difficulty feedback, while validation outcomes guide subsequent task generation. Across six spatial reasoning benchmarks and three VLM backbones, Spatial-Zero yields consistent gains through iterative self-evolution. After three iterations, Qwen3.5-9B improves average accuracy by 3.23 percentage points; with Qwen3.5-4B, Spatial-Zero also outperforms existing VLM self-evolution methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/YutongLi2024/Spatial-Zero
authors: Yutong Li, Haoyu Zhao, Daoguo Dong, Ziyi Ye, Yugang Jiang
bullets: Targets metric distance, 3D relationships, and viewpoint-dependent geometry in VLMs.
A proposer and Coder create object configurations, questions, executable scene programs, and multi-view images.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents repeatedly feed an ever-growing interaction trajectory to a specialized agent model. Prefix caching reuses computation over repeated history, but cannot prevent context growth or remove information irrelevant to the current decision. This is especially costly when the specialized agent lacks the cached-input discounts available to general-purpose models, making trajectory compression a natural alternative. However, existing compression methods on selective context risk losing global information, recursively rewriting summary leads to semantic drift, while repeatedly recompressing the full history shifts the growing cost to the compressor. Therefore, we introduce DMC-5 (Dual-Model Collaboration with CaChe-aware Context Compression), an asymmetric framework that assigns full-history integration to a general compression model and action generation to a specialized agent model. DMC-5 maintains the raw trajectory as an Append-only Canonical View, preserving global access while allowing the compressor to reuse a stable historical prefix instead of recursively rewriting or recomputing prior context. The agent operates only on a compact Decision View with recent raw interactions, reducing repeated input while retaining the information needed for the next action. DMC-5 further incorporates YAMATO (integritY-Aware Memory Abstractions for Tool Operations) to preserve execution-critical information during lossy compression. Experiments on AppWorld, OfficeBench, and 8-objective QA show that DMC-5 reduces agent model input by 38.5-57.0% and end-to-end cost by 14.5-28.0% with 78.0-85.0% compressor cache-hit rates, while improving task performance by 1.0-5.8% over the uncompressed baseline.
authors: Haochen Li, Xiaobing Tu, Yinggui Wang, Jinkui Ren, Xiantao Zhang
bullets: Addresses growing trajectory context, irrelevant history, semantic drift, and repeated recompression costs.
Uses an Append-only Canonical View for stable full-history access and a compact Decision View for action generation.
Combines dual-model collaboration with YAMATO to preserve execution-critical tool information during lossy compression.
On AppWorld, OfficeBench, and 8-objective QA, reduces agent input by 38.5–57.0% and end-to-end cost by 14.5–28.0%.
Reports 78.0–85.0% compressor cache-hit rates and 1.0–5.8% higher task performance than the uncompressed baseline.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents operating on Web development platforms can interact with repositories, issue trackers, and continuous integration services to carry out long-horizon software engineering tasks. However, behavioral drift remains a major bottleneck in such multi-turn reasoning and action trajectories. To mitigate this, activation steering has emerged as a promising approach for regularizing agent behaviors by intervening on the LLM's transformer residual streams. Nonetheless, existing methods typically apply a static steering policy across all tasks, overlooking the fact that a single policy is rarely effective across heterogeneous tasks and varying execution turns. This limitation motivates dynamic online selection among candidate steering policies. Yet, doing so in long-horizon agentic settings is challenging: verifiable task-level feedback is only revealed upon task completion, leaving the contributions of individual steering turns unobserved. To address this challenge, we formulate online steering-policy selection as a multi-armed bandit problem with delayed task-level feedback and turn-level predictive hints derived from residual-stream activations. Within this formulation, we introduce Online Optimistic Activation Steering, a meta-framework that uses hints to guide within-task steering policy selection and leverages terminal task-level feedback to correct cumulative reward estimates. Theoretically, against the best fixed policy in hindsight, we prove regret bounds that tighten with increasing hint accuracy and establish a matching lower bound with respect to prediction error and candidate policy count. Empirical evaluations on realistic coding benchmarks demonstrate that our framework outperforms both static steering policies and naive online adaptive baselines.
authors: Hao Luan, Hao Qiu, Zhi Zheng, See-Kiong Ng, Zhiyong Huang
bullets: Addresses behavioral drift in long-horizon LLM coding-agent trajectories.

Uses hints for within-task decisions and completed-task outcomes to update cumulative reward estimates.
Proves regret bounds that improve with hint accuracy, plus a matching lower bound tied to prediction error and policy count.
Experiments on realistic coding benchmarks outperform static steering and naive online adaptive baselines.

papers.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast zero-shot with accuracy exceeding that of task-specific models, and the smaller ones fit on edge devices. Operational deployments must refresh their forecast as new observations arrive, and privacy and latency requirements often force this refresh onto resource-constrained edge devices. To serve as a forecasting system there, a TSFM must refresh quickly, keep latency and peak memory bounded as the stream grows, and retain its accuracy as the observed history accumulates. Refreshing incrementally without altering the forecast requires temporal causality: non-causal models recompute at every update, causal attention admits a KV cache that grows linearly, and causal recurrent models update a fixed-size state in constant time and memory. We make these states persist across refreshes for every causal architecture and verify equivalence to full recomputation. We evaluate nine TSFM configurations on univariate forecasting against all three requirements, measuring accuracy as a function of context length, single-refresh latency, and latency and memory on streams of up to one million time steps on a server-grade GPU and three edge devices. No model gains on average accuracy beyond its trained context and most lose it well before the full history is reached, while KV caches leave latency and memory growing linearly with the retained history. TiRex-2 is the only one of the nine configurations meeting all three requirements: it refreshes in 14 ms on the GPU and 120 ms on a Raspberry Pi 5, keeps latency, energy and peak memory constant over a million steps, and retains its accuracy on the untruncated history.
authors: Marco Pichler, Patrick Podest, G\"unter Klambauer, Sepp Hochreiter
bullets: Edge forecasting requires fast refreshes, bounded latency and memory, and stable accuracy as observations accumulate.
Causal recurrent models support fixed-size state updates, unlike non-causal models and KV-cache approaches whose costs grow with history.
The authors persist recurrent states across refreshes and verify equivalence with full recomputation.
Nine TSFM configurations are evaluated on univariate forecasting across a GPU and three edge devices.
Most models lose accuracy beyond their trained context; only TiRex-2 meets all requirements, including constant resource use over one million steps.

papers.abstract: Driving models need to choose which capabilities to use and when to reconsider their decisions. We introduce AgentMoT, a Mixture-of-Transformers with built-in agent reasoning and system scheduling. Combinations of agent, world, and action experts form three jointly trained pathways for direct-action, vision-language-action, and world-action computation. The Router selects a native pathway, while the agent expert supplies reasoning and selects skills. Execution feedback raises wake-up requests, and the agent self-scheduler learns whether to reconsider the task decision or keep it. Mandatory requests invoke the agent directly. The relative-capability principle guides these choices by relating the benefit of additional computation or intervention to its cost. After open-loop initialization, dual-loop evolution trains the Router, agent, and self-scheduler from closed-loop experience while failure-driven updates refine skills and execution feedback. AgentMoT achieves state-of-the-art results on Bench2Drive v0.0.3 and v0.0.4, with 94.48/92.33 driving score and 85.45/82.73% success rate, respectively. With skills disabled, learned routing improves over the strongest fixed pathway by 1.79 driving-score points and 4.09 percentage points of success rate on v0.0.3. Ablation studies further show gains from closed-loop agent learning, two-view queries, and event-triggered wake-up.

Learns from closed-loop driving experience, with execution feedback triggering wake-up requests and failure-driven updates refining skills.
Achieves 94.48/92.33 driving scores and 85.45/82.73% success rates on Bench2Drive v0.0.3/v0.0.4.

papers.abstract: Navigation systems in colonoscopy are advancing from guiding the endoscopist to steering the scope autonomously. Since an incorrect motion can injure the patient, developing and evaluating these systems calls for a world model of colonoscopy. Such a model must follow a commanded scope motion, keep the colon anatomy consistent, and show lesions and procedural events. Yet camera-controlled generators trained on general scenes lose the colon's structure under motion, and endoscopic generators offer no camera control. We present ColonoWorld, a colonoscopy world model conditioned on a camera trajectory and a coarse 3D tube of the colon, trained on in vivo videos. From a whole-colon tube, it generates a full cecum-to-rectum procedure, even for unseen colon shapes. It also places polyps, instruments, and irrigation at specified locations and times. ColonoWorld outperforms state-of-the-art video generators, reducing camera trajectory error by 32% and FVD by 29%. Our code and annotations will be released at https://aidaslab.github.io/ColonoWorld.

papers.abstract: Dense feed-forward networks are unaffected by how their neurons are grouped: every neuron is evaluated. Sparse execution makes this grouping consequential, because each input can access only a few experts. An arbitrary partition can therefore retain pretrained weights while separating computations that an input needs together. We argue that upcycling should organize neurons according to their responses to similar inputs. To establish this correspondence, we introduce a context-guided upcycling approach REACT, Response-based Expert Assembly from Contextual Trajectories, that uses frozen denoising trajectories to connect input contexts with pretrained neuron responses. We first identify contexts after timestep-wise centering to account for distribution shifts across noise levels, then use their associated responses to allocate intact neurons to routed experts. The same contexts initialize the corresponding router entries, aligning expert contents with their intended inputs, while global activation statistics select an always-active shared expert. Layer-wise reconstruction and end-to-end adaptation refine this initialization for sparse execution. On ImageNet-1K, our approach achieves better generation quality while activating only 37.5% of the original FFN parameters and reducing total per-token activated parameters by 27.6%.
authors: Hesen Yang, Yuxue Liu, Yanzhe Chen, Weibo Zhao, Junwei Su, Dan Hu, Shenggan Cheng, Xuanlei Zhao, Wenchao Zhou, Junhua Wang, Lansong Diao, Yang You
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between arbitrary neuron partitioning and the input-dependent computation required by sparse execution.
Uses frozen denoising trajectories to identify timestep-normalized contexts and associate them with pretrained neuron responses.
Allocates intact neurons to routed experts, initializes router entries from the same contexts, and adds a globally active shared expert.
Refines the initialization through layer-wise reconstruction and end-to-end adaptation.
On ImageNet-1K, achieves better generation quality while activating 37.5% of original FFN parameters and reducing total per-token activation by 27.6%.

papers.abstract: Efficient robotic manipulation requires temporally coordinated actions with low inference latency. Multi-step diffusion and flow policies progressively refine action trajectories but require costly iterative inference, whereas one-step policies eliminate iterative trajectory refinement to reduce inference cost. We introduce **SOAR**, a structure-guided one-step generative policy that improves action quality while preserving one-step efficiency. SOAR predicts an observation-conditioned discrete cosine transform (DCT) representation of future actions, capturing temporal variations across multiple frequency bands to provide explicit guidance from key temporal structural information. Unlike velocity-parameterized one-step flow policies that recover clean actions indirectly from a predicted velocity field, SOAR directly generates clean action trajectories in action space. This aligns the model output with the executable control target and provides a direct interface for structural calibration. The predicted structure further corrects the generated trajectory according to their spectral discrepancy, without requiring an additional evaluation of the generative backbone. During training, the corresponding MeanFlow velocity is derived from the calibrated clean action and used for consistency learning, while an endpoint objective aligns training with the pure-noise condition used for one-step inference. Across 53 Adroit and Meta-World tasks, SOAR achieves 83.9% overall success with only 8.7 ms inference latency. When applied to the VLA model, {\pi}0.5, SOAR further achieves 97.2% on LIBERO and 71.7% on RoboTwin 2.0. Real-world experiments and extensive ablations further validate its effectiveness and efficiency.
authors: Di Xin, Mingfei Han, Genming Cui, Yuanxiang Chen, Xiaolong Wu, Siyu Ning, Xiaojun Chang, Zhihui Li
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of iterative diffusion and flow policies while retaining temporal coordination.
Predicts observation-conditioned future actions in a discrete cosine transform (DCT) representation across multiple frequency bands.
Directly generates clean action trajectories in action space, rather than indirectly recovering them from velocity predictions.
Uses spectral discrepancy to calibrate trajectories without an additional generative-backbone evaluation, with consistency and endpoint objectives during training.
Reports 83.9% success across 53 Adroit and Meta-World tasks at 8.7 ms latency; with π0.5, it reaches 97.2% on LIBERO and 71.7% on RoboTwin 2.0.

During training, the calibrated action induces the corresponding MeanFlow transport velocity for consistency learning and inference-endpoint alignment. Inference requires a single U-Net evaluation.

papers.abstract: Point supervised temporal action localization is becoming the need of time in this era of ever growing and non-stop video data. Existing method mainly rely on snippet level action response to generate pseudo labels. However, these labels often suffer from boundary ambiguity, over extended proposals, and weak temporal structure. To address these issues, we propose STAR, a structure-aware Temporal Action Recovery framework for point supervised temporal action localization. STAR works by enhancing the base S model with temporal difference interaction with attention module to capture forward and backward snippet changes, and introduces the learning of start, core, and end roles to model the internal temporal structure of actions. In addition, STAR further improves the pseudo label generation through All point proposal ranking and Rolebank based structural re-ranking, which suppress neighbor crossing and structurally inconsistent proposals. Finally, temporal action detector to STAR feedback supervision transfers high quality detector prediction back to the STAR model through soft start, core, end, action, and background targets. This helps to further refine the pseudo labels. Extensive experiments on four standard benchmarks shows the effectiveness of STAR. By using I3D features, STAR achieves 67.2% at AVG@0.1:0.7 on THUMOS'14, 58.1% on GTEA, 74.6% on BEOID, and 31.7% at AVG@0.5:0.95 on ActivityNet-1.3, outperforming previous point supervised methods across multiple benchmarks.
authors: Yawar Rehman, Min Young Kim
bullets: Addresses ambiguous boundaries, overextended proposals, and weak temporal structure in point-supervised localization.
Models forward/backward snippet changes with temporal-difference attention and represents actions through start, core, and end roles.
Refines pseudo-labels using all-point proposal ranking and Rolebank-based structural re-ranking to reduce neighbor crossing and inconsistency.
Uses detector feedback with soft structural targets to iteratively improve pseudo-label quality.
Reports strong results across THUMOS’14, GTEA, BEOID, and ActivityNet-1.3, outperforming prior point-supervised methods in the reported comparisons.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overall architecture of the proposed STAR framework. STAR calculates the attention based temporal difference interations using the I3D snippets. The enhanced features are then forwarded to the S model for class activation sequence scores and action seeds. Using those seeds, STAR constructs soft Gaussian target for temporal role learning. St, C, Ed, and Bkg represents Start, Core, End, and Background roles, respectively. Once candidate proposals are generated using the snippet level action responses those are refined through All point ranking and Rolebank re-ranking schemes to select the high quality action proposals. The selected action proposals are then converted to pseudo labels for the training of temporal action detector. Detector prediction are fed back to the STAR model as soft supervision for start, core, end, action, and background targets for further refinement of pseudo labels

Fig. 6. Error analysis of the proposed STAR method using I3D features on THUMOS’14 dataset and ActionFormer as temporal action detector. We report three profiles. (a) The false negative (FN) profile, (b) The false positive (FP) profile, and (c) The sensitivity profile

Fig. 1. STAR at a glance: Structure-aware temporal action recovery (STAR). For snippet video features with point annotations, STAR model calculates temporal difference interaction between neighboring snippets. This enhance feature information is then forwarded to estimate CAS of action and background snippets. To recover the action structure from point supervision, STAR learns role aware representations for start, core, and end regions of action and background. Candidate action proposals are refined by All point ranking, which rejects action proposal that crosses neighboring point annotations. Action proposals are re-ranked with Rolebank re-ranking that penalizes action proposals whose structure is not similar to the action structure. Pseudo labels are then created and TAD is trained. papers.title: STAR: Structure-Aware Temporal Action Recovery for Point Supervised Temporal Action Localization

papers.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical account of Transformer attention by organizing existing probabilistic and information-theoretic results. It identifies the assumptions under which attention computes a posterior mean and the additional conditions required for accurate next-token prediction. Posterior-mean optimality under squared-error loss does not by itself establish predictive sufficiency; even a sufficient representation requires a prediction head that uses its information correctly. An excess-log-loss decomposition makes this distinction precise by separating representation information loss from prediction-head error. The analysis clarifies the conditions required for predictive guarantees. Determining when these conditions hold in trained models, and how architectural or training choices can support them, could guide the development of AI systems that preserve and use predictive information more effectively.
authors: Fouad B. Chedid
bullets: Organizes probabilistic and information-theoretic results on Transformer attention.
Identifies assumptions under which attention computes a posterior mean.
Shows that posterior-mean optimality under squared-error loss is insufficient for predictive sufficiency.
Uses an excess-log-loss decomposition to separate representation information loss from prediction-head error.
Highlights open questions about whether trained models and design choices satisfy the required conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of Transformer attention and predictive sufficiency; relevant to LLM architecture understanding.
papers.title: Toward a Theoretical Understanding of Transformer Attention: Bayesian Estimation and Predictive Sufficiency
papers.tldr: The paper clarifies when Transformer attention can be viewed as Bayesian estimation and why posterior-mean representations alone do not guarantee accurate next-token prediction.

papers.abstract: 3D indoor scene synthesis requires generating objects to form a complete and coherent scene. Existing approaches rely heavily on manually annotated datasets, leading to high costs and limited generalization. We present SceneCast, an annotation-free framework that trains on large-scale, unlabeled videos, addressing two key challenges: (1) Videos provide only partial views of a scene, requiring the model to extrapolate unseen 3D regions, which is inherently error-prone; (2) Raw videos available online are uncurated, suffering from uncontrolled conditions and variable data quality. First, we design a Transformer-based model that predicts objects sequentially and is fine-tuned with reinforcement learning (RL), where an LLM acts as a spatial common-sense evaluator. The LLM provides reward signals through chain-of-thought reasoning and code-executable geometric checks to refine object configurations. Second, we introduce \trim, a data curation approach that generates training videos with controllable video generation models. Crucially, it retains only high-quality prefix clips via multi-criteria quality assessment with an entropy-based weighting strategy. Evaluated on curated synthetic video sets, our annotation-free approach outperforms state-of-the-art supervised methods in scene quality.
authors: Ziyang Zong, Canming Xia, Haoran Xu, Guang Tan
bullets: Addresses costly annotations and limited generalization in existing indoor scene synthesis methods.
Uses a Transformer to sequentially predict objects and extrapolate unseen 3D regions from partial video views.
Fine-tunes scene configurations with RL using LLM rewards based on spatial reasoning and executable geometric checks.
Curates synthetic training videos by retaining high-quality prefix clips selected with multi-criteria, entropy-weighted assessment.
Outperforms state-of-the-art supervised methods in scene quality on curated synthetic video sets.

figures.caption: Figure 1. SceneCast overview. (a) Our generation model predicts 3D objects sequentially, starting from an initial set of objects. The model is fine-tuned with a reinforcement learning phase with LLM feedback. (b) Our ViTrim strategy removes low-quality tail segments from generated video using multiple quality assessment criteria, ensuring only valid clips are used for training.

Figure 2. SceneCast pipelines. (a) Transformer-based autoregressive 3D indoor scene completion backbone network. (b) LLM-driven reinforcement learning fine-tuning loop incorporating CoT spatial reasoning, automatic geometric code execution, and multi-dimensional reward fusion. (c) ViTrim pipeline for high-quality video segment selection.

Figure 3. Generation samples from an empty scene. SceneCast performs well in producing reasonable and complete object layouts, with correct collision avoidance. ATISS and DiffuScene generate misaligned objects and unnatural layouts. Perhaps restricted by the video generation model, VIPScene generates a small number of objects with narrow coverage of the scene, missing objects that are commonly found in realistic scenes (e.g., wardrobe for bedroom, sofa for livingdiningroom). SAGE [52] lacks the understanding of the actual physical space, resulting in the generation of duplicate or poorly arranged objects (e.g., bedroom without bed, impassable passageway).

Figure 5. LLM reasoning process. (a) Position refinement for minor spatial overlap; (b) Size correction for severe object interpenetration; (c) Layout saturation detection and generation stopping. The LLM Agent applies CoT reasoning and self-programmed geometric computation. In each case, Size[x,y,z] denotes the corrected 3D dimension of an object, Position[x,y,z] its refined 3D centroid. CONTINUE indicates proceeding with object generation, while STOP terminates the process when layout is complete or spatially invalid.

Table 2. Ablations on the bedroom set. (a) Unified reward ablation. Each row augments the previous one with a single component, isolating its effect. The LLM reward outperforms handcrafted rules, and code execution provides a further gain over language-only reasoning. (b) ViTrim ablation. All models share identical architecture and training hyperparameters, while only the data curation strategy differs. Rows 1–2 isolate the effect of trimming, row 3 isolates the spatial IoU signal and rows 4–5 compare entropy-based vs uniform weighting.(c) SceneCast completion quality across condition coverage on held-out 3D-FRONT scenes.
