papers.selection_reason: Presents SceneCast, a framework for 3D indoor scene synthesis using synthetic videos and LLM-based rewards. This fits the 3D Vision topic as a foundation model for scene generation.
papers.title: SceneCast: Learning Indoor Scene Synthesis from Curated Synthetic Videos with LLM Reward
papers.tldr: SceneCast learns coherent 3D indoor scene synthesis without manual annotations by combining curated synthetic videos with LLM-guided reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Many large language models (LLMs) use chain-of-thought (CoT) to solve complex problems, but hide their CoT traces to prevent reasoning capabilities from being distilled. While recent studies have shown that hidden CoTs can be reconstructed, existing methods typically require training a separate attacker for each target LLM. This paper studies model-agnostic CoT reconstruction, aiming to reconstruct hidden CoT traces from arbitrary target LLMs using only input prompts and visible final responses. We propose Final-Output Preference Learning (FOPL), which trains a single reconstruction model that generalizes to unseen LLMs without target-specific adaptation. To achieve this, the reconstruction model must learn which reasoning patterns match a given final response without knowing the target LLM's identity. We address this using preference optimization, training the reconstruction model to prefer native CoTs over synthetic alternatives for the same question and final response. By learning these preferences from LLMs with accessible CoTs, the reconstruction model learns to distinguish reasoning patterns based on visible responses. Experiments show that reconstructed CoTs capture distinct reasoning patterns across LLM families, including a family unseen during training. Moreover, students trained on reconstructed CoTs match or outperform those trained on native CoTs across several reasoning benchmarks.
authors: Hongli Shen, Shaopeng Fu, Qinbo Zhang, Jian Li, Di Wang
bullets: Addresses model-agnostic reconstruction of hidden reasoning without target-specific attacker training.
Uses preference optimization to favor native CoTs over synthetic alternatives sharing the same prompt and final response.
Learns reasoning-pattern preferences from models with accessible CoTs, without identifying the target LLM.
Reconstructed CoTs capture distinct patterns across LLM families, including one unseen during training.
Students trained on reconstructed CoTs match or outperform those trained on native CoTs across several reasoning benchmarks.

papers.title: Learning Teacher Output Preferences from Final Responses for Reasoning Distillation
papers.tldr: FOPL reconstructs hidden chain-of-thought from prompts and final answers with one model that generalizes across unseen LLMs.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models enable streaming synthesis chunk by chunk, yet invoking the large model for every chunk remains costly. While chunk-level speculative decoding can offload chunks to a lightweight draft model, existing approaches suffer from two limitations: (1) an off-the-shelf draft diverges from the target's trajectory, compounding errors in history; and (2) they either omit verification or rely on costly post-decode aesthetic scores rather than verifying consistency against the target. We address both with Draft Forcing, a framework coupling target-guided drafting with an on-policy trained verifier. Specifically, to align the draft for high acceptance, we opt for feature-level drafting, conditioning it on multi-layer target hidden states persisted from committed chunks, whose outputs are pushed to match target trajectories with multi-aspect losses. For verification, we propose an on-policy trained feature-space verifier predicting CDF-calibrated frame-wise relative RMSE against the target. It is trained on speculative rollouts as contexts anneal from random to inference-aligned mixtures, and gates proposals without VAE decoding. On the 14B Self-Forcing target, Draft Forcing achieves $1.63\times$ DiT and $1.57\times$ end-to-end speedups on VBench with minimal quality loss, and up to $1.93\times$ DiT ($1.82\times$ end-to-end) when combined with orthogonal KV compression. It generalizes to accelerate a streaming variant of MiniMax-H3, generating over $50\%$ draft frames with competitive quality.
authors: Chenkai Xu, Yuji Ren, Zihui Liu, Yijie Jin, Yuhao Shen, Xin Wang, Yajing Chen, Keyang Luo, Shengju Qian, Litong Gong, Tiezheng Ge, Zhijie Deng
bullets: Addresses draft-model divergence and expensive or target-inconsistent verification in chunk-level speculative decoding.
Conditions feature-level drafts on multi-layer hidden states from committed target chunks and trains them toward the target trajectory.
Uses an on-policy verifier to predict calibrated frame-wise relative error and gate proposals in feature space.
On a 14B Self-Forcing target, reports 1.63× DiT and 1.57× end-to-end speedups with minimal quality loss.
Reaches up to 1.93× DiT and 1.82× end-to-end speedups with KV compression, and generalizes to MiniMax-H3 by drafting over 50% of frames.

papers.selection_reason: Focuses on autoregressive video generation using speculative decoding (drafting and verification). This directly addresses the Video Generation and Understanding topic, specifically autoregressive video models.
papers.title: Draft Forcing: Target-guided Speculative Drafting and Learned Verifier for Autoregressive Video Generation
papers.tldr: Draft Forcing accelerates autoregressive video generation by using target-guided feature drafting and a learned verifier to accept reliable speculative chunks without costly decoding.

papers.abstract: Distilling localization knowledge into compact detection transformers (DETRs) requires consistent teacher-student query correspondence across decoder layers. However, in DETRs with encoder-based query selection, the teacher and student select top-K proposals independently. Same-rank queries can originate from different spatial locations and correspond to different objects, making rank-based layer-wise supervision unreliable. To address this problem, we propose Trajectory-Aligned Encoder-Decoder Distillation (TAED), a framework for knowledge transfer between DETRs of different capacities. Encoder feature distillation matches normalized multi-scale features to strengthen student representations and increase the number of teacher-student query pairs from the same encoder locations. Source-indexed query alignment pairs native queries from the same encoder locations and retains pairs associated with the same object for which the teacher provides reliable and more accurate final localization than the student. Trajectory-aligned localization distillation maintains these correspondences and uses teacher proposals and corresponding decoder-layer box predictions to guide student refinement, without introducing additional queries. On COCO, TAED improves DINO-R18 and two-stage Deformable DETR-R18 by 2.5 and 1.7 AP, respectively. Further gains on D-FINE and ECDet demonstrate applicability to recent real-time DETRs at no additional inference cost.
authors: Zilong He, Zhangchi Hu, Hebei Li, Yijun Pan, Yifan Zhao, Xiangyu Yu, Yansong Peng, Xinghao Wang, Dongsheng Jiang, Xiaoyan Sun
bullets: Addresses unreliable rank-based supervision caused by independently selected top-K proposals in teacher and student DETRs.
Distills normalized multi-scale encoder features to improve student representations and increase shared-location query matches.
Aligns native queries by source encoder index and keeps pairs where the teacher offers more accurate localization for the same object.
Transfers teacher proposal and decoder-layer box trajectories to guide student refinement without adding queries.
Improves DINO-R18 by 2.5 AP and two-stage Deformable DETR-R18 by 1.7 AP on COCO; also applies to D-FINE and ECDet without extra inference cost.

This concept of aligning latent trajectories is highly transferable to World Models (Latent Action Models) and Embodied AI (memory/trajectory understanding).
papers.title: TAED: Trajectory-Aligned Encoder--Decoder Distillation for Detection Transformers
papers.tldr: TAED improves compact DETR detectors by aligning teacher–student queries through shared encoder locations and decoder trajectories for more reliable localization distillation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a powerful approach for improving language-model reasoning, but its supervision is inherently sparse: a sequence-level verifier reward is propagated only through sampled trajectories and provides no direct signal for alternative actions. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a complementary form of supervision by providing dense teacher feedback over the full next-token distribution, but this signal is not grounded in verified task outcomes. Simply co-optimizing the two objectives does not couple these signals: verifier feedback remains sparse and does not inform the dense teacher supervision. We introduce Verifiable On-Policy Distillation (VOPD), which transfers sparse verifier feedback into dense, verifier-grounded supervision. Our key observation is that the implicit-reward view of OPD places teacher supervision and verifier feedback in a common reward space while retaining a reward signal available for every next-token action. Under this view, VOPD projects verifier preference onto the teacher's implicit-reward direction and Rao--Blackwellizes the resulting signal over the full vocabulary, propagating verifier-grounded supervision to actions that were never sampled. The resulting objective can also be interpreted as adaptively extrapolating the distillation target according to teacher--verifier agreement. Across two teacher--student configurations and eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VOPD consistently improves both final performance and learning efficiency over vanilla OPD and other on-policy distillation baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/juntongshi48/VOPD.
authors: Juntong Shi, Stefano Ermon, Jure Leskovec, Minkai Xu
bullets: RLVR rewards only sampled trajectories, while on-policy distillation provides dense teacher feedback that is not tied to verified outcomes.
VOPD combines both signals in a shared implicit-reward space and projects verifier preferences onto the teacher’s reward direction.
Rao–Blackwellization propagates this verifier-grounded signal across the full vocabulary, including unsampled actions.
The method adaptively extrapolates distillation targets based on teacher–verifier agreement.
Across two teacher–student settings and eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VOPD improves final performance and learning efficiency over vanilla OPD and other on-policy baselines.

(C) VOPD projects verifier preference onto the teacher’s implicit-reward direction, then Rao–Blackwellizes the resulting signal over hypothetical next-token actions to obtain dense, verifier-grounded supervision across full vocabulary.

papers.abstract: In video temporal grounding, a correct interval can come from finding the event, answering blind or fitting one annotation style, and Recall at IoU scores them alike. We measure evidence dependence, how much the answer rests on the event's frames. Our fixed-answer audit edits either the frames inside the annotated interval or, as a placebo, as many frames elsewhere in the same video, and compares the two drops in the annotated answer's likelihood. Supervised fine-tuning and three public checkpoints trained with IoU-reward reinforcement learning raise the accuracy of Qwen2.5-VL-7B by 9 to 20 points, partly by answering blind and by fitting one annotation. Yet their answers rest on the event no more than the base model's, and the same holds for IoU-reward training on our data at the audit's frame rate. This comparison is a difference of the model's own likelihoods, so we can train on it. A placebo contrast and a bound on the placebo drop rule out learning to react to any edit. With them, evidence dependence rises in all five base models we train, and the weight on clean supervision controls how much. Added to IoU-reward training, the objective raises evidence dependence while keeping the accuracy gain. Masking the event's frames makes the trained models decline or miss the event more often than their base; masking as many other frames does not. The dependence moves to another event when the query names it, and holds on a second dataset and under patch scrambling, an edit never used in training.
authors: Zijie Jin, Shuai Zhao, Haoran Tao, Chaomin Huang, Liwen Luo
bullets: Introduces an evidence-dependence audit comparing likelihood drops after editing frames inside the annotated interval versus an equal number of frames elsewhere.
Finds that supervised fine-tuning and IoU-reward reinforcement learning improve accuracy but do not increase reliance on event frames.
Uses a placebo contrast and a bound on placebo effects to train models against generic edit sensitivity.
Evidence-dependence training increases reliance on relevant frames across five base models, while preserving IoU-reward accuracy gains.
The effect transfers to other queried events, a second dataset, and patch scrambling not seen during training.

figures.caption: Figure 5: The placebo-controlled models respond to the query and to the evidence. (a) Each point gives a model’s change from its base (mask, nats per token) in the partner contrast, the drop when the event’s frames are masked minus the drop when a partner event’s frames are, with the event’s own query (horizontal) and with the partner’s (vertical). Marker shape gives the base (circle Qwen-7B, square TimeZero, triangle Time-R1, inverted triangle VideoChat-R1); half-filled markers were evaluated text-first, with the query before the video. (b) The tick shows how often a model answers There are none. to a query about this video, and the marker how often it does so for one about another video. (c) Each row gives the change from the base in the evidence share, the fraction of the accuracy under the placebo mask that the evidence mask removes, with its 95% interval.

Figure 1: Accuracy and evidence dependence are separate axes. Left: the audit scores the same correct answer, the annotated interval y⋆, with the event’s frames masked (xE) and with as many frames masked elsewhere, the placebo (xO). The schematic bars show the two drops in the answer’s log-likelihood, dE and dO , and their difference ψ for three kinds of model. Right: each point places one post-trained model by its change from its own base (the origin) in R@0.5 (horizontal) and in evidence dependence Γ, the change in ψ (vertical), with R@0.5 on the full test split and Γ on the first 200 test questions; lines are 95% intervals. The grey band is the audit’s resolution, the farthest from zero that the 95% interval of Γ reaches between two seeds of one recipe (Section 2). Accuracy-oriented training (dark grey) moves models right but not out of the band; SFT, IoU-GRPO and mDPO-style are trained from Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and the public checkpoints (open diamonds) are compared with it. The placebo-controlled objective (green) moves them up. Marker shape gives the base model, its several points differ in α or β, and light-filled points use the smaller β=0.03 (Section 4).

Figure 2: Part of the added accuracy comes from answering blind or fitting one annotation; Γ keeps its sign under both label sets. (a) shows, for all-black videos under Time-R1’s prompt template, the fraction of questions still given an interval (open circles) and answered correctly (dots); the dashed line is a fixed (0, 10) s window on the real videos, and green rows are our placebo-controlled Qwen models at weight α. (b) scores each model on the questions annotated in both Charades-STA and TimeLens against each label set; the two rankings of the nine 7B configurations barely agree (Spearman 0.15). Open diamonds are public checkpoints; open grey circles are the Qwen2.5-VL-7B base (Qwen-7B); thin lines are our 7B models (green) and SFT (dark grey); thick lines are TimeLens-8B (dark) and our adapter of it trained on the original labels (green). (c) gives Γ (mask, nats per token, first 200 test questions) with 95% intervals for each label set as the fixed answer (filled: Charades-STA; open: TimeLens), with the audit’s resolution as a grey band; the TimeLens-8B SFT row has only the TimeLens value.

Figure 6: On each question, the audit scores one fixed answer while editing either the evidence frames or as many other frames. The annotated answer y⋆ and the query q are held fixed and scored by teacher forcing. Editing the frames inside the annotated interval gives xE ; editing as many frames outside it with the same operator gives the placebo xO . The drops of the answer’s log-likelihood under the two edits are dE and dO , and ψ = dE − dO . The figure shows one mask draw; the audit averages dO over three draws. The right panel shows how a trained model is compared with its base: Γ is the mean trained-minus-base change in ψ over H∩, the questions both models localise on the clean video (IoU ≥ 0.5), and the trained model’s placebo drop dO is reported next to it, under the mask and the swap operator.

Figure 7: Two models give the same correct interval for different reasons. Panels (a) and (b) each show a test question on which the Qwen2.5-VL-7B base and its placebo-controlled model (α=0.5) predict the same interval, with IoU above 0.7. The top rows show the native frames with the annotated ones outlined, followed by the annotated interval and both predictions. The bars below give the drop in the answer’s log-likelihood (nats per token) when the evidence frames are swapped out and when as many frames outside the interval are swapped the same way. In (a), for the same correct interval, the base loses 0.06 nats per token under the evidence swap and its trained model 3.81, with placebo drops of 0.11 and 0.00.

Figure 8: The placebo-controlled objective scores each training pair on the clean video and on both edits. The trainable model and the frozen base score the fixed annotated answer on the clean video x, the evidence edit xE and the placebo edit xO . Their log-likelihood differences rθ enter the evidence margin and the placebo contrast, the placebo drops of both models enter the placebo bound, and the total loss adds clean supervision to the operator losses (Equations 3–4).

Figure 10: The query-crossed design scores the same answer under the question’s own query and under a partner event’s query. Both conditions score the annotated interval of event A and use the same two edits: masking A’s frames, or masking the frames of a partner event B of the same video. Only the query changes, from A’s own to B’s. A model that reads the query shows a contrast that reverses under B’s query; a model that responds to edits at the answer’s timestamps shows the same contrast under both queries. The bars are schematic; Figure 5a and Table 16 give the measurements.

Figure 11: On QVHighlights, the placebo-controlled models keep a positive Γ (mask) while SFT stays at zero, and the placebo-controlled TimeZero model answers far fewer black videos than its base. (a) Each Charades-trained model is placed by its paired change in R@0.5 on QVHighlights (horizontal) and its Γ (mask) (vertical), with 95% intervals; the grey band marks the out-of-domain accuracy resolution (Appendix A.1). Qwen-7B is Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Green points are placebo-controlled models, trained at β=0.1 unless the label gives β; the β=0.03 model uses α=0.5. (b) For each base model on Charades-STA (STA) and QVHighlights (QVH), the black-video answer rate of the base (open) is set against that of its placebo-controlled model at α=0.5 (filled); squares are TimeZero and circles Qwen-7B.

Figure 9: Evidence dependence grows throughout training; SFT’s stays within the audit’s resolution from the start. Checkpoints are taken every 50 steps (400 pairs) of one placebo-controlled run (α=0.5, β=0.1) and of two SFT runs from Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and each checkpoint is audited against the base. (a) The curves give Γ (mask) with 95% intervals, and the grey band marks the audit’s resolution. (b) The curves give the trained model’s placebo drop on the same questions, and the dashed line marks the base’s.

Figure 3: The placebo contrast, and then the bound, bring the trained model’s own placebo drop back to the base’s. The left panel plots, for objectives trained from Qwen2.5-VL-7B on the same pairs and audited on the same questions, the trained model’s evidence drop dE and own placebo drop dO under masking (nats per token), from the base (top) to the full objective at α=0.5 (bottom); the dashed line is the base’s placebo drop.

Figure 4: Evidence dependence falls with the weight on clean supervision; the accuracy change depends on the base. The top row shows Γ (mask, nats per token, first 200 test questions) and the bottom row the change in R@0.5 from the model’s own base (points, full test split), with 95% intervals. (a) Each column plots one base against α at β=0.1; TimeLens-8B is built on Qwen3-VL, and the grey band is the audit’s resolution. (b) plots Qwen2.5-VL-7B at α=0.5 against β, with SFT at β → 0.

Each row pairs a model with its base: our trained models, the three public checkpoints against the Qwen2.5-VL-7B base (the pairs of Table 1), and TimeLens-8B against Qwen3-VL-8B. The columns give the clean-video negative log-likelihood (NLL) of the annotated answer in nats per token for the base and the trained model, then Γ (mask), its sign fraction (the fraction of H∩ on which ψ rises) and Γc, the change in the bounded index c = (dE − dO)/(|dE |+ |dO|+ 0.05), with its 95% interval. Under the mask, SFT and IoU-GRPO lose a smaller share. Each block compares a trained model with its base on the same 1,000 questions, edited frames and placebo draws. The first six columns give R@0.5 on the clean video, with the evidence frames (E) or as many frames outside the interval (O) masked or swapped, and on all-black versions of these questions. The ∆ columns give trained-minus-base changes in points in two readouts (Appendix D.4). Table 16: The audited contrast moves with the query: Γspec is positive in every placebo-controlled model and zero in SFT. All values use the mask operator and are in nats per token; Appendix D.2 defines them. In every table, brackets give 95% bootstrap intervals over videos unless its caption says otherwise.

Γ (mask) is in nats per token on the first 200 test questions, over all of H∩ and over the part of H∩ on which the trained model still returns an interval when the evidence frames are masked in its regenerated answers, with 95% intervals over videos. Each model is paired with its base re-run on the same software stack, whose R@0.5 on the full test split heads each block. The TimeZero entry for the annotated interval is that of Table 3; every other entry is a re-run, paired with its base re-run on the same software stack. Brackets give 95% intervals over videos.

Qwen2.5-VL-7B models on the 600 new questions, each paired with its base re-run on the same software stack. papers.tldr: Accuracy alone can hide blind or annotation-fitting behavior, so the paper measures and trains models to rely on the event evidence in video temporal grounding.

papers.abstract: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) aims to categorize unlabeled data from both known and unknown classes using labeled data from only the known classes. While recent GCD methods have shown promise on static images, their performance degrades in videos due to temporal dynamics, larger intra-class variation, and the lack of temporal consistency in existing approaches. We introduce VideoGCD, a framework tailored for video action recognition under the GCD setting. Our method integrates (i) a partitioned Mixture-of-Experts module that encourages specialization for known and novel categories, (ii) a novel-class balancing loss to reduce bias toward known classes, and (iii) a temporal optimal transport loss that promotes consistent routing across frames. Experiments on three video benchmarks demonstrate that VideoGCD significantly improves performance over existing GCD methods, particularly on novel categories. Our findings highlight the importance of combining temporal modeling and expert specialization for video GCD.
authors: Bardia Safaei, Vishal M. Patel
bullets: Addresses video GCD, where temporal dynamics, greater intra-class variation, and weak temporal consistency hurt recognition.
Uses a partitioned Mixture-of-Experts module to specialize processing for known and novel categories.
Introduces a novel-class balancing loss to reduce bias toward known classes.
Applies temporal optimal transport to encourage consistent expert routing across video frames.
Experiments on three video benchmarks show improved performance over existing GCD methods, especially for novel categories.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the proposed VideoGCD framework for Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) in video action recognition. Frameglobal representations (g1, gt, gT ) are obtained via temporal pooling and routed through the MoE module, which consists of known and novel experts. The router predicts expert assignment probabilities, and each expert applies low-rank adapters (Ue, Ve) for parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Three auxiliary losses are used: (i) Balancing Loss promotes uniform expert usage, (ii) Novel-Class Balancing Loss ensures sufficient learning signal for novel-class experts, and (iii) Temporal OT Loss enforces consistent expert assignments across frames. The updated representations are integrated back into the transformer backbone. For simplicity, LoRA fine-tuning on the multi-head attention modules is not shown.

papers.tldr: VideoGCD adapts generalized category discovery to videos by combining expert specialization, novel-class balancing, and temporally consistent frame routing.

papers.abstract: Physics-based human-object interaction (HOI) has enabled multiple characters to cooperatively transport objects, but existing cooperative controllers largely assume homogeneous embodiments and predefined interaction tasks. We ask whether a single physics-based policy can enable cooperation across diverse embodiments, team compositions, and interaction skills. We present MorphHOI, a decentralised framework built on a key insight: effective heterogeneous cooperation requires a unified representation across embodiments while accounting for differences in their physical capabilities. To realise this insight, we introduce a canonical body interface that unifies observation and action spaces, together with an embodiment-conditioned transformer that adapts cooperative decisions to the physical capabilities of each agent and its teammates. To extend cooperation to new interaction skills, we reuse the learned cooperative policy through task-specific tokens and lightweight adaptation, preserving its original capabilities. Our framework achieves success rates of up to 96.7\% on seen embodiments, 95.6\% on unseen embodiments, and 91.4\% on novel payloads. Furthermore, the learned cooperation extends to diverse interaction skills with high success rates, including box carrying, transport on stairs, and waypoint following, while preserving previously acquired cooperative capabilities.
authors: Zhihao Cao, Tianxu An, Chenhao Li, Chenyangguang Zhang, Stelian Coros, Marco Hutter
bullets: Addresses the limitation of prior cooperative controllers that assume homogeneous agents and predefined tasks.
Uses a canonical body interface to unify observations and actions across different embodiments.
Applies an embodiment-conditioned transformer to account for each agent’s physical capabilities and teammates.
Extends the policy to new skills using task-specific tokens and lightweight adaptation while preserving prior abilities.
Reports success rates up to 96.7% on seen embodiments, 95.6% on unseen embodiments, and 91.4% on novel payloads, including box carrying, stairs, and waypoint following.

papers.selection_reason: Single physics-based policy for heterogeneous cooperative human-object interaction; relevant to embodied robot learning.
papers.title: One Policy, Many Bodies: Cooperative Human-Object Interaction with Heterogeneous Teams
papers.tldr: MorphHOI enables one decentralized physics-based policy to coordinate heterogeneous teams across embodiments, payloads, and interaction skills.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot embodied systems are typically designed to collaborate by coordinating actions, sharing trajectories, or learning joint policies. We ask a complementary question: can collaboration emerge before decision-making, by first building a shared understanding of the environment? We introduce Shared Environmental Understanding, a policy-agnostic representation that aggregates partial egocentric observations from multiple robots into a shared latent world model. This shifts collaboration from the policy space to the representation space, enabling decentralized decision-making with shared environmental context. To this end, we propose Shared Environment Encoding and Retrieval (SEER), a framework that organizes multi-robot observations into a shared memory, retrieves relevant context via spatio-temporal similarity, and encodes it using a predictive latent world model. The resulting representations are injected into downstream navigation agents as tokens. Experimental results demonstrate that SEER captures action-relevant environmental structure and consistently improves navigation performance across both specialized VLN agents and general vision-language model agents, while preserving single-agent capabilities.
authors: Haihong Hao, Lei Chen, Mingfei Han, Chenglong Yan, Dong An, Yuqiang Yang, Changlin Li, Minghao Guo, Salman Khan, Xiaojun Chang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coordinating robots without requiring shared policies or coordinated actions.
Aggregates partial egocentric observations into a shared environmental understanding for decentralized navigation.
Stores observations in shared memory, retrieves relevant spatio-temporal context, and encodes it with a predictive latent world model.
Injects the resulting shared representations as tokens into downstream navigation agents.
Improves navigation across specialized VLN and general vision-language agents while preserving single-agent capabilities.

papers.tldr: SEER enables multi-robot collaboration by sharing a predictive latent representation of the environment before decisions are made.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual perception and language understanding from vision-language models (VLMs) with action prediction for robotic manipulation. Although multi-view observations provide complementary scene information, VLMs model cross-view interactions based on 2D feature similarity, which can lead to physical inconsistency in the form of cross-view incorrect association between distinct entities and cross-view information fragmentation about the same entity. To address these challenges, we propose ConsisX, a novel VLA framework that integrates cross-view association and entity coherence to enable cross-view consistency thinking in 3D for physically consistent robotic manipulation. Specifically, Cross-View Association Modeling (CAM) is proposed to introduce cross-view spatial proximity constraints in a shared 3D space to reduce cross-view incorrect association. Entity Coherence Organization (ECO) is designed to organize cross-view local information into coherent 3D entity evidence, thereby addressing cross-view information fragmentation. Consistent Action Conditioning (CAC) is introduced to condition action prediction on task-relevant 3D entity evidence for cross-view consistent action execution. Experiments on 3 real-world manipulation tasks and 4 simulation benchmarks establish ConsisX as an effective and competitive framework for robotic manipulation.
authors: Yunhe Zhang, Long Gao, Yuedong Fu, Gang He, Li Xu, Chang Wu, Pengyu Li
bullets: Addresses incorrect cross-view associations and fragmented information about the same entity caused by 2D feature-based interactions.
Uses Cross-View Association Modeling to impose spatial proximity constraints in a shared 3D space.
Uses Entity Coherence Organization to combine local observations into coherent 3D entity evidence.
Uses Consistent Action Conditioning to guide actions with task-relevant, cross-view-consistent 3D evidence.
Evaluated on 3 real-world manipulation tasks and 4 simulation benchmarks, where it is reported as effective and competitive.

papers.tldr: ConsisX improves vision-language-action models for robotic manipulation by enforcing physically consistent reasoning across multi-view observations in 3D.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can localize through their text interface, grounding open-vocabulary objects, complex referring expressions, text lines and layout regions with strong semantic understanding. They write the boxes one after another as a single sequence, although the instances of a query, unlike the words of a sentence, form an unordered set with no sequential dependence. The number of decoding steps therefore grows with the number of instances, which makes dense scenes the most expensive. Decoding the instances in parallel avoids this growth, but streams that cannot see each other duplicate some instances and miss others. We propose \method, which writes a single point into each query as a spatial anchor and asks for the matching instance nearest to that point within a local radius, or \none. Given the image, the anchored queries are independent, so they are decoded in parallel as leaves of a prefix tree that shares the image and the query, and the model is trained on the same tree. Coarse-to-fine anchors refine only the regions where instances are found, duplicate suppression keeps one box per instance, and set-level reinforcement learning optimizes the set F1. Only the prompt and the attention mask change, not the architecture. On three different VLMs and 12 benchmarks covering detection, OCR, layout and referring, \method is at most 5.5 F1 below sequential decoding trained on the same data, while its speedup grows with instance density and reaches 21.9$\times$ on dense scenes.
authors: Shuxuan Li, Jialiang Kang, Yanghao Zhou, Ziye Zhu, Zhilin Zhao, Xiao Yang
bullets: Sequentially grounding unordered object instances is inefficient because decoding steps grow with scene density.
Each query receives a spatial anchor; the model finds the nearest matching instance within a local radius or returns none.
Anchored queries are decoded independently in a shared prefix tree, with coarse-to-fine refinement and duplicate suppression.
Set-level reinforcement learning optimizes set F1 without changing the model architecture.
Across three VLMs and 12 detection, OCR, layout, and referring benchmarks, performance is at most 5.5 F1 below matched sequential decoding.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces PinGround for parallel grounding in VLMs using spatial anchors. This advances Multimodal Foundation Models by improving spatial reasoning and grounding efficiency.
papers.title: PinGround: Pinning Queries to Points for Parallel Grounding in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: PinGround enables parallel VLM grounding by anchoring each query to spatial points, achieving near-sequential accuracy with up to 21.9× speedup in dense scenes.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically rely on vision-language model (VLM) features as the primary perceptual source for action prediction, showing strong generalization across diverse robotic manipulation tasks. Although VLM features can identify which entities are relevant to action prediction, precise manipulation also requires understanding where task-relevant entities are located within the spatial layout, how their geometric structure constrains physical interaction, and when spatial or geometric information should make a greater contribution to action prediction. To this end, we introduce {\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}}-VLA to organize VLA perception and action prediction around which, where, how, and when. Specifically, {\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}}-VLA retains VLM-based semantic entity perception which and further introduces spatial distance perception where and geometric structure perception how with adaptive spatial-geometric guidance when to enrich the perceptual information available for action prediction. Experiments across real-world settings and simulation benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and superior performance of {\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}}-VLA.
authors: Yunhe Zhang, Long Gao, Yuedong Fu, Gang He, Li Xu, Chang Wu, Songyuheng Gao
bullets: VLM features identify which entities matter, but may lack information about their location and physical structure.
The framework organizes perception around which, where, how, and when.
It adds spatial distance perception and geometric structure perception to semantic entity understanding.
An adaptive spatial-geometric guidance mechanism determines when these cues should influence action prediction.
Experiments in real-world and simulated settings demonstrate its effectiveness and superior performance.

papers.abstract: Recent work has sought to localize the internal mechanisms underlying visual reasoning skills in vision-language models. These methods largely overlook separability and composability in both mechanism identification and evaluation. We propose separability and composability as two important desiderata for skill localization. Separability requires identified mechanisms to contribute primarily to their target skills while having limited effects on other skills, enabling precise diagnosis and targeted intervention. Composability requires skill mechanisms to be combinable to support complex tasks, allowing a small set of mechanisms to account for broader capabilities. In this work, we propose a multi-skill interpretability framework DISCO, built around these two properties. For identification, we propose Separable Head Selection, which selects skill-specific attention heads based on their contributions across skills. For evaluation, we are the first to design metrics for measuring separability and composability of identified heads. Extensive experiments on three VLMs and four fundamental visual reasoning skills demonstrate the effectiveness of DISCO. It achieves the highest separability, outperforming the strongest baseline by 24.80, 18.38, and 13.75 points across the three models, respectively, while also achieving the highest composability on all three models.
authors: Miaoyu Li, Boyang Li
bullets: Existing skill-localization methods largely overlook whether mechanisms are separable across skills and composable for complex tasks.
DISCO introduces a multi-skill interpretability framework centered on separability and composability.
Separable Head Selection identifies attention heads that contribute primarily to their target skills.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) is a fundamental task in multimedia understanding, where state-of-the-art methods have achieved prominent success relying on the assumption of complete, well-aligned multimodal inputs. However, real-world unconstrained scenarios often suffer from unpredictable modality degradation and information loss, leading to catastrophic performance collapse of existing MER models that heavily depend on facial cues as the core inference anchor. However, few systematic works evaluate model robustness under diverse, fine-grained incomplete settings, as prior works are limited to coarse-grained full-modality removal and neglect interpretable analysis of emotional reasoning. To bridge this gap, we formally define the Incomplete Multimodal Emotion Recognition (IMER) task, which benchmarks model generalization and robustness under multi-grained modality and emotional information loss. We further construct MIME, a dedicated IMER benchmark with 2,000 video segments covering realistic fine-grained facial-detail degradation, severe facial degradation, and extreme full-modality loss, surpassing the limited coarse-grained settings of prior works. We also propose the Chain of Emotion (CoE) analysis paradigm with tailored metrics to dissect the fine-grained emotional cue perception and reasoning process of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Extensive experiments on seven mainstream MLLMs reveal that body language and scene context act as critical compensatory mechanisms under facial degradation, while a pronounced gap exists between models' basic visual perception ability and high-level cognitive reasoning. Our work provides a focused evaluation platform and actionable insights for advancing robust multimodal emotion recognition. Our dataset and code are public at https://yuxinokk.github.io/MIME.
authors: Yuxin Jia, Xing Lan, Wensong Wang, Jian Xue, Feiliang Ren, Ke Lu

Proposes Chain of Emotion (CoE) analysis and tailored metrics to examine emotional-cue perception and reasoning in MLLMs.
Experiments with seven mainstream MLLMs show that body language and scene context can compensate for degraded facial information.
Finds a gap between basic visual perception and higher-level emotional reasoning; dataset and code are publicly available.

papers.abstract: AI agents accumulate conversations, images, and documents through long-term interactions with users. Answering later questions often requires connecting evidence across these records, yet the resulting understanding is rarely retained, allowing mistakes to recur on related questions. Existing multimodal memory methods largely focus on storing and retrieving records, with limited mechanisms for learning from completed tasks and consolidating task-specific experience. We therefore propose MMMem, a task-aware multimodal memory framework that extracts and consolidates experience from completed tasks through four complementary strategies. First, source-linked multi-view memory organizes original text, images, and rendered pages alongside generated scene images that combine clues across records for retrieval. Second, source-generated tasks support knowledge alignment at two levels: warm-up consolidates source knowledge into task-relevant experiences in external memory, while self-training adapts the model's parametric knowledge to task demands. Third, the same vision-language model distills completed tasks into experiences that record the task context, conclusion, and support links. Finally, task-aware retrieval recalls source views and relevant experiences for answering and verification, while source-supported reuse guides long-term retention. Across three memory benchmarks and two vision-language readers, MMMem outperforms eight baselines. With Qwen3.5-9B, MMMem achieves relative gains of 36.9%, 17.6%, and 15.2% over the best-performing baselines on LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2, respectively. Ablations show consistent gains from training and memory warm-up, while case studies illustrate how individual components work in practice.
authors: Yuxuan Chen, Changwei Lv, Yunfei Li, Zhongjing Du, Kehui Tan, Zijun Liao, Ruochong Zheng, Hao Chen, Can Deng, Zheni Zeng, Chang Liu, Jie Chen
bullets: Addresses the problem of agents storing multimodal records without retaining task-level understanding, causing repeated mistakes.
Uses source-linked multi-view memory for text, images, rendered pages, and cross-record scene images.
Combines source-generated task warm-up, self-training, and task distillation into experiences containing context, conclusions, and supporting links.
Task-aware retrieval supports answering, verification, and evidence-backed long-term reuse.
Outperforms eight baselines across LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2; ablations show benefits from training and memory warm-up.

papers.abstract: Adversarial object attacks pose a threat to BEV-based 3D object detectors in autonomous driving. Existing attacks typically target a single modality, coordinate camera and LiDAR observations at the current timestamp, or model temporal persistence mainly in camera streams. Without a unified construction of current and historical observations, attacks can leave part of the detector's accumulated evidence unsuppressed, limiting their effectiveness. In this paper, we propose AdvMTO, a 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) framework for suppressing detection of persistent adversarial objects. Its oriented surfels encode appearance, geometry, and opacity in one object state, from which camera images and scanline LiDAR returns are generated. AdvMTO then constructs current and historical inputs through detector-native processing, regenerating LiDAR returns in each native source sweep for fusion detectors. We optimize bounded appearance perturbations for each detector, propagating gradients through historical BEV memory for temporal camera detectors. For fusion detectors, bounded geometry refinement along local normals further perturbs both sensing modalities. Experiments on nuScenes demonstrate effective suppression of traffic-cone detection across three BEV detectors. Temporal ablations further highlight the importance of detector-native history modeling for both attack construction and optimization.
authors: Zhiyang Cui, Hao Tan, Ruonan Li, Shibin Wu, Junjian Zhang, Hong'an Lin, Zhaoquan Gu
bullets: Targets a gap in attacks that fail to jointly suppress current and historical camera–LiDAR evidence.
Represents objects with oriented surfels encoding appearance, geometry, and opacity, enabling camera and scanline LiDAR generation.
Builds detector-native current and historical inputs, including native-source LiDAR sweeps and temporal BEV memory.
Optimizes bounded appearance perturbations, with additional local-normal geometry refinement for fusion detectors.
Experiments on nuScenes show effective traffic-cone suppression across three BEV detectors; temporal ablations emphasize native history modeling.

papers.abstract: Post-training large language models routinely pools reasoning trajectories from diverse teachers or algorithms, yet it remains unclear whether standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can learn such heterogeneous strategies without explicit mode conditioning. We study the learnability and local bottlenecks of heterogeneous reasoning through a formal mixture formulation and controlled experiments. We first formalize the representational compatibility of the optimal autoregressive model with latent reasoning mixtures: the target next-token distribution weights modes by their prefix posteriors and concentrates on a single mode once alternative modes assign negligible likelihood to the prefix. In a verifiable symbolic graph-search environment with paired breadth-first and depth-first search trajectories, no consistent disadvantage is observed for unlabeled mixed SFT relative to homogeneous or labeled baselines under matched token budgets while preserving both modes. Scaling across 0.6B--14B models and data budgets largely eliminates global mode confusion, shifting the primary bottleneck to local state-tracking transitions. Because a local mistake affects the final outcome only when subsequent reasoning is sensitive to that step, we find that only a small fraction of local errors are outcome-determining \emph{Critical Reasoning Nodes (CRNs)}, and that single-step repairs at these nodes rescue failing trajectories across symbolic search and natural language benchmarks whenever the model has sufficient downstream competence to complete the remaining derivation. Our environment is open-sourced at https://github.com/Bowen1911/Symbolic_graph_env.
authors: Sunbowen Li, Dandan Song, Shengkun Ma, Xuanning Cao
bullets: Formalizes how an autoregressive model represents mixtures of latent reasoning modes using prefix-dependent mode posteriors.

Defines Critical Reasoning Nodes (CRNs) as the small fraction of local errors that determine outcomes; repairing them can rescue failed trajectories when downstream competence is sufficient.
The symbolic graph-search environment is open-sourced; results also extend to natural-language benchmarks.

papers.abstract: A UAV that flies without GNSS has to estimate its absolute position and heading without any external signal. Most existing methods for UAV-to-satellite cross-view geo-localization (U-S CVGL) treat the task as image retrieval: they compress the UAV image and each satellite tile into separate descriptors, rank the tiles by their similarity, and return the center of the best tile. The output can therefore only lie on a pre-defined grid, its accuracy is limited by the tile size, and no heading is produced. Regressing the pose in a single pass removes the grid, but it leaves no chance to correct the estimate afterwards. We observe that satellite tiles are not independent samples. They are laid on the map at a fixed spacing, scale and orientation, so neighboring tiles join into one continuous satellite block with a consistent metric, and a nadir UAV view of that block differs from it by a planar rigid transform only, i.e. a 2D translation plus an in-plane rotation. We therefore reformulate U-S CVGL as solving for this transform between two images of different sizes. Position and heading then become parts of one geometric quantity, and the accuracy is no longer limited by the tile grid. We propose RigidAnchor, which solves the transform iteratively. The network encodes the two images and builds a multi-level correlation pyramid between them. At each iteration, it indexes the pyramid with every aerial cell carried through the current estimate, pools the descriptors of all cells into one hidden state, and lets two decoupled heads predict a translation increment and a rotation increment, the latter being composed rather than added. On Bearing-UAV-90K, the cross-view mean errors are 78.6% lower in position and 69.7% lower in heading than Bearing-UAV, and HSR@15 increases by 19.06 points. Code is available at https://github.com/wwsource/RigidAnchor.
authors: Bo Wang, Dekang Zhu, Jian Li, Zhipeng Meng, Bo Wang, Dewen Hu
bullets: Addresses GNSS-denied UAV localization, where retrieval methods are grid-limited and typically do not estimate heading.
Models a nadir UAV view and a continuous satellite-image block as related by a 2D translation and in-plane rotation.
Uses a multi-level correlation pyramid and iterative updates, with separate translation and composed rotation prediction heads.
On Bearing-UAV-90K, reports 78.6% lower position error, 69.7% lower heading error, and a 19.06-point HSR@15 increase versus Bearing-UAV.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of RigidAnchor. A UAV view Iu and the satellite block Ib that contains it are encoded by two independent branches and correlated into a four-level pyramid C1, . . . , C4, so that one volume serves every candidate pose. At each iteration the pyramid is indexed at the current estimate, the descriptors of all aerial cells are reduced by a motion encoder and a GRU to one hidden state hk, and two heads predict a single rigid increment. After K iterations the estimate is read out as localization and heading.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes RigidAnchor for UAV cross-view geo-localization. This addresses autonomous navigation and pose estimation for UAVs, fitting Robot Navigation.
papers.title: RigidAnchor: Cross-View Geo-Localization for UAV via Iterative Planar Rigid Alignment
papers.tldr: RigidAnchor reformulates UAV-to-satellite geo-localization as iterative planar alignment, jointly refining position and heading beyond the satellite tile grid.

papers.abstract: By accumulating spikes over multiple timesteps, rate coding approximates the real-valued activations of an ANN, a principle that underpins numerous ANN-to-SNN conversion methods. However, the converted SNNs typically incur loss in accuracy compared to the original ANN. Existing methods either increase a number of timesteps or introduce more complex neuronal dynamics to reduce this accuracy gap. Yet, both approaches ultimately lead to the same outcome: redundancy either in information or in computation, thereby suffering from efficiency degradation. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{PRIME} (\underline{P}otential-\underline{R}esidual \underline{I}ntegration for \underline{M}ulti-threshold \underline{E}ncoding), a multi-threshold concurrent spiking neuron framework redesigned from a hardware data representation perspective:a) We introduce the Residual Membrane Potential Amplification (RMPA) mechanism, which replaces rate coding with Integration Coding by actively amplifying the residual membrane potential. RMPA enables the binary representation of spikes to carry substantially more information, achieving near-lossless conversion with as few as two timesteps.b) Complementarily, we implement concurrent spike firing in multi-threshold neurons, where spikes are decoded directly from the binary representation of floating-point data, eliminating membrane potential--threshold comparisons and replacing multiplications with lightweight bit-shift and accumulation operations that align with hardware computation primitives. At $T=2$ and $D=3$, we achieve competitive performance across both vision and language benchmarks with only 40.6\% of the FP32 bit-transmission cost and 13.4\% of the FP32 multiplication energy consumption. The PRIME framework establishes a new design principle for efficient ANN-to-SNN conversion, bridging the gap between algorithmic efficiency and hardware constraints.
authors: Shaohong Gu, Jiyuan Zhang, Yimeng Shan, Chenxiao Dou, Wei Hua, Malu Zhang, Honglin Cao, Choonghyun Lee, Jingwei Chen
bullets: ANN-to-SNN conversion often loses accuracy or requires redundant timesteps and complex neuron dynamics.
PRIME uses Residual Membrane Potential Amplification to replace rate coding with higher-information Integration Coding.
Multi-threshold neurons decode concurrent spikes from floating-point bit representations, avoiding membrane-potential comparisons.
At T=2 and D=3, the method achieves competitive results across vision and language benchmarks.
The reported cost is 40.6% of FP32 bit transmission and 13.4% of FP32 multiplication energy.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Spike-driven FP16 multiplication. Sign, exponent, and mantissa of x and w are processed in parallel: (a) So = Sx ⊕ Sw via XOR; (b) Eo = Ex + Ew − bias via a 5-bit adder and 6-bit subtractor; (c) the mantissa Fx is decomposed into T spikes {st} with traces Trt = 1 + (t− 1)D; (d) each partial product Fo|t = st × Fw is computed by a Conditional Shift-add Module of MUXes and an adder tree, replacing the 11× 11 multiplier array; (e) partial products are trace-aligned via right shifts and summed to form Fo, truncated to 11 bits.

Figure 1: Comparison between the traditional MTN and the proposed MTN with RMPA. Upper: traditional MTN. Repeated current input introduces redundant addition operations, while fixed threshold initialization requires the membrane potential to be compared with multiple thresholds, resulting in extra hardware computation overhead. Lower: the MTN with RMPA, which uses a single current input and adaptive threshold initialization for more hardware-friendly implementation.

papers.abstract: Off-policy safe reinforcement learning (RL) faces a challenging trade-off between task optimality and constraint feasibility. In primal-dual methods, the coupled optimization of cumulative reward and constraint penalties through adaptive Lagrange multipliers may induce oscillatory policy updates near the safety boundary and amplify the effect of unreliable reward estimates outside the safe set. To address these issues, we formulate a new constrained optimization problem (COP) for safe RL by introducing a Safety-Guiding Policy (SGP) and a corresponding Safety-Guiding Policy Constraint (SGPC). The proposed COP augments the standard COP in safe RL with a conditional safety-guidance constraint. During actor updates, the current actor is evaluated using the learned cost critic. If it is predicted to be outside the safe set, SGP provides a nearby lower-cost training reference, and SGPC guides actor optimization toward this reference. Once the policy enters the safe set, the added constraint becomes inactive, and the formulation reduces to the original COP. This formulation leads to a plug-in actor-training constraint that can be integrated into off-policy safe RL algorithms. By applying primal-dual optimization to the auxiliary COP, we finally derive an SGPC-based off-policy safe RL algorithm and implement it in two representative off-policy algorithms, yielding SAC-SGPC and TD3-SGPC. Experiments on multiple Safety-Gymnasium benchmarks demonstrate that SGPC achieves a better optimality-safety trade-off by substantially reducing constraint violations and cost oscillations while maintaining competitive or better task returns.
authors: Yifan Liu, Nan Zhang, Yang Cong
bullets: Addresses instability near safety boundaries and unreliable reward estimates outside the safe set in primal-dual off-policy safe RL.
Introduces a conditional Safety-Guiding Policy Constraint that is active only when the current policy is predicted to violate safety constraints.
Uses a nearby lower-cost Safety-Guiding Policy as a training reference during actor updates.
Provides a plug-in formulation implemented as SAC-SGPC and TD3-SGPC.
On multiple Safety-Gymnasium benchmarks, reduces constraint violations and cost oscillations while maintaining competitive or better returns.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in diffusion policies have demonstrated strong effectiveness when integrated into hierarchical skill-based learning frameworks, leveraging offline data to capture multimodal and temporally abstracted behaviors. However, prior approaches have rarely considered the diffusion process as a learnable component, adopting fixed noise schedules applied uniformly across skills, regardless of their distinct behavioral contexts. Such a design fundamentally limits the achievable performance, particularly for contact-rich and dexterous manipulation tasks where different skills exhibit distinct couplings between action dimensions. In this paper, we present a skill-adaptive noise diffusion framework (SaND) which introduces a learnable, skill-conditioned noise schedule that modulates the diffusion process per action dimension, adapting the noising dynamics to each skill. To prevent the learned noise schedule from collapsing into trivial solutions, we employ an auxiliary inverse objective that reconstructs the skill embedding from the Legendre coefficients of the derivative of the noise schedule, encouraging the schedules to remain skill-discriminative. This formulation naturally enables adaptive control over the denoising steps for each skill, where noise schedules are clustered in the Legendre coefficient space, and the appropriate number of denoising steps is determined at the point where reconstruction error abruptly increases. At inference, we identify each skill embedding's cluster from its noise schedule and apply the corresponding number of denoising steps, dedicating more compute to skills requiring fine-grained control and less to simpler ones. In simulation and on real robot hardware, SaND outperforms existing skill learning and planning baselines on contact-rich and dexterous manipulation tasks, achieving higher success rates while requiring fewer denoising steps.
authors: Woo Kyung Kim, Gwangpyo Yoo, Eunyoung Park, Honguk Woo
bullets: Fixed noise schedules ignore behavioral differences between skills, limiting performance in contact-rich and dexterous manipulation.
SaND conditions a learnable noise schedule on the skill and adapts noising dynamics per action dimension.
An auxiliary inverse objective uses Legendre coefficients of schedule derivatives to keep schedules skill-discriminative.
Skills are clustered by schedule, with denoising steps selected based on reconstruction-error changes.
Simulation and real-robot experiments show higher success rates than existing baselines with fewer denoising steps.

This enables skill-adaptive inference with reduced computational cost.

papers.abstract: In quantum pulse sequences, spacecraft attitude control and in-hand reorientation, actions act on a hidden physical state as non-commuting operators, so the outcome of a plan depends on the order of its actions. We let the value function carry this structure: each Q(s,a) is an N x N operator, and the Bellman backup applies the action's dual map to the continuation value, Q(s,a) = K_a^*(R(s,a) + gamma E V(s')). Unrolled along a plan, the recursion builds the ordered product of the actions' operators, and the value at any latent state is a linear trace readout. It is exact for policies that do not observe the latent, the backup contracts for unitary and orthogonal dynamics, and an asynchronous operator TD scheme learns it with almost-sure convergence. Classical values live in a lattice, so a maximum over actions exists; self-adjoint operators form an anti-lattice (Kadison) and have none. An operator log-sum-exp still gives one operator per state-action pair whose readout upper-bounds the value of every policy at every latent state. The sampled update converges to it for a finite horizon, and it reduces to soft Q-learning and the QMDP bound when actions commute. We prove that scalar values on observations that ignore action order must confuse swapped histories, that exact history tables grow exponentially for free action groups but polynomially for nilpotent ones, and give a Hankel-rank lower bound on the operator dimension. In experiments the learned policy matches 1000-simulation tree search on SO(3) pointing for horizons up to 20 at ~10^4 times lower decision cost, transfers zero-shot to unseen initial states, and acts exactly on its belief mean when the initial state is hidden, where plugging the mean into a DQN does not. A planner with the same model knowledge is more sample-efficient at short horizons, and a DQN given the operators matches or exceeds OpQ.
authors: Swagatam Das, Swagato Das
bullets: Scalar values cannot represent plans where swapping action order changes outcomes, while operator-valued Q-functions preserve ordered compositions.
The Bellman backup applies each action’s dual map to continuation operators; an asynchronous operator TD method converges under stated dynamics and finite-horizon soft backups.
An operator log-sum-exp provides a per-state-action upper bound on every policy’s latent-state value and recovers soft Q-learning and the QMDP bound when actions commute.

On SO(3) pointing, the learned policy matches 1000-simulation tree search through horizon 20 at roughly 10^4 lower decision cost, transfers to unseen initial states, and handles hidden initial states via belief-mean actions.
Scope includes theoretical dimension and history-complexity bounds; model-based planning is more sample-efficient at short horizons, while DQN with operator inputs matches or exceeds OpQ.

papers.abstract: The physical world is open-ended, dynamic, and partially observable. While foundation models have advanced embodied intelligence, standalone models struggle with long-horizon execution, and simply integrating models with agents may lead to inconsistencies between planning and physical control. To support reliable and adaptive behaviors in the physical world, we introduce Innata-0, a native embodied world system. Innata-0 jointly designs an embodied world-action model and an agent to combine their complementary strengths. The model, Innata-0-WAM, adopts a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that integrates understanding, prediction, and action generation. The agent, Innata-0-Agent, coordinates long-horizon execution through memory, verification, and recovery. A co-design protocol is further proposed to align model training with agent execution and leverage validated experiences to support subsequent adaptation and model improvement. Extensive evaluations demonstrate strong embodied capabilities across understanding, world prediction, and robotic manipulation. Innata-0 represents our first step toward physical intelligence, and we see it as the beginning of a much longer journey.

Karlsson, Jintao Li, Zhiyu Li, Xiongkun Linghu, Guang Liu, You Liu, Zhen Luo, Mengsi Lyu, Yufeng Lyu, Zheng Lyu, Quanyue Ma, Chunlei Men, Ziqiang Ni, Tengfei Pan, Yijun Shen, Liang Sun, Shaoxuan Xie, Xiang Yang, Guocai Yao, Hongjun Zhang, Yingli Zhao, Yonghua Lin, Zhongyuan Wang, Huan Yang

papers.abstract: Interactive segmentation models turn a few clicks into a segmentation prediction across domains, so annotators only decide where the prediction still needs correction. Annotation thus becomes a loop of inspecting the prediction and clicking again. Each step of this loop is a visual judgment, which suits general-purpose multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents. In this work, we focus on letting these agents run this loop on 3D volumes. However, the MLLM in such an agent takes only 2D images as input, so the agent must observe the 3D volume in 2D. Since the loop calls the MLLM many times, this observation must be token-compact enough to keep every call cheap, yet informative enough to show error regions in the 3D prediction. We meet both needs with tri-planes, the three orthogonal planes that cross at one point in the volume. We show, both theoretically and empirically, that tri-planes are context-efficient yet keep sufficient detail to show error regions in the 3D prediction. Building on tri-planes, we introduce TriSegAgent, an MLLM agent that refines the 3D prediction iteratively. Within the agent, the MLLM only judges the prediction on tri-planes, while a visual harness turns each judgment into a 3D action in code. To make the loop reliable, the harness places each click at an exact voxel in the volume and checks whether to accept the 3D prediction. To evaluate the agent, we build a diverse benchmark of 690 regions of interest (ROIs) from 35 public medical datasets across three imaging modalities. With frontier MLLMs, TriSegAgent reaches an overall Dice about 10 points above the strongest baseline, and its lead is even larger on targets below 3 cm. With flash-level MLLMs, it outperforms a recent 3D segmentation agent built on a frontier MLLM.
authors: Qingqiao Hu, Jialin Li, Meilong Xu, Kehan Qi, Yipeng Zhang, Lin Tian, Hongwei Bran Li, Klaus Mueller, Xiaoling Hu

Achieves about 10 Dice points over the strongest baseline with frontier MLLMs, with larger gains for targets smaller than 3 cm; also outperforms a recent 3D agent using flash-level MLLMs.

papers.abstract: GUI grounding requires precise clicks at low latency. Recent models such as GUI-Decisions and GUI-Swift predict coordinates in one forward pass using fixed global bins with local refinement. However, screenshot downsampling removes detail needed to locate small controls, while fixed bins cover larger pixel ranges at higher resolutions. We introduce PixelOne, which transfers spatial knowledge from a search teacher to a student that predicts clicks directly from screenshots at native resolution. The teacher uses VideoJEV's text-option scorer to select rows and columns and progressively zoom into candidate regions. The student inherits the teacher's parameters and matches its distributions over explored regions through spatial distillation alongside box supervision. At inference, the same decision head selects a visual token, and a lightweight pixel head predicts the click within it, all in one forward pass. A click-aligned loss encourages pixels inside the target box to score above those outside. Across four benchmarks, PixelOne-Pro-35B-A3B achieves 83.8% mean accuracy, the highest among the evaluated single-forward grounders, with a mean latency of 0.43 s per target.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures have emerged as a promising approach for scaling deep learning models while maintaining computational efficiency. However, existing MoE adaptations for Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) models suffer from significant computational overhead during sequential training and degradation of zero-shot capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose CLIP-FMoE, a novel approach that integrates MoE architecture into CLIP fine-tuning. Our method uses Isolated Constrained Contrastive Learning, a pipeline that trains specialized experts on cluster-based data partitions to accelerate expert specialization. Additionally, we introduce a Fusion Gate mechanism to mitigate catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained knowledge. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves consistent improvements on downstream tasks while preserving zero-shot capabilities. Furthermore, our method demonstrates robust performance across varying context lengths, making it particularly suitable for diverse real-world applications.
authors: Luong Tran, Lan-Cuong Nguyen, Huynh Dang Nguyen, Dat Nguyen Cong, Dung D. Le, Van Nguyen

papers.abstract: Long-lived Web assistants require effective memory and retrieval mechanisms to access information from past user interactions. While these capabilities can be learned through specialized policies, it remains unclear whether specialists trained independently in different environments can be effectively composed without joint optimization. This paper investigates compositional transfer through policy distillation. Memory-writing and sequential retrieval policies are independently distilled from frontier-model action trajectories into 3B models and combined with a fixed answer generator without downstream training. On a LongMemEval-based benchmark, the distilled composition achieves 73.1% accuracy, compared with 36.2% for a composition of existing RL-trained specialists, and also outperforms the evaluated RL-trained compositions on PersonaMem-v2. Component ablations reveal that improvements in individual policies depend on their composition, highlighting the importance of cross-specialist compatibility. Further task-specific adaptation improves accuracy to 75.2% on LongMemEval through RL and 48.9% on PersonaMem-v2 through supervised distillation. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of independent specialist distillation for modular multi-agent systems. Source code and datasets of teacher-generated memory-editing and retrieval trajectories are released to facilitate reproducibility and further research.
authors: Grigorii Davydenko, Artem Sakhno, Igor Pavlov, Julia Belikova, Andrey Savchenko, Maksim Makarenko
bullets: Addresses whether policies trained independently across environments can transfer and work together.
Distills memory-writing and sequential-retrieval policies from frontier-model trajectories into 3B models, then combines them with a fixed answer generator without downstream training.
The composition reaches 73.1% accuracy on LongMemEval versus 36.2% for a composition of existing RL-trained specialists, and also outperforms evaluated RL compositions on PersonaMem-v2.
Ablations show that individual policy gains depend on cross-specialist compatibility.
Task-specific adaptation further raises accuracy to 75.2% on LongMemEval via RL and 48.9% on PersonaMem-v2 via supervised distillation; code and teacher-generated datasets are released.

The reader remains fixed in both settings.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for spatial tasks such as navigation and manipulation, where they must infer geometry and object relationships from visual input in order to act correctly. Existing benchmarks usually test perception and reasoning in isolation, making it hard to tell whether failures come from visual understanding, downstream reasoning, or the bridge between them. We introduce VeriWorld, a benchmark for spatial reasoning in interactive 3D environments with executable actions and deterministic verification. For task families where all three channels are well-defined, we evaluate matched visual, structured, and combined input conditions on the same instance, environment, and verifier; families without a clean visual/structured/combined split are reported separately. This design supports controlled comparisons of perception, reasoning, and their interaction. Using this setup, we uncover two diagnostic findings. First, models often perform much better when task-relevant information, such as object identity, current state, or target location, is given explicitly than when it must be read from the rendered scene, revealing a recurring visual-to-structure gap. Second, action-space and harness design can change outcomes even under the same task and information condition, showing that interaction protocol is itself a confounding variable. VeriWorld is open-sourced to support reproducible and fine-grained evaluation of spatial reasoning in VLMs.
authors: Yan Zheng, ShengYun Peng, Xuyao Liang, Xiaoyan Cong, Nuo Chen, Bangya Liu, Zihan Wang, Wenyan Cong, Zhiwen Fan, Zhangyang Wang
bullets: Targets failures in navigation and manipulation where models must infer geometry and object relationships from visual input.
Compares matched visual, structured, and combined inputs on identical instances, environments, and verifiers when possible.
Finds a recurring gap: models perform better when object identity, state, or target location is provided explicitly than when inferred from rendered scenes.
Shows that action-space and interaction-harness design can alter results, making protocol a confounding factor.
Open-sourced for reproducible, fine-grained evaluation of spatial reasoning in VLMs.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the 11 tasks in VERIWORLD, spanning four families. Interactive Control (closedloop, multi-round): MazeNavFPS (first-person grid maze navigation), Billiards (2D pool trajectory planning), TunnelNav3D (curved-tunnel flythrough), PlaceOnBottom (object stacking). Trial-and-Error Prediction (submit-and-check): BoxFold (predict the folded shape), MovingShooter (aim at a moving target), LightWar (aim and launch a projectile at a distant beacon across a large outdoor terrain). Photoreal Grounding (photorealistic 3D scenes): SceneGrounding (recover the camera pose of a given screenshot in two photoreal interior levels), ObjectGrounding (localize named kitchen objects with 3D markers in a photoreal apartment scene). Computational Physics (Slang/CUDA simulation): CurvyBilliards (ball dynamics on a parametric surface), DropToTarget (surface design for target landing). Family colours match the row banners in Table 2; Sec. 5 reports these tasks using separate core, specialized, and harness-diagnostic tracks.

Figure 1: Batch control improves performance under both evaluated information channels at an equal move budget. Same task (MazeNavFPS, 30 mazes), same model (Gemini-3.1-Pro), and the same budget of primitive moves for both protocols (125/170/210 moves for 3×3/4×4/5×5 grids): switching the action interface from Single (one move per call) to Batch (3–6 moves per call) lifts Pass@1 from 0.57 to 0.93 under VP (vision + position log) and from 0.57 to 0.97 under VRP (VP + raycast), while Batch uses fewer moves on average. Under an equal budget of 50 model calls, Batch also outperforms Single for every evaluated model (Sec. 5.3 and Table 10). This motivates VERIWORLD’s three-axis design — task, information channel, and action harness — in which the harness is treated as a first-class experimental variable rather than a fixed implementation detail.

Figure 2: VERIWORLD evaluation pipeline. A Python generator maps a seed to task parameters and instantiates the scene in Unreal Engine 5 (rendering + game-runtime bridge for in-process code execution). A VLM agent runs a closed step loop: screenshot + action log → thoughts / actions / updated knowledge → execute in UE5; the new screenshot and log feed back for up to T rounds. A deterministic Python verifier checks pass / fail at runtime for every task; some families additionally have a solvability certificate (Lean 4 or deterministic simulation, depending on the task; §3.3).

Figure 4: LightWar successful arc, V+Telemetry condition. A 2×3 stack of arc replay frames sampled at t = 0.51, 1.53, 2.54, 3.56, 4.58, 5.59 s after launch, taken from a Gemini 3.1 Pro Pass@1 episode on seed=0 (hit_forest_hilltop_beacon). The agent fires a glowing projectile from a low-elevation forest clearing (frame 1) and tracks the ballistic arc until it intersects a hilltop beacon (frame 6, bright impact flare). Each frame is the harness’s per-tick render passed back to the agent at the next round; together they form the visual evidence the agent uses to plan the next shot. Per-round screenshots like these are part of the V condition; V+Telemetry additionally reports the scalar miss distance of each shot. Without the miss distance (V-only), the mid-tier panel models (Sonnet, Opus, Kimi, Qwen3-VL-30B) drop from 0.33 to 0.00 Pass@1.

Figure 5: Six rendering variants of the ObjectGrounding harness. The main-table V/C contrast (grid-marker family, fourth column) compares 9 bboxes with small index labels inside the boxes vs. the same bboxes with enlarged, camera-facing labels under an offcenter camera; the harness-diagnostic V/C contrast (single-marker family, second column) repeats the same label-rendering ablation under a sparser, single-bbox scaffold. Auxiliary numbered-ball variants (first and third columns) are the original baselines from which the bbox variants were derived; they are not used for the V/C tables but are the scene context the seed sampler draws from. Within each family, V and C differ only in how the index labels are rendered; both include the marker-to-world-coordinate table.

Prior benchmarks typically capture only subsets of these capabilities—focusing on perception, interaction, or evaluation in isolation—while VERIWORLD integrates all components within a unified and verifiable framework. ✓ = supported, ✗ = not supported, ∼ = partial.
Table 2: Task families in VERIWORLD. We organize 11 tasks into four families by interaction paradigm and the type of spatial reasoning required. Family colours match the row banners of Table 3.

Table 4: Grid mazes under an equal primitive-move budget: batch outperforms single-step control under both information variants. Pass@1 over 30 mazes per cell (grids 3, 4, 5 × 10 seeds). Batch and single share a budget of 125, 170 and 210 primitive moves for 3×3, 4×4 and 5×5 grids; the batch prompt asks for 3–6 commands per model call and single sends one.
