VP = rendered observation + position history; VRP = VP + a 4-direction raycast scan. These are auxiliary harness variants, not core V/S/C conditions.

Table 8: MazeNavFPS auxiliary information-channel sweep, 5×5 grids, 9-seed extension. Maze navigation does not cleanly fit the core V/S/C taxonomy: a closed-loop ReAct agent inevitably accumulates an action-history memory across rounds, so even the rendered-observation-only condition retains an implicit structured channel. We sweep four auxiliary information channels (all under batched action control, Bf ), holding the model lineup fixed at four frontier VLMs: V – rendered observation only; no harness-tracked position log; RP – 4-direction raycast wall distances + harness-tracked position log; no rendered observation; VP – rendered observation + position log; VRP – rendered observation + raycast + position log. We restrict to the hardest 5×5 grid for an apples-to-apples shape comparison and use nine seeds {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 42} that produce different maze topologies. Each per-model cell reports Pass@1 over valid episodes; Avg pools them across the four models. Each cell has n = 9 except RP (Gemini 7, Opus 4, GPT-5.2 5), VP (Opus 7) and VRP (Opus 4, GPT-5.2 8).

Table 10: Grid mazes under an equal budget of 50 model calls. Each cell shows Pass@1, with average rounds (model calls) in parentheses. The batch prompt asks for 3–6 commands per call and single executes one, so batch can execute more primitive moves. VP = rendered observation + position history; VRP = VP + a 4-direction raycast scan.

Table 3: Core V/S/C information-condition results. We include tasks for which visual (V), structured-only (S), and combined (C) conditions are defined on seed-generated task instances with the same action interface and verifier; ObjectGrounding has no structured-only condition and is reported with V and C. V provides rendered observations and task-specific metadata describing the scene setup and action interface, while retaining task-specific demands for visual identification or state estimation. S provides explicit information such as object attributes, current or target coordinates, and physical parameters without images. papers.abstract: Generating 3D indoor scenes requires a representation that captures object semantics, instance identity, height structure, and orientation while respecting room geometry. Methods that model scenes as sequences of object vectors learn spatial constraints implicitly, leaving collisions and boundary violations to losses or post-processing; semantic-map methods make occupancy explicit, but collapse instance and directional structure. We introduce RoomTokens, a sliced structured-token representation in which each token stores semantic class, instance-color identity, and facing field. This representation allows a scene to be generated as a discrete grid while preserving cues for instance grouping, orientation estimation, and 3D extent prediction. To learn the RoomToken distribution, we propose MDIRT (Masked Diffusion over RoomTokens), a masked discrete diffusion model that denoises semantic/instance-color/facing channels jointly with a shared cross-slice backbone. Architectural tokens are clamped as explicit floor- plan constraints, so the model samples furniture layouts that respect room geometry while retaining instance and object-attribute structure. Experiments on 3D-FRONT show that RoomTokens with MDIRT improve layout fidelity and physical consistency over sequence/vector- and map-based methods, suggesting structured spatial tokens as a practical choice for discrete 3D scene synthesis.
authors: Xiaohao Sun, Angel X. Chang
bullets: Represents scenes with tokens encoding semantic class, instance identity, and facing direction across spatial slices.
Uses masked discrete diffusion to jointly denoise these channels with a shared cross-slice backbone.
Clamps floor-plan tokens as explicit constraints, helping generated layouts respect room boundaries and geometry.
On 3D-FRONT, the approach improves layout fidelity and physical consistency over sequence/vector- and map-based methods.
Scope: targets discrete 3D indoor scene synthesis and relies on floor-plan constraints for geometry control.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of MDIRT. Given selected height slices and an architectural mask, we clamp the fixed room structure and denoise masked interior RoomTokens with a shared UNet with cross-slice attention. The denoiser predicts semantic, instance-color, and facing slices under semantic-gated validity constraints: architecture/background tokens carry no instance-color or facing cues, while furniture tokens do. The valid RoomToken grid is then grouped into object records, whose category, size, and pose are used to retrieve and place matched 3D assets.

Figure 1: Top. Comparison of scene representations for indoor scene generation. Object sequences (a) encode object attributes but lack explicit spatial relationship information. Semantic maps (b) make spatial structure explicit, but lack vertical, instance, and orientation information. We propose RoomTokens (c) to address these missing factors by encoding semantic occupancy, instance identity, and facing cues in a sliced spatial grid. Bottom. We introduce MDIRT (d), a masked discrete diffusion model over RoomTokens, which denoises missing token fields while keeping architectural tokens fixed so generated scenes respect room boundaries.

Baselines show boundary violations, collisions, or blocked door/window openings, while MDIRT preserves clear openings, room geometry, and structured object cues.

(b) Each slice encodes three aligned 2D channels: semantic class, instance-color identity, and the facing field. Stacking these channels over all heights forms a sliced token volume. (c) The resulting 3D representation of stacked slices (RoomTokens) stores semantic, instance, and orientation information, with height derived from the slice index.

papers.abstract: Pretrained robot policies decide what to do from camera images, yet some of the physics that decides whether their plans succeed is not visible. An object may look light but be 100 times heavier, and a weakened joint or a lagging controller leaves no trace in the image. When the physics at deployment differs from training, the plan is often still right but is executed as if nothing had changed. Training on such variations in advance cannot handle unseen changes, while adapting once deployed either changes the plan, leaving the miscalibrated commands in place, or updates a robot model by gradient steps that do not know how reliable they are and can make the robot worse even when nothing has changed. We propose RoboAda, which keeps the policy and its plan unchanged and corrects the commands that carry it out by inferring at test time how the robot turns commands into motion. The key observation is that the robot's own motion reveals the change: after each action chunk, an inverse-dynamics model of the original robot converts the observed motion into the commands it would have needed, yielding free labels at every step. Competing hypotheses of how the robot responds, including that nothing has changed, are weighted by how well they predict these labels, and the next chunk is sent with the commands that best realize the plan under them. RoboAda needs no reward, no gradient step and no data from the changed robot. We evaluate RoboAda with five frozen policies on LIBERO, two world action models and three vision-language-action models. Under eleven physical shifts, it more than doubles their average success, from 27.8% to 62.9%. It beats the best of seven test-time adaptation methods by 17.3 points on Cosmos Policy, and largely preserves the policies' success when nothing has changed. On bimanual RoboTwin 2.0 in joint space, it raises success under joint-target offsets from 24.9% to 78.8%.
authors: Yunbei Zhang, Zijian Jin, Shuaicheng Niu, Baian Chen, Weirui Ye, Jihun Hamm, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses hidden deployment shifts such as altered object weight, weakened joints, and controller lag.
Uses observed robot motion and an inverse-dynamics model to infer the commands the original robot would have needed.
Weights competing robot-response hypotheses, including no-change, by how well they predict inferred command labels.
Requires no reward, gradient updates, or data collected from the changed robot.
Across 11 physical shifts, improves average success from 27.8% to 62.9% and preserves performance when physics is unchanged.

papers.abstract: Looped language models reuse one block of weights T times per token, trading parameters for test-time depth, but autoregressive decoding then pays T sequential passes per token. Self-speculative decoders recover 2-10x for a single request, yet their gains fade as requests share a GPU, and current practice is to speculate less as load grows. We show that what fails under load is the layout of speculative work, not speculation. In concurrent decoding the unit of cost is the row, one request advancing on one loop, which reads that loop's key-value (KV) cache once; additional positions inside a row are nearly free. Pipelined schedules such as the wavefront place every speculative position on a different loop, hence in a row of its own, so each token is still read T times. We present PackLoop, built on one principle: speculate only inside rows that are read anyway. Deep loops accumulate positions and advance them as a block in one row, context-copy proposals join the row that the first loop already reads, and a closed-form admission rule, the economic order quantity of inventory theory, sets how long to accumulate from a cost model calibrated once per engine. PackLoop is exact: in FP32 its output is token-for-token identical to autoregressive decoding, also under sampling and early exit. Across 164 load points spanning three GPUs, four Ouro models, six benchmarks, and contexts up to 32K tokens, one PackLoop configuration is faster than the best existing schedule, chosen per point, at 161 points (median 1.25x, up to 1.76x) and never significantly slower. Its lead grows with concurrency and context length, the regime in which existing self-speculation gains least.
authors: Runguo Li, Dezhen Lu
bullets: Looped language models require multiple sequential passes per token, and existing self-speculation loses efficiency as concurrency increases.
The key bottleneck is speculative-work layout: separate rows repeatedly reread the same loop-specific KV caches.
PackLoop packs deep-loop and context-copy proposals into already-used rows, with an economic-order-quantity rule controlling accumulation.
It is token-for-token exact in FP32, including sampling and early exit.
Across 164 load points, it beat the best existing schedule at 161 points, with a median 1.25× and maximum 1.76× speedup, without significant slowdowns.

papers.abstract: Flow-based robot policies generate actions by repeatedly evaluating a conditional velocity field, so test-time bias correction seems simple: query the action expert under a task-agnostic condition and subtract that velocity from the task-conditioned prediction. We show this is often wrong. On Fast-WAM across 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, mean-instruction predictions align strongly with task-conditioned velocities (cosine approximately 0.94-0.95). Averaging eight completed-state references barely cancels this direction: their mean norm is 98.3% of the mean individual norm. References thus contain a large shared transport component, not only harmful bias, and aggressive subtraction damages generation. We propose a same-state diagnostic and shrinkage analysis showing that the optimal correction scale depends on reference signal-to-noise. This motivates geometry-calibrated action debiasing, which removes only the component orthogonal to the task velocity and predicts a small task-dependent scale from instruction geometry. In controlled RoboTwin experiments, corrupting instructions still permits 25.1% success (50 tasks, 20 episodes), whereas dynamic visual corruption nearly eliminates success. A fixed centered orthogonal correction reaches 92.7% versus a 92.1% baseline in one randomized 1000-trial sweep, but gains are non-monotonic and within run-to-run variation. An angular scale pilot has an offline oracle-gated bound of 94.5%; its best learned online realization reaches 92.5%. These results identify shared flow and train-serve mismatch as central obstacles and provide a reproducible foundation for conditional correction.
authors: Xufeng Zhan, Yuanzhi Liang, Ye Lu, Haibin Huang, Chi Zhang, Xuelong Li
bullets: Mean-instruction and task-conditioned velocities align strongly (cosine ≈0.94–0.95), so references are not pure harmful bias.
Averaging eight completed-state references leaves 98.3% of the individual mean norm, indicating a large shared transport component.
The proposed diagnostic and shrinkage analysis link correction strength to reference signal-to-noise.
Geometry-calibrated correction removes only the component orthogonal to task velocity and predicts a task-dependent scale.
In controlled RoboTwin experiments, centered orthogonal correction achieved 92.7% versus a 92.1% baseline in one sweep; gains were non-monotonic and within run-to-run variation.

Figure 1. Correction-aware fine-tuning for Fast-WAM. (a) Task and mean instruction contexts query the same WAM with identical observation o, proprioception p, noisy action xt, and flow time t. The mean context averages 8,192 cached training contexts. The no-op inset repeats the current unnormalized joint positions over the action horizon and applies the action normalizer to obtain anoop(p). The analytic no-op field is defined for σt > 0 (Equation 5); a stationary endpoint generally requires nonzero transport from the noisy state. (b) The tip-to-tip arrow forms the centered residual b = vmean − vnoop. After masking padded and gripper entries, orthogonal projection retains r. papers.abstract: World action models guide robots by predicting the effects of actions or generating commands from observations. A model may compare hundreds of candidate futures before acting, repeatedly reading weights that must fit in device memory. Post-training quantization reduces the number of bits used to store pretrained weights, but a smaller model is not necessarily a deployable one: temporary tensors can exceed graphics processing unit (GPU) memory limits, while even small prediction errors can change the selected action. This creates two coupled challenges: identifying bit assignments that preserve task performance and determining which of them meet real execution constraints, without exhausting costly task trials. We present PTQ4WAM, a framework for choosing layer-wise bit assignments and execution routes under memory, latency and task-evaluation budgets. Calibration measurements guide candidate proposals, optionally with a language model agent. We profile full-model routes on the GPU before spending task trials on feasible assignments. Fusing group rescaling and reading visual history in place can make an otherwise infeasible assignment deployable. Across 15 workloads from four model families, the median task score is 99.2% of the corresponding 32-bit floating-point (FP32) score. On fixed GPU replays, the median speedup over FP32 is 2.36 times and the median reduction in peak allocated memory is 71.5%. The code will be released soon.

bullets: Addresses the gap between smaller quantized models and actual deployability, where temporary tensors, latency, and action-sensitive errors matter.
Chooses layer-wise bit assignments and GPU execution routes under memory, latency, and task-evaluation budgets.

Across 15 workloads and four model families, achieved a median 99.2% of FP32 task score, 2.36× speedup, and 71.5% lower peak allocated memory.
Scope: results focus on fixed GPU replays; code release is forthcoming.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) has recently become a central paradigm for advancing Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), as demonstrated by systems such as OpenAI's o3 and the R1 series. Despite significant progress in LLMs, how to leverage RFT to unify visual perception, step-by-step reasoning, and agentic tool use into one coherent training paradigm remains an open challenge. In this work, we present Visual Reinforcement Fine-Tuning++ (Visual-RFT++), a unified framework that extends RFT to both visual perception tasks and multimodal agentic workflows, enabling LVLMs to reason with images, act upon images, and evaluate their own outputs using verifiable reward. With Visual-RFT++, open-source LVLMs not only show significant gains on diverse visual perception tasks, but also acquire agentic abilities such as web searching for real-time information and code-based image manipulation (e.g., cropping, rotation, and analysis). Across visual perception tasks, including fine-grained classification, few-shot detection, reasoning grounding, and open-vocabulary detection, Visual-RFT++ delivers strong gains over SFT, including a +24.3 percentage points improvement in one-shot fine-grained classification and +21.0 percentage points on COCO's 4-shot setting and +15.4 percentage points on LVIS with around several hundred samples. To evaluate agentic behaviors, we introduce the Multimodal Agentic Tool Bench (MAT) with MAT-Search and MAT-Coding. Visual-RFT++ surpasses its baseline by +18.6 F1 / +13.0 EM percentage points on MAT-Coding and +10.3 F1 / +8.7 EM percentage points on MAT-Search. It also shows gains of 29.3 F1 and 25.9 EM percentage points on multi-hop QA benchmarks such as 2Wiki and HotpotQA, demonstrating strong cross-modal generalization. Visual-RFT++ introduces a data-efficient and reward-driven framework that strengthens both visual reasoning and agentic adaptability.
authors: Ziyu Liu, Zeyi Sun, Xiaoyi Dong, Yuhang Cao, Haodong Duan, Dahua Lin, Jiaqi Wang, Yuhang Zang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of unifying visual perception, step-by-step reasoning, and agentic workflows in LVLMs.

Introduces the Multimodal Agentic Tool Bench (MAT) for evaluating search and code-based image manipulation.
Reports gains on MAT tasks and multi-hop QA, indicating cross-modal generalization with relatively few training samples.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) deliver fast visuomotor control, yet degrade sharply in challenging scenes and act blindly when about to fail; conversely, foundation-model-based agents generalize and recover reliably, but incur prohibitive latency and cost when queried at every step. To achieve both WAM (System 1)-level speed and agent (System 2)-level reliability--- we propose \textbf{\oursfull (\ours)}, a framework that calibrates WAMs' confidence--- adaptively triggering System~2 only when necessary, and distilling System~2's knowledge to form an evolving System~1. First, \ours equips a frozen WAM with \textbf{calibrated self-assessment}: a single lightweight judgment token reading internal video--action features is trained via our proposed \textbf{cross-fitted temporal-difference (TD) learning} using only binary rollout success/failure signals. It can predict a \textbf{calibrated success probability} at negligible overhead without affecting action predictions. Second, this calibrated success probability schedules control chunk by chunk---invoking System~2 to resolve bottlenecks when confidence drops, and handing control back to the WAM once confidence recovers, preserving WAM-like speed while approaching System~2 reliability. Third, as System~2 intervenes only when the WAM lacks confidence, its takeover trajectories directly capture the WAM's capability gaps. JiL distills these takeovers into the WAM to repair those gaps so System~1 can operate standalone without System~2 at test time, while our mastered-skill anchoring and dynamic confidence gating prevent degrading existing capabilities.
authors: Wenhao Li, Yu Han, Xiu Su, Dehao Wu, Keke Huang, Shan You, Fei Wang, Chang Xu
bullets: Addresses WAM failures in challenging scenes and the high latency and cost of invoking System 2 at every step.
Trains a lightweight judgment token with cross-fitted temporal-difference learning from binary rollout success/failure signals.
Uses calibrated success probabilities to switch between WAM control and System 2 assistance chunk by chunk.
Distills System 2 takeover trajectories into the WAM to repair capability gaps and support later standalone operation.
Mastered-skill anchoring and dynamic confidence gating aim to preserve existing capabilities during self-evolution.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the Judgment-in-the-Loop (JiL) framework. (1) Non-Invasive Calibrated Self-Assessment (Sec. 3.2): A lightweight judgment token J attends to the frozen WAM’s internal video and action streams through a causal mask and token-gated adapters, predicting calibrated success probability qθ via our proposed cross-fitted TD learning without affecting action predictions. (2) Adaptive System 1 & 2 Takeover (Sec. 3.3): At each decision step, qθ schedules control chunk by chunk; the WAM hands control to a GPT-6-Astra-based agent when qθ < τ and reclaims execution once confidence recovers above τback. (3) Capability-Gap Consolidation (Sec. 3.4): Keeping πbase frozen, successful agent takeovers (Dhelp) are combined with mastered-skill anchor data—the WAM’s own confident successes (Down) and pre-training replay (Dreplay)—into Dmix to train a separate repaired action expert πrep, distilling System 2’s recovery skills into System 1. (4) Erosion-Free Confidence-Gated Deployment (Sec. 3.5): During standalone deployment, πbase dynamically switches to πrep when base confidence qbase drops below τ and reclaims control once confidence recovers, repairing hard states without degrading mastered skills or invoking System 2 (scores shown: Fast-WAM on RoboTwin 2.0, 1 round).

papers.abstract: Persistent object maps must incorporate new surfaces while retaining valid identities and correcting earlier associations. We present a map-revision module that separates historical identity changes from new-surface admission. Proposed merges are tested against shared and separate mask explanations across views; a merge is allowed only if its evidence margin remains positive after removing any one observed frame. New measured points are assigned through local identity competition, with a mask witness and a seed-frame stability check. On two preselected KITTI-360 windows, the fixed method increases mean building/car instance AP50:90 from 17.259 to 18.762 under a local evaluation protocol. Controlled output interventions attribute the gains to fragment consolidation, protection against harmful overwrites, and local assignment of new points. Four additional spatial holdouts increase mean AP from 20.263 to 23.171, although unconditional revision is slightly higher at 23.251. The extra seed-frame check yields no AP gain over nearest-seed assignment in either set. A 330-frame garage recording demonstrates offline integration with LiDAR--inertial--visual odometry. These results identify where observation-supported revision improves object maps and where conservative decisions still limit recovery.

Assigns new points through local identity competition with mask-witness and seed-frame checks.
Improves mean instance AP50:90 from 17.259 to 18.762 on two KITTI-360 windows; spatial holdouts rise from 20.263 to 23.171.
Seed-frame stability adds no AP gain over nearest-seed assignment, highlighting limits of conservative revision.

papers.selection_reason: The paper presents a map-revision module for persistent object maps in SLAM, which is a core capability for embodied agents to maintain accurate world representations. The technical focus on evidence-based identity correction and new-surface admission is relevant to embodied world modeling.
papers.title: OmniSLAM: Evidence-Authorized Revision of Persistent Object Maps
papers.tldr: OmniSLAM revises persistent object maps conservatively by requiring observation-backed evidence for identity merges and new-surface assignments.

papers.abstract: Treating independent layers as the minimal pruning unit allows layer pruning to efficiently eliminate many redundant parameters and achieve high compression rates. Layer pruning has become a promising and prevalent structured pruning technique for large language models (LLMs). However, multi-layer removal can lead to significant performance degradation for LLMs. Although some works have explored various compensation methods for pruned layers, they are inefficient and costly. Observing that the expression of a large proportion of information is concentrated on a small number of pivotal channels, we propose a novel post-pruning compensation method for layer pruning, called pivotal channel compensation (PCC). PCC can achieve significant performance improvement by compensating for a small number of channels through learnable linear transformations at the pruning interface. Besides, we propose a new evaluation metric, called channel-wise average performance improvement (CAPI), which can measure the efficiency of channel-wise compensation. Our experimental results across various LLMs demonstrate that PCC can achieve significant and consistent improvements and high CAPI on language modeling and zero-shot question answering for the state-of-the-art cross-layer and consecutive-layer pruning methods. Compared with existing compensation methods, PCC can achieve competitive results with fewer additional parameters and less training cost.
authors: Xiangqian Wang, Yucheng Zhang, Zhaohong Jia, Kun Jing, Chunchun Li

Compared with existing compensation methods, PCC achieves competitive performance with fewer added parameters and less training cost.

papers.abstract: Sustained lunar-base operations require robots that restore equipment and deliver cargo under conditions unforeseen before deployment. Flown space autonomy executes pre-validated procedures and enters a safe hold outside their scope, whereas foundation models synthesize plans on site that cannot be verified before execution. We formulate these operations as safety-constrained contingent planning with irreversible actions, erroneous records, three-valued physical evidence, and costly, deadline-constrained sensing. We propose asymmetric knowledge-level replanning (AKR), which treats the planner as an untrusted black box: reversible actions run on the planner's assumptions, and irreversible actions run only after a minimum-cost sensing cover verifies every precondition. Under sound measurements, no irreversible action executes on a false precondition for any planner or record, the sensing cost before an irreversible action is bounded below for every sound knowledge-based policy, and execution with a complete planner ends in a verified goal or a certified hold. AKR executed no hazardous action in 21,000 Monte Carlo trials with sound observations or in 58 full-stack runs; the FF-Replan acting rule executed one in 7% of those trials. The median AKR run took 1.10 times the fastest run on the same mission, against 1.50 under the K-replanner acting rule. AKR completed 20 of 21 contingency and sequential-fault runs with an unchanged task model; the original PLEXIL and EUROPA$\rightarrow$PLEXIL procedures completed none.
authors: Bingqi Huang, Bingchuan Wei, Yingkai Cai, Zhaokui Wang
bullets: Addresses lunar operations where prevalidated procedures cannot handle unforeseen faults and foundation-model plans cannot be verified in advance.
Models safety-constrained contingent planning with irreversible actions, erroneous records, three-valued evidence, and costly deadline-limited sensing.
Treats the planner as untrusted: reversible actions follow assumptions, while irreversible actions require a minimum-cost sensing cover.
With sound observations, AKR executed no hazardous actions in 21,000 Monte Carlo trials and 58 full-stack runs; FF-Replan acted hazardously in 7% of comparable trials.
AKR completed 20 of 21 contingency and sequential-fault runs with an unchanged task model, while baseline procedures completed none.

papers.title: Trustworthy agentic lunar robotics: safety-constrained contingent planning with a foundation-model planner
papers.tldr: AKR enables foundation-model lunar robots to replan contingencies safely by verifying every precondition before irreversible actions, avoiding hazards while preserving near-fastest execution.

papers.abstract: Deploying large vision-language-action (VLA) models on resource-constrained robots demands extreme compression, yet existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods frequently collapse at ultra-low bit-widths ($\le$ 2 bits). We trace this failure to two mismatches in standard pipelines. First, calibrating on static offline demonstrations induces distribution shift: minor quantization perturbations drive the policy into unseen states where uncalibrated errors compound. Second, minimizing the layer-wise weight reconstruction error is a flawed proxy, as action generation depends only on the representations consumed by the action head. We present LoopQ, an on-policy ultra-low-bit quantization framework. LoopQ closes the loop by calibrating on states from the quantized policy's own rollouts. It then adds readout-aligned fine-tuning, which freezes the trellis codes and optimizes only lightweight lookup tables and scaling factors to align the backbone readout with the full-precision teacher. With all linear layers at 2 bits, LoopQ achieves a 60.4% success rate on LIBERO-Plus with GR00T N1.7, close to the 61.8% of full precision. Even at 1 bit per weight, $\pi_{0.5}$ still completes 80.0% of LIBERO tasks. With 8-bit activations, the 2-bit $\pi_{0.5}$ runs on integer kernels on an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor, with 4.1$\times$ smaller weights and 44% less memory. On a real AgileX Piper arm, it stays within one success of full precision on each of three tasks. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/LoopQ
authors: Yanlong Chen, Thongthornpatch Chamadol, Yichen Guo, Yunfei Gao, Mohan Liu, Addison Lin Wang, Yawei Li
bullets: Standard PTQ fails at ≤2 bits because static calibration misses quantization-induced state drift and layer-wise reconstruction does not reflect action-generation needs.
LoopQ uses on-policy rollouts from the quantized policy for drift-aware calibration.
Readout-aligned fine-tuning updates lightweight lookup tables and scaling factors while keeping trellis codes fixed.
At 2-bit weights, LoopQ reaches 60.4% on LIBERO-Plus with GR00T N1.7 versus 61.8% full precision; 1-bit π₀.₅ completes 80.0% of LIBERO tasks.
The 2-bit π₀.₅ model uses integer kernels on Jetson AGX Thor, reducing weight storage by 4.1× and memory by 44%, and remains close to full precision on three real-arm tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Ultra-low-bit quantization of VLA models with on-policy calibration; directly relevant to embodied action models and efficient deployment.
papers.title: Quantizing in the Loop: Drift-Aware Ultra-Low-Bit Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: LoopQ enables ultra-low-bit VLA models to retain near-full-precision robot performance by calibrating on their own rollouts and aligning quantized representations with action readouts.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) estimate, understand, and predict human motion, but mainly from RGB cameras. Depth, LiDAR, mmWave, and WiFi complement RGB under poor lighting, through occlusions, and in privacy-sensitive applications, but existing multisensory models cover only some of these sensing tasks. Covering all of them from any sensor subset is challenging, since the tokens of heterogeneous sensors are semantically inconsistent and spatially misaligned, paired multisensory data are scarce, and the tasks need different temporal granularities. We present OmniSenMo, a multisensory language model that takes the human skeleton as a common reference for all sensors. Its skeleton-grounded motion representation turns each sensor into joint tokens, one per body joint, so that any sensor subset is fused joint by joint and expressed in the motion vocabulary that the language model learned from motion capture and text. We pretrain it on all five sensors generated by our multisensory simulator, and Multi-Granularity Observation gives each task the frames it needs. On a cross-action split of MM-Fi, the same model with all five sensors outperforms the models compared on each task, including LEO-Fuse in pose estimation (84.1 vs. 89.0 mm MPJPE) and HoloLLM in unseen-action recognition (69.2% vs. 42.8%). Even without RGB, it outperforms both methods that use RGB, and in a cross-dataset validation on XRF55, it recognizes unseen actions far better than HoloLLM.
authors: Cheng Guo, Qiming Cao, Pu Perry Wang, Pu Wang, Hongfei Xue
bullets: Addresses heterogeneous, spatially misaligned sensors, scarce paired data, and task-specific temporal requirements.
Represents each sensor as joint-level tokens using the human skeleton as a common reference for fusion.
Pretrains on simulated multisensory data and uses Multi-Granularity Observation to match task-specific frame needs.
On MM-Fi, achieves 84.1 mm MPJPE for pose estimation versus 89.0 for LEO-Fuse, and 69.2% unseen-action recognition versus 42.8% for HoloLLM.
Maintains strong recognition without RGB and generalizes to unseen actions on XRF55; evaluation focuses on the reported datasets and simulated pretraining setup.

papers.selection_reason: Multisensory language model unifying heterogeneous sensors for human motion tasks; directly fits multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: OmniSenMo: A Unified Multisensory Language Model for Generalizable Human Motion Estimation, Understanding, and Prediction
papers.tldr: OmniSenMo unifies five sensing modalities through skeleton-grounded tokens to estimate, understand, and predict human motion across flexible sensor combinations.

papers.abstract: Dense visual SLAM built on learned two-view geometry is evaluated in good light; in low light it fails silently. Two frames of 9-level quantized noise, no scene at all, give MASt3R-SLAM's network a cross-view geometric self-consistency of 0.936; a real dark frame pair gives 0.935. Starved of structure, the network invents the same geometry for both views and the system trusts the agreement: on a dark sequence it consumes 1,605 frames, emits 7 keyframes, rejects no factor-graph edges and reports full frame rate, while over 95% of the correspondences it accepts violate the ground-truth epipolar geometry. One inflated statistic is read by two subsystems against thresholds in opposite directions, so keyframing starves while relocalization accepts almost every candidate. The same statistic, read at keyframe-pair baselines, separates the confident collapse from working runs on the ETH3D dark sequences without ground truth or extra computation (in-sample). Low-light-adapted weights take tracked trajectories from 1/6 to 5/6, as does retuning two thresholds; neither yields accurate ones, because the adaptation withdraws confidence from wrong geometry rather than finding right geometry. Replayed on a Jetson AGX Orin carried by a legged robot, the mechanism's signature reproduces on the two darkest of four routes, and which of its faces appears varies with route geometry and sensor encoding. The network does not lose confidence in the dark; it manufactures it.
authors: Shrikrishna Bhagirath Rajule, Srinath Neelamagam, Aniket Bera
bullets: Noise-only and real dark frame pairs produce nearly identical, high self-consistency, masking the absence of reliable scene structure.
On a dark sequence, the system processed 1,605 frames and produced 7 keyframes while rejecting no factor-graph edges; over 95% of accepted correspondences violated ground-truth epipolar geometry.
A single inflated statistic is interpreted in opposite ways by keyframing and relocalization, starving keyframes while accepting almost every relocalization candidate.
Reading the statistic at keyframe-pair baselines separates confident collapse from working runs on ETH3D dark sequences without ground truth or extra computation, in-sample.
Low-light weights and threshold retuning increased tracking but did not recover accurate geometry; the failure signature also reproduced on the two darkest of four Jetson robot routes.

Starved of structure, the network invents geometry that agrees with itself, the statistic rises to about 0.7, keyframing starves (7 keyframes in 1 605 frames) and relocalization accepts wrong anchors (497 of 543 on plant_dark). papers.selection_reason: Analyzes silent failure and confidence miscalibration in learned dense visual SLAM; relevant to embodied perception and 3D foundation model reliability.
papers.title: Confidently Lost: Silent Failure and Edge Deployment of Dense Visual SLAM under Photon Starvation
papers.tldr: Under photon starvation, dense learned visual SLAM can generate highly consistent but incorrect geometry, causing silent failure in real-time edge deployment.

papers.abstract: We introduce Audio-Visual Rearrangement (AVR), a novel task in which an agent hears a spoken request, retrieves a suitable object, and delivers it to the requesting user or an instruction-specified destination. AVR requires the agent to understand the spoken request and acoustically localize the speaker for delivery. To support this task, we construct a dataset covering three query types: explicit target specification, speaker-relative spatial references, and implicit user intent, spanning eight subtypes with diverse object selection and delivery requirements. Moreover, we propose a framework that integrates a motion-aware spatial audio module into an audio-visual large language model to encode spatial cues from the spoken request and update them as the agent moves. We further incorporate auxiliary supervision for speech understanding, spatial audio perception, and visual grounding through multitask instruction tuning to improve action prediction. Experiments establish baseline performance in both seen and unseen environments, laying the groundwork for future research on embodied intelligence and human-robot interaction. The code will be publicly available soon.
authors: Ruohao Guo, Jiatong Ye, Chenwei Dong, Jinxing Zhou, Dantong Niu, Guangyao Li, Zhenbo Li
bullets: Defines a task combining speech understanding, object retrieval, speaker localization, and delivery.
Provides a dataset with three query types, eight subtypes, and varied object-selection and delivery requirements.
Integrates motion-aware spatial audio into an audio-visual large language model to track spatial cues during movement.
Uses multitask instruction tuning for speech understanding, spatial audio perception, and visual grounding.
Reports baseline results in seen and unseen environments; code is planned for public release.

papers.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents enable automated interactions with mobile, web, and desktop interfaces. However, their large memory footprint and repeated model calls hinder deployment on resource-constrained devices, motivating post-training quantization (PTQ) without full retraining. Quantization can degrade GUI response accuracy and distort the instruction-vision affinities and local spatial relations needed for GUI target selection. Small coordinate errors can cause missed clicks, while early action errors can alter subsequent interface states and disrupt task execution. Local reconstruction error alone does not directly assess whether these responses and relations are preserved. We propose GUI-Q, a PTQ framework that targets response and relation preservation with 4-bit weights and 16-bit activations (W4A16). Task-Sensitive Granularity Allocation (TSGA) allocates finer groups under a scale-byte budget by combining response sensitivity with the measured reduction in activation-weighted distortion. Relation-Preserving Symmetry Selection (RPSS) then selects symmetric or asymmetric grids to preserve instruction-vision affinities and local spatial relations in GUIs. Across three GUI-capable models, GUI-Q improves mean grounding TargetHit by 8.04 to 12.55 points over the strongest evaluated 4-bit configurations, while reducing static peak graphics processing unit (GPU) memory by 49.9% to 56.2% relative to bfloat16 (BF16). Fixed-output replay with packed 4-bit execution provides 1.7 to 2.8 times model-call speedups. The code will be released.
authors: Tianqi Li, Yang Wang, Xin He, Le Zhang, Yun Liu
bullets: Addresses GUI-agent deployment constraints from large memory use and repeated model calls.
Uses Task-Sensitive Granularity Allocation to assign finer quantization groups where response-sensitive distortion is reduced most.
Uses Relation-Preserving Symmetry Selection to retain instruction–vision affinities and local spatial relations.
Across three GUI-capable models, improves grounding TargetHit by 8.04–12.55 points over evaluated 4-bit baselines.
Reduces peak GPU memory by 49.9%–56.2% versus BF16 and achieves 1.7–2.8× model-call speedups with packed 4-bit execution.

papers.abstract: Pathologists reach a diagnosis by integrating morphological evidence across regions and magnifications along viewing trajectories. Existing pathology AI rarely reflects this process: models predict from selected image regions, answer questions within fixed visual contexts, or navigate slides autonomously. We formalize pathologist-led streaming diagnosis, in which the pathologist controls navigation while a copilot selectively describes incoming views and synthesizes accumulated evidence into a final diagnosis. We record five pathologists' viewing trajectories on 1,791 TCGA whole-slide images (WSIs) spanning ten organs, with response labels, morphological descriptions, and session-level findings and diagnoses. We construct PathStreamBench to assess response timing, morphological description, and session-level diagnosis, alongside auxiliary video understanding. We introduce PathStream, which jointly learns streaming responses and diagnosis through two-stage training, with a diagnosis-attention loss guiding attention during diagnosis to relevant visual and textual evidence accumulated as the examination unfolds. PathStream outperforms 14 vision-language models and three domain-fine-tuned baselines on the core tasks, achieving a trajectory WSI Relevance score of 77.87, surpassing the strongest domain-fine-tuned baseline's 62.76. Without additional training, its diagnostic capabilities generalize to new educational pathology videos, three external centers, and an unseen organ.
authors: Dankai Liao, YuFeng Wu, Ziyue Wang, Guanxi Liu, Tianyi Zhang, Zeyu Liu, Linghan Cai, Yueming Jin
bullets: The work addresses the gap between pathology AI and pathologists’ trajectory-based, multi-region, multi-magnification diagnostic workflow.
Five pathologists’ viewing trajectories across 1,791 TCGA whole-slide images and ten organs support PathStreamBench, covering response timing, morphology, session-level findings, and diagnosis.
PathStream jointly learns streaming responses and diagnosis, using a diagnosis-attention loss to focus on relevant accumulated visual and textual evidence.
It outperforms 14 vision-language models and three domain-fine-tuned baselines; its trajectory WSI Relevance score is 77.87 versus 62.76 for the strongest domain-fine-tuned baseline.
Without additional training, the model generalizes to educational pathology videos, three external centers, and an unseen organ.

papers.abstract: Can a language model learn more from the same information simply by encountering it in different forms? We answer this in the affirmative by introducing Multimodal View Training (MVT), a simple training approach that presents identical information through text, speech, and images, without requiring new facts or supervision. Starting from a text sample, MVT generates corresponding audio and rendered-text image views, and trains a multimodal language model to produce the same target output across all three views. To further bring these benefits to text-only large language models (LLMs), we train lightweight connector modules to pretrained audio and vision encoders, allowing the LLM to learn from multimodal inputs while retaining its text-only architecture at inference. Across question answering, machine unlearning, and knowledge editing, adaptive MVT improves QA recall by +15.2 percentage points, forget quality by +40.7 points, and editing generality by +25.2 points over text-only training. Combining MVT with standard augmentation further improves QA and editing generality. Our theoretical analysis illustrates how training across modalities can shift weight updates toward shared factual content and reduce their reliance on features specific to each view.
authors: Devang Kulshreshtha, Priyanka Kaswan, Minh Pham, Chinmay Hegde, Niv Cohen
bullets: Uses identical content in text, audio, and rendered-text image views, training the model to produce the same output from each.
Connects pretrained audio and vision encoders to text-only LLMs through lightweight modules, preserving text-only inference.
Improves question-answering recall, machine unlearning, and knowledge-editing generality over text-only training.
Combining MVT with standard augmentation further benefits QA and editing generality.
Theory suggests multimodal training emphasizes shared factual content over view-specific features.

papers.abstract: A central challenge in generating instructional videos for reasoning-intensive topics is to show how and why the state changes at each step. Even when an animation renders successfully, the depicted object relationships and state transitions can conflict with the explanation, making the reasoning difficult to follow. We present ReVAgent, a multi-agent framework that solves a problem, generates keyframes for its explanation, and synthesizes an instructional video. The agents share the execution record of a solution program, reuse intermediate results and constructions in the scenes, and check rendered keyframes to guide revisions to the solution or the scenes. We also introduce a multidimensional rubric for assessing whether generated videos present the problem clearly, organize the steps coherently, and use visuals to explain the reasoning. We calibrate a multimodal judge using human ratings and apply it to instructional videos for mathematics and algorithms. In the evaluated samples, ReVAgent presents multi-step reasoning coherently and uses diagrams to show how key operations lead to subsequent states.

papers.abstract: Model routing assigns each query to a suitable foundation model, but tasks and available models keep changing, and existing routers are either untrained for the pool at hand or fit once and forget earlier tasks when updated. We present AdaptRouter, an adaptive router trained by policy learning: a compact multimodal decision model reads each question with cards describing the current experts and learns from native task feedback, without routing labels, to select one frozen expert. Open-weight and API experts share the router, its inputs, and the quality-cost trade-off but use different losses: cheap open-weight experts are explored with RL, whereas paid API experts are queried once and their cached feedback is reused as soft labels. New tasks are learned without replay, new experts enter as cards, and an open-weight quality-first advantage provably keeps cost from overriding quality. Across four task stages, AdaptRouter loses at most 0.4 points on earlier tasks, whereas feedback-trained routers lose up to 7.0, and as its pool grows from three to ten experts, its accuracy rises from 67.2% to 72.1%. On five API models, it exceeds GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra (low) by over 22 points at under a third of their cost.
authors: Jingpu Yang, Fengxian Ji, Tianhao Li, Juanfan Wu, Yufeng Wang, Shuxin Zheng, Xiaoqing Zhang
bullets: Addresses routers that cannot adapt to new tasks or forget earlier ones when updated.
Uses policy learning with a compact multimodal router that reads task questions and expert cards, requiring no routing labels.
Explores cheap open-weight experts with reinforcement learning and reuses cached feedback for paid API experts.
Adds new tasks without replay and incorporates new experts by adding their cards.

Across four task stages, earlier-task performance drops by at most 0.4 points; accuracy increases from 67.2% to 72.1% as the pool grows from 3 to 10 experts, while outperforming two cited API models by over 22 points at less than one-third their cost.

papers.abstract: Continual learning in language models is commonly studied in the incremental learning (IL) setting, where a model learns a sequence of tasks and is evaluated through its final classifier or language-model (LM) head. This interface, however, does not indicate where forgetting occurs: a drop in accuracy may reflect representation degradation in the backbone, readout mismatch in the head, or both. We therefore argue that backward transfer (BWT) and forward transfer (FWT) should be interpreted as interface-dependent quantities rather than as single modellevel properties. We study three evaluation interfaces: the trained head, which is updated sequentially with the backbone; a probe newly trained on frozen backbone features; and a classifier-free backbone diagnostic. They measure deployed performance, recoverability under a new readout, and representation separability, respectively. Across class-incremental experiments with encoder and decoder language backbones, plus task-incremental sanity checks, conclusions about forgetting and plasticity change with the interface: the trained head often indicates severe forgetting, the probe near-complete recoverability, and the backbone diagnostic intermediate representation drift with a consistent negative relation between stability and plasticity. This relation holds for clustering-free diagnostics such as nearest-class-mean accuracy and across five clustering algorithms and three metrics. Finally, Just LM-Head Tuning (JLT), a head-only intervention on a fixed incrementally trained backbone, recovers 96-99% of the gap to joint training for replayand distillation-based methods but only about three quarters for plain sequential fine-tuning, suggesting that many failures attributed to catastrophic forgetting reflect head-backbone mismatch plus partial representation drift. Our results call for reporting where forgetting is measured, not only how much.
authors: Keuntae Kim, Beomseok Lee, Hyunwoo Kim, Yong Suk Choi
bullets: Backward and forward transfer are interface-dependent, not single model-level properties.
A trained head often shows severe forgetting, while a new probe reveals near-complete recoverability; backbone diagnostics fall between these extremes.
Across encoder and decoder backbones, stability and plasticity show a consistent negative relationship, supported by multiple clustering-free and clustering-based diagnostics.
Just LM-Head Tuning recovers most of the joint-training gap for replay- and distillation-based methods, but less for plain sequential fine-tuning.
The study recommends reporting the evaluation interface alongside forgetting and transfer measurements.

We measure transfer through (a) the trained head, (b) a probe, and (c) the backbone diagnostic, a classifier-free proxy for representation separability. papers.abstract: Robot leading requires executing a route while continuously adapting to a designated follower. Existing robot-leading systems often mediate follower understanding and physical route execution through explicit states, planners, or modular interfaces; directly learning this coupling through end-to-end trajectory prediction can instead entangle route execution with follower response. We introduce LeadVLA, a structured multimodal policy that preserves the route as an explicit Path reference while learning a Pace for route progress and a Residual for local follower- and scene-conditioned adaptation. To make this problem trainable and measurable, we develop LeadInfra, a configurable Unreal Engine-based closed-loop data-generation infrastructure from which we instantiate an approximately 4M-sample training corpus, and LeadBench, a standardized benchmark with 108 fully held-out closed-loop episodes. LeadVLA achieves the highest task success (39.6%) among evaluated robot policies on LeadBench while maintaining strong route fidelity and follower responsiveness, and transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning. Project Page: https://louiszengCN.github.io/LeadVLA_PAGE/
authors: Tianle Zeng, Hanjing Ye, Bingyi Xia, Yuchen Zhou, Zibo Zhang, Yufei Huang, Yonggen Ling, Hong Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coupling route execution with continuous follower- and scene-aware adaptation.
Uses a structured multimodal policy with an explicit Path, learned Pace for route progress, and Residual for local adaptation.
Introduces LeadInfra for closed-loop Unreal Engine data generation and LeadBench with 108 held-out episodes.
Trains on an approximately 4M-sample corpus and reaches 39.6% task success, the highest among evaluated policies on LeadBench.
Transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Traffic forecasting is essential for intelligent transportation systems. However, traditional deep-learning models often rely heavily on high-quality observations. Recent LLM-based approaches incorporate pretrained knowledge to improve forecasting, but they remain sensitive to input perturbations and struggle to preserve long-term patterns. To address this, we propose STMemoLLM, a spatial-temporal memory-augmented LLM for robust traffic forecasting. STMemoLLM introduces memory prototypes to compress inputs into compact summary tokens while extracting reliable dynamics from residual signals, achieving a balance between stability and variability. Specifically, a memory-enhanced tokenizer encodes prototypes and sensor characteristics into attention biases to guide adaptive compression of correlated sensors into semantic summary tokens. A memory-calibrated router further evaluates contextual deviation, compression deficiency, and prototype alignment to identify reliable residual signals, which complement the summaries while suppressing noise. Extensive experiments on eight real-world datasets show that STMemoLLM achieves state-of-the-art performance. Additional experiments examine point masking, additive Gaussian noise, structured missingness, and limited training data, demonstrating strong robustness. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/STMemoLLM-70BF.
authors: Jian Zhou, Binqing Wu, Zongjiang Shang, Wanghui Qiu, Dongliang Cui, Chenxi Jin, Yue Yu, Xinyi Fu, Ling Chen

Experiments across eight real-world datasets report state-of-the-art performance and robustness to masking, Gaussian noise, structured missingness, and limited training data.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon, history-dependent robotic manipulation often requires acting on visual cues that have disappeared, such as an object indicated earlier or a target hidden under a moving cup. The key challenge is to maintain what past evidence means for the next action as the scene changes. We introduce Recurrent Memory Reasoning (RMR), an explicit reasoning step that connects memory to action inside a vision-language-action model (VLA), with no external reasoning model. At each update, the VLA first infers an event from visual evidence, then revises the task state and grounds a subgoal in the current scene to guide action generation. Carrying the state and subgoal across updates lets remembered identities and task progress determine the current target, doubling RoboMME success over an otherwise identical model without recurrence. Joint training lets one VLA both reason and act; because its memory decisions are text tokens with exact likelihoods, GRPO refines them from rollout rewards without making action generation stochastic. Among the compared methods, RMR-VLA achieves the best results on RoboMME (66.46% overall, 79.83% on the Reference category) and LIBERO-Mem (90.08%).
authors: Yiheng Du, Jingqi Tian, Xu Jiang, Jiexuan Zhang, Shuyu Wang, Zecheng Tang, Jian Zhang
bullets: Maintains task state and subgoals across visual updates so remembered object identities and progress guide current actions.

Jointly trains one VLA to reason and act without an external reasoning model.
Uses exact likelihoods of memory text tokens for GRPO refinement from rollout rewards while keeping action generation deterministic.
Reports 66.46% on RoboMME, 79.83% on its Reference category, and 90.08% on LIBERO-Mem; it doubles RoboMME success versus an otherwise identical non-recurrent model.

papers.abstract: LLM agents now propose research ideas and run the experiments that test them, but they train every run to its end, whereas a researcher reads a run's configuration and the beginning of its curve and stops the runs that show no promise. Reading a run this way takes more than describing or implementing a training method: it takes knowing what a design choice does to a run. We build Tea Leaves to measure this knowledge on 682 real training runs across pretraining, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning (RL): a forecaster sees the first 20% of a run with its configuration, description, and code, and predicts the rest. Across 11 LLMs and a range of forecasting baselines, the strongest LLMs match or exceed the best curve fitter on smooth loss curves (skill 0.66 against 0.62) and lead on noisy RL reward curves (0.43 against 0.13). What bounds every forecaster is what the log carries: on sparsely logged community runs all methods lose most of their skill, and none reliably flags a failing run in advance. Beyond the curve, information helps and effort does not: related runs in the prompt cut the error on loss curves by 39%, and knowledge of training dynamics lets the strongest LLMs order all 36 pairs of runs that differ by a described code change, which the early curves do not separate, whereas tools add little. This knowledge can be learned from logged runs: a small open model trained on public runs matches the best LLM on loss curves. Applied to the progress curves of research agents, the same reading ranks tasks by their remaining headroom, although for a single agent run it does not improve on the last value. We release the benchmark, the trained readers, and their training data to test and train LLMs' understanding of training and to help research agents decide which runs deserve their compute.

papers.title: Reading the Tea Leaves, Again: Can Large Language Models Predict Language Model Training Runs?

papers.abstract: General-purpose large language model (LLM) agents can develop complete solvers for combinatorial optimization problems. Their specialization, however, often relies on workflows engineered for individual problems, limiting the reuse of development expertise. We propose AutoSECO, an automated skill evolution method that learns reusable solver-development guidance from experience. The challenge is that external evaluation measures the completed solver, while the skill guides decisions during development. AutoSECO connects this feedback to guidance deficiencies by tracing performance shortfalls through solver code and recorded development decisions. Revisions are expressed as general instructions and retained only if a fresh solver developed under the revised skill achieves a lower mean evaluation gap. Evolved solely on the traveling salesperson problem (TSP), the skill guides fresh agents in developing solvers for capacitated vehicle routing, job-shop scheduling, and three-dimensional bin packing without further skill evolution. On TSP, the final mean benchmark gap is 0.52\%, compared with 0.98\% for the skill-evolution baseline SkillOpt. Across all four problems, the evolved skill achieves better aggregate results than no skill guidance, the initial skill, and SkillOpt. The same frozen skill also supports solver development under alternative model--harness configurations. These findings suggest that solver-development experience can be retained as reusable expertise for general-purpose LLM agents.
authors: Zirui Zhu, Cong Zhang, Ni Zhang, Kuan Xu, Zhiguang Cao
bullets: Addresses the limited reuse of problem-specific workflows for LLM-generated combinatorial optimization solvers.
Traces solver performance shortfalls through code and development decisions to identify deficiencies in reusable skill guidance.
Retains revised guidance only when a freshly developed solver achieves a lower mean evaluation gap.
A skill evolved only on TSP transfers to vehicle routing, job-shop scheduling, and 3D bin packing, including under alternative model–harness configurations.
On TSP, AutoSECO reaches a 0.52% mean benchmark gap versus 0.98% for SkillOpt; it also achieves better aggregate results than the listed comparison settings across all four problems.

papers.abstract: Personalized large language models (LLMs) should continually adapt to users' evolving preferences. Yet extracting preference changes from noisy interaction histories while supporting inexpensive updates remains challenging. We introduce WASP (Weight Adaptation for Streaming Personalization), a recurrent framework that captures fine-grained preferences directly from raw user interactions and generates personalized LoRA adapters without expensive per-user optimization. Specifically, WASP achieves this by training a shared hypernetwork that maintains a compact user representation and outputs adapter weights in a single forward pass. As new interactions arrive, WASP updates this representation without reprocessing full interaction history, enabling continual adaptation with per-update costs independent of history length. Experiments on personalization benchmarks and chronological interaction streams show that WASP sustains high-quality personalization over long horizons under fixed compute and storage budgets. Together, these results support efficient streaming personalization and facilitate privacy-preserving on-device deployment.
authors: Linxi Xie, Chonghua Liao, Mengxuan Wu, Guandao Yang, Zhangyang Wang, Kai Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting to changing user preferences from noisy interaction histories at low cost.
Uses a recurrent framework with a shared hypernetwork that maintains a compact user representation.
Produces personalized LoRA adapter weights directly, avoiding expensive per-user optimization.
Updates user representations incrementally, with per-update cost independent of interaction-history length.
Experiments show sustained personalization quality over long horizons under fixed compute and storage budgets, supporting on-device deployment.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has progressed from simple control tasks to complex real-world challenges with large state spaces. While RL excels in these tasks, training time remains a limitation. Reward shaping is a popular solution, but existing methods often rely on value functions, which face scalability issues. This paper presents a novel safety-oriented reward-shaping framework inspired by barrier functions, offering simplicity and ease of implementation across various environments and tasks. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed reward formulations, we conduct simulation experiments on the Unitree Go1 quadruped robot in Isaacgym. The policy was better than the existing baselines and reduced safety violations from 27% to 0.1% without almost any compromise on the performance.
authors: Janani S K, Manan Tayal, Shishir N. Y Kolathaya
bullets: Targets slow RL training and safety violations in complex, large-state-space tasks.
Introduces simple, broadly applicable safety-oriented reward formulations inspired by barrier functions.
Evaluated in simulation on the Unitree Go1 quadruped using Isaac Gym.
Outperformed existing baselines, reducing safety violations from 27% to 0.1% with little performance compromise.

papers.abstract: Rendering long text as images lets a vision-language model (VLM) read a document with fewer input tokens, and evaluations often count mainly these prefill tokens. We show that for reasoning models this accounting is incomplete. Across five models and two long-context benchmarks, reading the rendered document makes the model think longer: decode length grows by 1.5-3.5x on the four general-purpose VLMs tested, and under typical output pricing this decode tax makes image input more expensive than text for two of the five models on QuALITY. Unrecoverable information loss is not sufficient to explain the tax at moderate compression: Qwen's OCR of the same images recovers 98.7% of words, and feeding Kimi-K3 its own transcription as text restores text-mode reasoning length and accuracy. Whether compression pays off reduces to an exchange rate, (1-1/c)/(r-1), that must exceed the workload's price-weighted ratio of output to input tokens; this accounting decomposition shows why Kimi-K3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash can benefit and Qwen and GLM cannot. None of the training-free signals we test predicts the tax before generation. As a practical heuristic, an image-first policy that sends only inputs with a per-input compression ratio of at least 1.6 to images and falls back to text once image-mode reasoning costs as much as the input's prefill saving cuts the bill by 6-14% on Kimi-K3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at an accuracy cost of 0.3-1.2 points; on QuALITY, asking for a reasoning budget on both paths is a stronger lever.
authors: Ziqing Ge
bullets: Across five models and two long-context benchmarks, rendered documents increased decode length by 1.5–3.5× for four general-purpose VLMs.
The added reasoning cost is not explained solely by OCR loss: Qwen recovered 98.7% of words, while Kimi-K3’s text transcription restored text-mode reasoning length and accuracy.
Compression is worthwhile when its input-token savings outweigh the price-weighted output-token increase, favoring Kimi-K3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash but not Qwen and GLM.
An image-first policy using a 1.6× compression threshold reduced bills by 6–14% on two models, with a 0.3–1.2 point accuracy cost.
Training-free signals tested did not predict the decode tax before generation; matched reasoning budgets were a stronger lever on QuALITY.

papers.selection_reason: Decode-aware cost analysis of optical context compression in reasoning VLMs; relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: When Does Optical Context Compression Pay Off? A Decode-Aware Cost Analysis of Reasoning VLMs
papers.tldr: Optical context compression can reduce input tokens but often increases reasoning output enough to erase its cost advantage, so it pays off only under favorable model- and workload-specific conditions.

papers.abstract: Edge cases are not the long tail; they are the norm. An embodied system deployed across changing environments, bodies, objects, and tasks will routinely encounter combinations that were absent from its training data. General-purpose physical intelligence therefore requires world models that reuse prior knowledge, predict consequences, and adapt with little or no additional training. Yet current evaluations of conditional video generation emphasize visual quality, prompt alignment, or isolated physical plausibility, leaving systematic generalization difficult to measure. We introduce AxE Bench, a benchmark that organizes condition changes along eight factors of the acting agent and of its environment, and pairs every original condition with controlled variants that change one side or both. WBench-plus applies the same structure to an existing multi-turn benchmark, pairing each WBench scenario with variants on the environment side, through its world setting or camera behavior, or on the agent side, through its interaction instructions. Additionally, to score generated futures, we develop an evaluation harness that combines vision-language reasoning with targeted computer-vision evidence, converting each video into temporally localized events and comparing generated events with reference events in both time and semantics. We summarize each model with the AxE Score, event Fidelity weighted by its Stability across original-variant pairs. Across twenty models, generated events match reference events far more often in timing than in content: no model exceeds a Fidelity of 13.01, the highest Stability is 0.55, and the highest AxE Score is 7.10. Together, these components turn world-model generalization from an informal aspiration into a falsifiable evaluation program for real and simulated interactions. Our project website can be found at: AxEBench.github.io
authors: Haiyu Xu, Yiyang Chen, Jiayi Zhou, Jiaming Ji, Juntao Dai, Yaodong Yang, Boyuan Chen
bullets: Tests eight factors involving the acting agent and environment, including paired variants that alter one or both sides.
Extends the framework to WBench-plus with changes to world settings, camera behavior, or interaction instructions.
Scores generated futures using vision-language reasoning and computer-vision evidence to extract and compare localized events.
Across 20 models, event timing matched references more reliably than event content; reported maxima were Fidelity 13.01, Stability 0.55, and AxE Score 7.10.
Frames generalization as a falsifiable evaluation program for real and simulated interactions.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models can extract structured fields from scanned financial documents, yet they provide no indication of when a field might be wrong. We derive per-field confidence estimates from the token log-probabilities the model already produces, via a token-to-span alignment procedure that maps logprobs onto each extracted value within the structured JSON output. Evaluated on two benchmarks (CORD v2 receipts, Kleister NDA legal contracts) with three VLM families, the minimum token probability per field achieves Area Under the ROC Curve (AUROC) 0.74-0.91 for error detection, far exceeding verbalized confidence (0.53-0.56). The uncertain fields form a natural training curriculum: fine-tuning via Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO) improves accuracy from 78.5% to 87.5% on CORD (67 examples) and from 70.7% to 75.1% on multi-page NDA contracts (259 examples), while substantially improving error detection on Kleister NDA (AUROC 0.70 to 0.85, Area Under the Accuracy-Rejection Curve (AUARC) 0.78 to 0.92). The loop requires no annotation beyond the training-split ground truth, demonstrating that confidence-guided curriculum selection transfers to complex multi-page documents when combined with native multi-image training. A frontier model (Claude Sonnet 4) used as a pseudo-label judge achieves ~92% reward agreement with ground truth on both benchmarks, suggesting this loop can operate without human annotation.
authors: Varad Srivastava, Victor Casas Hernandez
bullets: Addresses the lack of trustworthy uncertainty estimates when VLMs extract structured fields from scanned financial documents.
Aligns token log-probabilities with extracted JSON spans; the minimum token probability per field is a strong error signal.
Across CORD v2 and Kleister NDA with three VLM families, token confidence reaches AUROC 0.74–0.91, outperforming verbalized confidence.
Using uncertain fields as a GRPO training curriculum improves extraction accuracy and, on Kleister NDA, error-detection AUROC from 0.70 to 0.85.
A frontier model can serve as a pseudo-label judge with about 92% reward agreement, suggesting reduced reliance on human annotation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Pipeline overview. Bottom: The uncertain fields form a training curriculum for GRPO fine-tuning, closing a self-improvement loop. Dashed arrow indicates an optional next iteration.

Figure 6: Selective prediction curves on Kleister NDA before and after GRPO fine-tuning. The baseline model’s confidence signal is noisy and barely exceeds overall accuracy at intermediate coverage; after GRPO, the curve is smooth and maintains near-perfect accuracy up to 20% coverage, enabling practical selective-prediction workflows on multi-page legal documents.

Figure 5: Selective prediction curves on CORD before and after GRPO fine-tuning. The post-GRPO curve is uniformly higher, reflecting both improved accuracy (87.5% vs. 78.5% on the expanded scoreable set) and better calibration (the model’s confidence ranking aligns more closely with actual correctness).

Figure 3: Reliability diagram (Qwen3-VL-8B, CORD, greedy). ECE= 0.165. Bars show observed accuracy per confidence bin; the gap below the diagonal indicates systematic overconfidence. Bottom: sample counts per bin.

Figure 4: Selective prediction curve (Qwen3-VL-8B, CORD). AUARC=0.942. Reviewing in confidence order catches errors rapidly.

Table 2: min_prob AUROC (with 95% bootstrap CI half-width) across three model families and two datasets. All CIs exclude 0.5; the signal is statistically discriminative in every condition. Table 5: Greedy vs. sampling on CORD (Qwen3-VL-8B). Sampling producesmore aligned fields but degrades every calibration metric. The temperature-scaled distribution no longer reflects true uncertainty.
Table 3: Error detection AUROC for individual signals and combinations (Qwen3-VL-8B, CORD, greedy). The composite uses domain-calibrated weights; the rank-average ensemble is parameter-free.

Table 9: Per-field accuracy on NDA before and after GRPO (8-page evaluation). Δ: percentage-point change. +/−: fields that switched from incorrect to correct or vice versa. AMBER accuracy is based on only 12 fields and should be interpreted cautiously.
Table 6: Platt scaling on min_prob (CORD, 500 random splits per size). GREEN accuracy rises substantially; AUROC is unchanged (monotone transform).

Table 7: Self-improvement on CORD (67 training examples, rank-16 QLoRA). The total field count exceeds the 285 scored fields in Table 1 because the improved model now produces valid JSON for fields previously left empty or unparseable (including nested sub-fields), expanding the scoreable set. Note: the Base A+R count of 285 is a coincidence—it refers to non-GREEN fields from the larger evaluation set, not the 285 aligned fields in Table 1. SFT maximises precision; GRPO maximises throughput.

papers.selection_reason: VLM confidence estimation and GRPO fine-tuning for document extraction; fits multimodal LLM topic.
papers.title: Could This BE Any More Wrong? Teaching VLMs to Know What They Don't Know in Document Extraction
papers.tldr: Token-level confidence from VLM outputs reliably identifies erroneous document fields and can guide training to improve both extraction accuracy and error detection.

papers.abstract: Robot policies act in real time but fail without knowing why, whereas a reasoning agent that watches the robot can often tell what went wrong. Existing systems either hand the agent control, which takes minutes per episode, or let it send instructions. Yet a policy follows a new instruction only from a fresh start, since a half-finished task leaves it in states outside its training data. Nor can an instruction fix how the robot moves. If a drift keeps pulling the hand to the left, "push right, slightly" is not a task the policy has learned. We propose RoboThink, in which the agent thinks and the policy learns to act on the agent's guidance. An instruction channel tells the policy what to do. When the user says "the milk, not the butter" after the robot has started, the agent rewrites the instruction and the robot undoes its own motion, with no training. A feedback channel tells it how to move. It is taught from the agent alone with agent-labelled DAgger, role tokens and counterfactual feedback, and is read only by the policy's action module. On LIBERO, RoboThink with Claude Opus 5.5 raises success from 0.09 to 0.87 under an unknown constant drift and from 0.42 to 0.84 under a random one. It also completes misheard and changed requests in 0.91 to 1.00 of the episodes. Acting alone, GPT-6 Astra needs 2.1 min per success and over a million tokens per episode, whereas RoboThink needs 55 s and 8k tokens. The same recipe works across policies, for both vision-language-action models and world action models, and across robots, from one arm to two arms and a mobile manipulator. On all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with two arms, success rises from 0.12 to 0.74 under the constant drift and from 0.31 to 0.56 under the random one. Finally, the agent is a plug-in. A policy taught by one agent works with other agents, including open-weight ones, and grows stronger with a stronger agent, without retraining.
authors: Yunbei Zhang, Zijian Jin, Janet Wang, Xingchen Zhao, Zhenyu Zhang, Weirui Ye, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses failures from unknown motion drift, mid-task instruction changes, and misheard requests that ordinary policy instructions cannot fix.
Uses separate instruction and feedback channels, agent-labelled DAgger, role tokens, and counterfactual feedback; only the policy’s action module reads the feedback.
On LIBERO, success improves from 0.09 to 0.87 under constant drift and from 0.42 to 0.84 under random drift.
The system handles changed or misheard requests in 0.91–1.00 of episodes while using 55 seconds and 8k tokens per success, versus 2.1 minutes and over 1M tokens for an acting agent.
Transfers across policies, agents, robots, and multi-arm tasks; agent replacement or improvement requires no policy retraining.

figures.caption: Figure 7. Does the policy do what the feedback says? Change of the first planned chunk when feedback describing a drift is added (one dot per case and arm axis). (a) Fast-WAM reacts to the presence of the text, not to what it says, and the opposite feedback moves it the same way. (b) DAgger alone follows the direction only partly. (c) RoboThink follows the feedback (cosine 0.95, gain 0.90) and moves the other way for the opposite feedback.

Figure 3. Qualitative examples on LIBERO (front camera). (a) Under the constant drift, the policy alone twists away from the bottle. With RoboThink, the agent infers the drift from the commanded and actual motion after the first chunk, and the policy, reading its feedback, grasps the juice and places it (five agent calls, 65 s in all). (b) Only the agent knows the user’s request. As told, the robot delivers the cream cheese. With RoboThink, the agent rewrites the instruction, and the robot undoes its two chunks and fetches the milk.

Figure 2. Teaching the feedback channel from the reasoning agent. (1) On training tasks under training drifts, the robot executes the policy’s plan corrected by the agent’s estimate. (2) Each state yields three kinds of training samples: the agent’s feedback with the corrected plan as target, counterfactual feedback for another drift with the matching target, or no feedback with the plan itself. These targets can only be fitted by reading the feedback. (3) Only the action module and the role tokens are trained, and the true drift is never used.

Figure 4. Success within a time budget on two arms. Share of RoboTwin 2.0 episodes under drift solved within a wall-clock budget, on the episodes of Tab. 1. Within two minutes, RoboThink solves more episodes than the agents alone do within thirty.

RoboThink (taught by Claude Opus 5.5) with ten reasoning agents on LIBERO: success rate under drift (mean of the two drifts) against the accuracy of the agent, measured on the same saved calls for every agent. Dashed: the policy alone. Every agent helps, and success grows with the accuracy of the agent (r = 0.96).
