Success rate on LIBERO with perfect feedback, read by different modules of the same policy, trained with agent-labelled DAgger from Claude Opus 5.5. Read by the video module, the feedback does not help. Read by the action module only, it gives the largest gain.

Table 7. What to do. Success rate. Top: reworded requests of LIBERO-Para [16]. Bottom, no drift: the robot is told another task or object and only the agent knows the request (misheard), or the user corrects it after three chunks (changed). Para.: reworded as in LIBERO-Para. No agent: the same policy without the agent. [INST], with undo before redo, needs no training, so it also works with Cosmos Policy off the shelf.

Table 1. The agent alone, the policy alone, and both on the same episodes. Time: median wall-clock time to success, agent calls included. Tokens: input tokens per episode, cached context included. RoboThink succeeds at least as often as the agents alone, in a fraction of their time and tokens.

Table 3. Other policies and robots, each before and after the recipe, with live Claude Opus 5.5. RoboTwin 2.0: two arms, joint drift, tasks outside the feedback training. RoboCasa: a mobile manipulator in unseen kitchens. The recipe works on a VLA, two WAMs and three robots.

Table 6. Building the feedback channel. Success rate on LIBERO, taught by and run with Claude Opus 5.5. All rows above the last are trained from the same agent-labelled episodes, one eighth of RoboThink’s. DAgger rows: only the action module reads the feedback unless stated. Each ingredient adds to the gain.

Table 4. RoboTwin 2.0 under its official protocol: success rate on all 50 tasks, mean over tasks. Last row: number of tasks on which RoboThink is better or worse than Fast-WAM. AW-0: numbers from its paper, which reports no drift (AW-0 under drift: Sec. E). The gain holds on almost every task.
Table 2. Feedback about the motion. Success rate on LIBERO with Fast-WAM, best in bold. The untrained policy is hurt by the feedback, whereas RoboThink acts on it, close to the privileged rule.

Table 9. Scenes that differ from training or change during the episode, success rate under random drift. LIBERO-Plus [10]: visually perturbed variants of the test tasks. LIBERO-MAX [42] Lite: one event during the episode. Agent: Claude Opus 5.5 with [FB]+[INST].

papers.selection_reason: Integrates LLM agent guidance with robot policy learning via DAgger and counterfactual feedback; directly relevant to embodied AI.
papers.title: RoboThink: Let the Agent Think, Let the Policy Act
papers.tldr: RoboThink lets a reasoning agent guide a robot policy through task instructions and motion feedback, enabling fast recovery from drift and changing requests without retraining.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting renders photorealistic views in real time. However, a single scene often needs millions of Gaussians, so these models are costly to store and render. Pruning reduces this cost by keeping a subset of the Gaussians. A common score is the leave-one-out importance, which is the loss increase when a Gaussian alone is removed. At high pruning ratios, many Gaussians are removed together, so Gaussians that are redundant alone but essential together are lost. We present LMnOP (Leave-Many-Out Pruning), which estimates the importance of each Gaussian under the removal of the other Gaussians. This leave-many-out importance is the average loss increase when a Gaussian is removed while the others are also removed at random. We compute the exact mean and variance of each pixel's color under random removal in closed form, and approximate the importance from them without sampling removal patterns. We refine each Gaussian's probability of remaining with its importance and prune once at the end. Without fine-tuning, LMnOP achieves the best results in 16 of 18 metrics on three datasets at 90% and 99% removal. It improves SSIM and LPIPS over GaussianPOP in all 13 scenes.
authors: Sunjae Jeong, Jaeseung Kim, Hyoseok Hwang
bullets: Targets the storage and rendering cost of scenes containing millions of 3D Gaussians.
Addresses the limitation of leave-one-out scores, which can miss Gaussians that are redundant individually but important together.
Computes exact per-pixel color mean and variance under random Gaussian removal in closed form, avoiding sampled removal patterns.
Updates each Gaussian’s retention probability from its estimated leave-many-out importance and prunes only once.
Without fine-tuning, achieves the best result on 16 of 18 metrics across three datasets at 90% and 99% removal; improves SSIM and LPIPS over GaussianPOP in all 13 scenes.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of LMnOP. We then move each keep probability halfway toward bi and compute the importance again. Here bi is 1 for the K Gaussians with the highest importance and 0 for the others. After R importance computations, we keep these K Gaussians and prune the rest in one final step.

papers.abstract: Robot foundation policies provide learned execution capabilities, while programming agents can reason about failures and construct recovery behaviors. Combining them effectively requires learning when intervention helps and when the policy can reliably resume. This challenge is inherently temporal: the physical world continues to evolve during reasoning, and a useful recovery may become infeasible before a decision takes effect. We introduce Agent on Guard (AoG), a hierarchical framework that improves collaboration between a frozen base policy and a programming agent through physical experience. An evolving outer planner allocates control as the physical state evolves, aligning decisions with the physical clock with attention to observation freshness, remaining recovery windows, and the time required for reasoning, recovery, and subsequent execution. Coupled inner loops jointly refine intervention timing, recovery skills, and handoff conditions. Rather than judging recovery by local correction alone, AoG uses downstream task progress, failure recurrence, final outcomes, and resource consumption to improve both recovery behaviors and scheduling. This turns temporary agent solutions into reusable collaboration capabilities that complement the frozen policy. On RoboDojo-Sim, AoG achieves a success rate of 50.57% and a task score of 57.26, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 11.22 percentage points and 10.68 points, respectively. It also reduces end-to-end episode latency by 80.4% and online token consumption by 85.1% relative to the GPT-6 Astra agent.
authors: Gengming Cui, Mingfei Han, Jiawei Zhang, Mozheng Liao, Yunkai Guo, Minghao Jin, Tingwen Du, Salman Khan, Xiaojun Chang, Zhihui Li
bullets: Addresses the temporal challenge of deciding whether intervention remains useful as the physical state and recovery window evolve.
Uses a hierarchical outer planner to allocate control based on observation freshness, available recovery time, and reasoning, recovery, and execution costs.
Jointly improves intervention timing, recovery skills, and handoff conditions through physical experience.
Evaluates recovery using downstream progress, recurring failures, final outcomes, and resource consumption rather than local correction alone.
On RoboDojo-Sim, reports 50.57% success and 57.26 task score, with lower latency and token use than the GPT-6 Astra agent.

papers.selection_reason: Runtime intervention framework for robust robotic manipulation with self-improving recovery; directly relevant to robot learning and control.
papers.title: Agent on Guard: Self-Improving Runtime Intervention for Robust Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: Agent on Guard enables a frozen robot policy and programming agent to learn when and how to intervene, improving manipulation robustness while reducing reasoning overhead.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a robot policy for a new target task requires target demonstrations, but only a few are available. Demonstrations of other tasks can fill this gap, and demonstration curation selects the useful ones among these candidates. Retrieval-based curation selects the candidates that are most similar to the target demonstrations. Since it does not use the policy, any candidate that looks similar receives a high score. Performance-aware curation therefore estimates the effect of each candidate on the policy. However, this requires training on the candidates and takes a long time. We propose a third branch, policy-intrinsic curation, which uses the policy and still takes little time. It estimates this effect with forward passes of the pretrained policy and needs no training. We instantiate this branch with PICKER (Policy-Intrinsic Curation from Known Errors). It selects the candidates on which the policy makes errors that agree with those on the target demonstrations. PICKER reaches success rates comparable to those of performance-aware curation and takes about as long as retrieval-based curation. Its selection is also stable across seeds.
authors: Sunjae Jeong, Geunhyeok Yu, Dowoon Lee, Hyoseok Hwang
bullets: Few target-task demonstrations motivate reusing demonstrations from other tasks.
Retrieval-based curation ignores the policy, while performance-aware curation is effective but computationally slow.
PICKER uses forward passes of a pretrained policy to identify candidates whose errors align with target-demonstration errors.
It achieves success rates comparable to performance-aware curation, with runtime similar to retrieval-based curation.
Selection remains stable across random seeds.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of PICKER for the candidates of Figure 2. The pretrained policy processes every candidate sample and target sample with forward passes only. Its encoder returns the observation representation ϕ(s), and its action head returns the error e, which the figure labels as the residual. After centering, the affinity compares the representations of a candidate sample and a target sample, and the agreement compares the directions of their errors. Their product is the utility U , which is averaged into a score T (τ) for each candidate. PICKER selects the N candidates with the highest scores.

Figure 4. Similarity is not usefulness. Two sets from LIBERO-X with SmolVLA, each with one sample of a target demonstration and of two candidates. Each row shows the demonstrated and the predicted path of the end effector over the 50 steps of a sample. The arrow shows the error at the end, projected onto the image. In Set 2, the middle panels are magnified twice.

The smaller rows divide the agreement of the displayed samples by action component. The target loss is that of the other target demonstrations after one training step on the sample.

papers.abstract: Professional documents are a long-context workload that retrieval-style benchmarks do not capture. In a ten-domain enterprise collection, a task's evidence is spread across a source document of median length 27 pages (mean 48.8, maximum 873); a third of tasks rest mainly on charts, drawings, and maps; and 70.9% require two or more reasoning hops. We post-train Kimi-K2.7, an open-weight foundation model, at its full context window on 1,465 expert-authored tasks with atomic rubrics from that collection, training rank-32 adapters with one round of privileged-context on-policy self-distillation followed by two rounds of rubric-reward reinforcement learning. We render each PDF as text for training and as extracted text plus selected page images at evaluation. The smoothed RL training reward rises from 0.37 in the first tenth of the run to 0.67 in the last. On the 100-task GDP.pdf holdout, served in a 262,144-token window, strict pass (all rubric criteria met) more than doubles after the second round, from 11.0% to 24.5%, with gains across input lengths up to 240K tokens. Mean tokens generated stay flat (9,803 to 9,733), so the gain does not come from longer outputs. GPT-5.6 Sol's leaderboard strict pass is 30.7% at a measured 3,422 tokens. On 220 out-of-domain GDPval tasks, where the model runs as a long-horizon tool-using agent, mean rubric reward rises from 0.571 to 0.746 after the third round and zero-credit tasks fall from 54 to 10, while messages per task fall 18%, from 70.9 to 58.2. In paired trajectories, the third round replaces a context-thrashing retry loop with one up-front check of all sources, and verification extends from checking that files exist to checking what they contain. We argue that long-context evaluation of agents should report accuracy jointly with tokens and turns, and that datasets of long documents should ship text and image renderings alongside each PDF.
authors: Sushant Mehta, Logan Ritchie, Edwin Chen
bullets: Evaluates professional-document tasks involving very long sources, visual evidence, and multi-hop reasoning across ten enterprise domains.
Post-trains Kimi-K2.7 using rank-32 adapters, one self-distillation round, and two rubric-reward RL rounds over 1,465 expert-authored tasks.
On a 100-task GDP.pdf holdout, strict pass rises from 11.0% to 24.5%, with gains up to 240K-token inputs while generated tokens remain nearly unchanged.
On 220 out-of-domain GDPval tasks, mean rubric reward increases from 0.571 to 0.746, zero-credit tasks decrease from 54 to 10, and messages per task fall 18%.
Argues that long-context agent evaluation should jointly report accuracy, tokens, and turns, and that document datasets should include both text and image renderings.

papers.abstract: As robotic arms undertake diverse manipulation tasks, a deployment may need to serve many task-specific vision-language-action (VLA) policies concurrently. Dedicating a GPU to each robot is costly, motivating shared-GPU inference. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) allows compatible policies to share a frozen backbone with lightweight policy-specific adapters, reducing model-weight memory and enabling cross-policy batching. However, robot inference must keep pace with physical execution. With action chunking, robots continue executing buffered actions while awaiting new predictions, and the remaining buffered time provides each robot's execution slack for serving its next request. Once this slack is exhausted, the robot stalls until new actions arrive, interrupting task progress. Observing earlier preserves more slack but can lead to disruptive replanning and lower task success, whereas delaying dispatch to form larger batches can improve GPU efficiency but consumes slack and risks stalls. To balance these competing demands, we present MotionServe, a shared-GPU serving system that coordinates robot observation timing with server-side batch formation. MotionExec selects observation triggers based on motion structure in predicted action chunks, allowing inference to overlap with remaining buffered execution. SlackBatch combines the resulting per-robot execution budgets with estimated outstanding GPU work to determine when to wait, which requests to batch, and when to dispatch them. We evaluate X-VLA on LIBERO and SimplerEnv's WidowX tasks and OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO, with up to 96 simulated robots sharing one NVIDIA H200 GPU. At 96 robots, MotionServe reduces mean stall per episode by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points, respectively, over each model's lowest-stall baseline. Backbone sharing also reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.
authors: Zikang Wen, Yuning Zhang, Dong Yuan
bullets: Shared-GPU inference reduces the cost of deploying many task-specific VLA policies, especially with LoRA adapters sharing a frozen backbone.
MotionExec triggers observations using motion structure in predicted action chunks to overlap inference with buffered execution.
SlackBatch uses per-robot slack and estimated GPU workload to decide when to wait, batch requests, or dispatch them.
With up to 96 simulated robots, it reduces mean episode stall by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points across evaluated settings.
Backbone sharing reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.

papers.title: MotionServe: Efficient Multi-Robot Serving by Exploiting Robot Execution Slack
papers.tldr: MotionServe improves shared-GPU serving for many robot policies by coordinating observation timing and batch formation around each robot’s execution slack.

papers.abstract: An artificial neuron computes and learns, but it does not live: the units of a network are fixed when it is designed, and every one of them is kept and paid for whether it is used or not. We give each neuron a second pathway. Beside its Task Path, the usual computation and gradient learning, a dual-pathway neuron has a Growth Path: a nutrient flows from the outputs back through the network, every layer receives the same fixed budget, and each unit is fed in proportion to how much the units above it use it. A well-fed unit divides and a starving unit dies. This allocation is not a separate analysis or pruning step: it runs throughout training and reads only activations and weights. The task is still learned from labels with the ordinary loss, and the training procedure gains no phase, no schedule and no target size. Because the budget is conserved, the competition is zero-sum and a single number sets the size of the network. Switched on in a pretrained network that is deployed on a narrower domain, the Growth Path shrinks the network while it keeps learning. With Adam the network ends 1.0 to 1.2 points more accurate on the domain than the same network trained ordinarily, at 24% to 60% of its compute, and at 12% of the compute it is still ahead; a random choice of the same number of units gives no gain. Letting starving pretrained units sleep instead of die keeps 1.2 to 4.6 points more of the rarely used content. Over 800 changing tasks a network with the Growth Path holds its accuracy while ordinary networks decline. With plain SGD the gains are smaller: at deployment the method trades compute against rarely used content, and on one of the two continual-learning streams it only ties networks of equal size. The experiments are small (three-layer perceptrons on MNIST-like data); what they show is that a conserved, loss-free second pathway can decide by itself which units a network needs.
authors: Tingan Jin, Haosong Li
bullets: Adds a second, label-free pathway alongside ordinary task learning: nutrient flows backward from outputs and is allocated according to unit use.
Well-fed units divide while starving units die or sleep; a fixed budget controls network size without a separate pruning phase, schedule, or target size.
On narrower deployment domains with Adam, networks retained higher accuracy while using 24–60% of the compute, with gains still reported at 12%.
Sleeping rather than deleting unused pretrained units preserved more rarely used knowledge; across 800 changing tasks, accuracy remained stable while ordinary networks declined.
Results were smaller with SGD and are limited to small three-layer perceptrons on MNIST-like data.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Switched on at deployment, the Growth Path shrinks the network while it keeps learning. Top: the deployment stream. Bottom: mean number of live units per hidden layer, accuracy on the common content (windows of 100 tasks) and on the rare content (windows of 250 tasks), means of five seeds. The size settles within about 200 tasks at a level set by the budget B. With Adam the smaller network is more accurate than the ordinary network on both kinds of content, and a random choice of the same number of units is not. With SGD it matches the ordinary network on the common content and falls behind on the rare content.

Figure 1: The Growth Path is a second pathway in every neuron. (a) An ordinary unit has a Task Path only: signals go up and gradients come back. A dual-pathway neuron also receives a nutrient from the units above it. (b) The nutrient enters at the outputs and is passed down; every layer receives the same budget B, split among its units in proportion to their use by the layer above. A well-fed unit divides, a starved unit dies, the others survive. The allocation is repeated every 100 updates while the network trains, and it never reads the loss. (c) Switched on in a pretrained network that is deployed on a narrower domain, the Growth Path shrinks the network while it keeps learning. Each point is one budget (B = 25 to 100). At 12% of the compute the network is still more accurate on the domain than the ordinary network at full size. (d) Trained from scratch on 800 tasks that keep rewiring the input, a network with the Growth Path holds its accuracy, while ordinary networks of the same size and of the starting width decline. Panels (c) and (d) are for Adam (means of five seeds); the results with SGD, which are less favourable at deployment, are in Sections 4 and 5.

Figure 3: The budget trades compute against accuracy along a smooth curve. Difference to the ordinary network against compute, for budgets B = 25, 35, 50, 65, 80 and 100 (left to right on each curve); bars are 95% intervals of the paired differences. Dotted lines mark the rules of Table 1. With Adam the Growth Path is above the ordinary network on the common content at every budget, down to 12% of the compute, and dormancy keeps the rare content as well. With SGD the common content holds down to about 30% of the compute and the rare content is lost progressively. Open squares: ordinary networks of the sizes reached at B = 50 and B = 100, trained from scratch on the whole stream.

Figure 4: The rule removes what the domain no longer needs, without ever seeing a label. Share of the pretrained units removed in the first 100 tasks after switch-on (B = 100), by the content a unit mattered for when the Growth Path was switched on (the content whose loss rises most when the unit is silenced; “none”: silencing it changes nothing). Bars are means of five seeds with 95% intervals. A random choice of the same number of units makes no such difference.

Figure 6: On a stream that keeps rewiring its input, a network with the Growth Path keeps learning. Left and middle: online accuracy over 800 pixel-permutation tasks (blocks of 20 tasks, five seeds; λ = 0). papers.abstract: Millimeter-wave radar offers weather-resilient sensing for 3D occupancy prediction. Existing radar occupancy methods mainly model geometry, with limited joint modeling of semantics and motion. Cascaded imaging radar provides fine spatial detail but has a limited unambiguous velocity range, whereas single-chip radar offers a wider range but coarser spatial resolution. We propose RadarOSV, to our knowledge the first radar-only framework that jointly predicts occupancy, dynamic object semantics, and ground-relative velocity from raw radar data in unified voxels, by exploiting complementary measurements from both radars. Its Polar-to-Cartesian Geometry (PCG) backbone maps polar imaging-radar features into Cartesian voxels through fixed and deformable sampling, guiding cross-radar fusion for geometry and attribute prediction. Single-chip detection outputs provide class evidence, while raw Doppler spectra supply motion features and radial-velocity candidates. The velocity readout selects from these candidates using fused features to resolve aliasing, then combines the selected radial estimate with learned motion. Ego-motion compensation uses radar-estimated velocity, so inference requires no external odometry or other sensors. On K-Radar, single-frame PCG achieves 40.7% mIoU within 12.8 m, compared with RadarOcc's reported 34.3%. On the BRIDGE-Liv dataset, compared with a cascaded-radar baseline predicting the same outputs with external ego velocity, RadarOSV improves macro-averaged accuracy across four dynamic object classes within annotated object regions from 63.1% to 75.5% and reduces object radial-velocity MAE against manual Doppler annotations from 1.03 to 0.51 m/s, while maintaining geometric occupancy mIoU.
authors: Yuan Fang, Long Zhuang, Xijia Wei, Jingqi Jiang, Fangzhan Shi, Simon Julier, Kevin Chetty
bullets: Addresses the limited joint modeling of geometry, semantics, and motion in existing radar occupancy methods.
Uses a Polar-to-Cartesian Geometry backbone with fixed/deformable sampling to fuse radar features into unified voxels.
Combines single-chip class evidence with raw Doppler spectra and candidate selection to handle velocity aliasing.
Performs ego-motion compensation using radar-estimated velocity, without external odometry or other sensors.
Reports improved occupancy, dynamic-class accuracy, and radial-velocity error on K-Radar and BRIDGE-Liv.

papers.abstract: Humanoid box pushing is challenging when the physical properties of the task, such as the box mass and the ramp inclination, are unknown before the push begins. This paper presents PushMimic, a framework that learns adaptive humanoid box pushing from a single level-ground kinematic reference motion. The learned policy adapts its pushing posture to these properties without observing them. PushMimic augments the reference motion into a dynamically feasible motion dataset over these properties with sampling-based trajectory optimization, and distills the dataset into one motion tracking policy in one stage of training. Simulation results over box masses from 5 to 15 kg and ramp inclinations up to 15 degrees show that PushMimic raises the success rate from 57.8% to 88.8% compared with a baseline that tracks the original reference motion. It also reduces the cost of push of the arms by 22%. Hardware experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid show that the policy adapts its torso pitch during continuous pushing on an inclined treadmill, with box masses up to 19 kg and ramp inclinations up to 12.6 degrees. PushMimic therefore needs only one reference motion, instead of one for every box mass and ramp inclination.
authors: Yulun Zhuang, Hanyu Zhang, Jingyu Liu, Yanran Ding
bullets: Addresses adaptive pushing when physical task properties are unknown before execution.
Augments one level-ground kinematic motion into dynamically feasible trajectories across varying masses and inclinations using sampling-based trajectory optimization.
Distills the augmented motions into a single motion-tracking policy in one training stage.
In simulation, success improves from 57.8% to 88.8% over tracking the original reference, while arm pushing cost decreases by 22%.
Hardware tests on a Unitree G1 demonstrate torso-pitch adaptation while pushing boxes on an inclined treadmill.

papers.abstract: Skill internalization offers a way for agents to learn useful behaviors from skills and use them without explicit guidance in context at inference time. A common approach is to generate demonstration trajectories with the skill in context and then fine-tune the same model on its own trajectories with the skill removed. However, this leads to the problem that the model may learn to reference the removed skill, which we named as context misalignment (CoMi). In this work, we first analyze agent behaviors related to CoMi under this common pipeline. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ARC-AGI-1, skill-removed fine-tuning consistently results in CoMi: 12.2-46.0% of test trajectories reference the removed skill. To address this problem, we develop Context-Grounded Skill Internalization (CGSI). CGSI uses a sentence detector to identify unsupported references and then masks or rewrites the selected sentences before fine-tuning. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of CGSI and reveal two key findings. (i) Compared with directly fine-tuning with the skill removed, CGSI reduces CoMi at test time by 72.5-94.6% while preserving task success. (ii) Compared with existing reinforcement learning-based skill-internalization baselines, CGSI achieves comparable performance with substantially less training time. CGSI also significantly reduces processing costs compared with large-scale trajectory auditing and correction.
authors: Jinlin Liu, Yumeng He, Qihan Huang, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Han Peng
bullets: Skill-removed fine-tuning causes context misalignment (CoMi), with agents referencing removed skills across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ARC-AGI-1.
CGSI detects unsupported references in demonstration trajectories and masks or rewrites the affected sentences before fine-tuning.
CGSI reduces test-time CoMi by 72.5–94.6% while preserving task success.
It matches reinforcement-learning-based internalization baselines with substantially less training time and lowers processing costs versus large-scale trajectory auditing.
Scope: results are demonstrated on the three evaluated benchmarks and focus on sentence-level reference correction.

papers.abstract: Autonomous exploration is widely used to map unknown environments, yet maintaining both path efficiency and low online computation remains difficult as environment scale increases. Hierarchical planners reduce global search through coarse regional representations but often rely on handcrafted local viewpoint-selection rules. Graph-based reinforcement learning can improve local decisions, but its inference cost grows with the exploration graph and global direction is usually represented only implicitly. To address these limitations, we present HERO, a hierarchical framework that assigns distinct responsibilities to global planning and learned local decision-making, enabling each level to focus on the function it is best suited to perform. To reduce the growing inference cost of graph-based policies, HERO restricts learned target selection to reachable candidates within the current region while using region-level planning to provide long-horizon guidance. To avoid informative targets causing excessive deviation from this global direction, the proposed Dual-Branch Graph Policy balances Frontier Utility with guidance toward the next region, improving both local exploration and global progress. Experiments on unseen 2D maps show the lowest overall mean path length and target-decision cost among the evaluated methods. MARSIM simulations and deployments at three real-world sites further demonstrate the framework's applicability with LiDAR-based mapping and chassis dynamics.
authors: Xulin Xiao, Shengyi Liang, Mingjie Zhang, Chengkai Wu, Chen Chen, Zhigang Li, Jinni Zhou, Jun Ma, Boyu Zhou
bullets: Targets the trade-off between path efficiency and online computation as exploration environments grow.
Uses hierarchical planning: global regions provide long-horizon direction, while learned decisions select reachable targets within the current region.
Introduces a Dual-Branch Graph Policy balancing frontier utility with progress toward the next planned region.
Achieves the lowest reported mean path length and target-decision cost among evaluated methods on unseen 2D maps.
MARSIM simulations and deployments at three real-world sites demonstrate applicability with LiDAR mapping and chassis dynamics.

papers.abstract: Multimodal embedding models map heterogeneous inputs into a shared representation space, yet text-only, image-only, and composed inputs are still presented in distinct formats and follow different routes through the model. This fragmentation prevents heterogeneous tasks from jointly optimizing the same end-to-end encoding process, limiting supervision transfer across input configurations. To address this issue, we propose unification before encoding and instantiate this paradigm in RenderEmbed. The framework uses Visual Substrate Rendering to convert heterogeneous inputs into a common visual substrate for encoding with a VLM. From the resulting visual tokens, Progressive Hierarchical Anchor Encoding produces compact retrieval representations by interleaving learnable anchors and fusing their states across layers, retaining broad context and fine-grained cues. Interventional Rendering Learning trains these representations to remain sensitive to content changes and stable across rendering variations through complementary semantic and rendering interventions. Extensive experiments on MMEB and ViDoRe v2, spanning diverse retrieval tasks, show that RenderEmbed outperforms prior state-of-the-art models at the same scale and exhibits strong out-of-domain generalization. Compared with MetaEmbed, RenderEmbed improves MMEB Overall Precision@1 by 1.7 points, with a larger 2.1-point gain on out-of-domain tasks. Transfer and scaling analyses further show that a shared visual pathway enables more effective learning from heterogeneous supervision.
authors: Xu Yuan, Pangjing Wu, Wenqi Fan, Qing Li
bullets: Addresses fragmented encoding pathways that limit shared supervision across heterogeneous inputs.
Uses Visual Substrate Rendering to convert all inputs into a common visual substrate for a vision-language model.
Progressive Hierarchical Anchor Encoding creates compact retrieval representations while preserving global and fine-grained information.
Interventional Rendering Learning promotes sensitivity to content changes and robustness to rendering variations.
Outperforms prior same-scale models on MMEB and ViDoRe v2, including a 1.7-point MMEB Overall Precision@1 gain over MetaEmbed and stronger out-of-domain performance.

papers.abstract: World models support planning by predicting how the environment evolves under candidate actions. However, one-step predictive accuracy alone does not characterize multi-step planning utility, which depends on distinguishing candidate futures. This raises a natural question: How does latent transition geometry shape planning? We investigate this through an action-conditioned transition-field view, using curvature regularization as a controlled intervention. Across four continuous-control tasks, appropriately tuned regularization improves planning, while excessive regularization can be detrimental. By decomposing the transition field into affine and non-affine components, we find that regularization reduces action sensitivity mainly through the non-affine component. To assess its role in planning, we directly manipulate the non-affine action response in frozen models and show that it affects candidate selection and closed-loop success. Further analysis shows that curvature generally brings predicted futures closer together, while preserving more of the differences along the goal direction. This helps explain why the planning effects vary across tasks. We observe broadly consistent planning trends across five sampling- and gradient-based solvers on LeWM and similar rollout-geometry trends on DINO-WM. Qualitative attention visualizations reveal accompanying shifts toward task-relevant visual structure. Together, these findings clarify how latent transition geometry influences multi-step planning.
authors: Xuanya Zhu, Da Li, Xiatian Zhu
bullets: The study examines how curvature in action-conditioned latent transition fields affects multi-step planning.
Moderate curvature regularization improves planning across four continuous-control tasks, whereas excessive regularization can hurt.
Regularization mainly reduces action sensitivity in the non-affine transition component.
Directly manipulating non-affine action responses changes candidate selection and closed-loop success in frozen models.
Curvature brings predicted futures closer together while preserving more goal-relevant differences, helping explain task-dependent effects across multiple planning solvers and world models.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Encoder attention across curvature regularization strengths. Maps compare the base and beneficial models on the same observations, with additional stronger regularization settings for PushT. Colors are normalized per panel and indicate relative spatial emphasis.

Figure 1: Overview of the transition field. LeWM encodes observations into latent states and predicts the latent change produced by an action, which we denote by the transition field F (zt, at). During planning, we repeatedly compose these predicted changes along candidate action sequences. Differences introduced by actions at one step are therefore transformed over later rollout steps, determining how separated the candidate futures remain at the planning horizon.
Figure 7: One-step prediction error and five-step candidate regret for the base models. Each point represents one held-out state–goal pair evaluated with 300 candidate sequences.

Figure 5: Rollout geometry and closed-loop CEM success across curvature regularization strengths. papers.abstract: Confidence estimation for large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) aims to assess how likely a particular generated response is to be correct. We investigate how learning this assessment can benefit from the model's predictive reliability on the underlying query. Binary correctness supervision, however, assigns identical labels to occasional errors and frequent failures, as well as isolated successes and consistent success. These outcomes can arise from substantially different predictive behavior under stochastic decoding. We propose a confidence-learning framework that supplements realized response correctness with query-level predictive reliability. We estimate reliability through repeated generations under a fixed model and decoding configuration, then combine the empirical success rate with individual correctness to construct a graded confidence surrogate. The surrogate differentiates responses sharing the same correctness label while preserving the average predictive reliability of the sampled response pool. To learn this target, we condition an independent confidence estimator on the query and its full generated response, and optimize backbone LoRA adapters together with a projection and scalar confidence head using mean squared error. Repeated sampling is required only for supervision construction; inference scores an individual response without additional generations. We establish ordering and mean preservation properties of the surrogate and derive a selective-risk bound connecting population surrogate prediction error to the error rate among accepted responses. We evaluate the framework across language and vision-language models, examining confidence calibration and selective prediction.
authors: Chen Li, Xiaoling Hu, Chao Chen
bullets: Binary correctness labels miss differences between occasional errors, frequent failures, isolated successes, and consistently correct behavior.
The method combines an individual response’s correctness with query-level empirical success rates from repeated generations.
An independent confidence estimator uses the query and full response, trained with LoRA adapters and a confidence head via mean squared error.
Repeated generations are needed only to construct supervision; inference evaluates each response in a single pass.
The paper proves ordering and mean-preservation properties and derives a selective-risk bound, then evaluates calibration and selective prediction in language and vision-language models.

papers.abstract: Moment Retrieval (MR) aims to identify the temporal segment in an untrimmed video that corresponds to a natural language query. Existing approaches commonly refine temporal predictions within the localization pathway, without explicitly verifying candidate-level semantic consistency. Moreover, directly reusing semantic scores as feedback can cause over-correction when the verification signal is unreliable. To address these issues, we propose Bi-Refine, a semantic verification-guided progressive refinement framework that formulates MR as a closed-loop verification-and-refinement process. A Heuristic Localization Branch first generates candidate moments, while a Semantic Verification Branch evaluates their query consistency in a semantically enriched latent space. Query supervision further trains the verifier with the same candidate moment but different queries, encouraging it to distinguish the matched query from semantically similar mismatched queries. The resulting verification features are incorporated into a Progressive Refinement Loop that updates both query representations and multimodal features. To suppress potentially harmful updates, a lightweight reliability estimator gates query updates and reweights candidate contributions in feature feedback. A convergence-based adaptive stopping strategy additionally terminates unnecessary refinement during inference. Experiments on three standard MR benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and state-of-the-art performance of our method.
authors: Mengnan Liu, Sanping Zhou, Kun Xia, Jiaxuan Lin, Yuxuan Wu, Gang Hua
bullets: Targets semantic inconsistency in temporal candidates and the risk of over-correction from unreliable verification signals.
Uses a Heuristic Localization Branch to generate candidate moments and a Semantic Verification Branch to assess query consistency.
Trains verification to distinguish matched queries from semantically similar mismatched queries for the same candidate moment.
Employs reliability-gated progressive refinement, adaptive candidate reweighting, and convergence-based early stopping.
Shows effectiveness and state-of-the-art performance on three standard moment-retrieval benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Robot agents built on frontier vision-language models now solve most robot memory benchmarks. Does this mean they can remember what they need in a home, where people and machines keep moving things? Existing memory benchmarks cannot answer this question, because they pause the simulator while the model thinks: nothing can change during a decision, so whatever the robot remembers is still true when it acts. We introduce RoboLiveMem, a benchmark that runs the same memory tasks twice, once with the world paused while the model thinks and once with the world running. It contains 29 task families in three tiers, from 16 realistic BEHAVIOR-1K scenes of homes, workshops and a restaurant to controlled ManiSkill tasks. Every task mixes real changes with harmless look-alikes and runs without any change, so that no fixed strategy succeeds, and most tasks have a twin that keeps the change in view, which separates forgetting from acting too late. Testing 16 models on 34,176 episodes, we find three surprises. (1) Paused results hide the problem: when a remembered object changes in a realistic scene, the 8 Claude and GPT models succeed in 97% of episodes on average with the world paused, but in only 50% with the world running, and their ranking changes: Claude Opus 5.5, which never fails when paused, succeeds in 44%. (2) Speed is not the fix: slower models do no worse, and models given only 2 s per decision still fall at least 36 points below their paused success. (3) Models see the change but act on camera frames from before it ended. Looking again just before acting closes most of the realistic gap, yet when identical objects are swapped several times, all nine models we test still lose points to memory.
authors: Yunbei Zhang, Yuyou Zhang, Janet Wang, Ming Liu, Yijiang Li, Yikai Wang, Weirui Ye, Ding Zhao, Jihun Hamm
bullets: Introduces a benchmark that compares robot memory with the environment paused versus continuously changing.
Covers 29 task families across realistic BEHAVIOR-1K scenes and controlled ManiSkill tasks, including distractor changes and no-change cases.
Across 34,176 episodes and 16 models, realistic changed-object success drops from 97% when paused to 50% when the world runs.
Slower reasoning does not solve the problem; models often perceive changes but act using stale pre-change camera frames.
Looking again before acting largely closes the realistic gap, but repeated swaps of identical objects still expose memory failures.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models generate virtual environments autoregressively from player actions and visual history. However, visual history alone cannot reliably capture the evolving states of independently acting non-player characters (NPCs) in real games, particularly when they are outside the camera view. Recent multi-agent world models address this challenge through joint multi-view generation or persistent shared state, but often rely on external observations, like maps or scene geometry, or predefined state transitions. We present SWAM, a State-aware World Action Model that separates agent-state evolution from autoregressive visual generation in interactive 3D environments. A lightweight state model propagates character dynamics from actions without consuming generated frames, combining motion priors with learned scene-dependent corrections. The predicted states then guide an autoregressive diffusion transformer alongside visual history through a novel conditioning scheme. Rather than requiring an explicit scene geometry map or visibility tests, the conditioning indicates where characters may appear, allowing the diffusion model to learn their appearance and occlusion. This design enables NPCs to evolve independently of visual generation while maintaining consistent observations across visibility changes, interactions, and respawns. Evaluations in a custom Godot-based first-person shooter game demonstrate improvements in visual fidelity, NPC consistency, and long-horizon stability over existing approaches.
authors: Jenna Kang, Bingxuan Li, Colin Groth, Anatolii Evdokimov, Sai Zhang, Qi Sun
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of tracking independently acting, off-screen NPCs from visual history alone.
Uses a lightweight state model to propagate character dynamics from actions, motion priors, and learned scene-dependent corrections.
Conditions an autoregressive diffusion transformer on predicted states and visual history without requiring scene maps or visibility tests.
Supports consistent NPC appearance and behavior across visibility changes, interactions, and respawns.
Experiments in a custom Godot first-person shooter show improved visual fidelity, NPC consistency, and long-horizon stability over existing approaches.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict how the world responds to actions and offer a promising path toward general embodied intelligence, but they are large and run the network many times per plan, so they are hard to deploy on robots. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) compute with sparse binary spikes and use additions instead of multiplications, which saves power. However, existing WAMs use dense videos as the world state, so a spiking version would spend most of its computation on the background. We therefore introduce SpikingWAM, the first spiking WAM, which uses a sparse task skeleton as the world state. Inspired by biological motor control, which attends only to the key positions of a task, the Task Skeleton State (TSS) keeps the keypoints of the arm and the task objects, and a small spiking front end estimates the object keypoints from images. Body Frame Spike Coding (BFSC) and Grid Coincidence Attention (GCA) keep millimetre precision, and the Persistent Single Step Readout (PSR) runs the network once per plan. On the simulated benchmarks LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, SpikingWAM achieves competitive success rates with far less energy than ANN methods and surpasses all compared methods on LIBERO-Plus. Real robot experiments further confirm its effectiveness. These results show that a task skeleton lets spiking networks implement WAMs at very low energy, offering a new solution for low power embodied intelligence. authors: Mingquan Liu, Peng Zhou, Shanming Yao, Shuai Wang, Simo Wu, Malu Zhang
bullets: Addresses the high computational and energy costs of large world-action models that repeatedly process dense video observations.

Introduces Body Frame Spike Coding, Grid Coincidence Attention, and Persistent Single Step Readout for precise, efficient planning.
Achieves competitive simulated-task success with substantially lower energy than ANN methods, surpasses compared methods on LIBERO-Plus, and works in real-robot experiments.

papers.abstract: Moment Retrieval (MR) aims to localize the temporal segment in a video that corresponds to a given textual description. However, a textual query often provides only a sparse semantic description of the target event, whereas the video contains rich and fine-grained visual variations. This mismatch creates an inherent gap between textual semantics and visual content, making a single textual input insufficient for precise cross-modal alignment. As a result, when multiple temporally adjacent or semantically similar segments exist, the model may struggle to distinguish the target moment from confusing candidates. To address this challenge, we propose a Multi-Perspective Auxiliary Representation (MPAR) framework, which aims to bridge this alignment gap by enriching a single textual input with complementary visual cues from multiple perspectives. Specifically, MPAR consists of three key components: (1) Auxiliary Representation Initialization (ARI) constructs multiple learnable representation slots from the original query, preserving the query intent while preparing flexible carriers for subsequent visual cue injection; (2) Visual-Induced Semantic Structuring (VISS) injects target-specific visual attributes into each representation while preserving semantic coherence with the original query; and (3) Multi-Perspective Semantic Aligner (MPSA) aligns each auxiliary representation with corresponding video regions to enhance discriminative localization. By constructing multi-perspective auxiliary representations and guiding the model to attend to relevant visual regions across these representations, our model achieves more accurate moment localization. Extensive experiments on MR benchmarks demonstrate that our MPAR outperforms state-of-the-art methods, validating the effectiveness of MPAR.
authors: Mengnan Liu, Sanping Zhou, Kun Xia, Jiaxuan Lin, Gang Hua, Le Wang
bullets: Addresses the semantic gap between sparse text queries and fine-grained visual content, especially among adjacent or similar candidate moments.

MPSA aligns each auxiliary representation with relevant video regions to improve discriminative localization.
Experiments on moment-retrieval benchmarks show MPAR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

papers.abstract: A 4-bit KV cache reads about half the bytes of FP8, but Hopper GPUs have no FP4 hardware and little instruction-issue capacity per byte of memory bandwidth, so 4-bit values must be decoded in software. On H200, vLLM's NVFP4 KV path (FlashInfer's decode) reaches 10-20% of memory bandwidth and is up to 1.7x slower than FP8. NVBit instruction counts show two causes: the kernels behind vLLM's 4-bit paths (FlashInfer NVFP4, Triton UltraQuant) execute 2-6x Hopper's issue budget per byte and serialize loading, decoding and matrix multiplies. Our Hopper-native decode kernel overlaps a TMA producer warp with two compute warpgroups, lays the cache out at write time so decoded values feed the tensor cores from registers, and swaps the matrix operands so small query groups need no padding. On H200 it reaches 67-75% of peak bandwidth at batch 32-128 and at all 11 shapes is 1.12-1.49x faster than the faster of XQA and FlashAttention-4's proposed native FP8. Inside vLLM, with an accuracy recipe (K mean removal and rotation, 4 BF16 sink tokens, BF16 layer 0), it decodes 1.12-1.64x faster per step on Llama-3.1-8B than vLLM's FlashInfer FP8 path at batch 8 and above (1.04-1.24x over FlashAttention-4's FP8), is level at batch 1, and holds 1.63x as many tokens. On one H200 under a reasoning-like request stream, the highest rate at which 99% of requests meet the latency targets is 1.23-1.32x FP8's on Llama-3.1-8B and 1.67-2.20x on Qwen2.5-72B, as the cache becomes the limit; prefill-heavy streams are worse (7% slower prefill). On five 7B-32B models, repeated runs show no significant accuracy difference from BF16 KV. In Qwen2-family models, whose reasoning variants collapse under FP8 KV, layer 0's key mean is almost entirely the key-projection bias identified by prior work, seen through RoPE and computable from the weights alone; keeping that layer in BF16 restores FP8 KV and, with K mean removal, 4-bit KV.
authors: Jian Zhang
bullets: Existing Hopper 4-bit KV kernels underuse memory bandwidth because decoding and matrix operations are serialized and exceed instruction capacity per byte.
The proposed kernel overlaps TMA loading with computation, stores the cache for register-fed tensor-core inputs, and avoids padding for small query groups.
It reaches 67–75% of peak H200 bandwidth and is 1.12–1.49× faster across 11 tested shapes than the faster of XQA and FlashAttention-4’s proposed native FP8 path.
In vLLM, it is 1.12–1.64× faster per decode step than FlashInfer FP8 at batch sizes ≥8 and supports 1.63× as many tokens; prefill-heavy workloads lose 7% speed.
K mean removal, rotation, BF16 sink tokens, and retaining layer 0 in BF16 preserve accuracy across tested models, including Qwen variants that degrade with FP8 KV.

papers.title: Fast 4-bit KV-Cache Decoding on Hopper GPUs: Why Existing Kernels Are Slow and How to Fix Them

papers.abstract: Humans dynamically adjust their reliance on sensory modalities across manipulation stages. Although existing World Action Models (WAMs) fuse multi-camera observations, they struggle to adapt their reliance on individual views based on the current observations. This raises a central question: how can the action expert integrate complementary visual evidence while prioritizing the views most relevant to the current action? FlexWAM addresses this challenge through three modules. First, we alternate within-view and cross-view attention to capture view-specific dynamics and complementary cues. For action prediction, View-Routed Action Attention uses an observation-conditioned router to prioritize relevant views. To calibrate routing, we train a critic using counterfactual view credit, estimated from action loss sensitivity upon suppressing each view's contribution to action attention. We evaluate FlexWAM with two video backbones on five challenging real-world manipulation tasks across two robot platforms. The two variants improve mean task success by 16.4 and 23.0 percentage points over the strongest baseline. Project website: https://flexwam.github.io/.
authors: Mingyu Mei, Haojie Xu, Zibo Dai, Hongjie Fang, Shirun Tang, Zhengrui Lv, Yang Liu, Chen Guang, Xingyue Zhao, Huiliang Shen, Zaixing He
bullets: Addresses the inability of existing multi-camera WAMs to adapt view reliance to the current observation and action.
Alternates within-view and cross-view attention to model view-specific dynamics and complementary visual cues.
Uses an observation-conditioned View-Routed Action Attention module to prioritize relevant views.
Trains routing with counterfactual view credit based on action-loss sensitivity when suppressing each view.
Across five real-world manipulation tasks and two robot platforms, variants improve mean success by 16.4 and 23.0 percentage points over the strongest baseline.

papers.abstract: Reliable 3D object detection for autonomous trucks requires both the semantic detail provided by cameras and the geometric and motion cues measured by 4D radar. Existing radar-camera detectors commonly construct global radar bird's-eye-view (BEV) representations, whose computational and memory costs grow with the perception range. Sparse query-based detectors offer greater efficiency, but global feature construction can obscure point-level radar geometry and motion information. We present QSRadar, a query-conditioned sparse radar fusion framework for efficient long-range 3D detection. Built on a Sparse4Dv3-style visual-temporal detector, QSRadar retrieves a compact set of raw radar points around each evolving object hypothesis. The selected points are represented in an anchor-aligned coordinate frame, augmented with motion residuals, radar cross section, and sweep timing, and aggregated by a query-conditioned set encoder. Radar neighborhoods are retrieved again after each anchor refinement, coupling evidence selection with object estimation. Under the official MAN TruckScenes validation protocol, QSRadar achieves 38.09 mAP and 52.20 NDS, compared with 37.08 mAP and 50.78 NDS for our reproduced Sparse4D-Radar global Radar-BEV baseline. In matched tests on an RTX 4090 D, QSRadar reduces latency by 45%, peak memory usage by 49%, and GFLOPs by 43%.
authors: Chenhao Yan, Hongyu Liu, Xiang Cai, Yifei Sun, Zhe Zhang
bullets: Avoids costly global radar BEV construction by retrieving sparse radar neighborhoods around each object hypothesis.
Encodes radar points in anchor-aligned coordinates with motion residuals, radar cross section, and sweep timing.
Re-retrieves radar evidence after each anchor refinement, linking point selection to object estimation.
On MAN TruckScenes validation, achieves 38.09 mAP and 52.20 NDS versus 37.08 mAP and 50.78 NDS for the reproduced global Radar-BEV baseline.
On an RTX 4090 D, reduces latency by 45%, peak memory by 49%, and GFLOPs by 43% in matched tests.

Current anchors guide visual sampling and local radar retrieval, while query features modulate radar point encoding. Visual and radar features are concatenated and fused to update queries and anchors. Updated anchors trigger new radar retrieval at the next layer, forming an iterative loop. Six decoder layers produce box, class, and velocity predictions.

papers.abstract: Residual world models forecast a driving scene through its temporal change, so feature components that stay constant over time vanish from the residual pathway. We ask whether evidence with weak temporal change, such as a waiting pedestrian or a stopped vehicle, can be used more effectively for planning, and introduce MOVER, a complementary event-routing mechanism. A training-time teacher measures how each spatially grounded event query responds when a past frame is removed from shared history and contrasts that sensitivity with the event's pooled temporal residual, prioritizing events that depend on history but receive weak residual evidence. A student predicts the resulting priorities from unperturbed history, so the teacher adds no inference cost. Under fixed total routing mass, one distribution scales a low-rank future bird's-eye-view update and biases trajectory-conditioned event reading. On nuScenes, MOVER reduces ResWorld's UniAD-style average L2 from 0.65 to 0.55 m and its collision rate from 0.23% to 0.12% without direct planner ego status (0.50 m and 0.09% with it), adding 4.1 ms per frame. Matched controls show that the complementary teacher outperforms either signal alone and that the allocation acts mainly during training. Adapted to BridgeDrive-LEAD, MOVER reaches a 96.52 +/- 0.65 driving score over three seeds on the 220-route Bench2Drive closed-loop benchmark, exceeding matched controls in each paired seed by a margin within seed variation.
authors: Xiangyu Li, Yu Jiang, Tianyi Wang, Liang He, Qixing Huang, Zhaomiao Guo
bullets: Residual world models may underrepresent static or slowly changing evidence, such as waiting pedestrians and stopped vehicles.
A training-time teacher identifies events that depend on past frames but receive weak temporal-residual evidence; a student predicts their routing priorities at inference.
The priorities allocate a fixed routing budget between low-rank future bird’s-eye-view updates and trajectory-conditioned event reading, adding no teacher cost at inference.
On nuScenes, MOVER reduces average L2 from 0.65 to 0.55 m and collision rate from 0.23% to 0.12%, with 4.1 ms/frame overhead.
On Bench2Drive, adapted MOVER achieves a 96.52 ± 0.65 driving score across three seeds and exceeds matched controls within paired-seed variation.

During training, a history-occlusion teacher produces complementary priorities from history sensitivity and residual evidence; a single-view student router distills these priorities. At inference, the learned allocation writes a low-rank update to the future BEV representation and provides a prior for trajectory-conditioned event reading. papers.abstract: A streaming video system must decide in a single pass what evidence to retain under bounded frame storage, before it knows which details a future question will require. Recent recursive self-improvement methods automate the design of the harness that stores and retrieves this evidence. They revise the harness in response to failures, but the editor must still devise each repair from its prior knowledge and a predefined set of tools. A failure that recurs across videos, however, may point to a problem that prior work has already addressed. We introduce MORSE (Memory Optimization with Recursive Self-Evolvement), an open-world auto-research framework that uses recurring failures to guide an online search for solutions. Its editor groups failures in training traces by cause, then searches papers, model cards, and code for methods it can adapt or pretrained perception models it can use. When the editor introduces a new perceptual capability, it can also revise how the harness stores and retrieves the resulting evidence for a frozen video-language model. On held-out validation streams, MORSE first selects revisions that improve answer quality, then seeks faster revisions that preserve those gains within a specified tolerance. Across three streaming video benchmarks, MORSE consistently achieves the highest answer accuracy within each frozen-backbone comparison. On OVO-Bench, our Qwen3-VL-8B harness answers queries in 0.30 seconds on average while achieving 75.1% accuracy, 3.1 percentage points ahead of the next-best evaluated harness using the same frozen backbone.
authors: Ce Zhang, Jianshu Zhang, Jinxi He, Xiyuan Yang, Pan Wang, Han Liu, Katia Sycara, Yaqi Xie
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retaining useful evidence in a single pass under bounded frame storage and unknown future questions.
Groups recurring failures by cause and searches papers, model cards, and code for adaptable methods or pretrained perception models.
Can jointly add perceptual capabilities and revise how their evidence is stored and retrieved.
Selects accuracy-improving revisions on validation streams, then optimizes for faster revisions within a quality tolerance.
Across three benchmarks, it achieves the best accuracy within frozen-backbone comparisons; on OVO-Bench, it reaches 75.1% accuracy with 0.30-second average response time using Qwen3-VL-8B.

papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces MORSE, a framework for optimizing the memory harness of a frozen video-language model (Qwen3-VL-8B). It addresses the problem of selecting evidence to retain in a streaming video system, which aligns with both Multimodal Foundation Models (VLMs) and Efficient AI (token eviction/pruning). The use of open-world auto-research to adapt the system is a novel approach to memory optimization.
papers.title: MORSE: Optimizing Streaming Memory Design via Open-World Auto-Research
papers.tldr: MORSE improves streaming video memory by using recurring failures to search for and integrate external research, achieving strong accuracy and efficient querying with frozen video-language backbones.

papers.abstract: LiDAR world models generate and predict metric 3D observations in the form of LiDAR scans. They typically synthesize scans following the scan pattern of their training sensor or render them from an intermediate 3D surface or field. However, following one scan pattern limits transfer to LiDARs with other patterns, and rendering from intermediate geometry can cause incorrect depths and false returns. In this paper, we propose a scan pattern agnostic 4D LiDAR world model that decouples the scene from sensor observation, so one spatial latent can be observed by heterogeneous LiDARs at the same mounting position without regeneration. Our decoder predicts the hit probability and depth of each ray directly from the latent, combining global scene context with local features retrieved at a preliminary depth. Without an intermediate surface or field, it reduces incorrect depths and false returns, and as each ray is decoded independently from one latent, LiDARs that share a ray receive the same return and observe one consistent scene. Finally, a diffusion transformer generates scenes in this latent and predicts 4D sequences from observed latents warped by the given ego and object motion. On KITTI-360 and nuScenes, our model generates realistic scenes and reduces the registration error between predicted frames by about 70% relative to the best compared world model. Its decoder yields 19 to 28% lower depth error than the rendering used by other world models, and generated scans benefit several downstream tasks. Our code will be open-sourced. More details are available at https://minwoo0611.github.io/OneLatentWorld.
authors: Minwoo Jung, Dongjae Lee, DongGuw Lee, Yeong Sang Park, Maurice Fallon, Ayoung Kim
bullets: Decouples scene representation from sensor scan patterns, enabling multiple LiDARs at the same mounting position to observe one shared latent scene without regeneration.
Directly predicts each ray’s hit probability and depth using global context and locally retrieved preliminary-depth features, avoiding intermediate surfaces or fields.
Uses a diffusion transformer to generate latent scenes and predict 4D sequences under ego and object motion.
On KITTI-360 and nuScenes, reduces predicted-frame registration error by about 70% versus the best compared world model and lowers depth error by 19–28% versus alternative rendering.
Generated scans also improve several downstream tasks; the scope is evaluated on KITTI-360 and nuScenes.

papers.title: One Latent World for Heterogeneous LiDARs: A Scan Pattern Agnostic 4D World Model via Direct Ray Decoding

papers.abstract: Next-token prediction relies on learned token embeddings whose dimension $d$ is much smaller than the vocabulary size $V$. Existing analyses of training dynamics either fix the embeddings with $d\ge V$ or train them only in restricted settings. It remains unclear whether jointly training the embeddings by gradient-based methods from random initialization leads to accurate prediction when $d<V$. In this paper, we study this question in the simplest setting where it is already nontrivial, namely next-token prediction with a one-token context, which we refer to as a state-transition model. The model consists of an input embedding and an output embedding, either untied or tied, and is trained from Gaussian initialization by perturbed gradient descent with weight decay on the population cross-entropy loss. We consider ground-truth transition laws whose centered log-probability table has low rank and bounded entries, and measure the prediction quality by the relative prediction gain (RPG). It is zero for the uniform predictor and one for the optimal predictor. For the untied model, we show that when $d=\Omega(\sqrt V)$, with probability at least $1-e^{-cd}$ for some constant $c$, the RPG is above $7/8$ at every iterate in the final $1-1/d$ fraction of training iterations. For the tied model trained on a subset of states, we prove that the RPG on the observed states is $1-O(V/d^2)$, and under a coverage condition on the ground truth and a bound on the learned embeddings, we further prove a prediction guarantee on the unseen states. Our analysis is based on the bounded trace of the Hessian of the softmax cross-entropy loss, which implies that the approximate second-order stationary points reached by training have high prediction gain. Numerical experiments with practical parameter choices illustrate the persistent training gain and the transfer of the tied model.
authors: Yee Man Choi, Fengchi Wang, Ruiquan Huang
bullets: Studies one-token-context next-token prediction with jointly trained input/output embeddings initialized randomly.
Analyzes untied and tied embeddings using perturbed gradient descent with weight decay on population cross-entropy.
For untied embeddings, dimension scaling as Ω(√V) yields RPG above 7/8 during most late training iterations, with high probability.
For tied embeddings trained on observed states, RPG is 1−O(V/d²), with additional guarantees for unseen states under coverage and embedding-boundedness conditions.
The theory uses a bounded Hessian trace to connect approximate second-order stationary points with high prediction gain; experiments illustrate persistent gain and transfer.

papers.abstract: As AI models evolve from text and vision to physical agents, embodied AI faces a fundamentally different attack surface. Prior attacks on embodied systems have used crafted instructions, adversarial visual inputs, and training-time policy modifications; we study environment-only object rearrangements with unchanged models and instructions. We reveal an attack surface in safety-critical spatial relations among existing objects. An adversary who rearranges objects, without modifying instructions or accessing models, can cause hazardous consequences. In this work, we propose EnvTrap, a diagnostic pipeline that constructs paired safe, trap, and null-trap (benign but misleading) embodied scenarios. We demonstrate that environment-only perturbations raise hazardous-action rates to an average of 83.4% across the five evaluated action policies, with similar vulnerability patterns confirmed in world models. On a consequence-prediction task, model accuracy remains near chance, while human evaluators achieve high accuracy. We further propose a consequence-aware defense that reduces trap trigger rates by an average of 76.3 percentage points across action policies in simulation and by 62.9 percentage points pooled across physical backends. Together, these findings link environment-only attacks to a broader deficit in physical reasoning: embodied models recognize task-relevant objects yet fail to anticipate how spatial relations change the consequences of acting on them. EnvTrap makes this gap directly testable and turns hazardous layouts into training scenarios for safer embodied action. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/INKSIR/Envtrap.
authors: Zehao Liu, Huashuo Lei, Xi Lin, Haoang Li, Yuliang Chen, Huarui Zhang, Yifan Wang
bullets: Problem: Embodied agents may be vulnerable to environment-only attacks even when models and instructions are unchanged.
Method: EnvTrap creates paired safe, trap, and benign null-trap scenarios to test action safety and consequence prediction.
Finding: Environment rearrangements produced hazardous actions at an average rate of 83.4% across five evaluated action policies.
Finding: Models performed near chance at predicting consequences, whereas human evaluators achieved high accuracy; similar vulnerabilities appeared in world models.

Defense and scope: A consequence-aware defense reduced trap triggers by 76.3 percentage points in simulation and 62.9 points across physical backends, while targeting a broader physical-reasoning deficit.

papers.abstract: Reliable video deepfake detection requires generalization to unseen generators while limiting false alarms on authentic footage. Although existing detectors capture diverse visual cues, they may produce overconfident errors under generator shift, limiting the reliability of confidence-based fusion. Threshold calibration is further complicated by shifts in authentic capture domains and the lack of future-generator examples. To address these challenges, we present Antiphony, a framework that combines calibrated fusion of four visual experts with selective investigation. Authentic videos serve as a shared reference for score fusion and threshold calibration, enabling threshold updates without target deepfakes. For this expert-fusion stage, we establish finite-sample false-alarm control when the scoring procedure is fixed independently of calibration and authentic samples are exchangeable. To refine decisions near the calibrated threshold, a tool-using multimodal investigator examines these videos and contributes an additional fusion score. We train the investigator on generator-held-out predictions and counterfactual expert outputs, to improve robustness to unreliable expert evidence. Across six benchmark protocols, Antiphony achieves a mean benchmark score of 88.3%, exceeding the strongest evaluated MLLM and conventional detector baselines by 14.7 and 11.5 points, respectively. It also outperforms ARGUS by 20.2 points on average and by 3.6 balanced-accuracy points on FaceVid's 20 unseen generators.
authors: Xinyu Yan, Yurong Hao, Zherui Li, Yebo Wu, Tiantong Wu, Jiaming Zhang, Zihao Zeng, Zheng Lin, Zijie Wang, Pengpeng Qiao, Yang Cao, Wei Yang Bryan Lim
bullets: Targets overconfident errors, false alarms, and difficult threshold calibration when future deepfake generators are unavailable.
Fuses four visual experts using authentic videos as shared calibration references, enabling threshold updates without target deepfakes.
Provides finite-sample false-alarm control when scoring is fixed before calibration and authentic samples are exchangeable.
Uses a tool-using multimodal investigator for cases near the calibrated threshold, trained with held-out-generator and counterfactual evidence.
Across six protocols, reports an 88.3% mean benchmark score and gains over evaluated MLLM, conventional-detector, and ARGUS baselines.

papers.abstract: Situated 3D reasoning requires embodied agents to interpret objects, scene geometry, and viewpoint dependent spatial relations. Existing methods learn grounded interactions from supervised traces, but largely imitate prescribed evidence acquisition patterns rather than optimizing the support that the returned evidence provides for the correct answer. Moreover, outcome rewards provide limited credit for intermediate tool choices and may leave infrequent tools underexplored. An effective agent should instead adaptively decide what to ground, which tool to invoke, and how to assess the utility of returned evidence. To this end, this paper presents CARE-3D, a reinforcement post-training framework for adaptive grounded reasoning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on grounding instructions first establishes valid interactions, after which Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) optimizes the agent while keeping the 3D grounding module frozen. CARE-3D combines Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence for evidence sensitive credit assignment, and Group Coverage Sampling to preserve tool coverage. Experiments on MSQA and Beacon3D show consistent gains over SFT and GRPO using only answer and format rewards, especially in spatial reasoning and grounding answer coherence. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/xiaoqian-UQ/CARE-3D}{CARE-3D}.
authors: Xiaoqian Hu, Ruihong Qiu, Yanran Tang, Sen Wang
bullets: Addresses the limits of supervised imitation and outcome-only rewards for embodied 3D reasoning.
Uses SFT to establish valid tool interactions, then applies GRPO while keeping the 3D grounding module frozen.
Introduces Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence for evidence-sensitive credit assignment.
Uses Group Coverage Sampling to maintain exploration across grounding tools.
On MSQA and Beacon3D, improves over SFT and answer/format-reward-only GRPO, particularly in spatial reasoning and grounding-answer coherence.

papers.abstract: Runtime model selection trades detection quality against energy and latency. However, comparing a selector only with a more costly static detector conflates detector choice with the benefit of adaptation. We present a framework for analysis and physical measurement that combines a pairwise reward criterion, matched static controls, paired blocks, a fixed load-prevalence factorial design, and reporting of actions outside training support. On one Raspberry Pi 4B with four frozen TON-IoT detectors, tabular Q-learning and a deep Q-network (DQN) both select LightLR throughout. A retrospective audit using validation data only rules out preference reversals for MedRF versus LightLR and HeavyMLP versus LightLR. However, TinyDT has a higher reward than LightLR in seven of the 2,500 windows, so the audit does not establish global LightLR optimality. We also evaluate a causal DeadlineGuard rule under a fixed factorial design with three arrival rates (50, 100, and 4,000 rows/s) and three attack prevalences (0.10, 0.50, and 0.90). Compared with Static-MedRF, DeadlineGuard saves 43.7 J per 500-s run (2.98%; 95% paired CI 41.4--46.0 J) and eliminates all 512 deadline misses among 5,000 windows, at a cost of 1.373 percentage points in F1. Outside training support, Tabular-Q's deterministic tie-breaking rule selects TinyDT, resulting in a false-positive rate of 67.76%. These single-board results motivate joint audits of reward attainability, realized actions, attribution against matched static controls, service feasibility, and default actions outside training support.
authors: Nuonan Ouyang, Bonan Zhang, Adrian Shatte, Zhigang Lu, Chao Chen, Wei Xiang
bullets: The study argues that comparing adaptive selectors only with costly static detectors can exaggerate adaptation benefits.
It combines pairwise rewards, matched static controls, paired blocks, fixed load–prevalence experiments, and audits of actions outside training support.
Tabular Q-learning and DQN selected LightLR in all observed windows; validation audits did not prove LightLR globally optimal because TinyDT performed better in 7 of 2,500 windows.
DeadlineGuard saved 43.7 J per 500-second run and eliminated 512 deadline misses, while reducing F1 by 1.373 percentage points versus Static-MedRF.
Outside training support, Tabular-Q selected TinyDT by deterministic tie-breaking, producing a 67.76% false-positive rate.
