papers.abstract: Parallel-trainable recurrences such as Mamba, linear attention, and DeltaNet offer constant-cost streaming inference, but they suffer from two limitations: 1) they struggle to track discrete state, and 2) they read every parameter at every step, tying model capacity directly to CPU latency. We introduce Yggdrasil, a recurrent architecture that decouples capacity from per-step compute by looking up each layer's transition in a large, tree-routed bank of recurrent experts. Each router addresses its bank using the current token and the state of the layer below. We prove that this cross-layer context is necessary---a single token-indexed layer of non-expanding transitions with finitely many reachable states cannot perform conditional resets---while avoiding feedback from the layer's own past preserves parallel-scan training. Because each step traverses one tree path and reads a single expert per layer, active weights stay within a few hundred kilobytes in CPU L2 cache while the full bank resides in RAM. Among the parallel-trainable models we evaluate, Yggdrasil is the only one to solve all five state-tracking tasks. At matched active parameter counts, it achieves the lowest test bits on enwik8 (1.540 bpb) and the human genome hg38 (1.567 bpb), while stepping $3.0\times$ and $3.3\times$ faster on a single CPU core ($6.7\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ and $5.8\,\mu\mathrm{s}$) than the fastest streaming baseline, and delivering the highest GPU throughput of all models at batch 1024. On the Genomic Benchmarks, it is the strongest causal model at matched active parameters (86.0% mean accuracy).
authors: Cosmo Santoni
bullets: Addresses state-tracking weaknesses and per-step latency that limit parallel-trainable recurrent models.
Routes each layer’s transition through a tree using the current token and the lower layer’s state, activating one expert per layer.
Cross-layer routing enables conditional resets while preserving parallel-scan training by avoiding feedback from a layer’s own past.
Active weights fit in a few hundred kilobytes of CPU L2 cache, while the larger expert bank remains in RAM.
It solves all five evaluated state-tracking tasks and reports strong language, genomic, CPU-speed, GPU-throughput, and genomic-classification results.

papers.abstract: Explicit reasoning enables autonomous vehicles (AVs) to interpret complex traffic interactions and support trajectory planning, but introduces additional computational demands. Determining when explicit reasoning can improve planning accuracy remains a key challenge, as its benefits vary across driving scenarios. To address this challenge, this study proposes Scene-Adaptive Gating of Explicit Reasoning for Driving (SAGE-Drive), a benefit-aware adaptive reasoning framework for autonomous driving planning. First, paired planning outcomes with and without explicit reasoning are analyzed to measure the reasoning benefit, i.e., the reduction in planning error achieved by explicit reasoning, which serves as the supervision label. SAGE-Drive then learns to predict these benefits using geometric features of the initial trajectory planned without reasoning and multimodal scene information, and invokes explicit reasoning only for the scenarios with the highest predicted benefits under a predefined reasoning budget. Experiments on 1,497 paired driving scenarios reveal that explicit reasoning improves planning accuracy in 53.5% of cases while degrading it in 46.5%, yielding a near-zero average benefit. On the test set, with a 20% reasoning budget, SAGE-Drive achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 1.5191 m, compared with 1.5252 m for random selection. At a 35% budget, it achieves an ADE of 1.5148 m, close to the 1.5141 m obtained when reasoning is applied to every scenario. These findings establish the predicted reasoning benefit as an effective criterion for reasoning selection, allowing explicit reasoning to be invoked where it improves planning accuracy at a fraction of its computational cost.
authors: Donglei Rong, Wenbin Yao, Congcong Bai, Xi Gao, Qiaoqiao Ren, Sheng Jin, Cheng Xu
bullets: Explicit reasoning is not uniformly helpful: it improves planning in 53.5% of scenarios and degrades it in 46.5%, producing near-zero average benefit.
The framework defines reasoning benefit as the reduction in planning error from using explicit reasoning versus not using it.
A predictor uses initial trajectory geometry and multimodal scene information to estimate this benefit.
Explicit reasoning is allocated to the highest-benefit scenarios under a predefined reasoning budget.
With 20% and 35% reasoning budgets, SAGE-Drive approaches the accuracy of reasoning on every scenario while outperforming random selection at 20%.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has demonstrated strong performance in improving large language model (LLM) reasoning, yet its credit-assignment signal remains coarse. Outcome verifiers provide scalable supervision by judging whether a completed response is correct, but they do not directly indicate which intermediate reasoning tokens contribute to success or failure. As a result, policy optimization can be inefficient, especially when training base models directly from sparse outcome feedback. In this paper, we introduce SAEPO, a Sparse AutoEncoder-guided token-level credit assignment method for outcome-supervised Policy Optimization. Rather than treating correctness only as a rollout-level (sequence-level) signal, SAEPO uses a pretrained sparse autoencoder (SAE) to build token-level semantic representations within reasoning trajectories; it scores each token based on the SAE concepts (e.g., penalizing wrong "final-answer" tokens but rewarding correct "reasoning-process" tokens), learned in an unsupervised manner, to achieve fine-grained credit assignment. SAEPO is a plug-in advantage-shaping module compatible with various policy optimization algorithms. We instantiate SAEPO with both GRPO and GSPO, covering token-ratio and sequence-ratio policy-gradient objectives, and evaluate SAEPO across three LLM backbones on six math and two code benchmarks. Empirical results show that SAEPO improves both the math and code benchmark averages over the matched baselines, with gains of up to 6.63% and 5.57%, respectively. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base, training curves also show faster early accuracy growth. Feature and token-level analyses suggest that the SAE-derived signal favors question-relevant concepts and reasoning tokens.
authors: Yusong Zhao, Zihao Zhao, Zirui Zhang, Tunyu Zhang, Ziyan Wang, Yi Wang, Chengzhi Mao, Hao Wang
bullets: Targets coarse credit assignment in outcome-supervised reinforcement learning, where verifiers judge only completed responses.
Uses a pretrained sparse autoencoder to represent reasoning trajectories and shape token-level advantages based on semantic concepts.
Can be plugged into multiple policy-optimization methods, demonstrated with GRPO and GSPO.
Evaluated across three LLM backbones on six math and two code benchmarks, improving matched-baseline averages by up to 6.63% in math and 5.57% in code.
Analyses indicate the learned signal favors question-relevant concepts and reasoning tokens; early accuracy growth was faster on Qwen3-1.7B-Base.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of SAEPO. A frozen SAE encodes token hidden states from grouped rollouts into sparse features. For each token, its counts of similar tokens in correct and incorrect rollouts determine its token-level reward, with higher reward assigned when more similar tokens appear in correct rollouts than in incorrect ones. The token-level reward is normalized and added to the outcome advantage, while the verifier reward, policy-ratio construction, clipping rule, and KL regularizer remain unchanged.

Figure 4 SAE features (concepts) associated with the highest and the lowest SAEPO token scores, computed from rollouts on the “Algebra” and “Geometry” subjects in MATH-500. Feature-level rewards are obtained by averaging semantic scores over tokens where each SAE feature is active. Rows show features with highest/lowest rewards and their top activating tokens; color intensity indicates normalized activation within each feature. Left: High-reward features correspond to subject-relevant concepts, such as spherical and coordinate vocabulary in Geometry, and computation and expression terms in Algebra. Right: Low-reward features mostly capture connectives, copulas, punctuation, stop words, and discourse markers. These results suggest that the SAEPO-derived signal concentrates on semantically meaningful reasoning features.

Figure 1 Comparison of credit assignment mechanisms in outcome-supervised policy optimizations. GRPO assigns the same rollout-level credit to all tokens in a generated reasoning trace, so decisive reasoning steps and incidental tokens receive identical credit. Our SAEPO assigns question-local, token-level semantic credit based on semantic representations from the SAE feature space; therefore it rewards question-relevant reasoning tokens while penalizing uninformative or misleading tokens with more fine-grained credit assignment. Top words of the most related concepts to an example rewarded token “interior” show that our SAEPO can achieve interpretable token-level credit assignment.

Figure 5 Examples of how SAEPO can assign a fine-grained credit signal to each token. For rollouts from different types of questions, we visualize the SAEPO-derived final shaped advantages Aqg,t = Aout qg + αŜqg,t from Eqn. (13) assigned to individual tokens in the rollouts. Green tokens represent positive credit that rewards the tokens, gray tokens represent near-zero credit, while red tokens represent negative credit that penalizes the tokens. SAEPO tends to reward semantically meaningful tokens like question-relevant tokens in incorrect trajectories and reasoning tokens in correct trajectories, while penalizing uninformative or misleading tokens even when they are in correct trajectories, achieving fine-grained token-level credit assignment over the reasoning trace.

Figure 3 Training dynamics on Qwen3-1.7B-Base. We plot training accuracy curves during RL training for GRPO and GSPO, comparing each vanilla policy optimization algorithm with its SAEPO-augmented variant and with credit-assignment baselines (i.e., KTAE, THR, and GTPO). SAEPO shows faster convergence in training accuracy and generally reaches higher training accuracy.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation enables the recognition of arbitrary categories through natural language descriptions and has recently been extended from natural images to remote sensing. However, existing approaches primarily focus on three-channel optical imagery or limited-band multispectral data, while pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to directly exploit the rich spectral information of hyperspectral imagery (HSI) without additional adaptation. More importantly, different land-cover categories rely on distinct spectral cues, which may be weakened by uniform fusion. To address these challenges, we propose SpectralRoute, a training-free framework for open-vocabulary hyperspectral segmentation. Specifically, we construct complementary spectral views from HSI and enrich category descriptions with external spectral knowledge, enabling frozen vision-language models to extract diverse spectral-semantic responses. We then introduce a class-adaptive spectral routing mechanism that selectively amplifies discriminative spectral responses for each category, overcoming the limitations of uniform fusion. Furthermore, physical spectral priors are incorporated to refine predictions for visually similar land-cover categories. Experiments on three hyperspectral benchmarks demonstrate that SpectralRoute consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods without additional training.
authors: Qingmei Li, Xiaoya Fan, Juepeng Zheng, Jianxi Huang, Haohuan Fu
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of applying vision-language models to hyperspectral imagery with rich, category-dependent spectral information.
Constructs complementary spectral views and enriches text descriptions with external spectral knowledge.
Uses class-adaptive spectral routing to amplify discriminative spectral responses instead of uniformly fusing them.
Incorporates physical spectral priors to refine predictions for visually similar land-cover categories.
Outperforms existing methods across three hyperspectral benchmarks without additional training.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SpectralRoute. The framework starts with knowledge-enhanced text representation and multiview spectral construction, followed by vision-language feature extraction using frozen CLIP to compute cross-modal similarities. Spatial pooling and softmax transform the similarities into routing weights. Class-adaptive spectral routing inputs both the routing weights and visual features to perform weighted summation and amplification. Physics-guided refinement integrates spectral prototypes, semantic gating, and initial scores to generate the final prediction.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison of segmentation maps on the Pavia University dataset. Previous methods suffer from severe category confusion and fragmented boundaries, whereas SpectralRoute achieves sharper boundaries and finer category separation.

Figure 4. Parameter sensitivity analysis of temperature τ and scaling factor γ. While simpler scenes favor smaller values, highly complex scenes rely more on strong spectral amplification. Our method adaptively scales with scene complexity and maintains robust performance.

Figure 1. Motivation of SpectralRoute. The task requires pixelwise prediction from HSIs and open vocabularies. However, RGBpretrained VLMs miss continuous spectra, causing visual ambiguity among certain categories. In contrast, hyperspectral signatures provide distinct physical evidence. SpectralRoute exploits this through multi-view routing, semantic enrichment, and physical priors to achieve fine-grained separation. in hyperspectral classification and semantic segmentation, existing methods predominantly operate under a closed-set assumption [35], where models are trained to recognize a predefined set of categories using annotated samples. Such dependence limits their flexibility in handling previously unseen categories [9, 18] and adapting to diverse Earth observation scenarios [28]. In practical applications, land cover categories may vary across regions, sensors, and requirements, making repeated data annotation and model retraining impractical [49]. Therefore, enabling flexible, textdriven recognition of land cover categories without additional training represents an important direction for hyperspectral image interpretation [15, 41].

Figure 6. Qualitative comparison of segmentation maps on the Washington DC Mall dataset. Previous methods exhibit category confusion in heterogeneous urban regions, whereas SpectralRoute better preserves the spatial organization of major land-cover categories and captures fine-grained structures.

Figure 7. Qualitative comparison of segmentation maps on the Houston 2018 dataset. SpectralRoute demonstrates favorable category discrimination and captures detailed spatial patterns in complex urban scenes.

papers.abstract: Mobile manipulators operating in homes and other complex environments must coordinate their base and arm over long horizons, navigating around obstacles, through narrow passages, and between constrained workspaces. Neural motion planners can provide fast closed-loop planning from partial observations, but scaling them to room-sized environments is difficult because generating high-quality training trajectories is itself a challenging motion-planning problem. To address this, we introduce MoMa-DemoSmith, a demonstration-generation pipeline that separates the problem into global path discovery for large complex scenes and local motion refinement for collision avoidance. This key separation enables the generation of millions of challenging whole-body trajectories across our procedurally generated scenes. We train MoMa-NMP on these demonstrations through behavior cloning (BC) followed by privileged on-policy distillation, achieving 87.0% success on our simulation benchmark and 77.5% across 80 trials in unseen real-world scenes. See video results at https://adamhkan.com/moma-nmp/.
authors: Adam Kan, Jason Jingzhou Liu, Jiahui Yang, Kenneth Shaw, Deepak Pathak
bullets: Targets long-horizon navigation and manipulation in complex, obstacle-filled environments with partial observations.
MoMa-DemoSmith separates global path discovery from local collision-avoidance refinement to generate challenging trajectories at scale.
MoMa-NMP is trained with behavior cloning followed by privileged on-policy distillation.
Achieves 87.0% success in simulation and 77.5% over 80 trials in unseen real-world scenes.

(1) We generate diverse scenes with varying arrangements of tables and obstacles, and sample start and goal poses in both open and confined workspaces. (2) We use cuRobo to plan global trajectories for the mobile base and arm. Relaxed planning constraints improve route discovery but can produce trajectories with insufficient obstacle clearance or unrealistic base motion. (3) We use Geometric Fabrics to refine the next five whole-body configuration targets at each cuRobo waypoint, generating action chunks with improved obstacle clearance for imitation learning.

papers.abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of scene-level memory design for efficient navigation across sessions and successive object goals. Recent methods commonly represent a scene using scene graphs or image--text records. However, dense scene-graph representations impose substantial reasoning and context overhead on multimodal large language models, while image--text records cannot be directly converted into executable geometric routes. To address these limitations, we propose SuperNav-1.5, an agentic navigation system equipped with a structured spatial memory constructed by the agent. The memory consists of an area-segmented occupancy map annotated with agent-maintained, map-grounded memory nodes. This map guides the agent toward unvisited areas and provides executable routes to known locations. For multi-session navigation, we introduce agent-guided relocalization, whereby the agent infers an area prior from current observations and stored memory records to constrain geometric matching and localize the robot within the stored map. Together, these designs enable efficient navigation across session and successive object goals. Experiments show that our method outperforms baselines on single-object, multi-object, and demand-driven navigation benchmarks, with particularly strong gains in path efficiency. Multi-session evaluation demonstrates that the constructed memory can be reused, while deployment on a real quadruped robot further shows the system's applicability.
authors: Jiarui Guo, Jinkai Zhang, Yuanhong Yu, Yongchen Zai, Futang Zhu, Ruizhen Hu, Sida Peng, Xiaowei Zhou

papers.abstract: A frozen language model can give a wrong answer because a fact is unavailable, a reliable passage is ignored, or an unsupported claim survives generation. We review 116 works on inference-time hallucination intervention and its foundations. We trace the development from retrieval and controllable generation to methods that act on input evidence, token scores, internal representations, completed claims, or the decision to answer. For each family we compare its source of evidence, model access, preparation cost, and the task on which a correction can be established. For activation steering, we distinguish estimating a subspace from applying a state-dependent edit and separate interventions on the prompt from those on the generated prefix. Published comparisons show why faithfulness to a source, factual correctness, informativeness, and answer coverage must be measured separately. Applications in time-sensitive question answering, document synthesis, and visual grounding identify when source authority, evidence availability, or capability preservation limits a reported gain.
authors: Can Huang
bullets: Hallucinations can arise from missing facts, ignored reliable evidence, or unsupported claims that persist through generation.
Interventions target input evidence, token scores, internal representations, completed claims, or the decision to answer.
The review compares methods by evidence source, required model access, preparation cost, and task-specific correction evidence.
For activation steering, it distinguishes subspace estimation from state-dependent editing, and prompt interventions from generated-prefix interventions.

Evaluation should separately measure source faithfulness, factual correctness, informativeness, and answer coverage; gains may be limited by source authority, evidence availability, or capability preservation.

papers.abstract: Underactuated grippers can form enveloping grasps through passive compliance, while the terminal pose and single width predicted by generic grasp generators do not fully capture the approach-closure process. Conventional collision filtering also struggles to distinguish harmful interference from acceptable contact. We present UnderGrasp, a post-hoc grasp refinement and evaluation framework for an underactuated gripper that reuses grasp candidates and quality priors from a frozen generator. The model jointly encodes the target, local environment, support surface, and approach-path geometry to propose diverse combinations of insertion depth, pre-grasp width, and target closing width for each candidate. These actions are ranked by combining separately predicted envelopment and interaction quality with upstream priors, balancing grasp feasibility, envelopment, and scene disturbance rather than rejecting all environmental contact. The back end is trained solely on configuration and interaction labels generated by gripper-specific simulations, without real-robot grasp labels. Real-robot experiments with an underactuated gripper show that UnderGrasp improves the overall success rate (SR) and the envelopment rate (ER) among successful grasps from 0.55/0.12 to 0.82/0.55 with AnyGrasp, and from 0.42/0.08 to 0.65/0.36 with GraspNet. In contrast, increasing the fixed insertion depth to 40 mm improves ER to 0.35 but reduces SR to 0.52, supporting the value of adaptive refinement. For trials involving target or environmental contact during approach, the conditional success rates increase from 0.36 to 0.89 and from 0.25 to 0.86, respectively, demonstrating more reliable execution under contact. bullets: Generic terminal pose and width predictions overlook the gripper’s approach-to-closure process and may mishandle acceptable environmental contact.
The framework jointly considers the target, local environment, support surface, and approach path to propose insertion depth, pre-grasp width, and closing width.
Candidate actions are ranked using predicted envelopment and interaction quality alongside the frozen generator’s grasp priors.
Simulation-generated configuration and interaction labels train the refinement back end without real-robot grasp annotations.
Real-robot experiments show improved success, envelopment, and contact-condition reliability compared with unrefined grasps and fixed insertion depth.

papers.abstract: Domain shift is a major problem for training machine learning models. While Continual Learning (CL) assumes distribution shift during training and Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) considers new domains at test time, setups that require explicit online adaptation to domain shift during both phases remain under-explored. We propose continual learning with domain preview (CL-P), a new combination of CL and TTA where both train and test data suffer from distribution shift. The training phase of CL-P is analogous to domain-incremental learning while the testing phase consists of a TTA phase on a future domain (which we call preview), and an evaluation phase on all seen domains. The model must then adapt to new domains at train and test time. In this paper, we evaluate mainstream CL and TTA methods that adapt only at train or test time, as well as their naive combination. Experimentally, TTA heavily damages the domain on which the CL method has just trained and increases forgetting. Notably, this damage mostly comes from the BatchNorm statistics shared by all domains. In that sense, we propose DOSE (Dosing by Online Statistics of Each domain), which allows a seamless combination of any CL and TTA methods by adaptive domain inference at test time, where the adaptation is applied to each image in proportion to the probability that it comes from the preview domain. Through extensive experiments with ResNet and ViT backbones, various combinations of CL and TTA baseline methods and datasets considering diverse domains, we show that DOSE matches or improves on CL methods alone in all 24 settings and on the naive combination in all but one. The code can be found in appendix.
authors: Fr\'ed\'eric Li Combeau, Nicolas Michel, Toshihiko Yamasaki
bullets: CL-P trains across shifting domains, then adapts online to a future preview domain before evaluating on all seen domains.
Naively combining CL and TTA can damage the recently trained domain and increase forgetting, largely due to shared BatchNorm statistics.
DOSE infers domain membership online and applies adaptation to each image in proportion to its likelihood of belonging to the preview domain.
Across 24 evaluated settings with ResNet and ViT backbones, DOSE matches or improves on CL alone in every setting and on the naive combination in all but one.

papers.tldr: The paper introduces CL-P, a setting combining continual learning and test-time adaptation under train- and test-time domain shifts, and proposes DOSE to reduce adaptation-induced forgetting.

papers.abstract: Current AI may have a model of how we use human language, but this does not translate into a reliable representation of physical reality. World models promise to fill this gap by learning how an environment changes over time and predicting the consequences of an action, and they are already used to steer robots and generate explorable worlds. This article asks how AI regulation in three major legal contexts, the European Union, California, and China, copes with the distinctive challenges they raise. I propose a definition and a taxonomy of world models based on who or what acts on their predictions, and identify the risks of misplaced reliance on them. I argue that existing rules tend to cover world models but leave three questions open, i.e., action provenance, trajectory validity, and the weight of simulated evidence, and recommend ways to fill these gaps.
authors: Claudio Novelli
bullets: World models learn environmental dynamics to predict the consequences of actions, supporting robotics and explorable virtual worlds.
The article examines regulation in the European Union, California, and China.
It defines and categorizes world models according to who or what acts on their predictions.
It highlights risks from misplaced reliance on simulated or predicted outcomes.
Three unresolved issues are action provenance, trajectory validity, and the evidentiary weight of simulations.

papers.selection_reason: Legal and policy analysis of world models is directly relevant to the world-models topic, though not a technical method.
papers.title: World Models and the Law
papers.tldr: Existing AI laws broadly cover world models but leave important gaps around how their predictions are used and trusted.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation is essential for interactive animation and humanoid robotics, where an agent must respond to changing instructions and spatial goals while moving. Existing autoregressive diffusion methods generate motion incrementally, but bounded attention caches limit access to distant history, while repeated denoising introduces substantial inference overhead. We present Motion Mamba 2.0, a Mamba-based root-body diffusion architecture that integrates local attention, resumable recurrent states, and persistent content memory (PCM) for long-horizon controllable motion generation. PCM transforms compressed motion history from Mamba recurrent states, together with state changes and text-conditioned features, into dynamically updated content slots accessible to local attention. To enable efficient inference, we further develop an execution scheme tailored to this architecture, combining CUDA Graph replay, fused kernels, and execution-flow simplification while preserving the canonical history update. Evaluations on retargeted HiPHI demonstrate accurate terminal control over rollouts of up to 39.52 s, while short-horizon comparisons on BONES Seed and retargeted HumanML3D show that the model also retains strong spatial control and text-motion matching. On an RTX 4090, the optimized execution reduces median complete-window latency from 1685.35 to 276.14 ms, achieving a median paired speedup of 6.138$\times$ while preserving identical outputs and committed states in the tested rollouts. Moreover, we conduct extensive real-world evaluation on the Unitree G1, demonstrating sequential text-guided action composition, expressive motion, and interactive locomotion through keyboard and mouse control.
authors: Yue Huang, Tianshan Zhang, Zeyu Zhang, Jayeon Kang, Akide Liu, Sungjoon Choi, Dacheng Tao, Hao Tang
bullets: Addresses limited long-range history and high inference cost in autoregressive diffusion motion generation.
Uses a Mamba-based root-body diffusion architecture with local attention, resumable recurrent states, and persistent content memory.
Persistent content memory converts compressed motion history, state changes, and text features into dynamically updated content slots.

Optimized execution with CUDA Graph replay, fused kernels, and simplified flow reduces reported median latency from 1685.35 ms to 276.14 ms, with a 6.138× paired speedup and identical tested outputs and states.
Evaluations cover long-horizon terminal control, short-horizon spatial and text-motion matching, and real-world interactive control on a Unitree G1.

figures.caption: Fig. 4: Overview of Motion Mamba 2.0. Conditioned on text, spatial controls, and accepted motion history, the framework generates motion autoregressively through a two-stage diffusion denoiser. At each denoising step, the root network predicts the global trajectory, whose local features condition body prediction. Both networks combine attention and Mamba-3 through a hybrid sequence mixer. After each clean motion window is accepted, the history states are updated for subsequent generation.
Fig. 1: Motion Mamba 2.0. Continuous text-guided motion generation for long-horizon humanoid control on the Unitree G1.

Fig. 8: Real-world qualitative results on Unitree G1. (a) T1, sequential action composition; (b) T2, expressive motion; (c) T3, keyboard-controlled locomotion; and (d) T4, mouse-controlled locomotion. Fig. 10: Qualitative comparison under a distant single-point constraint. ARDY (upper row) and Motion Mamba 2.0 (lower row) are shown at the same four timestamps. Both receive the common 18 m target and its 33.40 s deadline from the start. Bottom: (a) root trajectories in goal-aligned coordinates; (b) displacement along the goal direction over time. Our model makes greater progress by 25.04 s (15.05 versus 9.36 m) and has a lower final-second mean root speed (0.712 versus 1.992 m/s).

Fig. 2: Interactive motion generation with Motion Mamba 2.0. Text instructions specify the requested actions, while spatial controls constrain root motion and selected joint positions. From left to right, the panels show root trajectories, root waypoints, full-body pose sequences, and selected joint positions. Blue-to-gray poses indicate temporal progression, while red overlays visualize trajectories, waypoints, and joint locations. The panels show Viser motion references and a rollout tracked with SONIC.

Fig. 9: Simulated motion tracking with SONIC. Top left: forward to backward walking; top right: walking with a left turn; bottom left: waving followed by walking; bottom right: martial-arts motion followed by walking. Each quadrant compares simulated execution (upper row) with the corresponding Viser reference (lower row) at matching timestamps.

Fig. 6: CUDA Graph and Kernel Fusion. Stack-level CUDA Graph replay of the three CFG branches, with separate graphs for the root and body DiT stacks, and fused Mamba transition preprocessing.

Fig. 5: Streaming generation and hybrid attention–Mamba mixing. (a) Motion is generated window by window through root–body diffusion, with the history held fixed during denoising and updated only after the sampled window is accepted. (b) Base attention retrieves recent motion features, while PCM attention additionally accesses persistent content slots. Their gated residual difference is combined with the Mamba-3 output resumed from the committed recurrent state.

papers.selection_reason: Autoregressive diffusion Mamba for long-horizon humanoid motion generation and control; text-guided action composition on a real robot.
papers.title: Motion Mamba 2.0: Autoregressive Diffusion Mamba for Long-Horizon Humanoid Control
papers.tldr: Motion Mamba 2.0 enables long-horizon, real-time text- and spatially controlled humanoid motion by combining recurrent memory, local attention, and efficient diffusion execution.

papers.abstract: Particle filters flexibly represent complex, multimodal beliefs but expose them as weighted, unordered sets incompatible with conventional fixed-dimensional policies. We study particle-belief encodings as inputs to reinforcement-learning policies while holding belief estimation and policy optimization fixed. We compare statistical summaries, cumulant-generating-function (CGF) features, and permutation-invariant set encoders. Trainable encoders are learned end-to-end or pretrained through belief reconstruction or task-specific prediction. Across eight tasks, pooling-based set encoders and gradient CGF features are reliable end-to-end, while the Set Transformer achieves the highest performance with appropriate pretraining. Task-specific pretraining helps when its target captures decision-relevant belief structure, whereas reconstruction pretraining and latent alignment provide more selective benefits. For selecting and training particle-belief encoders in partially observable Markov decision processes, our results show that an encoding that reconstructs the belief well is not necessarily a good input for control.
authors: Himanshu Gupta, Brendan Crowe, Christoffer Heckman, Bradley Hayes, Zachary Sunberg
bullets: Particle filters produce flexible, multimodal beliefs, but their weighted, unordered particles are difficult for fixed-dimensional policies to use.
The study evaluates statistical summaries, cumulant-generating-function features, and permutation-invariant set encoders while keeping belief estimation and policy optimization fixed.
Pooling-based encoders and gradient CGF features perform reliably when trained end-to-end.
The Set Transformer performs best when given suitable pretraining; task-specific pretraining helps when it captures decision-relevant belief structure.
Scope: results span eight tasks and show that belief reconstruction quality is not a sufficient criterion for selecting control representations.

papers.selection_reason: Particle belief encodings for RL under partial observability are relevant to embodied agents.
papers.title: Particle Belief Representations for Reinforcement Learning under Partial Observability
papers.tldr: The study compares ways to encode unordered particle beliefs for reinforcement-learning policies under partial observability, finding that control-effective representations need not reconstruct beliefs accurately.

papers.abstract: Video corpus moment retrieval (VCMR) requires finding the video and time interval that match a text query in a corpus of videos. We present RELAY, a training-free framework for VCMR that shares memory across queries. RELAY processes a batch of queries in three stages: search with a query bank, ranking with video notes, and localization with video prompt caching. In the search stage, an embedding model scores each video by its best-matching frame. The query bank penalizes videos that score highly for many other queries in the batch. In the ranking stage, a vision-language model (VLM) writes notes on each candidate video's scenes, people, objects, and actions once. Then, a large language model (LLM) reranks the candidates from these notes. In the localization stage, a VLM predicts the time interval of the moment in the top-ranked video. When multiple queries select the same video, prompt caching lets the VLM reuse its frames. On the three VERIFIED benchmarks, RELAY outperforms the trained baselines in video retrieval R@1 without training. Without any labeled moment, its predicted intervals are shorter than the annotated ones. In VCMR, it achieves similar performance to VideoSearch-R1 on one benchmark and trails it at IoU 0.5 on the other two. Human annotators also mark shorter moments than the original annotations of the benchmarks. A single margin, calibrated on a few labeled queries, widens the predicted interval to the annotation convention of the benchmarks. With it, RELAY outperforms the trained baselines in VCMR at IoU 0.5.
authors: Chenwei Xu, Shang Wu, Zhenyu Pan, Jianshu Zhang, Pranav Maneriker, Lie Lu, Fan Du, Manling Li, Han Liu
bullets: Processes query batches through search, candidate ranking, and temporal localization.
Uses a query bank to reduce cross-query confusion and video notes for LLM-based reranking.
Caches video prompts and frames when multiple queries target the same video.
Outperforms trained baselines in video retrieval R@1 on three VERIFIED benchmarks.
Predicted intervals are initially shorter than annotations; a single calibrated margin improves VCMR at IoU 0.5.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Pipeline of RELAY. The top row follows one query of a batch through the three stages. The bottom row is the memory that the queries of the batch share. 1⃝ Search: the embedding model scores each video by its best-matching frame. The query bank subtracts a bias from each score. The bias is larger for a video that matches more queries. 2⃝ Ranking: a VLM writes notes on each candidate video once. An LLM orders the candidates from their notes. Reciprocal rank fusion merges this order with the embedding-based ranking. 3⃝ Localization: the VLM predicts the start and end of the moment in the top-ranked video. Queries for the same video share a prompt prefix containing its timestamped frames. Each request adds the current query.

Figure 5. Qualitative Example. (a) Success. The search ranks the annotated video 6th, the query bank raises it to 3rd, and RELAY ranks it first. Its notes name the bathroom, the red hooded sweatshirt and the dark gray pants of the query. They also record that the woman enters carrying a mug at 2.7–4.8 s. The predicted interval, 2.6–4.6 s, lies within the moment of the human annotator, 1.4–5.8 s. The annotation, 0.4–9.2 s, adds seconds on both sides. The margin widens the predicted interval to 0.6–6.6 s, closer to the annotation. (b) Failure. The search and the query bank rank the annotated Video 1 first. Its notes describe a man opening the door and taking out clothes, but they call the machine a washing machine. The notes of Video 2 describe a woman opening the door of a dryer, so RELAY ranks Video 2 first. Bars: dataset annotation, human annotation, the predicted interval, and the interval with the 2 s margin. Human annotation is from Otani et al. [30].

Figure 3. Margin around the predicted interval: VCMR R@1 (%) at IoU 0.5 on the three test splits when the predicted interval is widened by w seconds on each side, or shrunk for w < 0. Gray dashed lines: w = 0 and w = 2 s. Embedding only: our baseline that uses only Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, the embedding model of RELAY and VideoSearch-R1 [20], to retrieve the video and predict the moment. Its moment grows from the best-matching frame of its top-ranked video while the frames score above the midpoint of the video’s scores. VideoSearch-R1: its released predictions on Charades-FIG, widened the same way. Numbers: R@1 at w = 0 and w = 2 s. RELAY outperforms the embedding-only baseline at every w ≥ 0 on all three benchmarks. The 2 s margin raises RELAY and lowers VideoSearch-R1.
Figure 6. Video notes supplied to the ranker for the cabinet-opening example in Fig. 2. The timeline distinguishes opening the cabinet, removing a package and closing the door.

Figure 7. When a margin helps and when it hides an error. Each panel shows the Charades activity-class interval, independent annotators’ intervals and the model prediction for one Charades-STA test sentence. The displayed IoUs use the activity-class interval as reference. (a) The runner appears after the class interval begins. (b) The class interval covers drinking from a cup. The annotators place the queried action, eating a sandwich, later in the video.

Figure 4. Streaming Queries. Query bank: VR R@1 of the search minus that without a query bank, for a query whose bank holds the given number of streaming queries, itself included; with all of them, the bank is the batch. Video prompt caching: localization input tokens per query, by the number of queries for which the cache keeps unused frames (mean of 5 random orders). Dashed lines: all queries in one batch. A bank of a few queries lowers VR R@1, and ActivityNet-FIG needs the most queries for both.

Figure 1. Video corpus moment retrieval (VCMR). Given a text query and a corpus of videos, VCMR retrieves the video that contains the moment the query describes. It also localizes the start and end times of this moment. VCMR joins video retrieval (VR), which finds the video, and single-video moment retrieval (SVMR), which finds the moment in a given video.

Figure 8. Retrieval and localization on two test queries. (a) The DiDeMo-FIG reference covers two consecutive 5 s segments as a black car passes the camera. (b) The ActivityNet-FIG reference covers the entire pole-vault video.

Table 1. VCMR on the VERIFIED Benchmarks (test splits; search over the whole test corpus). VR R@1 and R@10: the percentage of queries whose ground-truth video is among the top 1 and top 10 ranked videos. VCMR R@1 at IoU 0.5 and 0.7: the percentage of queries whose top-ranked video is the ground-truth video and whose predicted interval has a temporal IoU of at least 0.5 or 0.7 with the ground-truth moment. RELAY: the interval that the VLM predicts. W/ margin: this interval widened by 2 s on each side, a value picked with 20 labeled training queries. Baselines as reported by VERIFIED [4] and by Lee et al. [20]. Qwen3-VL-2B: the zero-shot baseline of VideoSearch-R1, its VLM without fine-tuning. Without training, RELAY achieves the highest VR R@1 on all three benchmarks. It outperforms Qwen3-VL-2B, the other method without training, in every column, by about 10 points in VR R@1. With the margin, it also achieves the highest VCMR R@1 at IoU 0.5 on all three benchmarks, and at 0.7 on all benchmarks except DiDeMo-FIG.

Table 11. VCMR with the Original Queries and on TVR: R@1 (%) at IoU 0.5 and 0.7 on Charades-STA test, DiDeMo test, the first validation annotation of ActivityNet Captions, and TVR val. [12]. cWith automatic speech recognition (ASR) subtitles; split not stated. dSplit not stated. eR@10, as RefCap reports no R@1; RELAY predicts one interval per query, so its R@10 equals its R@1.

Tokens: localization input tokens per query, all and not read from the prompt cache (new); the first turn of a video’s conversation is shared over its queries. papers.abstract: Feedback tools and research on learner writing need transcriptions of handwritten essays that keep exactly what the student wrote: misspellings, line breaks, struck-through words and insertions. Vision-language models (VLMs) read handwriting well, but they also tend to rewrite it into correct language. We measure this on BRESSAY, 1,000 handwritten Brazilian Portuguese essays, with a benchmark that adds error preservation, invented errors, edit-markup precision and recall and line structure to the character error rate (CER) and uses paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We restrict the study to open-weight models that schools can run on their own hardware. Of 22 open baselines, the best, Qwen3-VL 235B-A22B, reaches 5.6% CER on the 199 test pages; none reproduces the edit markup reliably, and every VLM replaces 39-78% of the words absent from a Portuguese dictionary with dictionary words. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B on the 647 training pages in 85 minutes on one GPU. The resulting Escriba-OCR-1B reaches 2.06% CER, 3.5 points below the best baseline (95% CI [-4.2, -2.9]); under the ICDAR 2024 competition metric it reaches 2.1% CER, below the best published page-level results (2.2-2.4%). It recovers 67% of insertions and 77% of illegible deletions, and reproduces the line structure of 97% of the pages, but still normalises 60% of likely misspellings. Three seeds agree within 0.04 CER points, and quantised to 4 bits the model runs on an ordinary CPU at about one minute per page. On 40 letters of another corpus it matches its base model (without that model's appended comments) but misreads unseen words more often; weight interpolation recovers half the gap. A teacher's review finds that 45% of the judgeable apparent corrections are errors in the BRESSAY ground truth, so dictionary-based scores likely understate preservation. We release the model, the benchmark code and the review data.
authors: Tardelli Ronan Coelho Stekel
bullets: The benchmark evaluates transcription fidelity beyond CER, including invented errors, edit-markup precision/recall, and line structure on 1,000 Brazilian Portuguese essays.
Fine-tuning LightOnOCR-3-1B on 647 pages produced 2.06% CER, improving on the best open baseline’s 5.6% CER.
The model recovers 67% of insertions, 77% of illegible deletions, and preserves line structure on 97% of pages.
It still changes 60% of likely misspellings, and unseen words remain a challenge on another corpus.
The 4-bit model runs on ordinary CPUs at about one minute per page; released resources include the model, benchmark code, and review data.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel in open-world manipulation, yet their performance often saturates when training data are naively pooled across heterogeneous robots, tasks, and environments. Distributionally robust data mixture optimization, exemplified by Re-Mix, can recover much of this performance, but its weight search requires training full-scale policies twice on the entire corpus, placing it out of reach for most laboratories. We present ProMix, a compute-efficient instantiation of the proxy-reference DRO recipe for robotic imitation learning: a 15M-parameter proxy learns per-domain sampling weights by minimizing worst-case excess loss against a frozen reference model, and the learned weights transfer, without re-tuning, to VLA backbones up to 7B parameters. We further provide, to our knowledge, the first controlled analysis of the reference model's role in robotic DRO, showing that removing it induces over-pessimism toward noisy, low-quality domains (-3.8% average and -14.3% worst-domain success rate), and that entropy regularization is needed to prevent weight collapse. Evaluated on 9500 real-world episodes from the Open-X Embodiment dataset, ProMix improves the average success rate over uniform mixing from 68.4% to 76.2%, matching Re-Mix within evaluation noise while reducing mixture-optimization cost to a backbone-independent 11 GPU-hours - versus 16 GPU-hours at the 50M comparison scale and 192 GPU-hours at 7B for full-scale searches - with a +17.1% absolute gain on the worst-case domain.
authors: Qie Sima, Wei Xue, Yike Guo
bullets: Targets performance saturation caused by naively mixing heterogeneous robot, task, and environment data.
Uses a 15M-parameter proxy and frozen reference model to learn domain sampling weights via proxy-reference DRO.
Transfers learned weights without retuning to VLA backbones up to 7B parameters.
On 9,500 real-world Open-X Embodiment episodes, improves average success from 68.4% to 76.2% over uniform mixing and matches Re-Mix within evaluation noise.
Reference removal causes over-pessimistic weighting, while entropy regularization prevents weight collapse; optimization costs 11 GPU-hours and is backbone-independent.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: The ProMix Framework Architecture. The pipeline consists of two stages: (Stage 1) a proxy-reference optimization loop that learns optimal domain weights p∗ by minimizing the worst-case excess loss of a 15M trainable proxy against a frozen reference model; (Stage 2) single-pass training of the final VLA model using the transferred weights p∗. The entire mixture search costs 11 GPU-hours,whereas a full-scale Re-Mix search costs 16 GPU-hours at the 50M comparison scale and 192 GPU-hours at 7B.

Fig. 2: Evolution of the domain weights during the proxy search. Each panel traces the seven domain weights pi from uniform initialization (top to bottom: full method, without the reference model, without entropy regularization); the shaded band marks the final 10k-step window averaged into p∗.

Fig. 3: Summary of the main empirical effects. (a) Mixture-search cost: a full-scale search costs 16 GPU-hours at the 50M comparison scale and 192 GPU-hours at 7B, whereas the ProMix search is fixed at 11 GPU-hours regardless of backbone. (b) Per-domain improvement over uniform mixing at the 50M scale. (c) Transfer of the 15M-learned mixture to final models at three scales without re-tuning (95% CIs over 5 seeds).

papers.abstract: Reproducing and modifying a meter-scale humanoid remains challenging for research and teaching groups with limited fabrication resources and engineering support. This paper presents Arcadian, an open-source humanoid ecosystem that offers accessible and customizable humanoid hardware and software with community support. Arcadian aims to strike a balance among cost-effectiveness, structural durability, and full customizability, lowering the barrier to entry for research and education. Specifically, this meter-scale humanoid adopts metal-embedded 3D printing to achieve a high strength-to-cost ratio, eliminating the need for computer numerical control (CNC) machining while retaining design flexibility. Extensive simulation and hardware tests validate the design: a reinforcement-learning (RL) locomotion policy trained in simulation transfers to the hardware, and a virtual reality (VR) teleoperation interface drives both arms for simple manipulation tasks. The robot is around one meter tall and costs approximately $6,800 to build. All computer-aided design (CAD) models, the bill of materials, assembly documentation, and training and deployment code are publicly released, distributed through Tnkr.ai and MakerWorld and supported by a Discord server and a project forum through which community feedback informs design updates. The ecosystem resources are available at https://anonymous-humanoid.gitbook.io/docs.
authors: Zelin Shen, Gabriel Ramos Salinas, Qiyu Zhang, Yue Qin, Chen Qian, Yanran Ding

papers.abstract: Terraforming Mars is a long-horizon, action-conditioned control problem that requires predicting atmospheric responses to interventions over centuries to identify effective policies. This position paper argues that physics-regularized recurrent state-space world models are the most promising foundation for this setting. Data-driven climate emulators lack action-conditioning, and physics-based general circulation models (GCMs) are too expensive for policy search. Among learned world models, recurrent state-space architectures with physics constraints are better suited than transformer-based alternatives: they provide native uncertainty quantification through their stochastic-deterministic decomposition, remain stable under sparse non-terrestrial training data, and enforce physical consistency at each rollout step. To make this position concrete, we describe a potential architecture combining JEPA-inspired latent encoding, universal differential equation constraints, and a Dreamer-lineage planning head. We also introduce MarsWorld, an open benchmark proposal for intervention-conditioned planetary world models, and discuss broader implications and objections.
authors: Sameera S Kashyap, Akshitha Nagaraj, Razvan Marinescu
bullets: Terraforming requires long-horizon, action-conditioned predictions of atmospheric responses.
Climate emulators often lack intervention conditioning, while physics-based GCMs are too costly for policy search.
The paper favors recurrent state-space models over transformers for uncertainty estimation, sparse-data stability, and stepwise physical consistency.
A proposed design combines JEPA-inspired latent representations, universal differential equation constraints, and a Dreamer-style planning head.
The paper proposes MarsWorld, an open benchmark for intervention-conditioned planetary world models, but presents a position and architecture proposal rather than experimental validation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Proposed Mars atmospheric world model architecture. S1: A two-stage training strategy separates synthetic pre-training data (MCD v6.1) from observational fine-tuning sources (EMARS, OpenMARS; with TES/MCS as the underlying retrievals); intervention actions at enter the transition model as continuous vectors. S2: A state encoder maps atmospheric fields to a latent z; PINN constraints and UDE residuals regularize the latent and downstream dynamics, merged at the concatenation node. S3: An RSSM propagates stochastic latent zt and recurrent memory ht under action-conditioned transitions ρ(z | h, a) with physics enforced at every step; ht is updated from (ht−1, zt−1, at−1) via the recurrent backbone. S4: An actor-critic head trains within imagined latent rollouts; the actor π(a | z, h) outputs intervention policies, the critic V (z, h) estimates returns from (∆P,∆T,∆O2), and a decoder reconstructs gridded fields against EMARS as an auxiliary signal. S5: Outputs are a learned policy trajectory, a long-horizon atmospheric forecast, and a rollout uncertainty map from stochastic latent samples.

Table 1: Requirements for Mars terraforming simulation vs. existing systems. (i) Mars physical accuracy; (ii) tractable for policy search; (iii) action-conditioned rollouts; (iv) century-scale stability; (v) trainable on sparse non-terrestrial data.

papers.title: World Models Are the Right Foundation for Simulating Mars Terraforming

papers.abstract: Wrist cameras provide an action-centric view that is directly relevant to robot manipulation. However, collecting human wrist-camera videos at scale is challenging due to cumbersome setups that can interfere with natural hand movements. In contrast, head-mounted human egocentric videos are much easier to scale. We introduce Ego2Wrist, which synthesizes synchronized wrist-camera views from human egocentric videos and task descriptions. Trained on approximately 940 hours of paired head- and wrist-camera recordings, Ego2Wrist jointly generates three views. To evaluate generated wrist views without ground truth, we propose hand-centric cross-view consistency (HCC), which measures consistency between generated wrist views and corresponding hand regions in the input head view. HCC ranks model checkpoints comparably to ground-truth-based LPIPS, and human evaluators prefer HCC-selected generations in 77% of responses. Evaluated on four datasets, Ego2Wrist outperforms fine-tuned WorldWander, reducing LPIPS by 28% and receiving human preference in 76% of responses. More importantly, HCC facilitates recursive self-improvement on in-the-wild egocentric videos by selecting generated wrist views for further training. Generation quality progressively improves over three rounds. These results demonstrate a scalable approach to generating real-world wrist-view human manipulation videos for robot policy training.
authors: Ziyao Zeng, Xiatao Sun, Hao Wang, Ziyu Guo, Youheng Yao, Jingcheng Ni, Shenyuan Gao, Fengyu Yang, Renrui Zhang, Bangya Liu, Daniel Rakita
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of collecting large-scale human wrist-camera data without disrupting natural hand movements.
Generates synchronized wrist views and three total views from egocentric video and task descriptions.
Introduces hand-centric cross-view consistency (HCC) to evaluate generated wrist views without ground truth.
Across four datasets, reduces LPIPS by 28% versus fine-tuned WorldWander and receives human preference in 76% of responses.
HCC enables self-improvement on in-the-wild videos, with quality improving over three training rounds.

papers.title: Ego2Wrist: Bootstrapping Wrist-View Synthesis from Egocentric Video
papers.tldr: Ego2Wrist synthesizes robot-relevant wrist-camera views from scalable egocentric videos and uses cross-view consistency to enable recursive improvement.

papers.abstract: Runtime guardrails protect mobile GUI agents by assessing each proposed action before execution, but existing guardrails rely on cloud hosted large multimodal models, exposing every screen to a remote server, including private information such as payments, messages, and medical records. We propose MobileGrail, an on-device deployable model that addresses both. It maintains a recurrent task state that retains only the evidence subsequent safety decisions depend on, so that authorization and execution progress persist beyond the short context. To intervene early while keeping the safety boundary precise, it learns two labels, unsafe and block: unsafe marks the action that commits a violation, whereas block may be issued at any step of an intervention window, which spans from the first action that the user's authorization no longer explains to the committing action itself. To support training, we build an environment of 32 applications whose backends verify the effect of every action, supplying verified labels for supervision and rewards for reinforcement learning to calibrate intervention timing. We also build MobileVeto, an offline benchmark of unsafe trajectories largely on held-out applications, each paired with a benign counterpart. On MobileVeto, MobileGrail built on Qwen3.5-2B intercepts 76.2% of violations, up from 64.5% for its prompted backbone, while reducing premature intervention from 58.6% to 5.2%, outperforming the cloud-based OS-Sentinel on both. We further conduct online evaluation on GhostEIBench, where MobileGrail guarding a Qwen3.8-27B agent reduces fully successful attacks from 13 to 3 of 110 tasks while raising task completion from 48 to 58. Quantized to 4 bits, MobileGrail runs on a Snapdragon 8 Elite at a median latency of 4.7 s, comparable to the 5.1s of cloud-hosted Gemini 3.8 Flash.
authors: Zhiyu Zhang, Yuankai Li, Muhao Chen
bullets: Maintains recurrent task state so safety decisions retain relevant authorization and execution progress beyond short context windows.
Separates “unsafe” committing actions from “block” decisions allowed throughout an intervention window, enabling earlier but more precise intervention.
Trains with verified action-effect labels and reinforcement learning rewards in a 32-app environment, and evaluates on the offline MobileVeto benchmark plus online GhostEIBench.
On MobileVeto, its Qwen3.5-2B version intercepts 76.2% of violations and cuts premature intervention to 5.2%, compared with 64.5% and 58.6% for the prompted backbone.
Runs quantized on a Snapdragon 8 Elite at 4.7 s median latency; online evaluation reduces fully successful attacks from 13 to 3 of 110 tasks while improving completion from 48 to 58.

papers.selection_reason: Compact on-device guardrail model with 4-bit quantization for efficient deployment on mobile hardware.
papers.title: MobileGrail: Learning Compact Guardrails for On-Device deployable Mobile GUI Agent Safety
papers.tldr: MobileGrail is a compact on-device safety guardrail that protects mobile GUI agents without sending private screens to the cloud, while improving violation interception and reducing premature blocking.

papers.abstract: A transformer language model computes a deep hidden state for every token but uses it only to sample that token. Existing latent-feedback designs, which feed hidden states back across tokens, are mostly built in during pretraining and gain little when added to a pretrained model. We introduce the temporal residual, a second residual stream that every sublayer reads and writes and that is carried from each token to the next. It adds 2,752 parameters to a 4.2B-parameter model and starts exactly at the pretrained network. Retrofitted onto Qwen3.5-4B-Base with 5B tokens of training, it beats a standard model trained on the same data by 7, 13 and 5 points on AIME 2024, AIME 2025 and AMC 2023, writes shorter solutions, and stays ahead at matched training compute. The separate stream matters: prior designs that feed state into the existing stream recover at most 40% of the gain when retrofitted. Validation loss can mislead: the recipe with the lowest loss gains nothing at decoding. Trained with filler tokens in place of reasoning, the model reasons in its hidden state: its GSM8K accuracy with no visible reasoning rises from 21% to 40%, and falls back when the carried state is zeroed.
authors: Ziyang Cai, Xingyu Zhu, Sanjeev Arora
bullets: Addresses the limited effectiveness of adding latent feedback after pretraining.
Adds a separate residual stream that each sublayer reads, writes, and carries across tokens.
Retrofitting Qwen3.5-4B-Base with 5B training tokens improved AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and AMC 2023 performance by 7, 13, and 5 points, respectively, versus a same-data standard model.
The approach supports hidden-state reasoning: GSM8K accuracy without visible reasoning increased from 21% to 40%, but dropped when the carried state was removed.
Separate-stream design and decoding evaluations matter; validation loss alone did not predict gains, and prior retrofits recovered at most 40% of the improvement.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a temporal residual stream carrying latent feedback across tokens in pretrained LLMs, improving reasoning and acting as a lightweight recurrent memory.
papers.title: The Temporal Residual: Fast and Effective Retrofitting of Latent Feedback into Pretrained Language Models
papers.tldr: The temporal residual efficiently retrofits cross-token latent feedback into a pretrained language model, improving reasoning while enabling shorter or hidden reasoning traces.

papers.abstract: Causal video world models generate block by block from their own previous outputs. Small errors in early blocks are fed back as history and grow until the scene and the robot fall apart. Teacher forcing trains on clean ground-truth history, so the model never sees the history it will actually condition on, and it also finds a shortcut: copying the previous frame instead of predicting how the scene changes. We present Dynamics Forcing, a training scheme that keeps real video as the only supervision and reshapes how history is presented. History is perturbed in three ways: random noising, self-resampling by the model itself, and joint denoising, in which the most recent blocks are still partly noisy when the next block is predicted. On top of this we move history guidance and first-frame anchor guidance from inference into training, so that the model is pushed to use its history and its reference frame rather than ignore them. Dynamics Forcing needs no teacher model, no distillation, and no additional model at inference. Applied to a 5B video model with LoRA on 77 hours of manipulation video on a single GPU, it better matches unseen real continuations and reduces error accumulation.
authors: Xin Zhou, Cong Miao
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between clean teacher-forced histories and the model-generated histories used at inference.
Perturbs history through random noising, model self-resampling, and joint denoising of recent blocks.
Trains the model to use both temporal history and the first-frame reference via guidance applied during training.
Requires only real-video supervision, with no teacher model, distillation, or additional inference-time model.
Applied to a 5B video model on manipulation video, it better matches unseen real continuations and reduces error accumulation.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of Dynamics Forcing. Top: the block-causal attention pattern over latent blocks, where each block attends to the reference frame, all earlier blocks and itself, and future blocks are masked. Middle: the three history perturbations (random noising, self-resampling, joint denoising) applied to the history blocks while the target block stays real. Bottom: the training-time history guidance (σh=0.5) and first-frame anchor guidance (σa=0.8), which add no forward pass beyond the model’s standard classifier-free-guidance inference.

papers.selection_reason: Training scheme to reduce error accumulation in causal video world models directly fits video world models.
papers.title: Dynamics Forcing: Mitigating Error Accumulation in Causal Video World Models
papers.tldr: Dynamics Forcing trains causal video world models on realistic, perturbed histories to reduce error accumulation during long-horizon generation.

papers.abstract: Recent geometric foundation models can successfully convert a video sequence into frames of registered point clouds, but cannot predict moments beyond the observed temporal resolution. We propose a continuous-time 4D reconstruction method that extracts 3D structure and camera poses at any time instant, with additional guidance from event-camera measurements. While event cameras provide evidence at microsecond resolution to continuously fill the temporal gap, integrating them into existing RGB-based foundation models remains challenging. We formulate the problem as interpolation in the latent feature space and augment event-based losses in the image space as an auxiliary task to boost accuracy. Operating in the latent space leverages the powerful geometric priors of foundation models, while the event loss provides physically grounded guidance. To effectively address the lack of paired training data, we further propose a self-supervised training framework that uses pseudo-ground-truth labels of estimated geometry and simulated events generated from high-frame-rate RGB videos. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that the proposed pipeline outperforms baselines that temporally interpolate either the input RGB videos or the estimated geometry, and that it generalizes to unseen real-world scenarios. Controlled experiments with synthetic corruptions show that it remains robust under motion-blur and low-light conditions.
authors: Gwangtak Bae, Seunggu Kang, Junho Kim, Eun Sun Lee, Changwoon Choi, Young Min Kim
bullets: Addresses the limited temporal resolution of RGB-based geometric foundation models.
Interpolates in latent feature space while using image-space event losses for physically grounded guidance.
Uses self-supervision with pseudo-ground-truth geometry and simulated events from high-frame-rate RGB videos.
Experiments report better performance than RGB- or geometry-interpolation baselines and generalization to unseen real-world scenes.
Synthetic corruption tests indicate robustness to motion blur and low-light conditions.

figures.caption: Figure 8: Robustness analysis on the Sim4D dataset showing each method’s interpolated RGB frame at t = 0.5 paired with its corresponding reconstructed pointcloud.

papers.selection_reason: Continuous-time 4D reconstruction using event cameras and latent interpolation, fitting 3D vision research.
papers.title: Continuous-time 4D Reconstruction via Event-guided Latent Feature Interpolation
papers.tldr: A continuous-time 4D reconstruction method interpolates foundation-model features using event-camera guidance to recover geometry and camera poses between video frames, including under challenging visual conditions.

papers.abstract: A home robot that helps with chores needs to know where objects are, but people move objects according to routines that change and later change back. The robot's memory must adapt to the new routine without erasing experience that may become useful again. One approach is to have a language model maintain written summaries of the home from the robot's own observations, but existing evaluations of such memories use static worlds. We explore simulated households where a resident gets sick, recovers, and later gets sick again. We compare a rule that keeps every room an object has been seen in, language-model memories that store only written summaries, and language-model memories that can also read the raw history of sightings. The rule outperforms every summary-only memory, and giving language models the sighting history closes the gap. Surprisingly, writing summaries on top of the history adds nothing we can measure. When the illness returns, methods that keep the history search better than they did the first time, while summary-only methods show no consistent improvement. Deleting the first illness from memory removes all of the rule's gain and part of theirs. The summaries recorded where objects went during the illness but rarely distinguished sick-day patterns from normal routines. Our findings suggest that common approaches to summarizing robot memories struggle to remember facts about a routine that might return, highlighting the need for future benchmarks to evaluate this aspect of long-term robot deployment.
authors: Oliver Wang, Mani Srivastava
bullets: The study examines simulated homes where a resident becomes sick, recovers, and later becomes sick again.
It compares a room-history rule, language-model summaries, and language models with access to raw sighting histories.
The room-history rule outperforms summary-only memories; adding sighting history closes the gap.
Summarizing on top of the history provides no measurable benefit, while history-based methods improve when illness recurs.
Deleting the first illness removes the rule’s advantage and part of the history-based methods’ gains.

papers.selection_reason: Home-robot memory under changing routines directly fits embodied memory and long-term deployment.
papers.title: How Should a Home Robot Update Its Memories When Human Routines Change?
papers.tldr: Robot memories should preserve raw sighting history, because summary-only memories often forget routine-specific facts that become useful when circumstances recur.

papers.abstract: Real-time onboard robot control calls for a lightweight vision-language-action (VLA) model, yet shrinking the backbone leaves less capacity for deliberation at inference time. Chain-of-thought decoding, dual-system architectures, and larger backbones can restore deliberation but reintroduce the latency and memory costs that motivated going small. Recurrent action heads offer a lighter alternative by iterating in latent space before committing to an action, but existing designs refine a single undifferentiated state that must simultaneously encode slowly evolving task context and rapidly changing motor commands. We propose the Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head (HR-AH), which maintains two latent states updated at different frequencies: a low-level state that updates fast, grounded in action tokens and proprioception, and a high-level state that updates slowly, grounded in visual understanding and the instruction-informed low-level state. The two states exchange information through nested reasoning cycles. Because all iteration occurs in the compact head after a single backbone pass, HR-AH adds hierarchical reasoning without increasing the backbone size. With a 22.5M-parameter head, 3-4.3x smaller than those of RD-VLA and VLA-Adapter on the same backbone, HR-AH reaches 97.0% success rate on LIBERO and a 4.40 average chain length on CALVIN ABC->D, at the lowest latency among compared methods. We show that this hierarchy improves performance over a parameter-matched single-state head, and that routing distinct modalities to each level yields further gains in both accuracy and inference cost.
authors: Aditya Makineni, Amitesh Sahoo, Qing Tian
bullets: Addresses the loss of inference-time deliberation when VLA backbones are made lightweight.
Uses fast low-level and slow high-level latent states, updated from motor/proprioceptive and visual/instruction signals, respectively.
Performs nested reasoning cycles after one backbone pass, avoiding increases to backbone size.
A 22.5M-parameter head achieves 97.0% success on LIBERO and 4.40 average chain length on CALVIN ABC→D.
Reports the lowest latency among compared methods and gains over a parameter-matched single-state head.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head (HR-AH). The VLM backbone extracts multimodal features from a deep layer (hviz, ha) and the embedding layer (hemb viz ). Inside the HR-AH, iterative latent reasoning is performed over S segments, each comprising KH hierarchical reasoning cycles. Within each cycle, the executor (fL) attends to concise action and proprioceptive context for frequent updates of the detailed motor commands, while the planner (fH ) processes the larger vision context and the instruction-informed compact zL at a slower rate to maintain an abstract task representation. The refinement module (fR) feeds the updated plan back into the action state, closing the bidirectional loop. All three modules share the same UBAttn block architecture (Sec. 3.3) with different context inputs. After each segment s, the action state is projected to a candidate action chunk Âs, and the reasoning halts once the relative change δs between consecutive predictions falls below a threshold τ (Sec. 3.5). The final prediction is executed as Â ∈ RNact×7.
Figure 4. Real-world rollout comparison between RD-VLA (top) and HR-AH (bottom) on the Put task. Both methods succeed in this example, isolating the difference in execution speed.

Figure 6. Success rate versus latency on LIBERO-Spatial. HRAH (star) achieves 98.0% at 49.63 ms, combining the highest accuracy with the lowest latency among compared methods. Circle: end-to-end, triangle: CoT reasoning, square: iterative refinement. Numbers in parentheses give the action-head size.

Figure 1. Attention maps over reasoning steps for RD-VLA (top row) and our HR-AH (bottom row). The dashed ellipse highlights the task-relevant region. HR-AH halts after only 3 steps with attention sharply focused on the target bowl and destination plate, whereas the single-state baseline requires 8 steps and attends more diffusely. Both rows visualize attention from the vision-grounded latent state. Only the third-person view is shown.

Figure 5. Architectural ablation on LIBERO-Spatial. Each point plots success rate against average reasoning segments (upper left is best). Solid arrows follow the additive build-up from a parametermatched single-state baseline to the full model, and the dashed arrow shows the effect of removing learned initialization. Hierarchical recurrence raises success from 85.2% to 94.6% while reducing average segments from 7.44 to 5.71. Modality-specific routing further raises success to 98.0% and reduces segments to 4.96. Removing learned initializations drops success to 96.8% and raises average segments to 7.27.
Figure 3. Real-world experimental setup using the Kinova Gen3 Lite robot arm.

Table 1. LIBERO success rates (%) by suite. The number after each model name is the pretrained VLM size in billions of parameters. Head (M) denotes the action-head size in millions of parameters. Head size governs the memory footprint of the reasoning module on resource-constrained hardware. – indicates that a separately identifiable action head is not available. Bold: best; italics: second best. VLA-Adapter results are our reproduction of the released checkpoint.

Table 2. CALVIN ABC→D results. We report the percentage of successful chains of length 1 to 5, and the average chain length. The number after each model name is the pretrained VLM size in billions of parameters. Bold: best; italics: second best. VLAAdapter results are our reproduction of the released checkpoint.
Table 3. Real-world success rates (%) on the Kinova Gen3 Lite. We evaluate four manipulation tasks of increasing complexity.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a hierarchical action head for tiny VLA models, directly fitting embodied AI and robot learning.
papers.title: Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head for Tiny Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: HR-AH enables tiny VLA models to deliberate hierarchically in a compact action head, achieving strong robotic-control performance with low latency.

papers.abstract: AI agents can write programs that carry out a task without calling a model at every step, so the task runs fast and its logic stays open to inspection. Agents improve these programs by running them, studying their failures, and revising the code, a form of recursive self-improvement (RSI). We ask whether this process also yields runtime checks that can be trusted. In five task domains, with up to seven author models, agents bring their programs to high scores. Yet when the environment changes, the checks they were told to write stay silent on half or more of the resulting failures in four domains. These failures can be detected and repaired: a monitor built from records of normal runs catches most of them in three domains, and the same agents usually repair them once called. The checks do not examine the recorded relations that reveal the failures, and the strongest agent writes checks that catch most of them once told that its checks are the only thing that calls it back. An unreported failure stays unrepaired, which limits what self-improvement is worth in autonomous operation. Evaluations of self-improvement should measure not only scores but also whether a system notices its own failures.
authors: Teng Cao, Yu Deng, Kristian Kersting
bullets: Across five domains and up to seven author models, agents developed high-scoring task programs.
When environments changed, agent-written runtime checks missed at least half of the resulting failures in four domains.
A monitor trained from normal-run records detected most missed failures in three domains.
Agents generally repaired detected failures, but unrevealed failures remained unrepaired.
Self-improvement evaluations should measure failure detection—not just task scores.
