papers.selection_reason: Self-improving agents that detect and repair their own failures during deployment; test-time adaptation of agent code.
papers.title: Blind to What They Can Fix: A Detection Gap in Self-Improving Agents
papers.tldr: Self-improving agents can achieve high task performance yet fail to detect many environment-induced errors, revealing a critical gap between fixing failures and noticing them.

papers.abstract: Safety-critical scenarios are rare in recorded driving and must be generated to test and train motion planners of automated vehicles. In guided diffusion models, each scenario type needs its own weighted objective, separate from the validity check. Optimized together with the attacker, the vehicle under test can cancel the attack or draw it toward itself. We state each scenario as a signal temporal logic specification with clauses typed by role. Every clause names the agent it may change and the agents it may read, and the vehicle under test reads the attacker only from the attack onset. A large language model drafts the specification from a description, and a type checker accepts it. A compiler derives the optimization: it edits a diffusion model's samples by the smallest change that satisfies the specification, each clause moves only its owner, the attacker is solved against the unreacted vehicle under test before its response, and the monitor of the same specification decides acceptance. On nuScenes and CommonRoad, judged independently of the specification, one parameter set produced valid scenarios at a rate 0.14 above a weighted objective tuned per scenario type, and descriptions yielded at least one valid scenario for 11 of the 16 pre-crash types expressible in the public data. Learned planners fail more often on the generated scenarios than on their seeds. Fine-tuning on them lowers a planner's failure rate on critical scenarios, and the time headway one clause of the label requires, not the generator, sets the size of the gain.
authors: Zifan Zeng, Qunli Zhang, Peng Wang, Shiming Liu, Feng Liu, Zheng Hu
bullets: Targets the scarcity of rare, safety-critical driving scenarios for testing and training automated-vehicle motion planners.
Uses role-typed signal temporal logic: clauses specify which agents may be changed or observed, with restricted attacker–vehicle interactions.
An LLM drafts specifications; a type checker validates them, and a compiler derives constrained diffusion optimization and acceptance monitoring.
Across nuScenes and CommonRoad, one parameter set achieved a 0.14 higher valid-scenario rate than objectives tuned per scenario type.
Generated scenarios caused more learned-planner failures than their seeds; fine-tuning reduced failures, with gains limited by the labeled time-headway requirement.

figures.caption: FIGURE 2. Overview of the method for the description of a lead-vehicle braking scenario. Middle: an LLM drafts a role-typed specification, a type check returns errors for repair (contribution 1), and the compiler turns every clause φk into four objects. The exact robustness ρ, a minimum and maximum over time and agents, yields the monitor’s verdict ρ ≥ 0 and, for the observation clause, the onset t⋆. Its smooth lower bound ρ̃ enters a hinge loss whose gradient moves only the clause’s owner. Right: the solver runs in stages derived from the roles (contribution 2): the attacker keeps its seed during its hold time and is then edited against the unreacted seed of the ego, then the ego’s response is edited with the attack fixed, and the ego keeps its seed until the release t⋆ + δ. A specification may name a further guided role, such as a bystander that blocks the ego’s escape lane: it owns its clauses, whose gradients move only that role, and is solved in its own stage after the ego’s. All other agents are context agents and keep their seed trajectories. The monitor of the compiled specification accepts the result or restarts the role from maneuver primitives, and the K seeds of many windows are solved in one batch (contribution 3). Thumbnails (nuScenes, bird’s-eye view, true vehicle sizes): left, a seed scene with every agent’s trajectory (boxes at t = 0); bottom right, the generated scenario at t = 3 s: the lead vehicle brakes into the path of the ego’s unreacted seed (dashed), and the generated ego, identical to its seed until the release (circle), stays behind the lead vehicle.

FIGURE 3. Generated scenarios of six NHTSA pre-crash types, each from an LLM-drafted specification, with the parameter set of all other experiments and no weights: (a), (c)–(e) nuScenes, (b), (f) CommonRoad. The line under each title paraphrases the attack clause of the draft. In every panel the attacker’s seed (dashed red) did something else, the attack is turned against the unreacted seed of the ego vehicle (dashed black), with which it collides, and the generated ego vehicle responds from the release on with the smallest edit that keeps it clear of the attacker, by 0.1 to 0.7m at the closest point: it brakes in (a), (c), (e) and (f) and swerves in (b) and (d). The six pass the independent judges of their types. The drafted road clauses, which confine the attacker to the ego vehicle’s road corridor, are not met at the junctions, which is why the specification’s own monitor accepts only (b), (c) and (f) (Section VI). Footprints every 0.5 s (0.4 s on CommonRoad), light to dark; context agents in grey.

FIGURE 1. A cut-in on US-101 generated from the same seed in three ways; under each panel the speeds of the generated ego vehicle, the attacker and the unreacted seed (dashed), at the top right the monitor’s verdict. (a) Without ownership, the ego vehicle’s clauses also move the attacker and cancel the attack. (b) Without the stage order, the attacker is optimized against the responding ego vehicle: it chases the response, cuts in and brakes to a standstill, the unreacted seed collides with it, and the monitor rejects the output, since the specification asks for an unsafe gap and not a collision. papers.selection_reason: Generates safety-critical driving scenarios via diffusion models conditioned on specifications, fitting action-conditioned environment generation.
papers.title: Generating Safety-Critical Driving Scenarios from Role-Typed Signal Temporal Logic Specifications Drafted by Large Language Models
papers.tldr: A typed-logic compiler turns LLM-drafted driving specifications into diffusion-generated safety-critical scenarios that expose and help reduce planner failures.

papers.abstract: Policy gradient (PG) methods such as GRPO dominate LLM fine-tuning, yet recent work showed that Evolution Strategies (ES) also scale to fine-tuning models with billions of parameters. Which method needs fewer samples, and on which tasks, remains unclear. We view the two methods as estimators of the same gradient that differ in where they explore. Because ES perturbs parameters, its noise grows with the number of parameters, and because PG samples actions, its noise grows with the number of generated tokens. Only noise along the directions that change the reward slows learning. The cost of ES then depends on the effective dimension, the number of independent skills a task requires rather than its parameter count, while the cost of PG depends on the effective horizon, which counts only the tokens that share both credit and weights with the reward-carrying ones. We train both methods on a synthetic task where the number of skills and the effective horizon can be varied separately. PG is cheaper when the horizon is short, ES becomes cheaper once it is long enough, and this crossover moves to longer horizons as the number of skills grows. We then measure the effective horizons of 20 NLP, math reasoning, and agentic tasks and compare the two methods with Qwen2.5-7B. PG leads on short-horizon tasks, the two tie on the moderate-horizon math ones, and no task has a horizon in the regime where the theory predicts an ES advantage. Terminal-Bench has a far longer horizon. There, in a preliminary comparison with Qwen3.5-4B, ES without any credit assignment reaches a higher success rate than the PG checkpoint released with Tmax, as the theory predicts. ES should thus have the advantage on long-horizon tasks with few independent skills and a nonvanishing reward signal. Current benchmarks are only at the onset of this regime, so ES should become more competitive as agentic tasks grow longer.
authors: Qiyao Liang, Kajetan Schweighofer, Xin Qiu, Risto Miikkulainen
bullets: Both ES and policy gradients estimate the same gradient, but ES explores parameter space while policy gradients explore generated actions.
ES sample cost depends on effective dimension—the number of independent skills—whereas policy-gradient cost depends on effective horizon—the reward-relevant token dependencies.
On a controllable synthetic task, policy gradients win at short horizons; ES wins beyond a skill-dependent crossover horizon.
Across 20 NLP, math, and agentic tasks, policy gradients lead on short horizons and tie on moderate-horizon math tasks; no task reached the predicted ES-favorable regime.
On the much longer-horizon Terminal-Bench, preliminary results show ES without credit assignment outperforming a released policy-gradient checkpoint.

papers.selection_reason: Analysis of evolution strategies versus policy gradients for LLM fine-tuning; relevant to LLM training methodology.
papers.title: Dimension Is Free, Horizon Is Not: When Evolution Strategies Rival Policy Gradients for LLM Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: Evolution Strategies (ES) become competitive with policy gradients when tasks have long effective horizons but few independent skills, though most current benchmarks remain too short to show a clear ES advantage.

papers.abstract: Accurate chest X-ray radiology report generation (RRG) requires recognizing clinically relevant abnormalities and accurately describing them. Although Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves the clinical accuracy of generated reports, our analyses suggest limited improvements in visual representations for abnormality recognition. To address this limitation, we propose a selective regional visual distillation framework that enhances visual representations of challenging abnormalities while preserving existing visual capabilities. Specifically, we train a region-aware teacher with targeted supervision on challenging anatomical regions to acquire complementary visual knowledge. Rather than transferring all teacher features, we verify their utility through regional feature replacement and select only those that improve the original student's performance. We further introduce a Spatially Gated Residual Adapter (SGRA) to distill these verified features while minimizing interference with the student's existing visual representations. Experiments on MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray demonstrate improved clinical report accuracy and region-level abnormality recognition across different multimodal large language model backbones, while largely preserving performance on non-target findings.
authors: Rui Zuo, Qinyue Tong, Ziqian Lu, Zheming Lu
bullets: Targets the limited visual-representation gains of language-focused GRPO for radiology report generation.
Trains a region-aware teacher with targeted supervision on difficult anatomical regions.
Uses regional feature replacement to identify only teacher features that benefit the student.
Applies a Spatially Gated Residual Adapter to distill selected features while reducing interference.
Improves report accuracy and region-level abnormality recognition on MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray, while largely preserving non-target findings.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the proposed selective regional visual distillation framework. Region-Aware Teacher Training: A region-aware teacher is trained with region-specific questions and anatomical annotations to enhance visual representations of disease-associated regions in challenging cases. Regional Feature Utility Verification: Teacher features are substituted into the corresponding student regions, and the resulting changes in the student’s correct-answer scores are used to identify beneficial regional features for distillation. Selective Regional Distillation with SGRA: A Spatially Gated Residual Adapter (SGRA) learns from the selected teacher features through regional feature distillation, while a feature preservation loss constrains changes to non-target regions.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison of visual attribution before and after regional distillation. Representative error-correction cases from MedGemma 1 4B (top) and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (bottom), showing changes in generated reports and visual attribution to the corresponding abnormality regions. Attribution maps are computed using gradient × activation. For Qwen3-VL, attributions are aggregated from the final visual embeddings and DeepStack features, whereas for MedGemma, they are computed at an intermediate visual encoder layer. Due to differences in model architecture, feature resolution, and visualization settings, the attribution maps are computed differently and may exhibit distinct appearances. Therefore, we focus on before-and-after comparisons within each model rather than directly comparing attribution intensities across models.

Figure 1. Clinical performance and visual attribution before and after GRPO. We focus on Qwen3-VL, as its larger clinical gains from GRPO compared with MedGemma make the effects of GRPO more evident. (a) Representative CXR cases show similar disease-region attribution patterns despite corrected clinical predictions after GRPO. (b) Exchanging visual encoders between SFT and GRPO models has little effect on CheXbert F1 and RadGraph F1. The multimodal projector remains frozen in both stages. Parentheses indicate the source of the substituted visual encoder (VE), while the leading model name indicates the source of the remaining components. GT denotes ground truth.

Figure 2. The region-aware teacher, trained with region-level supervision, provides targeted guidance for enha cing the student’s visual representations in challenging regions. When the student incorrectly predicts a disease while the teacher correctly identifies it in the corresponding image region, that region is selected for distillation after passing regional feature utility verification. The visual tokens corresponding to the selected region are then extracted from both models, and the student’s tokens are aligned with their teacher counterparts to improve the visual representations associated with the student’s prediction errors.

Table 1. Comparison with state-of-the-art methods on MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray. All methods are trained on MIMIC-CXR for RRG and directly evaluated on IU-Xray without any further fine-tuning. papers.abstract: Conditional generation under constraints that can only be checked on a finished sample, such as a molecular property filter, remains challenging for diffusion models: most guidance methods require differentiable measurement operators, paired conditional data, or rollouts of the base model at every step. We present a framework grounded in the Doob $h$-transform that reduces conditional generation to learning a single function, the probability that a noisy sample denoises into the constraint set. We learn this function from binary clean-sample evaluations alone, by squared-error regression on forward-noised labels; the base model is frozen, one lightweight head is trained per constraint, and noisy-state classifier guidance arises as a special case. The exact guidance step fades where the constraint signal provably vanishes and carries a factor of the inverse probability across samples, which normalized guidance discards: with the schedule and mean step size held fixed, equalizing the step costs 17.0 to 18.5 points of constraint satisfaction on CIFAR-10 at comparable FID, across independently trained estimators. Guidance is more than 50$\times$ cheaper per satisfying sample than rejection sampling at a 1.7% base rate, raises a Lipinski-type property filter on QM9 from 54.3% to 96.8%, and lifts satisfaction on Stable Diffusion 1.5 from 7.2% to 60.0% at one sixteenth of the cost of derivative-free selection, which reaches 9.0%. These results demonstrate that binary evaluations of clean samples are sufficient supervision for constrained generation across pixel, latent, and molecular diffusion.
authors: Ssaumya Kammal Jaiswal, Mahfuza Farooque
bullets: Addresses constrained generation when constraints are only evaluable on completed samples and lack differentiable guidance or paired conditional data.
Learns one probability function per constraint by regressing forward-noised binary labels, while keeping the base diffusion model frozen.
Derives guidance whose strength vanishes when the constraint signal does and preserves inverse-probability weighting that normalized guidance loses.
Improves constraint satisfaction on CIFAR-10, QM9, and Stable Diffusion 1.5, while reducing cost relative to rejection or derivative-free selection.
Scope: requires binary clean-sample evaluations and separately trained lightweight guidance heads for each constraint.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a framework for constrained diffusion generation using Doob h-transforms, enabling guidance from binary evaluations without differentiable operators.
papers.title: Constrained Diffusion from Binary Evaluations via Learned Doob h-Functions
papers.tldr: A Doob $h$-transform-based method enables diffusion models to satisfy nondifferentiable constraints using only binary evaluations of clean samples, with strong gains across image and molecular generation.

papers.abstract: Perception systems often make discrete decisions: flag a hateful meme, predict whether a pedestrian will cross, detect a spoofed voice, or select the next move in a game. System-1 models, such as OneJev and Jev-Omni, read the media and return probabilities over the options in a single forward pass, while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) generate text. Which multimodal decisions can System-1 models handle, and where do MLLMs perform better? We introduce S1Arena-MM, a benchmark that gives every model the same decision requests and scores the probabilities it returns. It contains 51,060 questions across 94 tasks with image, video, and audio input, drawn from 94 public datasets and three program-generated ones. It also includes 102 closed-loop game environments that a model plays from screenshots; in real-time mode, the game continues while the model decides. We evaluate 33 open models: 12 System-1 models and 21 MLLMs read at the answer token. On static decisions, the best System-1 model leads the best MLLM by 4.9 percentage points on images and is within one point of it on video and audio. Post-training for decisions mainly improves the probabilities: on video, a System-1 model has a lower Brier score than the MLLM that it is post-trained from in 10 of 12 pairs. With up to 2,048 thought tokens per question, the most accurate MLLMs pass the best System-1 models only slightly, and thinking raises the Brier score of most MLLMs. Closed loops separate the models: three System-1 models built on a 27B MLLM reach 22.0-33.3% progression in BALROG, and no other model exceeds 9.7% with thinking off. In real-time GameWorld, latencies of up to 1.1 s per decision cause no measurable loss of progress for System-1 models. Code and data: https://github.com/zhaoyang02/S1Arena-MM.
authors: Lang Lin, Tianyu Chen, Yi Gu, Yang Zhao, Xinran Song, Xinyang Liu, Jianpeng Cheng, Mingyuan Zhou
bullets: Evaluates 33 open models—12 System-1 models and 21 MLLMs—on 51,060 questions across 94 image, video, and audio tasks plus 102 closed-loop games.
On static decisions, the best System-1 model leads the best MLLM on images and is nearly tied on video and audio.
Decision-focused post-training mainly improves probability calibration; on video, System-1 models generally achieve lower Brier scores than their MLLM counterparts.
Extended MLLM reasoning provides only slight accuracy gains and often worsens Brier scores.
In closed-loop games, System-1 models achieve markedly higher progression and tolerate up to 1.1-second decision latency without measurable loss in real-time play.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark comparing System-1 models and MLLMs on multimodal decisions, including video and closed-loop game environments, relevant to MLLM evaluation and video understanding.
papers.title: S1Arena-MM: Which Multimodal Decisions Can Be Left to System 1?
papers.tldr: S1Arena-MM benchmarks System-1 models and MLLMs on multimodal decisions, finding System-1 models highly competitive on static tasks and substantially better in latency-sensitive game loops.

papers.abstract: Whole-body humanoid manipulation remains bottlenecked by high-dimensional state-action spaces, contact-rich environments, and long task horizons. This trilemma is a challenge that state-of-the-art reinforcement learning (RL) methods are yet to resolve reliably. We address it with three contributions that add just enough structure to guide exploration: Sparse Interaction Edges (SIE) for whole-body manipulation, Interaction Gated Transport (IGT) for sustained transport over long horizons, and a Hinted Object Path (HOP) that resolves collision and search complexity bottlenecks. Across all three, the policy remains free to discover its own manipulation strategy. The method generalises from rigid object to human transport. As a flagship demonstration, we show, to our knowledge, the first bed-to-wheelchair transfer of a medical mannequin by a humanoid robot completed with no human intervention during execution. In the domain of human transfer, we show that a single policy can adapt across substantial variations in body mass, size, and random force perturbations, all while training on a single GPU in under an hour. Our approach offers a pathway to fully RL-driven humanoid manipulation, enabling assistive robots that can help humans. Website: https://elle-miller.github.io/into_my_arms
authors: Elle Miller, Reem Almheiri, Takuma Tsukakoshi, Ben Sanati, Tamon Miyake, Yushi Wang, Namiko Saito, Shigeki Sugano, Tetsuya Ogata, Rika Antonova, Oisin Mac Aodha, Sethu Vijayakumar
bullets: Targets high-dimensional, contact-rich manipulation with long task horizons.
Introduces Sparse Interaction Edges (SIE), Interaction Gated Transport (IGT), and Hinted Object Path (HOP) to guide exploration while leaving strategies policy-discovered.
Generalises from rigid-object transport to human transport under variations in body mass, size, and external force perturbations.
Demonstrates autonomous bed-to-wheelchair transfer of a medical mannequin with no human intervention during execution.
The abstract reports training on a single GPU in under an hour for the human-transfer setting.

papers.abstract: AI-generated video of politicians can pass for real footage, and once such fakes are common, real footage can be dismissed as fake. Platforms address both problems with detectors, but whoever uploads a clip controls its pixels. Existing datasets of political video are small, show real politicians, and test no attacks. We introduce CivicBench, with 10,800 generated clips of invented politicians from eight open generators and 2,632 public-domain or openly licensed real clips. Each clip can be attacked, to hide a fake or to frame real footage. Published detectors trained on a general benchmark reach at most .781 AUC on CivicBench. Adversarial changes of 1 gray level per pixel hide nearly every generated clip from the detectors not built to resist attacks. An attack's reach is how far it can move a clip's score. A clip keeps its label when its margin from the threshold exceeds this reach, and we find that the reach grows almost linearly with the budget. On this basis, we propose Tau-Anchor, which fine-tunes an encoder pretrained on attacked images. It attacks real and generated clips during training and adds a margin term at its deployed threshold. It reaches .941 AUC on CivicBench. It also keeps .668 of generated clips flagged at 2 gray levels, against at most .289 for published detectors. When real clips are framed at the same 2 gray levels, Tau-Anchor's false alarms rise only from 8% to 14%, whereas four published detectors flag nearly every framed real clip at just 1 gray level. External political footage and two general benchmarks show the same pattern under attack. Code and data are available at https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/CivicBench.
authors: Mert Onur Cakiroglu, Elham Buxton, Mehmet Dalkilic, Hasan Kurban
bullets: The benchmark contains 10,800 generated clips of invented politicians and 2,632 real clips, all attackable to hide fakes or frame real footage.
Published general-purpose detectors achieve at most .781 AUC, while near-imperceptible 1-gray-level changes evade detectors not trained against attacks.
Tau-Anchor fine-tunes an encoder on attacked real and generated clips and adds a deployment-threshold margin objective.
Tau-Anchor reaches .941 AUC and flags .668 of generated clips under 2-gray-level attacks, while limiting false alarms on framed real clips to 14%.
Similar robustness patterns appear on external political footage and two general benchmarks; code and data are released.

papers.abstract: We introduce MotionPort, which learns low-dimensional latent representations of body motion for accurate dynamics prediction and effective long-horizon planning. Existing world-model planners often search over action representations learned for prediction, yet we show that predictive accuracy alone does not ensure that optimization can discover successful trajectories. MotionPort addresses this mismatch by representing body trajectories rather than action chunks and organizing the search space by motion similarity, helping predicted improvements translate into successful execution. Without fine-tuning state encoders, MotionPort raises average goal-reaching success from 37.9% to 87.8% across three backbones and seven settings in four domains. On the evaluated AntMaze-OGBench tasks, it achieves 72% success, compared with 4% for the strongest baseline.
authors: Renhao Zhang, Abhranil Chandra, Bruno Castro da Silva
bullets: Predictive accuracy alone may not yield an action-search space that supports successful trajectory optimization.
MotionPort represents body trajectories and aligns the latent search space with motion similarity.
It requires no fine-tuning of state encoders.
Across three backbones and seven settings in four domains, average goal-reaching success increases from 37.9% to 87.8%.
On evaluated AntMaze-OGBench tasks, MotionPort achieves 72% success versus 4% for the strongest baseline.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving systems must not only interpret the current scene but also anticipate perceptual challenges such as occlusions, sparse observations, and recurring failure patterns. However, most existing LiDAR semantic segmentation methods operate in a frame-centric manner, processing each scan independently and discarding past contextual experience, which limits robustness under dynamic scene changes. We propose DREAM, a Dual-memory REAsoning framework for continual LiDAR seMantic segmentation that reframes perception as an experience-driven and anticipatory process. DREAM maintains two complementary memory banks in a strictly online setting: a latent memory that stores compact semantic abstractions of previously observed scenes, and an error memory that records representations associated with uncertain predictions. At each timestep, relevant memory entries are retrieved via cosine similarity and integrated into the feature space through a lightweight modulation mechanism, enabling the model to reinforce consistent semantic patterns while suppressing recurring failure modes. The backbone remains frozen and no past scans are replayed, ensuring computational efficiency and bounded memory growth. Extensive experiments on multiple large-scale LiDAR benchmarks demonstrate that DREAM achieves state-of-the-art performance, with consistent improvements on dynamic and small-scale objects, highlighting the effectiveness of persistent and error-aware memory for robust long-horizon perception.
authors: Sriram Mandalika, Athira Nambiar
bullets: Targets frame-by-frame LiDAR segmentation methods that discard contextual experience and struggle with dynamic changes, occlusions, and sparse observations.
Maintains a latent memory of compact semantic scene abstractions and an error memory of uncertain-prediction representations.
Retrieves relevant memories via cosine similarity and applies lightweight feature modulation to reinforce consistent patterns and reduce recurring failures.
Operates online with a frozen backbone, no past-scan replay, and bounded memory growth.
Experiments on multiple large-scale LiDAR benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance, especially for dynamic and small-scale objects.

papers.tldr: DREAM improves continual LiDAR semantic segmentation by using dual online memories to recall useful scene patterns and suppress recurring errors without replaying past scans.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in physics-based humanoid control enable teams of varying sizes to coordinate their movements and cooperatively transport shared objects. However, adapting learned cooperative behaviors to unseen environmental constraints remains challenging, particularly when obstacles require coordinated detours and changes in team configuration. We propose CarlHOI, a counterfactual predictive imagination framework built upon a counterfactual-anchored relational latent world model (CarlWM) for human-object interaction (HOI), enabling multi-humanoid teams to adapt to unseen environmental constraints without retraining their underlying cooperative control policies. CarlHOI explicitly represents the shared object, individual humanoids, and environmental obstacles as interacting entities. Trained offline using counterfactual simulator rollouts, the model imagines alternative collective futures under different shared waypoint commands, predicting how the coupled humanoid team and object would respond. By evaluating these imagined outcomes through predicted progress, failure, and contact risks, and long-horizon value estimates, CarlHOI selects adaptive guidance commands while preserving the pretrained cooperative controller. We introduce a benchmark comprising three challenging obstacle-constrained transport tasks to evaluate adaptation and generalization. Despite being trained exclusively with four humanoids, our model generalizes without retraining to teams of two to ten humanoids, unseen obstacle geometries and placements, unseen objects, and novel combinations of environmental constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved cooperative transport success over evaluated baselines across diverse configurations. Results highlight the potential of counterfactual predictive imagination to extend pretrained multi-humanoid cooperative skills beyond their original training conditions.
authors: Wenjie Lin, Jin Wei-Kocsis
bullets: Targets cooperative transport in environments requiring obstacle detours and changing team configurations.
Models humanoids, shared objects, and obstacles as interacting entities in a relational latent world model.
Imagines outcomes of alternative waypoint commands using offline counterfactual simulator rollouts.
Selects guidance commands using predicted progress, failure, contact risk, and long-horizon value.

Evaluated on three obstacle-constrained transport tasks, with generalization from four-humanoid training to teams of two to ten and unseen configurations; experiments report improved success over evaluated baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Uses a counterfactual latent world model for multi-humanoid cooperative manipulation, fitting robot learning and interactive/latent action world models.
papers.title: CarlHOI: Counterfactual Predictive Imagination for Generalizable Multi-Humanoid Object Interaction under Constrained Environments
papers.tldr: CarlHOI uses counterfactual world-model predictions to adapt pretrained multi-humanoid object-transport skills to unseen obstacles, team sizes, objects, and constraints without retraining.

papers.abstract: A zero-shot vision-language classifier is highly sensitive to the class names it receives. Even when images remain unchanged, replacing familiar labels with synonyms, abbreviations, or ontology terms can significantly alter predictions. We investigate this \emph{vocabulary shift} using a leakage-free evaluation protocol across Tiny ImageNet, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, and ImageNetV2. With CLIP ViT-B/16, alternative class names reduce top-1 accuracy by $14.8$--$17.6$ percentage points. To address this issue, we propose \emph{image-grounded concept linking}, a training-free method that maps class names to visual concepts and uses a reliability gate to improve predictions. The method outperforms a template ensemble across all four datasets, achieving a pooled gain of $1.8$ points. We further evaluate five vision-language backbones across four datasets. Our method improves performance in $16$ of $20$ backbone--dataset combinations, with no significantly negative results. It also reduces pooled negative log-likelihood across all five backbones. Stronger text linking and transductive refinement provide no consistent improvements, suggesting that accurate visual class-name linking remains the main challenge. A second CLIP ViT-B/16 seed confirms the improvement on ImageNetV2, but not on ImageNet-A.
authors: Behraj Khan, Shabir Ahmad, Tahir Qasim Syed, Syed Ahmad Chan Bukhari
bullets: Vocabulary shifts—such as synonyms, abbreviations, and ontology terms—reduce CLIP ViT-B/16 top-1 accuracy by 14.8–17.6 percentage points across four datasets.
The proposed training-free method maps class names to visual concepts and applies a reliability gate to improve predictions.
It outperforms a template ensemble on all four datasets, with a pooled gain of 1.8 points.
Across five backbones and four datasets, it improves 16 of 20 combinations and reduces pooled negative log-likelihood for every backbone.
Results suggest accurate visual class-name linking is the central challenge; gains were not consistently replicated for ImageNet-A with a second seed.

papers.title: Seeing Beyond Names: Image-Grounded Concept Linking for Robust Vision-Language Recognition
papers.tldr: Image-grounded concept linking makes zero-shot vision-language classifiers more robust to changes in class names without additional training.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved substantial progress across many domains, but training an agent \textit{tabula rasa} remains highly sample-inefficient. A common remedy is to initialize the agent using a neural network pretrained on demonstrations. However, collecting demonstrations is expensive, and the demonstrations themselves can be suboptimal. In this work, we use a large language model (LLM) to generate an advice policy that produces demonstration data with effectively no human cost. We use this data to warmstart a DQN agent, and use the advice policy itself to guide exploration during training. Because LLM-generated advice is often suboptimal, we further introduce a value warmstart method that initializes the agent to recognize promising states from the advice policy's behavior, without directly copying its actions. To characterize the robustness of this method, we systematically perturb individual sub-skills of an LLM-generated advice policy for a long-horizon, sparse-reward task. Degraded advice still meaningfully accelerates learning relative to unaided baselines. These results suggest that LLM-generated advice, though suboptimal, can be a cheap alternative to costly human demonstrations.
authors: Anurag Kadkol, Lawson L. S. Wong
bullets: Addresses the sample inefficiency and cost of collecting human demonstrations for RL.
Uses an LLM-generated advice policy to produce demonstrations and guide exploration during training.
Introduces value warmstart, which learns promising states without directly copying potentially suboptimal advice actions.
Systematic sub-skill perturbations show that degraded advice still accelerates learning versus unaided baselines.
Scope: evaluated on a long-horizon, sparse-reward task; the approach depends on the quality and coverage of LLM-generated advice.

papers.tldr: LLM-generated, imperfect demonstrations can cheaply warmstart and guide DQN agents, substantially improving learning in long-horizon sparse-reward tasks.

papers.abstract: Reasoning distillation offers a promising approach to transfer temporal reasoning capabilities of powerful Video-LLMs to open-source student models. However, teacher and student Video-LLMs may construct different temporal observations from the same video due to the adoption of distinct video sampling pipelines. A reasoning trajectory valid under the teacher's observations may rely on evidence inaccessible to the student and thus cannot be directly executed based on the student's observations. We formalize this as a conditional target mismatch, thereby revealing the Reasoning Acquisition-Execution Gap. To bridge this gap, we propose an acquisition-to-execution framework that first distills teacher trajectories into a student reasoning prior and then further optimizes the execution capability of this prior across multiple observations. We further introduce Execution-Aware Reference Regularization, which retains the existing prior when it is executable under current observations, while allowing a greater degree of adaptive adjustment when it is not. Experiments across multiple Video-LLM backbones and six video reasoning benchmarks show that explicitly optimizing observation-conditioned execution consistently outperforms supervised distillation and standard RL-based optimization, with gains extending to held-out out-of-domain benchmarks.
authors: Junzhou Chen, Jindong Wang, Gang Zhou
bullets: Different sampling pipelines can make teacher reasoning depend on evidence unavailable to the student, creating a Reasoning Acquisition-Execution Gap.
The framework first distills teacher trajectories into a student reasoning prior, then optimizes its execution across multiple observations.
Execution-Aware Reference Regularization preserves the prior when executable and permits adaptive changes when observations differ.
Across multiple backbones and six video reasoning benchmarks, the approach outperforms supervised distillation and standard RL-based optimization, including on held-out out-of-domain benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of our acquisition-to-execution framework. Reference regularization uses a larger KL weight when the frozen Stage-I model answers correctly under the current observation and a smaller weight otherwise.

papers.tldr: Observation-conditioned distillation helps Video-LLM students execute teacher reasoning despite differences in the video evidence they observe.

papers.abstract: Automated electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation has advanced substantially with deep learning, yet many methods remain task-specific and label-dependent. Large language models (LLMs) and time-series foundation models (TSFMs) offer complementary pretrained representations, but integrating them is challenging because of mismatched feature spaces and the lead- and scale-dependent structure of ECG signals. We propose LAF-ECG (Lead-Aware Foundation Fusion for ECG), a dual-foundation framework that extends MedTsLLM with a lead-aware interface to a frozen TSFM backbone while retaining its reprogramming pathway. The proposed framework captures multi-resolution temporal context, fuses temporal and language-aligned ECG representations through adaptive residual integration, and employs branch-specific supervision with cross-branch alignment. LAF-ECG achieves 71.10% accuracy and 62.43% macro-F1 on PTB-XL, and 89.73% accuracy and 65.94% macro-F1 on Chapman-Shaoxing, outperforming MedTsLLM on both datasets. These results highlight the value of preserving lead-specific temporal structure when combining temporal and language foundation representations for ECG classification. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/kkianamm/LAF-ECG.
authors: Kiana Taktehrani, Maryam Hosseini, Amir Keynia, Aram Montazami, Arash Mohammadi
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining time-series and language foundation models for lead- and scale-dependent ECG signals.
Uses a lead-aware interface to a frozen time-series foundation model while retaining MedTsLLM’s reprogramming pathway.
Fuses temporal and language-aligned representations with adaptive residual integration, branch-specific supervision, and cross-branch alignment.
Reports 71.10% accuracy/62.43% macro-F1 on PTB-XL and 89.73% accuracy/65.94% macro-F1 on Chapman-Shaoxing.
Outperforms MedTsLLM on both datasets; the approach is focused on ECG classification and preserves lead-specific temporal structure.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a dual-foundation framework fusing a time-series foundation model with a language model (MedTsLLM) for ECG classification, addressing modality mismatch through lead-aware fusion.
papers.title: LAF-ECG: Multi-Resolution Lead-Aware Fusion of Time-Series and Language Foundation Models for ECG Classification
papers.tldr: LAF-ECG improves ECG classification by fusing lead-aware, multi-resolution temporal features with language-aligned representations from frozen foundation models.

papers.abstract: Sequence models trained on game moves have been shown to encode world models, with structured linear probes revealing the underlying game states. World models, however, are inherently dynamic: in deterministic board games, a set of rules constrain how states evolve over time. We therefore ask if and how OthelloGPT, a transformer trained only on Othello move sequences, manifests the rules of the game in its activation space. We divide the rules of Othello, and symmetrically their violations, into three classes: placing a disc on an empty square (R1), flanking an opponent's disc (R2), and moving in turn (R3). We find that linear probes accurately separate legal from illegal moves, and also distinguish between the three kinds of rule violations. We introduce an unsupervised rule-violation detector based on the step length of activations between consecutive moves, which identifies illegal moves above chance. We further improve our detection metric by computing step length in the latent space of select sparse autoencoders. Together, we find that OthelloGPT follows game rules of Othello to a large extent, and that we can detect rule violations using structured detectors on model activations.
authors: David L. Cao, Sai Sumedh R. Hindupur, Demba Ba
bullets: Linear probes separate legal from illegal moves in activation space.
Probes distinguish violations involving placement, flanking, and turn order.
An unsupervised detector uses activation step lengths between consecutive moves to identify illegal moves above chance.
Measuring step length in selected sparse-autoencoder latent spaces improves detection.
The study finds that OthelloGPT follows Othello’s rules to a large extent.

(b) Less overlap in the distribution of the metric between legal moves and illegal moves is observed for GatedSAE latent space as opposed to that of residual stream activations (see Figure 3).

Figure 5: Accuracy of linear probe trained on Othello board state over each residual stream layer of OthelloGPT. A linear probe classifies each of the 64 squares on the board as {empty,mine, theirs} from the residual stream activations after each block ℓ ∈ {0, . . . , 7}, scored on n = 1000 held-out games (58,000 positions).

Figure 2: Rule violations can be distinguished using linear probes. (a) 2D Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) visualization of linear probe directions (ring is linear probe direction, point is re-fitted probe per square) of the five classes (legal, illegal, R1, R2, and R3) (b) Cosine similarity matrix between the five probe directions. Illegal moves are anti-correlated with legal moves, and illegal classes are also anti-correlated with each other. (c) AUROC of linear probes for distinguishing each class. Figure 1: OthelloGPT largely follows the rules of Othello. (a) Board state from a randomly chosen game at move t = 16, with black to move, illustrating a legal move and the three classes of rule violations (R1, R2, R3). This probability remains low throughout the game, reaching 7.1% at t = 58, indicating that OthelloGPT generally generates moves consistent with the rules of Othello.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates how a game-playing transformer (OthelloGPT) encodes game rules and dynamics in its latent space, introducing unsupervised detectors for rule violations.
papers.title: From States to Dynamics: Detecting Rule Violations in OthelloGPT
papers.tldr: OthelloGPT’s activations encode Othello’s transition rules, enabling legal-move classification and unsupervised detection of rule violations.

papers.abstract: Hand-driven egocentric interactive video generation aims to generate dynamic scenes with realistic interaction responses conditioned on hand movements and camera motion. However, existing egocentric video datasets struggle to provide scene diversity, meaningful hand-object interactions, and reliable motion annotations simultaneously. To address these limitations, we introduce HandiVid, a high-quality dataset comprising 200K curated and annotated egocentric interaction video clips for hand-driven interactive video generation. We develop a unified data processing pipeline that integrates public datasets, online videos and synthetic videos. Through video quality assessment, hand detection filtering, and multi-stage interaction validation using vision-language models (VLMs), we select high-quality video clips with meaningful hand-object interactions. Since 3D hand reconstruction relies on initial hand detections, we integrate SAM 3 into the hand detection pipeline to reduce missed detections and improve the completeness of 3D hand annotations. Each video clip is provided with high-quality hand renderings, camera trajectories, and interaction descriptions. Comprehensive dataset analysis and downstream video generation experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of HandiVid in terms of data diversity, annotation quality, and controllable video generation.
authors: Chaoyang Zhang, Shaohao Rui, Xiaofeng Mao, Yuanxun Xu, Haoyuan Xia, Xiaohong Liu, Qinghe Du, Weijie Ma
bullets: Addresses limited scene diversity, meaningful hand-object interactions, and reliable motion annotations in existing egocentric video datasets.
Combines public, online, and synthetic videos through a unified processing pipeline.
Uses quality assessment, hand-detection filtering, and VLM-based multi-stage interaction validation to curate clips.
Integrates SAM 3 to reduce missed hand detections and improve the completeness of 3D hand annotations.
Provides hand renderings, camera trajectories, and interaction descriptions; experiments support its usefulness for controllable video generation.

papers.abstract: Successful manipulation requires a policy to understand where things are and how they will move, yet action demonstrations leave this spatiotemporal structure implicit. While explicit 4D supervision has proven effective, reducing the cost of dense 4D prediction remains challenging. This paper introduces \method, a lightweight yet expressive decoder that efficiently injects holistic 4D scene understanding into policies and improves success rates. At its core is a query-based decoder attached to a pretrained policy, which casts many spatialtemporal tasks into one unified interface (e.g. depth, 2D/3D point motion, multi-view correspondence, and hand-eye relations). This design enables efficient training and inference without sacrificing expressivity: the policy learns rich 4D structure from a small number of sampled queries during training, while the decoder can be removed at inference with zero additional overhead. Across multiple backbones, simulated environments, and real-world settings, \method achieves state-of-the-art manipulation performance, outperforming competing methods while training up to $5\times$ faster. Probing analyses further reveal that this 4D structure is recoverable from the policy.
authors: Siyuan Xie, Jinxi Xiao, Ran Ji, Yikai Liu, Mingxi Li, Xuebing Li, Ye Shi, Yuxiang Gao, Jiayuan Gu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of learning where objects are and how they move from action demonstrations without costly dense 4D supervision.
Attaches a query-based decoder to a pretrained policy and unifies tasks such as depth, point motion, correspondence, and hand–eye relations.
Learns rich spatiotemporal structure from a small number of sampled queries during training.

papers.abstract: Effective long-horizon persuasion in recurring goal-oriented settings requires more than factual memory: it must track how a user's trust, negotiation behavior, and strategic receptiveness evolve across interactions. Existing persuasive dialogue systems are largely single-session, static, and unimodal, while cross-session memory systems, though temporally aware, retain only factual content and overlook persuasion-specific dynamics. We propose MERIT (Memory-augmented Experience-Rationale for Iterative Temporal persuasion), which pairs a graph-based memory of four persuasion-specific memory types with a per-persona experience rationale library that records which strategies succeed for each user and why. Together they enable adaptive persuasion through prompt composition alone, with no parameter updates. To support this setting, we introduce PERSIST (PERSona-driven InSurance Interactions over Time), a dataset of 60 curated personas spanning 10+ years of motor insurance renewal interactions, with probabilistic life events that shift negotiation behavior and receptiveness across sessions, verified through strict human-in-the-loop annotation. MERIT surpasses memory and experience-based baselines on every metric across two policy backbones, reaching persuasive-appeal scores of 4.10 and 4.74 (out of 5).
authors: Rohan Kirti, Akash Ghosh, Pratik Amrit, Aryan Vats, Niladri Ghosh, Sriparna Saha
bullets: Targets recurring persuasion settings where trust, negotiation behavior, and receptiveness evolve across sessions.
Uses a graph-based memory with four persuasion-specific memory types plus a per-persona library of successful strategies and rationales.
Introduces PERSIST, a human-verified dataset of 60 personas across 10+ years of motor-insurance renewal interactions and changing life events.
Evaluated with two policy backbones, MERIT outperforms memory and experience-based baselines on every reported metric, achieving persuasive-appeal scores of 4.10 and 4.74 out of 5.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers achieve remarkable recognition performance but incur substantial computational cost during inference, limiting their use in latency- and compute-constrained deployment scenarios. Early-exit inference offers a promising solution by allowing easy samples to terminate at intermediate layers. However, existing approaches typically couple early classification with the shared backbone, requiring intermediate representations to support both early classification and subsequent feature refinement. Under joint training, the corresponding optimization objectives jointly update shared backbone parameters, which can lead to conflicting gradient directions. Motivated by this observation, we introduce DeclareViT, a framework that decouples early classification from feature refinement. Each exit uses a dedicated query to read intermediate features through one-way cross-attention without modifying the backbone token stream. The query branches are optimized for early classification while the backbone and final classifier remain frozen. Across ViT, DeiT, and Swin on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K, and Food-101, DeclareViT consistently establishes a state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-off: It achieves 1.58 times to 2.57 times multiply-accumulate (MAC)-based speed-up with only a 0.39-1.91 percentage-point accuracy drop. Wall-clock measurements on CPU and GPU further demonstrate practical inference acceleration. Code is available at https://github.com/TUDa-HWAI/DeclareViT.
authors: Xinrui Gong, Yao Rong, Chuangtao Chen, Daniel Ochs, Ulf Schlichtmann, Bing Li, Kristian Kersting, Grace Li Zhang
bullets: Early-exit ViTs can reduce inference cost, but shared optimization may create conflicting gradients between early classification and later feature refinement.
Each exit uses a dedicated query with one-way cross-attention to read intermediate features without altering the backbone token stream.
Only the query branches are optimized for early classification, while the backbone and final classifier remain frozen.
Across ViT, DeiT, and Swin on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K, and Food-101, it delivers 1.58×–2.57× MAC-based speed-ups with 0.39–1.91 percentage-point accuracy drops.
CPU and GPU measurements also show practical wall-clock inference acceleration.

papers.abstract: Many generation tasks draw the next image from a visual history, such as storyboards, illustrated stories and multi-turn editing. A new request often states what happens next without restating how earlier objects look. Instead of recovering an object's current look from the history, generators often redraw it from the request alone or bring back an outdated look, and the error can carry into later steps. We call this failure prop drift. Existing evaluations rarely isolate it, because similarity to the history rewards copying and a judge that sees a single history cannot tell a look recovered from that history from one the generator happens to prefer. We introduce PROPS, a benchmark of 2,257 pairs of twin histories that end on the same request but show one prop in two different looks. A pair passes only if the generator draws the matching look on each side and carries out the request, so a look preferred by the generator or the judge passes at most one side. All 34 open and closed systems we test show prop drift, and even systems that carry out the requested action on most sides often lose the current look of the prop. Swapping the planners and editors of agents further shows that both history understanding and image generation limit agent performance. We also build PROPS-Train, 80,250 training chains in four tracks whose targets recover an earlier state or carry scripted changes forward, and fine-tuning on it clearly improves all four tested models. Both datasets will be publicly released.
authors: Xiangzhao Hao, Dianyi Wang, Keyan Zhou, Yiqian Zhang, Zefeng Zhang, Bailin Li, Kun Zhan, Junchi Yan
bullets: Prop drift occurs when generators redraw a prop from the latest request or revert to an outdated appearance instead of using its visual history.
PROPS uses 2,257 twin-history pairs with the same final request but different prop appearances; success requires matching each history while completing the request.
All 34 tested open and closed systems exhibit prop drift, even when they usually perform the requested action.
Agent tests indicate that both history understanding and image generation constrain performance.
Fine-tuning on 80,250 PROPS-Train chains improves all four tested models; both datasets will be released.

papers.abstract: Top-k sparse attention relies on an indexer, a lightweight per-layer module that ranks cached tokens so attention covers only the k highest-scoring ones. Indexers are usually distilled from dense attention at the full serving length, so every training step pays for long-context dense attention. We show that when an indexer is distilled on short sequences, its failure to generalise to longer contexts is driven mainly by rotary positional encoding (RoPE), not by degraded content matching. We propose position-skipped distillation: the indexer and the frozen teacher see short sequences whose position IDs contain a randomly placed gap, so neither ever processes more than the short training length. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B, an indexer distilled on 8K tokens this way matches a 32K-distilled indexer to within about 0.5 perplexity up to 32K, and on DeepSeek-V2-Lite matches a 64K-distilled indexer at 64K with roughly 6x less training compute per token. On Llama-3.1-8B it trails the stronger 32K run by 0.6 perplexity, and at 64K simple position compression is often as good, so the main gain is training cost rather than quality. We also quantise indexer keys to 3-4 bits without retraining and score them with a fused integer kernel: at 4 bits, perplexity changes by at most 0.05 and the scan is 1.6-2.2x faster than half precision. In a current serving engine, the indexer speeds up decoding only for long contexts with multiple concurrent streams.
authors: Fu Dai, Haodi Quan, Kamal Taha
bullets: Short-sequence failures are mainly attributed to rotary positional encoding rather than content matching.
Random gaps in position IDs let the indexer and frozen teacher learn long-range positions without processing long sequences.
An 8K-distilled indexer nearly matches 32K- and, on one model, 64K-distilled quality; the reported training-cost reduction is about 6× per token.
3–4-bit key quantization requires no retraining; 4-bit keys change perplexity by at most 0.05 and yield 1.6–2.2× faster scans.
Benefits vary by model and serving setting: position compression can be competitive, and decoding speedups appear mainly for long contexts with multiple streams.

(2) The frozen model computes dense attention under the same ids, and each layer’s indexer matches its head-summed attention pt,s with a KL loss; only the indexer receives gradients. papers.selection_reason: Improves sparse-attention indexer distillation for long-context serving with position-skipped training and quantization, relevant to efficient long-context LLMs.
papers.title: Position-Skipped Distillation of Sparse-Attention Indexers: Train Short, Serve Long
papers.tldr: Position-skipped distillation trains sparse-attention indexers on short sequences that generalize to long contexts, substantially reducing training cost while preserving quality in several models.

papers.abstract: Teams enable serving features such as prefix caching, chunked prefill and speculative decoding after checking that benchmark accuracy is unchanged, because the engine documents them as exact. Accuracy is an aggregate, so a feature can hold it while flipping which requests are answered correctly. We serve one 4B instruction model in vLLM under nine single feature configurations and five replicas of a reference configuration, grade 3,380 requests from five benchmarks in every run, and compare each candidate with a restart floor (fresh process) and a scheduling floor (same requests in a different order). With default kernels every configuration keeps accuracy within one point, and the seven exact features flip the graded outcome of 1.47% (95% CI 1.13 to 1.85) to 1.78% (1.39 to 2.20) of requests, none above the scheduling floor of 1.72%, while the FP8 KV cache flips 3.36% (2.80 to 3.96), as many as FP8 weights. With batch invariant kernels all seven exact features, speculative decoding included, reproduce the reference text on every request, while the FP8 KV cache still flips 3.91% (3.28 to 4.53) of graded outcomes. A gate that compares against a single replica pair rejected an unchanged configuration, so we recommend certifying a serving change under batch invariant kernels, where the floor is zero, or against a scheduling floor measured from at least three replicas.
authors: Sharven Rane
bullets: Aggregate accuracy can remain stable while individual graded answers change.
Across nine feature configurations, seven exact features flipped 1.47%–1.78% of requests, no higher than the 1.72% scheduling floor.
FP8 KV caching flipped 3.36% of graded outcomes, comparable to FP8 weights, and 3.91% with batch-invariant kernels.
Batch-invariant kernels made all seven exact features, including speculative decoding, reproduce reference text on every request.
Certification should use batch-invariant kernels or a scheduling floor measured from at least three replicas; single-replica comparisons can reject unchanged configurations.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLM serving efficiency shortcuts including FP8 KV cache compression and prefix caching, directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency research.
papers.title: Exact on Paper: Which LLM Serving Shortcuts Flip Graded Answers, Measured Against the Noise of Reordering the Same Requests
papers.tldr: Most exact serving features cause answer flips no more often than request-reordering noise, but FP8 KV caching produces substantially more changes unless batch-invariant kernels are used.

papers.abstract: Learning to predict the effects of contact-rich manipulation skills requires models that represent distinct outcome modes rather than a single expected result. Even for basic skills such as pushing, picking, and placing, small variations in contact conditions or object geometry can produce qualitatively different object motions under nearly identical states and actions. Deterministic and Gaussian models tend to average over these alternatives or represent them as a single broad distribution, obscuring distinct modes such as sliding, toppling, and rotating. We study probabilistic skill-effect models that learn multimodal distributions over object pose changes given partial point clouds and actions. We instantiate this abstraction with three representative model classes: mixture density networks, state tokenization, and flow matching, each paired with latent dynamics for next-step prediction. Across diverse objects and skills, explicitly multimodal models predict which outcome occurs more accurately than deterministic and Gaussian baselines. In planning, flow matching significantly improves task success over the deterministic baseline on every skill and achieves the highest success on every multi-step sequence. On a real robot, probabilistic models succeed at pick about twice as often as the deterministic baseline, providing evidence that probabilistic skill effects offer a practical abstraction for reasoning and planning under uncertainty.
authors: Siyeon Kim, Mohanraj Devendran Shanthi, Joseph C. Liechty, Tucker Hermans
bullets: Contact variations and object geometry can produce distinct outcomes such as sliding, toppling, and rotating from similar states and actions.
The study models distributions over object pose changes from partial point clouds and actions using mixture density networks, state tokenization, and flow matching with latent dynamics.
Explicitly multimodal models identify outcome modes more accurately than deterministic and Gaussian baselines across diverse objects and skills.
Flow matching improves task success over the deterministic baseline for every skill and performs best on all evaluated multi-step sequences.
On a real robot, probabilistic models achieve roughly twice the pick success rate of the deterministic baseline.

papers.abstract: Audio description (AD) makes visual media, such as video, accessible to blind or low-vision (BLV) audiences, but the high cost of professional production limits coverage. Due to recent advances in AI, numerous approaches to automatically generate intermediate AD scripts and/or final AD audios have been proposed. We present an expert evaluation of AI-generated AD scripts for movies in Italian and German that compares two AI systems, a GPT-4o- and a Qwen-based pipeline, against human-authored descriptions. Professional audio describers rated description quality and annotated errors using a detailed error taxonomy that includes content, character, fluency and coherence errors. The results show that while GPT-4o outperforms the Qwen models, both AI systems still fall short of human professional quality: the generated descriptions show substantially higher error rates and lower quality ratings. Based on the error annotations, we identify two key areas that require improvement: 1) character references, which includes both issues with identification and coherent naming, and 2) content errors and hallucinations, where the AD misrepresents or invents events. These error types are particularly critical, as they directly affect the viewer's ability to follow the narrative.
authors: Annette Rios, Lukas Fischer, Sarah Ebling
bullets: Professional audio describers evaluated movie AD scripts from two AI pipelines against human-authored descriptions.
Evaluation covered description quality and errors in content, character references, fluency, and coherence.
GPT-4o performed better than the Qwen-based systems, but both produced more errors and received lower quality ratings than human work.
The most critical issues were incorrect or inconsistent character references and content errors or hallucinations.
The study focuses on Italian- and German-language movie descriptions and does not establish human-level quality.

papers.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $\pi_0,\pi_{0.5}$ generate continuous action chunks by flow matching, and online reinforcement learning (RL) can improve them beyond supervised fine-tuning. Existing methods, such as Flow-GRPO and $\pi_{\mathrm{RL}}$, optimize likelihood ratios of stochastic denoising transitions, which reweight the sampled actions by their advantages but do not use the distances between them. We propose JKO-GRPO, which augments Flow-GRPO with Wasserstein proximal steps, with two contributions: (1) At each state, we treat the group of sampled actions as an empirical distribution and formulate policy improvement as a Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) step. We use a soft discrete $c$-transform to construct transport targets from group-relative advantages and combine shared-noise regression of the deterministic flow sampler onto these targets and combined with the clipped Flow-GRPO objective without Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. (2) We extend this approach to sequential VLA control through random-time branching: we select one or multiple action-chunk indices along old-policy trajectories and independently apply group-level JKO updates using candidate continuations from the corresponding states.
authors: Jiyong Kwon, Yikun Bai, Amirhossein Mollaali, Guang Lin
bullets: Existing Flow-GRPO-style methods reweight stochastic denoising transitions by advantages but ignore distances between sampled actions.
JKO-GRPO treats actions sampled at each state as an empirical distribution and formulates policy improvement as a Jordan–Kinderlehrer–Otto step.
A soft discrete c-transform converts group-relative advantages into transport targets, trained via shared-noise regression of the deterministic flow sampler.
The method combines these updates with clipped Flow-GRPO without KL regularization.
Random-time branching extends the approach to sequential VLA control by applying independent group-level JKO updates at selected action-chunk states.

(b) The first action chunks of a group share the state st. Flow-GRPO reweights them by advantage. The added JKO step constructs soft c-transform targets yi that trade advantage against action distance. (c) On the first branch chunk, the masked transport loss fits the deterministic ODE sampler to stop-gradient targets, reusing each sample’s initial noise ϵi. The clipped Flow-GRPO objective acts on the post-branch segment. Both terms train the same velocity field, and the transport loss requires neither a critic nor a policy density.

papers.abstract: Service robots that share corridors and lobbies with people must keep moving without endangering them. Reactive planners can stop indefinitely in dense crowds (the freezing robot problem), whereas the attention-based learned navigators that dominate the standard crowd benchmark assume holonomic motion or emit discrete actions unsuited to a differential-drive base. This paper presents TASC, a navigation system for a non-holonomic service robot that integrates an attention-based crowd encoder, an anticipatory collision feature, and a continuous-control policy. We adapt the dual-selection attention module, originally developed for discrete-action value learning, to proximal policy optimization for continuous velocity control, and add a closing-speed time-to-collision feature, a conservative estimate of the time to contact that serves as both an observation and a reward term. The policy is trained on a high-fidelity 3D robot model in NVIDIA Isaac Lab with 10,000 parallel environments, social-force-model pedestrians, and randomized crowd sizes. In 30,000 evaluation episodes, each run to its end, the policy timed out in fewer than 0.5% at every tested crowd density. This liveness comes at a cost: pedestrian collisions rise from 4.5% with five pedestrians to 17.4% with ten. In an ablation with four seeds per variant, policies retrained without the time-to-collision feature succeed 4 to 7 percentage points less often. The policy runs in Gazebo without retraining and on a commercial differential-drive service robot through a ROS 2 package with an inference latency below 10 ms, verified in a hardware-in-the-loop test with virtual pedestrians.
authors: Mohammadhossein Malmir, Mohammadali Rahmati, Mohammad Reza Kolani, Alois Knoll
bullets: Addresses the freezing-robot problem while supporting non-holonomic, continuous-velocity control.
Combines dual-selection attention for crowd encoding, time-to-collision anticipation, and a PPO policy.
Trained in high-fidelity simulated environments with randomized crowd sizes and social-force pedestrians.
Across 30,000 evaluation episodes, fewer than 0.5% timed out at every tested density.
Removing the time-to-collision feature reduced success by 4–7 percentage points; collisions reached 17.4% with ten pedestrians.

papers.abstract: High-resolution images contain rich visual details that require fine geometric structures for faithful 3D reconstruction. However, generating extremely detailed 3D geometry from images requires substantial computational resources and training data, making high-resolution geometry generation challenging for existing state-of-the-art models. In this paper, we present SuperFine3D, an efficient framework for generating extremely detailed 3D geometry through global-local recursive refinement. SuperFine3D learns a shared refinement operator from paired coarse-to-fine representations and recursively reuses it to progressively synthesize finer geometry beyond the training resolutions, without requiring additional paired supervision at target resolutions. To make recursive refinement computationally efficient, we introduce spatial-cell attention, which restricts high-resolution interactions to local spatial neighborhoods while maintaining bounded communication across neighboring cells. We further propose spatially anchored cross-scale guidance, which leverages globally contextualized coarse geometry to guide local detail synthesis and preserve structural consistency. In addition, geometry-aware training objectives encourage the refinement process to preserve stable geometric structures while introducing fine-grained surface details. Experiments demonstrate that SuperFine3D generates geometry at a $4096^3$ decoder-grid resolution, corresponding to a sparse $256^3$ latent lattice, using a shared refinement operator trained only on $512^3$--$1024^3$ representations. Compared with a full-attention recursive baseline, SuperFine3D achieves a $9.4\times$ speedup in end-to-end inference and reduces peak GPU memory usage by $23.0\%$, while improving cross-scale structural consistency and producing cleaner surfaces with finer geometric details.
authors: Lihan Li, Junwei Zhou, Yu-wing Tai
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and data demands of high-resolution 3D geometry generation.
Learns a shared coarse-to-fine refinement operator and reuses it recursively beyond the training resolutions.
Uses spatial-cell attention for efficient local interactions and spatially anchored cross-scale guidance for global structural consistency.
Trained on 512³–1024³ representations, it generates geometry at 4096³ decoder-grid resolution with a sparse 256³ latent lattice.
Compared with full-attention recursive refinement, it achieves 9.4× faster inference, 23.0% lower peak GPU memory, and cleaner, finer surfaces.

papers.abstract: Most LLM agent frameworks build a crew that runs a task and exits. Physical environments (e.g., homes, labs, factory floors) need agents that stay up for months, survive their own bugs, and run on whatever hardware is already next to the sensors. We present Wactorz, an open-source runtime in which LLM-generated agents are long-lived, supervised actors: a planner turns a chat request into Python, compiles it into a new actor at runtime, and a supervisor restarts that actor alone, with its state intact, when it crashes. All coordination rides on MQTT, so agents can be spawned on, and live-migrated between, edge nodes such as a Raspberry Pi, and every internal event is a topic external systems can subscribe to. The recorded demo builds a camera-to-lamp automation from one chat request, adds a second agent that is auto-wired to the first by topic and carries a deliberate division-by-zero, watches that agent repair its own code without losing its count, then deploys a fresh Raspberry Pi node and live-migrates the agent onto it, in under four minutes of wall-clock time and \$0.13 of model usage. This extended version adds what the two-page demonstration paper could not: the Wiring view of the topic graph, Wactorz as a library for hand-written agents, how trained models are stored, sent to nodes and replaced, the security model, and the system's limitations.
authors: Panagiotis Kasnesis, Lazaros Toumanidis, Amalia Contiero Syropoulou, Christos Chatzigeorgiou
bullets: Targets persistent agents in physical environments rather than short-lived task crews.
A planner generates Python actors at runtime, while supervisors restart crashed actors with state intact.
MQTT enables topic-based coordination, external event access, and live migration between edge nodes.
A recorded demo creates a camera-to-lamp workflow, repairs a deliberate division-by-zero, and migrates the agent to a Raspberry Pi.
The extended system includes topic-graph visualization, hand-written-agent support, model management, security details, and limitations.

papers.abstract: Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for real-time video synthesis, distilling pretrained diffusion models into few-step autoregressive generators. However, its reverse-KL objective is mode-seeking and can collapse the student's conditional video distribution onto a narrow subset of modes, leading to reduced sample diversity, diminished temporal dynamics, and color oversaturation. Existing methods mitigate this issue mainly via coverage-oriented student initialization, but we observe that such coverage is transient: across three initializations, the fraction of dynamic videos drops sharply during subsequent DMD training, indicating that the mode-seeking objective, not the initialization, drives this degradation. We propose Mass Forcing, a probability-mass-aware framework that moves on-policy DMD supervision from whole videos to individual states. Each update branches several continuations from a shared student-generated prefix, making the student's probability mass at that state measurable against the teacher. First, Mass Forcing estimates relative teacher-to-student density ratios among these continuations through latent-space score integration and uses them to rebalance conditional DMD updates, amplifying rollouts underrepresented relative to the teacher. Second, since mismatched mode probabilities do not necessarily induce strong local score corrections, it aligns generated rollout sets with a reweighted reference distribution defined by the same mass estimates, providing cross-rollout supervision. Experiments on MovieGen and VBench show that Mass Forcing improves video fidelity and sustains temporal dynamics throughout training, achieving the highest Total scores among compared methods and a Dynamic Degree of 83% after 1,000 generator updates, versus 12-32% for the baselines, with no additional inference-time overhead.
authors: Yiyu Li, Fei Wei, Yong Wang, Zaiquan Yang, Gerhard Petrus Hancke, Xiangxiang Chu, Rynson W. H. Lau
bullets: DMD’s reverse-KL objective can progressively reduce video diversity, temporal dynamics, and color fidelity despite broad student initialization.
The method branches multiple student continuations from shared prefixes to estimate relative teacher-to-student probability mass at individual states.
It rebalances conditional DMD updates toward underrepresented rollouts and adds cross-rollout supervision using a mass-reweighted reference distribution.
On MovieGen and VBench, it improves fidelity and preserves temporal dynamics, reaching 83% Dynamic Degree after 1,000 updates versus 12–32% for baselines.
It adds no inference-time overhead.

papers.abstract: Recovering globally consistent 3D human motion from monocular videos remains challenging under dynamic camera motion. Although SLAM and human mesh recovery (HMR) provide complementary camera and body estimates, directly combining them often leads to inconsistent orientations and accumulated trajectory drift. We present GravHMR, a training-free, plug-and-play framework that couples SLAM and HMR through a shared gravity-aligned reference. By allowing gravity to be estimated independently of the HMR backbone, GravHMR accommodates world-grounded HMR models with or without explicit gravity-view representations. Specifically, Yaw-Aware Orientation Optimization (YAOO) resolves heading inconsistencies by correcting body and velocity orientations about the shared gravity axis. Conditioned on these corrected orientations, Gravity-Aware Trajectory Optimization (GATO) anchors root trajectories in the metric SLAM world by jointly leveraging 2D reprojection, the metric scale implicit in the human body, and the body's own motion. On EMDB-2, GravHMR achieves state-of-the-art performance with 154.0 mm W-MPJPE100 using ViPE and 189.8 mm using masked DROID-SLAM, outperforming TRAM (222.4 mm) under the same masked DROID-SLAM camera estimates. It further reduces W-MPJPE100 by 44.3% over GVHMR (276.5 mm) and by 20.0% over GVHMR + HTD-Refine (192.4 mm) with the same HMR backbone.
authors: Hanglei Jin, Chenglu Sun, Junchen Ge, Yuchao Wang, Siqi Chen, Yuzhi Huang, Jingyan Jiang, Zhi Wang
bullets: Addresses orientation inconsistency and trajectory drift when combining SLAM with human mesh recovery under dynamic camera motion.
Uses independently estimated gravity to support world-grounded HMR models with or without explicit gravity-view representations.
YAOO corrects body and velocity heading around the shared gravity axis.
GATO optimizes root trajectories using 2D reprojection, metric body scale, and body motion in the SLAM world.
On EMDB-2, reports 154.0 mm W-MPJPE100 with ViPE and 189.8 mm with masked DROID-SLAM, outperforming listed baselines.

Gravity-Aware Trajectory Optimization (GATO) then recovers the global root trajectory from 2D pose observations under the corrected orientations and the SLAM camera geometry, and Flow-Aware Temporal Consistency (FATC) finally regularizes its temporal derivatives.
