papers.abstract: Human interaction with physical objects relies on a combination of dexterity and robustness. In robotic manipulation, dexterity requires not only flexible end effectors but also a diverse repertoire of manipulation strategies, while robustness requires closed-loop adaptation to disturbances and unexpected situations. Two prominent research directions in dexterous grasping have largely addressed these capabilities separately. Generative approaches model multimodal distributions to produce diverse grasp poses, but their reliance on open-loop execution can limit robustness. Reinforcement learning approaches learn closed-loop grasping policies, but can converge to a narrow range of successful grasping strategies, limiting behavioral diversity. We introduce a time-reversed curriculum with a coordinated reset mechanism that enables a simple MLP policy trained with PPO to capture multiple modes of the grasp-pose distribution while maintaining closed-loop control. Experiments demonstrate both diverse grasping behaviors and robust closed-loop execution. Trained on only approximately 400 objects, our policy further demonstrates strong generalization when evaluated on more than 20,000 unseen objects.
authors: Kunqi Xu, Xiaokang Sun, Xueyan Zou
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between diverse grasp strategies and robustness to disturbances.

papers.abstract: Latent world models enable planning from images, but their predictions do not directly establish whether a robot will satisfy physical constraints. We present JEPA-Shield, which connects a frozen action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world model to task-space safety enforcement. Two downstream models predict relative motion from imagined latent rollouts and decode unsafe geometry from the current image. Split conformal prediction turns end-to-end motion-prediction errors into multi-horizon uncertainty tubes. A backup-based shield checks these tubes against physical constraints and screens both candidate trajectories and final proposals in diffusion-inspired sampling-based model predictive control. Under the stated exchangeability and initial-backup assumptions, we establish probabilistic constraint satisfaction at action-block boundaries for a returned plan executed without replanning. We also introduce VParkBench, with geometric car and tractor-trailer parking tasks and a editable photorealistic Gaussian-splatting environment. In closed-loop evaluation, JEPA-Shield achieves success rates of 84.4%, 82.3%, and 99.0%, respectively, with no observed constraint violations. Ablations show complementary benefits from shielding and uncertainty calibration. The results demonstrate the importance of grounding latent world-model predictions in task-space quantities and explicitly accounting for prediction uncertainty in safety-critical planning.
authors: Taekyung Kim, Ege Yuceel, Steven Hong, Georgios Fainekos, Dimitra Panagou, Bardh Hoxha
bullets: Motivation: Image-based latent predictions alone do not guarantee that robot plans satisfy task-space safety constraints.
Method: A frozen action-conditioned JEPA predicts imagined rollouts, while downstream models estimate motion and unsafe geometry; split conformal prediction forms multi-horizon uncertainty tubes.
Safety mechanism: A backup-based shield checks candidate and final diffusion-inspired MPC trajectories against physical constraints.
Guarantee: Under exchangeability and initial-backup assumptions, the returned plan satisfies constraints probabilistically at action-block boundaries without replanning.

Evaluation: On geometric car and tractor-trailer parking tasks in VParkBench, success rates were 84.4%, 82.3%, and 99.0%, with no observed constraint violations; shielding and calibration provided complementary benefits.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of JEPA-Shield. (a) A latent world model predicts action-conditioned future representations from visual history. (b) Task-space probes recover relative motion and decode unsafe geometry from latent and spatial features. (c) Conformal motion tubes enable uncertainty-aware shielding against physical constraints. (d) Diffusion planner iteratively updates shielded action candidates and applies a final shield before execution. (e) VParkBench evaluates the framework in geometric and Gaussian-splatting parking environments.

Fig. 4: Qualitative JEPA-Shield results for (a) VParkBench Car, (b) VParkBench TT, and (c) GS Car. Left: conformal motion-tube visualization at one planning cycle. In (b), the red arrow highlights expansion of the yellow tube induced by hitch-angle uncertainty: although the nominal predicted motion is nearly straight, conformalization expands the possible articulated trailer placements, which are robustly checked by the shield. papers.abstract: As medical VLMs are increasingly evaluated for clinical decision-support scenarios, knowing when to trust their predictions is critical. Closed-ended medical VQA has become a common benchmark format because it enables automated scoring. Yet, systematic investigation into whether this format changes the reliability problem remains scarce. We identify a failure mode that we call stable wrongness: models can produce incorrect yes/no answers that remain confident and repeatable even when patient-specific visual evidence is removed or mismatched. This failure violates the premise behind sampling-stability uncertainty methods, including recent hallucination-aware calibration (HAC) variants: disagreement is informative only when errors are unstable. When shortcut-driven errors are themselves stable, sampling agreement can remain deceptively high. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity (CAS), which shifts reliability estimation from answer stability to evidence sensitivity. CAS uses cross-modal counterfactual interventions, such as text-only, black, and corrupted images, to audit whether a committed yes/no answer remains supported when visual evidence is invalidated. Across 7 VLMs and 3 benchmarks, CAS outperforms the best HAC-family scores across all evaluated settings, achieving a macro-averaged AUROC gain of +0.150 for error detection. Mechanistic analysis further shows that CAS recovers hidden errors in the HAC-confident region and that its strongest standalone signal is counterfactual decision-boundary shift rather than hard prediction stability. Our findings suggest that closed-ended evaluation should test visual dependence, not only answer stability, in safety-critical medical contexts.
authors: Qi Wu, Xiaoyu Liu, Ao Wang, Rongsheng Wang, Wenting Chen, Wenxuan Wang, Qingsong Yao
bullets: Identifies “stable wrongness”: incorrect yes/no predictions may remain confident and repeatable even when images are removed or corrupted.
Argues that sampling-stability uncertainty methods can miss shortcut-driven errors because agreement does not guarantee evidence-based reasoning.
Introduces Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity (CAS), which tests whether answers change appropriately under text-only, black, or corrupted-image interventions.
Across 7 VLMs and 3 benchmarks, CAS improved error-detection macro-AUROC by 0.150 over the best HAC-family scores.
Finds that counterfactual decision-boundary shifts are more informative than prediction stability and recover errors missed by HAC.

papers.abstract: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. We study how effectively coding agents use these new, potentially unfamiliar extensions to write fast code. We introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline and a set of environments for evaluating coding agents in kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures. Its agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline turns code repositories into benchmark instances, and its environments let agents optimize code with feedback from the target hardware. Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernels from real-world, actively developed repositories (ncnn, llama.cpp, Arm SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI), including inference workloads derived from real model executions. KernelShift supports incorporating new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer architectural extensions (Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), examining how performance changes as hardware evolves. On established extensions, agents beat the auto-vectorized compiler everywhere (2.4-19.8x) and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74x over its Neon kernels), but fall behind Arm's hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70x). In end-to-end inference of two LLMs, agent-written kernels achieve a 1.3-1.6x prefill speedup over llama.cpp's fast path. However, current agents do not yet reliably adapt to new extensions that require unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.
authors: Shuaiwei Huang, Weihua Du, Allen Wu, Ivan Fox, Manupa Karunaratne, Yiming Yang, Sean Welleck
bullets: Introduces a benchmark pipeline and hardware-feedback environments for agent-based kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures.

Agent-written kernels improve LLM prefill speed by 1.3–1.6× over llama.cpp’s fast path in two end-to-end inference workloads.
Agents do not yet reliably handle new extensions with unfamiliar programming models, particularly SME2 matrix tiles.

papers.abstract: Mid-generation abstention aims to stop an unpromising response before spending its remaining computation budget. Intermediate transformer states may help predict eventual correctness, but whether scalar summaries of their vocabulary predictions add useful evidence is less clear. We compare Tuned Lens entropy and divergence features with final-state and raw intermediate-state probes under matched, causal evaluation. Across eight instruction-tuned models on MATH-500, raw intermediate states improve ranking, whereas scalar-only probes usually trail the final-state baseline. Scalar hybrids have positive exceptions, but their advantage over position-matched permutation controls is small. Cross-fitted residual comparisons further show that gains over a final-state probe need not require aligned scalar features. Actual stopping runs on two model sizes and two benchmarks reveal a separate accuracy--computation trade-off, with token savings overstating wall-time savings for scalar policies. The evidence supports a restricted empirical conclusion about these scalar features, not a general negative claim about intermediate representations.
authors: Khurram Khalil, Khaza Anuarul Hoque
bullets: Evaluates entropy and divergence features from Tuned Lens summaries against final-state and raw intermediate-state probes.
Across eight instruction-tuned models on MATH-500, raw intermediate states improve ranking, but scalar-only probes usually underperform the final-state baseline.
Some scalar hybrids help, yet their gains over position-matched permutation controls are small and need not depend on aligned scalar features.
Stopping experiments show a separate accuracy–computation trade-off, with scalar policies saving fewer wall-clock resources than token counts suggest.
Conclusion is limited to these scalar features rather than intermediate representations in general.

papers.abstract: Steering one neuron of a small language model can impose a topic or a quirk without training, yet replications show that many published single-neuron recipes are fragile or nonspecific. This paper asks whether an interpersonal stance can be controlled in this manner. The stance studied is a distant crush, a chatbot character that is guarded, intermittently warm and inconsistent. In Qwen3.5, 4B, contrasting activations on hand-written guarded and eager replies identified neuron 7515 of layer 9 as a candidate for controlling this stance. Increasing this neuron activation made the characters replies more distant. Three language models rated this change as stronger than the effects of changing randomly selected neurons, and a blind human comparison supported the finding. Changing the interventions direction between messages also shifted replies between warmer and more distant styles. This suggests that a language model conversational stance can be personalized without finetuning.
authors: Naman Chawla, Chhavi Dhiman
bullets: The paper tests whether one-neuron steering can control an interpersonal stance rather than only topics or quirks.
Contrasting guarded and eager replies identified neuron 7515 in layer 9 of Qwen3.5 4B as a candidate.
Increasing its activation produced more distant replies, while reversing intervention direction shifted replies between warmer and more distant styles.
Three language models and a blind human comparison judged the targeted change stronger than changes from randomly selected neurons.
The findings suggest a possible route to personalized conversational character control without fine-tuning, but also highlight concerns about fragile or nonspecific single-neuron recipes.

papers.abstract: Deploying a conversational model and a specialist together could avoid maintaining a separate specialist service. We present LM2, which embeds a trained story generator into a larger conversational model. The larger model handles the conversation and invokes the generator for story requests. We constrain the generator arithmetic during training so its calculations can be compiled directly into added model layers. We compare this approach with QwenPU, which executes the stories260K language model on an embedded processor. LM2 requires one host token per generated character, compared with approximately 25,000 for QwenPU. However, its story generator predicts held out text less well, i.e. 1.145 bits per character versus 0.894 for stories260K, where lower is better. The Qwen3.5, 0.8B implementation occupies 18.1 GB and generates the same characters as a standalone integer implementation of the inner model in the tested runs. These results illustrate a tradeoff between host-token cost and text-prediction performance.
authors: Naman Chawla, Chhavi Dhiman
bullets: Embeds a trained story generator into a conversational model so one system can handle dialogue and story requests.
Constrains generator arithmetic during training to compile its computations into added model layers.
Uses one host token per generated character, versus approximately 25,000 with the QwenPU approach.
Achieves 1.145 bits per character on held-out text versus 0.894 for stories260K, where lower is better.
The tested Qwen3.5 0.8B implementation occupies 18.1 GB and matches the standalone integer implementation’s generated characters.

papers.abstract: Test-time compute has become an important paradigm in computer vision and language modeling, where additional computation at inference time enables models to explore multiple candidate solutions and select or refine the most reliable one. However, time series forecasting models typically produce predictions through a single forward pass, leaving them vulnerable to distribution shifts and non-stationarity that frequently arise in real-world temporal data. We propose Time Test Compute for Time Series (TTC4TS), an architecture-agnostic framework that improves the predictive performance of frozen forecasting models at inference time. Given a pretrained backbone, the generator produces multiple candidate forecast trajectories using augmentation, retrieval, adapter. The synthesizer then selects or combines these candidates using aggregation, classification, or candidate-scoring and ranking methods to produce the final forecast. By increasing the number of candidates, TTC4TS scales test-time compute without retraining the forecasting backbone. Beyond improving point-forecast accuracy, TTC4TS can exploit candidate forecasts for uncertainty quantification, which supports improved interval forecasts. We also theoretically analyze when additional test-time computation improves forecasting. Experiments across diverse datasets and backbones demonstrate consistent gains in accuracy and calibration. Code is provided in https://github.com/Anoise/TTC4TS.
authors: Daojun Liang, Xiao Hong, Pei Zhang, Yinglong Wang, Shuo Li, Jing Chen, Ying Guo, Hu Zhang
bullets: Addresses vulnerability to distribution shifts and non-stationarity caused by single-pass forecasting.
Uses an architecture-agnostic generator–synthesizer framework with augmentation, retrieval, or adapters for candidate generation.
Combines or ranks candidates through aggregation, classification, or scoring methods.
Scaling the number of candidates increases test-time compute and also supports uncertainty and interval forecasting.
Experiments across diverse datasets and backbones report consistent gains in predictive accuracy and calibration.

papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) agents have surpassed learned-policy baselines on existing robotic manipulation benchmarks. However, these agents still struggle with time-sensitive everyday tasks that existing benchmarks for VLM agents cover only partially. In these tasks, evolving physical processes create finite windows for successful intervention. These action windows are inherently temporal and impose a shared time budget on decision making and physical execution. Coordinating intervention within this budget requires agents to determine when the window opens. We introduce AWAIT, a simulation benchmark that evaluates task completion within action windows while accounting for decision and execution time. Our evaluation reveals difficulties in recognizing window onset and shows that successive decisions and movements can exhaust an action window even when each decision takes less than the window duration. Project page: https://eyja42.github.io/await-site/.
authors: Haoxiang Zhan, Haoqin Hong, Congcong Zhu, Jingrun Chen
bullets: Existing manipulation benchmarks only partially test time-sensitive everyday tasks.
AWAIT is a simulation benchmark that evaluates task completion under explicit action windows.
Agents must identify when an intervention window opens and coordinate decisions with physical movements.
Results show difficulty detecting window onset and that repeated actions can exhaust the window, even when individual decisions are shorter than it.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies complete most benchmark tasks but often violate safety constraints. Since they are stochastic, one remedy is to sample several candidate action chunks and execute one that a world model predicts is safe. We ask what such a model must do. In simulation, a lookahead safety filter with the simulator as an exact world model raises the safety rate of three VLA policies on LIBERO and of pi0.5 on LIBERO-Plus by 11.5 to 25.7 points. It also helps pi0.5 on three RoboCasa tasks. Learned critics trained on one policy's data detect dangerous states (pooled AUROC up to 0.864) but rank candidates at one state close to chance (within-decision AUROC 0.551-0.560), and the learned dynamics and video models we test do no better. When the simulator's state is perturbed, selection degrades long before detection. In the loop, a median position error of 3.18 mm removes 70% of the gain on LIBERO-Spatial, partly because the error also corrupts the displacement check. On LIBERO-10 the loss is smaller, and the intervals overlap. The median does not predict the cost: a pixel reader with a 0.56 mm median error keeps 6.5 points less of the gain than Gaussian error of a similar median. A world model for safety should thus be judged by within-state ranking, and its state must be accurate in the tail and on handled objects, not only in the median.
authors: Thanish Bolla
bullets: VLA policies can violate safety constraints despite strong benchmark performance, motivating safety filtering over sampled action chunks.
An exact-simulator lookahead filter improves safety rates by 11.5–25.7 points across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and selected RoboCasa tasks.
Learned critics detect dangerous states well (pooled AUROC up to 0.864) but rank candidates nearly at chance (within-decision AUROC 0.551–0.560).
Safety-selection gains degrade substantially when the world model’s state is perturbed; median position error can remove most of the benefit.
Evaluation should emphasize within-state ranking and state accuracy in tail cases and on handled objects, not just median error.

papers.title: Detecting Is Not Choosing: What a World Model Needs to Keep a VLA Policy Safe

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential for industrial anomaly detection and understanding. However, reliably identifying subtle anomalies remains challenging, as existing approaches often struggle to acquire and verify fine-grained visual evidence beyond global observations. To address this challenge, we propose EVAD, an evidence-guided visual search framework that enables MLLMs to actively seek and examine diagnostically informative visual evidence for reliable anomaly reasoning. Specifically, EVAD begins with a global visual assessment to identify potentially anomalous regions for further inspection. Building upon this observation, we introduce a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-guided exploration strategy that progressively acquires visual evidence through two complementary operations: semantic refinement for fine-grained inspection and spatial expansion for contextual verification. The acquired evidence is subsequently evaluated and integrated to support more informed and reliable anomaly decisions. Extensive experiments across multiple industrial anomaly detection tasks demonstrate that EVAD achieves state-of-the-art performance in most evaluated settings, highlighting the effectiveness of active evidence exploration for fine-grained anomaly understanding and reasoning. The code will be publicly available upon publication.
authors: Peng Chen, Chao Huang, Yangyang Liu, Maodong Wu, Jinyi Xu, Mingbo Yang, Yunkang Cao, Fangjun Huang
bullets: Targets the difficulty of detecting subtle anomalies that global visual observations may miss.
Starts with a global assessment to identify regions requiring closer inspection.
Uses Monte Carlo Tree Search to guide semantic refinement and spatial expansion of visual evidence.
Evaluates and integrates the acquired evidence for more reliable anomaly reasoning.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance in most evaluated settings across multiple industrial anomaly detection tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the proposed EVAD framework. EVAD consists of three key stages: (1) Inspection Planning, which performs global observation and generates spatially grounded semantic inspection targets; (2) Evidence Search, which employs Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with bidirectional evidence evaluation and asymmetric rewards to explore informative visual regions; and (3) Decision Reassessment, which selects diverse and informative visual evidence to reassess the initial prediction.

papers.abstract: Representation alignment markedly accelerates diffusion training, but one-step generators raise a question that diffusion does not: \emph{which training path should receive the loss?} A one-step generator sees two kinds of inputs. Corrupted real images come with their clean counterpart, which provides an instance-paired target. Samples generated from pure noise have no corresponding real image, yet this is where the final model operates. We study this question on Priming, which trains one-step generators from scratch by reconstructing corrupted images and then matching feature distributions with optimal transport. Aligning the generative path, the natural choice, collapses recall ($0.45\!\to\!0.15$--$0.25$) in all 17 configurations we test, including five target constructions and loss weights down to $0.05$. Aligning the paired reconstruction path with a frozen DINOv2 encoder instead helps in every setting we test. A short analysis explains this asymmetry: when the target carries no instance information about the input, the optimal aligned feature is constant within each class, so the loss pulls samples toward class prototypes. A control confirms this: aligning the paired path to a random same-class image instead of the input's own image removes most of the gain. Inside the generator, paired-path alignment creates an interface block through which post-training routes noise, and the image semantics carried through it predict sample quality across 16 models. The resulting recipe, \method, accelerates \emph{both} training stages on ImageNet $256\!\times\!256$: it matches the 160-epoch baseline with $2\times$ fewer priming epochs, surpasses its final quality with $4\times$ fewer post-training updates, and lowers FID to 1.30 (B) and 1.155 (L) at the standard budget. A joint single-stage variant trains native one-step generators and reaches FID 1.22 with 115M parameters.
authors: Mingxiao Li, Xuantuo Huang, Encheng Su, Aoran Wang, Han Zhang, Jinouwen Zhang, Shixiang Tang
bullets: Generative-path alignment consistently harms recall, collapsing it from 0.45 to 0.15–0.25 across 17 configurations.
Paired-path alignment with a frozen DINOv2 encoder improves performance in every tested setting.
Unpaired targets lack instance information and pull samples toward class prototypes; a same-class-image control confirms the importance of exact pairing.
The proposed recipe matches the baseline with 2× fewer priming epochs and exceeds its final quality with 4× fewer post-training updates.
At the standard budget, it achieves FID 1.30 (B) and 1.155 (L); a joint variant reaches FID 1.22 with 115M parameters.

(b) On the generative path, the same weights map noise to samples that are matched to real images by OT in frozen ConvNeXt/MAE feature spaces. papers.abstract: Rotating, translating, or rescaling an object in a photograph requires revealing unseen surfaces, preserving visible appearance, and updating shadows and reflections. Reconstructed 3D assets, rendered at the target pose as a 3D state, provide explicit geometric guidance, but their imperfect textures may conflict with the photograph, while standard paired training does not explicitly teach the editor which source to trust. To address this, we propose counterfactual state supervision, which constructs controlled photo--state conflicts through hidden-surface repainting, hidden geometry with re-rendered shadows and reflections, and visible-surface texture replacement. This teaches the editor to follow the 3D state for unseen content while preserving photograph-visible appearance. However, learning this distinction does not ensure that it is maintained during sampling. We therefore introduce symmetric counterfactual correction, which uses state-side and photo-side twins, which share the photograph and the state respectively, to construct directed latent perturbations toward condition-inconsistent targets and train recovery toward the target specified by the current condition. Both strategies operate only during training, requiring no architectural changes or additional inference steps. Experiments on OBJect and SpatialEdit-Bench demonstrate strong spatial editing performance and content preservation, while controlled ablations show improved source selection and sustained responsiveness to conditioning during sampling.
authors: Jian Zahng, Zhijun Zhang
bullets: Addresses object rotation, translation, and rescaling when unseen surfaces, shadows, and reflections must be generated consistently.
Introduces counterfactual state supervision with controlled conflicts between photographs and 3D states to teach source selection.
Adds symmetric counterfactual correction using photo-side and state-side twins to preserve conditioning responsiveness during sampling.
Training-only strategies require no architectural changes or extra inference steps.
Experiments on OBJect and SpatialEdit-Bench report strong spatial editing and content preservation, with ablations showing improved source selection.

papers.tldr: A 3D-aware editing framework trains models to trust reconstructed 3D states for unseen content while preserving photograph-visible appearance and conditioning this behavior during sampling.

papers.abstract: Cross-subject brain-to-image retrieval aims to identify viewed images from unseen subjects' brain signals. However, inter-subject variability hinders alignment of brain-image representations, while independent query ranking tends to concentrate predictions on a few candidates, making accurate retrieval difficult without target labels. We propose STAGE (Structured Test-Time Adaptation with Global Entropic Soft-coupling), a structured test-time adaptation framework for recovering cross-subject alignment from uncertain brain-image correspondences. Moment calibration reduces statistical discrepancies between features, while coupling-weighted initialization establishes initial alignment. Coupling-guided adaptation further refines residual feature mismatches, and soft-coupling ranking coordinates candidate competition across queries to prevent overly concentrated matching assignments. Using only unlabeled target batches, STAGE maintains consistent matching from feature calibration to image retrieval while keeping both encoders frozen. Experiments on three public datasets validate STAGE's retrieval performance. On THINGS-EEG2, STAGE achieves 68.25% Top-1 and 90.47% Top-5, improving Top-1 by 18.52 percentage points over SCORE recovery and CSLS on identical frozen NICE features. Calibrated on 200 queries and a 200-image gallery covering their identities, STAGE retains 42.05% Top-1 when ranking 1,854 images with the transform frozen.
authors: Yihang Zou, Ruixi Liang, Chunmei Qing, Junpeng Tan, Haichuan Wei, Wanxiang Luo, Gao Wu, Haodong Li, Xiangmin Xu, Yefeng Zheng
bullets: Addresses inter-subject brain-signal variability and prediction concentration in image retrieval without target labels.
Uses moment calibration, coupling-weighted initialization, and coupling-guided adaptation to refine brain-image alignment.
Applies global entropic soft-coupling to coordinate candidate competition across queries.
Validated on three public datasets; on THINGS-EEG2, it achieves 68.25% Top-1 and 90.47% Top-5 retrieval.
With a frozen transform, it retains 42.05% Top-1 when ranking 1,854 images after calibration on 200 queries and 200 images.

papers.abstract: Quantization is the standard way to shrink large language models, and it is usually judged by perplexity and task accuracy. We ask a different question: after quantization, which words can the model still say at all? A token is silenced when no hidden state can make it the top choice of the output layer, so a greedy decoder can never produce it. We give a simple, scalable way to estimate how many tokens a quantized output head silences, combining three checks: a direction that lets a token win (so it is safe), an upper bound on how close a token's row is to being trapped inside the others, and an exact match that proves a token can never win. Each count is therefore a certified range: exact matches give its lower end and flagged tokens can only raise its upper end. In nearly all settings we report down to 3 bits the two ends coincide, so the counts are exact. Across three open models we find that quantization silences tokens: on large-vocabulary models it already appears at 8-bit precision, up to a few hundred previously reachable tokens on a 1B-parameter model, and grows as precision drops, while a small-vocabulary model resists until 3 bits. The loss is far from uniform across languages: on a multilingual vocabulary the silenced tokens are overwhelmingly non-Latin (Korean, Chinese, Thai, Arabic and Hebrew), even though Latin tokens dominate the vocabulary. Silencing is thus a measurable, language-sensitive side effect that standard averages miss, and it should be reported alongside them.
authors: Giuseppe Pappalardo
bullets: Defines a token as silenced when no hidden state can make it the output-layer winner.
Introduces scalable certified lower and upper bounds using winning directions, geometric trapping bounds, and exact impossibility checks.
The bounds coincide in nearly all tested settings down to 3-bit precision, yielding exact counts.
Silencing appears at 8 bits in large-vocabulary models, reaches a few hundred tokens in one 1B model, and increases at lower precision; small vocabularies resist until 3 bits.
On multilingual vocabularies, silenced tokens are overwhelmingly Korean, Chinese, Thai, Arabic, and Hebrew rather than Latin.

papers.abstract: Test-time learning (TTL) enables large language models to adapt to unlabeled inputs during deployment. The model updates a lightweight adapter by minimizing the next-token prediction loss on the input it receives. When these updates persist across conversation turns, every user query serves both as the request answered in the current turn and as adaptation data for later turns. By choosing the queries used for adaptation, an attacker can influence parameter updates and weaken safety alignment through ordinary interactions with a TTL chat service. To demonstrate this risk, we introduce Progressive Test-Time Adaptation Poisoning (P-TAP), a query-only multi-turn attack that jailbreaks the model by poisoning its session adapter through the service's own updates. A sequence of escalating adversarial queries shapes the adapter turn by turn; the final harmful request is then answered under the accumulated state without itself being used for adaptation. Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, enabling updates raises attack success rates on average by 13.00 percentage points under greedy decoding and by 22.25 points under best-of-10 sampling, relative to matched sessions receiving the same queries without updates. Answering adversarial queries but adapting on unrelated text or on benign text about the same topic removes most of this increase. Among existing safeguards, screening incoming queries flags every attack stream before the final request, while a perplexity-based detector of unsafe adaptation flags none of the successful attacks.
authors: Honghao Feng, Shanhan Qu, Kai Tong, Shuquan Man, Huiping Zhuang
bullets: P-TAP gradually shapes a session’s lightweight adapter with escalating adversarial queries, then uses the accumulated state to answer a final harmful request.
Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, updates increased attack success by 13.00 percentage points with greedy decoding and 22.25 points with best-of-10 sampling.
The attack’s effect largely disappears when adaptation uses unrelated or benign same-topic text instead of adversarial queries.
Incoming-query screening caught every attack stream, whereas a perplexity-based unsafe-adaptation detector missed all successful attacks.

papers.selection_reason: Studies security risks of conversational test-time learning where LLM adapters update during deployment, directly matching test-time adaptation and LLM research.
papers.title: Adaptation or Poisoning? Security Risks of Conversational Test-Time Learning in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Persistent conversational test-time learning can be poisoned through ordinary multi-turn queries, weakening safety alignment and enabling jailbreaks.

papers.abstract: Agent frameworks typically orchestrate language models through prompt-and-response interfaces. We propose a harness design that exposes intermediate model states and layer-level execution controls to the agent runtime. By connecting state collection, policy fitting, and execution, the design enables policies to allocate computation within and across models based on intermediate states. We demonstrate the approach with a prototype that learns stitching bridges and state-conditioned execution policies from paired model states, then applies them during inference to select among continue, exit, and stitch. For dispatcher supervision, we select the least-computation action whose full-vocabulary next-token prediction matches the source model's full-depth prediction, using continue when neither early action matches. We train these components on a frozen proxy corpus of 5,000 typed-decision items authored using source texts sampled from WildChat conversations, then evaluate the prototype on JevBench measuring task accuracy, agreement with full-model predictions, and end-to-end latency including runtime overhead. Preliminary results show an approximately 15% reduction in mean latency while maintaining task accuracy comparable to full-model inference.
authors: Ran Guan, Yiqi Lin, Xiangxi Tian, Yige Luo, Mi Zhou
bullets: Addresses the limits of prompt-and-response-only agent frameworks by exposing intermediate model states and layer-level controls.
Learns state-conditioned execution policies and stitching bridges from paired states across models.
Selects the least-computation action—exit, stitch, or continue—based on agreement with the source model’s full-depth prediction.

Preliminary results report about 15% lower mean latency with task accuracy comparable to full-model inference.

papers.abstract: Robot co-design benchmarks rank bodies after training their controllers under a fixed episode protocol, but that protocol can change the ranking itself. Consequently, two studies can select different bodies from the same corpus even when they use the same task and evaluator. We study one part of that protocol, the reset rule, which ends a training episode when the robot's torso falls below a height threshold. We train proximal policy optimization (PPO) controllers for 100 DERL-evolved UNIMAL bodies with this threshold at 20% of each body's starting torso height (Standard), at 50% (Strict), or with no threshold (Reset-free), and score every controller with the same evaluator. The threshold changes which bodies look best: the rankings after Strict and Reset-free training correlate at only 0.21, against about 0.89 if seed noise were the only difference. Removing fall resets costs some bodies far more than others. Bodies evolved on flat ground lose 45% of their per-step reward relative to Standard training, and those evolved on variable terrain only 16%. Permutation tests over bodies support this difference, and on 24 bodies, flat-ground bodies gain the most from Strict over Reset-free training under both PPO and soft actor-critic (SAC). Choosing bodies by their worst reward across the three protocols costs little: in sample, they keep at least 91% of the reward of each protocol's best bodies, and over 80% averaged across held-out seeds. Co-design benchmarks should state their reset rule, test whether their rankings depend on it, and report bodies that stay strong across protocols. Project page: https://reset-dependence.github.io.
authors: Kevin Qiu, Zhao Yang, Marek Cygan
bullets: The study evaluates 100 DERL-evolved UNIMAL bodies with PPO under Standard, Strict, and Reset-free torso-fall reset rules, using a shared evaluator.
Morphology rankings differ sharply: Strict versus Reset-free rankings correlate only 0.21, compared with about 0.89 expected from seed noise alone.
Removing fall resets hurts flat-ground-evolved bodies more (45% lower per-step reward) than variable-terrain bodies (16%).
The pattern is supported by permutation tests and also appears with SAC on a 24-body subset.
Selecting bodies by worst-case reward across protocols preserves at least 91% of each protocol’s best-body reward in-sample and over 80% across held-out seeds.

papers.selection_reason: Studies how training protocol (reset rule) changes morphology rankings in robot co-design, directly relevant to learned robot control and co-optimization.
papers.title: Reset Dependence Is Embodied: Training Protocol Changes Which Morphologies Appear Optimal

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement asks a system to improve the very system that improves it. Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. We let the model write its own weights. In SELFWRITE, each generation the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives (singular directions, activation contrasts between its right and wrong answers, rank-one projections, tensor computations), with no training or gradient tool. Every candidate is graded once on a hidden gate set against the current model; the best strictly improving edit is merged into the weights, and the edited model writes the next edit. On Qwen3.8-27B and math problems from DAPO-Math, five generations of SELFWRITE raise gate accuracy from 73.95% to 76.45% and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees from 76.30% to 77.75% (avg@4) and from 82.60% to 84.80% (pass@4), without a single gradient step. A language model can author useful changes to its own weights without gradients, and the edited model keeps writing useful edits.
authors: Linghua Zhang, Yunhe Li
bullets: The model analyzes its reasoning, weights, and activations in a persistent Python session to design self-edits.
Edits use white-box primitives such as singular directions, activation contrasts, rank-one projections, and tensor computations.
Each candidate is evaluated on a hidden gate set, and only strictly improving edits are merged before the next generation.
On Qwen3.8-27B math problems, five generations improved gate accuracy from 73.95% to 76.45%.
Held-out performance also improved, indicating that the self-edits generalized beyond the loop’s gate set.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The gradient writes the weights, or the model does. Top: in existing self-improvement the model writes data or chooses hyper-parameters, and SGD computes the weight change. Bottom: in SELFWRITE the model reads its own wrong and right answers, contrasts its activations on them, and writes a program that projects the contrast direction out of one of its layers (code simplified). The rank-one edit is merged only if it improves the model on a hidden gate set, and the edited model Mg+1 writes the next edit. No gradient tool is used and no training step is taken.

Figure 2: One generation of SELFWRITE. (1) Observe: the current model Mg answers 500 freshly drawn problems four times, and the editor reads its own answers, reasoning included (Section 3.2). (2) Write: eight independent sessions of the editor Mg, each with up to 30 tool rounds over a white-box toolkit for its own weights, each return a program that builds one LoRA ∆Wk (Section 3.3). (3) Select: every candidate is graded once on the hidden gate, paired problem by problem with Mg; the largest strictly positive gain is merged, and Mg+1 becomes the next editor (Section 3.4); gate statistics reach the sessions of later generations. Bars are schematic. The test split is never shown to the editor.

papers.abstract: Existing Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) autonomy frameworks lack human contextual awareness, limiting real-time adaptability in unstructured Search and Rescue (SAR) environments. To address data availability, we propose a Robot Operating System (ROS2)-based human-in-the-loop (HITL) framework that translates human directional gestures (left/right) into UAV navigation commands using RGB-Depth (RGB-D) sensing and YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once). The deprecation of ROS1 necessitates migrating to ROS2, prioritising real-time communication, scalability, and long-term maintainability. Unlike approaches optimised for peak accuracy under ideal conditions, the proposed system prioritises robustness and real-time deployment in degraded SAR environments. Our system achieves 89% confidence in depth estimation under occlusion and varying environmental conditions in Gazebo-PX4 simulations. In foggy conditions, RGB-D fusion consistently provides more informative cues than RGB alone, with an average improvement of 46.7% across all scenarios and distances. The framework demonstrates superior occlusion handling (+15%), adaptive RGB-D fusion, temporal consistency modelling, and real-time deployment via a ROS2 data distribution service (DDS), with end-to-end latency below 50 ms. We evaluate the modified YOLOv11 and the depth-weighted pose estimation on a held-out simulated test set and on real people from the public UAV-GESTURE dataset, in clear air and in Koschmieder fog. Without retraining, the framework reads the gestures of real people with 80% accuracy, depth keeps 77% at a visibility of 10 m where RGB drops to 24%, and the modified YOLOv11 reaches 91% in simulation and 99% on held-out real people when trained on real data. The open-source ROS2 implementation eases the transition of SAR-UAV platforms from ROS1, enabling UAVs to act directly on operator gestures without complex path planning.
authors: Anubhav Pandey, Harshit Nagpal, Aditya Agarwal, Tejasvi Alladi, Fei Richard Yu
bullets: Translates left/right human gestures into UAV navigation commands using RGB-D data, modified YOLOv11, and depth-weighted pose estimation.
Targets unstructured SAR conditions by prioritizing robustness, occlusion handling, temporal consistency, and real-time deployment over ideal-condition accuracy.
Uses ROS2 DDS for scalable, maintainable communication, with reported end-to-end latency below 50 ms.
In simulation, RGB-D fusion improved cues over RGB alone by 46.7% on average in fog; depth retained 77% gesture accuracy at 10 m visibility versus 24% for RGB.
The open-source implementation supports migration from ROS1 and enables direct operator control without complex path planning.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) excel at robot manipulation by imagining future observations and decoding actions from them, yet remain confined to a single embodied agent. In practice, manipulation often requires multiple robots to collaborate across disjoint workspaces, coupled timing, and heterogeneous embodiments. Such coordination demands both spatiotemporal alignment of future interactions and awareness of individual embodiment and role identities, whereas existing decentralized per-robot policies, flat centralized models, and multi-robot VLAs fail to unite both. To bridge this gap, we present MAWAM, a multi-agent world action model that jointly predicts the future observations of multiple embodiments and decodes each agent's actions from them for collaborative manipulation. Through an agent-axis curriculum, MAWAM expands a single-agent WAM along an agent dimension to coordinate teams under shared weights. Within one unified causal sequence, joint self-attention spans all agents to spatiotemporally align their imagined futures, while hierarchical language, identity encodings, and embodiment masks bind each stream to its role, identity, and embodiment. We further formalize multi-agent-necessary manipulation along three axes (why, when, and who) and develop MA-Task Harness, a coding-agent pipeline where mutually constraining generators and evaluators co-evolve customizable simulation-data and evaluation packages. Using this pipeline, we build MA-Bench across all axes with seven tasks, pairing joint success rate with role and collaboration scores for fine-grained analysis. On MA-Bench, MAWAM reaches 82.7% mean joint success, 30.7% above the strongest baseline, and achieves real-time closed-loop collaboration on a real heterogeneous robot team.
authors: Rongze Tang, Chenyu Zhou, Jianjie Fang, Ziming Liu, Zhaolu Wang, Ziyou Wang, Xvyuan Liu, Wei Wu, Chen Gao, Yong Li, Zhibo Chen
bullets: Addresses multi-robot manipulation requiring spatial-temporal coordination, role awareness, and embodiment awareness.
Expands a single-agent world action model across an agent dimension using shared weights and an agent-axis curriculum.
Uses joint self-attention, hierarchical language, identity encodings, and embodiment masks to coordinate agent-specific behavior.
Introduces MA-Task Harness and MA-Bench, covering seven tasks with joint success, role, and collaboration metrics.
Achieves 82.7% mean joint success on MA-Bench and real-time closed-loop collaboration on a heterogeneous robot team.

papers.abstract: We introduce CoHABIT, a framework for evaluating furniture layouts through complementary spatial rules and household routines. Static assessment captures geometric validity, ergonomic access, functional organization, and configurable design preferences, including Feng Shui. Dynamic assessment uses learned resident policies to simulate everyday activities, resource sharing, coordination, and individual burdens in multi-agent households. Controlled comparisons show how spatial criteria and household behavior reveal distinct aspects of layout quality, while resident profiles and scheduling influence furnishing rankings. Independent verification of household needs grounds dynamic comparisons in observed outcomes, enabling interpretable assessments of how furnished environments serve different households.
authors: Ewsey Obzherin, Samira Atlangirieva, Anastasia Antsiferova, Valentin Khrulkov, Art Prosvetov, Andrey Kuznetsov

Simulates everyday activities, resource sharing, coordination, and individual burdens using learned resident policies.

Uses independent verification of household needs to support interpretable, household-specific comparisons.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning is an effective way to accelerate multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing methods degrade substantially under aggressive pruning, especially on visual grounding (VG). We analyze the sources of this degradation from the perspective of the output shift that pruning causes in decoder layers, and decompose this shift in closed form into two terms, an image summary error and an attention allocation error. The summary error stems from the loss of visual information, and the allocation error from the drop in the share of attention assigned to visual tokens. To reduce both errors, we propose CAR (Coverage selection and Attention Reallocation), a token pruning framework that restores attention share while maintaining information. Specifically, to minimize the summary error, whose upper bound tightens as the retained tokens better cover all visual tokens, our coverage selection retains tokens that are both salient and non-redundant, with saliency from encoder heads chosen by a label-free probe. To minimize the allocation error, our attention reallocation reassigns the attention of the discarded tokens to the retained ones through a closed-form logit bias. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B with $90\%$ of the visual tokens pruned, CAR retains $93.0\%$ of the unpruned accuracy on visual question answering (VQA) and $77.9\%$ on VG, against $26.5\%$ for the best existing method on VG; the logit bias alone raises the VG accuracy of existing methods by up to $24$ points. Experiments on multiple MLLMs across VQA, VG and video understanding show that CAR generalizes well and consistently outperforms existing methods.
authors: Xixi Jiang, Pingcheng Dong, Chen Yang, Xin Yang, Kwang-Ting Cheng
bullets: Visual token pruning accelerates MLLMs but can sharply hurt performance, especially visual grounding, due to decoder output shift.
The shift is decomposed into image summary error from lost information and attention allocation error from reduced visual-token attention.
Coverage selection keeps salient, non-redundant tokens using a label-free encoder-head probe.
Attention reallocation transfers discarded-token attention to retained tokens via a closed-form logit bias.
With 90% pruning on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, CAR retains 93.0% of unpruned VQA accuracy and 77.9% of visual-grounding accuracy; results generalize across MLLMs and tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses visual token pruning in MLLMs with a novel coverage-selection and attention-reallocation framework.
papers.title: CAR: Reducing Decoder Output Shift in Visual Token Pruning via Coverage Selection and Attention Reallocation
papers.tldr: CAR makes aggressive visual token pruning more reliable by preserving broad visual coverage and reallocating attention from discarded tokens to retained ones.

papers.abstract: Recent works align the intermediate features of vision-language-action (VLA) models with frozen vision encoders during fine-tuning, hoping to inject additional priors such as 3D awareness or affordances. Unlike in image generation, where teachers for representation alignment (REPA) are assessed with encoder-intrinsic metrics, teachers for VLAs are still chosen largely by heuristics. We show that this practice is unreliable: across 14 teachers and 16 manipulation tasks, under matched training budgets, no off-the-shelf vision encoder improves the clean success rate of $\pi_{0.5}$ by more than 1 point, and all of them reduce its success rate under perturbations by 10 to 39 points. Neither global semantics nor spatial structure, the criteria used in image generation, predicts which teachers help. We therefore propose the behavioral structure metric (BSM), which measures whether states that are close in a teacher's feature space are followed by similar expert actions within the same task. BSM correlates strongly with success rate under perturbations ($r=0.87$), and every off-the-shelf vision encoder scores below $\pi_{0.5}$ itself. Based on it, we introduce Behavior-Aware VLA Alignment (BAVA), a general VLA alignment protocol that favors vision encoders whose BSM exceeds the student's and stops alignment early according to the student's BSM during training. On SmolVLA, BAVA matches continuous alignment with one third of the alignment budget, and improves the average success rate by 4.6 points over unaligned fine-tuning. Our results suggest that representation alignment benefits VLAs only when the teacher encodes rich behaviorally relevant structure.
authors: Zhengfeiyang Zhang, Haoyuan Chen, Hexin Wang, Hanyu Zhou, Zhenglin Wan, Wangbo Zhao, Pengfei Zhou
bullets: Across 14 vision encoders and 16 manipulation tasks, off-the-shelf teachers provided little clean-task benefit and substantially reduced robustness to perturbations.
Common teacher-selection criteria such as global semantics and spatial structure did not predict VLA performance.
Behavioral Structure Metric (BSM) measures whether nearby teacher representations lead to similar expert actions and strongly correlates with perturbation success.
Behavior-Aware VLA Alignment (BAVA) selects teachers with higher BSM than the student and ends alignment based on the student’s BSM.
On SmolVLA, BAVA matched continuous alignment using one-third of the alignment budget and improved average success by 4.6 points over unaligned fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models have revolutionized generative tasks but incur high inference latency due to iterative denoising. Cache-based strategies accelerate inference by reusing intermediate features, yet they largely rely on static, sample-agnostic schedules. Our empirical analysis reveals two factors that these schedules overlook. (i) denoising dynamics and computational requirements vary across prompts, motivating adaptive computation allocation. (ii) sensitivity to caching errors varies across timesteps, so static schedules may reuse features at error-sensitive steps or waste computation at less sensitive ones. We therefore propose OnCache, a dynamic caching framework that makes prompt-adaptive decisions online about how much computation to allocate and when to refresh cached features. A policy is trained offline on paired compute and cache continuations from identical denoising states, using differences in terminal fidelity and the number of function evaluations (NFE) to account for the downstream consequences of each decision. To further improve the generation quality, a neural corrector compensates for caching-induced errors and mitigates their accumulation throughout the denoising trajectory. Both components are lightweight and introduce negligible additional inference latency. On FLUX.1-dev, OnCache achieves a nearly $3\times$ generation speedup at $1024^2$ resolution, with LPIPS of $0.156$ and SSIM of $0.860$. We further extend OnCache to video generation on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, achieving state-of-the-art efficiency--quality trade-offs across both modalities.
authors: Zhikang Xie, Xichen Ye, Yifan Wu, Yuxuan Liu, Qianlong Wang, Haoshen Yu, Peizhu Gong, Weizhong Zhang, Cheng Jin
bullets: Static caching schedules overlook prompt-dependent denoising costs and timestep-varying sensitivity to caching errors.
OnCache uses an offline-trained policy to allocate computation and refresh cached features online during denoising.
A lightweight neural corrector reduces caching errors and their accumulation with negligible added inference latency.
On FLUX.1-dev at 1024², it achieves nearly 3× speedup with LPIPS 0.156 and SSIM 0.860.
The framework also extends to video generation on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, yielding state-of-the-art efficiency–quality trade-offs across image and video modalities.

figures.caption: Figure 3. OnCache inference framework. (a) Conditioned generation repeatedly applies an OnCache denoising step, producing intermediate latents. (b) The policy πθ,b observes the causal state zi and selects full computation (ai = 1) or cache reuse (ai = 0). Full computation refreshes the residual cache with Ri = Bi(hi, c) − hi; cache reuse forms h̄i = hi + Rj , where j is the most recent refresh index. The corrector adjusts reused features before the output head; δi denotes the resulting adjustment to the denoiser output.

papers.abstract: Adaptive visual token routers aim to save computation while preserving the image detail needed to answer each question. A higher average score could reflect better choices for individual images or more frequent use of high resolution on tasks that need it. We distinguish the two by keeping action counts fixed within each task and comparing the router's assignments with random pairings of the same actions and images. On equally weighted ChartQA and TextVQA, both Qwen2.5-VL-3B and -7B gain from matching but lose more from their action frequencies relative to a task table, with a 1.71-point gain and a 3.95-point loss on 7B. Exchanging the continuous resolutions chosen by the external selector CARES also lowers quality on 7B. When requests arrive with task labels, the table outscores the discrete router by 1.92 points and saves 31.76 ms per complete 7B request on average.
authors: Chenxi Wang, Bin Wang
bullets: The study separates routing quality into action allocation and image–action matching while holding per-task action counts fixed.
On equally weighted ChartQA and TextVQA, both Qwen2.5-VL-3B and -7B benefit from matching, but deviate more from task-optimal action frequencies.
For Qwen2.5-VL-7B, matching adds 1.71 points, while its action-frequency choices cost 3.95 points relative to a task table.
Randomly exchanging CARES-selected continuous resolutions also reduces 7B quality, supporting the value of image–resolution matching.
With task labels, a task table beats the discrete router by 1.92 points and saves 31.76 ms per complete 7B request on average.

papers.selection_reason: Studies adaptive visual token routing to save computation, directly relevant to token-level efficiency in multimodal models.
papers.title: Separating Action Allocation from Image Matching in Visual Token Routing
papers.tldr: Visual token routers benefit from both choosing the right action frequencies and matching actions to images, with action allocation often having the larger impact.

papers.abstract: Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) store entities with photos and names and link them by facts. MMKG methods predict links between known entity IDs, and image retrievers, from CLIP to MLLM embedders, return entities that look like a query photo or match its description. Neither answers a common question about a new photo: which graph entity is related to the one shown, such as the team of a pictured player or the city of a landmark. We call this knowledge graph relational image retrieval (KRIR): given a photo and a natural-language relation, retrieve the related MMKG entity, which rarely resembles the photo, whether the depicted entity is in the graph (known) or not (unseen). We build three benchmarks from YAGO, Wikidata and in-the-wild OVEN photos. The task hides two hops: recognising which graph entity is shown, and recalling what it is connected to. GraphSeer bridges them inside one multimodal LLM: it links the photo to the graph, reads the facts of the best match, and retrieves with the hidden state at which the model is about to say the answer. An unseen entity has no facts of its own, but every candidate answer does, so a listwise verifier reads the other end of the graph: it re-ranks the top candidates by their facts and photos in one forward pass, and the facts matter far more than the photos. With Qwen3.5-27B, GraphSeer improves MRR on known entities by 24.2-70.0% over an MLLM embedder fine-tuned on the same data with the same budget. When it also fuses and verifies the embedder's candidates, it improves MRR on unseen entities by 12.5-25.6%, and on known entities it beats KG-completion models given the ground-truth entity ID.
authors: Linyu Li, Zhi Jin, Yuanpeng He, Haoran Duan, Dongming Jin, Wenchun Jing, Xuan Zhang, Gadeng Luosang, Nyima Tashi
bullets: Introduces knowledge graph relational image retrieval (KRIR), where the target entity may look unrelated to the query image.
Builds benchmarks from YAGO, Wikidata, and in-the-wild OVEN photos, covering known and unseen entities.
Uses an MLLM to link the image to the graph, read relational facts, and retrieve candidates from the answer-generation hidden state.
For unseen entities, a listwise verifier re-ranks candidates using their graph facts and photos; graph facts are substantially more useful than photos.

With Qwen3.5-27B, improves MRR over comparable MLLM embedding retrieval by 24.2–70.0% on known entities and 12.5–25.6% on unseen entities; it also surpasses KG-completion models when given the true entity ID.

papers.selection_reason: Uses multimodal LLMs for knowledge graph relational image retrieval.
papers.title: GraphSeer: Multimodal Knowledge Graph Relational Image Retrieval with MLLMs
papers.tldr: GraphSeer enables multimodal knowledge-graph retrieval by identifying the entity shown in a photo and finding the entity connected to it by a requested relation, even for unseen entities.

papers.abstract: Sequential recommender systems aim to predict a user's next interaction by modeling temporal dependencies in historical behavior sequences. To capture such dependencies, recent approaches increasingly rely on attention-based architectures, particularly transformers. While effective at modeling long-range sequential patterns, these models apply a fixed computation depth to all interaction items, treating them as equally complex. However, user behavior is inherently heterogeneous, with many interactions following simple repetitive patterns, whereas others require modeling higher-order dependencies. This mismatch leads to inefficient utilization of model capacity and unnecessary computational overhead, particularly in deep transformer-based architectures. To address this issue, we propose MoR4Rec, a sequential recommendation framework based on a Mixture-of-Recursion paradigm, which enables item-wise adaptive computation through a shared transformer backbone. A learned routing mechanism dynamically assigns each item to an appropriate recursion depth, allocating deeper computation to complex interactions while processing simpler patterns more efficiently. To improve computational efficiency, we develop a cascade-based strategy with key-value sharing across recursion steps. We further introduce a gated attention mechanism that adaptively regulates contextual information during recursive sequence modeling. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets show that MoR4Rec consistently outperforms strong transformer-based baselines, achieving average gains of 2.28% in Recall@5, 2.50% in NDCG@5, and 2.0% in MRR@5 over the strongest baseline. The improvements remain consistent across top-10 and top-20 recommendation cutoffs, while comparisons with vanilla transformers demonstrate the computational efficiency of adaptive recursive processing.
authors: Tiwari Ankit Satyaprakash, Adamya Shyam, Vikas Kumar, Bharti Rana, Venkateswara Rao Kagita
bullets: Targets inefficient fixed-depth computation in transformer-based sequential recommenders.
Uses a shared transformer backbone with learned routing to assign item-wise recursion depths.
Employs cascade-based key-value sharing for efficiency and gated attention for adaptive context regulation.
Outperforms strong transformer baselines across three benchmarks, with average gains of 2.28% Recall@5, 2.50% NDCG@5, and 2.0% MRR@5.
Gains remain consistent at top-10 and top-20 cutoffs; efficiency is demonstrated against vanilla transformers.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) extract structured data from documents by generating the requested JSON one token at a time, so their sequential steps grow with the length of the answer. Yet in key information extraction (KIE) the schema already fixes the answer's structure: keys, nesting and lists are known before decoding, and only the values are unknown. We exploit this with a non-autoregressive extractor that writes the structure from the schema, sizes every list with a count pass, and predicts all values in parallel, in a fixed number of passes that does not grow with the document. Each value is decoded with connectionist temporal classification (CTC) in its own block of slots, so its length never has to be predicted, and a value that is still open after its block gets a larger token budget. Zero-shot on VAREX, CORD and FUNSD, our 4B extractor is 3.5$\times$ faster than the diffusion-VLM competition on average (up to 5.6$\times$) and more accurate, with 4--6 forward passes per document where block diffusion needs 12--74. The same extractor also drafts for speculative decoding with its own autoregressive base: it runs 8.3$\times$ faster than autoregressive decoding (up to 10.4$\times$) within 0.4 points of its accuracy, and 3.3$\times$ faster than speculative diffusion decoding while 13.0 points more accurate. We release the model and code.
authors: Shaked Perek, Avihu Dekel, Ben Wiesel, Sivan Harary, Eli Schwartz
bullets: Problem: Autoregressive VLMs decode JSON sequentially even though KIE schemas already specify the output structure, causing latency to grow with answer length.
Method: Fill the schema directly, use a count pass to size lists, and decode each value in parallel with CTC slot blocks and adaptive token budgets.
Results: Zero-shot on VAREX, CORD, and FUNSD, the 4B model is 3.5× faster than diffusion-VLM competitors on average and uses 4–6 forward passes per document.
It also serves as a speculative-decoding draft model, running 8.3× faster than autoregressive decoding with accuracy within 0.4 points.
The model and code are released.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Decoding trace on a VAREX test form, coloured by the forward that wrote each token. The first bidirectional pass commits most of every value (blue) and the later confidence passes fill what it was unsure of (orange). The extended budget (green) writes the end of the longest value, the physician’s details, and all eleven values are exact. In the speculative mode the verifier accepts all eleven unchanged.

Figure 2. Schema-parallel CTC decoding. (a) A count pass reads the image and the schema and sizes every list. (b) The schema is written out as a skeleton in which every value gets a block of n [M] slots. (c) A bidirectional forward predicts all slots of all values at once; this is repeated for T passes, each but the last revealing the slots predicted with probability above τ and re-predicting the rest (blanks are never revealed; the last pass takes the argmax of every slot), with the image–prompt key/values computed once. (d) CTC collapse first merges repeats, then drops blanks (∅); a value still open after its block gets n more slots (budget +n).

Figure 4. Sequential cost vs. document size. Forward passes (left, log scale) and latency (right) per document against the number of keys in its schema, pooled over VAREX, CORD and FUNSD (1,924 documents; median and interquartile range per bin). Our forward count stays at 4–6 for every document, while block diffusion’s grows with the size of the JSON it generates. Masked diffusion on our own skeleton (value-decoder ablation, 8 steps) is also flat but needs more forwards than CTC and is slower.

papers.selection_reason: Non-autoregressive schema-parallel decoding for VLMs directly reduces inference latency and is a transferable efficiency idea.
papers.title: Fill in the Blanks: Non-Autoregressive Schema-Parallel Key Information Extraction with CTC Decoding
papers.tldr: A schema-aware, non-autoregressive KIE model uses CTC to decode all values in parallel, substantially reducing document-extraction latency while maintaining or improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Time-to-Transit (TTT) is a perceptual cue, proxy for depth, that can be computed in the visual cortex, allowing animals to estimate the time remaining to move past features in the environment. We show how TTT can be estimated and used for bio-inspired navigation of a mobile robot equipped with a monocular camera. The paper describes a lightweight neural network estimation method, named MobileNeTTT, that (1) uses the full field of view and provides a rich array of visual feature TTT estimates; (2) is relatively insensitive to camera rotation; and (3) automatically adjusts to the geometry of the path and the presence of obstacles. Because TTT is a coarse visual cue, it is far simpler to use for robot navigation than current large visual depth foundation models. Our navigation model uses a 1.95M-parameter network that is two to three orders of magnitude smaller than well-known large vision foundation models, making it able to run in real time on edge hardware. Simulation and actual laboratory experiments validate the proposed approach in dynamic and spatially complex environments. Code, data, and video are available.
authors: Chiara Boretti, Philippe Bich, Manuel Morteo, Roberto Tron, John Baillieul
bullets: Uses the full camera field of view to produce rich visual time-to-transit estimates.
Is relatively robust to camera rotation and adapts to path geometry and obstacles.
Employs a 1.95M-parameter network, substantially smaller than large vision foundation models.
Enables simpler navigation from a coarse depth-related cue rather than full visual depth estimation.
Validated in simulation and laboratory experiments involving dynamic, spatially complex environments.

figures.caption: Fig. 4. Overview of MobileNeTTT, which estimates Time-To-Transit from sequential RGB images I(t−1) and I(t) using a DNN-based depth estimator. Instead of predicting a dense per-pixel depth map, the network outputs a coarse depth map and a binary validity map indicating reliable values. Coarse depth values are then divided by the robot’s speed v, with a small constant ϵ added to prevent division by zero, to compute TTT values.

Fig. 5. Comparison of the estimation of TTT values coming from two areas of the input image using MobileNeTTT and the OF-based method. The image is acquired in a simulated environment. The red outer area represents the Region of Interest (ROI) where features are selected and tracked using optical flow. These ROIs are combinations of the grid cells provided by MobileNeTTT. MobileNeTTT offers superior, less noisy estimates, particularly in the central region close to the FoE.

Fig. 6. An example of an environment and the TTT estimates produced by the OF-based method and MobileNeTTT. MobileNeTTT enables a better understanding of the environment and the definition of dynamic left (blue), right (orange), and central (white) ROIs.

Fig. 1. In a) TTT estimation from sequential monocular images using sparse Optical Flow (OF), while in b) MobileNeTTT, which extends coarse TTT estimation across the entire image, enhancing estimation, maintaining real-time performance without imposing any motion constraint.

(Bottom) The corresponding top-down environment layout with the recorded MobileNeTTT odometry trajectory, demonstrating successful navigation through the corridor without collision at v = 0.4m s .

papers.selection_reason: Learning-based visual navigation for a mobile robot using a lightweight time-to-transit estimator, fitting robot navigation.
papers.title: MobileNeTTT: a Lightweight DNN-based Time-To-Transit Estimator for Visual Navigation
papers.tldr: MobileNeTTT is a compact monocular-vision network that estimates time-to-transit across the visual field for real-time, bio-inspired robot navigation on edge hardware.

papers.abstract: Latent world models plan toward a goal by predicting the outcomes of candidate actions, but under the distribution shift, prediction errors can lead the planner astray. Test-time training using executed actions helps, yet what it corrects and whether its updates should persist across episodes remains unclear. We address both by analyzing the world model's prediction error. On PushObj, an object-pushing task, we probe multiple actions from the same state and decompose the error into an offset shared across actions and an action-dependent component. The offset effectively shifts the planner's goal, and AdaJEPA mainly tracks it: the common shift alone recovers 91% of its planning gain. Part of the offset is episode-specific, so carrying its correction into the next episode does not help and may even hurt. The remaining offset recurs across episodes and action-dependent error can be or needs to be learned and retained from many episodes. Our sft-JEPA therefore uses two learners on different timescales: a fast learner that tracks the offset and resets each episode, and a slow LoRA learner that accumulates recurring knowledge across episodes. Across PushObj, PointMaze, zero-shot planning on RoboCasa (with DINO-WM), and OGBench (with LeWAM), sft-JEPA leads all benchmark averages, improving planning success over AdaJEPA by up to 22 points.
authors: Shuaicheng Niu, Guohao Chen, Kevin Z. Shen, Yunbei Zhang, Peilin Zhao, Yinan Zhang, Cyril Leung
bullets: Problem: Distribution-shifted prediction errors can mislead latent-world-model planners, and it is unclear which corrections should persist across episodes.
Method: Decompose prediction error into an action-shared offset and an action-dependent component.
Key finding: The shared offset shifts the planner’s goal; tracking it alone recovers 91% of AdaJEPA’s planning gain, while episode-specific corrections should not persist.
Contribution: sft-JEPA combines a fast, episode-resetting learner for transient offsets with a slow LoRA learner for recurring and action-dependent errors.
Results: It leads benchmark averages across PushObj, PointMaze, RoboCasa, and OGBench, improving planning success over AdaJEPA by up to 22 points.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes test-time training in latent world models and proposes a slow-fast approach for planning under distribution shift.
papers.title: What Test-Time Training Corrects in Latent World Models? A Slow-Fast Approach
papers.tldr: A slow-fast test-time training method separates transient from recurring world-model errors, improving planning across diverse benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Conversation history is infrastructure: deployed language models rely on application layers to store and reinject prior turns, and that stored state is writable. We formalize session-level contamination by attack layer, state a coverage theorem, and measure its scope: each deployment-layer verification tier covers exactly its layer and is sound with respect to the others; instruction overrides are not detectable without false positives; and composite vectors evade per-fragment verification. A standardized harness applied to eight mechanism families across 3,249 sessions and three model families makes these claims checkable. First, pattern-based detection pays a measured false-positive price: the classic defenses flag 35 to 50 percent of benign sessions, and the naive refusal floor reaches only 2.4 percent attack-cell adoption while destroying 33 to 100 percent of benign turns, whereas provenance-gated channel separation achieves adoption at or below 1.2 percent with zero false positives and zero utility loss. Second, in the exploratory instruction-override extension, the gates' boundary is a cliff: directives rephrased without shape markers bypass them at control-equivalent rates, 47.7 to 49.5 percent against 0.0 percent for the shaped class, placing that class in the model-internal lane. Third, the deterministic core is storage-layer detection at 126 of 126 per model with zero false positives. External anchors reproduce published attack pressure, with PoisonedRAG falling from 70 to 0 percent under the full stack. For practitioners: authenticate stored history and content provenance with deterministic tiers, scope instruction-layer mitigation to provenance-gated designs whose measured benign cost is zero, and monitor composition at the trajectory level rather than per fragment. All protocols and acceptance criteria are pre-registered; the stack and harness are released.
authors: Fahrell Giovanny, Geby Bayuningtyas, Sahrul Mukharom
bullets: Defines attack layers and proves that each deployment-layer verification tier covers only its own layer; composite vectors can evade per-fragment checks.
Evaluates eight mechanism families across 3,249 sessions and three model families using a preregistered, released harness.
Pattern-based defenses produced 35–50% benign-session false positives; provenance-gated channel separation achieved zero false positives and zero utility loss.
Instruction overrides without recognizable markers bypassed gates at 47.7–49.5% control-equivalent rates, identifying a model-internal detection boundary.
Storage-layer detection was deterministic across 126/126 cases per model with zero false positives; PoisonedRAG pressure fell from 70% to 0% under the full stack.
