papers.selection_reason: Addresses integrity of conversation history as external memory for LLMs.
papers.title: Detectable Epistemic Attack Layers: A Coverage Theorem and Standardized Harness for Conversation-History Integrity
papers.tldr: The paper formalizes conversation-history contamination and shows that layer-specific, provenance-gated verification detects storage attacks without false positives, while instruction overrides and composite attacks require broader safeguards.

papers.abstract: Distribution matching distillation (DMD) enables fast video generation by distilling a multi-step teacher into a few-step student. However, DMD-based methods often suffer from unnatural motion and costly training. We trace these limitations to the DMD gradient, which jointly optimizes appearance, layout, and motion without distinguishing their learning dynamics. Its static component, which carries appearance and layout, has a much higher signal-to-noise ratio than its motion component. As a result, per-frame quality converges within a few hundred iterations, whereas motion lags far behind. Beyond being noisy, the gradient also lacks two signals. (1) Video VAEs encode several frames into one latent frame (four in Wan2.1), and the gradient provides little guidance for spreading motion over these frames, causing periodic stutter. (2) DMD does not constrain the final sampling step to preserve the layout set by earlier steps, so objects merge and drift once the video moves. We propose HorizonFlow, which decouples the correction of motion from that of layout. It keeps the DMD loss and only shifts its regression target, with one training-only correction in the motion component and one in the orthogonal layout component. Chunk Evenness addresses (1) by spreading the motion of each latent chunk evenly over its frames, and Semantic Commitment addresses (2) by anchoring the coarse layout to the teacher's completion of the student's last step. In only 600 iterations, HorizonFlow distills Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B into a 4-step model using 8.4k training samples, 4.6-304$\times$ fewer than prior work. On VBench, HorizonFlow outperforms all released few-step Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B models. The same recipe transfers to Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B, where our student outperforms NVIDIA's distilled model. Code: https://github.com/XIANGLONGGUO/HorizonFlow-repo
authors: Xianglong Guo, Haobo Xu, Zanyi Wang, Zhen Lei, Chang Yu
bullets: DMD distillation often produces unnatural motion because appearance/layout signals dominate noisier motion signals.
Chunk Evenness spreads motion evenly across latent frames to reduce periodic stutter.
Semantic Commitment anchors the final sampling step to the teacher’s layout, limiting object merging and drift.
The method distills Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B using 8.4k samples and transfers to Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B.
It outperforms released Wan2.1 few-step models on VBench and NVIDIA’s distilled Cosmos model.‌

figures.caption: Figure 4. Qualitative comparison with released few-step models on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B. Every method gets the same VBench prompt and seed; columns are frames 1, 17, 33, 49, 65 and 81 of 81. Red boxes mark failures; insets enlarge them. rCM fuses the giraffe’s head with a zebra, loses the bird from its nest and smears the train. FastWan barely moves the giraffe, opens the bird clip with a blurred double exposure and melts the train into the rails. Self-Forcing cuts to a new shot halfway through the bird clip and pushes the bird out of the frame. HorizonFlow carries out each prompt: the giraffe bends down and drinks, the bird settles on its nest, and the train crosses the bridge toward the camera, with every subject intact from the first frame to the last. CoDMD and more prompts are in the supplementary material.

Figure 3. One student update of HorizonFlow. The student rolls out k ∈ {1, . . . , 4} steps from noise; gradients flow only through the last step, which maps (xin, tin) to xG. DMD (blue) re-noises xG and compares the critic with the guided teacher, giving the DMD gradient g. Chunk Evenness (orange) decodes a random window of xG with the frozen VAE, measures how evenly its motion is spread over the four frame phases of each latent chunk, and, where it is less even than the training clips, takes a few normalized steps that keep motion and detail, giving ∆CE. Semantic Commitment (green) lets the teacher complete the student’s last step from the same input and keeps only the block- and time-averaged difference, gated by tin and capped, as ∆SC. Both corrections only move the DMD target, x̃ = sg(xG − g + ∆CE − ∆SC), each in its own component of the update (CE: motion; SC: layout); the critic update, the sampler, and inference are those of a plain 4-step student.

Figure 2. Video DMD learns appearance before motion, and correcting the motion disturbs the layout. (a) After 4100 iterations of conventional DMD training, the glove’s fingers lose their shape from frame to frame; HorizonFlow keeps them intact after 600. (b) Plain DMD: imaging and aesthetic quality reach their final level by 300 iterations, while the dynamic degree is still 18. (c) Top: signal-to-noise ratio over noise draws of the static and motion components of the plain DMD gradient (dashed: signal = noise). Bottom: push of the update toward evenly spread motion, divided by its noise; the DMD gradient stays below the noise (dashed), while our update (DMD + CE + SC, same samples) exceeds it at every noise level. (d) Motion per frame transition in one clip, divided by its mean: plain DMD (300 iterations) moves mostly at the transitions between latent chunks (shaded); the teacher moves evenly. (e) The stutter amplitude A4, the period-4 component of these changes, peaks at 4.6 times the teacher’s level at 200 iterations. (f) Chunk Evenness alone (600 iterations) removes the stutter and raises the dynamic degree from 76 to 97, but the dog fuses with the horse, the bear with the zebra, and the drummer’s head leaves the frame. Details are in Secs. D and E.

papers.selection_reason: Few-step distillation of video diffusion models directly advances video generation efficiency and quality.

papers.tldr: HorizonFlow distills video generators into four steps in just 600 iterations by separately correcting motion and layout, improving motion quality and temporal consistency.

papers.abstract: Staged robotic procedures may reuse a fixed-dimensional policy output even though the admissible motions and physical meanings of its coordinates change across phases. We call this action-semantic shift. To address it, we propose a phase-conditioned executable policy that separates learned action proposal from deterministic command formation. Phase-specific heads generate proposals, while an action contract removes inadmissible components, enforces state-dependent bounds, and decodes the remaining action into phase-dependent task-space commands. We further introduce failure-focused local repair and a read-only provenance trace for exact command replay and rule-level auditing. Across three held-out retinal-injection evaluation blocks, our method achieves $94.27\pm0.64\%$ procedural completion and $64.40\pm2.43\%$ success within $35\,\mu\mathrm{m}$, with no hard violations. Applying the contract and decoder to the same frozen Correction network raises completion from $12.27\%$ to $90.47\%$. The trace exactly reconstructs 96,350 commands, and all 1,996 binding interventions follow their declared effects. These results show the importance of explicit executable action semantics for auditable staged microsurgical control.
authors: Jiaxi You, Yiwei Shi, Yanlin Li, Rihui Song, Weibing Li, Kai Huang, Weiru Liu
bullets: Addresses action-semantic shifts when fixed-dimensional policy outputs change meaning across procedure phases.
Uses phase-specific proposal heads followed by deterministic filtering, state-dependent bounds, and phase-dependent task-space decoding.
Adds local repair for failures and a read-only provenance trace for command replay and rule-level auditing.
Across three held-out retinal-injection blocks, achieves 94.27±0.64% completion, 64.40±2.43% success within 35 μm, and no hard violations.
On the same frozen Correction network, contract-based decoding raises completion from 12.27% to 90.47%; all 1,996 binding interventions matched their declared effects.

papers.abstract: Answering questions over long multimodal documents requires locating relevant evidence across pages containing text, tables, and figures. When the document exceeds the model's context window, selective retrieval becomes necessary. We introduce VistaTree, a document question-answering agent that builds a summary tree directly from rendered page images. VistaTree segments documents into contiguous page spans, recursively groups them into a topic hierarchy, and refines sibling summaries to distinguish neighboring sections. At query time, the agent uses node summaries to select relevant nodes and reads the corresponding pages, using hierarchical navigation when the full outline exceeds the context budget. Experiments on MMLongBench-Doc and LongDocURL evaluate answer quality and retrieval cost using a locally hosted vision-language model, and quantify the performance gap between global and hierarchical access to the index.
authors: Yexiang Cheng, Xiaochen Zheng, David Tokar, Tatyana Y. Doktorova
bullets: Addresses evidence retrieval across long documents containing text, tables, and figures when context windows are limited.
Builds a topic hierarchy by recursively grouping contiguous page spans and refining summaries of neighboring sections.
Uses node summaries to select relevant pages, with hierarchical navigation when the full outline cannot fit in context.
Evaluated on MMLongBench-Doc and LongDocURL for answer quality and retrieval cost using a locally hosted vision-language model.
Measures the performance gap between global and hierarchical index access.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) models can now generate visually plausible short clips, but multi-shot generation requires a different set of skills: composing multiple shots with intended cut timing, transition style, camera language, and cross-shot continuity. How far this multi-shot output can be controlled from text remains unmeasured: existing benchmarks either evaluate single shots or, when they provide shot-level scripts, typically check whether the requested shots appear but not when they change or how they are joined. We introduce MSBench, a benchmark for controllable text-driven multi-shot video generation built around structured Scene-Entity-Shot mini-scripts that specify each shot's time span, camera state, content, and outgoing transition. MSBench defines a four-dimensional hybrid evaluation framework spanning Visual Quality, Dynamic Quality, Semantic Alignment, and Cross-Shot Consistency with 11 sub-metrics. Experiments on 14 commercial and open-source systems show that visual quality does little to separate the systems, whereas multi-shot control does: many models cut mainly on scene changes and render requested gradual transitions as hard cuts. Human evaluations further validate MSBench, with its system ranking reaching a Spearman correlation of 0.87 with human preferences. The project page is available at https://totalhuang.github.io/MSBench-page/.
authors: Tao Huang, ZiHao Liang, Junhao Liu, Junzhe Li, Yuancheng Wei, Sifan Zuo, Beiming Yu, Taojin Liu, Zhuoyang Li, Bing Cao
bullets: Introduces structured Scene-Entity-Shot mini-scripts specifying shot timing, camera state, content, and outgoing transitions.
Evaluates four dimensions—Visual Quality, Dynamic Quality, Semantic Alignment, and Cross-Shot Consistency—through 11 sub-metrics.
Tests 14 commercial and open-source systems, finding visual quality alone poorly distinguishes them while multi-shot control reveals larger differences.
Many systems favor hard cuts at scene changes and struggle to produce requested gradual transitions.
MSBench rankings correlate strongly with human preferences, with a reported Spearman correlation of 0.87.

papers.tldr: MSBench benchmarks how well text-to-video systems control multi-shot composition, timing, transitions, and continuity—not just visual quality.

papers.abstract: When two musicians in an ensemble play the same instrument, they sound alike and their instruments look alike. Audio-only separators, and audio-visual separators that rely on appearance, cannot tell them apart. What still differs is how each player moves, and when. We study same-instrument per-player separation: a user clicks one musician in a video and receives that musician's sound alone, even when other players in the video play the same instrument. Our model follows the clicked player and describes them with high level video features and the velocities of body and hand keypoints. A pretrained music separator attends to these tokens through cross-attention. Earlier motion-based separators were scored only on synthetic mixtures of solo videos. We give the first per-player evaluation of same-instrument separation on real ensemble recordings. On 58 players in URMP, each sharing an instrument with at least one other player in the piece, our model reaches a median SDR of 5.3 dB, while four released separators, audio-only and audio-visual, stay at or below 0.3 dB. The gap is wider on same-instrument duets, and our model also beats the audio-visual baselines on their own MUSIC benchmark. Tests show that the gain comes from movement: replacing the video with a still frame removes it, and so does shifting the video by a fraction of a second against the audio.
authors: Abhinaba Roy, Ambuj Mehrish, Sebastiano Vascon, Dorien Herremans
bullets: Targets per-player separation when appearance and audio cues cannot distinguish musicians playing the same instrument.
Uses high-level visual features and body/hand keypoint velocities from the clicked player.
Feeds these motion-aware tokens via cross-attention into a pretrained music separator.
On 58 same-instrument players in URMP, it achieves a median SDR of 5.3 dB versus at most 0.3 dB for four released baselines.
Ablations show the improvement depends on synchronized movement, not static appearance; it also outperforms audio-visual baselines on MUSIC.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses same-instrument music separation from video using motion keypoints. This contributes to audio-visual multimodal models and action understanding in video.

papers.abstract: The domain of genomic language models (gLMs) has advanced rapidly, with models pretrained on diverse multi-species genomic corpora demonstrating their remarkable capabilities. While the effect of simple nucleotide-level tokenization on long-context modeling is well established, overlapping k-mer tokenization remains underexplored in causal pretraining, despite its rich neighborhood information. Here, we thoroughly revisit overlapping tokenization and introduce HGDNA, a hybrid linear-attention gLM with causal language modeling (CLM) pretraining and a shared token-prediction interface for downstream adaptation, using a species-classification auxiliary task and shared class tokens. HGDNA delivers competitive performance across sequence classification and frozen-embedding evaluations, supporting both short-range and long-range tasks with 30M parameters and 19B pretraining tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/Sophie10001b/HGDNA
authors: Xudong Wang, Siwei Cheng, Haozhe Hu
bullets: Addresses the limited study of overlapping k-mers for causal genomic pretraining, motivated by their richer neighborhood information.
Uses a hybrid linear-attention architecture pretrained with causal language modeling and a shared token-prediction interface for downstream adaptation.
Adds a species-classification auxiliary task with shared class tokens.
Achieves competitive results on sequence-classification and frozen-embedding evaluations spanning short- and long-range tasks.
The abstract reports a 30M-parameter model trained on 19B genomic tokens; broader generalization beyond the evaluated tasks is not specified.

Bottom: causal pretraining jointly learns sequence continuation and species-class token prediction, while downstream adaptation uses soft prompts for conditional generation and class-token prediction for classification.

Fig. 3. Ablation studies on tokenization, pretraining objectives, backbone selection, training corpus, auxiliary-task transfer, and other microdesign choices on the GUE benchmark. All models have 30M parameters and use 60% of the standard HGDNA pretraining budget.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a hybrid linear-attention genomic language model, directly relevant to efficient attention mechanisms.
papers.title: HGDNA: Overlapping k-mer Tokenization for Efficient Autoregressive Genomic Language Models
papers.tldr: HGDNA revisits overlapping k-mer tokenization in causal genomic language models and combines it with hybrid linear attention for efficient, versatile sequence modeling.

papers.abstract: Speech large language models are usually evaluated on questions that have answers. We ask what they do when a recording establishes none, and whether the standard way of finding out is sound. Diagnosed on synthesized speech the answer looks clear: Qwen2-Audio fabricates an answer to 92.5% of unanswerable questions, while an ASR cascade reading the same recordings reaches 2.5% hallucination at 6.7% over-refusal, placing the failure in reasoning rather than in perception. The identical protocol on 376 native SQuAD 2.0 questions over human-read recordings removes that conclusion: the cascade hallucinates on 67.7% against the end-to-end model's 69.8%, at a higher over-refusal cost. A paired subset asking the same questions of a synthesized and a human recording of each passage localises the effect in the ASR stage -- the end-to-end model's abstention behaviour does not move with the speaker, the cascade's goes from 11.1% to 65.9%. Reliance on synthesized speech has been named as a limitation of audio benchmarks but not quantified; we quantify it, and show it large enough to reverse a finding. Since no prompt we tested repairs the residual failure, we transfer pre-generation attention probing to the multimodal setting. A probe over frozen prompt representations reaches 0.773 AUROC at predicting which unanswerable questions the model will answer anyway, where semantic entropy over ten sampled generations is at chance: the model fabricates the same answer every time, so sample disagreement cannot see a failure it is confident about.
authors: Vladislav Nesterenko, Polina Doronicheva, Olga Golubeva, Polina Sheviakova
bullets: Qwen2-Audio fabricated answers to 92.5% of unanswerable questions on synthesized speech, while an ASR cascade hallucinated on 2.5% with 6.7% over-refusal.
On human-read recordings, the cascade hallucinated on 67.7% of questions versus 69.8% for the end-to-end model, reversing the synthesized-speech diagnosis.

A paired comparison localised the speaker-dependent effect to the ASR stage: cascade abstention changed from 11.1% on synthesized speech to 65.9% on human speech, while the end-to-end model remained stable.
Prompting did not repair the residual failure; a probe over frozen prompt representations predicted problematic answers with 0.773 AUROC.
Semantic entropy over ten sampled generations was at chance because the model repeatedly produced the same confident fabrication.

papers.selection_reason: Studies speech LLMs (multimodal) and proposes probing mitigation for hallucination.
papers.title: Can Speech LLMs Recognize When Audio Evidence Is Insufficient? A Diagnostic Study and a Pre-Generation Probing Mitigation
papers.tldr: Speech LLMs often answer confidently when audio evidence is insufficient, and synthesized speech can substantially distort diagnosis; pre-generation probing offers a promising mitigation.

papers.abstract: Understanding a scene requires both geometry and semantics: geometry recovers its spatial structure, and semantics separates it into objects. Current models obtain the two from separate networks or separate passes. We present PINE, a one-step Omni Diffusion Transformer that predicts the point map, the surface normals, and the instance map of an image in one forward pass. PINE treats each map as a token stream, and a stream mask decides which streams interact. A camera-aware ray encoding positions every token by its camera ray rather than its pixel. Grounding attention adds the affinity of pretrained DINOv3 features to the attention logits. Trained on only 139K synthetic images for geometry, PINE achieves state-of-the-art point maps whether or not intrinsics are given and the best average rank on surface normals. It also exceeds SAM on large objects with less than 1 percent of its training images, and it predicts all three maps 5.7x faster than MoGe-3 with SAM.
authors: Zeyu Ren, Jie Ni, Rui Qian, Jiahao Wei, Hao Tang, Yongtai Liu, Zeyu Zhang
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of estimating geometry and semantics with separate networks or passes.
Uses an Omni Diffusion Transformer with separate token streams for point maps, surface normals, and instance maps.
Employs stream-masked interactions, camera-ray token encoding, and DINOv3-based grounding attention.
Trained on 139K synthetic geometry images, it achieves state-of-the-art point maps and the best average rank for surface normals.
Outperforms SAM on large objects and predicts all three maps 5.7× faster than MoGe-3 with SAM.

papers.selection_reason: Generalist one-step model jointly predicting point maps, normals, and instance maps qualifies as a broad 3D perception foundation model.
papers.title: PINE: Point, Instance and Normal Estimation in One-Step Diffusion Model
papers.tldr: PINE jointly predicts scene geometry and object instances in one diffusion-model forward pass, achieving strong accuracy with substantially faster inference.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models typically use flow-based generative modeling to learn a rich, often multimodal, distribution of robot actions. Generating samples from flow-based methods involves iteratively updating random noise, and distinct noise samples from the same state can result in distinct trajectories and task outcomes. Existing test-time scaling methods improve action chunk generation via selection, aggregation, or correction, but commonly require the generation of large ensembles of candidates or the training of an external corrector. We adapt Predict-and-Perturb (P&P), a self-refinement procedure for flow-based models originally used for mode-seeking in video generation, to the robotics domain. We find that applying P&P to VLA models requires modifications to the refinement process used in video generation due to differences in the underlying structure of the data. Across 400 episodes of LIBERO evaluated using SmolVLA, P&P improves upon the stock baseline by 5.3 percentage points. Further, episode-level P\&P uncertainty correlates strongly with task failure (AUC 0.851).
authors: Jeff Duan, Arjun Sharma, Jennifer Cruden, Vansh Tibrewal
bullets: Flow-based VLA models can produce different action trajectories from different noise samples, leading to variable outcomes.
The work adapts Predict-and-Perturb (P&P), a self-refinement method originally developed for video generation, to robot action sampling.
P&P requires robotics-specific changes because action data differ structurally from video data.
On 400 LIBERO episodes with SmolVLA, P&P improves the stock baseline by 5.3 percentage points.
Episode-level P&P uncertainty correlates strongly with task failure, with AUC 0.851.

Top left: a schematic of the P&P refinement process, where a sample z (0) s is at an intermediate integration step . Top right: an example of stock sampling from the policy demonstrating unstable behavior for a task, resulting in failure, while P&P-based refinement improves the stability of generated actions and ultimately enables a successful rollout. Bottom: our P&P-based aggregation strategy more effectively leverages additional test-time computation than naively reducing the execution horizon with the stock policy or utilizing the original refinement technique [1].

papers.selection_reason: Self-refinement of flow-based VLA action sampling at test time for robot manipulation.
papers.title: Self-Refining VLA Sampling
papers.tldr: Self-refining flow-based VLA sampling improves robot task success without large candidate ensembles and provides an uncertainty signal linked to failure.

papers.abstract: World models support robotic manipulation by predicting how the scene evolves under a planned action. For garments this prediction is notoriously difficult: deformations are complex, and self-occlusion leaves much of the cloth unobserved. Planned gripper trajectories provide a useful motion prior because cloth held by a gripper moves with it, while the remaining deformation must be predicted. We introduce ClothCast, a world model that applies this prior to the cloth's points and learns the residual motion. ClothCast takes one RGB-D observation, the camera pose, the robot's own model and the planned gripper trajectories, with no cloth mesh or material parameters. It lifts the observation to a layered point set that includes hypothesized occluded layers, carries the points with a blended rigid prior derived from the gripper poses, and predicts the residual motion with a video-diffusion point-flow model. Over entire 4- to 11-second episodes at 10 Hz, the moved points are rendered into depth, from which a geometry-conditioned completion model synthesizes RGB; after release, a hand-designed settling step replaces the learned motion. We further release ClothCastBench, 10,000 simulated dual-arm cloth-manipulation episodes with the ground-truth cloth mesh, including occluded layers, at every frame. On 492 held-out episodes, ClothCast achieves 2.5x lower sequence-averaged visible-surface Chamfer distance than Flex-{\pi}, the strongest baseline in geometry (14.0 mm vs. 35.6 mm), and 3.7 dB higher cloth-region PSNR than Cosmos-Predict2.5, the strongest baseline in cloth PSNR. On a 50-episode ablation subset, the rigid prior alone, applied to ClothCast's learned initial geometry with the same post-processing, already outperforms both geometry-capable baselines, and the learned residual lowers its error by about a third.
authors: Yushen Hu, Yilong Song, Zhen Zhou, Apurv Kushwaha, Harshvardhan Chandirasekar, Zhu-Tian Chen
bullets: Addresses cloth world modeling from a single RGB-D observation despite complex deformation and self-occlusion.
Uses camera pose, robot model, and planned gripper trajectories without requiring a cloth mesh or material parameters.
Lifts observations into layered point sets, applies a blended gripper-motion prior, and predicts residual motion with a video-diffusion point-flow model.
ClothCastBench provides 10,000 simulated dual-arm cloth-manipulation episodes with ground-truth meshes and occluded layers.

On 492 held-out episodes, it reports 14.0 mm visible-surface Chamfer distance and higher cloth-region PSNR than the cited baselines; a rigid prior alone already outperforms geometry-capable baselines, while residual learning further reduces error.

papers.title: ClothCast: Generative Cloth World Modeling under Partial Observability
papers.tldr: ClothCast predicts garment motion under occlusion by combining gripper-driven rigid motion priors with learned residual deformation.

papers.abstract: Clinical trials are costly and often take years to complete, making early outcome prediction valuable for trial planning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to forecast clinical-trial outcomes, yet their predictions remain unreliable and their rationales may not faithfully reflect the evidence underlying their answers. On tasks such as predicting whether a registered clinical trial will complete or terminate early, frontier LLMs perform only modestly above chance in our experiments. We introduce SAE-Audit, which optimizes a black-box LLM at inference time with evidence obtained from a deployable open model. A frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is converted into a vocabulary of clinical concepts. Sparse probes fitted on past trials determine which concepts are associated with the outcome. For a new protocol, the concepts detected by the probe are written as evidence, each with the direction and strength of its association with the outcome, and the LLM being audited optimizes its answer in the light of this evidence. Without additional training, SAE-Audit raises balanced accuracy of deepseek-v4-flash by 9.6--12.0 points on five clinical-trial prediction tasks and raises GPT-5.6-terra by 8.0 points on trial completion, exceeding other agentic inference-time optimization methods by a large margin. As an auxiliary, SAE probes module within SAE-Audit is itself accurate and auditable, providing natural-language explanations directly derived from verified concept contributions and protocol evidence, without requiring additional LLMs at inference time. SAE-Audit provides verifiable, concept-level evidence for more accurate and auditable clinical-trial prediction. It can also be embedded into biomedical AI agents such as Biomni to optimize their performance.
authors: Junbo Shen
bullets: Clinical-trial outcome predictions by frontier LLMs are unreliable and only modestly above chance in the reported tasks.
A frozen SAE on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is used to identify clinical concepts, while sparse probes estimate each concept’s association with trial outcomes.
For each new protocol, the system provides concept evidence with outcome direction and strength, which the audited LLM uses to revise its prediction.
The method improves balanced accuracy by 9.6–12.0 points for deepseek-v4-flash across five tasks and by 8.0 points for GPT-5.6-terra on trial completion.
The probe module also produces auditable natural-language explanations directly from verified concept contributions, without an additional inference-time LLM.

papers.title: SAE-Audit: Clinical-Trial Prediction via Inference-Time Optimization of Black-Box LLMs Audited by Sparse Autoencoder Evidence
papers.tldr: SAE-Audit improves black-box LLM predictions of clinical-trial outcomes at inference time by supplying auditable, concept-level evidence derived from sparse autoencoders.

papers.abstract: Current MLLM methods largely focus on whether models attend to the right visual regions, implicitly treating spatial attention map as the primary key of effective visual perception. To examine this assumption, we introduce a medical VQA dataset with paired non-contrast (NC) and contrast-enhanced (CE) images that share corresponding anatomy while providing different cues. We show that this view is incomplete: across paired NC and CE medical images, MLLMs often exhibit similar attention patterns despite producing contrasting answers, while controlled bidirectional interventions induce substantially larger prediction changes on visual values than attention weights. These results identify the visual content retrieved through values as a critical factor in improving perception beyond spatial attention alone. Guided by this finding, we propose VIVID (VIsual Value Intervention Distillation), which uses enhanced visual values to identify and refine teacher corrections aligned with useful visual evidence to improve on-policy distillation from CE to NC images. Across six internal and external test sets, VIVID consistently outperforms existing on-policy distillation methods across different model scales and architectures, requires only NC images at inference, and maintains strong zero-shot performance on general-domain VQA benchmarks. The project page is available at https://qiuzyc.github.io/VIVID.
authors: Yichen Zhao, Fenghe Tang, Wenxin Ma, Rongsheng Wang, Zihao Wan, Shaohua Kevin Zhou
bullets: Paired non-contrast and contrast-enhanced medical images reveal that similar attention patterns can produce different answers.
Bidirectional interventions show visual values affect predictions more than attention weights.
VIVID uses enhanced visual values to select and refine teacher corrections for on-policy distillation from contrast-enhanced to non-contrast images.
It consistently improves over existing on-policy distillation methods across six internal and external test sets, model scales, and architectures.
VIVID uses only non-contrast images at inference and retains strong zero-shot general-domain VQA performance.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes VIVID to improve medical MLLMs by focusing on 'visual values' rather than just attention maps, offering a novel perspective on multimodal perception.
papers.title: Beyond Attention Maps: Understanding and Improving Medical MLLMs via Visual Values
papers.tldr: Visual values, not attention maps alone, are crucial for medical MLLM perception, motivating VIVID to improve non-contrast image understanding through value-guided distillation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models have become a new kind of describer, writing about almost anything people see, and their descriptions now shape how cultures are known by people and by other models. Descriptions of cultures tend to turn particular things into types, and what a description loses shows what its describer lacks. We introduce Polytropos, a benchmark that measures what model descriptions of cultural objects keep of the particular object by turning each description back into an image and comparing it with the original photograph. On 374 objects from the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Getty, with 1,870 descriptions from five models and 230 written by curators, reconstructions are recognised as the recorded culture more often than the photographs, at 54.55% to 59.09% against 52.14%, yet 16% to 21% of objects change outcome and only 0.49% of reconstructions are identified as the specific object. On the same objects, models lose recorded cultures at a rate similar to curators but gain more. Model descriptions give each object many faces, each typical of its culture and almost none the object itself.
authors: Yuechen Jiang, Enze Zhang, Yuyan Wang, Mohsinul Kabir, Chenying Lin, Sijia Li, Qianqian Xie, Stavroula Golfomitsou, Konstantinos Arvanitis, Sophia Ananiadou

papers.selection_reason: Investigates how VLMs describe cultural objects and reconstruct them, providing insights into the fidelity of multimodal descriptions.
papers.title: Polytropos: What Do Vision-Language Model Descriptions Make of a Cultural Object?
papers.tldr: Polytropos shows that vision-language model descriptions often preserve an object’s cultural type better than its specific visual identity, giving artifacts many culturally typical but object-inaccurate “faces.”

papers.abstract: Deep learning has shown promise for estimating human pose with multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) radar through walls. Building paired radar and pose datasets demands considerable time and manual effort, while large visual pose datasets provide no corresponding radar echoes. Physical simulation can supply synthetic signals, but requires expertise in scattering models and can leave a gap between simulated and real data. To address this challenge, we introduce MIMORPHEUS, a framework that generates radar echoes from 3D human poses through conditional diffusion. To prepare echo and pose representations, MIMO-VAE compresses the echoes according to their channel and fast time sample structure, while SkeleCoder learns pose features through contrastive alignment with echo features. These pose features then guide diffusion in the MIMO-VAE latent space, and the VAE decoder reconstructs echoes from the generated latents. Once trained, the generator augments radar data by producing different echoes for a recorded pose and supplies the radar modality for pose annotations in existing visual datasets. In data augmentation experiments, our method reduces MPJPE by 6.8%-11.2% across four radar pose estimators. Transfer experiments with three public pose datasets also show that visual pose annotations can supply useful radar training data. Code will be made publicly available on GitHub.
authors: Shizhao Zhang, Yanyan Zhang, Deshui Yu, Jun Pan, Guangyou Fang
bullets: Addresses the cost of collecting paired radar–pose data and the simulation-to-real gap.
Compresses radar echoes with MIMO-VAE and learns pose features via contrastive alignment in SkeleCoder.
Generates radar echoes conditioned on 3D poses through diffusion in the VAE latent space.
Augmentation reduces MPJPE by 6.8%–11.2% across four radar pose estimators.
Transfer experiments indicate that visual pose annotations can provide useful radar training data.

figures.caption: Figure 1. MIMORPHEUS generates complex echoes from poses and random noise. The generated pairs support pose estimation directly from echoes or after radar imaging. The framework provides a new strategy for radar data augmentation and a potential route for cross-modal data transfer.

Figure 5. Echo generation and downstream pose estimation examples. (a,b) Measured and generated echo amplitudes, with fast-time indices horizontally and MIMO channels vertically. (c) Skeletons predicted by the corresponding estimators, overlaid on 3D BP reconstructions of the generated echoes.

Figure 4. Conditional 1D latent generation. Training latents come from the frozen MIMO-VAE mean, followed by scaling and noise addition. SkeleCoder joint and geometry features are concatenated before conditioning. FiLM modulates features at every scale, while radar queries read the condition tokens through cross-attention at the coarser encoder scales. Diffusion generates a latent that the frozen MIMO-VAE decoder converts to complex echoes.

Figure 3. Skeleton–radar alignment with SkeleCoder. SkeleCoder retains joint order during skeleton aggregation, while a learned query reads radar fast-time tokens derived from the frozen MIMOVAE posterior mean. The loss aligns global features from the two modalities. The full joint tokens remain available for diffusion conditioning.

papers.abstract: Latent reasoning lets Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models deliberate at a fraction of the cost of explicit chain-of-thought, increasingly through visual foresight, which we show to be indispensable for predicting actions. Yet this paradigm is inherited from Vision-Language Models, where it serves understanding rather than action: each latent is aligned with an isolated future frame, often enriched with further modalities of that frame. We find that this binds the policy to the appearance of its training scenes, so that it degrades sharply once the scene changes. We argue that visual latents for action should capture not what a future frame looks like, but how the scene evolves toward the goal. We therefore propose Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning, which redirects visual latents from the whole frame to the interaction that the action must bring about. Semantic latents, following the stages of embodied chain-of-thought, first establish what to accomplish and how. Conditioned on them, motion-oriented latents anticipate each future step from coarse to fine: from the global scene, to the interaction region spanned by the manipulated object and its destination, to the robot state. Relative to the state-of-the-art latent VLA LaST$_0$, our method raises the mean success rate on SimplerEnv-WidowX from 37.5% to 55.2% in distribution and from 22.4% to 30.2% under out-of-distribution shifts, and on an AgileX Piper dual-arm platform from 60.8% to 90.8% in training scenes and from 6.7% to 37.5% under environmental changes.
authors: Xin Zhang, Yushuo Hou, Anqi Zhao, Moyun Liu, Xingwei Zhao, Bo Tao, Jiawei Du, Joey Tianyi Zhou
bullets: Visual foresight is important for action prediction, but frame-aligned latents overfit to training-scene appearance.
The method separates semantic latents, which determine what and how to accomplish, from motion-oriented latents that predict future interactions.
Motion reasoning progresses from the global scene to the object–destination interaction region and then to the robot state.
Compared with LaST₀, it improves success across simulated and real dual-arm settings, including out-of-distribution environments.
The approach targets scene-change robustness; its scope is demonstrated on the reported SimplerEnv-WidowX and AgileX Piper tasks.

papers.abstract: Recently, GPT-6 Astra demonstrates strong generalization in robot control, yet limited disclosure of its training leaves open how such capabilities can be reproduced. We introduce nanoAstra, an approach to training vision-language models (VLMs) for generalizable manipulation that combines semantic action modeling with capability-preserving supervised fine-tuning (CP-SFT). nanoAstra represents robot behavior as semantic steps composed of reusable, parameterized action primitives, guided by explicit progress descriptions. Meanwhile, CP-SFT uses an explicit robot-specific system prompt to constrain manipulation outputs to a structured action space, aiming to focus adaptation on robot-specific contexts and promote specialization while minimizing interference with broader pretrained capabilities. With this formulation, we train nanoAstra on more than 5,000 hours of robot data together with general VQA data. On RoboTwin 2.0's randomized benchmark, nanoAstra-9B achieves a 17.8% zero-shot success rate, substantially outperforming advanced VLA and WAM baselines as well as similarly sized VLMs. With inference faster than the corresponding motion execution on a single H20 GPU, our model supports action-chunk-like streaming execution that overlaps inference with motion, reducing the robot's idle time from 35.0% to 6.9%.

Trained with over 5,000 hours of robot data plus general VQA data; nanoAstra-9B reaches 17.8% zero-shot success on RoboTwin 2.0’s randomized benchmark.
Streaming inference overlaps computation with motion, reducing robot idle time from 35.0% to 6.9% on a single H20 GPU.

papers.abstract: Prompt learning provides a parameter-efficient way to adapt pretrained vision--language models through text and visual prompts, but noisy labels prevalent in real-world data inevitably bias prompt updates and thereby undermine adaptation effectiveness. Prior work on robust prompt learning focuses on suppressing unreliable updates under noisy supervision. We uncover a pivotal yet overlooked aspect--prompt allocation: shifting the parameter budget between text and visual prompts can substantially enhance robustness while keeping the training objective and total budget fixed. However, suitable prompt allocations vary across tasks and are unknown a priori, rendering brute-force candidate training computationally prohibitive. We propose GPrompt, a training-free method that derives allocation between text and visual prompts using only loss gradients at initialization before prompt optimization. Using a small sample of images and generated pseudo-labels as shared supervision, GPrompt performs an initialization probe to extract paired text and visual loss gradients, and characterizes the geometry of their trace-normalized Gram matrices through both concentration within each modality and overlap between modalities. GPrompt then derives a closed-form allocation, and projects it onto feasible prompt counts under the exact parameter budget, enabling task-specific selection without training candidate configurations. Experiments across eleven datasets show that GPrompt outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 7.75% while selecting configurations close to the best allocation identified through exhaustive training. The average runtime of gradient probe across datasets is 99.9% lower than that of exhaustive candidate training.
authors: Jiazhe Zhang, Zibin Geng, Qiang Ma, Xuefeng Jiang, Yijun Lin, Jingyi Wang, Yu Yan, Xingzhou Zhang, Min Liu, Yuwei Wang, Sheng Sun
bullets: Prompt allocation between text and visual prompts strongly affects robustness under noisy labels, but the best split is task-dependent.

papers.abstract: Experimental platforms that enable multiple participants to engage in spoken dialogue and perform physical actions concurrently in a shared environment are important for studying cooperation between humans and embodied AI agents. In this paper, we propose EMIP (Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform), a virtual environment platform built on Minecraft. Through an Internet-based client-server architecture, EMIP connects multiple humans and multiple AI agents to the same virtual environment and supports full-duplex speech communication and simultaneous physical interaction. It provides interfaces based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for environmental observation, physical action execution, and audio input and output, enabling researchers to develop their own agent control methods using large language models (LLMs). Additional features include centralized control of an agent group through a single EMIP agent client, collaborative object transportation by multiple agents, and experimental support functions such as recording and retrieving observation histories. By integrating these features into a reusable platform, EMIP aims to support research on human-human, human-agent, and agent-agent cooperation under different participant configurations and agent control methods. Usage examples illustrate concurrent speech and physical action, task coordination, and overlapping speech. The source code for the platform is publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/AI-Humans-Lab/EMIP-Embodied-Multi-Party-Interaction-Platform).

papers.abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) enables contactless physiological monitoring from facial videos, but facial motion, particularly mouth and jaw movements during cognitive and communicative tasks, can severely degrade signal reconstruction. We present SKIA, a lightweight, mask-guided framework that suppresses motion-prone lower-face regions while preserving physiological cues from the forehead and cheeks. Using the UBFC-rPPG benchmark, we first investigate static lower-face suppression in the classical CHROM pipeline. Static masking improves waveform Pearson correlation from 0.3507 to 0.4166 (p < 0.001) and reduces heart-rate mean absolute error (MAE) from 33.50 to 23.44 bpm. Building on this finding, we introduce SKIA-Net, a compact spatiotemporal architecture that combines raw facial frames, statically masked representations, and temporal motion differences to reconstruct blood volume pulse (BVP) waveforms. The full model achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.7522 and a heart-rate MAE of 3.73 bpm on UBFC-rPPG, outperforming single-stream variants. Ablation studies show that the static mask provides complementary information to raw appearance and that static anatomical priors outperform the tested dynamic optical-flow-based masking strategy. These results suggest that spatially informed, temporally stable masking can improve motion-robust rPPG estimation. Code: https://github.com/lee-vtruong/SKIA-rPPG
authors: Van-Truong Le, Viet-Tham Huynh, Minh-Triet Tran

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning can reduce the inference cost of vision language models, but its effectiveness depends on preserving complementary visual information under a limited token budget. A central challenge is to quantify the additional information a candidate token contributes beyond the retained set, a contribution that conventional scores based on attention or similarity struggle to capture directly. In this work, we revisit visual token pruning from the perspective of information gain and use mutual information to characterize the incremental value of candidate tokens. We further establish theoretically that frame potential serves as an effective surrogate for mutual information. Building on this observation, we propose FP-Prune, a training-free visual token pruning method that iteratively removes tokens with low information gain to preserve as much complementary visual information as possible. Experiments on three widely used VLMs and eight datasets demonstrate that FP-Prune outperforms baseline methods in both accuracy and inference efficiency. Further analysis shows that the surrogate objective closely aligns with model performance. Our work provides theoretical grounding and an effective method for visual token pruning.
authors: Haozhe Zhao, Junxiang Zhang, Junxin Wang, Yuan Ge, Xiangchen Song, Dingyang Zhang, JingBo Zhu, Tong Xiao
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of measuring a candidate token’s additional information beyond retained tokens.

papers.abstract: Cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) aims to locate an object indicated by a click point in a ground or drone query image within a satellite reference image. Through a quantitative prompt-sensitivity evaluation, we find that existing CVOGL methods suffer from a prompt-disobeying overfitting problem: when the click point is moved or removed, their predictions barely respond, indicating that the models rely on spurious feature correlations rather than genuinely following the prompt semantics. We trace this behavior to the limited scale of the benchmark dataset, which contains only 4,343 prompt-object pairs per task, so that the models simply memorize the object associated with each scene instead of learning the true prompt-to-object correspondence. To address this, we propose two plug-and-play components. First, we construct the CVOGL-MO dataset by expanding the existing training and test sets with diverse multi-object annotations, mitigating the memorization that induces shortcut learning. Second, we propose the Cross-View Co-Scene Multi-Object Contrastive Loss (CVMCL), which enforces distinct feature representations for different click points within the same scene, compelling the model to follow prompt instructions. We further design a prompt-sensitivity evaluation protocol with prediction-shift metrics, providing the first quantitative measurement of prompt-following capability for CVOGL. Both components are architecture-agnostic and can be integrated into existing methods without any architectural modification. Experiments on three representative backbones show that our components substantially improve prompt-following accuracy on the new multi-object test sets and markedly increase prompt sensitivity. Our dataset and code will be publicly released at https://github.com/Sunny-Fresher/CVOGL-MO.

papers.abstract: Unifying visual understanding and generation requires representations that preserve both semantic information and fine-grained image details. Continuous tokenizers trained primarily for semantic alignment may omit fine-grained reconstruction details, whereas discrete tokenizers face information loss from codebook quantization. Conventional multi-codebook designs assign every token the same number of codewords regardless of local content. We instead view codewords as reusable visual primitives whose allocation and composition adapt to each token. We introduce PrimiTok, a compositional visual tokenizer that represents each visual token through adaptive allocation and weighted composition of learned codebook primitives. PrimiTok integrates two complementary components: Diverse Quantitative Primitives (DQP), which encourages diversity among sub-codebook centroids to reduce redundancy, and a Dynamic Primitive Allocator (DPA), which selects primitives according to token complexity. Embedding quantization error supervises how many primitives are selected from each sub-codebook, and DPA aggregates them with input-dependent weights. Joint reconstruction and image--text contrastive learning encourage the resulting representations to retain visual fidelity and semantic alignment. Experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction and semantic alignment over SOTA baselines, with further evaluations on multimodal understanding and visual generation.
authors: Yizhu Chen, Chen Ju, Donghao Zhou, Ziyu Guo, Shuai Xiao, Jinsong Lan, Xiaoyong Zhu, Ying Chen, Haodong Li
bullets: Addresses information loss and detail omission in existing continuous, discrete, and fixed multi-codebook tokenizers.
Uses Diverse Quantitative Primitives (DQP) to reduce redundancy among sub-codebook centroids.
Employs a Dynamic Primitive Allocator (DPA) to select and weight primitives based on each token’s complexity.
Trains with quantization-error supervision, image reconstruction, and image–text contrastive objectives.
Reports improved reconstruction and semantic alignment over state-of-the-art baselines, with evaluations in multimodal understanding and visual generation.

papers.abstract: Today's MLLMs can count objects in natural images. However, when asking them how many bolt holes appear in a mechanical drawing or how many nitrogen atoms are in a chemical structure, they often struggle. Counting in technical drawings remains challenging, as objects can be small, densely packed, or even implied by drawing conventions. To study this problem, we introduce CountDrawBench, a benchmark including floor plans, electrical schematics, mechanical drawings, and molecular structures, with 1,574 counting questions and instance-level annotations where available. Besides evaluation, we introduce Code-Verified RL, a reinforcement learning framework that teaches MLLMs to count with executable feedback. Our method combines three complementary rewards: a count reward that checks the final answer, an instance-matching reward that verifies object locations, and a zoom-based reward that checks counting consistency across local image regions. All three are integrated into a unified GRPO objective. Extensive experiments reveal that even leading MLLMs struggle on CountDrawBench, with the best evaluated model achieving only 59.3% accuracy. Our method improves Qwen3.5-9B from 49.3% to 54.3% accuracy, outperforming all evaluated open-source baselines. These results establish CountDrawBench as a challenging testbed for technical drawing understanding and demonstrate the value of code-verified rewards in these tasks. Code and data will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Junxian Li, Ruixuan Yang, Zhenhua Xu
bullets: Introduces 1,574 counting questions across floor plans, electrical schematics, mechanical drawings, and molecular structures, with instance-level annotations where available.
Proposes Code-Verified RL with count, instance-matching, and zoom-consistency rewards combined in a unified GRPO objective.
Leading evaluated MLLMs achieve only 59.3% accuracy, showing that technical-drawing counting remains difficult.
Improves Qwen3.5-9B from 49.3% to 54.3% accuracy, outperforming evaluated open-source baselines.
Scope: focuses on counting objects that may be small, densely packed, or implied by technical drawing conventions.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents improve by retaining feedback as reusable memories or skills, but every mistaken approval can shape many future behaviors. Two updates can provide exactly the same evidence to a verifier yet produce opposite safety outcomes, so the verifier cannot distinguish them from that evidence alone. We introduce DoppelVet, a verification framework that checks proposed updates before they enter an agent's persistent state. Without access to safety labels, DoppelVet constructs an alternative that matches every signal used by the existing verifier. It replays both updates from the same state and directly compares their behaviors in both presentation orders before deciding whether to retain the candidate. We evaluate DoppelVet on DoppelVet-Grid and DoppelVet-Tool, covering executable programs and natural-language memories. Across nine open-weight and proprietary verifiers, DoppelVet raises mean harmful-update detection AUC from 0.762 to 0.940 on DoppelVet-Grid and from 0.681 to 0.826 on DoppelVet-Tool, outperforming VaG and AgentDoG 1.5. On DoppelVet-Grid, it reduces trajectories experiencing degradation from 30.39% to 0.43% over a ten-generation self-update loop and leaves no final degradation.
authors: Yifan Duan, Du Yin, Siyuan Zheng, Chao Xue, Lihuan Li, Flora D. Salim

papers.abstract: Clinical computed tomography (CT) interpretation inherently requires progressive visual exploration, where radiologists navigate from whole scans to individual slices and regions of interest and interact with external tools when necessary. However, existing 3D medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) typically connect a specialized 3D visual encoder to a language model, without fully leveraging the native 2D visual and agentic capabilities of generalist MLLMs. Trained on large-scale one-hop CT instruction-following data, these models also have limited ability to perform iterative reasoning and explicitly ground their conclusions in visual evidence, limiting their support for traceable CT interpretation. To solve these problems, we propose \textbf{agentic perception} as an alternative paradigm inspired by radiologists' interpretation workflows. We introduce \textbf{CT-Navigator}, a framework that harnesses generalist MLLMs' 2D visual and agentic capabilities to progressively ground CT interpretation in explicit, traceable visual evidence through hierarchical visual exploration and radiology tool invocation. To build these capabilities, we curate 8,904 visual chain-of-thought (V-CoT) trajectories for cold-start agentic supervised fine-tuning. We then optimize the policy through reinforcement learning on 33,219 questions, with data selection and dynamic rollout sampling prioritizing informative learning signals. Finally, we introduce CTNavi-Bench, a 3D CT visual question answering benchmark comprising 7,000 questions spanning anatomical regions throughout the human body. CT-Navigator achieves 79.50\% accuracy on CTNavi-Bench, surpassing the strongest baseline by 17.59\%, and demonstrates strong generalization across three external CT benchmarks. The code, model, and benchmark will be released on \href{https://github.com/fyb99/ct_navigator}{GitHub}.
authors: Yibing Fu, Huidong Xie, Yihao Niu, Wei Ji, Heming Dong, Ziyue Wang, Jingyu Chen, Jun Zhao, Haoyuan Hu, Hongming Shan, Lai Jiang, Mai Xu, Yueming Jin

papers.abstract: Cooperative perception with roadside LiDARs (RSLs) extends the sensing range of autonomous vehicles and resolves onboard-sensor occlusions, particularly at curves and intersections. Because infrastructure deployment is costly, existing work optimizes RSL configurations once, against road geometry and aggregated traffic statistics, and treats them as fixed thereafter. Traffic flow, however, is inherently dynamic, and a placement optimal on average can be far from optimal at any given moment. We introduce RSLaA (Roadside LiDARs as Agents), a framework in which each RSL adaptively adjusts its pose to the evolving traffic scene over decision-time windows. Since ground truth is unavailable at decision time, the framework centers on surrogate metrics computed solely from a probabilistic occupancy grid of historical observations, which predicts the next-window perception performance of candidate poses. We construct a co-simulation benchmark pairing five candidate surrogates with detector-agnostic ground-truth perception labels at every decision window, identifying the multi-view coverage metric J_mv as the most reliable predictor. Upon this validated surrogate we build two adaptive configuration methods, a receding-horizon (MPC) optimizer and a lightweight MAPPO-based multi-agent reinforcement learning scheme with centralized training and decentralized execution. Across 10 sites and 89 six-hour traffic scenarios (890 evaluation runs), adaptive configuration consistently improves the composite perception score over static deployment. Our results indicate that RSLs could be benefitted from being treated as agents.
authors: Yang Ma, Yichen Sun, Yubing Zheng, Zhongxiang Feng, Zeyang Cheng, Said M. Easa

papers.abstract: Geometry-aware rotary positional encodings, such as RayRoPE, help attention reason about the 3D spatial relationships between tokens and the query camera. However, they implicitly assume a static scene, encoding each key at its observed position regardless of when it was captured. For dynamic scenes with temporally separated input views, this mismatch places the same moving object at a different position in each input frame, so it can be rendered at an inaccurate position. While temporal encodings inform attention when a token was observed, they do not resolve where its content should be at the query time. We introduce a simple and general approach that aligns positional encodings with dynamic scene geometry through Galilean transport. Before positional encoding, each key's 3D position is transported to the query time using its estimated velocity and the temporal offset. By modifying only key positions, our method integrates directly with existing encodings, including RayRoPE and URoPE, without altering their formulations. Velocities can be obtained from arbitrary sources. By default, we estimate them from token correspondences within the network. Integrated into LVSM, our method improves dynamic view synthesis on Syn4D, dynamic Objaverse, and real-world Stereo4D videos over baselines. Ablations show that encoding velocities as token features yields smaller gains, while attention visualizations reveal that our method attends to query-time locations of moving content, unlike RayRoPE. Beyond view synthesis, our method also reduces tracking errors on dynamic objects in a pretrained 3D point tracker and improves moving-vehicle generation in a video generator.
authors: Youngmin Kim, Seonghyun Jin, Jong Chul Ye
bullets: Static geometry-aware positional encodings can misplace moving content when input views were captured at different times.

Integrated into LVSM, it improves dynamic view synthesis across synthetic and real-world benchmarks and also benefits tracking and video generation.
Velocity estimates can come from arbitrary sources; the default uses token correspondences within the network.],

papers.abstract: Long-sequence inference in large language models is constrained by the high cost of prefilling, where dense attention scales quadratically with context length. Exploiting similarity across attention heads offers a way to reduce redundant computation. Prior approaches in this direction have relied on localized query observations to determine head-level computation reuse or budget allocation. However, inter-head similarity does not imply uniform query requirements, leaving adaptation to varying budget needs and selection preferences across query regions a key challenge. We introduce QASparse, a Query-Adaptive Sparse attention mechanism with hardware-efficient execution. QASparse preserves the efficiency of shared cross-head importance estimation while adapting computational budgets and token selections to query requirements, and it executes these dynamic sparse decisions through dedicated kernels. Its query adaptivity stems from two complementary innovations: Local Budget Regression models local variations in computational demand along query positions to estimate budgets for different query regions and attention heads; Boundary Voting lets queries within each head vote over candidates near the selection cutoff using actual query/key scores, refining the retained set while preserving the initial selection size. To reduce the execution overhead of dynamic budgets, we further design length-specialized selection kernels that efficiently support query-adaptive sparse patterns across context lengths. Together, these designs efficiently combine shared estimation with local decisions while adapting both how much attention is computed and which interactions are retained. Experimental results demonstrate improved benchmark scores and faster prefill attention computation compared with existing sparse attention baselines.
authors: Zhiyuan Chen, Zihao Yang, Quanjiang Li, Haijiang Li, Jiancheng Pan, Qichao Zhao, Zihan Dong, Qiushi Shi, Jinshi Liu
bullets: Targets the quadratic cost of dense attention during long-sequence prefill and the limitations of uniform head-level sparsity.
Uses shared cross-head importance estimation, then applies query-specific decisions for computational budgets and token selection.
Local Budget Regression estimates attention budgets across query regions and heads.
Boundary Voting refines tokens near the selection cutoff using actual query–key scores without changing the initial selection size.
Length-specialized kernels reduce the overhead of executing dynamic sparse patterns; experiments report better benchmark scores and faster prefill attention than prior sparse-attention baselines.

papers.abstract: Force and tactile feedback provide essential information about physical interactions in contact-rich manipulation that visual observations alone cannot reliably capture.However, integrating these signals into vision-language-action (VLA) models remains challenging owing to the representational gap between visual-language semantics and physical measurements.To address this challenge, we propose A2I-VLA, a two-stage VLA framework that first learns semantically Aligned force-tactile representations and then Integrates them into a VLA model.In Stage I, a cross-modal alignment loss is introduced to promote correspondence between semantic and physical representations. The tactile and force feature streams are then integrated through a hierarchical multimodal fusion network, and the resulting representations are jointly supervised by future wrench and action prediction losses. The former encourages the model to anticipate physical responses, while the latter associates force-tactile observations with task-relevant manipulation behaviors.In Stage II, a gated cross-attention bridge module adaptively integrates the hierarchical physical features learned in Stage I into the VLA model to guide action generation.Real-world experiments demonstrate that the proposed A2I-VLA significantly outperforms the baseline PI05 across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, improving the success rate from 70% to 95%.
authors: Kun Dai, Tianqi Wang, Haibo Lei, Chaoyang Li, Kai Zhang, Fuyuan Qiu, Lijun Zhao, Ruifeng Li, Chuqing Cao, Tao Xie, Wenming Tan
bullets: Addresses the gap between semantic visual-language features and physical force-tactile measurements.
Uses a two-stage design: semantic-physical alignment and subsequent VLA integration.
Learns hierarchical multimodal physical representations with cross-modal alignment, future wrench prediction, and action prediction.
Employs a gated cross-attention bridge to incorporate physical features into action generation.
Outperforms the PI05 baseline across three real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: World Action Models anticipate visual outcomes to guide robot actions, yet humanoid interaction also depends on how the robot's body responds. Visual foresight alone can miss body motion, while latent-distance losses do not directly supervise action responses. We present $\zeta_0$, a framework that turns vision-language-action policies into World Action Models by foreseeing future visual features and measured joint trajectories in a shared latent representation. During training, a teacher conditioned on recorded futures provides a reference action response, and dual-response transfer trains the causal predictor to match it through the teacher and the executing policy. All components are trained jointly, and deployment uses only causally predicted futures. On seven HumanoidArena tasks, $\zeta_0$ built on $\Psi_0$ and GR00T N1.7 reaches 63.6% and 79.5% mean success, 18.8 and 9.0 points above these bases. On six real-world tasks, it reaches 78.3% and 85.0%, gains of 16.7 and 10.0 points. On GR00T, its 79.5% tops all compared seven-task joint policies. Project page: https://chenyizhi123.github.io/zeta0-project/
authors: Yizhi Chen, Zhanxiang Cao, Yitong Wang, Junyu Liu, Hongchu Zeng, Xinyi Peng, Chuxuan Huang, Yicheng Su, Zihao Zhou, Shengcheng Fu, Haoyang Li, Liyun Yan, Tianyue Zhan, Jianming Ma, Yang Zhang, Keqi Zhu, Xiaxi Si, Jinming Yao, Qiao Sun, Shizeng Zhang, Jiangwei Zhong, Yue Gao
bullets: Addresses the gap between visual foresight and accurate body-response prediction in humanoid interaction.
Transforms vision-language-action policies into World Action Models with shared-latent visual and joint-trajectory foresight.
Uses a future-conditioned teacher and dual-response transfer to train causal predictions without requiring future observations at deployment.
Improves mean success on seven HumanoidArena tasks to 63.6% and 79.5%, and on six real-world tasks to 78.3% and 85.0%, depending on the base policy.
Scope: evaluation covers seven simulated and six real-world humanoid tasks.

papers.abstract: Video world models predict how a scene will evolve, and their sampled futures are increasingly used in place of the real one, from planning to simulation. These uses assume that the samples are aligned with real-world odds, with each future appearing among them as often as it would follow the same history in reality, yet current evaluations only score how real each sample looks. Testing this assumption on real driving data is hard for three reasons. Each recorded history has only one real future, so the true probabilities are unknown. Physical quantities must be read from video, where reading errors can look like model errors. Finally, the many possible analyses invite selective reporting. We introduce DriveOddsBench, a pre-registered benchmark that addresses all three. First, if the samples follow the real distribution, the rank of the real outcome among them is uniform in every history, so pooled ranks test them without probability labels. Second, one validated instrument reads the same quantities, such as the lead-vehicle gap and the ego motion, from the generated futures and from the real future, which first passes through the world model's autoencoder so that both are read alike. Third, all confirmatory analyses were frozen before any test clip was measured. We test eleven general and driving world models on 200 held-out Argoverse 2 histories in five scenario families, with 35,200 generated futures. None is aligned, and every model underestimates its uncertainty. The real outcome falls outside the range of all 16 samples in 28-61% of cases instead of the 11.8% expected under the real distribution. Five models are significantly skewed, in opposite directions, and the largest errors are in the ego motion. Nine models beat climatology without being aligned, and among these models neither type nor scale predicts which comes closest.
authors: Jiaxi Liu, Keshu Wu, Bin Ran, Xiaopeng Li
bullets: Addresses evaluation challenges caused by unknown true probabilities, video measurement error, and selective analysis.
Uses uniform ranks of the real future among sampled futures to test distributional alignment without probability labels.
Applies a shared validated measurement instrument and preregistered, frozen confirmatory analyses.
Evaluates 11 models on 200 held-out Argoverse 2 histories across five scenario families with 35,200 generated futures.
No model is aligned; all underestimate uncertainty, with the real outcome outside 16-sample ranges in 28–61% of cases versus 11.8% expected.

papers.abstract: Continual learning requires a model to learn multiple new tasks sequentially while retaining performance on previous tasks. Projecting model parameters onto the Jacobian null space of previous tasks after unconstrained training on a new task has emerged as an effective paradigm. However, unidirectional projection merely minimizes the parameter distance to the new-task optimum, overlooking the new-task loss landscape. To address this limitation, we propose DUET, a bidirectional projection algorithm that imposes Jacobian null-space constraints from both previous and new tasks during post-training projection. Specifically, DUET formulates the post-training adjustment as a dually constrained optimization problem. It minimizes the distance between parameters before and after training on a new task, subject to loss preserving constraints on both tasks. To solve the optimization problem, we develop an alternating bidirectional projection algorithm, whose convergence is guaranteed by the contraction mapping theorem. For reliable multi-step projection, we rectify existing step size selection criteria via an effective-rank aware formulation, overcoming their failure under rank-deficient Jacobians. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DUET consistently outperforms existing unidirectional projection methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets.
authors: Bowyn Tan, Zhilong Zheng, Yang Guan, Liming Xiao, Liye Tang, Xiao Li, Naizheng Wang, Keqiang Li, Shengbo Eben Li
bullets: Continual learning must acquire sequential tasks without forgetting earlier ones.
Existing unidirectional Jacobian-null-space projection overlooks the new task’s loss landscape.
DUET formulates post-training adjustment as a bidirectionally constrained optimization problem.
An alternating projection algorithm solves the problem, with convergence guaranteed by the contraction mapping theorem.
An effective-rank-aware step-size criterion enables reliable multi-step projection, and experiments report state-of-the-art results across multiple datasets.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models deliberate over multiple answer proposals, often resulting in excessively long traces due to backtracking, even when the correct answer has already been reached (Across three 32B models, ~87% of rollouts contain 1 unique answer yet still make ~8 answer proposals on average). Given this potentially "decorative" chain of thought (CoT) reasoning, can we look to the model internals to determine if the model will backtrack or commit to an answer proposal? Operating under the hypothesis that models maintain an internal representation of their uncertainty, we seek to extract this representation and characterize its relationship with backtracking behavior at answer proposals. By querying the model's verbalized confidence following answer proposals throughout a response trace, we extract a linear direction for latent confidence that separates high and low verbalized confidence. This direction can steer verbalized confidence as expected, but it surprisingly can also steer the next token probability of backtracking, performing on par with a linear direction extracted directly from backtracking examples. We then test the direction under progressively more realistic interventions. Steering continuously from a mid-trace answer proposal modulates response length (~-1.3k - ~+2.5k tokens) and the number of answer proposals (-4.18 - +4.75) in both directions, with minimal cost to accuracy. Applying the confidence direction from the start of generation, where proposal positions are unknown, still shortens traces at comparable accuracy, and its effect surfaces in the linguistic confidence of proposals. Overall, our study reveals the intricate interplay between a model's internal confidence and its proclivity to backtrack or commit to an answer.
authors: Stephen Cheng, Zahra Sodagar, Sandeep Soni, Dinesh Manocha, Sarah Wiegreffe
bullets: Many rollouts repeatedly propose answers despite containing only one unique answer, suggesting potentially unnecessary chain-of-thought backtracking.
A linear direction extracted from verbalized confidence separates high- and low-confidence states and also influences the probability of backtracking.
Steering this direction mid-trace changes response length by roughly −1.3k to +2.5k tokens and answer proposals by −4.18 to +4.75, in both directions.
Applying the direction from generation start shortens traces at comparable accuracy, even without knowing proposal positions.
The findings link internal confidence representations to a model’s tendency to commit or continue reasoning.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents accomplish complex tasks by coordinating multiple reasoning steps and tool operations, which form dependencies among their operations. Existing orchestration methods primarily consider hard dependencies that determine when an operation can legally begin, but overlook soft dependencies, i.e., information that is not required for execution but may improve an already executable operation. We identify soft-dependency scheduling as an important problem in agent execution. To this end, we introduce Neural Agent Compiler (NAC), a learned scheduler that predicts the task-quality and resource consequences of three execution modes and selects the highest-utility legal mode at a scheduling boundary. NAC represents the executable continuation, pending information event, and resource state in a shared memory, and uses a utility function to adapt the consequence predictions to different resource preferences. Across AppWorld, WebShop, and $\tau^2$-bench, NAC achieves 276/417 AppWorld task completions, a 74.69 WebShop Task Score, and 59/100 $\tau^2$-bench successes. Additional studies show that the learned scheduler reduces execution work, establishing soft-dependency scheduling as a promising solution for orchestrating tool-using agents.

Reports 276/417 AppWorld completions, a 74.69 WebShop Task Score, and 59/100 τ²-bench successes.
Additional studies find reduced execution work, though the abstract does not specify the study setup or limitations.

papers.abstract: Agents in complex, stochastic environments must contend with dynamics that can exceed their world models' predictive capacity and randomness that obscure the consequences of their actions. We hypothesize that, compared to imagining entirely new trajectories in such complex environments, it can be easier to transform observed trajectories with alternative actions. Counterfactual world models condition on observations to predict alternative outcomes under the same underlying environmental randomness, using experience as a reference for predicting action-dependent changes. We present a policy gradient estimator, REINFORCE Look Back (RLB), that uses counterfactual returns as baselines to distinguish action effects from environmental luck, and prove conditions for unbiasedness and variance reduction. In settings where environmental evolution is harder to predict than action-induced changes, we show that counterfactual world models are easier to learn and support better policy learning than ordinary world models. Our findings suggest that counterfactual thinking can help agents learn effective behavior without independently reproducing the full complexity of their worlds.
