papers.abstract: With the growing demand for large language model (LLM) services, optimizing LLM serving systems is becoming increasingly complex, and the bottleneck is no longer predicting how a given configuration will perform. The harder problem is deciding what to investigate: which mechanisms matter for a workload, which configurations are worth testing, and what evidence a decision still needs. In this work, we present NoeVera, an agentic Second Brain that goes beyond just one-shot retrieval by turning papers, code, benchmarks, and experimental results into a persistent, provenance-preserving knowledge base with three planes: source evidence, reusable synthesis, and agent memory. Decision-aware retrieval assembles compact evidence packs, role-specific agents reason over them and invoke a simulator (Vidur or GAUSS) whenever quantitative support is needed, and every finding is written back as a scoped evidence record, so knowledge guides experiments and experiments refine knowledge. In configuration search over four serving scenarios, NoeVera comes within 5% of the optimum in a median of 6-7 simulator calls, versus 9 for Bayesian optimization and 15 for a knowledge-free agent with the same tools; on A100 GPUs, its representative configurations deliver ~1.30x vLLM-default throughput and meet every scenario's latency objective. When reused, provenance-preserving evidence records over-generalize on only 8% of applicability traps, versus 28% for a general-purpose agent memory. On the held-out 48-task split of a 72-task benchmark, NoeVera scores 29% higher than an equally equipped agent and 36% higher than its single-call retrieval counterpart (0.80 vs. 0.62 and 0.59), and even when baselines receive NoeVera's own prompts, a statistically significant part of its evidence-evolution advantage remains.

papers.abstract: Force-aware manipulation requires robots to infer appropriate interaction forces from task context and tactile feedback. We present Tacinf, a low-cost, modular infrastructure that enables policies to predict robot actions and fingertip forces from task language, vision, and touch. Task instructions can optionally specify the desired force level. Tacinf integrates simulation data synthesis and tactile benchmarking (Tabero), vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policy learning, handheld data collection using the same gripper as robot deployment (Tacumi), and task-aligned sim-to-real evaluation (Taco). Together, these components form an integrated workflow connecting data collection from multiple sources, foundation-model training, and hardware deployment. We validate each component, including the simulation data, benchmark, controller, and Tacumi, and are releasing the full stack as open source. A foundation model fine-tuned solely on tactile simulation data transfers zero-shot to different real-robot tasks. Across eight policy variants, mean task success rates are strongly correlated between simulation and the real robot (Pearson r=0.998, mean maximum rank violation MMRV=0.010). For the four policies with reported force measurements, mean grip force is higher under firm instructions than under gentle instructions on all three tasks in both domains. When both object positions and instances are randomized, a mixture of teleoperation, simulation, and Tacumi data raises mean real-robot task success from 20% with teleoperation alone to 60%.

A model fine-tuned only on tactile simulation data transfers zero-shot to different real-robot tasks.
Simulation and real-robot success rates are highly aligned across eight policy variants (Pearson r=0.998; MMRV=0.010).

papers.abstract: Effective task execution requires embodied agents to select observation positions that provide sufficient task-relevant information. Existing approaches typically predict viewpoints with learned models or score discrete candidates, but they either struggle to incorporate new constraints such as reachability or require extensive candidate evaluation to search. We introduce InfoField3D, which lifts geometry-bound information into a differentiable analytic field, whose value at each 3D observation position represents the task-required information accessible there. It uses low-order spherical harmonics to encode directional information responses and analytic line integrals of Gaussian occupancy functions to model occlusion along lines of sight. This formulation casts task-driven camera placement as a well-studied constrained continuous optimization problem, enabling both flexible incorporation of constraints through the feasible domain and efficient viewpoint search even in the presence of occlusion. Experiments show that InfoField3D compactly preserves the pointwise information landscape with high fidelity and generally recommends higher-quality, more robust viewpoints at lower search cost than the evaluated baselines. Controlled evaluations with a frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policy further suggest that the recommended views can improve downstream task performance under information-limited initial viewpoints.
authors: Huan Lyu, Yawei Luo
bullets: Addresses viewpoint selection when agents need task-relevant information and constraints such as reachability.
Uses low-order spherical harmonics for directional information and analytic Gaussian-occupancy line integrals for occlusion.
Formulates camera placement as constrained continuous optimization rather than costly discrete candidate search.
Experiments find high-fidelity information landscapes, generally better and more robust viewpoints, and lower search cost than evaluated baselines.
Frozen VLA-policy evaluations suggest improved downstream performance when initial viewpoints are information-limited.

The field is then restricted to the feasible domain (A3, B3), and the recommended observation position is obtained through constrained optimization over this field (A4, B4). Within the same scene, viewpoints recommended according to different task requirements are provided to a frozen VLA to execute the corresponding tasks.

papers.abstract: We introduce Egocentric Human Motion Bridging, a task that generates a coherent 3D human motion sequence from two endpoint egocentric images. Unlike conventional motion in-betweening, which requires structured 3D endpoint poses, this setting uses raw first-person observations available from wearable devices in VR/AR and robotics. It presents challenges due to viewpoint variations, partial body visibility, and temporal ambiguity under cross-modal endpoint constraints. To address these challenges, we propose Ego-HMB, a unified diffusion-based framework that learns endpoint pose estimation and temporally consistent motion infilling within a single model through two training stages. First, Egocentric-to-Canonical Pretraining uses a hierarchical curriculum with progressively increasing temporal spans to strengthen endpoint pose priors. Second, Motion Bridge Diffusion Training incorporates endpoint and physics awareness, diffusing from neighboring poses to promote temporal continuity while preserving global endpoint constraints. Extensive experiments compare our approach with one-stage methods that directly generate motion from two egocentric images and two-stage pipelines that combine endpoint pose estimation with motion interpolation. Ego-HMB consistently outperforms these baselines in endpoint accuracy and motion generation quality. Code is available at https://github.com/gaogehan/Ego-HMB.
authors: Gaoge Han, Yongkang Cheng, Shaoli Huang, Jing Zhang, Mingming Gong, Fakhri Karray, Tongliang Liu
bullets: Addresses motion in-betweening from raw first-person images rather than structured 3D endpoint poses.

Applies endpoint- and physics-aware motion bridge diffusion to preserve endpoint constraints and temporal continuity.
Outperforms reported one-stage and two-stage baselines in endpoint accuracy and motion quality.
Targets wearable-device applications in VR/AR and robotics despite viewpoint variation, partial visibility, and temporal ambiguity.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires a robot to regulate the force it applies, not only where it moves. Existing force-aware policies learn this force from demonstrations and therefore reproduce the force levels they were trained on, which fails once the interaction demands more force than any demonstration. We present Force2Act, a hybrid force-position policy built on two complementary mechanisms. A global force policy plans the motion and the interaction force once per action chunk, with force represented relative to the measured interaction, so that the planned force scales with the load. Between planning steps, a reactive compliance policy, termed Mixture of Force Experts, identifies at every control step the force expert that governs the interaction and regulates the force through it, so that the contact holds when it changes within a chunk. We further introduce Force2Act-Bench, a simulation benchmark of five contact-rich tasks that gives the community a common and repeatable way to test force-aware policies and measure how well they regulate the interaction force. Force2Act achieves an overall success rate of 93.8%, compared with 77.0% for the strongest baseline, and its reactive regulation reduces the failures on block pivoting from 30 to 10 of 150 trials. On a real robot, Force2Act reaches an average success rate of 94.2% over four tasks, against at most 27.5% for the baselines.
authors: Keerthi Vasan Murugan, Fangguo Zhao, Jiafei Duan
bullets: Problem: Demonstration-trained force policies may fail when tasks require forces beyond those seen during training.
Method: A global force-position policy plans motion and load-relative force per action chunk, while Mixture of Force Experts reactively regulates contact between plans.
Contribution: Introduces Force2Act-Bench, a five-task simulation benchmark for evaluating force-aware manipulation.
Results: Achieves 93.8% overall simulation success versus 77.0% for the strongest baseline, and 94.2% average real-robot success across four tasks versus at most 27.5% for baselines.
Scope: Evaluations focus on five simulated contact-rich tasks and four real-robot tasks.

papers.tldr: Force2Act combines force-aware planning with reactive compliance to generalize contact-rich robot manipulation across changing interaction demands.

papers.abstract: In difficult driving scenes, a learned scorer can select a poor trajectory from a fixed pool even when a better candidate is available. Nearby vehicles and road boundaries can also leave only a narrow range of high-scoring maneuvers. These constraints vary with the scene and are difficult to cover exhaustively during training. We introduce DriveTTO, a training-free method that searches around native proposals and checks each proposed refinement against a retained trajectory. A frozen scorer evaluates completed paths at the endpoints they actually reach, guiding resampling in progressively smaller neighborhoods. From a shared reference, one branch draws on planner proposals and another perturbs vehicle controls. DriveTTO blends their poses at matching times and accepts a branch or fusion update only when both frozen scorers predict a gain. On Navtest, DriveTTO recovers nonzero predictive driver model scores (PDMS) in 51.35% of native zero-score cases on average. Accounting for new failures, the zero-score rate falls from 1.63% to 1.13%. Benchmark-specific configurations achieve 95.54 PDMS and 92.30 extended PDMS (EPDMS) on Navtest, 57.10 EPDMS on Navhard, and 40.1 HD-Score on HUGSIM under observed commands. With a single frozen scorer, DriveTTO-S improves all six evaluated planners on both Navtest and Navhard.
authors: Xinyao Rao, Zecheng Tang, Zheyuan Lai, Liuxuan Sun, Minjun Yu, Xun Cao, Wei Li
bullets: Addresses difficult scenes where a learned scorer selects a poor trajectory despite better candidates being nearby.
Searches around native planner proposals and vehicle-control perturbations using progressively smaller neighborhoods.
A frozen scorer evaluates completed trajectories, while updates are accepted only when both branch scorers predict improvement.
Recovers nonzero PDMS in 51.35% of native zero-score cases and lowers the zero-score rate from 1.63% to 1.13% on Navtest.
With one frozen scorer, DriveTTO-S improves all six evaluated planners on Navtest and Navhard.

papers.abstract: Dexterous functional grasping is critical for robotic tool use, yet current dexterous hands exhibit substantial morphological diversity. This hardware heterogeneity makes cross-embodiment functional grasping a fundamental but largely unexplored problem. Existing functional grasping methods use retargeted hand poses as guidance, tying task representation to a specific embodiment and failing to explicitly capture object-centric functional contact intent, limiting generalization across hands. To address this, we propose FunGrasp-Zero, a reinforcement learning framework for zero-shot cross-embodiment functional grasping. Instead of relying on embodiment-specific joint configuration, FunGrasp-Zero captures functional intent via an object-centric, cross-embodiment-consistent contact map, adapted to heterogeneous hands through morphological mapping. We construct a hand-object potential field from mapped contact regions, yielding attractive and repulsive guidance vectors. A Field-Conditioned Graph Attention Network (FC-GAT) leverages these vectors to coordinate multi-finger motion across hands, while a potential field reward guides fingers toward target regions and penalizes non-target collisions to enforce functional alignment and stability. We further establish X-FunBench for cross-embodiment functional grasping, evaluating both physical grasp success and functional intent preservation across hands. Evaluated on X-FunBench, our unified policy, co-trained on four embodiments, achieves 86% average grasp success rate across five unseen hands on novel objects. Deployed on four unseen physical hands (Leap, Inspire, Sharpa, Wuji) for novel object grasping, the policy achieves 80% average success rate without fine-tuning. To our knowledge, FunGrasp-Zero is the first RL-based framework to achieve zero-shot cross-embodiment functional grasping across unseen hands in both simulation and the real world.
authors: Yanhan Lin, Yuliang Wu, Yihao Guo, Wei-Jin Huang, Jianwen Li, Jiawei Tang, Xiaolong Huang, Yuquan Wang, Ancong Wu, Wei-Shi Zheng
bullets: Addresses cross-embodiment functional grasping, where hand morphology differences hinder transfer.
Represents functional intent with a hand-independent contact map and adapts it to each hand through morphological mapping.
Uses a field-conditioned graph attention policy with attractive/repulsive guidance and collision-aware rewards.
Introduces X-FunBench to evaluate grasp success and preservation of functional intent across embodiments.
Achieves 86% average simulated success on five unseen hands and 80% average real-world success on four unseen hands without fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Physical counterfactual video editing turns a source video and a language-specified physical edit at a given execution frame into a counterfactual video that shows how the scene would evolve after the edit. Existing evaluations with counterfactual target videos mainly cover object removal or specific rigid-body motions, although real scenes also involve elastic deformation, fluid flow, and interactions among rigid bodies, elastic solids, and fluids. We introduce PhyCoVE, a benchmark of 533 cases on 110 source videos that covers rigid, elastic, and fluid dynamics in five interaction patterns, with edits that remove an object, change a physical quantity, or insert a new object. For the simulated cases, a language model proposes scene designs, coding agents build them with solvers suited to each material and physically based rendering and then simulate each edit from the source scene state, and humans check every stage. For the real cases, we record continuously from one camera position before and after each edit. We also propose counterfactual fidelity, a metric that applies across materials and their interactions and measures how much of the physical change from the source video to the target video a generated video reproduces. We evaluate seven open-source and commercial video editing models and find that counterfactual fidelity ranks them nearly as human preference does, but even the best model reproduces only about one seventh of the physical change. The models change how a scene looks but rarely how it evolves, whereas a physical edit requires understanding the dynamics that it changes. Physical counterfactual video editing thus remains far from solved, and PhyCoVE provides a foundation for developing and evaluating methods for it.
authors: Conghan Yue, Yuanjie Chen, Yunyan Xiao, Zeyu Peng, Xingsong Ye, Ya Gao, Yanglin Huang, WeiYao Zhang, Yue Han, Zhineng Chen, Yu-Gang Jiang
bullets: Introduces 533 benchmark cases from 110 videos spanning rigid, elastic, and fluid materials across five interaction patterns.
Covers object removal, physical-quantity changes, and object insertion in simulated and real-world videos.
Proposes counterfactual fidelity, a cross-material metric that measures how much of the physical change is reproduced.
Evaluates seven open-source and commercial models; the metric closely matches human preferences.
Even the best model reproduces only about one seventh of the physical change, showing that the task remains largely unsolved.

papers.abstract: Standard dense visual prediction architectures scale representation capacity by stacking deep feedforward decoders (6-16 transformer layers with 50M-200M parameters). This explicit layer stacking brings substantial activation memory overhead during backpropagation, requires high off-chip memory bandwidth for non-tied weights, and uses static computational allocation that cannot adapt to spatial image complexity. We propose loopxDINO, which replaces physical decoder depth with iterative latent reasoning. It has two decoupled components: (1) a frozen DINOv2-Base backbone extracting spatial features in one forward pass and caching static Key-Value representations in GPU memory; (2) a compact weight-tied Looped Cross-Attention Decoder (7.96M core, 14.85M total trainable parameters) that recurrently updates queries across T iterations. Recurrence is stabilized by step-conditioned adaLN, LayerNorm-based hyper-ellipsoid manifold regularization, and learnable residual contraction damping. Intermediate mask predictions are fed back as spatial attention biases to guide queries toward ambiguous contours with no extra parameters. On Pascal VOC 2012 semantic segmentation with a single RTX 5060 Ti 16GB GPU, loopxDINO (T=2) achieves 85.66% mIoU and 65.01% Boundary IoU. It outperforms 6-layer DINO-Trans6L (54.06M params) by +1.09% mIoU and +7.41% Boundary IoU with 72.5% fewer parameters. Compared to 4-layer DINO-FCN4L probe (2.43M params, 83.82% mIoU), loopxDINO improves boundary delineation by +6.43% bIoU and occlusion resilience by +6.76% mIoU (60% patch masking). With Adaptive Computation Time (ACT), it reaches 87.3 FPS and retains 29.64% mIoU under 60% occlusion (+5.83% over DINO-Trans6L). Source code, pre-trained weights and evaluation suites are open-sourced under Apache 2.0 at https://github.com/loopxDINO/loopxDINO
authors: Xiangjing An, Zhibin Jiao, Aiting Chen
bullets: Addresses activation-memory, bandwidth, and fixed-compute costs of stacked transformer decoders.
Uses frozen DINOv2-Base features with cached key-value representations and a weight-tied Looped Cross-Attention Decoder.
Stabilizes iterative reasoning with step-conditioned adaLN, manifold regularization, residual damping, and feedback from intermediate masks.
On Pascal VOC 2012, T=2 achieves 85.66% mIoU and 65.01% Boundary IoU, outperforming a 6-layer baseline with 72.5% fewer parameters.
ACT enables adaptive computation, reaching 87.3 FPS and retaining 29.64% mIoU under 60% patch masking.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Architectural overview of loopxDINO. (a) Immutable Perception Base: An input image X ∈ R3×H×W is processed in a single forward pass by a frozen foundation backbone (∇θ = 0), producing spatial features and a persistent Key-Value cache (Kv,Vv) ∈ RHpWp×D. (b) Looped Latent Reasoning Engine: A compact, weight-tied Looped Cross-Attention Decoder (≈ 7.96M core parameters) iteratively refines learned queries Qt across t = 1 . . . T . Recurrent updates are modulated by step-conditioned Adaptive Layer Normalization (adaLN), regularized by LayerNorm hyper-ellipsoid projection, and guided by spatial attention biases derived from intermediate mask predictions. (c) Readout & Dynamic ACT: Multi-scale representations from layers 4, 8, and 12 are fused to generate dense masks Mt, while a halting controller predicts termination probabilities ht for adaptive computational allocation.

Figure 2: Compute-Optimal Pareto Frontier on Pascal VOC 2012. (a) Latency-Accuracy Pareto Frontier: Trade-off between inference latency (RTX 5060 Ti) and validation mIoU. loopxDINO (T = 1, 2) and Dynamic ACT define an optimal Pareto frontier, outperforming the 6-layer physically stacked baseline (DINO-Trans6L, 54.06M) and substantially exceeding the boundary precision of the convolutional probe anchor (DINO-FCN4L, 2.43M). (b) Parameter Efficiency Scaling: Achieving +1.09% higher mIoU and +7.41% higher Boundary IoU with 72.5% fewer trainable decoder parameters than DINO-Trans6L.

Figure 3: Dynamical Stability and Recurrent Contraction Analysis. (a) Latent Norm Boundedness on Hyper-Ellipsoid Manifold: Norm evolution ∥Qt∥2 over 32 recurrence steps. Naive additive embeddings diverge past 140, whereas loopxDINO (adaLN + LayerNorm) stabilizes on the invariant manifold ∥q∥2 ≈√ D = 27.71. (b) Exponential Velocity Decay & Fixed Point: The step displacement ∥Qt −Qt−1∥2 exhibits geometric decay alongside the analytical Lipschitz contraction bound (ρ = 0.74 < 1.0).

Figure 5: Dynamic Halting and Occlusion Robustness. (a) Adaptive Pondering vs. Occlusion Depth: Under increasing patch masking (0% to 60%), the differentiable ACT controller autonomously shifts halting probability mass toward higher reasoning iterations (mean steps shift from µ = 2.9 to µ = 7.4). (b) Occlusion Retention: Evaluated across clean and randomly occluded inputs on Pascal VOC 2012. Both DINO-FCN4L and DINO-Trans6L degrade under heavy masking, whereas loopxDINO (T = 4) achieves 29.64% mIoU (+5.83% over DINO-Trans6L, +6.76% over DINO-FCN4L).

Figure 4: Boundary Refinement and Attention Sharpening Dynamics. (a) Edge Boundary IoU vs. Recurrent Loops: Boundary IoU across trimap bands (1px, 3px, and overall) on Pascal VOC 2012. Fine boundary precision peaks at T = 2 (65.01% bIoU), outperforming the 6-layer baseline by +7.41%. (b) Attention Sharpening & Spatial Focusing: Cross-attention entropy drops steadily as queries transition from diffuse scene exploration to concentrated boundary saliency.

papers.selection_reason: Replaces deep decoder with weight-tied iterative latent reasoning, reducing parameters and memory for dense visual prediction.
papers.title: loopxDINO: Dense Visual Prediction via Iterative Latent Reasoning
papers.tldr: loopxDINO replaces deep dense-prediction decoders with a compact recurrent decoder that improves segmentation boundaries and robustness while reducing parameters.

papers.abstract: Many deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms store agent-environment interactions in a replay buffer and later learn by sampling transitions from it. However, this approach can be memory-inefficient and can delay learning because the agent can learn from a transition only when the buffer samples it. Additionally, most of these methods use one-step or short multi-step temporal-difference (TD) updates, which are slow at credit assignment. An alternative approach is to learn from the stream of observations as they arrive without relying on a buffer. Eligibility-trace algorithms allow these incremental updates and can also assign credit over many steps. These algorithms were common with linear function approximation but have only recently been used in deep RL. Basic questions, such as how to use vector step sizes with eligibility traces in the deep RL setting, remain open. In this work, we first show that adaptive vector step sizes must be part of the eligibility trace to keep the equivalence between the forward and backward views. We then show that the step sizes of common optimizers, such as Adam, do not have an online backward view. We introduce a new optimizer, Function-Space Distance (FSD), that maintains the forward-backward equivalence. We test four eligibility-trace algorithms covering semi-gradient and gradient TD updates, as well as value-based and actor-critic methods. We show that FSD performs better than SGD or naively applied Adam. The resulting algorithms outperform or match other streaming methods and are comparable to or better than PPO, which uses a buffer, in most environments. Code available at https://github.com/esraaelelimy/ada_traces
authors: Esraa Elelimy, Martha White
bullets: Replay-buffer methods delay learning and often use short-horizon TD updates, limiting fast credit assignment.
The work shows that vector-valued adaptive step sizes must be included in eligibility traces to maintain forward–backward equivalence.
Common optimizers such as Adam lack an online backward view when combined with eligibility traces.
The proposed Function-Space Distance (FSD) optimizer preserves this equivalence and is evaluated across four streaming eligibility-trace algorithms.
FSD outperforms SGD and naively applied Adam, while the resulting methods match or exceed other streaming approaches and are comparable to or better than PPO in most tested environments.

papers.abstract: Multi-step reasoning requires models to preserve and update intermediate information as computation unfolds. State tracking captures this fundamental requirement, but models that succeed within a fixed range of state transitions may not generalize when substantially more updates are required. Recurrent Transformers offer a natural mechanism for addressing this challenge by repeatedly applying shared Transformer blocks, allowing computation to scale with problem length. We study when such recurrent computation generalizes beyond the training range in a controlled state-tracking task, varying operation representation, positional encoding, and recurrent capacity. We find that recurrence alone is insufficient: multi-token template representations and absolute positional encoding can severely limit extrapolation, whereas atomic operation representations enable substantially stronger length generalization. The effect of positional structure also varies with recurrent depth, with periodic positional encoding achieving the strongest mean performance at greater recurrent depth. Most importantly, scaling the recurrent operator extends the extrapolation horizon, reaching 35.1% exact-match accuracy on sequences of 20-40 operations after training only on 2-10, while substantially larger fixed-depth Transformers remain at 0%. Additional recurrent computation at test time can extend the range over which the model generalizes, but does not eliminate failure on much longer sequences. These results suggest that recurrent computation can support length-generalizable state tracking, but that its effectiveness depends critically on whether the learned computation remains reusable across sequence lengths.
authors: Yoonsung Jung, Sunghun Jung, Louise Nayeong Koh, Yongjun Choi
bullets: Studies length extrapolation in a controlled multi-step state-tracking task.
Atomic operation representations generalize substantially better than multi-token templates.

Scaling the recurrent operator reaches 35.1% exact-match accuracy on 20–40 operations after training on 2–10, while larger fixed-depth Transformers reach 0%.
More recurrent computation at test time extends generalization but does not prevent failure on much longer sequences.

papers.abstract: Modifying 3D assets requires enacting targeted structural transformations while strictly preserving the geometric identity of unedited regions. While recent probability flow models enable training-free editing, bounding these modifications within a high-dimensional latent space presents severe mathematical challenges. Current inversion-free trajectories rely on global velocity updates, which often cause spatial bleed into preserved structures and induce trajectory under-commitment, causing edits to stall mid-path. To resolve these dual failures, we introduce FocusFlow, a segmentation-free framework that structures the integration trajectory into two disjoint phases. During early coarse structure formation, FocusFlow applies Feature-Divergence Localization (FDL) to spatially gate the velocity field using intrinsic cross-attention. Once coarse structure has formed, FocusFlow applies Reference Generation Guidance (RGG), a trajectory-correction term that drives convergence to the target shape by pulling the trajectory toward an explicit clean-latent target. Evaluated on the joint Google Scanned Objects and PartObjaverse-Tiny benchmarks, FocusFlow obtains the best preservation scores and the largest edit magnitude among compared methods, suggesting that it can reduce the traditional preservation-modification trade-off. By providing stable, localized geometric control without manual spatial annotations, this phase-scheduled approach lowers technical barriers to the modification of synthetic 3D media.
authors: Tri Ton, Siwoo Lim, Joshua Tian Jin Tee, Chang D. Yoo
bullets: Addresses spatial bleed and stalled edits in inversion-free probability-flow editing.
Uses Feature-Divergence Localization to gate velocity updates during early coarse structure formation.
Applies Reference Generation Guidance later to pull the trajectory toward a clean latent representing the target shape.
On Google Scanned Objects and PartObjaverse-Tiny, reports the best preservation scores and largest edit magnitude among compared methods.
Requires no segmentation or manual spatial annotations, though its scope is evaluated on these benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: FocusFlow framework. Left: Precomputation of the DINO distance, the edit region and the reference latent zref . Top: Per-step velocities and the alignment gradient. Center (localization phase): FDL gates the velocity field via soft mask m to confine the edit. Right (guidance phase): RGG applies a ramped pull toward zref , driving structural commitment.

The inset under each result shows the per-point deviation of the output from the source mesh (blue: unchanged, red: changed), so a well-localized edit appears blue outside the edit region. papers.abstract: Hand pose estimation aims to recover the spatial configuration of hand joints from visual observations and serves as a fundamental perception module for downstream systems that rely on complete and topologically consistent hand representations. Most existing methods are developed under the assumption of fully articulated hand structures and tend to produce unstable or implausible predictions when parts of the kinematic structure are persistently absent, resulting in degraded performance or even system failure despite available partial observations. To study this challenge, we construct IncNYU, a physiologically constrained benchmark that simulates structural incompleteness through morphological modification of complete hand models and retains reference locations for both intact and synthetically removed regions. Based on this benchmark, we propose InsHaPE, an Inclusive Hand Pose Estimation framework designed to remain robust under structural incompleteness while preserving performance on standard, fully articulated hands. Built on hierarchical kinematic modeling, InsHaPE introduces two complementary components. First, a topology-aware distillation strategy transfers joint-level and relational priors from fully articulated hand representations, providing anatomically consistent initialization under missing structures. Second, a progressive kinematic reasoning module performs structured inference along the kinematic chain, enabling complete and anatomically consistent pose estimation under severe structural variations. Extensive experiments on NYU/IncNYU, together with external validation on MSRA, demonstrate that InsHaPE improves robustness under structural incompleteness while maintaining competitive performance on complete hands. System-level evaluations further show that InsHaPE improves robustness for downstream applications that require fixed-topology hand pose representations.
authors: Kanglei Zhou, Zikai Hao, Liyuan Wang, Xiaohui Liang
bullets: Introduces IncNYU, a benchmark simulating physiologically constrained structural incompleteness with reference locations for intact and removed regions.
Uses topology-aware distillation to transfer joint-level and relational priors from fully articulated hands.
Applies progressive kinematic reasoning to infer complete poses along the hand’s kinematic chain.
Experiments on NYU/IncNYU and external validation on MSRA show improved robustness under structural variation and competitive results on complete hands.
System evaluations indicate benefits for downstream applications requiring fixed-topology hand representations.

papers.abstract: Agents built on large language models must maintain continuity across repeated interactions with users. However, long-term conversations scatter facts across turns and sessions, making it difficult to retrieve the right evidence with enough context. Memory for such conversations must therefore preserve facts with their context while keeping evidence selectively accessible. We first study how memory construction and retrieval-unit boundaries affect answerability and evidence access. Reading the entire memory bank reveals gaps that cannot be resolved by retrieval selection alone, showing that some context must be preserved during memory construction. Adjacent-turn grouping improves evidence access at matched unique-turn budgets, while wider windows do not consistently help. This motivates keeping fact-specific context local while organizing cross-session evidence separately. We propose ContextFact, which links context-preserving fact memories with source-grounded entity representations. Within sessions, it gathers the context needed to interpret each fact. Across sessions, it aligns recurring referents and revisits the source dialogue to reconstruct coherent entity representations linked to the supporting facts. At query time, ContextFact retrieves fact and entity views, reranks them independently, and uses entity-linked expansion to surface related facts; complete entity representations then provide organized cross-session evidence. With Qwen3.5-27B as the backbone, ContextFact achieves state-of-the-art performance while using only $21\%$ of the evidence tokens consumed by the strongest evaluated baseline, obtaining $86.49\%$ overall judge accuracy on LoCoMo and $91.00\%$ on LongMemEval-S. Controlled ablations support context-preserving fact boundaries and source-grounded entity reconstruction, while entity readout improves multi-hop accuracy beyond adding more facts.
authors: Jiayu Huang, Yichao Cai, Xinyu Li, Zhen Zhang, Javen Qinfeng Shi
bullets: Long-term conversations scatter facts across turns and sessions, making context-aware evidence retrieval difficult.
Studies show memory construction and retrieval-unit boundaries affect answerability; adjacent-turn grouping improves access, while wider windows do not consistently help.
ContextFact links context-preserving fact memories with source-grounded entity representations across sessions.
At query time, it independently reranks fact and entity views and expands retrieval through entity links.

Using Qwen3.5-27B, it reports 86.49% judge accuracy on LoCoMo and 91.00% on LongMemEval-S while consuming 21% of the evidence tokens used by the strongest baseline; entity readout particularly helps multi-hop questions.

papers.abstract: Multi-video understanding requires systems to combine evidence from different videos for cross-video reasoning. Answering such questions involves two kinds of decisions. Observation decisions must adapt to each video's content, whereas cross-video judgments require relating evidence from different videos based on the question. Most existing agents make both kinds of decisions in one controller, whose context accumulates observations from every video. We separate them in MVAgent, a training-free Multi-Video Understanding Agent framework with one LocalAgent per video. Each LocalAgent plans observations of its own video and keeps a private observation history. A GlobalAgent coordinates cross-video reasoning by instructing the LocalAgents and combining their reports with joint observation. We evaluate MVAgent on CVBench, MVU-Eval, and CrossVid, using three Qwen3.5 models of different sizes and GPT-6-sol. With Qwen3.5, our framework improves aggregate benchmark scores by 5.1 points on average over Single-pass inference with the same model and by 5.0 points over the strongest prior agent using the same model. With GPT-6-sol, the average gain over Single-pass inference with the same model is 4.3 points. On the same hardware, MVAgent also runs 1.8-2.7 times faster than prior agents of comparable size.
authors: Kewei Wei, XueXiang Wen, Bocheng Hu, Weili Xu, Haiyang Yu, Kaiyue Zhou, Gaoang Wang
bullets: Separates per-video observation from cross-video judgment to avoid one controller accumulating all observations.
Each LocalAgent plans observations for its own video and maintains a private history.
A GlobalAgent directs LocalAgents and combines their reports through joint reasoning.
Across CVBench, MVU-Eval, and CrossVid, it improves average scores over single-pass and prior-agent baselines, while running 1.8–2.7× faster than comparable prior agents.
The framework is training-free and evaluated with multiple Qwen3.5 model sizes and GPT-6-sol.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) tokenize images using fixed spatial grids, so visual token count grows with pixel area rather than scene content. We propose to group neighboring patches based on their visual appearance, allowing tokens to represent coherent image regions rather than fixed spatial windows. We introduce RVLM, a VLM trained to use regions rather than patches as its visual units. Analyzing region construction for general-purpose VLMs, we find that regions must cover the full image, stay spatially connected during end-to-end training, and preserve fine structure such as small text, while semantic grouping adds little. RVLM therefore partitions images using training-free Felzenszwalb-Huttenlocher segmentation, assigns each ViT patch to a region, and pools patches within each region into a variable-length sequence of visual tokens. The patch-to-region assignment is retained to support spatially precise prediction through coarse-to-fine decoding. Across tasks spanning VQA, pointing, counting, segmentation, and depth estimation, RVLM matches or improves example-weighted task performance while using 21.5% fewer visual tokens than an identically trained patch baseline. The advantage grows with image resolution, reaching a 5.3-point gain while using 51.8% fewer visual tokens at the highest-resolution setting. The gains are largest on spatially demanding tasks, where prior token-reduction methods degrade most sharply. RVLM adds no model parameters and improves inference throughput by up to 35.9%. On unseen pathology and satellite images and on video benchmarks without any video training, RVLM performs on par with the patch baseline while using 2-3$\times$ fewer visual tokens. These results establish regions as a scalable alternative to patch-based visual representations while preserving the spatial precision required for grounded prediction.
authors: Savya Khosla, Chris Dongjoo Kim, Alex Schwing, Derek Hoiem, Christopher Clark, Sangho Lee
bullets: Uses training-free Felzenszwalb–Huttenlocher segmentation to group patches into variable-length, spatially connected regions.
Preserves full-image coverage and fine structure, including small text; semantic grouping is not essential.
Retains patch-to-region mappings for coarse-to-fine spatial prediction.
Matches or improves performance across VQA, pointing, counting, segmentation, and depth estimation while using 21.5% fewer tokens overall.
At higher resolutions, gains reach 5.3 points with 51.8% fewer tokens; inference throughput improves by up to 35.9%, with strong transfer to pathology, satellite, and video benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of RVLM. We generate content-adaptive regions using FelzenszwalbHuttenlocher segmentation and assign each ViT patch to a region. This is a CPU-side preprocessing that runs in parallel to the model execution. Patch features within each region are aggregated through attention pooling to produce a sequence of region tokens for the LLM. The retained patch-to-region correspondence enables coarse-to-fine spatial grounding, where the LLM selects a region, then a patch within it, and finally a precise point within the patch.

For instance, in the first example, it incorrectly describes some initiatives as “on the table” for Obama, even though the image lists none. PVLM and FH-based RVLM do not show these failures.

papers.title: RVLM: Fewer Tokens, Better Resolution Scaling, Fine-Grained Spatial Grounding
papers.tldr: RVLM replaces fixed-grid image patches with connected visual regions, reducing visual tokens while preserving fine-grained spatial grounding and improving high-resolution efficiency.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves multimodal reasoning, but response-level feedback provides limited guidance on which intermediate decisions to correct. Visual interventions reveal sensitivity to image content, yet this sensitivity alone does not establish reward alignment or support across questions. We introduce RAVEC (Reward-Aligned Visual Evidence Correction), which selects visual corrections using local and cross-question reward support and jointly determines their strengths within each response. Paired Visual Evidence Contrast (PVEC) compares predictions from an exponential moving average teacher at the same sampled response prefix under the original image and a version with its annotated evidence region suppressed, yielding signed correction directions. Credit-Risk Allocation (CRA) screens these directions using local reward alignment and reward support from other questions, excluding all responses to the source question. It then solves a response-level budgeted allocation problem, assigning additional cost to directions that locally reduce predictive entropy. The resulting signed visual loss augments Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) during training. Inference uses only the original image and question. Across ten multimodal benchmarks, RAVEC achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared methods with both 3B and 7B Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct models, outperforming GRPO by 2.67 and 1.39 percentage points, respectively. Component ablations support the combined design of evidence alignment, credit qualification, and risk-aware allocation. The project is available at https://yangjj007.github.io/ravec/.
authors: Junjie Yang, Rui Qian, Xutao Mao, Yuhe Wu, Mingda Zhang, Jiaxuan Luo, Yang Tan, Qiang Huang, Zhisheng Chen, Yanfeng Li, Dawen Tian, Changmiao Wang, Tao Tan
bullets: Addresses the weak guidance of response-level rewards for correcting intermediate visual reasoning decisions.
Uses PVEC to derive signed visual correction directions by contrasting original images with evidence-suppressed versions.
Uses CRA to filter corrections by local and cross-question reward support, then allocates correction strength under a response-level budget.
Augments GRPO with the resulting signed visual loss; inference uses only the original image and question.
Achieves the best average accuracy among compared methods across ten benchmarks, improving over GRPO by 2.67 points for 3B and 1.39 points for 7B models; ablations support the combined design.

papers.tldr: RAVEC improves multimodal reasoning by training models to correct visual evidence with reward-aligned, risk-aware interventions while requiring no extra inputs at inference.

papers.abstract: A pretrained image representation helps train a diffusion transformer in several roles, including as an alignment target, which the model's hidden states learn to match, as in representation alignment (REPA), and as a condition, an extra input describing the image to be generated. Combined, they would give the model an input and a target, but whether they conflict is unknown. To test this, we let the condition carry only part of REPA's target: we split the representation of each image patch into an image-level (global) part, shared by all patches of the image, and a within-image (local) part, the patch's difference from the image-level part, and use one token carrying the image-level part as the condition. Then, the two roles overlap on the image-level part, where they could conflict, while only REPA supervises the within-image part, where we can see whether the token helps REPA. We find that the token and REPA together teach both the image-level part and the within-image part, the main source of REPA's FID improvement, far more than the sum of what each teaches alone, so they cooperate rather than conflict. These findings give one design rule for combining REPA with an image-level condition, supply the global, supervise the local, which we implement as Global-Condition REPA (GC-REPA): REPA with the token as an extra input; the token carries no information beyond REPA's target and is drawn at sampling from a separately trained token prior. GC-REPA greatly accelerates convergence: on ImageNet 256*256, SiT-XL/2 + GC-REPA reaches REPA's 4M- and SiT-XL/2's 7M-iteration FIDs within 200K and 100K iterations (20 and 70 fewer).
authors: Chaojie Ji, Sergio Quiroga-Sandoval, Ruxin Wang, Zheju Zheng, Yankai Cao
bullets: REPA uses pretrained image representations as alignment targets, while conditioning provides them as model inputs; their interaction was previously unclear.
The method separates each patch representation into a shared global component and a patch-specific local component, then supplies the global component as a single conditioning token.
The condition and REPA cooperate: together they teach both global and local features far more effectively than either alone, rather than conflicting.
This leads to Global-Condition REPA (GC-REPA), where the token is an extra input and is sampled from a separately trained prior at generation time.
On ImageNet 256×256, GC-REPA reaches REPA’s 4M-iteration and baseline SiT-XL/2’s 7M-iteration FIDs within 200K and 100K iterations, respectively.

papers.abstract: World-action models learn from future prediction, but accessing their future representations directly at test time can require costly frame generation. Methods that generate future frames before planning incur additional forward passes, while future co-training methods omit explicit future predictions at inference. We introduce \method, a planner that reads the hidden states of masked future tokens without decoding future frames. We pretrain MMaDA-Parallel-M on driving video using frame-level masked world modeling, which predicts a masked suffix of future frames and explicitly includes inputs with all future frames masked. Learned planning queries attend to these masked positions and the observed context, and a continuous head predicts the trajectory in the same forward pass. With a single front camera, \method reaches 92.0 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 89.3 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, with an end-to-end latency of 60.3\,ms.
authors: Ziyu Zhao, Casey Sun, Zeyu Wang, Shicong Ma, Emily T Zhang, Cheng Lu
bullets: Addresses the inference cost of generating future frames before planning.
Pretrains a masked world model on driving video, including inputs where all future frames are masked.
Uses planning queries over masked future states and observed context, with a continuous trajectory head in one forward pass.
Achieves 92.0 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 89.3 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 using a single front camera.
Runs with 60.3 ms end-to-end latency.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based planners capture the multimodality of human driving behavior well, yet covariate shift in closed-loop driving can lead them to generate trajectories that result in collisions or road departures. Reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning offers a promising way to tackle this issue, but applying it to diffusion-based planners is complicated by their iterative denoising process and receding-horizon execution. We find that small adjustments to the planned trajectories can prevent many of these unsafe outcomes. Motivated by this observation, we propose PlanNudge, which preserves the learned planning capabilities of a pretrained diffusion-based planner by freezing it and trains a lightweight policy that we call the nudge policy. At each planning step, the nudge policy outputs a nudge, a two-dimensional adjustment of the speed and curvature of the plan from the frozen planner. The nudge policy is a multilayer perceptron that predicts the nudge in a single forward pass, and both dimensions directly change the motion of the vehicle, so standard off-policy RL can train it in closed-loop simulation. We evaluate PlanNudge on nuPlan, a large-scale autonomous driving benchmark based on real-world driving data. In all six settings, PlanNudge matches or exceeds the final scores of the previous state-of-the-art RL finetuning method while using about one sixth as many environment steps and less than one fifth as much model compute. We also provide guidelines for reward shaping, value learning, and exploration when using off-policy RL to post-train autonomous driving planners. Our results are reported with means and standard deviations over six training runs. Project page: https://zerlinwang.github.io/plannudge/
authors: Zilin Wang, Guozheng Ma, Saeed Rahmani, Jiong Yang, Antyanta Bangunharcana, Yiluan Guo, Jakob Nicolaus Foerster, Shimon Whiteson
bullets: Diffusion planners model diverse driving behavior but can fail under closed-loop covariate shift, causing collisions or road departures.
The method freezes the pretrained planner and trains a lightweight MLP nudge policy to adjust each plan’s speed and curvature in one forward pass.
These direct trajectory adjustments make standard off-policy RL practical despite iterative denoising and receding-horizon execution.
On nuPlan’s six settings, PlanNudge matches or surpasses the prior RL fine-tuning method using roughly one-sixth the environment steps and less than one-fifth the model compute.
The paper also gives guidance on reward shaping, value learning, and exploration for off-policy RL planner post-training.

papers.selection_reason: RL finetuning of diffusion-based driving planners via a lightweight nudge policy, directly relevant to learned navigation and planning.

papers.abstract: As multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) get increasingly used as collaborative partners across embodied robotics, AR/VR, and multi-user systems, spatial reasoning is now often distributed across agents with partial environment visibility, necessitating spatial reasoning integration. Prior work in language-mediated spatial integration is however strictly limited to simplified two-agent scenarios. To address this gap, we first formalize the general problem of decentralized multi-view spatial reasoning, where N agents observe distinct viewpoints, exchange budget-constrained natural language messages, and collaborate to enable a listener to answer spatial queries. We then introduce a novel multi-view spatial benchmark to isolate queries that demand non-trivial multi-view integration. Through an extensive empirical study, we discover that the penalty of restricting decentralized spatial reasoning to natural language with limited budget is far smaller than suggested by prior two-agent literature. Nevertheless, we observe that substantial headroom still remains for multi-agent spatial reasoning in this setting, as evidenced by a significant gap between current centralized performance and an oracle best-of-K ceiling. Moreover, we show that reinforcement learning with credit assignment substantially bolsters the decentralized model, effectively closing the gap with the centralized baseline.
authors: Soumyabrata Chaudhuri, Joydeep Ghosh
bullets: Studies N agents with partial, distinct views that exchange budget-limited natural-language messages to answer spatial queries.
Introduces a benchmark targeting queries requiring non-trivial integration across multiple viewpoints.
Finds that limited-language communication is less damaging than prior two-agent results suggest, but substantial reasoning headroom remains.
Shows a significant gap between current decentralized performance and an oracle best-of-K ceiling.
Reinforcement learning with credit assignment substantially improves decentralized reasoning and closes the gap with the centralized baseline.

papers.abstract: Human videos promise a scalable way to reduce expensive robot data collection, but the embodiment gap limits the resulting policies to coarse behaviors, and they fail at precise tasks such as insertion. Existing methods co-train or finetune a single policy on both data sources, treating each source as equally useful in every state: the policy either absorbs the embodiment error at precision-critical steps or spends scarce robot data relearning free-space motion. We observe that the value of each source depends on the state: human data is useful where precision requirements are low, while robot data is disproportionately valuable near precision-critical states. We therefore propose \textbf{DUO Policy} (Dual-Actor Policy), which decouples a manipulation skill into a hand policy, pretrained on human videos for global free-space motion, and a robot policy, trained on sparse in-hand data for local precise corrections, with a gate learned from human interventions switching between them. This design is robust to moderate embodiment error in human data and generalizes to scene layouts beyond the coverage of the robot data. On tasks such as K-cup coffee making, desk cleanup, and cluttered candy sorting, DUO Policy outperforms the baseline with the highest average success by 12.9 percentage points over four simulated tasks and by 51.7 points over three real-world tasks, and matches robot-only training with 2.75$\times$ less data-collection time. Project Webpage: https://mingxi-jia.github.io/duo_policy_site/
authors: Mingxi Jia, Patton Jiyang Yin, Haojie Huang, Ivy Xiao He, Xuanru Liu, Gefei Liu, Dian Wang, Stefanie Tellex
bullets: Human videos scale data collection but are unreliable for precision-critical actions such as insertion.
The method uses separate hand and robot policies: human-pretrained motion for free-space behavior and robot-trained corrections for precise states.
A gate learned from human interventions switches between policies based on the current state.
The approach handles moderate embodiment error and generalizes beyond robot-data scene layouts.
It improves average success over the strongest baseline by 12.9 points in simulation and 51.7 points in real-world tasks, while matching robot-only training with 2.75× less collection time.

papers.abstract: Generative priors are state-of-the-art for modeling medical images in image reconstruction tasks, but reconstruction with video priors takes tens of seconds to minutes per frame. Latent priors inherit the errors of their autoencoder, the memory of pixel-space whole-frame priors grows with the frame size, and pixel-space patch priors are slow for two reasons. First, their deep networks process every frame at full resolution at every sampling step, even though early steps resolve only low frequencies. Second, their samplers spend many network evaluations per sampling step on overlapping windows, multiple re-noising rounds, or backpropagation through the prior. We introduce TesseraFlow, a complex-valued pixel-space flow prior that reduces the first cost. A global encoder reads a low-resolution view of every frame once per sampling step. A single shallow decoder operates on this view during early steps and on full-resolution space-time tiles during later steps, so no network processes a whole frame at full resolution. Our sampler, ReTile, addresses the second reason. We use randomized grid shifting at every sampling step along with re-noising, which acts as a stochastic gradient instead of computing overlapping tiles, so a single network pass per sampling step suffices. On its own, ReTile speeds up an existing global-context patch prior by 6-9x, and our prior adds a further 3-5x speedup. TesseraFlow reconstructs about one 256x256 frame per second, 20-367x faster than patch and latent video priors, and can match or exceed the best generative baseline on cardiac, brain, and abdominal MRI and lung CT, at a fraction of its GPU time.
authors: Atakan Topcu, Mohammadhossein Momeni, Alfredo De Goyeneche, Michael Lustig
bullets: Addresses the high latency and memory costs of video priors for medical image reconstruction.
Uses a complex-valued pixel-space flow prior with a global low-resolution encoder and a shallow decoder that shifts from low-resolution views to full-resolution space-time tiles.
Introduces ReTile, which uses randomized grid shifting and re-noising to replace overlapping tile evaluations with one network pass per sampling step.
Achieves about one 256×256 frame per second and reports 20–367× speedups over patch and latent video priors.
Matches or exceeds the best generative baseline across cardiac, brain, and abdominal MRI and lung CT while using less GPU time.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate sequences of actions from visual observations, proprioceptive states, and language instructions. In embodied interaction, executing these actions influences subsequent observations and robot states, providing a natural predictive signal for policy learning. However, standard action-supervised fine-tuning does not explicitly capture these action-conditioned temporal dependencies in the guidance consumed by the action predictor. We introduce JEPA-Tuner, a predictive fine-tuning framework that regularizes the VLA's native policy guidance through action-conditioned future prediction. During fine-tuning, a predictor in JEPA-Tuner learns to match guidance encoded from a future observation given the current guidance and committed actions. This objective encourages a cross-modal guidance adapter to capture how the scene and robot state evolve under those actions, while jointly training the action expert on both observed and predicted guidance keeps the representation informative for control. In addition, when deploying the VLA model with asynchronous action-chunk inference, the pre-trained predictor will anticipate the guidance needed at the next chunk boundary. The policy can thus generate the next chunk in advance and execute it from its first action without overlap correction or additional predictor training, enabling efficient and high-quality asynchronous execution. Experiments on LIBERO and Meta-World show that JEPA-Tuner improves task success under synchronous inference with better multi-modal guidance embeddings. For asynchronous control, JEPA-Tuner improves performance and smoothness across different latency settings on both LIBERO simulator and multi-size real robot demonstrations. The project website with video demos is at https://qujx.github.io/JEPA-Tuner-Website.
authors: Jingxiang Qu, Tian Xie, Youngjin Hong, Changhyun Choi, Yang Katie Zhao, Yi Liu
bullets: Addresses the missing modeling of how actions alter future visual observations and robot states during standard VLA fine-tuning.
Trains a predictor to forecast future guidance from current guidance and committed actions, while jointly training the action expert on observed and predicted guidance.
Uses the pretrained predictor at deployment to anticipate guidance at the next action-chunk boundary, allowing execution without overlap correction or extra predictor training.
Improves synchronous task success and multimodal guidance embeddings on LIBERO and Meta-World.
Improves asynchronous-control performance and smoothness across latency settings in LIBERO simulation and real-robot demonstrations.

Figure 2. Predictive fine-tuning and asynchronous execution with JEPA-Tuner. During fine-tuning (bottom), the cross-modal adapter, JEPA predictor, and action expert are trained jointly while the VLM encoder stays frozen. The adapter fuses visual, language, and state embeddings into policy guidance. Given this guidance, the current robot state, and d intervening demonstrated actions, the predictor estimates visual guidance and robot state at t + d. During asynchronous execution (top), the same predictor anticipates guidance at the next chunk boundary. For instance, with chunk size H = 12, execution horizon E = 8, and latency ∆ = 4, inference starts from o5 and uses the committed actions a5, . . . , a8 to predict guidance for step 9. The expert decodes Chunk 2 from this guidance. Its first eight actions, a9, . . . , a16, follow the Chunk 1 immediately without overlap correction.

papers.abstract: Judgments about the beauty of buildings and streets inform architectural design, urban planning, and heritage conservation, yet increasingly rely on scanned 3D models over material fabric. Automatic aesthetic assessment remains largely confined to 2D photographs. We ask what survives when image aesthetic assessment crosses this dimensional gap to produce dense, per-point aesthetic descriptions of heritage and urban point clouds. We examine three routes that sidestep costly, and sometimes ethically dubious, human labeling at scale: (1) lifting scalar scores from image aesthetic models (NIMA, SAAN) onto geometry; (2) training Aesthetic Visual Analysis (AVA) regression heads on frozen vision backbones (DINOv3, TIPS, SigLIP2, PE, RADSeg) or, in a 3D-native variant, a generalist point encoder on feed-forward AVA reconstructions; and (3) querying lifted vision-language features with a natural-language aesthetic label, taking similarity as a score. The two supervised routes transfer poorly: heads fitting AVA in-domain produce architectural class profiles that neither reproduce one another nor track other signals, while the 3D-native probe stays near chance due to reconstruction geometry quality. Text querying is markedly more coherent. Projecting out the class-text direction from point features raises mean cross-model agreement on architectural part profiles from +0.035 to +0.352, and from +0.113 to +0.293 per point; the four backbones passing a semantic sanity check correlate at 0.31-0.73, while the failing one remains an outlier. Since model agreement is not agreement with human aesthetic perception, we detail a part-aware rating protocol to clarify where human and automatic ratings disagree. We provide a reproducible transfer protocol, an account of which pseudo-labeling routes carry signal, and dense aesthetic pseudo-labels meant as hypotheses rather than ground truth.
authors: Sophia Kovalenko, Alexander M. Rusnak, Vittoria Meroni, Yasmine Kroknes-Gomez, Fr\'ed\'eric Kaplan
bullets: The work addresses automatic aesthetic assessment for scanned 3D buildings and streets, extending methods beyond 2D photographs.
It compares image-score lifting, supervised AVA regression heads on frozen vision backbones, a 3D-native probe, and natural-language querying of lifted vision-language features.
Supervised transfer routes perform poorly: their architectural profiles are inconsistent, and the 3D-native probe remains near chance because of reconstruction quality.
Text querying improves cross-model agreement after projecting out the class-text direction, with agreement rising from +0.035 to +0.352 for architectural profiles and from +0.113 to +0.293 per point.
The authors provide a reproducible transfer protocol and a part-aware human-rating protocol to identify disagreements between automatic scores and human perception.

papers.abstract: Image policies are scalable but remain brittle to camera viewpoint changes. On LIBERO, we identify proprioception as an input shortcut: masking robot states sharply degrades several policies, while retraining from images alone recovers much of the loss. We introduce ViewPACT, an image policy trained with privileged geometric supervision. Auxiliary objectives recover end-effector and task-relevant object poses in the camera frame, while deployment requires only RGB observations. Joint geometric supervision improves mean simulation success from 37.4% to 78.4% under unseen external-camera viewpoints, with more modest gains under separately evaluated object, scene, and camera-intrinsic shifts. Across four real-robot tasks, combining simulated and real-image geometric supervision achieves 68.1% mean success, versus 3.1% for fixed-view behavior cloning and 30.6% for the strongest evaluated alternative. These results support geometric supervision for viewpoint robustness in the evaluated fixed-view demonstration setting.
authors: Chenglang Tu, Feng Chen, Ruizhe Liu, Pei Zhou, Binbin Huang, Chen Xu, Yanchao Yang, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
bullets: Image policies can exploit proprioception and degrade under camera viewpoint changes.
Auxiliary objectives predict end-effector and task-relevant object poses in the camera frame.

Across four real-robot tasks, combined simulated and real-image supervision reaches 68.1% mean success; results are scoped to the evaluated fixed-view demonstration setting.

papers.abstract: A diffusion language sampler makes two choices for every position in its denoising window: where the next token comes from, and when the position is committed to the KV cache. Using the entropy-bound sampler in DiffusionGemma, we study two extremes of the second choice. Committing each token as soon as it is accepted removes the chance to revise it, which hurts when the entropy bound is relaxed to trade accuracy for speed. When accepted tokens are frozen, macro accuracy falls from 73% to 20% as the bound is relaxed, while the unfrozen sampler stays near 70%. Committing a whole block at once wastes computation, since tokens converge in a largely left-to-right order and more than half of the window holds already-final tokens by twenty denoising steps. These findings motivate the Rolling Entropy Sampler (RES), which commits a contiguous accepted prefix once it reaches a minimum length and keeps positions farther ahead open to revision. Unlike earlier rolling samplers, RES runs on uniform diffusion, where accepted tokens can still change, and it needs no training. Across seven benchmarks, RES increases tokens per forward pass from 19.3 to 25.5, while macro accuracy goes from 80.7% to 78.8%, and it extends the speed-quality Pareto frontier beyond what tuning the entropy bound alone reaches.
authors: Patrick Pynadath, Nicolas Perez-Nieves, Bobak Shahriari, Jean Tarbouriech, Ruqi Zhang, Ivan Lobov
bullets: Immediate commitment harms quality when the entropy bound is relaxed, whereas leaving tokens revisable maintains accuracy.
Committing entire blocks wastes computation because tokens typically converge in a left-to-right order.
RES commits a contiguous accepted prefix after it reaches a minimum length and keeps later positions open for revision.
Across seven benchmarks, RES raises tokens per forward pass from 19.3 to 25.5, with macro accuracy decreasing from 80.7% to 78.8%.
RES requires no training and extends the speed–quality Pareto frontier beyond entropy-bound tuning alone.

figures.caption: Figure 3 | Columns in the top and middle rows show LiveCodeBench, GPQA Diamond, and Natural2Code. Top row: Spearman 𝜌 and Kendall 𝜏 between the acceptance order of the DiffusionGemma EB sampler and the AR generation order; across all tasks the sampler is strongly biased towards left-to-right order. Middle row: Percentage of wasted denoising slots averaged across canvases for LCB v6, GPQA Diamond and Natural2Code. For a given sampling step, a slot is wasted if it belongs to a contiguous prefix that has already converged to its final token. By denoising step 20, the mean fraction of wasted canvas slots exceeds 50% on all three tasks. Bottom row: Accepted tokens are revised more often at higher entropy bounds (in both argmax and sampled-token stability), independent of renoising.

Figure 4 | Three passes of the rolling sampler. Every pass spends a fixed budget of ten positions (dashed frame), split between an encoded prefix of the tokens committed on the previous pass and the remaining denoising window; the mask panel on the right is exactly that block of ten. Left: positions keep their column, so each slot can be read down its column. Out-of-order acceptances wait for a contiguous prefix (w at 𝑡) and unaccepted slots stay mutable (column ten: r→ o). The prefix completing at 𝑡+1 is four slots long, so four slots must be encoded at 𝑡+2: the block advances by however many positions graduated into the KV cache, and the split is 0+10, then 2+8, then 4+6. Right: rows are queries, columns are keys; a coloured cell means the query attends to the key. The encoded prefix is causal, so its KV-cache entries depend only on committed tokens and are never revised, while denoising positions are bidirectional among themselves and attend fully to the prefix. Committing more positions per pass therefore moves the KV cache forward faster, but leaves fewer positions to denoise on the next pass. Every query additionally attends to the whole KV cache (white cells), which the panels omit for space.

Figure 1 | (a) The unified stopping criterion matches the original at a slight speedup. (b) Simulation of per-position commitment in DiffusionGemma: freezing each token upon acceptance removes the chance for later revision. Frozen variants degrade much faster than unfrozen variants as the entropy bound is relaxed, showing the cost of losing this sampler flexibility.

Figure 2 | Where the denoising slots go. Both samplers denoise a width-8 window per pass in the same order, and the colours are those of Figure 4: teal = still denoising, amber = accepted on this pass, white = already encoded and in the KV cache, gray = not yet admitted. Brick marks a slot spent re-denoising a position that was already accepted but is still waiting for its prefix, that is, wasted work. (a) The block sampler appends only once the block is fully resolved, so converged positions idle and each block re-pays warm-up. (b) The rolling sampler appends the accepted prefix immediately and admits fresh positions in its place, wasting far fewer slots.

(6)), 𝐴𝜏 the confidence set, ℓ(𝐴) the longest accepted prefix, 𝐴<𝑡 the positions accepted at earlier steps. papers.abstract: Personalized LLM agents rely on an agent harness, the surrounding memory and control code, to connect user history with downstream decisions. Existing methods typically employ either a single shared memory workflow across all users, which is efficient to deploy but cannot adapt how evidence is retrieved and interpreted across diverse histories, or per-user harness optimization, which customizes behavior for each user but requires costly repeated candidate evaluation at deployment and suffers from sparse, noisy supervision in raw logs. To address this trade-off, we present HyperHarness, a framework that learns a shared history-to-harness generator to synthesize executable, user-specific retrieval and answer-guidance code directly from user histories. Given a user's permitted history, HyperHarness prompts a construction LLM to write personalized retrieval and guidance functions, while downstream task scores across training users supervise iterative refinements to the shared generator without reference harnesses or answering-model updates. At deployment, the frozen generator constructs a harness for each unseen user in a single pass from history alone, eliminating per-user task-scored search. Across three benchmarks (PersonaMemv3, Mem-PAL, and MemoryCD) and three answering models (Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.8-27B, and GPT-5.6-Luna), HyperHarness achieves the highest aggregate score in seven of nine settings and ranks second in the remaining two, improving over the strongest baselines by up to 5.95 points while cutting matched answer-time tokens by 90.32% over long-context prompting. Analyses show that optimization tailors context allocation to each executor, transfers to unseen user clusters, and amortizes adaptation costs.

Analysis suggests the method adapts context allocation to executors, transfers across unseen user clusters, and amortizes adaptation costs.

papers.abstract: Real-world point clouds are not naturally bounded: 3D scans grow as sensors move through rooms, LiDAR surveys extend across forest plots, and 4D captures can span thousands of frames. Yet most point-cloud encoders are designed for fixed-size inputs, forcing inference-time cropping or tiling that loses long-range context and requires ad-hoc output stitching. We formulate arbitrary-extent point-cloud segmentation as recurrent sequence-of-chunks processing and introduce PoinTTT, a recurrent point-cloud encoder built on Point Transformer V3 (PTv3). PoinTTT augments PTv3 with residual Large Chunk Test-Time Training (LaCT) layers in both the encoder and decoder. Each LaCT layer maintains compact fast weights as recurrent state: tokens from each chunk update the fast weights, which are then applied to produce chunk features and passed to the next chunk. This design allows PoinTTT to train on fixed-size chunks while processing scenes of arbitrary spatial or temporal extent, with activation memory bounded by the chunk size. A pilot study on ScanNet and nuScenes shows that recurrent TTT improves segmentation over PTv3 baselines. On FOR-instanceV2, PoinTTT achieves state-of-the-art forest semantic segmentation of 87.9 mIoU with nearly constant memory. On HOI4D, online full-sequence recurrent inference carries state across clips rather than resetting at benchmark boundaries, reaching 42.6 mIoU; a matched full-sequence Mamba control reaches approximately 39.9. These results suggest that test-time training is a practical primitive for scalable spatial and temporal point-cloud understanding.
authors: Wentao Zhou, Xuweiyi Chen, Charles Saunders, Aruni RoyChowdhury, Zezhou Cheng
bullets: Addresses fixed-input limits that otherwise require cropping, tiling, and output stitching, which can lose long-range context.
Extends Point Transformer V3 with residual Large Chunk Test-Time Training layers in both encoder and decoder.
Processes chunks sequentially: tokens update recurrent fast weights, which generate features for the current chunk and carry state forward.
Pilot results show improved segmentation over PTv3; PoinTTT reaches 87.9 mIoU on FOR-instanceV2 with nearly constant memory.
On HOI4D, carrying state across clips achieves 42.6 mIoU versus approximately 39.9 for a matched full-sequence Mamba control.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Qualitative comparison between PoinTTT and PTv3. Two examples per dataset show semantic predictions and ground truth; red boxes mark enlarged regions. PoinTTT (Ours) reduces chunk-boundary artifacts on (a) ScanNet [10], better preserves tilted trunks and irregular branches on (b) FOR-instanceV2 [53], and more clearly separates moving objects from the background on (c) HOI4D [28].

Figure 2. PoinTTT uses recurrent fast weights for unified spatial and temporal point-cloud inference. Each step processes one spatial or temporal chunk with a shared PTv3-based [50] backbone augmented by a residual LaCT [60] block. LaCT maps chunk features Ht to Q,K, V , updates fast weights from Wt−1 to Wt using K,V , and applies the updated weights to Q. The readout is normalized and linearly projected before being added to Ht through the gate tanh(λ). Solid arrows denote causal propagation for temporal streams, while dashed reverse arrows indicate bidirectional propagation over spatial chunks. The resulting compact recurrent state enables large-scene and streaming 4D inference without storing full-scene activations.

Table 4. Ablations of recurrent aggregation and model design. Metrics are percentages except (i). Panels (a)–(g) use FOR-instanceV2; (h)–(i) use ScanNet. Panel (a) disables aggregation in training and evaluation; (b) matches total training epochs. In (d)–(g), † marks the default. Random membership removes within-chunk spatial coherence. Panel (i) compares full-scene PTv3 with chunked PoinTTT.

Table 3. Semantic segmentation on HOI4D. † marks published offline supervised results from PointNet4D [30], Table 9; P4Mamba is its online result from Table 7. PTv3 uses fixed windows; PTv3+Mamba and PoinTTT share the PTv3 backbone and fullvideo streaming protocol.

Table 1. Pilot results on ScanNet with 10,240-point chunked inference and on nuScenes with single-pass evaluation without TTA. The training-input setting applies to both datasets. PointMamba [26] is a point-cloud state-space baseline; recurrent PoinTTT improves under the same bounded-memory protocol.
Table 2. Semantic segmentation on the FOR-instanceV2 test split. Best results are in bold, second-best are underlined.
