papers.title: Recurrent Point Transformer via Test-Time Training
papers.tldr: PoinTTT enables point-cloud segmentation over arbitrarily long spatial or temporal sequences by recurrently updating compact test-time weights while keeping memory bounded by chunk size.

papers.abstract: Conventional geometric measures of visual representations are symmetric, assigning equal costs to forward and reverse motion along the same path. We propose DiRGeo, a framework for learning directional geometry over frozen visual representations. Grounded in Randers geometry, DiRGeo learns a state-dependent directional field from ordered image trajectories through self-supervised contrast, without semantic labels. Sphere-tangent correction and attractor-relative decomposition distinguish learned directional structure from normalization artifacts and common convergence. Experiments across 17 visual processes, three encoder families, and multiple representation depths demonstrate consistent directional discrimination and whole-path asymmetry beyond simple attractor-based explanations. The learned fields become increasingly process-specific in deeper representations, while natural-video experiments reveal event-dependent directional preferences. As functional validation, DiRGeo guides restoration selection. These results establish directional geometry as a useful complement to symmetric representation analysis.
authors: Muhammad Ahtesham, Xin Zhong
bullets: Addresses the limitation of symmetric geometric measures, which treat forward and reverse paths identically.
Uses Randers geometry, self-supervised contrast, and state-dependent directional fields to model visual-process directionality.
Sphere-tangent correction and attractor-relative decomposition separate directional structure from normalization artifacts and shared convergence.
Across 17 visual processes, three encoder families, and multiple depths, it finds consistent whole-path asymmetry that becomes more process-specific in deeper representations.
Event-dependent directional preferences in natural videos and restoration-selection guidance demonstrate practical functional value.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Learning directional geometry from ordered trajectories. (a) Opposite motions on a representation manifold can have different costs. (b) A lightweight network learns a bounded Randers wind over frozen features; sphere-tangent correction removes normalization artifacts during evaluation. (c) Directional contrast favors observed motion over reversed, shuffled, and random alternatives, regularized by smoothness and multi-step consistency.

Figure 8. Whole-path asymmetry across visual processes and representations. Sphere-projected R/ρ for all 17 trajectory families and 10 encoder representations, grouped by global appearance transformations, object-level processes, and matched controls. Points are averaged over three training seeds, with pointwise 95% source-image bootstrap confidence intervals. All intervals lie above zero, indicating lower accumulated forward cost. The magnitude varies substantially across processes and representation depths.

The dashed line marks the 12.5% randomselection reference for eight candidates. Adding other-process sink penalties substantially reduces overcorrection, while the learned own-process term improves exact-inverse selection over the matched sink reference. (a) Object-level processes: INSERT, ENTER, GROW, and COLOUR. (b) Matched controls: Insert-blob, Insert-scramble, Insert-blur, Grow-blob, and Enter-blob. Figure 1. Directional geometry of visual representations. Left: Forward and reverse visual trajectories can have different costs despite sharing the same states. Middle: A state-dependent wind defines local directional preferences. Right: The learned ruler distinguishes opposite motions and guides visual restoration.

Figure 5. Representative visual trajectories. Left to right: progressive Gaussian blur (global appearance), bus entering (objectlevel), matched blob control, and cat approaching (natural video). Each column shows three ordered states, top to bottom. Controlled trajectories train the geometry; natural video tests transfer without adaptation. Further examples and construction details appear in the appendix. Representations and training. We use three frozen encoders with different pretraining objectives: CLIP ViTB/16 [17], DINOv2 ViT-B/14 [15], and a supervised ViTB/16 [6]. We extract CLS features after blocks 4, 8, and 12, together with CLIP’s projected image embedding, yielding 10 representations and 170 family–representation combinations. All features are ℓ2-normalized. For each combination, we train a separate three-layer wind network with hidden width 512 and norm bound ρ = 0.9 for 30 epochs using three random seeds. Training uses ordered trajectories without semantic class labels. Results are averaged over three seeds, with 95% confidence intervals obtained by bootstrapping source images (2,000 resamples); full evaluation protocols

Both geometric scores share other-process penalties. The fitted sink overcorrects (23.6 dB), while DiRGeo selects the exact inverse (53.2 dB). Clean references are used only for evaluation; aggregate results appear in Table 5, with further examples in the appendix.
Figure 3. Sphere-tangent correction. Both the observed displacement and the bounded learned wind are projected onto the sphere’s tangent space, removing radial components.

Figure 13. Identical endpoints, different visual journeys. Figure 12. Additional colour-correction examples across four degradation families. Rows show red, cyan, blue, and yellow casts. Columns show the degraded image, correction selected by the fitted spherical sink with other-process penalties, correction selected by DiRGeo with the same penalties, and the clean reference. PSNR values are displayed beneath the first three images in each row. DiRGeo selects the more accurate correction in these examples, illustrating its ability to distinguish candidate paths beyond the fitted attractor. Figure 9. Process-specific fields become less aligned with depth. Mean cosine similarities among INSERT, GROW, and ENTER fields across L4, L8, and L12 in CLIP, DINOv2, and supervised ViT. Solid lines show full fields; dashed lines show sink-removed residuals. All comparisons use identical evaluation states and average three seeds. Both full and residual field similarities decrease with depth.
Figure 4. Sink–residual decomposition. The learned tangent field separates into a sinkaligned component and an orthogonal residual.

Table 6. Aggregate sphere-tangent directional accuracy (%). Global appearance rows average eight transformation families; object-dataset rows average four object-level processes and five matched controls. Results are averaged over three training seeds. L4, L8, and L12 denote transformer-block features, and the CLIP embedding is its projected image representation. All accuracies use 50% as the chance reference.

Table 7. Per-family sphere-tangent reverse accuracy (%). Held-out evaluation averaged over three training seeds. Reverse discrimination compares each observed displacement with its negation at the same state; 50% is the chance reference. All 170 pointwise 95% confidence intervals lie above chance, with a minimum lower bound of 62.4%. Individual intervals are omitted for compactness.

Table 8. Per-family sphere-tangent shuffled accuracy (%). Held-out evaluation averaged over three training seeds. Shuffled alternatives are length-matched displacements sampled from other test images of the same process family. All 170 pointwise 95% confidence intervals lie above the 50% chance reference, with a minimum lower bound of 54.2%. Individual intervals are omitted for compactness.

Table 5. Colour-correction selection on 200 held-out images. Top-1 accuracy identifies the highest-PSNR candidate across four casts. MUSIQ, BRISQUE, and NIQE are noreference quality estimators; nearest-to-degraded and random are sanity checks. Clean references are used only for evaluation.

Table 3. Process-dependent directional fields. Mean cosine similarity between INSERT and ENTER fields at identical states, before (βtan θ ) and after (δβ) sink removal. L4, L8, and L12 denote transformer-block features. Values near one indicate alignment; near zero, orthogonality. Both similarities decrease with depth across encoders. Accumulated asymmetry depends on the process and the observed event. Global appearance transformations exhibit greater whole-path asymmetry (R/ρ = 0.129–0.962) than object-level processes (0.014–0.413) within each representation. Matched controls often produce comparable or stronger asymmetry than real-object processes, showing that directional strength alone does not establish semantic dependence. We further test whether these preferences transfer to natural video, where chronological order need not correspond to the direction learned from a particular photo-editing process.

Table 4. Event-dependent directionality in natural video. Wholepath R/ρ from photo-trained fields evaluated without adaptation on 10-state video windows (0.2 s stride), averaged over 10 representations and three seeds. Positive and negative values favor forward and reverse traversal, respectively.

Table 9. Learned field versus the field-fitted spherical sink. Sphere-tangent shuffled-accuracy differences ∆local in percentage points across all 170 configurations, averaged over three training seeds. Positive values favor the learned field. Table 10. Predictive directional structure after sink removal. Sphere-tangent shuffled accuracy (%) of the orthogonal residual δβ(z), evaluated without retraining and averaged over three seeds. Table 12. Sink-aligned energy across representations. Mean Qsink (%) over held-out states, measuring the squared projection of βtan θ (z) onto the fitted sink axis relative to total field energy. The quantity is unsigned: it measures axis alignment rather than convergence toward the attractor. L4, L8, and L12 denote transformer-block features; Emb. is the projected CLIP image embedding.

All values are positive, with every pointwise 95% confidence interval above zero. Larger values indicate greater relative preference for forward traversal.

Table 41. Representation-specific directional preference margins and reciprocal rates. Mean learned-field margins are reported alongside reciprocal preference rates for the learned field and the fitted sink. All 10 representations have positive mean margins under both the original and unseen journey constructions, although reciprocal rates vary substantially across representations.

Table 21. Per-video event asymmetry. Sphere-projected R/ρ at a 0.2 s stride, averaged over 10 representations and three seeds. Multiple annotated intervals of the same event within a video are grouped together. The number of contributing windows is reported to indicate the support underlying each mean.

Table 32. Final restoration-selection confirmation outcomes. A representation-level criterion is satisfied only when at least 8/10 paired confidence intervals lie above zero. The learned and fitted-sink scores use identical other-process penalties unless stated otherwise. Top-1 gains are percentage points; percentile and Spearman gains are differences in their respective metrics.

Table 1. Directional discrimination and whole-path asymmetry. Ranges over family–representation combinations, averaged across three seeds. In all 170 cases, pointwise 95% confidence intervals exceed 50% for both accuracies and zero for R/ρ. 4.3. Beyond a Common Attractor We next ask whether the learned directional preferences can be explained simply by motion toward a common destination in representation space. We examine this explanation through two complementary tests.

Insert–Blob, Grow–Blob, and Enter–Blob compare each object-level process with its matched blob-control field. The 30 cases comprise 10 representations and three whole-video strides. Reverse accuracy uses sphere-tangent comparisons; path ranges and confidence counts use the original chord-based evaluation.

Table 42. Directional margins for the qualitative examples. All values are pooled over 10 representations and three wind seeds. Positive values indicate that each field favors its corresponding journey. The selected examples illustrate the effect; the full 200- image confirmation provides the statistical evidence.

Table 36. Cases satisfying the predefined category-effect criterion. A case passes when its five-split mean Dcat is positive and at least four of five split effects are positive. papers.abstract: Collaborative agents joining an ongoing team rely on shared context to connect multi-party interaction histories with downstream coordination decisions. Existing work typically focuses either on retrieving historical facts from conversation logs, which surfaces isolated evidence without capturing who knows or owns what, or on evaluating end-to-end interactions, which conflates preparation with execution and lacks direct supervision because a team's history has no single ground-truth summary. To bridge this gap, we formulate group briefing, the task of reconstructing task-relevant group cognition across participants' expressed beliefs, group dynamics, and grounding gaps, and introduce a four-domain benchmark of 1,351 requests and 9,975 verified reference points paired with a two-stage evaluation pipeline combining reference-point coverage and downstream collaboration simulation. Using this pipeline, we show that GroupBrief, a simple task-guided approach that iteratively probes the message history and synthesizes a structured brief without offline memory indexing or graph construction, outperforms ten retrieval and agent-memory baselines in overall coverage with gpt-5.4-mini, while benchmarking nine language models reveals that prospective friction remains harder to recover than past state across model scales. We further use reference-point coverage as a feedback signal for harness optimization, refining GroupBrief's retrieval and synthesis instructions while keeping model weights frozen. On held-out Test projects, GroupBrief (optimized) improves coverage by 2.54 percentage points for gpt-5.4-mini and 12.88 for gpt-5.6-luna, achieving 64.46% and 68.42% preference over no brief in downstream simulations. These results establish our benchmark and evaluation pipeline as a foundation for measuring and optimizing how collaborative agents ground in group cognition.
authors: Zhaoxuan Tan, Mengting Wan, Jingbo Yang, Kwei-Herng Lai, Renyi Qu, Lorenzo Jaime Flores, Meng Jiang, Longqi Yang, Victor Poznanski, Pei Zhou
bullets: Defines group briefing as recovering participants’ beliefs, group dynamics, and grounding gaps—not merely retrieving historical facts.
Introduces a four-domain benchmark with 1,351 requests and 9,975 verified reference points, evaluated through coverage and downstream collaboration simulation.
GroupBrief iteratively probes message histories and synthesizes structured briefs without offline memory indexing or graph construction.
It outperforms ten retrieval and agent-memory baselines in overall coverage with gpt-5.4-mini; prospective friction remains harder to recover than past state.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) generators produce detailed images but remain slow at inference. Speculative decoding can reduce this cost, yet its behavior across the rendering requirements of T2I prompts remains insufficiently understood. We introduce T2ISpec, a benchmark of 1,400 prompts balanced across seven rendering topics and two difficulty levels. It evaluates autoregressive and diffusion/flow accelerators by latency, work performed by the target model, and image quality. Our study reveals three key findings: (1) aggregate results hide large differences between topics, (2) alignment and preference scores can disagree with prompt constraint satisfaction, and (3) large reductions in target work can yield limited latency gains. Motivated by these findings, we propose TopicRoute, a plugin that combines prompt routing with speculative and cache controls without retraining the generator. Across six model--method pairs, it achieves a geometric mean speedup of 1.0308x over the native methods, and the speedup carries over to external prompts with the same settings, while quality gains and losses vary across configurations.
authors: Yifan Zhang, Shatong Zhu, Hui Shen, Yunta Hsieh, Jianing Ma, Muxin Fu, Xin Wang, Ping Zhang, Qian Chen, Chaofan Tao
bullets: Benchmarks 1,400 prompts spanning seven rendering topics and two difficulty levels.
Evaluates autoregressive and diffusion/flow accelerators using latency, target-model work, and image quality.
Finds that aggregate scores can hide topic differences, preference metrics may miss prompt-constraint satisfaction, and reduced target work does not always improve latency.
TopicRoute combines prompt routing with speculative and cache controls across six model–method pairs.
Reports a 1.0308× geometric-mean speedup over native methods, with configuration-dependent quality changes and transfer to external prompts.

papers.abstract: As with conventional AI agents, a common source of misalignment between Large Language Models (LLMs) and their human users is misspecified goals. Often, this happens when the human has skewed beliefs about the system's model and provides it with information that causes behavior different from what they expected, with potentially unwanted side effects. To ensure goal alignment, one solution would be for the LLM to ask the human questions about their objectives. However, it has been well-documented that LLMs most often provide default responses to user requests rather than try and ask questions to clarify their true intent. In this paper, we address these challenges by adapting a novel formulation for the objective misspecification problem to work with LLMs. We then test if LLMs that are prompted to ask questions about a user's true underlying objectives are better at identifying them compared to those that do not. We evaluate our method using four state-of-the-art LLMs tested on five standard IPC domains, showing that for some domains, asking questions greatly improved model performance.
authors: Kelsey Sikes, Sarath Sreedharan
bullets: Addresses goal misalignment caused by misspecified objectives and users’ inaccurate beliefs about LLM behavior.
Adapts a formulation of objective misspecification to LLM-based agents.
Tests whether prompting models to clarify users’ true objectives improves intent identification.
Evaluates four state-of-the-art LLMs across five standard IPC domains.
Question-asking substantially improves performance in some domains, though gains are domain-dependent.

papers.abstract: Avatars created from a single photo are fixed once made: regions the photo never showed, such as the back of a garment, are hallucinated and remain that way. We present Refreshable Animatable Gaussian Avatars (RAGA), a full-body Gaussian avatar that is created from a single image in about one second and can be refreshed whenever new images of the same person become available, without retraining or gradient-based optimization. RAGA maps each new observation into canonical UV space, accumulates it as visibility- and angle-weighted running sums, and re-decodes the fused map with the same decoder used for the photo. Although this decoder is trained only on single images, it makes use of the fused evidence. On 163 clips from five datasets, RAGA created from one photo outperforms LHM, LHM++ and IDOL, including on three datasets never used in training. Refreshing from later frames adds 0.49 dB PSNR overall and 0.68 dB on views turned at least 135{\deg} from the photo, where SSIM and LPIPS also improve. Given the same 16 images on all clips, LHM++ gains 0.15 dB, against 0.48 dB for RAGA. Creating an avatar takes 1.08 s and animating it 48.1 ms per frame on a laptop RTX 3080 GPU, with body fitting and matting included in creation and pose estimation included in animation. Code will be released on GitHub.
authors: Sadia Mubashshira, John Quarles, Kevin Desai
bullets: Addresses fixed, hallucinated unseen regions in single-photo avatars, such as the back of clothing.
Maps new observations into canonical UV space, fuses them using visibility- and viewing-angle weighting, and re-decodes the result with the original decoder.
Evaluated on 163 clips across five datasets, including three unseen during training; it outperforms LHM, LHM++, and IDOL from a single photo.
Refreshing with later frames improves reconstruction quality, especially for views turned far from the original photo.
Runs in 1.08 seconds for creation and 48.1 ms per animation frame on an RTX 3080 laptop GPU.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is one of the most popular post-training paradigms for large language models. RLVR typically trains a single model under hyperparameters chosen before training begins, while researchers tune hyperparameters across consecutive runs. We introduce Population-Based Post-Training (PBPT), which trains several models in parallel and lets the training process do the tuning through population-based training. PBPT periodically evaluates models on a validation set. High-performers are duplicated and their hyperparameters perturbed to explore new configurations. Low-performers stop training and are replaced by these copies. On reasoning benchmarks (Enigmata, Nemotron) and interactive tool-use environments (Gaia2, AppWorld), PBPT produces stronger agents than compute-matched groups of independent RLVR learners. Furthermore, PBPT is able to recover from poor initial hyperparameters, automatically discovering better settings over the course of training.
authors: Yixuan Even Xu, Aleksei Petrenko, Raja Giryes, Jackson Hamburger, Kevin Chen, Fei Fang, J. Zico Kolter, Philipp Kr\"ahenb\"uhl
bullets: RLVR commonly trains one model with hyperparameters fixed before training, requiring manual tuning across runs.
PBPT trains a population of models in parallel and periodically evaluates them on validation performance.
High-performing models are copied with perturbed hyperparameters, while low-performing models are replaced.
It outperforms compute-matched independent RLVR learners on reasoning and interactive tool-use benchmarks.
PBPT can recover from poor initial hyperparameter choices by discovering better settings during training.

papers.abstract: Min-of-K (MoK) training is widely used to train models that produce diverse outputs from random noise. For each target, it draws K outputs from the model and backpropagates only through the one closest to the target. However, MoK generally does not make the generated distribution match the data distribution. In this paper, we analyze the MoK bias across all values of K and show that tuning K shifts between failure modes, from mode dropping at small K to distribution flattening at large K. We further prove that every nontrivial loss based only on target-candidate distances fails to recover some data distribution, since these distances do not reveal how the candidates are placed relative to each other. Based on these analyses, we propose mirrored MoK (MMoK), a drop-in modification of MoK training that draws one extra sample from the model, applies the closest-candidate selection rule against it, and subtracts the resulting distance. Since this distance is measured between samples of the model, it provides additional information about how the candidates are placed relative to each other. We prove that MMoK can in principle recover data distributions that MoK cannot. We empirically validate MMoK on five scenarios, namely synthetic mixtures, pedestrian and vehicle trajectory prediction, tropical cyclone forecasting, robotic policy learning, and ambiguous medical image segmentation. The results confirm the effectiveness and generality of MMoK in both distribution learning and task performance.
authors: Jiaru Zhang, Zeyun Deng, Hyunsoo Yun, Yupeng Zhou, Bingyao Du, Juntong Peng, Zichong Yang, Can Cui, Chuheng Wei, Ruqi Zhang, Ziran Wang
bullets: MoK can shift from mode dropping at small K to distribution flattening at large K, without generally matching the data distribution.
Distance-only objectives cannot recover every data distribution because they ignore how generated candidates relate to one another.
MMoK adds one extra model sample and subtracts a closest-candidate distance measured between model samples.
Theoretical analysis shows MMoK can recover distributions that standard MoK cannot.
Experiments across five synthetic and real-world scenarios support its effectiveness for distribution learning and task performance.

papers.abstract: The decay exponent $\alpha$ in KV-cache eviction is an intrinsic property of the model: calibrated once on a single corpus, it transfers directly across domains. Attention-based accumulation (H2O) and recency-based sliding windows (StreamingLLM) are two dominant eviction frameworks, often treated as unrelated, but we show that they are the two endpoints of a single power-law family: by scoring each token as $s_i = A_i \cdot (t-i)^{-\alpha}$, where $A_i$ is cumulative attention and $\alpha$ controls the age penalty, H2O and StreamingLLM correspond to $\alpha=0$ and $\alpha\to\infty$, respectively (with StreamingLLM additionally hard-coding an attention-sink patch). The no-hair mechanism of \citet{xiang2026nohair} bounds the admissible range of $\alpha$, and the measured exponents agree: calibrating once on WikiText yields $[0.556, 0.822]$ for a representative model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct). The per-model ranges are consistent across five models (410M--1.5B) and independently match the optimal regions from perplexity sweeps. \textsc{NoHairCache} achieves the lowest perplexity across three datasets (WikiText, PG19, and arXiv) without per-dataset tuning, outperforming both H2O and StreamingLLM ($p < 0.05$ on all three datasets, with $0.06$--$0.10$ PPL gains over StreamingLLM at budget $512$). On downstream four-way multiple-choice QA, it matches or outperforms StreamingLLM across all nine (task, budget) cells, retaining $98.2\%$ of full-cache accuracy on NarrativeQA at $25\%$ retention versus $91.1\%$ for StreamingLLM; per-cell McNemar tests are not significant, so QA is corroborating only. We release our calibration script and drop-in scorer upon publication.
authors: Shuyang Xiang
bullets: Frames H2O and StreamingLLM as endpoints of a shared score: cumulative attention weighted by token age via exponent α.
Calibrating α on WikiText produces model-consistent ranges that also align with perplexity-based optimal regions across five models.
Achieves the lowest perplexity on WikiText, PG19, and arXiv without per-dataset tuning, outperforming H2O and StreamingLLM.
Matches or exceeds StreamingLLM on all evaluated QA task–budget cells; QA results are treated as corroborating because per-cell tests are not significant.
The approach is scoped to calibrated model-specific exponent ranges and is accompanied by a calibration script and drop-in scorer.

papers.title: NoHairCache: Calibrate-Once KV Cache Eviction with One Power-Law Exponent

papers.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) has been widely adopted in autoregressive (AR) models for high-quality image generation. Despite its strong empirical performance, its mechanism in AR models remains unclear. This paper demystifies the mechanism of CFG through both empirical and theoretical studies. By examining the top-ranked semantics of different components in CFG, we show that texture information is primarily encoded in the difference between the conditional and unconditional logits, whereas both logits share previous-token repetition as their leading semantics. This strong repetition semantics obscures the desired texture information, causing greedy decoding from the conditional logits alone to produce nearly pure-color images. Through a training-dynamics analysis of shallow transformers, we prove that this shared repetition semantics does not arise from limitations or failures of pretraining, but instead originates from the texture sparsity of images. We further show that CFG improves generation quality by rectifying this repetition bias during inference. Motivated by the shared semantics between conditional and unconditional logits, we propose Attention Weight Reuse (AttnReuse), which reuses intermediate attention computations from the conditional-logit forward pass to accelerate the unconditional-logit computation. AttnReuse reduces about $25\%$ of attention computation with little performance degradation across different models.
authors: Zhiling Zhou, Jiachun Pan, Fengzhuo Zhang, Dirk Bergemann, Zhuoran Yang
bullets: CFG’s conditional and unconditional logits both strongly encode previous-token repetition; their difference primarily captures texture information.
Greedy decoding from conditional logits alone can yield nearly pure-color images because repetition semantics obscure texture.
Theoretical and empirical analyses attribute this shared repetition bias to image texture sparsity, not pretraining failure.
CFG improves quality by rectifying the repetition bias during inference.
Attention Weight Reuse cuts about 25% of attention computation with little performance degradation across models.

figures.caption: Figure 7: Overview of the proof. (1) Training WV makes text and background tokens favor background repetition, while feature tokens favor feature repetition. (2) Training WQK makes the conditional branch attend to text when predicting the first feature token. Inside the block, both branches attend to earlier feature tokens. (3) CFG uses the logit difference to generate the first feature token. Repetition then completes the feature block; without CFG, generation repeats the background.

Figure 8: Illustration of the proposed AttnReuse method. In selected layers, we reuse conditional attention weights by masking out text-token entries and renormalizing over image tokens. We then apply these weights to the conditional value vectors to approximate the unconditional attention output.

papers.abstract: Multi-step retrieval over long contexts is a key capability for retrieval-augmented generation, but strong existing approaches are costly and complex to train. Supervised retrievers are far simpler and cheaper, yet they fall well behind in this setting. We show that this gap stems not from supervised training itself, but from three misalignments between training and inference: easy training negatives, noisy retrieval prefixes, and position-agnostic scoring. Guided by this analysis, we introduce S$^2$LMR, a simple yet effective supervised sequential retriever that models multi-step retrieval as the evolution of an explicit textual state encoded by a single shared Transformer. On long-context reasoning, multi-hop QA, and needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks with context lengths ranging from 4K to 10M tokens, S$^2$LMR achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, substantially outperforming prior supervised retrievers. Notably, it requires only $\sim$2 hours of training on a single A6000 for contexts of up to 10M tokens, while remaining robust across a wide range of hyperparameter settings.
authors: Qiang Hu, Kaiyi Ji
bullets: Identifies three training–inference misalignments: easy negatives, noisy retrieval prefixes, and position-agnostic scoring.
Models multi-step retrieval as the evolution of an explicit textual state using one shared Transformer.
Performs well on long-context reasoning, multi-hop QA, and needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks from 4K to 10M tokens.
Achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods while substantially outperforming prior supervised retrievers.
Trains in about 2 hours on a single A6000 for contexts up to 10M tokens and is robust across hyperparameters.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of S2LMR, which performs sequential multi-hop retrieval with a shared biencoder. During training (blue), gold chunks provide per-hop supervision; during inference (orange), S2LMR greedily selects and appends the highest-scoring chunk.

papers.abstract: Modern monocular hand estimators recover detailed 3D meshes from individual images, yet effectively leveraging their predictions across multiple views remains challenging. Independently predicted meshes can disagree in scale, placement, and articulation, limiting the integration of complementary multi-view information. Hence, we present AlignHand, a calibrated multi-view framework that builds on a frozen monocular hand reconstruction prior to align and enhance its predictions. Specifically, AlignHand refines cross-view joint observations and estimates their reliability to establish a shared metric reference for alignment. Once the meshes are brought into a common frame, their complementary surface evidence is selectively fused across anatomical regions, followed by pixel-aligned refinement that predicts bounded residual displacements from local image features. This global-to-local integration enables AlignHand to exploit complementary observations while preserving the strong monocular prior. Extensive experiments on DexYCB-MV, HanCo, and HO3D-Eval-MV demonstrate that AlignHand achieves the lowest MPVPE and MPJPE among the compared methods under the respective evaluation protocols, reducing MPVPE by 30.1%, 29.1%, and 8.0%, respectively, compared with a matched geometry baseline.
authors: Zhilu Yang, Kun Yang, Shiyan Wang, Anqi Xu, Xinran Huang, Yizheng Jiao, Huan Yang, Rolandos Alexandros Potamias
bullets: Addresses inconsistencies in independently predicted meshes across scale, placement, and articulation.
Refines cross-view joints and estimates their reliability to establish a shared metric reference.
Fuses aligned surface evidence by anatomical region, then applies pixel-aligned bounded residual refinement.
Evaluated on DexYCB-MV, HanCo, and HO3D-Eval-MV, achieving the lowest reported MPVPE and MPJPE among compared methods.
Reduces MPVPE by 30.1%, 29.1%, and 8.0% versus a matched geometry baseline under the respective protocols.

papers.abstract: Marine robots face partial observability, non-stationary dynamics, and sparse communication, motivating WMs that learn compact predictive states for planning. This review develops a functional taxonomy of WMs for ocean engineering, focusing on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) and AdaJEPA's test-time adaptation within model predictive control, mapping them to navigation, adaptive sampling, digital twins, and biodiversity monitoring, and separating demonstrated evidence from prospective applications. The synthesis identifies key Gaps: benchmarks, uncertainty calibration, safe adaptation and proposes a research agenda for physics-informed, deployment-adaptive marine WMs validated through simulation and field missions.
authors: Basma Dokkara, Esteban W. G. Cluab, Luiz M. G. Goncalves, Paolo Spagnolo, Cosimo Distante
bullets: Marine robots must operate under partial observability, changing dynamics, and limited communication.
It provides a functional taxonomy spanning navigation, adaptive sampling, digital twins, and biodiversity monitoring.
The review focuses on JEPAs and AdaJEPA-style test-time adaptation integrated with model predictive control.
It distinguishes demonstrated evidence from prospective applications.
Key gaps include benchmarks, uncertainty calibration, and safe adaptation; it proposes physics-informed, deployment-adaptive validation in simulation and field missions.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance on vision-language tasks but often remain vulnerable to distribution shifts due to their fixed parameters during inference. While Test-Time Training (TTT) offers a pathway for dynamic adaptation, existing approaches suffer from prohibitive computational overhead due to multiple sampling and the risk of error reinforcement from biased self-generated supervision. In light of this view, we propose RoTTT (Rotation-based Test-Time Training), a simple and efficient TTT approach that enables instance-specific refinement at inference time. For each test instance, RoTTT performs a small number of gradient updates by predicting the rotation angle of the input image. The known rotation angles naturally serve as a reliable self-supervised signal, enabling lightweight and stable adaptation without requiring additional annotations. Extensive experiments across multiple vision-language benchmarks demonstrate that RoTTT consistently improves performance across different MLLMs, providing a practical and efficient paradigm for on-the-fly MLLM adaptation.
authors: Changyu Liu, Fei Zhao, Yiyang Liu, Xi Xiao, Tianyang Wang, Cheng Han
bullets: Targets MLLM vulnerability to distribution shifts caused by fixed inference-time parameters.
Uses a small number of gradient updates to predict known image rotation angles for each test instance.
Employs rotation labels as reliable self-supervised signals, avoiding costly sampling and biased generated supervision.
Experiments across multiple vision-language benchmarks report consistent performance gains across different MLLMs.
Designed as a practical, efficient approach for instance-specific adaptation at inference time.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Rotation-based Test-Time Training (RoTTT). Given a test instance (x, q), RoTTT first generates an auxiliary transformed view x̃ by applying a controlled rotation to the input image x. The image pair (x, x̃) is then processed by the pretrained MLLM with trainable LoRA parameters to perform a structured textual rotation prediction task, where the supervision signal yrot is directly derived from the rotation parameter r. The resulting auxiliary loss Lrot is used to update the LoRA parameters during test-time training. After adaptation, the updated MLLM performs inference on the original image x and query q to generate the final prediction.

Figure 1: Comparison of RoTTT with other test-time training methods (i.e., MM-UPT (Wei et al., 2025) and TLM (Hu et al., 2025)) on Qwen2.5VL-3B (Bai et al., 2025b). As seen, RoTTT consistently achieves the best results across benchmarks, demonstrating superior effectiveness and stability. More visualizations are provided in Appendix §S5.

Figure 3: Loss Landscape Visualization of Qwen2.5VL-3B on an MMVet sample. The top row shows the loss landscapes, while the bottom row presents the corresponding 2D heatmaps. From left to right, the columns correspond to the baseline model, the oracle model, and the RoTTT-adapted model.
Figure 4: Blur perturbation analysis. RoTTT exhibits consistently smaller performance drops than the baseline under various blur perturbations

Table 1: Main results on multimodal understanding benchmarks. Best results are highlighted in bold. The symbol “-” represents missing results under specific configurations: MM-UPT is inherently incompatible with the open-ended generative format of MMVet, and it suffers from out-of-memory (OOM) failures on LLaVANeXT-13B due to its GRPO-based optimization. As shown, our method consistently improves performance across all models and benchmarks, demonstrating strong effectiveness, stability, and generalization.

Table 4: Impact of LoRA Position. We evaluate the effect of applying LoRA to different components of the MLLM. The results show that applying LoRA to all layers consistently achieves the best performance across models and benchmarks.

Table 5: Comparison of Computational Efficiency. We report the total test-time training cost in GPU hours for each benchmark. The “× Cost” column indicates the relative speedup factor. RoTTT consistently reduces computational overhead across all benchmarks and models, offering a more resource-efficient paradigm for onthe-fly MLLM adaptation.
Table 3: Impact of LoRA Rank.The results show that rank 8 consistently achieves the best performance across models and benchmarks, while both lower and higher ranks lead to suboptimal results.
Table 2: Impact of Prediction Label. Structured labels consistently outperform simplified labels.

papers.title: Learning from Another Angle: Rotation-Based Test-Time Training for Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: RoTTT adapts multimodal large language models at test time through lightweight rotation-prediction training, improving robustness to distribution shifts without extra annotations.

papers.abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has achieved state-of-the-art performance across diverse tasks, but its high computational cost remains a major barrier. We introduce PruneNAS, a novel framework that integrates structured pruning into NAS to efficiently explore high-performing architectures while leveraging pretrained models. Unlike conventional NAS methods that train each candidate from scratch, PruneNAS generates a candidate pool by pruning pretrained networks at multiple granularity levels and formulates the selection as a global optimization problem using training-free importance metrics. This approach enables rapid evaluation of candidate architectures under strict resource constraints, dramatically reducing search time from hundreds of GPU hours to mere minutes. Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that PruneNAS discovers compact, high-accuracy architectures that nearly halve the computational cost (MACs) of prior methods on ResNet-50, while also showing strong generalization on object detection tasks with YOLO. Our method bridges structured pruning and NAS, offering a practical solution for resource-constrained model deployment.
authors: Sudhakar Sah, Nikhil Chhabra, Honnesh Rohmetra, Andy Li
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of conventional NAS under strict deployment constraints.
Builds candidate architectures by pruning pretrained models at multiple granularity levels.
Uses training-free importance metrics and global optimization to select architectures without training each candidate from scratch.
Reduces search time from hundreds of GPU hours to minutes, according to the abstract.
Finds compact architectures with nearly half the MACs of prior methods on ResNet-50 and generalizes to YOLO object detection.

papers.abstract: A world model should tell us not only what will happen, but what would happen under a different action. Learned Earth models now forecast remarkably well, yet forecast skill says little about what their state means or how it responds to a changed driver. We build LandWM, a world model of land-surface water in which rain is the action, learned from seven years of SMAP and CYGNSS observations: physical observation operators tie its latent state to soil water, and a mass-conserving balance governs how that state responds to rain. Over the U.S. Southern Great Plains, the model, never shown a soil-moisture value, tracks 28 in-situ probes as well as the operational SMAP Level-4 product, even from CYGNSS alone, and a storm added to the forcing of a station's cell wets its soil as natural storms wet the probes. Replace either piece and the forecasts stay, but the meaning goes: with neural operators, only a probe fitted to the stations finds the soil water; with a generic recurrent transition, rain on a single cell barely moves it. Yet when the same rain covers the whole region the two transitions swap roles, and the conserving one responds too weakly. Grounding makes a world model readable; its response to actions must be tested under more than one kind of intervention.
authors: Suya Li, Zekun Qi, Xiaochong Xu, Duo Zhang
bullets: Addresses the gap between accurate forecasting and understanding what model states mean or how they respond to changed rainfall.
Learns from seven years of SMAP and CYGNSS observations, using physical observation operators and a mass-conserving water-balance transition.
Over the U.S. Southern Great Plains, it tracks 28 in-situ probes comparably to operational SMAP Level-4, including from CYGNSS alone.
Adding a storm to a station cell produces soil wetting consistent with natural storms, demonstrating action-response behavior.
Intervention tests show that both state grounding and transition design matter, with responses depending on the spatial scale of rainfall.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) involves detecting the underlying emotion behind each utterance within a conversation, which is essential for emotionally aware human-computer interaction. While omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) demonstrate strong capability for MER by jointly processing modalities including text, audio, and vision, different modality combinations yield different prediction outcomes across utterances: acoustic and visual inputs can help recover annotated labels missed by text-only inference, but can also turn correct predictions into errors. Processing all modalities for every utterance is also computationally expensive. To this end, we introduce EmoRouter, a training-free, model-agnostic framework for adaptive modality cascading that selects an exit tier for each utterance along a predefined modality order. The routing is guided by prediction-uncertainty estimates derived from Conformal Prediction. EmoRouter routes each utterance through a sequence of increasing-cost modality levels and exits at the first level when the model is confident in the emotion. To determine when to exit, we propose Conformal Set Contraction, a structural calibration criterion that calibrates the per-tier CP error budgets used for these exit decisions. Comprehensive evaluations on 4 MER benchmarks and 3 Omni-LLMs reveal that EmoRouter matches or outperforms the full modalities while reducing inference latency by 67.9--94.5%. Furthermore, EmoRouter demonstrates high transferability across different models, validating its robustness. Code is available at https://github.com/tianyi-lab/EmoRouter.
authors: Fangxu Yu, Lingzhi Yuan, Dehai Min, Tao Feng, Ge Liu, Furong Huang, Tianyi Zhou
bullets: Addresses the variable usefulness and high cost of processing text, audio, and vision for every utterance in multimodal emotion recognition.
Uses a training-free, model-agnostic cascading router that evaluates increasingly expensive modality combinations and exits when sufficiently confident.
Introduces Conformal Set Contraction to calibrate per-tier error budgets for reliable exit decisions.
Evaluated on 4 MER benchmarks and 3 Omni-LLMs, matching or outperforming full-modality inference while reducing latency by 67.9–94.5%.
Transfers effectively across models, supporting the framework’s robustness.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of EmoRouter. Given an utterance with text, audio, and visual modalities, EmoRouter cascades the Omni-LLM through three modality tiers of increasing cost: Tier 1 (T), Tier 2 (T+A), and Tier 3 (T+A+V). At each non-terminal tier, a conformal prediction set is constructed using the CSC-selected error rate α˚ ℓ . If the set contains at most one label, the cascade exits and returns the top-1 prediction; otherwise, it escalates to the next tier. The per-tier error budgets are obtained by maximizing Conformal Set Contraction (CSC) on the calibration set.

papers.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) built on vision-language models are increasingly entrusted with long-horizon tasks in live desktop, web, and mobile environments, where the screen keeps changing on its own. However, current CUAs lack real-time situational awareness: they perceive the environment through discrete snapshots, and the substantial inference latency of VLMs, compounded by highly dynamic interfaces, opens a perception-action gap in which the observed state frequently becomes stale before the corresponding action is executed. To bridge this gap, we present NightWatch, a plug-and-play framework that endows any CUA with continuous, temporally grounded perception without changing the agent's model, prompt, or action space. NightWatch couples the VLM agent with NightWatch-0.8B, a lightweight System-1 model that performs streaming monitoring of the interface state and keeps the agent synchronized with the evolving environment at low computational cost and latency, thereby grounding each decision in the current state rather than an outdated snapshot and reducing both stale actions and idle waiting while preserving task success. Experiments on desktop and dynamic web environments (OSWorld-Verified and DynaCU-Bench) show that NightWatch, driven by a watcher of only 0.8B parameters, reduces non-reasoning wall-clock time by 33% and wasted time by 53% on OSWorld while keeping task success on par, raises success on DynaCU-Bench from 39.5% to 44.2% with the large VLM agent, and is more efficient than passive-watching baselines such as AOI and PUSV under the same screenshot-only input, as well as a System-1 decision model more than $30\times$ its size. Overall, NightWatch demonstrates that the timing of perception is as critical as its content, marking a step toward agents that maintain continuous awareness of their environment rather than perceiving it turn by turn.
authors: Jiaqi Su, Jie-Jing Shao, Yichen Liu, Long-Kai Huang, Haiyan Yin
bullets: Targets the perception–action gap caused by snapshot-based observation, VLM inference latency, and rapidly changing interfaces.
Pairs the existing VLM agent with NightWatch-0.8B, a lightweight streaming System-1 watcher, without changing the agent, prompts, or action space.
On OSWorld-Verified, reduces non-reasoning wall-clock time by 33% and wasted time by 53% while keeping task success on par.
On DynaCU-Bench, improves success from 39.5% to 44.2% with the large VLM agent.
Outperforms passive-watching baselines and a System-1 decision model over 30× larger under screenshot-only input.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of NightWatch. Left: the screen is watched as a stream, and NightWatch-0.8B reads a visual context built from recent frames and the pending action and answers every question of a fixed, generic bank with a probability. Middle: in proactive triggering, fixed thresholds turn these probabilities into three interventions on an unmodified agent: interrupt its reasoning when a new event appears, void a pending action whose target is lost, and wake it as soon as the screen settles. Right: NightWatch-0.8B is trained offline on decision points from the agent’s trajectories, with teacher, gold, and hindsight labels and a calibration-preserving objective.

Figure 1: Observation and execution control in computer-use agents. (a) Fixed scheduling. Reasoning continues after a dialog appears, and fixed waits continue after the page is ready. (b) Passive watching. Buffered frames inform later observations, while pre-dispatch checks can reject actions after reasoning completes. (c) Proactive perception. NightWatch combines a 0.8B System-1 watcher with threshold rules to interrupt reasoning, void pending actions, and end post-action waits based on estimated interface state. (d) OSWorld-Verified results. NightWatch reduces non-reasoning time by 33% and the wasted-time share from 16.3% to 7.7% at comparable success with the same agent.

Figure 3: Results at a glance for the large VLM agent. (a) Success against non-reasoning time per task on OSWorld, with error bars showing the standard deviation over three runs. (b) Share of steps with a premature observation or a stale action on OSWorld. papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) leverage the world knowledge of video generation models to improve action generation by aligning visual prediction with action prediction. However, their prediction overhead prevents real-time deployment on edge devices, and they usually lack an effective long-term memory. We introduce SANA-Robot, a 4.5B WAM with minute-level memory that runs in real time on edge devices, built on the following core designs: (1) hybrid memory at constant cost: our WAM relies on linear attention to maintain a global memory with a fixed-size state, and on sliding window softmax attention layers that propagate previous information, enabling high success rates on tasks requiring whole-episode memory while keeping an efficient and constant inference speed; (2) a unified model: by dynamically applying different noise levels to action and video tokens, SANA-Robot can serve not only as a policy but also as a world simulator; (3) a full-stack infrastructure for both memory training and inference, including efficient data packing and shuffling as well as memory-phase-based asynchronous execution. SANA-Robot achieves the best performance on the memory dimension of RoboDojo among models of medium size (about 5B) and the highest success rates on LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro and LIBERO-Max. In real-world deployment, SANA-Robot takes 135 ms per action chunk on an RTX 5090 with FP8 GEMMs and 115 ms with NVFP4 GEMMs, and achieves closed-loop, real-time asynchronous robot control at 30 Hz on edge devices, demonstrating both the efficiency and the effectiveness of SANA-Robot. Project page: https://nvlabs.github.io/Sana/Robot/
authors: Yuyang Zhao, Zekai Li, Yicheng Pan, Jiaming Tang, Zhuoyang Zhang, Jiaxu Xing, Moritz Reuss, Quanquan Peng, Junsong Chen, Enze Xie, Zhijian Liu, Song Han
bullets: Addresses WAM inference overhead and weak long-term memory for real-time, whole-episode robot tasks.

Dynamically assigns noise levels to action and video tokens, allowing one model to function as both a policy and a world simulator.
Includes infrastructure for memory training and inference, including efficient data handling and asynchronous memory-phase execution.
Reports strong memory-task performance and real-time deployment: 135 ms per action chunk on an RTX 5090 and 30 Hz control on edge devices.

papers.abstract: We present XShot, a framework for cross-shot video object insertion, which adds objects to a shot by watching another shot of the same scene. Video productions show a scene through many shots, and objects added to one shot must appear consistently in the others. Most video editors take the appearance of new objects from reference images and their location from a text prompt, a mask or an edited keyframe, leaving this consistency to the user. XShot reads both from a reference video of another shot, which need not be aligned with the target, and needs no mask, box or camera pose. We build on a video Diffusion Transformer and formulate the task as in-context generation over the reference video, a few images of the objects and the target video. A geometry-aware cross-shot attention estimates the epipolar geometry between the two shots from the model's own correspondences and uses it to guide where the target reads the reference and the exemplars. We train XShot with an erase-and-restore data engine: objects are erased from one shot of a film or a multi-camera recording and restored from another shot of the scene. Experiments show that XShot places objects more accurately and renders them more faithfully than open-source and commercial video editors, while leaving the rest of the shot intact.
authors: Bangxun Tang, Chen Chen
bullets: Addresses cross-shot object consistency, reducing manual placement and appearance specification by editors.
Uses in-context generation with a video Diffusion Transformer, reference video, object images, and target video.
Geometry-aware cross-shot attention estimates epipolar relationships from learned correspondences to guide reference information.
Trains via an erase-and-restore pipeline using shots from films or multi-camera recordings.
Experiments report more accurate placement, more faithful rendering, and preservation of the unchanged scene compared with open-source and commercial editors.

papers.abstract: Accurate material identification is important for robotic manipulation, yet vision-based methods face challenges when materials have similar appearances. Herein, we report T-Tac, a soft, thin, active thermal tactile sensor that identifies materials through their transient thermal responses. T-Tac integrates a polyimide film heater with an ionic conductive film temperature sensor, providing controlled thermal excitation and resistance-based temperature measurement in a film assembly suitable for mounting on robotic grippers. Single-sided transient plane source modeling and finite element simulations relate the thermal response to material thermal properties, while calibration and repeated measurements characterize the heating and sensing performance. Loading experiments at room and elevated temperatures further characterize the sensor response under an applied force. A hybrid classification framework concatenates extracted thermal descriptors with multiscale convolutional neural network features and uses an ExtraTrees classifier for material prediction. Experiments on 12 materials achieve a mean classification accuracy of 92.69\% using a 3 s heating pulse and a 10 s observation window. These results support T-Tac as a compact approach to integrating active thermal material sensing into robotic end effectors. This work shed a light on the new approach for robotic material identification.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based sequence models have achieved strong performance in language and time-series modeling, but self-attention remains computationally and memory intensive for deployment on resource-constrained edge accelerators. We propose STEdgeFormer, a lightweight, hardware-aware sequence architecture designed for efficient execution on embedded neural accelerators. STEdgeFormer combines polynomial mixture layers and DyT normalization with an accelerator-aware causal memory block, replacing pairwise self-attention with compact causal aggregation. On TinyStories, the fully NPU-supported STEdgeFormer (MW) achieves a perplexity of 7.39 with 4.12M parameters and 6.51 MB RAM, with an end-to-end latency of 40 ms. In comparison, the standard 4.12M-parameter configuration achieves a lower perplexity of 6.79 but requires CPU fallback for unsupported operators, resulting in 1450 ms latency. Vanilla Transformer, on the other hand, achieves a perplexity score of 5.71 using a 4.40M-parameter model, but it cannot be deployed on the hardware. On downstream tasks, STEdgeFormer achieves 94% accuracy on ECG5000 and 93% accuracy on Speech Commands with 1.39M parameters. These results demonstrate that hardware-aware architectural choices and operator compatibility can have a substantial impact on practical inference latency, beyond model size and task accuracy alone. Rather than targeting state-of-the-art accuracy on individual benchmarks, STEdgeFormer is designed to provide a deployable sequence modeling architecture under the memory, computational, and operator constraints of embedded neural accelerators.

papers.abstract: Adapting spoken language understanding (SLU) systems to novel or revised label taxonomies conventionally requires additional labeled data and retraining, creating a bottleneck for real world deployment. While in-context learning with few-shot demonstrations offers an alternative, multi-modal generalization and scaling has been challenging. In this work, we investigate whether natural-language definitions alone can guide zero-shot SLU without demonstration exemplars, finding that symbolic definitions serve as the primary supervisory driver for adapting speech-text models. We operationalize this principle as Definition-Guided In-Context Learning (DG-ICL), a fine-tuning framework that decouples semantic categories from fixed lexical names. By replacing labels with dynamically randomized definitions (arbitrary synthetic tokens in DG-ICL-Sym or permuted vocabulary words in DG-ICL-Flip), DG-ICL avoids lexical shortcuts and encourages the model to ground acoustic representations in contextual definitions. Novel categories can thus be introduced at inference simply by defining them through the instructions. Across three speech-text models (AUDIO FLAMINGO 3, QWEN2-AUDIO, and SALMONN), DG-ICL outperforms standard instruction tuning on held-out tasks under novel symbols (0.663 vs. 0.449 macro-F1 on Audio Flamingo 3; 0.703 vs. 0.620 on Qwen2-Audio; 0.582 vs. 0.399 on SALMONN), while remaining competitive on original labels. Furthermore, counterfactual evaluations demonstrate instruction following abilities, where it is shown that DG-ICL-Sym retains 68% of its performance when definitions contradict pre-trained lexical priors, whereas standard instruction tuning elicits significantly reduced retention of 21%. Finally, we show that DG-ICL enables zero-shot speech clustering into user-defined categories specified on the fly

papers.abstract: Multimodal System One models answer visual tasks with typed decisions and native probabilities, yet no holistic evaluation compares them with general VLMs or maps either class's capability boundaries. We introduce OmniDecisionBench, a holistic benchmark of multimodal System One models. Its main evaluation assigns 45 datasets (192,975 records) to five capability families and twelve primary angles across four typed interfaces, scoring accuracy and candidate-probability calibration. A validation layer adds three single-factor diagnostics varying visual presentation, textual evidence sufficiency, and target dataset. Across three System One models and two general VLMs, three regularities emerge. First, strengths depend on angle and metric: System One models lead discrete tasks overall with lower ECE15 on most perception, reading, and reasoning angles (Jev 1.14: 80.14% accuracy, 4.50% ECE15), while general VLMs lead ordinal grading and outperform Jev 1.14 among the three models tested on direct Box grounding. Second, multi-image and abstract reasoning bound every model, where confidence rather than accuracy separates them. Third, reliability shifts with the input: rendering only options nearly triples Jev 1.14's selective risk at nearly flat mean signed bias, and donor risk cutoffs often exceed target risk across unseen datasets and task families. OmniDecisionBench thus maps which model class suits each angle and where reliability ends. The code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/Glax147/OmniDecisionBench.

papers.abstract: Visual world models enable goal-conditioned planning by predicting the outcomes of candidate actions in latent space. However, planning depends on how well a model ranks candidates, whereas training optimizes how accurately it predicts each one. We identify the Decision-Relevant Residual (DRR), the part of the cost error that can reorder candidates, and show that the more training reduces the DRR, the more it improves selection (Spearman $\rho = 0.82$, vs. $0.61$ for prediction error). Building on this insight, we introduce Decision-Aligned Selection (DAS), a plug-in selection rule that scores candidates by the standardized consensus of several independently trained checkpoints, which averages out their checkpoint-specific residuals. Across two model families (LeWorldModel and DINO-WM) and five tasks, DAS selects better actions than single checkpoints in 12 of 18 configurations and outperforms training one model three times longer in 14 of 18. In closed loop, DAS improves success over single checkpoints in 6 of 9 pre-registered LeWM comparisons.
authors: Chan Aristella Lu, Arya Fayyazi, Junil Yeo, Jin Lu, Kyu Hyung Lee, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram
bullets: Prediction error can differ from decision quality because only residual cost errors that reorder candidates affect action selection.
The Decision-Relevant Residual (DRR) correlates more strongly with selection quality than overall prediction error (Spearman ρ = 0.82 vs. 0.61).
Decision-Aligned Selection (DAS) scores actions using standardized consensus across independently trained checkpoints.
DAS selects better actions than single checkpoints in 12/18 configurations and beats training one model three times longer in 14/18.
In closed-loop evaluation, DAS improves success over single checkpoints in 6/9 pre-registered LeWM comparisons.

papers.abstract: 3D affordance grounding aims to localize 3D regions specified by an interaction query. Existing methods predict a single affordance mask, overlooking the inherent diversity of human-object interactions. We introduce diverse 3D affordance grounding, a new task that requires predicting multiple plausible regions for a given object and affordance query. We then propose Div3DAffordNet, a transformer-based set prediction model capable of generating diverse affordance regions. To address the scarcity of diverse 3D affordance data, we develop an automated pipeline leveraging 2D generative models and 3D reconstruction techniques to synthesize 3D affordances, followed by lightweight human verification (reducing the annotation time by 72X), yielding the Div3DAfford benchmark. Extensive experiments show Div3DAffordNet effectively captures multi-mask affordance regions. Our method achieves the SOTA affordance grounding performance in the multi-mask setting, reducing GED-SIM from 0.745 to 0.492, while maintaining competitive single-mask performance on the standard benchmark of 19.0 mIoU.
authors: Haomeng Zhang, Raymond A. Yeh
bullets: Addresses the limitation of single-mask methods, which miss diverse human–object interactions.
Proposes Div3DAffordNet, a transformer-based set prediction model for generating multiple affordance regions.
Builds the Div3DAfford benchmark using 2D generative models, 3D reconstruction, and lightweight human verification.
The automated annotation pipeline reduces annotation time by 72×.
Achieves state-of-the-art multi-mask performance, reducing GED-SIM from 0.745 to 0.492, while retaining 19.0 mIoU on single-mask grounding.

papers.abstract: Unified 3D understanding and generation require compact sequences preserving spatial structure. Dense grids yield long sequences, while serialization can separate spatial neighbors. We propose Sparse Proximity Aware Compression (SPAC), a shared sparse SDF vocabulary combining sparse encoding with reversible spatial merging. A Sparse SDF VQ-VAE quantizes near-surface features while retaining explicit coordinates, using reconstruction supervision for surface fidelity and detail. 3D Byte-Pair Encoding (3D-BPE) merges recurring face-adjacent patterns using relative offsets before serialization. Macro tokens expand exactly into leaf tokens and coordinates. After Morton serialization, a shared LLM reads geometry for captioning and predicts tokens that decode into meshes for text-conditioned generation. With fixed geometry, architecture, and band width in voxels, sparse encoder cost grows approximately quadratically with resolution. 3D-BPE reduces mean complete LLM sequence length by 45.4 percent, including coordinates, text, and control tokens. SPAC achieves strong results in both 3D captioning and text-conditioned mesh generation. Ablations show gains over leaf tokens and Morton 1D-BPE in both tasks. The project page at https://yangjj007.github.io/spac/ .
authors: Junjie Yang, Rui Qian, Yijiang Li, Jinyi Xu, Yuhao Yan, Xinjian Yi, Yanfeng Li, Mingxuan Li, Xiang Wan, Jicong Fan, Siqi Liu, Ahmed Elazab, Changmiao Wang
bullets: Targets long sequences from dense 3D grids and spatially disconnected serialization.
Uses a sparse SDF VQ-VAE with explicit coordinates and reconstruction supervision to preserve surface detail.
Applies 3D-BPE to merge recurring face-adjacent patterns using relative offsets; macro tokens decode exactly to leaf tokens and coordinates.
Reduces mean complete LLM sequence length by 45.4% and achieves strong captioning and text-conditioned mesh-generation results.
Ablations report gains over leaf-token and Morton 1D-BPE baselines; encoder cost still grows approximately quadratically with resolution under fixed settings.

papers.abstract: Skill-augmented reinforcement learning enables LLM agents to reuse task-solving knowledge across episodes, but existing systems typically expose agents to a flat skill pool and update skills only from coarse, episode-level outcomes. This conflates two distinct uses of experience: a stable strategy that should frame the whole episode, and tactical know-how that should be retrieved only when the agent reaches a local execution gap. We propose STRIDE (Strategy-to-Tactics Retrieval-guided skIll Disclosure and Evolution), a framework that brings progressive skill disclosure into agentic reinforcement learning. STRIDE keeps the selected strategy visible as episode context, exposes a compact tactic menu, and loads full tactic content only after an explicit retrieval action. This interface turns each retrieval into an event-level credit unit: the same event provides process feedback for learning when to retrieve and supplies evidence for skill-bank evolution. On ALFWorld, STRIDE achieves a 92.7% average success rate with Qwen3-4B and a 94.9% average success rate with Qwen3-8B. On WebShop, it improves over the strongest reproduced skill-augmented baseline by 4.5 score points and 1.9 success-rate percentage points. These results show that skill reuse is most effective when persistent strategies preserve global task structure and tactics are disclosed only at local decision bottlenecks.
authors: Shixin Hong, Wanqing Cui, Yibo Hu, Naen Xu, Zhiwei Huang, Meiguang Jin, Junfeng Ma
bullets: Addresses the limitations of flat skill pools and episode-level skill updates, which fail to distinguish global strategies from local tactics.
Uses progressive skill disclosure: a selected strategy remains visible, a compact tactic menu is exposed, and full tactic details require an explicit retrieval action.
Treats retrieval events as credit units for learning retrieval timing and evolving the skill bank.
Reports 92.7% and 94.9% average success on ALFWorld with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, respectively.
On WebShop, improves over the strongest reproduced skill-augmented baseline by 4.5 score points and 1.9 success-rate percentage points.

The Analyst assigns event-level feedback to retrieval decisions, and the Strategist uses retrieval traces and rollout outcomes to create, update, or prune the strategy-tactic skill bank.

Figure 1: Comparison of skill delivery paradigms. (a) Flat skill injection exposes the same skill pool across decisions and updates skill quality from trajectory-level outcomes. (b) STRIDE keeps the strategy visible, discloses tactics through a compact menu, and records each retrieval event as evidence for policy feedback and skill-bank updates.

Figure 3: Skill-bank evolution on ALFWorld. (a) Bank growth occurs mainly in the tactic layer, while the number of strategies changes little and utility rises early before stabilizing. (b) Under a fixed final policy, success increases from 93.4% with the Step-50 bank to 94.9% with the Step-150 bank.

Figure 5: A stuck-state recovery example. The retrieved tactic redirects the agent from repeating already checked locations to broadening the search over remaining receptacles.

(a) STRIDE reaches GRPO’s peak success rate in 1/3.2 as many training steps and maintains an approximately 17-point advantage near the end of training. papers.abstract: Video generators can now render convincing short clips, yet complete audiovisual works require coordinating visuals, sound, and editing across multiple stages. Existing benchmarks focus on individual generators or video agents under narrower production settings, leaving end-to-end creation by general multimodal large language models (MLLMs) underexplored. We introduce StudioBench, a benchmark comprising 160 tasks across eight video genres and five task types, spanning diverse audiovisual production requirements. Models produce minutes of finished audiovisual content using 33 atomic generation, editing, and inspection tools, without shell access or workflow templates. We evaluate the delivered films, while analyzing reconstructed workflow graphs to characterize production behavior and diagnose failures. Across seven MLLMs, explicit requirements are nearly saturated, yet production quality varies substantially in picture clarity and composition, object structure, motion, and lip sync. All models spontaneously organize multi-stage production workflows without predefined templates. However, higher-quality models exhibit more selective production workflows, whereas additional tool calls alone show little association with quality. These findings identify the missing quality loop of effective inspection, selection, and revision as a key bottleneck in productive audiovisual creation.
authors: Xinglong Xu, Yuxia Zhu, Siyuan Li, Lixu Tian, Xiaofei Zhao, Yuxin Liu, Caijun Jia, Jintao Chen, Bihui Yu, Alden Cai, Asher Qin, Jingxuan Wei, Cheng Tan
bullets: Introduces 160 benchmark tasks across eight video genres and five audiovisual production task types.
Models create minutes-long finished works using 33 generation, editing, and inspection tools without shell access or workflow templates.
Across seven MLLMs, explicit requirements are nearly saturated, but quality varies in clarity, composition, object structure, motion, and lip sync.
All models form multi-stage workflows spontaneously; stronger models use more selective workflows, while extra tool calls show little relationship to quality.
The main bottleneck is an effective quality loop of inspection, selection, and revision.

papers.abstract: Purpose: Analyzing clinicians' visual attention from exocentric camera views can support surgical scene understanding without requiring wearable eye trackers. However, existing gaze-following research in the operating room (OR) estimates only 2D gaze locations without identifying attended scene entities or localizing gaze targets in 3D space. In this work, we investigate gaze graphs as a scene-level representation of visual attention that connects clinicians to attended scene entities, and evaluate their utility for fine-grained surgical action recognition and semantic scene graph (SSG) generation. Methods: We extend the public EgoExOR dataset with gaze annotations to create EgoExOR-Gaze, the first benchmark for multi-view gaze graph generation in the OR. We propose a novel architecture that jointly estimates 3D gaze targets and predicts attended entities using only exocentric camera views. Specifically, our approach exploits 3D gaze geometry to sample local visual features across multiple views for attended entity prediction. We further utilize predicted gaze graphs for fine-grained surgical action recognition and SSG generation. Results: For gaze graph generation, our model outperforms both exocentric-only and combined exocentric-egocentric baselines. For surgical action recognition, our model incorporating predicted gaze graphs outperforms both exocentric and egocentric baselines across all evaluated metrics, with particularly strong gains in temporal metrics. For SSG generation, incorporating gaze graphs improves macro-F1 from 0.42 to 0.52 compared to exocentric inputs alone, although performance remains below that achieved with egocentric inputs. Conclusion: Our results demonstrate the value of gaze graphs for surgical action recognition and SSG generation, highlighting the importance of explicitly modeling scene-level visual attention even when egocentric views are unavailable.
authors: S\'eraphin Baributsa, Keqi Chen, Vinkle Srivastav, Nicolas Padoy
bullets: Introduces EgoExOR-Gaze, a multi-view operating-room benchmark with gaze annotations.
Proposes a model that jointly predicts 3D gaze targets and attended entities using multi-view exocentric features.
Predicted gaze graphs outperform exocentric-only and combined exocentric–egocentric baselines for gaze graph generation and action recognition.
Gaze graphs improve semantic scene graph macro-F1 from 0.42 to 0.52 over exocentric inputs alone.
Semantic scene graph performance remains below that achieved using egocentric inputs.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the gaze graph generation architecture. A frozen DINOv3 backbone extracts raw and text-aligned visual features. The initial 3D gaze point is computed from the estimated gaze direction and depth. The role prediction module estimates each clinician’s role, and the corresponding role embedding is added to the initial appearance query. Decoder layers iteratively refine the 3D gaze point and appearance query through projective attention. Finally, the appearance query is compared with ‘dino.txt’ vocabulary embeddings using cosine similarity to identify attended entities.

Fig. 1: An example of dataset annotations. On the left, we show the annotated head bounding box, clinical role, and corresponding gaze point of each person. On the right, we show the annotated gaze graph where arrows denote “looking” relations pointing from clinical roles to one or multiple entities within the attended regions.

papers.title: Gaze Graphs: A Scene-Level Representation of Visual Attention in the Operating Room
papers.tldr: Gaze graphs use exocentric video to link clinicians’ attention to 3D scene entities, improving surgical action recognition and semantic scene understanding without eye trackers.

papers.abstract: Executable code can preserve a world's structural layout, yet video renderers frequently alter the appearance of previously visited places once they leave the camera view. We present Paintress, a code-conditioned world model that couples an executable geometric proxy with an independently parameterized 3D Gaussian appearance memory in a shared metric coordinate frame. While the proxy enforces structural and visibility constraints, 3D Gaussians capture the visual realization synthesized by emitted observations. To balance stable incremental fusion with consistent readout, Paintress separates writing from reading: newly emitted frames update a persistent raw Gaussian map under confidence-gated selection, whereas a cloned reader copy is globally refined against the observation archive and rendered with coverage masks to condition generation. We also introduce Expedition-33, a benchmark for generated-appearance retention across 11 static scenes, five route families, and 15, 30, and 60 s target absences (165 settings per system). Excluded from the opening image, targets are synthesized during a shared prefix and scored against each system's own first visit at matched return cameras. Across ten systems (1,650 videos), Paintress achieves 0.1220 ROI-LPIPS, 0.0613 MAE, and 52.12% detail retention (vs. 0.2731, 0.1401, and 10.91% for CWM), with lower discrepancy at 60 s (0.1630) than CWM, AgentGarten, and Lyra 2.0 achieve at 15 s.
authors: Wenqing Tian, Zijian Zhang, Qiang Liu, Liang Wang
bullets: Video renderers can alter previously visited places after they leave the camera view.
Paintress combines an executable geometric proxy with a separately learned 3D Gaussian appearance memory in shared metric coordinates.
A persistent raw map is updated with confidence-gated observations, while a refined reader copy supports consistent rendering and generation.
On the Expedition-33 benchmark, Paintress achieves 0.1220 ROI-LPIPS, 0.0613 MAE, and 52.12% detail retention, compared with CWM’s 0.2731, 0.1401, and 10.91%.
The benchmark covers 11 static scenes, five route families, and target absences of 15, 30, and 60 seconds; results are limited to generated-appearance retention in these settings.
