papers.tldr: Paintress improves visual consistency in code-conditioned world models by persistently remembering scene appearance across out-of-view periods.

papers.abstract: Action tokenizers let robot policies treat control as autoregressive next-token prediction. As these policies are trained on larger and more diverse datasets, they will need a universal tokenizer that can encode actions from many embodiments and data sources, including ones it has not seen. We study action tokenization at scale, training on 49k hours of action data from real-world robots, handheld grippers, simulation, and humans. We introduce Neural Action Tokenizer (NAT), a causal tokenizer whose decoder lets actions be executed as their tokens are generated. Across four simulation benchmarks, NAT outperforms FAST and prior neural action tokenizers when tokenizing unseen robot embodiments, and in vision-language-action models it outperforms FAST+ across four benchmarks and on a real robot when acting through its tokens. NAT tokens also close the performance gap to a flow-matching action head on some benchmarks while lowering the inference latency for first actions. Our experiments also find that robot data may not be necessary to learn an effective action space: a NAT trained only on human hand motion performs close to tokenizers trained on robot data.
authors: Ahad Jawaid, Alexander Swerdlow, Yu Xiang
bullets: Trained on 49k hours spanning real robots, handheld grippers, simulation, and human motion.
Its causal decoder executes actions as tokens are generated, reducing latency for first actions.
Outperforms FAST and prior neural tokenizers across four simulation benchmarks, including unseen embodiments.
Improves vision-language-action models over FAST+ across four benchmarks and on a real robot.
Human-hand-motion-only training performs close to robot-data-trained tokenizers, suggesting robot data may not be essential.

papers.title: NAT: Scaling Causal Neural Action Tokenizers Across Embodiments
papers.tldr: NAT is a scalable causal action tokenizer that enables fast, autoregressive robot control across unseen embodiments and diverse action sources.

papers.abstract: Existing surgical world models often leave implicit how instrument motion drives localized tissue responses and how interaction history informs subsequent actions. We introduce KineState-SWAM, a surgical world-action model coupling action prediction and video generation through a persistent interaction state, separating kinematically determined instrument motion from learned scene evolution. A flow-matching policy predicts joint trajectories conditioned on interaction state, robot configuration, and task instruction. Kinematic Geometry Conditioning converts these trajectories into surface-motion tokens and spatially aligned instrument renderings using calibrated URDF kinematics. Causal Interaction Dynamics recurrently updates the state through geometry-guided attention and motion-aligned feature transport, carrying interaction history into subsequent action predictions without intermediate video synthesis. The State-Geometry Adapter combines state-dependent spatial modulation with localized geometric residuals to guide video generation. Interaction-aware supervision emphasizes tissue responses near instrument working regions. We introduce dVRK-Chole5.2k, comprising 5,255 videos spanning 17 surgical tasks. Experiments demonstrate improved action accuracy and video fidelity over evaluated baselines within matched action-conditioning settings. Ablations support preserving and transporting interaction states for long-horizon prediction.
authors: Rulin Zhou, Yujie Ma, Rui Tang, Qiujie Song, Wanhao Liu, Guoheng Ma, Liangjing Shao, An Wang, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Addresses the missing link between instrument motion, localized tissue response, and interaction history in surgical world models.
Uses a flow-matching policy to predict joint trajectories from interaction state, robot configuration, and task instructions.
Converts trajectories into geometry-aligned motion tokens and instrument renderings via calibrated URDF kinematics.
Maintains interaction history through recurrent geometry-guided dynamics and guides video generation with state and geometric residuals.
Introduces dVRK-Chole5.2k with 5,255 videos across 17 tasks; reports improved action accuracy and video fidelity over evaluated baselines, with ablations supporting state preservation and transport.

papers.abstract: Civil infrastructure is designed, built, and maintained through engineering drawing sets, yet preparing and revising them remains labour-intensive and calls for automation. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are promising candidates, but assessing them requires a benchmark grounded in real engineering practice. We introduce CivilCADBench, a benchmark for understanding, reconstructing, and designing civil engineering drawing sets, built from real infrastructure drawings and source CAD files containing over 250,000 CAD entities. Unlike parametric 3D CAD models, these drawings are dense, layered, and multi-sheet; and since prints are lossy projections with no pixel trace of layers, a file can print correctly yet remain wrongly organised. CivilCADBench comprises three task families of increasing difficulty: understanding tasks are evaluated with 2,183 expert-reviewed questions ranging from single sheets to whole sets, while reconstruction and design tasks are agentic, requiring models to rebuild printed pages as editable CAD files, either as single pages or entire drawing sets, and to produce new designs. These tasks are performed across 232 pages, 28 sets, and 19 design tasks, and evaluated by a deterministic scorer that compares model outputs with the designers' source files on geometry, layers, text, and dimensions. We evaluate seven frontier MLLMs on CivilCADBench, and find that they read and redraw printed content accurately but recover the file structure poorly: the best model scores above 90% in understanding and single-page reconstruction, yet only 60% on layer assignment and 48% on design. Grounded in real engineering practice, CivilCADBench exposes both the capabilities and the limitations of frontier models in professional civil engineering, laying a foundation for next-generation models and agentic systems for intelligent civil engineering.
authors: Zelin Zheng, Difei Wu, Xinyan Liu, Minghong Chen, Antoni B. Chan, Difan Zou
bullets: Benchmarks three increasingly difficult task families: understanding, editable-CAD reconstruction, and design.
Uses real infrastructure drawings and source CAD files spanning over 250,000 entities, 232 pages, 28 sets, and 19 design tasks.
Understanding is tested with 2,183 expert-reviewed questions from individual sheets to complete drawing sets.
A deterministic scorer compares outputs with source files across geometry, layers, text, and dimensions.
Seven frontier MLLMs exceed 90% on understanding and single-page reconstruction, but reach only 60% on layer assignment and 48% on design.

(b) Reconstruction and design, in rising difficulty: rebuild one page as an editable CAD file (L1), a whole set whose shared values must agree (L2) and a withheld page from its reference page and new parameters (L3), all scored against the source file.

Figure 10: An example of an L1 episode: input, agent loop and scoring. (a) The agent receives one raster page, a task card that fixes paper-millimetre coordinates and nine named layers, and tools; the source file, the ground truth and the scorer stay outside the sandbox. (b) It writes and runs its own code, plots its DXF in the input’s style and compares the plot with the input (grey: in both; blue: input only; orange: output only), then submits once. Its file groups the page into six named blocks, and it restores a garbled bar glyph of the input from the unit weight in the bar schedule. (c) The scorer matches entities with the source file and weights five component F1 scores; here the agent puts a centre line and a slope triangle on the symbol layer, where the source has them on its centre-line and dimension layers. L2 runs the same loop over a whole set, and L3 starts from a reference page and new parameters.

Figure 9: Examples of reconstruction and design tasks (L1 to L3) on one set. The approach-slab set of five pages carries a task at each level: (a) L1 rebuilds its second page, (b) L2 rebuilds the whole set and (c) L3 produces its third page from the second and the new slab width. Inputs are shown as the agent receives them, and CAD files are plotted with one colour per layer.

Figure 11: Case studies of reconstruction (a, b) and understanding (c). (a) Within the set, the agent keeps 26 of the 69 dimensions as dimension entities and redraws the rest as loose lines whose labels are truncated or missing: the dimension score falls from 100 to 36.0 and the stray text lowers the text score. (b) The outputs range from a page that matches the designer’s file to one that keeps the section outline and loses most of the reinforcement and its labels. (c) In Full-Set, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol open all four evidence pages and answer every probe correctly, including the one on the seam group, yet count that group twice.

papers.abstract: When visual context makes an ordinary request unsafe to answer as asked, a blanket refusal may leave the user's need unresolved. Choosing how to help requires distinguishing an established hazard from a condition that still needs verification, a distinction that binary safety labels leave unspecified. We formulate this decision through four actions: allow, warn, review, and refuse. To ground these decisions in verifiable evidence, we build a corpus of 20,126 training audits and the JudiBench benchmark, connecting each action to diagnostic judgments, source evidence, and controlled context changes. Our guard, JudiAct, separately states what the source establishes, what condition governs the help, and how the rules apply. It then checks these three brief review items against the original inputs to predict diagnostic labels and a handling action. Supervised training learns individual judgments while comparing label assignments across related cases. A second stage swaps one review item at a time, using the resulting audit feedback to refine review generation. On JudiBench, JudiAct improves request and answer Macro-F1 by more than 28 percentage points over its 4B backbone. Across nine public benchmarks, it outperforms state-of-the-art guards on the mean delivered-answer score in both pre-generation and post-generation settings, cutting MM-SafetyBench attack success from 40.78% to 25.30%.
authors: Jipei He, Cheng Cheng, Liuguo Wang, Zihan Wen, Changlin Yu, Wentao Song, Suyun Zhao
bullets: Addresses the limits of binary safety labels when visual context makes a request conditionally unsafe.
Uses three review items—established facts, governing conditions, and rule application—to ground interventions in source evidence.
Trains on 20,126 training audits and is evaluated on the JudiBench benchmark.
Improves request and answer Macro-F1 by over 28 percentage points over its 4B backbone on JudiBench.
Outperforms existing guards across nine public benchmarks and reduces MM-SafetyBench attack success from 40.78% to 25.30%.

figures.caption: Figure 4. JudiAct’s audit and two-stage training. The model generates a source fact e, condition c, and rule link r independently, then audits them with the original inputs X and rules P. Request audits predict S1–S4; answer audits predict S5. Both select a handling action. After deciding, the model can locate evidence in source text and images. SFT combines individual supervision with conditional matching across related cases. Stage 2 replaces one short item at a time, shown here for c. Each review is audited separately, and its utility updates generation and judgment. Deployment uses one greedy review.

papers.abstract: Two visually identical animated characters can respond differently to the same action command because their body dynamics differ. For example, a stiff blob and its bouncy twin reach different heights when both receive the jump command. Given only the first frame and the action command, a visual world model has no information to distinguish these twins, because their initial appearances are identical. We therefore propose an in-context world model that encodes clips of a character's other actions into a body representation, using a contrastive loss to separate look-alike characters. We introduce ToonTwins, a benchmark of 144 2D cartoon characters that run, jump, fall, turn and crouch. Its characters form look-alike groups of four that differ only in their dynamics profile, and we also evaluate the model on 32 animated animals from DeformingThings4D. Even with a body code from these clips, the latent pixel world model we tested recovered at most 25 percent of the twins' jump height difference. On new shapes, our model identified the correct twin in 85.9 percent of cases, compared with 76.7 percent for a transformer baseline that reads the same clips without a body summary, and in a controlled ablation the contrastive loss gave more than half of this gain. On the animated animals, it reduced the mean path prediction error by 8.5 percent against a model without body information.
authors: Amarnath R
bullets: Problem: Identical-looking characters can respond differently to the same action because their body dynamics are unobserved from a single frame.
Method: Encode clips of a character performing other actions into a body representation using an in-context world model and contrastive loss.
Benchmark: ToonTwins contains 144 cartoon characters in look-alike groups with differing dynamics; evaluation also uses 32 animated animals from DeformingThings4D.
Results: The model identified the correct twin in 85.9% of new-shape cases versus 76.7% for a transformer baseline, while contrastive learning accounted for more than half the gain.
Scope: The model recovered at most 25% of twins’ jump-height differences, indicating substantial limitations in predicting dynamics.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models benefit from strong semantic representations that support object recognition and instruction understanding. However, precise manipulation also depends on resolving object locations and workspace relations, and on selecting actions with an estimate of how the scene will evolve. Existing geometry-aware methods make the current scene more explicit, while predictive methods model future observations or representations. Yet future information is often neither grounded in a control-relevant spatial state nor directly used to guide action generation. We introduce Spatially Grounded Latent Lookahead (SG-LL), which uses the grounded present as the reference for predicting an actionable near-future representation. A frozen spatial teacher first distills geometric priors into policy-connected spatial tokens. A current-conditioned bottleneck then learns a compact latent that captures future information relative to the present scene. This latent is predicted from the current policy context and initial Action Expert features, without access to future observations or the spatial teacher. Finally, zero-initialized residual fusion incorporates the predicted latent into the Action Expert to refine action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and three real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improvements over in both simulation and real-robot settings.
authors: Qihang Chen, Tengjie Li, Hongwei Lu, Jason Wu, Chyna Qu, Shikui Tu, Lei Xu
bullets: Addresses the gap between geometry-aware perception and predictive action selection in precise manipulation.
Distills geometric priors into policy-connected spatial tokens using a frozen spatial teacher.
Learns a compact, current-conditioned latent representing actionable near-future information without future observations at inference.
Fuses the predicted latent into the Action Expert through zero-initialized residual connections.
Shows improvements across LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and three real-world manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Frontier language models can now read and edit the weights of a neural network much like code and thereby improve a small model, an approach known as Weight-Space Programming (WSP). We further explore applying WSP to a language model itself, which we call Self-WSP. Specifically, Qwen3.5-0.8B reads its own weights, proposes an edit, and then continues with the edited weights as both problem solver and editor. We find many cases of genuine self-improvement. Self-edits can raise GSM8K accuracy from 11.8% to 62.2% and MATH500 accuracy from 7.0% to 32.2%, sometimes by changing only 16 parameters, and in some cases repeated self-editing keeps improving the model. A closer look, however, reveals that these gains lack interpretability. The model shows little understanding of the edits it makes, and WSP driven by random search sometimes performs comparably. Self-WSP thus holds promise as a path toward recursive self-improvement (RSI), but realizing this promise requires further exploration.
authors: Guoming Ling, Shanshan Zhong, Kaixuan Zhang, Zhongzhan Huang
bullets: Qwen3.5-0.8B reads and edits its own weights, then uses the edited model for both solving and further editing.
Self-edits improved GSM8K accuracy from 11.8% to 62.2% and MATH500 accuracy from 7.0% to 32.2%.
Some improvements required changing as few as 16 parameters, and repeated self-editing sometimes continued to help.
The model showed little understanding of its edits; random-search WSP sometimes achieved comparable results.
The approach suggests potential for recursive self-improvement but remains difficult to interpret and validate.

papers.abstract: In Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training, loss curves can conceal substantial instability, i.e., even small perturbations may lead to dramatically different predictions while leaving loss nearly unchanged. To investigate this phenomenon and reveal the underlying mechanisms, we first formulate LLM pre-training as a non-autonomous dynamical system that jointly evolves model weights and Adam optimizer states. Based on this formulation, we introduce a normalized sensitivity score in optimizer-relative coordinates to identify sensitive training checkpoints. At one such checkpoint, a weight perturbation of only 10^(-5) leads to 35.7% disagreement in top-1 predictions and 16.2% disagreement in benchmark answers after 200 training steps, with only 0.8% of greedy generations remaining identical despite similar validation losses. Furthermore, we find that perturbations to Adam's first and second moments induce comparably large effects, with similar sensitivity patterns observed in OLMo-1B. Finally, guided by our diagnostic, targeted stabilization reduces top-1 disagreement to 0.83% and increases generation exact match to 88.3%, at the cost of a 0.11-nat increase in validation loss. Our findings reveal a hidden form of optimizer-state-dependent sensitivity in LLM pre-training that conventional loss-based evaluations may overlook, while demonstrating its potential for diagnosis and mitigation.
authors: Bo Liu, Yuan Xie, Junan Chen, Fujun Han
bullets: Models are framed as non-autonomous dynamical systems jointly evolving weights and Adam optimizer states.

Targeted stabilization reduced top-1 disagreement to 0.83% and raised generation exact match to 88.3%, while increasing validation loss by 0.11 nat.

papers.abstract: Learning deformable physical world models requires dynamics that generalize beyond observed motion. Accurate reconstruction alone does not ensure accurate future prediction, motivating us to learn how observations should influence physical identification. However, visual reliability alone does not determine how informative an observation is about physical dynamics. We propose ViTrust to learn 3D observation trust, determining how strongly each tracked point influences physical identification. Its key design is a visual-contact trust adapter that combines pointwise spatiotemporal evidence with interaction history on a persistent contact graph to predict time-varying observation weights. A single-stage, shared-forward objective jointly optimizes these weights and physical parameters through weighted geometry and correspondence losses, with constraints to prevent observation-weight collapse. All learning uses only the observed prefix. The fitted physics remains fixed for future prediction under supplied controls. Experiments on real-world sequences demonstrate improved future prediction over the evaluated baselines, alongside qualitative demonstrations of novel-control rollouts and cross-object transfer.
authors: Zhihao Guo, Zhihao Li, Xu Ge, Lijian Zhong, Yu Lu, Haitao Wu, Longqing Zhao, Yue Ma
bullets: Addresses the gap between reconstructing observed motion and identifying dynamics that generalize to unseen future motion.
Uses a visual-contact trust adapter combining pointwise spatiotemporal evidence with persistent contact-graph history.
Jointly learns observation weights and physical parameters from weighted geometry and correspondence losses, while preventing weight collapse.
Trains only on the observed sequence prefix, then keeps the fitted physics fixed during controlled future prediction.
Real-world experiments show improved future prediction over evaluated baselines, with qualitative novel-control and cross-object transfer results.

Contact graph message passing and a temporal GRU encode interaction history on persistent patches defined by fixed point-to-anchor assignments. Patch-level contact adjustments are broadcast back to points and fused with pointwise visual scores to predict relative observation weights Wψ for physical identification. (c) Single-Stage Training. A regularized objective jointly updates physical parameters θ and adapter parameters ψ through trust-weighted geometry and tracking losses from a shared forward simulation on the observed prefix. (d) Future Prediction. Frozen physical parameters predict motion under future controls without refitting or future object observations, with 3D Gaussians used for rendering. papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow-based models have achieved remarkable success in generation, yet their samples often remain suboptimal in fidelity and text alignment. Two lines of inference-time methods address this: extrapolation guidance, such as classifier-free guidance (CFG) and its variants, and reward guidance, which aligns samples with reward models of human preference. Extrapolation guidance needs only forward passes, but it builds its reference by heuristic rules unrelated to the reward and therefore cannot steer sampling toward a given reward. Gradient-based reward guidance steers sampling directly toward a higher reward, but backpropagates through the entire generator at every step. This trade-off raises the question of whether extrapolation guidance can steer sampling toward a higher reward without a full backward pass. To answer this, we introduce Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance (RadAG), which constructs the reference by perturbing the attention logits of a single block against their reward gradient and extrapolates away from it. We prove that this update increases the reward of the clean estimate to first order, while its backward pass stops at the perturbed block instead of traversing the entire generator. On FLUX.2-klein-4B and 9B with PickScore and aesthetic rewards, RadAG achieves the highest target reward in every setting with 30-65% less time than gradient-based and candidate-based baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces an efficient inference-time alignment method for diffusion models using reward-attentive guidance, reducing computational cost while improving alignment.
papers.title: RadAG: Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance for Efficient Inference-Time Alignment of Diffusion Models

papers.abstract: Looped transformers do not acquire new knowledge during a forward pass. Prior work shows that they store as many bits in their weights as non-looped models. It remains unclear how recurrence makes this knowledge available during inference. We study this question using synthetic factual recall and multi-hop reasoning, measuring depth-resolved readable information in bits with native readouts and tuned lenses. Under final-loop supervision, single-hop facts become readable progressively: heavier memorization loads delay retrieval despite comparable final readable information. Untied baselines of equal unrolled depth concentrate retrieval near the end of their stacks, whereas looped models expose facts earlier. This delay is not intrinsic to the tested recall tasks: training with supervision and depth-specific readouts at every loop makes near-final information readable after the first loop in all tested configurations. Representational analysis shows value-related structure emerging within states organized by the query key. We then study multi-hop chains whose facts are stored in the weights rather than given in the prompt. Intermediate entities become decodable in chain order, and aligned transitions show next-entity structure developing while current-entity structure remains dominant. Interventions in a released six-recurrence model establish a causal role for these representations. Counterfactual replacements of a probe-defined entity component at a single prompt position redirect downstream bridge entities and the final answer. Conversely, replacements from queries that reach the same entity through different preceding relations, preserving the remaining relation suffix, retain the original answer in over 99.5\% of tested cases. These results distinguish a training-dependent schedule for factual recall from the causal role of retrieved-entity representations in subsequent composition.
authors: Fabio Valerio Massoli, Arnau Padr\'es Masdemont, Jordi Ros Giralt, Arash Behboodi
bullets: Under final-loop supervision, heavier memorization loads delay when facts become readable, despite similar final information.
Loopy models expose facts earlier than equally deep untied transformers, while depth-specific supervision can make near-final information readable after the first loop.
In multi-hop recall, intermediate entities become decodable in chain order as next-entity structure develops around query-key-organized states.
Interventions show that replacing a retrieved entity redirects downstream bridge entities and answers; matched relational substitutions preserve the original answer in over 99.5% of tests.
The findings separate a training-dependent retrieval schedule from the causal role of retrieved entities in composing answers.

papers.selection_reason: Studies knowledge availability and factual recall in looped transformer architectures, relevant to LLM architecture and reasoning.
papers.title: When do stored facts become available in looped transformers?
papers.tldr: Looped transformers can retrieve stored facts progressively during recurrence, with learned entity representations causally driving later multi-hop reasoning.

papers.abstract: Practical highway infrastructure inspection entails progressive diagnostic reasoning from visual perception to maintenance decisions, yet existing benchmarks remain confined to isolated tasks, leaving Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) insufficiently evaluated across sequential inspection stages. Meanwhile, current datasets focus primarily on highway pavement defects, falling short of real-world inspection across diverse infrastructure components such as highway pavements, guardrails, glare screens, and drainage systems. To address these gaps, we formulate the Highway Infrastructure Inspection Progression Chain (HIIP-Chain), spanning Anomaly Detection, Anomaly Recognition, Condition Analysis, and Maintenance Resolution, and introduce HighwayVerse. HighwayVerse comprises 14,143 real-world Ground and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) inspection records spanning 100 and 17 anomaly categories, respectively, with 84,858 expert-reviewed question-answer pairs. We evaluate 12 open-source and closed-source MLLMs using the chained metric Final, which credits a correct maintenance decision only when all preceding diagnostic stages are completed correctly. Results show that although models achieve relatively high accuracy when initially judging whether an anomaly is present, their markedly lower Final scores expose struggles across downstream recognition, analysis, and decision-making. This discrepancy indicates that current MLLMs do not fully comprehend specific highway anomaly patterns beyond superficial initial judgments. Furthermore, we propose LaneRAG, a training-free retrieval-augmented framework that provides hierarchical reference guidance achieving consistent performance improvements across diverse MLLMs. Our dataset, evaluation benchmark, and source code will be publicly released.
authors: Junyi Yang, Zheng Si, Yilin Zhai, Pengpeng Ouyang, Hongxi Wang, Kangze Li, Mo Chen, Sicong Zhang, Hua Wang, Dongyuan Wu, Dong Chen, Mingliang Xu
bullets: Introduces HIIP-Chain, a four-stage inspection progression: detection, recognition, condition analysis, and maintenance resolution.
Covers diverse highway components—including pavements, guardrails, glare screens, and drainage systems—using ground and UAV inspection records.
Provides 14,143 real-world records and 84,858 expert-reviewed question-answer pairs across 100 ground and 17 UAV anomaly categories.
Evaluates 12 open- and closed-source MLLMs with Final, which requires every preceding diagnostic stage to be correct before crediting the maintenance decision.
Finds that models detect anomalies relatively well but struggle with downstream recognition, analysis, and decisions; LaneRAG consistently improves performance without training.

Figure 2. HighwayVerse construction through image filtering, visual-spatial verification, QA generation, and human review.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires timely decisions based on instructions and visual observations. However, autoregressive VLN models generate action descriptions token by token, introducing substantial inference overhead. Decision models offer an efficient alternative but face challenges in maintaining short-horizon action coherence and long-horizon goal alignment. To address these challenges, we propose NavDecision, an efficient multi-step VLN decision model. We introduce parallel multi-step action prediction (PMAP) to predict multiple action distributions from a shared vision-language state, and memory-augmented self-referential policy optimization (M-SRPO) to learn from unsuccessful trajectories using successful trajectories as references. A cross-iteration success memory further accumulates historical successful trajectories to provide informative training feedback. NavDecision achieves success rates of 64.60% on R2R-CE and 64.57% on RxR-CE with a 4B backbone. Compared with existing autoregressive VLN methods, it delivers significant inference speedups of up to $22.28\times$ and $18.96\times$ while maintaining comparable navigation performance.
authors: Kai Wu, Yufan Hu, Quan Fang, Boning Zhang, Junyu Gao
bullets: Targets autoregressive VLN inference overhead and difficulties with short- and long-horizon decision coherence.
Uses parallel multi-step action prediction (PMAP) to generate multiple action distributions from one shared vision-language state.
Introduces memory-augmented self-referential policy optimization (M-SRPO), with cross-iteration success memory for learning from unsuccessful trajectories.
Reports 64.60% success on R2R-CE and 64.57% on RxR-CE with a 4B backbone.
Achieves up to 22.28× and 18.96× inference speedups over autoregressive VLN methods while maintaining comparable navigation performance.

papers.title: NavDecision: Parallel Multi-Step Action Prediction with Persistent Self-Referential Learning for Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: NavDecision accelerates vision-and-language navigation by predicting multiple actions in parallel while using successful trajectories as persistent training references.

papers.abstract: Streaming 3D reconstruction must preserve geometry under limited memory, yet STAC's fixed-resolution spatial key-value (KV) cache grows as scenes expand. We propose STAC++, a plug-and-play, training-free framework that compresses and reuses spatial memory for long-term reconstruction in unbounded scenes. Adaptive Spatial KV Cache (ASKC) organizes KV states into an octree with adaptive resolutions across regions and layers. Response-Aware Cache Compression (RACC) guides KV merging by measuring attention-output changes, balancing storage savings with geometric preservation. Temporal Context Refinement (TCR) reuses cached intermediate features and recomputes only a short backbone suffix to refine historical predictions with later observations. Integrated into four pretrained streaming backbones, STAC++ reduces spatial memory consumption while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality on long sequences and large scenes, with further quality gains from refinement at limited computational overhead. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
authors: Boyi Zhu, Youcheng Cai, Dong Wang
bullets: Addresses the memory growth of STAC’s fixed-resolution spatial KV cache as scenes expand.
Uses an adaptive-resolution octree cache, with resolutions varying across regions and network layers.
Merges KV states based on attention-output changes to balance memory savings and geometric preservation.
Refines historical predictions by reusing cached features and recomputing only a short backbone suffix.
Integrated with four pretrained backbones, it reduces memory while maintaining competitive quality and adds refinement gains at limited computational overhead.

ASKC organizes spatial KV states in an adaptive octree; RACC guides cache compression using attention-output changes. papers.tldr: STAC++ is a training-free, plug-and-play framework that compresses and refines spatial memory to enable long-term streaming 3D reconstruction in large, unbounded scenes.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive diffusion world models deliver strong video generation performance, yet they typically output only RGB frames rather than explicit 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene representations, creating a gap between learned visual world dynamics and usable 3D assets for downstream robotics, simulation and rendering. To bridge this gap, we introduce ArgsWorld, an autoregressive diffusion model that also produces an explicit 3DGS scene. For each generation chunk, the diffusion transformer jointly processes clean historical image latents and noisy latents for new views. It keeps the historical image latents fixed and refreshes the scene features so that the Gaussian representation can be revised as new regions come into view. Our 3D Self-Forcing Distillation trains the model on its own generated histories using a mixture of single-view and multi-view data. Distribution matching supervises direct image latents and latents of Gaussian renderings at both generation and additional cameras. ArgsWorld unifies 3D scene reconstruction from posed images, scene generation from image or text prompts, and scene extrapolation across camera segments with disconnected endpoints. Experimental results demonstrate that ArgsWorld achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple 3D scene modeling tasks. Project page: https://m4a1tastegood.github.io/ArgsWorld/
authors: Weiming Chen, Shuaiyan Liu, Xinyu Shao, Zhewen Chen, Tian Guan, Yonghong He, Xitong Ling
bullets: Addresses the gap between RGB-only video world models and usable 3D scene representations.
Jointly processes fixed historical image latents and noisy new-view latents while refreshing Gaussian scene features as regions are revealed.
Uses 3D Self-Forcing Distillation with single- and multi-view data, plus distribution matching for direct and Gaussian-rendered image latents.
Supports 3D reconstruction, image- or text-prompted scene generation, and camera-segment extrapolation with disconnected endpoints.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across multiple 3D scene modeling tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. ArgsWorld inference. (a) We process a camera trajectory in successive chunks, using available reference images to condition the first chunk. Multiple input images enable scene reconstruction, while a single input image supports open-ended scene generation. (b) Each DiT call attends jointly to the current views and their clean history, predicting new RGB latents and refreshing features for Gaussian decoding across all views processed so far. 3DGS latents and DiT features feed the next denoising step within a chunk. Across chunks, the model carries forward its final direct RGB latents and 3DGS latents.

papers.title: ArgsWorld: Unifying 3DGS Scene Reconstruction, Generation and Extrapolation with Autoregressive Diffusion Transformer

papers.abstract: As code agents evolve, their scope is expanding from generating simple static 3D meshes to constructing structurally complete, complex, interactive 3D scenes. However, existing datasets mainly rely on converting or captioning pre-existing 3D assets, consisting mostly of single-turn code data for static single objects and struggling to scale task diversity and scene complexity, leaving such training data scarce. We present 3DCodeFactory, an automated framework that directly constructs diverse, complex 3D training data from abundant raw text (e.g., diffusion prompts and product descriptions). The framework first leverages an image generator to synthesize 3D reference images from raw text as visual anchors, guiding the generation of concrete modeling specifications and interactive functional requirements; meanwhile, it jointly constructs visual, specification, and functional rubrics from the reference images and requirements to automatically score and filter multi-turn agent rollouts. Based on this framework, we release 3DCodeFactory-Data, comprising 5,045 high-quality task instances and multi-turn interaction trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B on 3DCodeFactory-Data significantly improves performance on BlenderWorld, P3D-Bench, and 3DCodeBench, consistently outperforming models trained on existing open-source 3D code datasets, with our 27B model further surpassing the same-series 2.4T flagship Qwen3.8-Max in overall performance.
authors: Zhaoyu Wang, Xueru Wen, XingYu Li, Jie Lou
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of training data beyond static, single-object 3D code generation.
Uses image-generated 3D references to guide modeling specifications and interactive requirements.
Automatically creates visual, specification, and functional rubrics to score and filter agent rollouts.
Releases 3DCodeFactory-Data with 5,045 high-quality task instances and interaction trajectories.
Fine-tuned Qwen3.5 models improve performance across BlenderWorld, P3D-Bench, and 3DCodeBench; the 27B model surpasses Qwen3.8-Max overall.

papers.tldr: 3DCodeFactory automatically turns raw text into diverse, multi-turn training data for agents that build complex interactive 3D scenes.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents can read and edit the weights of neural networks without gradients, and this is increasingly presented as a new way of repairing models. We ask what such an agent adds, in a setting with a known answer. A vision model moved into a new system may be broken by a preprocessing, weight-conversion or output-convention fault; an agent restricted to forward passes must decide whether a fault exists, name it, and undo it by editing the weights. Over 183 runs on classification, segmentation and detection, scored against the fault-free model, we find three things. When the kind of fault is known, the agent is not needed: a script written afterwards repairs 30 of 48 faults against the agent's 33. But the agent did not have to be told: on five fault types outside every script it repairs 15 of 15 where that script repairs 4, and it never edits any of 21 fault-free models. And its limits are predictable: it needs a trustworthy per-layer reference for the model's activations and a fault that is an invertible structured transformation; without them, small faults are missed and repairs stay partial. We derive guidance on when to use an agent and when a script.
authors: Zhuangzi Li, Shilv Cai, Jian Jin, Weisi Lin
bullets: The study evaluates blind fault detection, diagnosis, and weight-based repair using only forward passes.
Across classification, segmentation, and detection, agents are compared with post hoc scripts over 183 runs.
For known fault types, scripts repair 30/48 faults versus 33/48 for the agent, so the agent adds little.

papers.abstract: World models hold great promise for autonomous driving planning, yet their ability to imagine the future often comes at a formidable computational cost. Efficiency efforts, such as knowledge distillation and domain-specific pre-training, often shift this burden to costly teachers or training pipelines, leaving lightweight world modeling an open challenge. We introduce FastWorld, a natively lightweight world-model framework for efficient autonomous driving planning. FastWorld reduces computation through compact scene representations, short-horizon action-conditioned prediction, and selective candidate verification and score refinement. These designs support efficient future-informed planning without teacher distillation or additional domain-specific pre-training. On NAVSIMv1, FastWorld achieves 92.2 PDMS at 132 FPS on a single 4090 GPU. It also achieves 89.4 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2 and an average L2 of 0.40 over 3 seconds at 17 FPS on nuScenes. Code and models can be found at https://github.com/MoyangSensei/FastWorld.
authors: Feiyang Jia, Lin Liu, Zhicheng Bao, Caiyan Jia, Ziying Song, Shengkai Zhang, Lina Han, Yan Zhao, Xiaoshuai Hao
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of imagining future driving scenarios for planning.
Uses compact scene representations, short-horizon action-conditioned prediction, and selective candidate verification with score refinement.
Avoids costly teacher distillation and additional domain-specific pre-training.
Achieves 92.2 PDMS at 132 FPS on NAVSIMv1, 89.4 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2, and 0.40 average 3-second L2 at 17 FPS on nuScenes.
Scope is demonstrated on NAVSIM and nuScenes benchmarks; the abstract does not report broader deployment limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 2. FastWorld Pipeline. FastWorld achieves efficient planning through a natively lightweight architecture. (c) Future-Aware Utility Scoring refines candidate scores using the predicted futures and selects the final trajectory. (d) Future-informed trajectory selection yields the final driving decision.

papers.abstract: Gigapixel whole-slide images (WSIs) exceed single-pass vision-language model (VLM) capacity at cellular resolution, while multiple instance learning relies on query-agnostic offline patching without interactive reasoning. Multi-step VLM navigation agents inspect regions on demand, yet face two bottlenecks: (1) autoregressive action decoding incurs heavy latency, throttling exploration and online multi-trajectory RL; and (2) offline distillation suffers from an existential-versus-universal stopping asymmetry between positive detection and negative exclusion, inducing thumbnail and kinematic shortcuts while leaving policies prone to passing metastases without stopping. Under the Jev (System One) paradigm, a model predicts distributions over predefined decision spaces in one forward pass (0 generated tokens) while deterministic code executes navigation. We build JevNavAgent, a 2B-parameter agent combining factorized stopping, spatial-candidate, and contextual-bilinear answer heads with overview modality dropout. We pair Stage-1 offline counterfactual trajectory alignment (mitigating depth and panning shortcuts) with Stage-2 online trajectory-level GRPO (Traj-GRPO), using decoding-free rollouts to optimize branch-level lesion discovery, in-polygon stopping, and step-wise confidence gain. On Clean Visual WSI-VQA, JevNavAgent achieves 51.57% multi-scale (50.43% terminal-step) overall and 51.39% focal accuracy, outperforming frontier VLM agents and 4B-11B open-source cascades while running nearly 12x faster than frontier APIs (5.63s vs. 66.64-70.04s). On CAMELYON16 Official Test, Traj-GRPO reaches 22.45% localization (converting 11/12, or 91.7%, of visited tumors into grounded stops) with 93.75% specificity and 69.77% slide accuracy, surpassing Stage-1 SFT under matched stopping rules alongside zero-shot budget scaling.
authors: Yonghuang Wu, Zhenyang Liang, Pengfei Wang, Yize Ma, Guoqing Wu, Jinhua Yu
bullets: Addresses slow autoregressive navigation and stopping failures in whole-slide image analysis.
Uses one forward pass with factorized stopping, spatial-candidate, and contextual-bilinear answer heads; deterministic code executes navigation.
Combines counterfactual trajectory alignment with online Traj-GRPO to optimize lesion discovery, in-polygon stopping, and confidence gain.
Achieves 51.57% multi-scale accuracy on Clean Visual WSI-VQA and runs nearly 12× faster than frontier APIs.
On CAMELYON16, reaches 22.45% localization, 93.75% specificity, and 69.77% slide accuracy; scope is gigapixel pathology navigation.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the JevNavAgent architecture and two-stage trajectory alignment framework. (a) Deterministic environment code supplies a multi-scale observation ot (whole-slide thumbnail Iov, up to K = 3 recent crops shown with illustrative nested 2.5 × –40× fields from a CAMELYON16 Official Test episode, query Q, options A, trail V1:t, and candidate pool Ct, without B − t prompt counters) to Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct. Under the Jev (System One) interface, one forward pass (0 generated tokens) yields ptype, pcand (scoring Ct), and pans (reusing shared LM logits with bilinear keys); deterministic orchestration executes READ (next view vt+1) or STOP (final diagnostic prediction). (b) Stage-1 SFT offline counterfactual alignment balances long-horizon and panning stops via eligible multi-region negatives (Mneg), synthetic positives, and stop-decoupled supervision (LSFT). (c) Stage-2 Traj-GRPO rolls out forced-READ groups over restricted pools Sg,t for two specializations: + GRPO (CAM16) (L(2) CAM) and + GRPO (VQA+KL) (L̃(2) VQA + CAM).

(a) Clean Visual WSI-VQA (351 questions): JevNavAgent + Traj-GRPO attains the highest multi-scale accuracy (51.57%, filled star) and focal accuracy (51.39%), with Step-T accuracy (50.43%, hollow star) on par with the strongest 4B baseline, at 5.63 s per episode, 11.8× –12.4× faster than frontier multi-turn agents (GPT-6.1-Sol/Terra); the SFT variant is shown with Step-T readout. Top bars: Strict Loc+Spec (%); bottom bars: mean reads on positive (solid) and negative (hatched) slides.

Fig. 3. Zero-shot test-time compute scaling and Stage-2 online reinforcement learning dynamics on CAMELYON16. (a, b) Decoupling the execution budget B from the policy prompt lets the same checkpoint scale across B ∈ {4, 6, 8, 10, 12} without retraining: Dev positive localization hit rate rises from 8.70% to 30.43% and slide accuracy from 54.35% to 71.74% (Stage-1 SFT); on the held-out Test split, Stage-2 Traj-GRPO raises the hit rate from 12.24% to 22.45% and slide accuracy from 67.44% to 69.77%, while Stage-1 SFT reaches 10.20% and 66.67% (Traj-GRPO uses the calibrated stopping rule of Table IV). (c) Across the 60-step Stage-2 training log (10-step window averages), in-polygon stopping probability P (STOP | Tumor) rises from 70.1% (steps 1–10) to a peak of 94.9% (steps 41–50) before settling at 67.5% (steps 51–60), benign-follicle false-positive risk falls from 7.58% to 2.35% (steps 31–40), and the branch search reward increases 5.0× (0.072 → 0.362).

papers.abstract: Aligning pre-trained diffusion models with multiple context-dependent preferences requires adapting generation at test time rather than relying on offline fine-tuning, which requires hyperparameter tuning and a new training run for each preference trade-off. Existing approaches compress diverse preferences into a single scalar reward objective for fine-tuning or test-time guidance rather than directly reusing existing generative experts released for different purposes and obtained through different fine-tuning methods. In this work, we propose Contrastive Gradient Guidance (CGG), a test-time compositional generative framework that reformulates multi-preference alignment as a composition of distributions. CGG represents each preference as a contrastive preference pair of favored experts and unfavored anti-experts, whose score difference forms a contrastive gradient guidance signal that combines denoising directions (gradients) from off-the-shelf diffusion models during sampling. Experiments show that CGG reuses pre-trained and fine-tuned models as favored experts or anti-experts to control output style and safety, and that it can be combined with existing sampling-based reward guidance. With a single fixed scale per pair, CGG composes five preferences at once and gives a more balanced trade-off across text-image preference, concept control, photographic fidelity, and safety than offline fine-tuning, weight-space merging, and reward steering.
authors: Po-Yi Lu, Jui-Chao Lu, Paul Kuo-Ming Huang, Shih-Hsin Wang, Chun-Liang Li, Hsuan-Tien Lin
bullets: Addresses multi-preference alignment without a new offline fine-tuning run for each preference trade-off.
Forms each preference from a favored expert and an anti-expert, using their score difference as a guidance signal.
Combines denoising gradients from existing diffusion models at sampling time and can integrate reward guidance.
Controls style and safety while composing five preferences with one fixed scale per preference pair.
Reports more balanced trade-offs across text-image preference, concept control, photographic fidelity, and safety than several baselines.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion models can render convincing frames while failing to produce the requested action. Increasing classifier-free guidance (CFG) can strengthen motion, but also saturates and shifts colors. Scalar CFG assigns the same coefficient to the averaged and frame-varying components of its prediction difference, limiting independent control of temporal variation. THAW, Temporal Harmonic Amplification during Warm-up, retains stock CFG and adds a separately weighted residual during an initial denoising window. Its dose specifies the added norm relative to the current CFG difference, giving the extra guidance a consistent relative budget across sampling steps. THAW is training-free and reuses CFG's two model predictions with an unchanged network evaluation count. It improves cost-matched motion over scalar and scheduled CFG on five video models, with positive point estimates against existing guidance methods on three of them. On VBench, THAW raises dynamic degree by about 14 to 15 points over stock CFG while increasing total scores on a different set of three models.
authors: Xuanhua Yin, Boyu Wei, Chengkun Yue, Shunqi Mao, Chuanzhi Xu, Wei Guo, Weidong Cai
bullets: Scalar CFG can strengthen motion but may saturate and shift colors because it controls averaged and frame-varying components together.
THAW adds a separately weighted residual during an initial denoising window while retaining standard CFG.
Its dose is normalized to the current CFG difference, providing a consistent relative guidance budget across sampling steps.
The training-free method improves cost-matched motion across five video models and shows positive point estimates against existing guidance methods on three.
On VBench, THAW increases dynamic degree by about 14–15 points over stock CFG, while total-score gains occur on a different set of three models.

papers.abstract: We present OSplit, an exact analytical method that enables efficient partitioning of a GPU L1 domain into prefill and decode workers, including sharding for classical and advanced GPUs. OSplit takes into consideration model parameters, enabling any inference model to be partitioned into prefill and decode workers with a goal of producing the maximum throughput possible. OSplit is based on a capacity model that takes as inputs the model, the loading scheme (batch size, max sequence length), and models an inference serving framework (vLLM) and computes the efficiency of each GPU. For this, we model H100 and GB300 GPUs, and model a scale-up domain, along with FlashAttention-based kernels. OSplit first computes an optimal collective generation policy, which gives inputs to the capacity model that enables optimal split of prefill and decode GPUs. We evaluate our scheme over H100 (NVL8) and GB300 (NVL72) using vLLM inference serving and show throughput, predicted and measured latency, showing near-perfect theoretical-to-measured values over leading LLMs (Llama and Qwen)
authors: Akshat Pandey, Dominic Cheng, Sidharth Sharma, Ashwin Gumaste
bullets: Models GPU capacity using the inference model, batch size, sequence length, loading scheme, vLLM, and FlashAttention-based kernels.
Supports sharding and partitioning across classical and advanced GPU configurations, including H100 NVL8 and GB300 NVL72.
Computes an optimal collective generation policy before selecting the prefill/decode GPU split.
Evaluation on Llama and Qwen shows near-perfect agreement between predicted and measured latency and throughput.
Scope is evaluated on modeled H100 and GB300 scale-up domains with vLLM serving.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion models have enabled the synthesis of high-fidelity, visually compelling videos. However, despite being trained on internet-scale video data, understanding underlying physical laws and generating physically plausible dynamics remain challenging. To mitigate this, conditioning video generators on explicit physical reasoning has emerged as a promising direction. Nevertheless, existing conditioning approaches often fail to incorporate detailed physical guidance into generation, resulting in physically implausible motion or visual artifacts. We propose PSC-Gen, a training-free framework that employs an agentic approach to synthesize visual conditions and inject their core dynamics via low-frequency filtering. By iteratively planning physical states and verifying generated keyframes, our Physics Agent constructs visually and physically consistent keyframe sequences. We then interpolate these keyframes into a continuous physical sequence and inject only its low-frequency components, steering the video model to preserve physical dynamics while synthesizing fine visual details. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations across physics-informed and robotic manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that PSC-Gen faithfully follows instructions and generates physically plausible videos.
authors: Wonsik Shin, Jinju Jang, Junhoo Lee, Yeonjin Chang, Jimyeong Kim, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Addresses physically implausible motion and artifacts in video diffusion models despite large-scale video training.
Uses a training-free Physics Agent to iteratively plan physical states and verify generated keyframes.
Interpolates verified keyframes into continuous physical sequences and injects their low-frequency components into the video generator.
Evaluations on physics-informed and robotic manipulation benchmarks show improved instruction following and physically plausible videos.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method Overview. PSC-Gen generates physically plausible videos through (a) Agentic Visual Planning and (b) Physical Sequence Conditioning. A vision-language model (VLM) acts as a Physics Agent to plan physical states and iteratively generate and verify keyframes. These keyframes are interpolated into a physical sequence, which guides diffusion sampling through low-frequency velocity injection. This design effectively transfers physical dynamics while allowing the diffusion model to synthesize fine visual details.

Figure 5. Ablation Study on Physical Sequence Conditioning. The top row shows the variant without Physical Sequence Conditioning, and the bottom row shows our full pipeline. While the ablated variant simply reconstructs and interpolates the static keyframes, our full pipeline achieves more natural, physically plausible motion guided by the physical sequence.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free physical-sequence conditioning improves physical plausibility of video diffusion, relevant to video generation and world-model-style dynamics.
papers.title: PSC-Gen: Physical Sequence Conditioning for Video Generation via Agentic Visual Planning
papers.tldr: PSC-Gen improves physical plausibility in video generation by planning, verifying, and injecting physically consistent visual sequences without training the generator.

papers.abstract: Strong vision and text encoders can be trained independently, but their representations are not directly comparable. Connecting them usually requires paired image-text data, which may be unavailable. Unpaired alignment instead fits a map between a vision and a text encoder from feature-space geometry alone, enabling text-based retrieval and zero-shot classification without paired data. Treating each pair independently leads to fragile searches, repeated fitting, and uncertain map quality. A collection of encoders supplies additional supervision: all vision encoders embed the same images and all text encoders the same texts. Correspondences within each modality are therefore known exactly, while the cross-modal correspondence remains hidden. ConsensusAlign pools each modality into a shared space, fits one unpaired cross-modal bridge, and transfers it in closed form to every encoder pair. New encoders join through same-modality fitting without repeating the cross-modal search. On 21 vision-text encoder pairs and five seeds, pooled fitting aligns every pair, whereas pairwise fits fail in 68 of 105 pair-seed cells. Mean alignment error (FOSCTTM) falls from 0.1457 to 0.0099, and zero-shot accuracy nearly doubles on ten datasets. Gains persist across the tested within-modality pooling constructions with a WP bridge. New corpora reuse the bridge through native maps fitted to unlabeled target features from every source encoder. Agreement with separately fitted reference maps detects failures on COCO.
authors: Xuanhua Yin, Shunqi Mao, Chuanzhi Xu, Boyu Wei, Wei Guo, Weidong Cai
bullets: Unpaired alignment enables text retrieval and zero-shot classification without paired image-text data, but pairwise fitting is fragile.
ConsensusAlign pools same-modality encoder representations, fits one cross-modal bridge, and transfers it in closed form to all encoder pairs.
New encoders can be added through same-modality fitting without repeating the cross-modal search; new corpora can reuse the bridge via native maps.
Across 21 encoder pairs and five seeds, pooled fitting succeeded for every pair, while pairwise fits failed in 68 of 105 pair-seed cases.
Alignment error decreased from 0.1457 to 0.0099, and zero-shot accuracy nearly doubled across ten datasets; agreement with reference maps helps detect failures.

papers.abstract: Neural networks are typically trained separately for individual datasets or tasks, resulting in many task-specific models. This redundancy increases memory footprint, deployment costs, and energy consumption limiting their scalability. We propose UNIFY, a unified learning framework that enables a single model to jointly learn and perform inference across multiple datasets via Batch Normalization Switching (BNS). Instead of maintaining separate models for each dataset, UNIFY shares the parameter-intensive backbone while maintaining dataset-specific BN statistics and parameters, along with dataset-specific classification heads. We validate our framework using five datasets (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet) across six Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) of different sizes (SqueezeNet 1.1, WideResNet-40-2, WideResNet-16-8, ResNet-18, ResNet-34, ResNet-50). Notably, a single UNIFIED ResNet-34 trained on these datasets achieves accuracies of 99.53%, 94.84%, 96.12%, 80.32%, and 67.67%, respectively, outperforming the average performance of the corresponding independently trained task-specific models while reducing the memory footprint by approximately 4.94x, from 428.30 MB (five separate models) to 86.71 MB (one unified model). UNIFY aims not only to consolidate (K) models into a single model but also to enhance model-effectiveness by leveraging complementary knowledge across datasets. It paves the way for scalable, efficient, and unified learning capable of handling diverse image classification tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/saktx/UNIFY.
authors: Shaharyar Ahmed Khan Tareen, Xiaojing Yuan
bullets: Addresses the memory, deployment, and energy costs of maintaining separate models for different datasets or tasks.
Uses Batch Normalization Switching with shared backbone parameters, dataset-specific BN statistics/parameters, and dataset-specific classification heads.
Evaluated across five datasets and six CNN architectures.
A unified ResNet-34 achieved the reported accuracies while reducing memory from 428.30 MB to 86.71 MB—about 4.94× lower than five separate models.
The framework is scoped to jointly learning and inferring across diverse image-classification datasets.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: An example UNIFIED architecture for 3 datasets, having 4 feature-extraction layers, 2 switchable BN layers, and an output layer. Each switchable BN layer maintains 3 sets of BN parameters (and statistics), while the output layer contains 3 classification heads, corresponding to the 3 participating datasets. To preserve dataset-specific parameters, the corresponding BN layers and classification head are switched while routing the data from different datasets. The shared feature-extraction layers can be linear, convolutional, or residual connections, depending on the architecture used (UNIFY is architecture-flexible framework that can be adopted in various CNN architectures). Batch Normalization Switching (BNS) and dedicated classification heads preserve dataset-specific representations while enabling joint optimization through a shared backbone.

Fig. 1: (a) A UNIFIED model jointly trained across multiple datasets enables effective inference on all datasets through Batch Normalization Switching (BNS) and dataset-specific classification heads. (b) A UNIFIED model trained on K datasets, reduces the memory footprint to approximately 1/K of that required by K independently trained models, while preserving strong performance. (c) A UNIFIED ResNet-34, jointly trained on 5 datasets, achieves overall superior performance compared with independently trained ResNet-34 models on these datasets.

Fig. 3: Visualization of the feature statistics in a Switchable BN layer of a UNIFIED SqueezeNet 1.1 during training. BN Heads 1 to 5 correspond to MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet, respectively. The differences in the statistical distributions across the 5 BN sets highlight the importance of BNS in accommodating dataset-specific feature characteristics. These results suggest that sharing a single BN configuration is ineffective and sub-optimal for accommodating distinct data characteristics of the 5 datasets, resulting in degraded performance, as also supported by the results in Table IV.

TABLE III: Comparison of parameter count and memory footprint between dataset-specific and UNIFIED models at Float32 precision. The percentage parameter and memory overhead introduced by the dataset-specific BN layers and classification heads is reported in parentheses. The deployment-size reduction shows the reduction achieved by replacing 5 independently deployed models with 1 UNIFIED model.

TABLE II: Performance comparison of independently trained dataset-specific models with corresponding UNIFIED models jointly trained across all datasets (bold blue and bold black indicate superior performance achieved by UNIFIED and dataset-specific models, respectively). Results demonstrate that a single UNIFIED model can provide comparable or even superior performance on all datasets as compared to independently trained models.

TABLE IV: Performance of UNIFIED models without the use of Batch Normalization Switching (BNS). After 200 epochs of training, the results demonstrate that a common BN configuration does not adequately accommodate the distinct feature distributions of the 5 datasets even if dedicated classification heads are used, leading to overall degraded performance.

papers.selection_reason: Single model with dataset-specific BN and heads reduces memory and deployment cost, transferable to efficient multi-task and continual adaptation.
papers.title: UNIFY: Unified Learning with One Model via Batch Norm Switching
papers.tldr: UNIFY consolidates multiple image-classification models into one by sharing the backbone while switching dataset-specific batch normalization and classification components.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models can state the rules of a video game, but do they apply them when they only see the game? We introduce RuleCraft, 1,240 image questions over 155 Minecraft rules with outcomes verified in the game engine, each asked in text, on the image with the game named, and on the bare image. Six widely used models know the rules and recognize the game, yet answer the bare image by real-world physics: naming the game raises their accuracy on rules where the game departs from reality by 8.2-19.8 points on a main set and by 33.8-52.7 on a hard stress-test set. Their errors pick the real-world outcome, the gap is largest where the game leaves a scene unchanged, and reasoning traces state the game's rule, then answer by reality. On the main set, naming the game mostly swaps the real-world default for the game's. The pattern holds with reasoning, recurs in two more games, and persists on questions the models themselves take to be about the game; one neutral sentence asking for the rules of the world shown recovers much of the gap. Evaluations that name the game measure knowledge of its rules, not world selection.
authors: Jianxin Gao, Bohan Chen, Runze Li, Qi Zhang

The models may state the correct game rule in their reasoning but still answer according to real-world physics; the effect also appears in two other games.
A neutral prompt asking about the rules of the depicted world recovers much of the performance gap.

papers.abstract: Learning-based optical flow estimation approaches generally rely on both inter-frame correspondence evidence and intra-frame contextual guidance, yet features from general-purpose image encoders may not fully support these roles. Strongly activated but weakly discriminative channels can outweigh more informative ones when computing inter-frame feature similarity, while context feature affinities can be low within motion-coherent regions yet high across motion boundaries. To address these mismatches, this study proposes TO-Flow, a task-oriented feature adaptation framework that aligns matching and context features with their respective requirements through dedicated channel modulation and spatial reorganization approaches. An affinity-based soft partition distinguishes motion-region interiors from boundary-adjacent regions to guide both processes. Channel modulation uses simulated flow refinement to assess whether each channel assigns higher similarity to estimated correspondences than to nearby competing candidates. The resulting similarity differences are aggregated within each region type and averaged across iterations to derive channel weights that emphasize informative channels and suppress ambiguous ones. Spatial reorganization combines affinity-guided feature attraction and repulsion from coarse to fine to simultaneously improve consistency within motion-coherent regions and distinctiveness across motion boundaries, with feature resampling mitigating boundary blurring during cross-scale fusion. Extensive experiments on the MPI Sintel, KITTI 2015, Spring, and LayeredFlow datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and general applicability of TO-Flow across diverse iterative refinement architectures as well as supervised and unsupervised training paradigms. The source code will be publicly available at https://mias.group/TO-Flow upon publication.
authors: Mengtan Zhang, Dazhong Wang, Haoran Zhang, Hongbo Zhao, Yuhang Ming, Weihao Yuan, Wei Ye, Hanli Wang, Rui Fan
bullets: General-purpose features can overemphasize weak channels and confuse motion interiors with boundaries.
An affinity-based soft partition separates motion-region interiors from boundary-adjacent regions.
Channel modulation reinforces features that distinguish estimated correspondences from competing matches.
Coarse-to-fine spatial reorganization improves within-region consistency and cross-boundary distinctiveness while reducing boundary blur.
Experiments on MPI Sintel, KITTI 2015, Spring, and LayeredFlow show effectiveness across iterative, supervised, and unsupervised flow systems.

papers.abstract: Image enhancement spans degradations with distinct spectral characteristics. Standard convolutions use fixed kernels, whereas dynamic convolutions gain adaptability at additional inference cost. We propose Dynamic Spectrum Re-parameterized Convolution (DSRC), a plug-and-play module that learns task-adaptive spectral responses during training while retaining standard convolution at inference. DSRC decomposes convolution kernels into frequency bands, applies learnable high/low-pass modulation, and incorporates lightweight residual branches. Owing to the linearity of these operations, all training-time components are analytically fused into a single kernel for inference. Experiments on low-light enhancement, underwater enhancement, and image super-resolution show consistent PSNR gains and generally improved or preserved SSIM and LPIPS across twelve backbone-task configurations, with unchanged deployed parameter counts and theoretical FLOPs, and no additional inference operators.
authors: Zhiyan Zhou, Hailong Yan, Hanlin Liu, Yongrui Zhang, Xiangtao Zhang, Le Zhang
bullets: Targets the mismatch between fixed convolution kernels and degradations with different spectral characteristics.
Decomposes kernels into frequency bands and learns high-/low-pass modulation with lightweight residual branches.
Uses analytical re-parameterization to fuse all training-time components into one standard convolution.
Across 12 backbone–task configurations for low-light, underwater enhancement, and super-resolution, it reports consistent PSNR gains and generally improved or preserved SSIM and LPIPS.
Deployed parameter counts and theoretical FLOPs remain unchanged, with no extra inference operators.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables foundation models to perform unseen tasks from context without parameter updates. In robotic manipulation, a human video provides the context that specifies how a task should be performed. However, scaling human-video ICL on world-action models (WAMs) faces two challenges: task-level human-robot pairs are not temporally aligned with robot actions, and standard action losses allow policies to rely on initial-scene or task-identity shortcuts rather than tracking the context. We present Entangle, an in-context world-action model that maps a single human video and current robot observations to future visual states and executable actions. To scale temporally aligned training data, we convert recorded robot videos into matched human contexts via video-to-video generation, supplemented by real paired recordings. For model training, we combine variable-length video windows with an intra-task contrastive objective that distinguishes the paired action trajectory from other executions of the same task, preventing task-identity shortcuts. Without task-specific fine-tuning, Entangle improves steadily as aligned training data scales, reaching an average score of 83.5/100 across six unseen tasks on an Astribot S1 robot, and achieves a 69.5% average success rate on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, outperforming Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points. Under Context-OOD, although trained only on scene-aligned pairs, Entangle transfers context-specified behaviors across rearranged layouts and substituted tools.
authors: Chendong Xiang, Chengwen Zhang, Ruowen Zhao, Zeyuan Wang, Shuhe Huang, Rongxu Cui, Min Zhao, Fan Bao, Hengkai Tan, Jun Zhu
bullets: Addresses temporal misalignment between human demonstrations and robot actions, plus shortcut reliance on scene or task identity.
Generates matched human contexts from recorded robot videos and supplements them with real paired recordings.
Uses variable-length video windows and intra-task contrastive learning to make actions track the provided human context.
Achieves 83.5/100 across six unseen Astribot S1 tasks and 69.5% success on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, surpassing Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points.
Transfers context-specified behaviors to rearranged layouts and substituted tools despite training only on scene-aligned pairs.

papers.abstract: Planning in a visual world means reading the layout, foreseeing how the state will change, and following the task rules all at once. When a plan fails, a model should also use what went wrong to fix it. We call these two abilities spatiotemporal planning and plan repair, and test them with Railbound-Bench. A model sees a railway puzzle, adds tracks under a budget, and submits one complete layout; a simulator then moves all cars at once and decides whether the layout works. After a failure, the model sees what happened and may submit a new layout, up to five attempts in total. On the 200-puzzle main set, the best of nine models solves 59.5% within five attempts, the next 39.5%, and the other seven at most 10.0%; a 1,000-puzzle extended set with a wider range of difficulty is far easier, at 90.9% for the best model. Controlled studies on 180 fixed puzzles show that knowing the task is not the same as using it. GPT-6.1 Terra copies 97.2% of boards exactly and, given a correct layout as text, predicts all four requested future states in 91.3% of cases, yet only 22.8% of its first layouts work. Planning fails more often as the cars' routes interact, even among puzzles that a search solver finds equally easy. Visual feedback removes the reported fault in 175 of 417 first revisions, but only 43 of these revisions solve the puzzle, and at an equal budget of 40k tokens it does no better than fresh retries. The code and data are open-sourced on GitHub at https://github.com/liaoyanqing666/Railbound_Bench.
authors: Siyuan Li, Ethan Lin, Xiang Li, Tianming Liu
bullets: Railbound-Bench evaluates visual spatiotemporal planning and iterative plan repair under a track budget and up to five attempts.
Performance varies sharply: the best model solves 59.5% of 200 main-set puzzles, while seven of nine models solve at most 10.0%.
Strong board copying and state prediction do not translate into reliable planning: one model achieves 97.2% board copying and 91.3% future-state prediction but only 22.8% valid first layouts.
Planning becomes harder when car routes interact, even when a search solver considers the puzzles equally difficult.
Visual feedback often removes the reported fault but rarely yields a solution and performs no better than fresh retries at equal token budget.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark probing spatiotemporal planning and plan repair in multimodal LLMs; relevant to spatial reasoning in visual environments.
papers.title: Seeing Is Not Planning: Spatiotemporal Planning and Plan Repair in Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: Multimodal LLMs can perceive railway puzzles and predict outcomes, but still struggle to construct valid plans and effectively repair failures.

papers.abstract: Searching from high altitude and navigating to a target instance specified by a reference image is a common application for UAVs. In such tasks, high-altitude observations provide broad ground coverage for efficient search, but targets occupy fewer pixels, making instance verification and action selection more difficult. We present AERIN, a visual world model that uses action-conditioned prediction to guide the UAV toward the target while adjusting its viewpoint to obtain higherquality observations for subsequent instance verification. Highaltitude navigation requires fine-grained target details and scene context relevant to visibility, but repeatedly predicting dense visual representations of this information is computationally expensive. AERIN addresses this challenge with a compact, fixedsize, target-conditioned latent state that separately represents both for efficient action evaluation. Experiments demonstrate that AERIN outperforms the evaluated baselines in target approach and observation quality, while requiring substantially less decision time than similar world models.
authors: Zhenzhen Jiao, Rui Tian, Zhineng Chen
bullets: High-altitude UAV search offers broad coverage but makes target recognition and action selection harder because targets appear small.
The model predicts action-conditioned outcomes to guide target approach and select viewpoints that improve subsequent observations.
AERIN uses a fixed-size latent state that separately encodes fine-grained target details and visibility-relevant scene context.
Experiments show better target approach and observation quality than evaluated baselines, with substantially lower decision time than similar world models.

papers.abstract: We present KMed-31B, a medical large language model post-trained from an open-weight model for on-premises deployment with limited hardware. Post-training a model for diverse medical tasks remains difficult, because improving one kind of task can lower performance on another. We attribute this to differences between tasks in expected output and available feedback. Medical question answering and diagnosis prediction have reference answers, whereas clinical inquiry has no single correct response and is judged with rubrics. We therefore divide medical training tasks into four categories by these two properties, train one specialist per category with a reward that its feedback supports, and integrate the specialists into a single student with Multi-teacher On-policy Delta Distillation (MOPD$^2$). For clinical inquiry, we build Synthetic Health Dialogue, a simulated corpus of consultations with lay users and clinicians whose patient cases span common clinical presentations in primary care. Relative to its base model, KMed-31B raises HealthBench Hard from 22.95 to 41.87 and HealthBench Professional from 37.92 to 50.20 in non-thinking mode, and from 23.80 to 51.48 and from 41.97 to 59.18 in thinking mode, while its scores on four multiple-choice medical benchmarks are maintained or slightly improved. KMed-31B has the highest unadjusted HealthBench Hard score among the compared models, including proprietary ones, and scores higher on HealthBench Professional than every open-weight model we compare, including models with more than ten times as many total parameters. Applied to another base model, Qwen3.8-27B, the same training recipe also raises both HealthBench scores. We describe the training recipe, data construction, and settings in detail so that institutions requiring on-premises deployment can develop medical models from open-weight foundations.
