Trains four task-category specialists, then integrates them using Multi-teacher On-policy Delta Distillation (MOPD²).

papers.abstract: Autoregressive Large Vision-Language Models solve multimodal reasoning tasks by retaining hundreds or thousands of visual tokens, allowing every generated token to attend to the visual tokens at any time during the generation process. However, whether continuous access to these visual tokens is necessary remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate how visual token influence evolves along two dimensions: generation time and transformer depth. Using long-form visual reasoning benchmarks and multiple model scales, we first analyze the attention dynamics across generation time and transformer depth. We identify a temporal and depth-wise structure in the use of visual information. Visual attention peaks during the initial generation steps and then rapidly declines as attention shifts toward previously generated reasoning tokens. Across depth, visual influence is concentrated in intermediate layers and becomes very weak in the final layers. We further verify these observations with causal intervention that removes all visual tokens across generation time and model depth. These interventions confirm that visual-token dependence in multimodal reasoning is neither temporally persistent nor uniformly distributed across transformer depth. Thus, retaining the complete visual context at every layer and decoding step may be unnecessary. Our experiments demonstrate that we can remove up to 59\% of tokens from the full input prompt across generation time and 11\% across all transformer layers, while incurring only a very small performance drop. On video benchmarks, up to 65\% of the input prompt tokens can be removed during generation without affecting performance.
authors: Fawaz Sammani, Nikos Deligiannis
bullets: Visual-token influence declines rapidly after the initial generation steps as models rely more on previously generated reasoning tokens.
Across transformer depth, visual influence is concentrated in intermediate layers and is weak in final layers.
Attention analyses and causal interventions show that visual dependence is neither temporally persistent nor uniform across depth.
The approach removes up to 59% of input-prompt tokens during generation and 11% across all layers with only a very small performance drop.
On video benchmarks, up to 65% of prompt tokens can be removed without affecting performance.

papers.abstract: 3D scene understanding tasks are often approached by building explicit 3D scene representations or by training specialized multi-modal models over point clouds, voxels, or scene graphs. We take a complementary view: for many queries, the main bottleneck is not the absence of a stronger 3D representation but the selection of a small subset of multi-view RGB views that actually makes the query answerable. We present a training-free, query-conditioned multi-view pipeline that performs diverse tasks using only 2D images and a set of tools used purely for inference. Our method first decomposes each query into a set of concepts that identify unique attributes that assist with reasoning. This drives a coarse-to-fine evidence selection process: a coarse retrieval selects and scores all views, a diversity-aware selector reduces redundancy, and a reranking stage helps shortlist views by target visibility or answerability. The resulting evidence is optionally grounded for queries that benefit from explicit localization, and a self-verification step helps refine the final response, especially for open-ended cases. Despite using no task-specific training and no explicit 3D representations at inference time, our approach provides approximately 10% gain on 3D VQA and 5% gain on dense captioning and Embodied QA while being applicable across different scenarios. We further propose a unique judge-based evaluation system, motivating a judge who takes into account many semantically correct or partially correct answers, thereby improving holistic scene understanding.
authors: Sarosij Bose, Arindam Dutta, Konstantinos Karydis, Amit K. Roy Chowdhury
bullets: Targets the bottleneck of identifying which views make a query answerable, rather than constructing stronger 3D scene representations.
Decomposes queries into concepts and uses coarse-to-fine retrieval, diversity selection, and reranking based on visibility or answerability.
Optionally grounds evidence spatially and applies self-verification to refine responses, particularly for open-ended queries.
Reports approximately 10% gains on 3D VQA and 5% gains on dense captioning and Embodied QA.
Introduces a judge-based evaluation approach that accommodates semantically correct or partially correct answers.

papers.abstract: Video world models generate plausible novel views but often lack persistent memory, failing to preserve a place's geometry and appearance when an agent revisits a scene. A central challenge is how previous views should be effectively used for creating memory. Reconstructing them independently underutilizes geometric constraints between nearby views, while repeatedly reconstructing a growing history can propagate later prediction errors into earlier geometry. We introduce RecallWorld, a persistent embodied video world model that jointly reconstructs short multi-view episodes into Scenelets while keeping geometry independent across episodes. Starting from a single source image, camera-aware ray lifting places perspective and native fisheye images in a common world frame, retaining wide-field content for perspective generation. Each generated segment extends the Scenelet memory and conditions subsequent generation. Coverage-based retrieval selects complementary Scenelets from the full history, while target-view visibility is resolved geometrically before appearance fusion, providing consistent memory conditioning for guiding subsequent generation. Across four datasets, RecallWorld improves revisit PSNR over the strongest evaluated baseline by 2.6 dB on partial revisits and 3.9 dB on full cycles, demonstrating substantially stronger preservation of scene identity across exploration and return.
authors: Sarosij Bose, Gitika Karumuri, Chenqi Li, Allen Tu, Srikumar Sastry, Mellon Zhang, Avinash Ravichandran, Alexander Schwing, Konstantinos Karydis, Amit K. Roy Chowdhury

Retrieves complementary Scenelets by coverage and resolves target-view visibility geometrically before fusing appearance.
Improves revisit PSNR by 2.6 dB on partial revisits and 3.9 dB on full cycles across four datasets.

papers.abstract: Asking a vision-language model (VLM) to think step by step often makes it worse at spatial questions, even though the image stays in context. We show that short chain-of-thought (CoT) turns a perception problem into a transcription problem. Once a VLM writes a spatial relation, its answer follows that sentence instead of the image, so whether CoT helps or hurts depends largely on whether the written relation is more accurate than answering directly. Studying 15 open VLMs (2B-38B) and six frontier closed models, we rule out token count, turn format, and visual forgetting in open models and trace the failure through three stages. First, writing re-weights visual cues, weakening a "lower is closer" shortcut in all 13 open models tested but also discarding valid cues, which produces false relations. Second, the written text takes over. With the model's own conclusion-removed rationale held fixed, swapping in an opposite-depth image moves the answer by 2-9 points on rendered twins (vs. up to 77 for direct answers) and by 3.0-3.4 points on average on natural photographs (vs. 20.5-69.6). Third, the concluding sentence can invert even a true relation, mainly on converse questions. Together, false relations and conclusion mis-mapping account for four in five CoT losses. Scale does not remove this bottleneck: Qwen3-VL-32B shows the same pattern. Frontier closed models are not hurt: they write relations as accurately as they answer, and three of six re-check the image after writing. The three queried with reasoning off lock in like open models, so re-grounding co-occurs with answer-turn reasoning; we identify answer-step re-grounding as the step open VLMs lack. In a single-model pilot, fine-tuning on fixed rationales with image-determined labels restores it on natural photographs. We open-sourced all our datasets and code at https://ming-zch.github.io/seeing-right-writing-wrong.
authors: Chenhao Zhang
bullets: CoT turns spatial perception into transcription: once a relation is written, the model tends to follow the text rather than re-checking the image.
Writing can weaken useful visual shortcuts and produce false spatial relations; the final sentence can also invert a correct relation, especially for converse questions.
These two failure modes explain about four in five CoT losses across tested open VLMs, including larger models.
Frontier closed models avoid the harm when they re-ground their answer in the image after writing; models without re-grounding show the open-model pattern.
A pilot suggests fine-tuning with fixed rationales and image-determined labels can restore re-grounding on natural photographs.

papers.abstract: Event cameras capture brightness changes with high temporal resolution and dynamic range, but converting event streams into videos remains fundamentally ill-posed due to the lack of absolute intensity information. Resolving this ambiguity calls for a brightness reference that complements the intensity changes recorded by events. Inspired by the complementary spatial and temporal processing of the parvocellular and magnocellular pathways in human vision, we propose EvDualDiff, a dual-stream framework that combines a brightness reference from temporal-mapping events with motion-event cues for video reconstruction. Conditioned on both streams, our video diffusion model autoregressively reconstructs long sequences from a single temporal map. Photometric constraints and finetuning on self-generated rollouts reduce accumulated drift. At the hardware level, our approach requires only a minimal light-modulation mechanism on the lens of an event camera. We build this setup and collect a dataset comprising temporal-mapping events, motion events and synchronised ground-truth RGB frames. Experiments on a public benchmark and on our collected EvDual dataset demonstrate that EvDualDiff outperforms existing event-to-video reconstruction methods in fidelity, perceptual quality and video-level realism. The code and dataset will be released.
authors: Lei Sun, Zhendong Li, Chenxin Shao, Weilun Li, Ruibo Ming, Kaiwei Wang, Jinjin Gu, Danda Pani Paudel, Luc Van Gool
bullets: Addresses the ill-posed nature of event-to-video reconstruction caused by missing absolute intensity information.
Uses temporal-mapping events as a brightness reference alongside motion events, inspired by complementary visual pathways.
Autoregressively reconstructs long sequences with photometric constraints and rollout finetuning to reduce drift.
Requires only a minimal lens-based light-modulation mechanism and introduces the EvDual dataset with synchronized RGB frames.
Outperforms existing methods on a public benchmark and EvDual in fidelity, perceptual quality, and video-level realism.

papers.abstract: Industrial anomaly inspection requires not only accurate anomaly discrimination but also trustworthy explanations for operators, while satisfying the strict latency constraints of online inspection. Existing methods, however, typically apply a fixed computational path to all samples, making it difficult to strike a good balance among detection accuracy, inference efficiency, and interpretability. To address this issue, we propose UACR, an uncertainty-aware collaborative routing framework for explainable industrial anomaly inspection. UACR aims to deliver reliable anomaly decisions together with operator-facing explanations under the online inspection budget, while adaptively allocating computation so that ambiguous cases receive deeper scrutiny. The framework consists of two stages. Stage I, Offline Training and Routing Hyperparameter Search, learns the anomaly inspection modules and calibrates the uncertainty estimator that drives routing. Stage II, Uncertainty-Aware Adaptive Routing, collaboratively dispatches each input across inspection paths according to its estimated uncertainty. Experimental results on multiple public datasets show that UACR achieves over 5.16% improvement in accuracy compared to the baseline method, while reducing latency by over 31.5%. It also enhances the interpretability of industrial detection by over 15%.
authors: Yiwei Li, Qiyang Chen, Zheming Yang
bullets: Targets the trade-off among anomaly detection accuracy, online inference efficiency, and trustworthy operator-facing explanations.
Uses uncertainty estimation to allocate deeper computation to ambiguous samples while avoiding unnecessary processing for easier cases.
Operates in two stages: offline module training and routing calibration, followed by uncertainty-aware adaptive routing at inference.
Experiments on multiple public datasets report over 5.16% higher accuracy, over 31.5% lower latency, and over 15% improved interpretability than a baseline.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence, the ability to reason about 3D space from visual observations, becomes essential as multimodal large language models (MLLMs) move into the physical world. Beyond perceiving each view, it rests on two cornerstones of human cognition: fusing multiple views into one coherent 3D scene and mentally transforming that scene to new viewpoints as reasoning unfolds. Yet our spatial probes reveal that MLLMs largely lack both capabilities, even after spatial fine-tuning. We therefore present S-Mind, which internalizes multi-view geometry within the MLLM through a compact set of spatial tokens. It supervises these tokens to hold the fused 3D scene and re-emits them to re-express this scene from every viewpoint the reasoning adopts. Across four spatial benchmarks, S-Mind improves its Qwen3.5 backbones by up to 22.26 points and surpasses frontier general models such as GPT-6-Astra (+0.45), Kimi-K3.1-Pro (+1.97), and GLM-5.3-Flash (+7.80) in average accuracy. Moreover, the same probes confirm that it acquires both capabilities, reaching fusion and transformation accuracies of 65.11% and 82.17%, against at most 16.02% and 37.28% for the baselines. At inference, S-Mind also runs about 100x faster than a tool-based agent on the same backbone. Instilled through these spatial tokens during training, spatial capability becomes intrinsic to the backbone and persists even when the tokens are withheld, offering a promising path toward spatial intelligence in MLLMs.
authors: Muxin Fu, Peike Yu, Guibin Zhang, Wenrui Zhou, Runze Liu, Lang Feng, Fuchao Yang, Feng Chen, Yixuan Li, Mengao Zhang, Shiying Zhang, Wen Shen, Ling Pan, Shuicheng Yan, Bo An
bullets: MLLMs often lack coherent multi-view fusion and mental viewpoint transformation, even after spatial fine-tuning.
S-Mind supervises compact spatial tokens to encode a fused 3D scene and re-express it from reasoning-dependent viewpoints.
Across four spatial benchmarks, it improves Qwen3.5 backbones by up to 22.26 points and exceeds several frontier general models in average accuracy.
Probe accuracies reach 65.11% for scene fusion and 82.17% for viewpoint transformation, versus substantially lower baseline results.
The learned spatial capability persists without the tokens at inference, while running about 100× faster than a tool-based agent on the same backbone.

papers.abstract: Freehand orthographic drawings capture early design intent, yet recovering executable sketch--extrude CAD programs from raster front, right, and top views remains challenging: noisy, dimension-free 2D layouts must be reconciled into an ordered construction history. We introduce Hand2CAD, a benchmark of 215K ABC-derived synthetic orthographic-drawing--CAD program pairs and 1,000 real three-view sets drawn by CAD-trained participants. Recovering CAD programs from orthographic drawings requires both cross-view geometric reasoning and alignment between visual features and program representations. We propose OrthoLatentCAD to address these two challenges. It fuses local geometry with global context on canonical planes, exchanges evidence between paired plane lines indexed by the same shared-axis coordinate, and maps the spatial representation to ordered program latents through queries inherited from a frozen CAD autoencoder. Across the evaluated one- to three-view configurations, OrthoLatentCAD outperforms protocol-matched baselines in procedural accuracy, compiled geometry, and CAD-kernel validity while benefiting from additional views. Without real-data fine-tuning, it also outperforms the baselines on held-out real drawings. We will release the dataset, code, and evaluation scripts.
authors: Xiaolei Zhou, Xinjie Zhu, Chuangjie Fang, Chenyu Wang, Jianwei Zheng
bullets: Introduces Hand2CAD, comprising 215K synthetic orthographic-drawing–CAD program pairs and 1,000 real three-view sets.

Uses canonical-plane spatial features that combine local geometry and global context, exchange evidence across shared-axis-aligned plane lines, and map to ordered program latents via a frozen CAD autoencoder.
Outperforms protocol-matched baselines in procedural accuracy, compiled geometry, and CAD-kernel validity across evaluated view configurations.
Benefits from additional views and outperforms baselines on held-out real drawings without real-data fine-tuning.
Dataset, code, and evaluation scripts are planned for release.

papers.abstract: A correct answer to a scientific-figure question can conceal an incorrect account of the experiment. Reading evidence across panels requires keeping each observation attached to the object and conditions that give it meaning. We introduce CrossPanel, a benchmark of 2,650 human-reviewed questions that exposes this answer-evidence gap. Its tasks combine parallel observations or follow dependent queries, while a response audit separates object selection, experimental conditions, cross-panel binding, and local readout. Across 15 vision-language models on 251 diagnostic questions, 8.42%-56.64% of correct answers contain explicit factual errors. The audit distinguishes coherent readings of the wrong target from incorrect readings of the right one. Controlled interventions then test how these failures can be repaired: verified object-condition hints, which withhold the requested measurement, raise Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's target-query success by 22.81 percentage points on 57 questions, while additional image tiles alone yield little improvement. Other models benefit most from combining both forms of assistance. These findings identify experimental attribution as a distinct requirement alongside local perception, and make both measurable beyond final-answer accuracy.
authors: Zhengyang Lu (University of Science and Technology of China), QianhongWen (Sichuan Agricultural University), Chenpeng Wang (YiXin-AI Lab), Qiang Huang (Fudan University), Ziyang Ling (University of Science and Technology of China), Huan Li (University of Science and Technology of China), Chenziao (Peking Union Medical College), Yibo Qiu (University of Science and Technology of China), Xiaojie Cheng (YiXin-AI Lab)
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 2,650 human-reviewed questions involving parallel observations and dependent cross-panel queries.
Audits responses across object selection, experimental conditions, cross-panel binding, and local readout.
Across 15 models, 8.42%–56.64% of correct answers contain explicit factual errors.
Verified object-condition hints improve target-query success, while extra image tiles alone provide little benefit; combining both helps some models.
Findings show that experimental attribution must be evaluated separately from final-answer accuracy.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented language models answer well when the relevant document comes first or last and poorly when it sits in the middle. Some fine-tuning recipes lift the middle by lowering the start. We show how training contexts teach positional bias. With a uniform answer slot and shuffled distractors, the optimal reader ignores position. Building on this result, Exchangeable Self-Distillation (ExSD) trains a small adapter on shuffled contexts to reproduce the model's answer when it reads the answer document alone. It needs no gold answers and only a few thousand examples. On six models from 1.5B to 32B parameters, ExSD raises both average and worst-position accuracy against the frozen model, including on a held-out test split. In controlled LoRA comparisons, it significantly improves both criteria over Pos2Distill. Against CORD, mean differences are not significant, while worst-position accuracy improves significantly in the 20- and 30-document settings. ExSD also matches or beats gold-answer fine-tuning, changes behavior on other tasks far less, and transfers to unseen tasks. Head probes show greater reliance on content over position.
authors: Qingsen Ma, Dianyun Wang, Jiahong Liu, Irwin King
bullets: Uniform answer placement and shuffled distractors motivate making document position uninformative during training.
ExSD trains a small adapter on shuffled contexts to match the model’s answer from the relevant document alone, without gold answers.
Across six models ranging from 1.5B to 32B parameters, it improves average and worst-position accuracy, including on held-out data.
ExSD outperforms Pos2Distill on both criteria; it matches or beats gold-answer fine-tuning and transfers to unseen tasks.
Head probes indicate increased reliance on content over position, while behavior on unrelated tasks changes less.

papers.abstract: Long video question answering requires finding relevant evidence before reasoning over it. With a limited frame budget, single-pass frame selection can miss critical evidence, while adaptive search often relies on repeated text generation to decide where to look. We introduce LoopSeek, a framework that decouples evidence search from answer generation through a division of labor between a non-thinking System I and a generative System II. Our key insight is that search can be expressed as a sequence of small, typed decisions, allowing System I to find the evidence that System II needs. Four System I role agents navigate a tree of video windows and coordinate through probability outputs to select frames, assess evidence, and revise the search without generating text. To align search with System II, System I learns from annotated evidence on questions that System II answers correctly only from that evidence, and the verifier's evidence estimates steer the search without calling System II, which stays frozen and answers once from the selected frames. On five long-video benchmarks, with a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B reading 32 frames, LoopSeek improves average accuracy from 53.5 to 63.9 over the uniform baseline and takes 32--80\% less GPU time per question than agentic methods.
authors: Chengzhong Wang, Lang Lin, Xinyang Liu, YueQin Yin, Mingyuan Zhou, Shengwei An
bullets: Addresses missed evidence under limited frame budgets and the cost of repeated text-based search.
Uses four non-generative System I agents to navigate video-window trees, select frames, assess evidence, and revise searches.
Trains search using annotated evidence from questions that a frozen System II answers correctly from that evidence.
On five long-video benchmarks, accuracy rises from 53.5 to 63.9 with 32 frames, while using 32–80% less GPU time than agentic methods.

papers.abstract: Grounded vision-language models write boxes as text, and the mean probability of their coordinate tokens says little about whether a box is right. We study a single-pass signal for boxes on another object, which matter when only the object counts. A linear map, fitted per model to its own answers without labels, reads a box from the hidden state before writing. Its disagreement with the written box, the self-prediction residual, flags boxes on another object although the read-out is far less accurate; the residual's weight was fixed with labels on two models. On a replication list of 1,200 RefCOCOg test items, the residual, averaged over six models, raises the detection of these errors for each of fifteen single-pass scores, by 0.026 to 0.049 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) on a label-free probe and probes trained on 2,000 labelled items. Over all errors, adding it to the label-free probe moves AUROC, averaged over the models, by less than 0.02 (95% interval). With a fifth of answers reviewed, the share of all errors caught moves from 0.518 to 0.524, that of boxes on another object from 0.505 to 0.607 (post hoc): the residual changes which errors are found, not how many, and in cost-weighted recall it breaks even when such a box costs about 0.86 times another error, and its gain is positive in point estimate at equal costs. These gains come from RefCOCOg lists of MS-COCO images.
authors: Enhao Cui, Junzhi Yang, Yaoshun Lin, Yuhan Feng, Zijian Chen
bullets: Coordinate-token probabilities are poor indicators of box correctness.
A per-model linear readout predicts the box from its pre-generation hidden state; disagreement with the emitted box forms the residual.
Across six models and 1,200 RefCOCOg items, adding the residual improved wrong-object detection AUROC by 0.026–0.049 across 15 scores.
With 20% of answers reviewed, wrong-object error recall rose from 0.505 to 0.607, while overall error recall changed little.
Results are limited to RefCOCOg lists of MS-COCO images; the residual mainly changes which errors are detected, not the total number.

papers.abstract: Vision-based 3D occupancy prediction infers voxel-wise geometry and semantics from multi-view images, where 2D-to-3D view transformation is a crucial step. Many existing methods adopt a backward-projection paradigm, projecting uniformly distributed 3D reference points onto image planes to aggregate multi-view features. However, their scene-agnostic sampling patterns overlook the non-uniform distribution of scene geometry, allocating many references to empty space and reducing sampling efficiency under a fixed sampling budget. To address this challenge, we propose SAP, a scene-adaptive projection framework that leverages depth-based geometric priors to guide view transformation. Specifically, we back-project metric depth maps predicted by a frozen depth model into 3D space to obtain geometric priors. To leverage these priors, we design a Scene-Adaptive Projection Encoder comprising two complementary components. First, Prior-Guided Reference Generation constructs a hybrid reference set for feature sampling, allocating references within prior-supported height regions and retaining full-range sampling where valid support is unavailable. Furthermore, to account for potential spatial misalignment caused by depth estimation errors, Radial-Structured Feature Aggregation explores multiple candidate locations through learned radial offsets to aggregate potentially displaced feature evidence. Extensive experiments on Occ3D demonstrate that SAP achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently improves results across diverse occupancy frameworks.

papers.abstract: A fundamental question in reinforcement learning is how many sampled transitions are needed to learn a near-optimal policy, and whether direct policy optimization can attain this statistical limit. To answer this question, we consider natural policy gradient (NPG), a widely used policy optimization method. We study tabular finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) with known rewards and unknown horizon-dependent transition kernels, accessed through a generative model. Our sample-based NPG algorithms update the policy by backward sweeps and do not estimate transition probabilities. Under three different batch-size and step size schedules, we establish last-iterate guarantees with sample complexity $\widetilde O(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$, where $S$, $A$, and $H$ denote the number of states, the number of actions, and the horizon length, respectively. In this setting, horizon-dependent transition kernels contribute a factor of $H$ to our transition-query bound. Our information-theoretic lower bound of $\Omega(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$ shows that the resulting $H^4$ dependence is unavoidable in the worst case, even for agents that select their queries adaptively. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first last-iterate guarantees for NPG whose sample complexity matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, our results demonstrate that direct policy-space optimization through NPG can achieve the fundamental statistical limits of reinforcement learning while guaranteeing the performance of the final policy. Furthermore, for known kernels, we prove that exact NPG with a constant step size $\eta=1/H$ requires $\Omega(H^2/\varepsilon)$ iterations in the worst case, matching the known upper bound for that step size.
authors: Asha Barua, Sajad Khodadadian
bullets: Studies tabular finite-horizon MDPs with known rewards, unknown horizon-dependent transitions, and access to a generative model.
Introduces sample-based NPG algorithms using backward policy updates without explicitly estimating transition probabilities.

Proves a matching lower bound of $\Omega(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$, even for adaptively selected queries, showing the $H^4$ dependence is unavoidable.
For known transition kernels, exact NPG with step size $1/H$ may require $\Omega(H^2/\varepsilon)$ iterations in the worst case.

Their guarantees hold with probability at least 1−δ. Our NPG methods return a last iterate πT that is ε-optimal in expectation under the fixed initial state distribution ρ.

papers.abstract: How much interaction experience is needed to distill a capable visual agent? We study learning from few tasks and recorded interaction histories. Our framework selects representative trajectories using skill-context coverage and ordered visual-decision similarity. On-policy distillation (OPD) learns through fresh interaction on selected tasks or fresh student responses at fixed histories. Across Navigation, Sokoban, and spatial mapping, even one online training task supports transfer to other tasks. Four fixed trajectories raise a 4B student's success from 49.17% to 82.08% on standard Navigation and from 60.16% to 85.55% on Sokoban, recovering over 90% of the measured gap to a 27B teacher on these panels. On an independent Navigation panel, replay improves success from 45.83% to 76.67%, retaining 91.36% of the same-task online gain without new interaction during optimization. Training repetitions, matched supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and a 9B extension further support the value of compact experience.

papers.abstract: Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control is central to online planning for model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL), but its iterative refinement incurs planning latency. Reducing refinement iterations often degrades performance, motivating stronger policy guidance learned from the planner. However, existing methods typically learn from the planner through action-level alignment, which does not directly capture the complete $H$-step planner proposal. Moreover, planner imitation leaves further target improvement to online refinement. To address these limitations, we propose FaSt World PlANner (SWAN), an advantage-aware MPPI-based MBRL framework that explicitly represents and improves the complete $H$-step planner proposal to improve policy guidance for efficient online planning. For proposal representation, SWAN combines k-MPPI, a multimodal MPPI extension, with a mixture of factor analyzers (MFA) action-chunk policy to capture multiple modes and correlations across time and action dimensions. For proposal optimization, we introduce Advantage-Guided Proposal Optimization (APO), which reuses MPPI evaluations to construct an improved target using advantage estimates and trains the policy toward this target while preserving planner alignment. Experiments across 31 high-dimensional continuous-control tasks from DMControl, HumanoidBench, and MyoSuite show that SWAN substantially improves control performance and sample efficiency while using 50% fewer MPPI refinement iterations than state-of-the-art planning-based MBRL methods. Finally, SWAN demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a physical Unitree Go2, achieving stable velocity-tracking locomotion with high-frequency control. (see our demo at https://swanfastworldplanner.github.io/)
authors: Jiangtao Kong, Yuchen Wang, Yandong Luo, Rongchao Xu, Guang Wang, Yanbing Mao, Lu Gan, Tianyi Zhou, Huajie Shao

Introduces Advantage-Guided Proposal Optimization, which uses MPPI evaluations and advantage estimates to improve policy targets while maintaining planner alignment.
Improves control performance and sample efficiency across 31 continuous-control tasks while reducing MPPI refinement iterations by 50%.

papers.abstract: To surface "objective" fact-check notes, X's Community Notes uses Biased Matrix Factorization (BMF) on crowd-sourced ratings to separate note quality from reviewer ideology. We show that for any correctly specified model that decomposes ratings into quality and ideological alignment, this separation requires fixing an ideological anchor: a reference point for what counts as neutral. We give a characterization for the standard implementation: with $L_2$ regularization, BMF anchors quality at a point proportional to the mean reviewer ideology, recovering objective quality if and only if the mean reviewer is neutral, assuming note quality is uncorrelated with note leaning. This parallels the Condorcet Jury Theorem: collective judgment recovers truth when the pool is unbiased on average. When that assumption fails, BMF's recovered ranking shifts toward maximizing aggregate reviewer satisfaction, which coincides with social welfare only when the pool is representative. This is not specific to BMF; the rating matrix admits a continuous family of gauge-equivalent decompositions, each implying a different quality ranking, so no mechanism based on ratings alone can recover quality without implicitly choosing such an anchor. What appears to be routine hyperparameter tuning is in fact a normative choice about whose preferences define quality.
authors: David Gamba, Seura Ha, Daniel M. Romero, Grant Schoenebeck
bullets: Quality–ideology separation has a continuous ambiguity: multiple equivalent decompositions of the same ratings imply different quality rankings.
In standard Biased Matrix Factorization with L2 regularization, the anchor is proportional to the mean reviewer ideology.
Objective quality is recovered only when the reviewer pool is neutral on average and note quality is uncorrelated with note leaning.
Otherwise, rankings favor aggregate reviewer satisfaction, matching social welfare only when reviewers are representative.
The issue is general to rating-only mechanisms, not specific to BMF; tuning effectively selects whose preferences define quality.

papers.abstract: Parametric memory enables large language models (LLMs) to retain information from past experience and reuse it in subsequent tasks. Yet how training data supports the internalization of reusable task rules remains unclear. We introduce FSMem (Finite-State Machine Memory), a state-transition framework for constructing training data and studying how data content and organization shape memory formation. We evaluate rule reuse across synthetic worlds, classical planning, and code execution through valid-action identification and execution-outcome prediction, complemented by next-operation prediction in code. Our experiments reveal several systematic learning patterns. Under matched training conditions, even unchanged task rules become harder to internalize when learned alongside a larger variety of action types; by contrast, scaling the training data to provide broader state-action coverage generally improves rule learning. We further find that training at a single execution depth produces depth-specialized behavior, with models performing best when training and test executions have similar lengths. Motivated by this finding, we construct cumulative corpora that combine short and long trajectories, which can outperform long-trajectory-only training while using fewer training tokens. Together, these results demonstrate that the same task rules can be internalized differently depending on how execution experience is constructed, and that understanding these learning patterns can guide the design of more effective training data for parametric memory.
authors: Xianxuan Long, Xinnan Dai, Kai Guo, Jiliang Tang
bullets: Rule internalization becomes harder when unchanged rules are mixed with a wider variety of action types.
Broader state–action coverage generally improves learning of reusable rules.
Training at one execution depth leads to depth-specialized behavior, with best performance at similar train/test lengths.
Cumulative data combining short and long trajectories can outperform long-trajectory-only training with fewer tokens.
Findings span synthetic worlds, classical planning, and code execution tasks.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we conduct a systematic study on improving permutation robustness while preserving accuracy. First, we categorize permutation bias phenomena into four representative scenarios. Then, we take the multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) dataset as an example under text-option reordering scenario to analyze the root cause of permutation bias. Based on this root cause analysis and set encoding strategy, we investigate shared positions with blocked cross-unit attention (SP-B) and extend this design to bidirectional cross-unit attention (SP-V) for modality exchange. However, these structural changes may reduce predictive accuracy. To recover model capability across different scenarios under the SP structure, an attention-only distillation from frozen native models is proposed. Shared positions reduce permutation sensitivity, and attention-only distillation improves accuracy under the shared-position structure. Across all three models, our method is comparable to or better than majority voting in macro-average all-permutation accuracy, and outperforms supervised fine-tuning by 1.95-4.20 percentage points. This work provides valuable insight into permutation bias mitigation and model capability recovery.
authors: Yifei Cheng, Xiaolin Zhang, Yu-Xuan Qiu
bullets: Analyzes permutation bias across four representative scenarios, focusing on text-option reordering in multiple-choice QA.
Introduces shared positions with blocked cross-unit attention (SP-B) and bidirectional cross-unit attention (SP-V).
Uses attention-only distillation from frozen native models to recover accuracy affected by structural changes.
Across three models, achieves macro-average all-permutation accuracy comparable to or better than majority voting and 1.95–4.20 percentage points above supervised fine-tuning.
Scope: evaluation centers on permutation robustness, including text-option reordering and multiple-choice QA.

papers.abstract: Decoding with large language models at small batch sizes is limited by memory bandwidth, so the bits stored per weight largely set its cost. Group-wise integer quantization stores every weight of a group at the same precision, although the input channels of a group differ in sensitivity. We present BITSHARE, a codebook-free weight format that keeps the integer grid and the dequantizer of group-wise quantization but varies precision within each group. Sensitivity-aware binning places the channels of each group into three bins at fixed positions, and static bit sharing with optimal bit-value allocation lets the less sensitive weights share their lower bits, each stored once per group or once per pair of weights. A sharing-aware version of GPTQ chooses every stored value, with no fine-tuning and no codebook. BITSHARE has two modes. BITSHARE-U gives every group the same layout, so its decoder routes bits by fixed wiring, while BITSHARE-N chooses a layout per group within the same bit budget. With calibration on the Pile and at the same storage, both modes have lower perplexity than GPTQ at 3 and 2 bits on WikiText-2 and C4. At 2 bits across Llama-2 and Llama-3 models, BITSHARE-N lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by up to 70% against SliM-LLM and up to 35% against GPTAQ. At the 2-bit perplexity of SliM-LLM, BITSHARE-U stores 13.6-19.4% fewer bits per weight, cutting DRAM weight traffic by the same fraction. A verified hardware decoder implementation synthesized in SkyWater 130 nm reconstructs BITSHARE weights at the throughput of INT-n and SliM-LLM decoders.
authors: Qiuyu Ren, Sudipta Paria, Aritra Dasgupta, Swarup Bhunia
bullets: Targets memory-bandwidth bottlenecks in small-batch LLM decoding, where bits per weight determine weight traffic.
Bins channels by sensitivity and applies variable precision within each quantization group, without codebooks or fine-tuning.
BITSHARE-U uses a fixed layout for simple decoding; BITSHARE-N selects layouts per group under the same bit budget.
At 2–3 bits, both modes achieve lower WikiText-2 and C4 perplexity than GPTQ at matched storage; BITSHARE-N also outperforms reported SliM-LLM and GPTAQ baselines.
A verified SkyWater 130 nm decoder reconstructs weights at the throughput of INT-n and SliM-LLM decoders.

papers.selection_reason: Bit sharing for LLM weight compression, relevant to memory efficiency.
papers.title: BitShare: Sensitivity-Aware Binning and Bit Sharing for Compacting LLM Weight Storage
papers.tldr: BITSHARE reduces LLM weight-storage cost by sharing lower bits among sensitivity-binned weights while preserving efficient integer-grid decoding.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from large language models to smaller students, yet stronger teachers do not always yield better students. Recent studies report diminishing or even negative returns from teacher scaling. We hypothesize that these limitations arise in part from insufficient student capacity to absorb the teacher's knowledge. We therefore investigate loop and recurrent computation as a way to expand the student's effective capacity by modifying its computation graph while keeping the backbone parameter count fixed. Under teacher-forced KD during pretraining, weight-shared looping improves performance but retains teacher-size saturation, whereas cross-token recurrence avoids the observed reversal with larger teachers. In mathematical post-training under both teacher-forced KD and on-policy distillation (OPD), recurrent students scale better with increasing teacher size than looped and vanilla LLMs do. Crucially, we show that a pretrained LLM can be readily fine-tuned into a looped or recurrent architecture jointly with OPD, without repeating pretraining. Our recurrent Qwen model improves with larger teachers and consistently outperforms looped and vanilla LLMs. This suggests a new post-training paradigm that integrates architectural conversion into distillation, avoiding a separate conversion stage while substantially improving student performance and maintaining near-vanilla inference latency.
authors: Zeyi Huang, Jiuxiang Gu, Eli Shechtman, Yong Jae Lee, Zongze Wu
bullets: The work addresses teacher-size saturation and performance reversals in knowledge distillation, partly attributing them to limited student capacity.
It compares weight-shared looping and cross-token recurrence under teacher-forced KD and on-policy distillation.
Cross-token recurrent students scale better with larger teachers than looped and vanilla LLMs, especially in mathematical post-training.
A pretrained LLM can be fine-tuned directly into a recurrent or looped architecture jointly with OPD, avoiding repeated pretraining or a separate conversion stage.
The recurrent Qwen model consistently outperforms the looped and vanilla variants while maintaining near-vanilla inference latency.

papers.title: Bridging Teacher-Student Capability Gaps with Recurrent Computation

papers.abstract: Memory-efficient Muon methods aim to reduce storage overhead while preserving strong performance, yet existing approaches compromise either convergence guarantees or practical efficiency. In this paper, we focus on subspace optimization for Muon, where the choice of subspace determines the gradient information retained for updating. To preserve dominant information while providing the coverage needed for stochastic convergence guarantees, we construct a principal-random subspace that combines leading singular directions of the stochastic gradient with random directions sampled from their orthogonal complement. Under a fixed rank budget, there is a trade-off between principal exploitation and complementary coverage, making rank allocation important for practical optimization. Our key observation is that the preferred balance shifts from principal-heavy early in training to random-heavy later. Motivated by this shift, we propose \dram, a memory-efficient Muon optimizer that reallocates principal and random ranks across stages while maintaining momentum and performing matrix-sign normalization entirely in the subspace. Theoretically, we establish convergence guarantees for general rank-allocation schedules with nondecreasing coverage factors, obtaining rates of $O(T^{-1/4})$ in the stochastic setting and $O(T^{-1/2})$ in the deterministic setting, with fixed allocation as a special case. Using a simple linear reallocation schedule, \dram achieves the best low-memory performance across three pre-training scales and nine fine-tuning settings.
authors: Haomin Bai, Dingzhi Yu, Xuling Zhao, Sifan Yang, Yibo Wang, Lijun Zhang
bullets: Targets the trade-off between preserving dominant gradient information and maintaining stochastic convergence coverage under a fixed rank budget.
Builds a principal-random subspace from leading stochastic-gradient singular directions plus random orthogonal-complement directions.
Reallocates principal and random ranks from principal-heavy early training to random-heavy later training, while keeping momentum and matrix-sign normalization in the subspace.
Proves convergence rates of O(T^-1/4) for stochastic optimization and O(T^-1/2) for deterministic optimization under general allocation schedules.
A simple linear schedule achieves the best low-memory performance across three pre-training scales and nine fine-tuning settings reported in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models translate visual observations and language instructions into robot actions, enabling general-purpose robotic control. However, environmental perturbations, such as objects moving during execution, can undermine their reliability. Different policies exhibit complementary failures under mid-rollout perturbations, motivating selective switching between policies for recovery. Such switching can stall the robot during inference of the newly invoked policy or, if performed asynchronously, act on stale observations. We present AsyncMixVLA, an adaptive inference framework for proactive, asynchronous switching across heterogeneous VLA policies. A learned trigger balances recovery potential against intervention harm to selectively escalate to a higher-compute policy. AsyncMixVLA overlaps its inference with committed outgoing actions and aligns its context to the anticipated takeover state. On LIBERO-Long with mid-rollout perturbations, AsyncMixVLA improves perturbed task success from 69.5% to 77.1% over the lightweight policy. It achieves 84.9% overall success, comparable to 84.5% for synchronous switching, while reducing median exposed handoff latency from 226.5 ms to 0.1 ms. Without retraining or recalibration, it achieves 75.1% success across three unseen perturbation families, compared with 71.3% for the stronger constituent policy in aggregate.
authors: Tamoghno Das, Keyon Jazayeri, Yerin Cho, Nazmul Takbir, Arshia Aravinthan, Nikil Dutt
bullets: Addresses reliability failures when objects move during robot execution and policy switching causes stalls or stale observations.
Uses a learned trigger to selectively escalate from a lightweight policy to a higher-compute policy based on recovery potential and intervention risk.
Runs the incoming policy asynchronously alongside outgoing actions and aligns its context with the expected takeover state.
On LIBERO-Long, perturbed-task success rises from 69.5% to 77.1%, with 84.9% overall success—comparable to synchronous switching at 84.5%.
Reduces median exposed handoff latency from 226.5 ms to 0.1 ms and generalizes to unseen perturbations without retraining or recalibration.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents have shown promising capabilities in task-oriented environments. However, they still struggle when queries are deferred until after exploration, requiring them to retain visual evidence before knowing which details will matter. We introduce EvoViM, a recursively self-evolving framework in which a frozen multimodal model turns its own interaction experience into one visual program for memory and skills. The program retains images and computes directly on pixels, and its operations decide how this evidence is used in each task. During memory evolution, the same model traces failures in its visual trajectories to the operations that lost or misused evidence and revises them. It also rewrites the notes and analysis tools that guide later revisions, which then build on earlier findings and skip changes that have already failed. We evaluate EvoViM with three multimodal models on six tasks covering visual matching, spatial recall, and sequential decision-making, including three tasks with deferred queries. Across the six tasks, EvoViM improves the average score over AutoMem, the strongest baseline in the main comparison, by 31.3-47.6 points on held-out episodes. Programs written once from the initial environment instructions perform substantially worse, highlighting the value of interaction experience in shaping how visual evidence is retained and used. Code and dataset are available at https://evovim.github.io/.
authors: Xinyu Cao, Tianjie Ju, Zhuosheng Zhang
bullets: Targets tasks where agents must preserve visual evidence before knowing which details will later be queried.
Uses a frozen multimodal model to create and revise a pixel-based visual program for memory, skills, and evidence use.
Analyzes failed visual trajectories to identify operations that lost or misused evidence, then updates those operations and revision guidance.
Evaluated with three multimodal models across six tasks spanning visual matching, spatial recall, and sequential decision-making, including three deferred-query tasks.
Improves average held-out performance over AutoMem by 31.3–47.6 points; programs written only from initial instructions perform substantially worse.

papers.abstract: Related sources can improve multivariate time series forecasting when the target history is short, but their usefulness varies across source groups and historical periods. A key challenge is to identify informative historical contexts from the sources. This paper proposes Hierarchical Context Transfer (HiCT), a framework that adaptively weights source groups and their historical contexts to determine both \emph{where} and \emph{when} to transfer. A shared context encoder and cross-attention are used to learn weights over source groups and historical contexts. These weights guide regularized transfer estimation, followed by an optional target-specific correction. This paper establishes a target excess-risk bound for the context-weighted transfer estimator. Experiments demonstrate competitive predictive performance across four multivariate forecasting datasets and a favorable accuracy--runtime trade-off against the evaluated baselines. Source-corruption ablations illustrate the roles of group-level and within-group weighting in adapting to unreliable source histories.
authors: Huiling Yuan, Yize Wang, Guodong Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge that source usefulness varies across groups and historical contexts when target history is limited.
Uses a shared context encoder and cross-attention to weight source groups and historical contexts.

Experiments on four multivariate forecasting datasets show competitive accuracy, favorable accuracy–runtime trade-offs, and robustness mechanisms under source corruption.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly rely on external visual tools to access fine-grained visual evidence, but repeated tool execution incurs substantial inference overhead and deployment dependencies. Moreover, conventional tool-use RL can improve visual-task performance, yet the resulting tool gains are often unstable. Motivated by this, we propose Tool-to-Self (T2S), a tool-scaffolded reinforcement learning framework that turns external visual tools into temporary training scaffolds. T2S cold-starts tool-use ability and observation prediction from tool-repairable examples, then progressively anneals tool execution on a per-tool basis during RL. By combining answer-correctness and observation-consistency rewards with privileged on-policy self-distillation from actual tool observations, T2S effectively teaches the model both to reproduce tool outputs and to reason from them. Experiments across diverse visual perception and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over both explicit tool-use models and implicit zooming models while enabling tool-free inference with reduced latency.
authors: Jin Cui, Hao Dong, Xinyue Long, Boran Zhao, Pengju Ren
bullets: Addresses the inference overhead and deployment dependence caused by repeated external visual-tool use.
Uses tool-repairable examples to cold-start tool use and observation prediction, then gradually reduces tool execution during reinforcement learning.
Combines answer-correctness and observation-consistency rewards with on-policy self-distillation from actual tool observations.
Reports consistent gains across diverse visual perception and reasoning benchmarks over explicit tool-use and implicit zooming approaches.
Produces models capable of tool-free inference with reduced latency.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly use external visual tools to acquire evidence during reasoning, yet learning when to invoke these tools remains challenging. Existing tool-use reinforcement learning (RL) methods often rely on call-contingent rewards to encourage beneficial tool use, but such reward engineering can distort the task objective and lead to degenerate calling behaviors. We argue that effective tool-use learning requires identifying not merely which questions are difficult, but which failures are attributable to missing visual evidence and can therefore be corrected through tool observations. We propose AOVO, a data-centric framework that enables MLLMs to learn effective tool use through perception attribution and policy-adaptive data sampling (PADS), without introducing tool-specific rewards. It counterfactually probes the model's reasoning states to identify observation-sensitive questions, distinguishing them from reasoning-dominated ones. PADS then periodically estimates category-level observation effects from recent policy rollouts and dynamically reallocates the training distribution toward questions where visual observations provide informative learning signals, while optimizing solely for final-answer correctness. Experiments across diverse visual perception and multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over competitive tool-use MLLMs, with causal analysis further validating the data-centric perspective for learning effective visual tool use.
authors: Jin Cui, Xinyue Long, Jiepeng Zhou, Boran Zhao, Pengju Ren, Hao Dong
bullets: Tool-use RL rewards tied to tool calls can distort objectives and encourage degenerate calling behavior.
AOVO uses perception attribution to distinguish failures caused by missing visual evidence from reasoning-dominated failures.
Policy-adaptive data sampling reallocates training toward questions where visual observations provide informative learning signals.
The framework optimizes final-answer correctness without introducing tool-specific rewards.
Experiments across visual perception and multimodal reasoning benchmarks show consistent improvements, with causal analysis supporting the data-centric approach.

papers.abstract: Mobile embodied agents continuously alter their observations through their own motion, while external dynamics further shape future interactions. Different mobile embodied tasks therefore capture complementary patterns of state evolution, yet jointly learning world dynamics across such interactions remains less explored. We investigate this problem through Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) and Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT), which respectively involve navigation toward a stationary goal and interaction with a moving target. We propose WorldWeave, a cross-task world model that couples shared predictive dynamics with task-specific adaptation. Instead of conditioning state transitions on heterogeneous physical actions, WorldWeave learns latent actions from observed state changes via inverse-forward dynamics, establishing a shared transition representation across tasks. The resulting future-state predictions are adaptively integrated into task-specific representations for downstream decision making. Experiments across multiple VLN and EVT benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over specialized baselines.
authors: Xuan Yao, Jiahao Zhang, Rongjunchen Zhang, Kaixuan Huang, Junyu Gao, Changsheng Xu
bullets: Addresses underexplored cross-task world modeling for embodied agents whose actions and environments continually change future observations.
Uses inverse-forward dynamics to learn latent actions and a shared transition representation instead of relying on heterogeneous physical actions.
Combines shared predictive dynamics with task-specific adaptation for downstream navigation and tracking decisions.
Evaluations across multiple VLN and EVT benchmarks show consistent improvements over specialized baselines.

papers.abstract: Action Quality Assessment (AQA) aims to evaluate the quality of human actions, yet existing methods are predominantly developed and evaluated on individual datasets with different task formulations and assessment criteria. We introduce X-AQA, the first unified training and evaluation framework for general-purpose AQA with multimodal large language models (MLLMs). We construct X-AQA-40K, a training corpus comprising 40,163 samples from 22 data sources across four domains: competitive sports, fitness exercises, rehabilitation, and general skills. We convert heterogeneous annotations into a unified question-answering format, incorporating dataset-specific annotation guidelines and official scoring rules when available. Using this corpus, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B to develop a single MLLM capable of handling diverse AQA tasks. We further establish X-AQA-Bench, which evaluates both in-distribution (ID) performance on datasets represented during training and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization on four held-out datasets. The resulting model outperforms all evaluated open-source MLLMs on X-AQA-Bench and achieves competitive performance relative to proprietary MLLMs. Ablation studies further demonstrate that multi-domain joint training and explicitly providing assessment criteria in prompts both improve OOD generalization. X-AQA establishes a unified foundation for advancing general-purpose AQA across diverse real-world domains. Data and models are released at \hyperlink{https://huggingface.co/collections/Kelly0510/x-aqa}{here}.

papers.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by the memory demands of the key-value (KV) cache, whose size scales linearly with context length. Dynamic sparse attention reduces this bottleneck by fetching and attending only to a critical subset of tokens. The dominant primitive in dynamic sparse attention research and deployment is fixed-budget top-$k$ selection, which is favored because its deterministic block count aligns with the static memory allocation that systems like vLLM rely on. Top-$k$ uses a fixed budget regardless of how attention mass is distributed across heads, layers, and decode steps, leading to either wasted bandwidth on heads with peaky attention or dropped context on heads with diffuse attention. Top-$p$ (nucleus) selection adapts naturally to this variation but has seen limited adoption in production serving systems due to two system-level challenges: variable block counts that break deterministic block allocation and computationally expensive selection kernels that exceed the cost of attention itself. We present DisSparse, a serving system that integrates top-$p$ sparse attention into vLLM end-to-end. DisSparse decouples block selection from the scheduler's critical path, hides selection latency behind layer computation via a two-stream pipeline, and introduces a single-pass histogram-based top-$p$ kernel. We further observe intra-block sparsity, the inflation of selection budgets caused by mixing high- and low-importance tokens within fixed-size KV cache blocks, and address it with a token relocation kernel guided by accumulated prefill attention scores. Across long- and medium-context benchmarks on multiple models, DisSparse achieves 1.17x to 1.80x speedup in sparsity analysis (block selection) over state-of-the-art top-$p$ methods with negligible accuracy loss and supports up to 8x larger maximum batch sizes than dense vLLM under the same memory budget.
authors: Nurlan Nazaraliyev, Elaheh Sadredini, Nael Abu-Ghazaleh
bullets: Top-$p$ selection adapts computation to attention distributions, avoiding top-$k$’s fixed-budget waste or context loss.
Integrates top-$p$ sparse attention into vLLM with scheduler-decoupled block selection and a two-stream pipeline that overlaps selection with layer computation.
Uses a single-pass histogram-based top-$p$ kernel to reduce selection cost.
Relocates tokens based on prefill attention scores to reduce intra-block sparsity and inflated selection budgets.
Reports 1.17×–1.80× faster sparsity analysis, negligible accuracy loss, and up to 8× larger maximum batch sizes than dense vLLM under the same memory budget.

papers.abstract: Video generation models are widely used as 3D priors for novel view synthesis and 3D scene generation. Fine-tuned for perception, generation models also excel at dense prediction such as depth estimation. However, methods that apply video generation models to 3D reconstruction either predict depth without cameras or generate geometry and estimate cameras through many iterative denoising steps, which makes them slower. In this paper, we present $\textbf{VG3R}$, which turns a pretrained video generation model into a feed-forward 3D reconstruction model. Our key observation is that such a model already captures the depth and camera motion of a video, but not in the form required for reconstruction. We introduce two components: $\textit{clip-level shift prediction}$, which corrects depth distortion caused by the unknown shift in decoded inverse depth, and a $\textit{multi-layer camera head}$, which predicts per-frame cameras parameters by combining features across transformer blocks. Using Wan2.1 as its video backbone, VG3R reconstructs a scene and estimate the camera of every frame without iterative denoising. It achieves the lowest ATE and reconstruction errors among methods built on video generation models, runs about 4 and 14 times faster than Aether and Geo4D. VG3R also demonstrates competitive depth estimation and 3D reconstruction performance compared with geometry foundation models. Project page: https://github.com/KTH-RPL/VG3R
authors: Jingong Chen, Qingwen Zhang, Lin Lian, Xinxin Zuo, Yang Wang, Chulwoo Pack, Kyle Gao, Patric Jensfelt, Kwanghee Won
bullets: Addresses the slowness and incomplete camera modeling of prior video-generation-based 3D reconstruction methods.
Corrects decoded inverse-depth distortion using clip-level shift prediction.
Predicts per-frame camera parameters with a multi-layer camera head that fuses features across transformer blocks.
Using Wan2.1, reconstructs scenes without iterative denoising and reports the lowest ATE and reconstruction errors among comparable video-generation methods.
Runs about 4× faster than Aether and 14× faster than Geo4D, while remaining competitive with geometry foundation models.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview. VG3R encodes the input video with the frozen VAE of Wan2.1 and processes its latents with a LoRA-adapted transformer at a fixed timestep, with blocks ordered from bottom to top. The final-block features are decoded into inverse depth x̂ through the output layer and VAE decoder D. ClipShift uses these features to predict a single shift ĉ for a video clip, recovering depth up to a global scale. LayerTap combines features from multiple transformer blocks and pairs each latent frame with the first to predict per-frame cameras. Depth and cameras yield the reconstructed point maps. Gray losses are used only during training.

papers.selection_reason: Turns a pretrained video generation model into a feed-forward 3D reconstruction model with camera estimation; relevant to generalist 3D perception from video priors.
papers.title: VG3R: Video Generation Model for Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction

papers.abstract: Reasoning-based driving vision-language-action (VLA) models propose multiple candidate trajectories at each decision, yet only one is executed. Standard evaluation scores the best candidate, assuming an oracle selector that deployment lacks, and leaves the risk of the executed candidate unexamined. Existing online evaluators typically close this gap with a purpose-trained scene or world model, often rolling out each candidate through it at inference time. We introduce AlpaSafe, a risk-aware trajectory selector that reuses the scene representation a frozen driving VLA computes while proposing its candidates. AlpaSafe reads the last hidden token of the VLA's prompt prefill. A lightweight head, trained on the closed-loop simulation outcomes of the candidates, fuses this token with each candidate trajectory and predicts a relative score and collision/offroad logits. A fixed rule removes candidates dominated on the two risk logits and selects the highest-scoring candidate among those remaining, adding neither rollouts nor VLA training. Experiments on 525 AlpaSim scenes show that AlpaSafe outperforms Alpamayo's default first-sample rule and uniform random selection in selected regret and top-1 agreement, and reduces the collision-at-fault or offroad rate from 6.41% and 6.10% to 4.93%. The selector has 1.7M parameters and takes 0.75 ms per decision.
authors: Qiren Wang, Mingyu Guo, Weisong Shi
bullets: Addresses the gap between oracle-based evaluation and the risk of the single trajectory actually executed.
Uses the frozen VLA’s last prompt-prefill hidden token with each candidate trajectory to predict relative quality and collision/offroad risk.
Filters candidates dominated on both risk predictions, then selects the highest-scoring remaining trajectory.
On 525 AlpaSim scenes, improves selected regret and top-1 agreement over first-sample and uniform-random selection.
Reduces collision-at-fault or offroad rate to 4.93%, from 6.41% and 6.10%; adds 1.7M parameters and 0.75 ms per decision.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. AlpaSafe overview. (a) One forward pass of the frozen Alpamayo-1.5 generator yields the K=8 candidate trajectories and the prompt-prefill hidden states H; the selector reads only the last token h = H[−1]. (b) The selector head encodes each candidate, fuses it with h through one cross-attention block with a residual connection, and outputs a bounded relative score si and collision/offroad logits (ci, oi); the group-mean, future-trajectory, and progress heads supervise training only. (c) Candidates dominated on the two risk logits are removed, and the highest si among the survivors is executed. Camera frames, candidates, scores, and logits are recorded data from one decision group of the evaluation pool (LASTTOKEN).

Fig. 6. Recorded outcomes for one evaluation-pool decision group, 3.8 s after the decision. Each panel shows the top-down view with metric summary above the front camera. Orange (light gray in grayscale print) marks the executed trajectory and green (mid gray) the navigation route and, in the top-down view, the recorded human drive. LASTTOKEN selects the only one of the eight candidates without a recorded safety failure. The groups in Figs. 6 to 8 were chosen retrospectively for camera legibility and show individual selections, not average performance.

Fig. 7. Recorded outcomes for the scene-information ablation, 6.1 s after the decision, with conventions as in Fig. 6. NULL has selected the only colliding candidate of its group, whereas LASTTOKEN and FULL selected event-free candidates.

Fig. 8. Recorded outcomes for the last-token versus full-sequence comparison, 5.2 s after the decision, with conventions as in Fig. 6. The candidates selected by FULL and NULL have left the road, whereas the LASTTOKEN selection has not.

Fig. 2. Same-prefill representation extraction. One production predict() call per decision group runs one prompt prefill (camera, ego-history, and text tokens) through the frozen generator and yields two products of that forward pass: the K=8 candidates, decoded by the flow-matching action expert from K sampled chain-of-causation (CoC) reasoning traces, and the final-layer hidden states H of the 3,086-token prefill. The selector consumes only the last row h = H[−1]. The candidates shown are the recorded outputs of the decision group in Fig. 1.

Fig. 3. Expanded view of the selector head, panel (b) of Fig. 1. Blue marks the products of the frozen generator (τi, h); the other blocks are trained: yellow runs per candidate, red is the scene reader, computed once per group, and green marks the heads read by the rule of panel (c). The scene memory M has one row for LASTTOKEN and 3,086 rows for FULL, and ⊕ denotes a residual add.
TABLE I RESULTS ON ALL 525 SCENES AND 1,575 GROUPS, WITH K=8. SCORE IS THE SELECTED CANDIDATE’S TRUE OFFICIAL SCORE, AND ALL VALUES ARE SCENE-MACRO MEANS.

TABLE II MATCHED SCENE-INPUT ABLATIONS, WITH SCENES, GROUPS, AND COLUMNS AS IN TABLE I. ONLY THE SCENE INPUT DIFFERS: THE LAST TOKEN FOR LASTTOKEN, ONE ZERO TOKEN FOR NULL, AND ALL 3,086 TOKENS FOR FULL.

TABLE III COST OF ONE EIGHT-CANDIDATE DECISION: CLOSED-LOOP SIMULATION OF EVERY CANDIDATE VERSUS THE LASTTOKEN SELECTION PATH. BOTH COLUMNS WERE MEASURED ON THE SAME NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU. SIMULATION ENTRIES USE THE MEDIAN OF 24 CANDIDATE ROLLOUTS (104.5 S) PLUS OFFICIAL SCORING (6.8 S); THE SELECTOR ENTRY IS THE MEDIAN OVER 315 HELD-OUT GROUPS. A ROLLOUT CANNOT BE SPLIT ACROSS GPUS, SO ONE ROLLOUT BOUNDS THE SIMULATION LATENCY FROM BELOW.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a risk-aware trajectory selector for VLA models in autonomous driving that reuses internal VLA states to select safe trajectories without rollouts.
papers.title: AlpaSafe: Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection for Vision-Language-Action Models in Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: AlpaSafe selects safer trajectories from VLA-generated candidates using existing scene features, reducing collision/offroad risk without extra rollouts or VLA retraining.

papers.abstract: Coupling a property-graph database to an external language-model server imposes a three-part socket tax: serialization overhead dwarfing microsecond graph reads, repeated prefill of verbose schemas, and blind decoding divorced from the live catalog and multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) engine. We present Shoonya, from-scratch commercially clean (0.0% non-commercial or share-alike data) tri-modal (Python, Rust, OpenCypher) small language models (16.8M to 1.07B parameters) co-designed with shoonya-infer, a zero-dependency pure-Rust runtime embedded inside the samyama-graph-enterprise address space. Direct GraphStore references unlock three database-native primitives: (1) an epoch-invalidated SchemaPrefixCache over a copy-on-write PagedKvArena accelerating warm CPU time-to-first-token by 4.91x--13.68x with O(1) DDL invalidation; (2) a 36 us columnar catalog and source-span logit mask enforcing valid ontology identifiers and verbatim spans; and (3) a sub-65 us read-only MVCC gate serving Tier-0 queries inside 389.8 MiB INT8 RSS (59.8--67.9 tok/s) with 0.0% hallucination leak. Rank-factorized tied embeddings (-74.5% vocabulary weights), atomic indentation tokens (0/421 indentation errors), 4:1 grouped-query attention with 2:1 cross-layer KV sharing (-93.75% INT8 KV memory), Warmup-Stable-Decay training, KnOTS SVD merging, Step-GRPO, and Rust Jacobi SVD governance keep 100% of layers heavy-tailed ($\alpha \in [1.88, 2.20]$). Finally, we synthesize nine lessons across v0.1--v1.0, resolving a Reverse-Token-Density Distillation Trap via teacher scaling and zero-VRAM Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation (AdvKD), recovering +13.61 MBPP points (33.07%) while reaching 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool planning.
authors: Madhulatha Mandarapu, Sandeep Kunkunuru
bullets: Targets serialization cost, repeated schema prefill, and decoding that is unaware of live catalogs and MVCC.
Uses an in-process Rust runtime with Python, Rust, and OpenCypher models ranging from 16.8M to 1.07B parameters.
Introduces epoch-invalidated schema KV caching, catalog/source-span logit masking, and an MVCC gate for read-only queries.
Reports 4.91–13.68× faster warm CPU time-to-first-token, 0.0% hallucination leak, and 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool-planning tasks.
Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation recovers 13.61 MBPP points while operating without VRAM for the distillation verifier.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Zero-socket in-process architecture coupling samyama-graph-enterprise (v1.15.0) and shoonya-infer inside one Rust address space. Direct &GraphStore references enable DDL-epoch KV prefix caching, 36 µs columnar catalog and source-span logit masking over the 50, 264-token vocabulary, and sub-65 µs read-only MVCC verification.

Figure 4: (a) Longitudinal sample efficiency of Shoonya-350M (0.43M → 796.7M verified tokens) vs. external 350M–360M baselines (335B–4, 000B tokens). (b) Resolution of the M3 Reverse-TokenDensity Trap (v0.9.4) via 6.53× teacher scaling (1.3B-v1.0) and AdvKD (350M-v0.9.5).

Figure 2: Live zero-socket samyama-graph-enterprise v1.15.0 CPU evaluation. (a) Cold schema prefill vs. warm SchemaPrefixCache TTFT across scoped threads (v0.9.2) and the persistent OnceLock + AVX2+FMA worker pool (v0.9.3/1.3B-v1.0). (b) Four-surface accuracy progression from unaligned M1 (v0.9.2) to M4 (v0.9.5-AdvKD / 1.3B-v1.0) at 0.0% MVCC hallucination leak.

Figure 3: (a) Full-depth Rust Cyclic Jacobi SVD Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization (HTSR) exponent α across normalized depth. Shoonya-1.3B v1.0 (24/24 layers, ᾱ = 2.075) and Shoonya-350M v0.9.5 (20/20 layers, ᾱ = 1.983) remain strictly inside the ideal α ∈ [1.85, 3.5] corridor, whereas multi-trillion-token sub-500M baselines exhibit α < 1.85 correlation traps. (b) Six-arm Iso-Step kernel throughput vs. perplexity.

Table 2: Complete longitudinal progression (v0.5.0 → v0.9.5-AdvKD and 1.3B-v1.0) and samehost competitor evaluation across all 593 SHA-256-decontaminated problems and full-depth Rust Cyclic Jacobi SVD.

Table 1: Controlled six-arm Iso-Step wind-tunnel on RTX 4050 (BF16). Dense-GQA-XKV2-WSD preserves FlashAttention-2 SRAM fusion while halving KV memory on top of 4:1 GQA (87.5% total BF16 KV reduction) and enabling spike-free WSD continual pretraining.
