papers.selection_reason: Introduces efficient LLM inference techniques for graph databases, including Schema-Epoch KV caching and Verifier-Advantage Distillation.
papers.title: Shoonya: Zero-Socket In-Process Small Language Models for Graph Databases with Schema-Epoch KV Caching, Live Catalog Logit Masking, and Verifier-Advantage Distillation
papers.tldr: Shoonya embeds small language models directly inside a graph database to reduce socket overhead, reuse schema context, and constrain generation using live database state.

papers.abstract: Vision Banana showed that a closed image generator, instruction-tuned to paint perception outputs as RGB images, becomes a generalist vision model. Does this carry over to \emph{open} generators, and if not, what fails? We answer with \textbf{Open Vision Banana (OVB)}, an open framework that adapts the 7B diffusion generator of Qwen-Image-2.1 into one instruction-driven model for metric depth, semantic, instance, and referring segmentation, using a single shared low-rank adapter and public data. Each task is a \emph{task contract} whose RGB encoder, instruction, and decoder share one specification and are checked before training. Studying 42 externally evaluated checkpoints from two 100k-update runs, six exact weight-space merges, and eight controlled shorter runs, we find that the gap to the closed system is specific and measurable. Geometry is learned early while absolute scale is not: median-aligned NYUv2 $\delta_1$ stays at 0.89--0.93 throughout training as unaligned $\delta_1$ wanders between 0.11 and 0.50. The scale is not committed by a single sample: a ten-seed ensemble lifts unaligned $\delta_1$ from 0.348 to 0.516 without retraining. Depth and 2D segmentation compete for the shared adapter, and weight merging moves along this trade-off without escaping it. Finally, lower validation flow loss comes with lower Cityscapes accuracy (Spearman $\rho\approx-0.9$ between loss reduction and mIoU), so the loss cannot select checkpoints. We release code, contracts, training data, and all evaluation outputs.
authors: Xu Lin, Ruilin Yao, Haoran Xu, Zixiang Wang, Ming Ma, Yu Zhao, Pu Miao, Chonghan Liu
bullets: Adapts Qwen-Image-2.1 into one instruction-driven model for metric depth, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and referring segmentation.
Uses a shared low-rank adapter, public data, and task contracts that align each task’s encoder, instruction, and decoder before training.
Geometry is learned early, but absolute depth scale remains unstable; ensembling predictions improves unaligned depth accuracy without retraining.
Depth and 2D segmentation compete for adapter capacity, and weight merging does not remove this trade-off.
Lower validation flow loss correlates with worse Cityscapes mIoU, making the loss unreliable for checkpoint selection; code, data, contracts, and evaluations are released.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Open Vision Banana overview. A source image x and a task instruction pq condition a frozen generative backbone (Qwen-Image-2.1 in all experiments; the backbone is a configuration choice) that carries one newly initialized rank-64 LoRA adapter δ shared by all tasks. The source enters as visual tokens and reference latents, the instruction as the text condition, and the target latent is generated from noise in 50 flow steps. The generated RGB image r̂q is converted by a parameter-free decoder Dq into a structured prediction ŷq: metric depth, a class-ID map, instance masks, or a binary mask. Bottom: a task contract Cq = (Eq, pq, Dq; Sq) ties encoder, instruction, and decoder to one specification and is validated before training. The scene is a rendered illustration; its RGB tiles are produced by the contract encoders from exact annotations and are not model predictions.

Fig. 3. Training data and task mixture of the main runs. (a) The 1,098,435 training records by task and source; one record is an image–instruction–target triple, so an image can appear in several records. Small sources are listed to the right of their bar; “Indoor observed” combines ARKitScenes, DIODE, and SUN RGB-D frames with at least 98% observed depth, and “Earlier pool” is the segmentation data of the earlier OVB stages. (b) Each task’s share of the pool (light) against its per-update sampling probability (dark), and the expected number of times each record is drawn over the 3.2M draws of a 100k-update run. Sampling reweights the pool: semantic segmentation and editing replay are drawn more often than their size implies, referring segmentation less often.

Fig. 4. Training trajectories of the two 100k-update runs (A: lr 3 × 10−5, B: lr 1 × 10−5; EMA “best” checkpoints, external evaluation). (a) Median-aligned NYUv2 δ1 is flat at 0.89–0.93 from the first evaluated checkpoint, while unaligned δ1 moves between 0.11 and 0.49: training changes the scale, not the geometry. (b) Cityscapes mIoU declines in both runs while depth improves; ReasonSeg peaks early in B and recovers late in A.

Fig. 5. Qualitative results: metric depth and semantic segmentation of Qwen-Image-2.1 with run B at 20k updates (EMA adapter, merged) on benchmark validation images. Depth is the RGB code before decoding.
Fig. 6. Qualitative results: instance and referring segmentation, same model as Fig. 5. Instance colors are arbitrary per instance and need not match the ground truth.

Fig. 2. Task contracts, contract check, and training. (a) Each task is an explicit, decodable RGB code given by a specification Sq, an encoder Eq, an instruction pq, and a decoder Dq; the depth card shows the colormap path along the edges of the RGB cube, each vertex labeled with the metric depth it encodes under Eq. (2). (b) Checks that run on the training manifest and configuration before the first update. (c) Training: an annotation is encoded into an RGB target and then into a latent b by the frozen autoencoder; conditional flow matching updates the shared adapter while the backbone stays frozen. Run A uses peak lr 3 × 10−5 (shown) and run B uses 1 × 10−5; editing replay is included with the intent of preserving generation, which we have not measured (Sec. 6).

Table 8 gives all metrics and Table 9 the gap to interpolation. Cityscapes is above interpolation for every merge, ReasonSeg below for every merge, and unaligned NYUv2 δ1 below for all merges except P6. P2, P3, and P4 show unstable DIODE AbsRel (1.1–2.9), while P1 and P5 stay at 0.50–0.56, close to the 17.5k checkpoint (0.51), and P6 is 0.79.

Table 10 extends Sec. 5.5. Only Cityscapes has a consistent sign, and it is negative in both runs. Across runs, A ends at a lower loss than B (3.079 vs. 3.120 × 10−2) while being worse on unaligned depth and Cityscapes.

papers.selection_reason: Unified perception through generation in RGB space, including metric depth and segmentation, directly relevant to 3D foundation models and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Open Vision Banana: An Open Framework for Unified Visual Perception through Generation in RGB Space
papers.tldr: Open Vision Banana shows that an open 7B diffusion generator can unify depth and segmentation perception tasks, but shared-adapter interference, unresolved depth scale, and misleading validation loss limit performance selection.

papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of AI-generated content (AIGC) video generation and editing technologies has raised growing societal concerns about the authenticity and reliability of digital videos. Existing video detection methods primarily exploit temporal inconsistencies through holistic frame-level representations, whereas manipulation localization methods focus on artifacts within individual spatial regions. However, holistic representations may obscure localized artifacts through global feature aggregation, while region-centric approaches may overlook disagreements between individual regions and their surrounding spatiotemporal context. To address these limitations, we propose VIdeo Contextual Agreement (VICA), a unified framework that masks individual video regions and leverages a frozen V-JEPA model to predict their representations from the surrounding spatiotemporal context. Complementary masking ensures complete regional coverage, while context-conditioned predictions establish references for assessing regional agreement with the broader video context. By comparing predicted and observed representations, VICA derives spatial residuals that characterize intra-frame discrepancies and bidirectional temporal residuals that capture inconsistencies across preceding and subsequent frames. These residuals characterize contextual disagreements, providing a shared forensic representation for both tasks and shifting the focus from identifying isolated manipulation artifacts to assessing regional agreement with expectations inferred from the broader video context. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VICA achieves state-of-the-art performance on both tasks across multiple benchmarks, with strong generalization to unseen video generators and editing methods.
authors: Runheng Lin, Jialiang Shen, Jiyang Zheng, Ruiqi Liu, Zonglin He, Yu Yao, Huajie Chen, Chris Russell, Runqi Lin
bullets: Addresses limitations of frame-level holistic features and isolated region-artifact analysis.
Masks video regions and uses a frozen V-JEPA model to predict each region from surrounding context.
Computes spatial residuals for within-frame discrepancies and bidirectional temporal residuals for cross-frame inconsistencies.
Provides a shared forensic representation for both AIGC video detection and manipulation localization.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks with strong generalization to unseen generators and editing methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of VICA. Given an input video clip, the frozen V-JEPA 2.1 target encoder extracts observed features Y , while the frozen context encoder and predictor generate context-conditioned predictions from two complementary masked views. The resulting predictions are combined into P̂ , providing a predicted representation for every spatiotemporal token. Spatial residuals S are computed between predicted and observed features at the same time step, whereas bidirectional temporal residuals F and B capture discrepancies across paired time steps. Finally, a shared readout integrates [S, F,B] to support both video-level detection and region-level localization.

Figure 2. The video is generated by Vidu and sourced from AIGVDBench, which does not provide localization annotations. P̂t and Yt denote the predicted and observed regional features at temporal step t, respectively. The three rows show the spatial residual P̂1 − Y1 and the bidirectional temporal residuals P̂2 − Y1 and P̂1 − Y2. The columns display the input frame, channel-wise signed residual sums, and ℓ2 norms, with and without overlays on the input frame. The right boxer’s glove appears malformed, while the spatial residual P̂1 − Y1 produces a localized response around the fist. In comparison, the bidirectional temporal residuals P̂2−Y1 and P̂1−Y2 exhibit stronger and more extensive ℓ2 responses along the moving arms and gloves, highlighting motion-dependent discrepancies that are less apparent in the spatial residual. This visualization illustrates how spatial and bidirectional temporal residuals reveal complementary patterns of contextual disagreement in AI-generated videos.

papers.abstract: We show that an AI agent can write new capabilities into a pretrained language model by adding gated attention heads and MLP neurons inside its existing layers, without backpropagation and without fitting any weight to the answers of task examples. It has a budget of 50 model passes and sees no validation or test instance. Composed in one model, its modules for six BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) subtasks raise the normalized BBH score of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct from 19.95 to 41.05 (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: at most 35.01) and that of Gemma-3-1B-it from 10.25 to 32.86. Against the unmodified model at the same precision, both composites leave the next-token distribution on 1,023,000 WikiText tokens unchanged (KL exactly 0), give identical answers on 15,845 items of five other Leaderboard tests and identical scores on the other 18 BBH subtasks. The agent also writes exact multiplication up to 20 digits, running the model only up to 6 (100.0% on the absent lengths of the sealed test in both models; a LoRA with the same budget: at most 2.1%). Sets, rules and report sentences were sealed in git before the first session (manifests timestamped in Bitcoin), with dated amendments listed in Appendix D; a frozen evaluator ran the sealed test once. Verdicts (H5: tracking; H6: composite; H8: one pass vs. chain of thought; H9: fresh and rewritten instances; H10: side effects; H12: multiplication), on the preregistered sealed test, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct: H5 success, H6 success, H8 (web_of_lies) success, H9 success, H10 (composite) success on (i) to (iii), (iv) confirmed, H12 success; Gemma-3-1B-it (H7: H5, H6, H8 and H9 in this model): H5 success, H6 success, H8 (web_of_lies) success, H8 (tracking 3) success, H9 partial, H10 (composite) success on (i) to (iii), (iv) confirmed, H12 success. Not everything worked: 4 of 45 single modules show small side effects and 5 of 50 sessions hit the 12-hour limit without a module.
authors: Santiago Rivadeneira Quintero
bullets: The approach adds gated attention heads and MLP neurons within existing layers using at most 50 model passes and no validation or test examples.
A single model composed of modules for six BBH subtasks improved normalized scores from 19.95 to 41.05 on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and from 10.25 to 32.86 on Gemma-3-1B-it.
The written modules achieved exact multiplication up to 20 digits while the base models ran only up to 6 digits; a same-budget LoRA reached at most 2.1% on the absent lengths.
On tested WikiText tokens and other benchmark items, the composites produced unchanged next-token distributions or identical answers/scores outside targeted capabilities.
Limitations include small side effects from 4 of 45 modules and 5 of 50 sessions that timed out without producing a module.

papers.selection_reason: Directly writes new capabilities into LLM weights via gated heads and neurons, a novel architectural modification relevant to large language model research.
papers.title: Don't Train It, Write It: An AI Agent Writes New Capabilities into Language Model Weights
papers.tldr: An AI agent can add targeted capabilities to pretrained language models by writing internal modules into their weights—without backpropagation or answer-fitting—while largely preserving existing behavior.

papers.abstract: Social simulations often use language model agents to represent people who differ on several measurable traits. However, describing a trait profile in a prompt does not guarantee the agent will express each trait at its intended level. We propose a method that calibrates agents to multidimensional profiles using activation steering: (i) extract steering directions for each trait, (ii) learn a shared mapping from steering strengths to measured trait scores, and (iii) search for a steering intervention for each target. We use Bayesian optimization for this search and evaluate the method on the Big Five personality scores of 500 OpenPsychometrics respondents. In each of five rounds, the assigned interventions yield lower mean absolute error across respondents than the prompting and steering baselines. Further, the model's responses to a given intervention yield the same trait profile regardless of whose target motivated it, so a poor match for one respondent can be the best match for another. When we match each respondent to the closest profile found across all tested interventions, Bayesian optimization yields 16.6% lower mean absolute error than uniform random search at the same evaluation budget. Our method thus offers a way to build social agents whose measured traits dovetail with those of the people they seek to represent. Whether this closer fit translates to improved predictions of downstream behavior remains an open question.
authors: Niuniu Zhang
bullets: Prompted trait descriptions may not reliably produce the intended personality levels.
The method extracts trait-specific steering directions, learns a shared strength-to-score mapping, and searches for interventions for each target profile.
Evaluated on Big Five scores from 500 OpenPsychometrics respondents across five rounds.
The approach reduced mean absolute error versus prompting and steering baselines; Bayesian optimization also beat uniform random search by 16.6% at the same evaluation budget.
A limitation is that improved personality-profile matching has not yet been shown to improve downstream behavior prediction.

papers.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization provides a computationally efficient approach to fine-tuning large language models (LLMs), but conventional methods typically rely on isotropic perturbations that ignore the anisotropic structure of neural-network parameter spaces. We introduce Preconditioned Activation-Metric Subspace (PAMS), a ZO optimization framework that uses forward-pass activation statistics to construct structured, layer-wise perturbation geometries without computing gradients or forming dense curvature matrices. PAMS tracks a low-rank approximation of the dominant activation subspace and its associated spectrum online, and uses the spectrum to softly reweight perturbation variance while preserving exploration in directions outside the retained subspace. A trace normalization separates the perturbation geometry from its overall scale, enabling consistent perturbation magnitudes across layers. We show theoretically that the resulting perturbation covariance induces right-side preconditioning of the gradient of the corresponding Gaussian-smoothed objective. We further characterize the estimator's smoothing bias and second moment and derive a nonconvex convergence guarantee that captures the effects of the perturbation geometry and smoothing radius. The proposed low-rank tracking procedure requires $\mathcal{O}(n_l r)$ persistent memory for a layer with input dimension nl and retained rank r, avoiding the $\mathcal{O}(n_l^2)$ memory required by a dense activation covariance. Experiments on transformer-based language-model fine-tuning tasks across GLUE and SuperGLUE demonstrate that PAMS improves the effectiveness and stability of zeroth-order optimization while retaining its gradient-free and objective-evaluation-based advantages.
authors: Pradeep Kumar Ragu Chanthar, Saksham Sahai Srivastava, Jaewoo Lee
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of isotropic perturbations, which ignore anisotropic parameter structure.
Uses forward-pass activation statistics to track dominant layer-wise subspaces and softly reweight perturbation variance.
Applies trace normalization to maintain consistent perturbation scales across layers while preserving exploration outside the tracked subspace.
Provides theoretical analyses of preconditioning, smoothing bias, estimator variance, and nonconvex convergence.
Experiments on GLUE and SuperGLUE transformer fine-tuning tasks report improved zeroth-order effectiveness and stability while retaining gradient-free optimization.

papers.tldr: PAMS improves zeroth-order LLM fine-tuning by using activation-informed, low-rank perturbation geometries instead of isotropic noise, without gradients or dense curvature matrices.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a model using unlabeled test data to help it handle distribution shifts. However, prior work has found that image corruption causes a vision-language model (VLM) to produce more similar features for different images, a phenomenon known as feature compression. Under compression, entropy minimization, the most common TTA objective, can cause the model to favor a few classes and perform worse than before adaptation. Despite these observations, a detailed analysis of how these failures are connected and an effective strategy for preventing them are still lacking. In this paper, we first analyze why entropy minimization fails for VLMs. We then propose CAMA, a new test-time adaptation objective that maximizes batch mutual information to encourage confident predictions for individual images while maintaining diverse predictions across the batch. CAMA also estimates a reference class distribution early in the test stream and aligns each batch's average prediction with this reference during adaptation. We prove that feature compression biases the predictions and that entropy minimization amplifies this bias into collapse, whereas CAMA is guaranteed to preserve every class. Across standard corruption benchmarks, we observe collapse on nearly every VLM backbone evaluated. CAMA prevents collapse in every observed case and, in turn, achieves the best accuracy on every backbone. Quantitative and qualitative analyses confirm that CAMA reverses the feature compression behind the collapse, and ablations show that each of its components contributes.
authors: Jinho Kang, Yunhui Guo
bullets: Feature compression under corruption makes different images produce similar VLM features, biasing predictions toward a few classes.
Entropy minimization amplifies this bias, causing class collapse and potentially degrading performance below the pre-adaptation model.
CAMA promotes confident per-image predictions while maintaining diverse batch predictions through mutual-information maximization.
It aligns each batch’s average prediction with a reference class distribution estimated early in the test stream.
On standard corruption benchmarks, CAMA prevents collapse in all observed cases and achieves the best accuracy across evaluated backbones; ablations support both components.

papers.selection_reason: Test-time adaptation objective for vision-language models that prevents feature-compression collapse; directly relevant to test-time learning.
papers.title: CAMA: Calibrated Anti-Collapse Marginal Alignment for Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Models

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is commonly adopted as one of the components in post-training of large language models (LLMs), but in multi-turn agentic tasks we find that the student model increases their reasoning lengths after training. Our empirical analysis shows that the reasoning token lengths is affected by how much the student can distract the teacher's scores. We introduce Muted Distillation (MD), a simple variant of OPD that hides the student's reasoning from the teacher, so the teacher judges what the student does without the interference of student's reasonings. MD takes a few lines of code and adds no extra data or hyperparameters. On the knowledge-work benchmarks OfficeQA Pro and SpreadsheetBench, it reduces output tokens per episode by 57\% and 53\% compared with standard OPD, making the student more concise than it was before training. At the same time, it matches OPD's accuracy on OfficeQA Pro and improves pass@1 by 4.8 points on SpreadsheetBench.
authors: Yuwei Zhang, Ian Miao, Wentao Zhang, Chen Qu, Bill Bi, Jingbo Shang, Donna Schut
bullets: Standard on-policy distillation can lengthen student reasoning in multi-turn agentic tasks.
Muted Distillation prevents the teacher from seeing the student’s reasoning, reducing score interference.
The method requires only a few lines of code and adds no data or hyperparameters.
It cuts output tokens per episode by 57% on OfficeQA Pro and 53% on SpreadsheetBench versus standard OPD.
Accuracy matches OPD on OfficeQA Pro and pass@1 improves by 4.8 points on SpreadsheetBench.

papers.selection_reason: Novel distillation variant for LLM post-training that reduces reasoning token length; fits LLM methods research.
papers.title: Muted Distillation: Sealing Reasoning from Teacher Unlocks Token-Efficient Agents
papers.tldr: Muted Distillation hides student reasoning from the teacher during on-policy distillation, producing substantially more token-efficient agents without sacrificing benchmark performance.

papers.abstract: This paper introduces LoKiTO, a 3D local kinodynamic trajectory optimizer that combines a Chebyshev polynomial parameterization with an online neural Euclidean Signed Distance Field (ESDF) representation for aerial robotics. While current gradient-based planners often struggle with the high memory requirements of explicit volumetric maps or fail to strictly enforce dynamic limits, LoKiTO embeds kinodynamic constraints directly into a modular cost function and exploits the numerical conditioning properties of the Chebyshev basis. Collision awareness is provided by a continuous, memory-efficient neural ESDF updated online from LiDAR measurements, which drastically reduces map memory consumption to approximately 1.0 MB. Benchmarking in highly cluttered simulated environments against state-of-the-art baselines (Fast-Planner and EGO-Planner) demonstrates the superiority of our approach. Experimental results show that LoKiTO achieves over 99.4% dynamic feasibility compliance, significantly outperforming the baselines, and maintaining higher median clearance from obstacles. By coupling a well-conditioned continuous parameterization with explicit kinodynamic reasoning, LoKiTO provides a practical and extensible basis for local replanning in aerial robotics.
authors: Guillermo Gil-Garcia, J. A. Cobano, L. Merino, F. Caballero
bullets: Addresses the memory demands of volumetric maps and weak enforcement of dynamic limits in gradient-based local planners.
Uses Chebyshev polynomial trajectory parameterization with kinodynamic constraints embedded in a modular cost function.
Maintains an online neural ESDF from LiDAR for continuous collision awareness with approximately 1.0 MB of map memory.
In cluttered simulations, achieves over 99.4% dynamic-feasibility compliance and higher median obstacle clearance than Fast-Planner and EGO-Planner.
Provides a practical and extensible framework for local UAV replanning; results are reported in simulation.

papers.selection_reason: Local kinodynamic trajectory optimization using a learned neural ESDF, fitting learning-based local planning and obstacle avoidance.
papers.title: LoKiTO: Local Kinodynamic Trajectory Optimization for UAVs based on Memory-Efficient Neural Distance Fields
papers.tldr: LoKiTO enables memory-efficient, collision-aware UAV trajectory optimization with explicit kinodynamic constraints and strong feasibility in cluttered environments.

papers.abstract: The advancement of large language models (LLMs) has significantly enhanced the capabilities of agents across various tasks. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) loops, in which a language model repeatedly rewrites a program and builds on its previous version, now perform well in machine-learning tasks, but they rely on frontier models and hundreds of calls per run. Small open-weight models are far cheaper, yet when used alone, their programs often crash and their improvements stall. We propose DiVE (diverse models evolve), an ensemble method for RSI that aims to improve creativity and diversity of generated solutions. DiVE uses three components: a shared memory, a failure log, and best-idea-wins rounds. This allows models to write candidate solutions from the same context and retain the best idea at each iteration. On 22 MLE-bench Lite competitions, an ensemble of five 8-12B open-weight models has 25.4% less test error than its average member and 16.7% less than Llama 3.3 70B, and comes within 7.1% of Qwen 3.5 122B-A10B at 75% of its cost. Diversity among small models can thus stand in for part of the scale that RSI relies on.
authors: Navapat Nananukul, Mayank Kejriwal
bullets: Small models used alone often produce crashing programs and stall during recursive improvement.
DiVE combines shared memory, a failure log, and best-idea-wins rounds to coordinate candidate solutions.
Across 22 MLE-bench Lite competitions, five 8–12B models achieved 25.4% less test error than their average member.
The ensemble had 16.7% less test error than Llama 3.3 70B and came within 7.1% of Qwen 3.5 122B-A10B at 75% of its cost.
The results suggest model diversity can partially substitute for scale in RSI, within the evaluated competition setting.

figures.caption: Figure 2. A comparison of simplified OpenEvolve and DiVE. (a) OpenEvolve, the standard RSI loop, draws one model per iteration by a fixed weight and adds every scored child to a program database from which the next parent is drawn. (b) DiVE adds three components. (1) Shared memory, (2) Failure log, and (3) Best idea wins: all K models write a candidate from the same prompt, and the best-scoring one replaces the memory if it beats it. Components 1 and 2 are part of every run in our study, single-model or ensemble. Scores are from a real ML evaluator at each round.

papers.selection_reason: Ensemble recursive self-improvement for small open-weight LLMs using shared memory and failure logs; relevant to LLM agent memory and self-improvement.
papers.title: Diversity over Scale: Recursive Self-Improvement with Ensembles of Small Open-Weight Models
papers.tldr: DiVE shows that ensembles of small open-weight models can improve recursive self-improvement by using diversity, shared memory, failure tracking, and best-idea selection.

papers.abstract: Online surface reconstruction from LiDAR scans requires observation models that respect the sensor's physical measurement geometry. Unlike unordered point sets, LiDAR returns carry anisotropic range noise along known rays, which also implicitly identify free space. We introduce the Occupancy Planar Patch (OPP), an incremental bounded planar patch representation that evaluates surface likelihoods and free space directly in range-space, allowing sensor noise, plane uncertainty, and ray clearance to be explicitly modelled during reconstruction. A single ray-to-patch association weight jointly updates plane geometry, refines surface boundaries, and blends camera imagery. The method is evaluated using six sequences from the Oxford Spires and Multi-Campus datasets. OPP achieves the highest precision and lowest reconstruction error among evaluated methods, while producing stored maps among the most compact. By conservatively admitting surfaces only where geometric evidence is certain, OPP prioritises structural precision over unconstrained completeness, which is well suited for architectural modelling. Geometric reconstruction operates in real time, requiring 81 ms per frame on a representative sequence, with texture projection adding 134 ms.
authors: Jiahao Wang, Chaehyeon Song, Dongjiao He, Jan Quenzel, Lintong Zhang, Ayoung Kim, Maurice Fallon
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between unordered point-set models and LiDAR’s anisotropic, ray-based measurements.
Represents surfaces as bounded planar patches evaluated in range-space, incorporating sensor noise, plane uncertainty, and ray clearance.
Uses a single ray-to-patch association weight to jointly update geometry, refine boundaries, and blend camera imagery.
Across six Oxford Spires and Multi-Campus sequences, it achieved the highest precision and lowest reconstruction error among evaluated methods, with compact maps.
Prioritises conservative structural precision over complete surface coverage; reconstruction ran in real time at 81 ms per frame, with texture projection adding 134 ms.

Insets in row 3 (b–d) highlight walking pedestrians: dense motion trails visible in raw LiDAR scan (b) and integrated into the volumetric mesh (c) are cleanly carved away in OPP (d) via range-space transmission clearance (Sec. III-E). In textured OPP (e), patch areas left unobserved by MCD’s narrower camera coverage remain white.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a novel planar patch representation for LiDAR reconstruction that explicitly models sensor noise and geometry, relevant to 3D perception.
papers.title: Occupancy Planar Patch: Incremental Probabilistic Bounded-Plane Reconstruction from LiDAR Data
papers.tldr: OPP incrementally reconstructs precise bounded planar surfaces from LiDAR by modelling measurement uncertainty and free space directly along sensor rays.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion streams a video chunk by chunk, but large AR models are too slow for real-time use. We ask where in an AR rollout a large model is actually needed. Pairing Krea-Realtime-14B with Self-Forcing-1.3B, which share their latent space and denoising schedule, we find that the order of the two models matters: when the 14B model generates only the first chunk and the 1.3B model continues, the rollout keeps 95\% of the 14B model's semantic advantage, whereas the reverse allocation keeps 16\% at about ten times the cost. The large model decides what the video shows; the small model only has to carry it forward. We turn this into BigSmall, a training-free planner--renderer sampler. The 14B model plans the opening chunk and sketches the chunks in which content changes, which preserves motion, and the 1.3B model renders the rest; a faster variant, BigSmall, plans only the opening chunk. A cross-model KV cache that is approximate, windowed and lazy lets the planner leave and re-enter the rollout at low cost. On VBench, BigSmall is $3.02\times$ faster than the 14B model at an unchanged semantic score and motion, and $1.55\times$ faster than SDVG, which lets the small model draft first; BigSmall reaches $3.77\times$ at the same semantic score, trading away 10\% of the motion. On minute-long videos (LoCoT2V-Bench), where the 14B model degrades when it reads its own long history, BigSmall is $3.14\times$ faster than the 14B model and scores higher ($+1.78$).`
authors: Yixuan Luo, Yanjing Li
bullets: Large-model computation is most valuable at the rollout’s beginning and when video content changes; reversing the model order largely loses the semantic benefit.
BigSmall is a training-free planner–renderer sampler: the 14B model plans the opening and selected transition chunks, while the 1.3B model renders the rest.
An approximate, windowed, lazy cross-model KV cache enables the large planner to leave and re-enter generation efficiently.
On VBench, BigSmall is 3.02× faster than the 14B model with unchanged semantic score and motion; a faster variant reaches 3.77× speedup with a 10% motion trade-off.
On minute-long videos, BigSmall is 3.14× faster and scores 1.78 points higher than the 14B model.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of BIGSMALL on a real rollout (“a teddy bear and a frisbee”). Top: a zero-cost change score decides, chunk by chunk, whether the 14B planner is called. The planner generates the plan chunk c0 with all four denoising steps and only the first step t1 of each sketch chunk; the 1.3B renderer takes all other steps (squares: denoising steps t1–t4; orange: 14B, blue: 1.3B). Bottom: each model reads its own KV cache; dashed arrows write a finished chunk into a cache, solid arrows read from it. The renderer’s cache is exact: every chunk is written. The planner’s cache is windowed: a planner call reads only the sink c0 and the previous chunk. It is lazy: that previous chunk is written only when the planner needs it (c1 when c2 is sketched, c4 when c5 is sketched), and other chunks are never written. It is approximate: a chunk is re-encoded sparsely, only its moving tokens, while the others copy K/V from the previous frame with re-rotated RoPE; it is re-encoded densely if the chunk before it was never written, as for c4. Right: inside sketch chunk c5, the planner’s first step from noise already fixes the layout (x̂(1) 0 ); it is re-noised to σ2, keeping 6% of the signal, and the renderer completes the chunk from its own cache.

papers.selection_reason: Semantic-aware computation allocation between large and small autoregressive video models with a cross-model KV cache; relevant to video generation and inference efficiency.
papers.title: Plan Big, Paint Small: Semantic-Aware Computation Allocation for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation

papers.abstract: Instruction-based image editors are trained on millions of edit pairs and follow instructions far more reliably than current video editors. We show that this ability can be transferred to video editing without any training. Our key observation is that a growing number of image editors and video generators share the same latent space. Their velocity fields can therefore be combined at sampling time: the difference between the editor's velocity under the instruction and under a neutral prompt, which we call the \emph{edit velocity}, can be added to the sampler of a video model. Added naively, however, it blurs the video, alters the background and flickers. An analysis of the edit velocity explains why. It is small and reliable only at coarse scales and high noise levels, not concentrated on the edited object, and uncorrelated across frames. From these properties, we derive a simple guidance operator that amplifies the edit velocity and restricts it in noise level, space, and time. The video model then turns the incoherent per-frame signal into a temporally coherent edit. Our method, TOGO, combines Qwen-Image-Edit with the Wan2.1 video model without training or fine-tuning. On FiVE-Bench, it raises the edit success rate from 47.0\% (the same video model without the editor) to 65.6\%, above the best published method (59.2\%). At the same time, it maintains the background PSNR and obtains the best LPIPS and SSIM of all methods. Because the video editor is assembled at inference time, it can be upgraded to any newer image editor that shares the latent space with no cost.
authors: Yixuan Luo, Jose Caballero, Yanjing Li
bullets: Addresses unreliable instruction following and artifacts in current video editors.
Combines image-editor and video-model velocity fields through an edit-velocity guidance operator.
Restricts guidance by noise level, spatial region, and time to reduce blur, background changes, and flicker.
Combines Qwen-Image-Edit with Wan2.1 without training or fine-tuning.
On FiVE-Bench, improves edit success from 47.0% to 65.6% while maintaining background PSNR and achieving the best reported LPIPS and SSIM.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of TOGO. Two frozen models that share a latent space are combined at sampling time. At every step, the video model provides the FlowEdit velocity ∆σ , and the image editor provides, for each latent frame k, the edit velocity ∆vk between the instruction and a neutral prompt. The raw ∆v is weak, unlocalized and incoherent across frames; G amplifies, windows, smooths and gates it, and the video model turns G(∆v) into a coherent edit that keeps the motion and background of the source.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison between TOGO and other baselines on FiVE-Bench. Each example shows frames 0 and 39 of a source video edited with the instruction above it. Wan-Edit, which uses the same video model and sampler as TOGO but no edit velocity, makes weak or no change. Other baselines apply the edit only partially or alter the background over time. TOGO applies the edit in both fra es while keeping the background and motion of the source.

Figure 3. What the edit velocity ∆v contains (8 local edits from DAVIS-2017 [28], two noise seeds). Top: for “make the rhino shiny gold” (latent frame 0), the residual D of the editor’s full edit concentrates on the object M⋆, whereas ∆v spreads over the whole frame. (a) ∆v is a small fraction of the full velocity. (b) Its alignment with the ideal direction −D (latent frame 0) grows with noise level and spatial pooling (mean ± s.e. over videos). (c) Its energy fraction outside the object (mean over videos) matches that of a spatially uniform signal. (d) Cross-frame cosine similarity at σ = 0.7 (latent frames 0–20, sampled): D is shared across frames; ∆v is not.

papers.title: TOGO: Take One Image Editor, Get One Video Editor for Free
papers.tldr: TOGO transfers instruction-following ability from an image editor to a video model at inference time, enabling training-free, temporally coherent video edits.

papers.abstract: Payload-carrying robots, such as delivery robots and autonomous trucks, must choose motions that keep them and their payload safe, so their planners predict the outcome of each candidate motion. Modern planners compare thousands of candidates per step on a GPU, using world models such as batched simulators or learned predictors. Most of them assume a rigid payload, but a liquid payload keeps moving after a maneuver, and its state is rarely measured. Near a safety limit, small prediction errors can make an unsafe plan look safe. Coupled fluid simulations are accurate but too costly for every candidate, while low-order slosh models are cheap but accurate only away from resonance. We study this trade-off on a ground vehicle with a partly filled tank near its rollover limit. First, we build PLiMB (Parallel Liquid-MultiBody), a GPU-parallel slosh simulator that, to our knowledge, couples FLIP liquid two-way with many multibody vehicles for the first time. It provides training data and a high-fidelity reference. Second, we propose a scalable physics-anchored world model that combines a modal-slosh and roll prior, an estimate of the hidden liquid state from the vehicle's own motion history (no sensor in the tank), and a learned correction. Without simulating the fluid, it scores thousands of candidate plans in one batched pass within a 20 Hz control tick on one GPU. We judge each world model by the plans it leads a planner to choose. Near the rollover limit, planners that treat the liquid as a rigid payload or use published low-order slosh models repeatedly pick unsafe plans when a safe one exists. Ours never does in our standard tank and makes about half as many in a wide tank whose sloshing mode lies in the maneuver band. There, the liquid state left by earlier driving can change the best plan, and reading it from the vehicle's history halves our model's near-limit prediction error.
authors: Yicheng Zhu, Linfeng Tian, Yang Chen, Tao Li, Zilin Bian
bullets: Liquid payloads can continue sloshing after maneuvers, making rigid-payload and simple slosh assumptions unsafe near rollover limits.
PLiMB is a GPU-parallel, high-fidelity simulator coupling FLIP fluid dynamics with many multibody vehicles to generate training data and references.
The proposed model combines modal slosh and roll physics, history-based hidden-state estimation, and a learned correction without requiring tank sensors.
It evaluates thousands of candidate plans in one GPU-batched pass within a 20 Hz control cycle.

Near rollover limits, it never selected an unsafe plan in the standard tank and made about half as many unsafe choices in a wide tank; history-based state estimation halved near-limit prediction error there.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The physics-anchored response model. Once per tick, the liquid ROM (Fig. 3) is stepped on the vehicle’s on-board signals to estimate the hidden liquid state ξ̂g , and a recurrent latent z summarizes the same history. For all candidate plans in one GPU batch, the physics prior rolls vehicle and liquid forward together, and a second ROM copy, started from ξ̂g , feeds its roll moment Mx back into roll (green). The fitted constants are ca, cM , ωr , ζr , amax and ky . A learned correction, one head per label source, refines the prior’s response series, and a peak head predicts ℓ̂ and ê (and an uncertainty σ that Eq. (1) does not use).

Figure 6. Scaling on one GPU (pre-registered). Left: median time per call against the number of candidate plans per call. Below the dashed line, a call fits one 20 Hz tick. Right: peak GPU memory. Our deployed model fits the tick up to 4,096 plans, while its as-scored implementation, the physics-only planners and every simulator in the loop miss it at every batch size. FLIP stops at 256 plans (median call over 300 s). In memory, B, K and Q coincide, as do R and E and the two implementations of ours.

Figure 5. Predicted against reference peak LTR for every evaluation plan, before calibration (643 plans in the standard tank, 960 in the wide tank), with bias and MAE in each panel. In the standard tank the published models and rigid payload underpredict by 0.04 to 0.05 on average but rank plans well. In the wide tank, the published models scatter widely, and rigid payload under-predicts every plan, by 0.28 on average.

Figure 4. One standard-tank decision group at the calibrated operating point: each candidate’s reference peak LTR against its progress, with the predictions of our model and of Q. Q picks the plan with the most progress among those it predicts safe, which is an avoidable unsafe choice. Ours picks the best safe plan.

The large marker is the pre-registered τ = 0.6, the other thresholds are pre-declared secondary analyses. A planner can avoid unsafe choices by caution, at the cost of rarely picking the best safe plan, so a good model sits in the upper left.

Figure 7. One wide-tank contrast: the same road and identical vehicle state, with the liquid settled (left) or carrying a past maneuver (right). Top: the FLIP liquid’s lateral shift before the decision in the two groups. Bottom: the 16 candidates’ reference peak LTR and the calibrated predictions, and triangles mark each planner’s choice. Without the liquid state, Nc predicts the same loads in both cases and keeps its choice, which becomes unsafe, while Cc raises its predictions and switches to the best safe plan. It is one of 7 contrasts in which the reference’s best plan changes and only Nc’s choice becomes avoidably unsafe. In the settled case both planners are more cautious than necessary.

papers.abstract: Enterprise agents must maintain an up-to-date understanding of work distributed across heterogeneous artifacts, evolving over time, and unevenly visible to different collaborators. We formulate this challenge as persistent project-state understanding (PPSU) and introduce PULSE, a benchmark of 1,573 questions over 30 enterprise project histories. PULSE constructs deterministic, time-indexed project state and documented collaborator views from source-linked records, and evaluates three families of questions: open loops, project evolution, and view gaps. Across retrieval agents, graph- and memory-augmented retrieval, long-context, and oracle conditions, we find substantial headroom for current systems. Retrieval and extraction account for the largest share of the gap, but providing explicit project state on top of gold evidence yields further substantial gains, showing that PPSU cannot be reduced to retrieval alone. Further analysis shows that questions requiring information to be reconciled across multiple parts of the project history remain difficult even when the relevant evidence is provided, while project-state synthesis and perspective conditioning remain persistent challenges. These results motivate enterprise agents that explicitly maintain and reconcile temporally grounded state across sources, actors, and time.
authors: Jiexin Ding, Lin Ai, Adam Davies, Scott Counts
bullets: Introduces 1,573 questions across 30 enterprise project histories, covering open loops, project evolution, and view gaps.
Evaluates retrieval, graph- and memory-augmented retrieval, long-context, and oracle settings.
Finds substantial headroom: retrieval and extraction are major bottlenecks, while explicit project-state representations provide additional gains.
Cross-history reconciliation remains difficult even with relevant evidence; state synthesis and perspective conditioning are persistent challenges.
Motivates agents that track temporally grounded state across sources, actors, and time.

papers.abstract: This paper shows that transformer networks trained with next-token prediction (NTP) and gradient descent do not learn to make predictions using only causally-relevant tokens in the left context, irrespective of the causal ordering of tokens during training, and identifies the learning deficiencies responsible. We introduce a causal world-model setup, for which, we characterize the Bayes-optimal predictor under the causal view of the data. We then prove that, a function that distills its predictions to non-causal views of data, when realized under Occam's Razor, recovers the true causal predictor. Based on this analysis we propose CausalNTP, a practical training algorithm that approximates this theoretical recipe and trains transformers to depend only the causally relevant tokens in left-context. Empirically in the world-model setup, CausalNTP achieves out-of-distribution generalization that vanilla NTP cannot due to its theoretical limits, regardless of data and model scale. We show similar gains and behavior in the natural language question-answering setting as a proof-of-concept.
authors: Devansh Arpit
bullets: Vanilla next-token prediction can learn dependencies on non-causal left-context tokens, regardless of their training-time causal ordering.
The paper analyzes a causal world-model setup and characterizes its Bayes-optimal predictor under a causal view of the data.
It proves that distilling predictions across non-causal data views under an Occam-style principle recovers the true causal predictor.
CausalNTP approximates this recipe in practice and improves out-of-distribution generalization in the world-model setting.
Similar gains are observed in natural-language question answering as a proof of concept.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The Proposed Causal World-model Setup: See section 3.1 for details.

Figure 4: Choice of token-ordering is insufficient: Same models as those trained for fig. 3, except these models are now evaluated on out-of-distribution eval sets. CausalNTP achieves close to Bayes-error at large model width in this setting across all ndesc-before-q strata as well, showing strong evidence of causal dependence on left-context to make predictions.

Figure 2: Bayes-predictor-like behavior under NTP training: Both Model 2 and Model 2R are trained and evaluated on permuted data with the constraint pa(q) ≺ q. Model 2 training allows attending to the full left-context for predicting q while Model 2R training enforces not using descendants of q present in its left-context for predicting q. Empirically, attending to descendants leads to lower training loss but higher eval loss, similar to the prediction of theorem 3.1.

Figure 9: The proposed CausalNTP algorithm for natural language question-answering. See section 4.3 for details. This is an illustration; each node category can contain many tokens in natural language. Notation: pa - parent, An - ancestor, U - unrelated, De - descendant.

Figure 3: Choice of token-ordering is insufficient: The plot shows that choice of tokenordering in training– causal vs. permuted– is insufficient for learning a causal predictor. This is evident from Model 1 (trained on causal token-ordering) and Model 2 (trained on permuted tokenordering) achieving high eval loss on eval samples graded by ndesc-before-q (number of descendants of q in its left-context). Larger ndesc-before-q strata have more descendants in left-context, while smaller ndesc-before-q strata have more ancestor/unrelated nodes in left-context. CausalNTP learns a much more faithful causal predictor that is closer to Bayes-error across all ndesc-before-q strata, especially as model width (dmodel) increases.

Figure 6: Choice of token-ordering is insufficient: Same models as those trained for fig. 5, except these models are now evaluated on out-of-distribution eval sets. CausalNTP achieves error closer to Bayes-error in this setting across all ndesc-before-q strata as well.

Figure 8: Choice of node categories in left-context is insufficient: Same models as those trained for fig. 7, except these models are now evaluated on out-of-distribution eval sets. CausalNTP achieves close to Bayes-error as data scales across all ndesc-before-q strata in this setting as well, showing strong evidence of causal dependence on left-context to make predictions.

Figure 7: Choice of node categories in left-context is insufficient: The plot shows that the choice of node categories in the left-context during training is insufficient for learning a causal predictor. Model 1 is trained on parents+ancestor+unrelated nodes in the left-context, Model 1PO is trained on only parents in the left-context, Model 2 is trained on all four node categories in the left-context. However, all three models achieve high eval loss on eval samples graded by ndesc-before-q (number of descendants of q in its left-context). Larger ndesc-before-q strata have more descendants in left-context, while smaller ndesc-before-q strata have more ancestor/unrelated nodes in left-context. CausalNTP learns a much more faithful causal predictor that is closer to Bayes-error across all ndesc-before-q strata, especially as data scales.

papers.abstract: For on-policy distillation (OPD), more capable models are a natural choice as teachers. However, higher task performance does not necessarily imply greater teachability. A controlled token intervention study suggests that even a model weaker than the student can serve as an informative contrastive reference. Building on this observation, we propose Contrastive On-Policy Distillation (cOPD), which provides dual branch supervision by contrasting strong teacher, weak teacher, and student predictions at student generated prefixes. Our analysis explains how this three way comparison helps select token candidates associated with better or worse reasoning outcomes under an idealized model. We evaluate cOPD across diverse teacher student configurations spanning different training stages, parameter scales, and model families, on tasks including mathematical reasoning, instruction following, and question answering with abstention. cOPD achieves the best or top-tier performance among the evaluated baselines across all three tasks, improving overall Pass@16 on mathematical reasoning by up to 7.51\% over the strongest baseline. Further analyses show that cOPD suppresses undesirable response patterns and suggest that it facilitates exploration.
authors: Zhibo Hou, Fan Zhao, Yiping Li, Zhiyu An, Wan Du
bullets: Motivation: A teacher’s task accuracy does not necessarily determine how teachable it is; even weaker models can provide useful contrastive signals.
Method: cOPD applies dual-branch supervision by contrasting strong-teacher, weak-teacher, and student predictions at prefixes generated by the student.
Analysis: The three-way comparison helps identify token candidates linked to better or worse reasoning outcomes under an idealized model.
Results: Across varied teacher–student configurations, cOPD achieves the best or near-best performance on mathematical reasoning, instruction following, and abstention-based question answering.
Scope: Further analyses indicate that cOPD suppresses undesirable response patterns and may promote exploration.

papers.title: Contrastive On-Policy Distillation via Dual-Branch Supervision
papers.tldr: Contrastive On-Policy Distillation uses strong and weak teachers together to guide student-generated reasoning, improving performance and exploration across several tasks.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now tune neural networks, yet without cross-session memory they spend costly trials rediscovering known lessons. Reuse is difficult because production models differ in architecture, training setup and inference budget. We present Engram, a memory system that links past trial outcomes with the hypotheses and rationale behind them and assesses whether this evidence applies to the current model. An online agent curates evidence at the decision points where it is needed: Initial Guidance supplies validated lessons at the start, Session Retrieval supplies related past sessions before each batch of hypotheses is generated, and Trial Candidate Review checks each trial candidate against matching past trials. Between sessions, an offline agent distills validated lessons, making the memory self-improving. On two ads models, Engram reaches the 32-trial result of a no-memory control with 47% fewer trials and also ends with a better model on average.
authors: Huanran Li, Nhat X. T. Le, Kevin De Angeli, Yao Xuan, Alireza Vahdatpour, Djordje Gligorijevic
bullets: Addresses costly rediscovery when agents tune models across sessions and heterogeneous architectures, training setups, and inference budgets.
Links trial outcomes to their hypotheses and rationale, while assessing whether past evidence applies to the current model.
Uses three retrieval stages: initial guidance, session retrieval before hypothesis generation, and candidate review against related trials.
An offline agent distills validated lessons between sessions, enabling the memory to improve over time.
On two ads models, it matches a no-memory system’s 32-trial result with 47% fewer trials and achieves a better final model on average.

papers.title: Engram: Multi-Stage Memory for Agentic Tuning of Heterogeneous Models
papers.tldr: Engram helps agents tune diverse neural networks more efficiently by reusing and validating lessons from past optimization trials.

papers.abstract: JEPA world models are trained to predict logged transitions but used to compare counterfactual actions from one state. The logged behavior data show one action per state, and under a local linear approximation we prove the action response is unidentified along any direction the policy never varies within a state. We therefore supplement behavior data with measured outcomes of alternative actions from the same state. Our fork futures execute two actions from one restored state, and their outcome difference cancels the state term, identifying the action response on the sampled span. The resulting model, Fork-JEPA, matches predicted to measured differences, anchors the logged successor with behavior prediction, and adds a lookback head that keeps the predecessor recoverable, all at training time, leaving planning unchanged. On three visual control tasks, behavior-only training leaves the predicted action effect no better than a constant guess. Fork-JEPA makes it readable and raises planning success by up to 14\% over LeWM, its base model. Where the action response changes across hidden zones, it nearly doubles cross-zone success, and 1,024 fork pairs beat 1.2M extra behavior steps. Our project is available at https://fork-jepa.github.io/.
authors: Yihao Wu, Runjia Zeng, Tongyan Wang, Renzhong Huang, Chongzhou Fang, Qifan Wang, Fan Heng, Dongfang Liu
bullets: Behavior logs contain only one action per state, leaving action responses unidentified where the policy does not vary.
Fork futures execute two actions from one restored state; subtracting their outcomes cancels the shared state effect.
Fork-JEPA combines measured action differences with logged-transition prediction and a lookback head that preserves predecessor information.
Across three visual-control tasks, it improves planning success by up to 14% over LeWM; 1,024 fork pairs outperform 1.2M extra behavior steps.
When action effects vary across hidden zones, it nearly doubles cross-zone success; scope is limited to sampled action-response directions and tested tasks.

papers.abstract: Under structured outputs (JSON schemas, regexes, tool calls), speculative drafters do not see the grammar constraint and repeatedly propose invalid keys, delimiters, and indentation, while the grammar engine already knows which tokens must come next. We present Grammar-as-a-Draft (GaaD), which treats the grammar as a second drafter. Before each verify step, the scheduler merges the drafter's proposal with grammar-forced tokens into one draft row: matching tokens stay as GRAMMAR, the proposal is cut where it leaves the forced path, and forced tokens fill the rest of a row wider than the drafter's proposal. The verify step accepts GRAMMAR drafts without computing their logits, composing with any drafter with no new kernels or compilation on the critical path. Because grammars fix text rather than tokens, committing canonical forced tokens changes the output distribution relative to grammar-masked target decoding. We implement GaaD in vllm-torchtpu and an independent Rust serving runtime, evaluating on TPU v7x with MTP, DFlash, and n-gram drafters on a JSON character-profile benchmark. GaaD raises average acceptance length from 2.06 to 5.43 (MTP, Qwen3.5-0.8B), 1.99 to 5.31 (MTP, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), 1.57 to 4.13 (DFlash, Qwen3-4B), and 1.30 to 3.64 (n-gram, Qwen3-4B), decoding 2.66-2.81x faster at batch size 1 and 1.14-1.70x at batch size 64. In Rust, MTP+GaaD is 2.23x faster on Qwen3.5-0.8B, 2.02x on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8, and 1.22x at 128 concurrent requests. Under mixed traffic (25-50% structured), GaaD finishes the workload 1.03-1.23x sooner (structured requests 2.2-3.2x sooner) while plain-text TPOT rises 7-42%. We also show grammar-masked greedy decoding can pick non-canonical tokenizations, so GaaD can yield different valid outputs that an fp32 reference finds equally likely.
authors: John Zhang, Silky Arora
bullets: Targets wasted speculative proposals for invalid JSON keys, delimiters, indentation, and other grammar-disallowed tokens.
Merges drafter proposals with grammar-forced tokens; forced-token drafts are verified without computing target logits and require no new critical-path kernels or compilation.
Works with MTP, DFlash, and n-gram drafters across TPU and Rust serving implementations.
Raises average acceptance length roughly 2.5–2.7× and delivers up to 2.81× speedup at batch size 1 and 1.70× at batch size 64 in the reported benchmark.

Canonical forced-token choices can change outputs relative to grammar-masked decoding, producing different but valid and equally likely results; mixed traffic also incurs a plain-text latency increase.

papers.selection_reason: Grammar-as-a-Draft improves speculative decoding throughput for structured outputs, directly reducing inference latency.
papers.title: Grammar-as-a-Draft: More Tokens per Speculative Decoding Step on Grammar-Constrained Structured Outputs
papers.tldr: Grammar-as-a-Draft accelerates grammar-constrained structured decoding by combining speculative drafts with grammar-forced tokens, substantially increasing accepted tokens per step and reducing latency.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in a wide range of robotic tasks. However, adversarial attacks in VLA models have shown strong transferability across robotic tasks, posing significant threats to robotic systems. Despite their different attack strategies, we observe that these transferable attacks share a common consequence: they disrupt the VLA model's perception towards the robot itself. Motivated by this observation, we propose a proprioception-grounded defense framework that leverages trusted proprioceptive information to detect and mitigate transferable adversarial attacks. Specifically, we utilize the robot's proprioceptive states to establish a trusted spatial reference, and compare it with the robot's perceived location inferred from visual features. Discrepancies between these two sources provide a reliable signal for detecting adversarial attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate effective detection of transferable adversarial patches and improved closed-loop performance. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our defense on real-world robotic tasks.
authors: Jiahao Wang, Ming F. Li, Han Xu
bullets: Transferable adversarial attacks can disrupt a VLA model’s perception of the robot itself across tasks.
The method compares the robot’s visually inferred location with a spatial reference derived from proprioceptive states.
Perception–proprioception discrepancies serve as an attack-detection signal and guide mitigation.
Experiments show effective detection of transferable adversarial patches and improved closed-loop performance.
Real-robot evaluations demonstrate effectiveness on real-world robotic tasks.

papers.abstract: Latent dynamic world models have proven to be highly versatile tools for embodied artificial intelligence systems, enabling online action planning, safe policy evaluation, and scalable policy learning. However, this versatility makes world models a vulnerable and centralized point of failure as a compromised model can impact planning, evaluation, and training at once. Therefore it is critical that the security and robustness properties of world models are properly understood before they are universally deployed in embodied AI systems. In this work we take a unifying approach towards this understanding, developing two novel attacks against world models, named state hallucination and dynamic shift attacks, aimed directly at impacting downstream systems, and proposing a new theoretical lens through which to study the robustness of latent dynamic world models. Through our analysis we identify robust latent space encoders as the key component of robust world models. We empirically validate this finding on four separate latent dynamic world model families, studying Dino World Model, Le World Model, r2Dreamer, and Cosmos 3, demonstrating significant improvements in robustness through adversarial encoder model training.
authors: Ethan Rathbun, Jonathan N\"other, Christopher Amato, Alina Oprea, Goran Radanovi\'c
bullets: World models are a centralized failure point because compromises can affect planning, evaluation, and policy learning.
Introduces state hallucination and dynamic shift attacks targeting downstream embodied-AI systems.
Provides a unified theoretical framework for analyzing robustness in latent dynamic world models.
Identifies robust latent-space encoders as the key component for improving model security.
Validates encoder adversarial training across four world-model families, including Dino World Model, Le World Model, r2Dreamer, and Cosmos 3.

papers.abstract: Materials science research is a non-linear, long-horizon process. Existing scientific agents, however, largely rely on specific task execution or predefined workflows, rendering them brittle in open-ended settings. To bridge this gap, we present MatHarness, an agent harness designed for open-ended, long-horizon computational materials research spanning the complete lifecycle from initial ideation to manuscript writing. MatHarness couples three mechanisms: execution robustness through pre-flight verification, expert-distilled skills, and just-in-time auditing; epistemic adaptability through persistent research artifacts and an evolving scientific mental model; and collective intelligence through a heterogeneous multi-agent round table under targeted human oversight. We evaluate MatHarness on adsorbate-induced surface segregation in Cu-Zn alloys, an open question in methanol-synthesis catalysis. Over a multi-week trajectory consuming roughly 10^3 GPU-hours (50 production DFT relaxations prescreened by 171 machine-learning-potential evaluations) the system revised its plan six times, recovered autonomously from failed calculations, and had an independent auditor overturn one of its own over-attributed claims before publication. Within the sampled metallic dilute-limit models, the validated DFT analysis supports an adsorbate-induced tendency toward greater surface Cu exposure at both composition endpoints, with facet- and coverage-dependent exceptions. These results were compiled into a complete manuscript with human involvement concentrated in specification, approval, and strategic steering gates. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/PrentisAI/pippin.
authors: Yanlin Fei, Lei Li, Shaolong Chen, Nazhou Liu, Xinmiao Yu, Madalina Ciobanu, Navan Preet Singh, Qingqing Mao, Ritankar Das
bullets: Addresses the brittleness of scientific agents built around fixed tasks or predefined workflows.
Combines pre-flight verification, expert-distilled skills, just-in-time auditing, persistent research artifacts, an evolving scientific model, and heterogeneous multi-agent collaboration.
Evaluated on adsorbate-induced surface segregation in Cu-Zn alloys for methanol-synthesis catalysis across a multi-week research trajectory.
The system revised its plan six times, recovered from failed calculations, and corrected an over-attributed claim through independent auditing.
Within sampled metallic dilute-limit models, DFT supported greater surface Cu exposure at both composition endpoints, with facet- and coverage-dependent exceptions.

Figure 8: Cu-rich model. Environmental segregation energy Eeseg(T, p) for the selected intermediate/facet case shown in the panel, plotted over temperature and adsorbate pressure with the equilibrium coverage overlaid. The departure from the clean-surface value is largest at low temperature and high pressure. The map is parametrized from the DFT dilute-limit segregation shifts through the lattice model described in Sec. 3.8; it is intended as a semi-quantitative illustration of the environmental trend rather than a precise surface phase diagram.

Figure 5: Zn-rich MLIP prescreen of () for all nine intermediates on the four hcp facets (bestsite placement, bulk-like Cu reference in the third layer). The coverage ladder adds up to eight adsorbates per cell, so the accessible range is set by the number of surface sites and differs by facet: it reaches≈ 1 on the smaller (101̄0)/(101̄1) cells but only≈ 0.5 on the larger (0001)/(112̄0) cells. CO, H, and HCO show the clearest tendency toward negative at low-tomoderate coverage, whereas O, OH, and the weakly interacting CO2/H2O cases generally remain near or above zero on the close-packed facets. The (0001)/(101̄0) trends are read qualitatively at low-to-moderate coverage; the open (112̄0)/(101̄1) surfaces and high-coverage tails carry the caveats discussed in Sec. 3.9. All quantitative segregation energies in the main conclusions are DFT results.

Figure 1: Cu-rich limit. Adsorbate-induced segregation shift as a function of coverage for the nine reaction intermediates on the four fcc facets, in the same format as the Zn-rich screen of Fig. 5. Lines are the 30LT MLIP screen; diamonds are converged DFT (reconstruction-free set, n = 17). Positive suppresses surface Zn, i.e. drives the minority Zn below the surface; the shaded band marks || ≤ 0.1. CO, HCO, and H stay positive across the coverage range on most facets, whereas O, OH, and formate can turn negative, providing the Cu-rich counterpart to the Zn-rich trends.

Figure 9: Zn-rich thermodynamic estimate of the CO-induced segregation reversal boundary as a function of temperature and CO chemical potential, plotted as an effective PCO. Open and stepped facets reverse at lower CO activity than close-packed (0001). Inputs are DFT adsorption and segregation energies with the Campbell–Sellers entropy approximation. The boundaries are semi-quantitative and PCO denotes the CO partial pressure, not the total reactor pressure.

Figure 4: Cu-rich limit. Adsorbate-induced segregation shift versus surface openness, quantified by the surface-atom coordination number (CN; fcc bulk = 12), decreasing from close-packed (111) to the stepped (211) edge. Each marker is one reconstruction-free DFT configuration, coloured by adsorbate; the boxed value is the per-facet mean ||. The close-packed (111) surface is nearly inert (|| = 0.05, all points within the ±0.1 neutral band), whereas the more open (100)/(110)/(211) surfaces carry larger and more scattered shifts (0.13–0.32), so the segregation response is governed by facet geometry as well as adsorbate identity. papers.abstract: Food assembly robots pick ingredients from a pan, and every pick must deliver a target weight. We learn a world model of food picking from 61,773 production picks, labeled automatically by a camera and a scale (self-supervised learning). From the pre-pick heightmap of the pan on a 2.5 mm grid, the commanded pick action, the food and the utensil, the model predicts the post-pick heightmap and the picked mass with uncertainty. We evaluate the mass prediction on 12,294 held-out picks of nine foods. The production controller keeps each pick near its commanded target. The model's root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 10.93 g is 9% lower than that of the commanded target or of a per-food mean. This RMSE is 24% lower than that of the controller's internal mass estimate. Gradient-boosted trees on 20 hand-crafted features have a 0.2 g lower RMSE, but they predict only the mass, not the next state that planning and policy learning need. Using the predicted uncertainty, we decline the most uncertain picks and answer 89.4% of picks with an RMSE of 10.28 g. The prediction barely responds to the commanded volume and depth, because they vary little in closed-loop production. The model also fails without warning at target weights not seen in training. Future directions include action-primitive conditioning and a more general model across foods and utensils. We give recommendations for learning world models from production data.
authors: Inkyu Sa, Gaurav Kuppa, Steve Van der Hoeven, Konstantin Stulov, Rajat Bhageria, Luis Rayas
bullets: Learns from 61,773 automatically labeled production picks using pre-pick heightmaps, actions, food, and utensil information.
Predicts post-pick heightmaps and picked mass with uncertainty; mass is evaluated on 12,294 held-out picks across nine foods.
Achieves 10.93 g RMSE, outperforming commanded-target/per-food-mean baselines and the controller’s internal estimate.
Rejecting the most uncertain picks yields 89.4% coverage with 10.28 g RMSE.
Performance is weakly sensitive to commanded volume/depth and can fail without warning on unseen target weights; broader food and utensil coverage is needed.
papers.selection_reason: Learns an action-conditioned food-picking world model from production data for robot planning and mass prediction.
papers.title: Learning a Food World Model That Predicts the Next State from Production Data
papers.tldr: A production-trained food-picking world model predicts both the next pan state and picked mass, enabling uncertainty-aware planning for assembly robots.

papers.abstract: Can changing which matrices receive 2, 4, or 8 bits improve a small language model without increasing its parameter storage? I compare two parent-selection rules in the same genetic algorithm: a binary-tournament variant and an Alternis-inspired rule. A separate baseline samples repaired random allocations without crossover or mutation. All three use the same MLX affine quantizer, byte ceiling, initialization and candidate allowance within each study. An exploratory study on Qwen3.5-2B evaluates 90 allocations per run. The main study on Qwen3-1.7B evaluates 500 distinct allocations per run over 10 paired seeds. Against uniform four-bit, tournament reduces held-out next-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) by 0.0616 on AG News and 0.0152 on IMDb on average, improving all 10 seeds on each corpus at identical parameter storage. Alternis improves five seeds and ties five on AG News; on IMDb its mean gain is near zero. Random returns uniform four-bit in every seed. The tournament representative answers 156 of 400 ARC-Challenge questions correctly versus 163 for uniform; no accuracy gain is demonstrated on this subset. The result favors this tournament variant for text prediction under the tested protocol, not for compression ratio or task accuracy.
authors: Smit Anand
bullets: The study asks whether assigning 2, 4, and 8 bits to different matrices can improve small language models without increasing parameter storage.
It compares binary-tournament and Alternis-inspired selection within the same genetic algorithm against repaired random allocation, using a shared MLX affine quantizer and byte ceiling.
On Qwen3-1.7B, tournament selection reduced mean NLL by 0.0616 on AG News and 0.0152 on IMDb across 10 paired seeds, improving every seed.
Alternis helped on AG News but showed near-zero mean gain on IMDb; random allocation matched uniform 4-bit in every seed.
The tournament representative scored lower than uniform 4-bit on the tested ARC-Challenge subset, so benefits are limited to the evaluated text-prediction setting.
