papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world action models (WAMs) are increasingly deployed on robots whose cameras and controllers differ from those used to collect their training data. Such deployment introduces two kinds of shifts. Visual shifts, such as a moved camera, change the observed images; actuation shifts, such as a retuned controller, latency or an added payload, change only how commanded actions translate into robot motion. Invisible to the policy, actuation shifts sharply degrade its success, even under domain randomization. In this work, we propose PEA, a test-time calibration method that identifies actuation shifts through active probing before task execution. Specifically, before each episode, the robot executes a short probe that moves one arm axis at a time with known commands, so that gain, delay and drift leave separable traces. A closed-form identifier estimates them from the response, and PEA compensates every subsequent command so that the robot executes the motion the policy intends. The identifier requires no policy training and thus applies to any frozen visuomotor policy. Since visual shifts remain visible to the policy, PEA further adapts the frozen policy with a removable low-rank adapter, addressing coupled visual and actuation shifts. Experiments on LIBERO with a WAM and a VLA show that, without any policy training, the identifier of PEA recovers most of the success lost to actuation shifts and generalizes to shifts unseen during training (e.g., from 61.0% to 89.7% on LIBERO-Spatial with Cosmos-Policy).
authors: Jie Liu, Hui Xie, Qinfeng Feng, Joaquin Vanschoren
bullets: Actuation changes such as controller retuning, latency, payload, or drift can severely reduce robot success without altering camera observations.
Before each episode, the robot performs short, axis-wise probes with known commands to reveal gain, delay, and drift.
A closed-form identifier estimates these effects, and PEA compensates subsequent commands without retraining the policy.
For combined visual and actuation shifts, a removable low-rank adapter adjusts the frozen policy to visible visual changes.
On LIBERO with a WAM and VLA, PEA recovered much of the lost performance and generalized to unseen actuation shifts, including 61.0% to 89.7% on LIBERO-Spatial with Cosmos-Policy.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PEA. Actuation shifts are invisible in images but revealed by motion, so PEA moves before it acts. (1) Probe: before each episode, the robot executes a 30-step probe that pushes one arm axis at a time with zero-sum commands, so that each gain, the delay and a constant drift leave separable traces. (2) Estimate: a closed-form identifier (orange), calibrated once offline and requiring no policy training, reads per-axis gain ĝ, delay d̂ and drift correction b̂ from the response (curves: logged x motion under gain 1.6 and a 1-step delay). (3) Act: every command of the frozen policy (gray) is rescaled and offset, and the arm holds for d̂ steps after each chunk; a lightweight LoRA adapter (blue) on the frozen weights, conditioned on the probe, handles visual shifts such as a moved camera.

Figure 4. Rollouts from the same initial state (Cosmos-Policy; last frame of each episode with the end-effector path, dot: start). Left, coupled camera and gain shift: the identifier alone corrects the gains but not the view, and the adapter completes the task. Middle, 30 N payload: the released model presses the gripper down; the identifier’s drift term lifts it. papers.abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are post-trained and deployed as agents inside a "harness", but standard harness designs accumulate context that the neural network is forced to generalize to, making training for long-horizon tasks expensive and time-consuming. We study an alternative emerging path: training inherently neurosymbolic LM harnesses, which externalize and manage context programmatically to compose existing LM capabilities. We hypothesize that training around these harnesses can offer a better return on compute by enabling compositional generalization, as they can learn to decompose complex problems so that every observation their neural LM receives is locally in-distribution, even when the full task is novel. We find that harnesses like the Recursive Language Model (RLM) learn such decompositions readily under reinforcement learning post-training: (1) we demonstrate that training only on short tasks can generalize to tasks 2-64$\times$ longer while the base neural LM improves less, and (2) training on one domain transfers to novel domains that share latent structure. On messier, complex tasks, we find that we can target individual LLM calls within a harness by generating and training on easier, synthetically generated surrogate environments with fake tool / sub-calls, a technique we call surrogate harness training. From this finding, we train RLM-27B on synthetic data, and show it improves Qwen3.8-27B in the same RLM harness on a hard suite of long-context tasks like CTC-Bench and ExpertLongBench by 26.9% on average while using $\sim$2$\times$ fewer tokens at inference time. Finally, we show that harnesses can compose over these newly learned decompositions using recursive sub-harness calls.
authors: Alex L. Zhang, Souradip Chakraborty, Omar Khattab
bullets: Standard harnesses accumulate context, making long-horizon training costly because the LM must generalize over increasingly complex inputs.
Recursive Language Model (RLM) harnesses trained on short tasks generalize to tasks 2–64× longer, while the base LM improves less.
Decompositions learned in one domain transfer to novel domains with shared latent structure.
Surrogate harness training uses easier synthetic environments to target individual LM calls within complex harnesses.
RLM-27B trained on synthetic data improves Qwen3.8-27B by 26.9% on average on CTC-Bench and ExpertLongBench while using about 2× fewer inference tokens.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Harnesses like Recursive Language Models (RLM) can enable compositional generalization on unseen tasks by shaping prompts for each individual language model call to be indistribution, a property we call locally-in-distribution (LID). “Trajectory-as-a-prompt” harnesses like ReAct rely on a root language model to generalize its policy to a growing trajectory as incontext prompts, frequently leading to erroneous behavior on out-of-distribution (OOD) prompts.

Figure 3: On six environments with controlled context lengths, we train several harnesses and the base Transformer on short tasks, and evaluate on longer variants. We plot their train reward (smoothing window=3) and evaluation reward (smoothing window=11) over training, and include a frontier model, GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026b), using the RLM as a reference. The evaluation reward of the RLM closely follows the trend of the training reward, while for the base Transformer it does not.

Figure 4: We choose three environments with splits that are completely disjoint in domain (e.g. math vs. essay writing questions), but share a similar decomposition structure (e.g. ranking). We train several harnesses and the base Transformer (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507) on one domain, and evaluate on the other, where the RLM generalizes the strongest among other harness abstractions and the base model.

Figure 5: For several harnesses, we train on short tasks and evaluate on their long-context variants. For each setting, we track the nearest three training trajectories by Weighted Jaccard Similarity to each long evaluation trajectory, and average their rewards. We find that context-offloading harnesses learn root-level trajectories that are re-used in longer tasks compared to “trajectory-as-a-prompt”, but training performance does not necessarily transfer for all harnesses, like Pi on OOLONG.

Figure 6: Harnesses that decompose tasks to be locally in-distribution (LID) are composed of individual LLM trajectories. (a) On the left, we describe surrogate harness training, a strategy for training on synthetic environments to target individual LLM behavior within a harness, using a surrogate synthetic environment that transfers behavior to the real environment when tools and sub-calls are real. (b) On the right, we describe how learned decomposition strategies invoked by the harness can be composed to be LID, by enabling the harness to invoke sub-harness calls recursively.

Figure 2: Several popular harness abstractions are useful for controlling what individual LM calls observe. (a) Context offloading keeps the full context in the environment and only allows the model to see slices. (b) Programmatic tool calling treats tools (e.g. sub-agents) as functions in code, which can manipulate intermediate state without the model needing to see it. (c) Sub-agent calling allows the model to explicitly fan out to other LMs, each with their own fresh context. These abstractions can be composed, yielding stronger task generalization effects.

papers.abstract: Scientific information extraction (IE) is a fundamental component of AI for Science, transforming experimental knowledge embedded in scientific literature into structured and traceable data for evidence synthesis, scientific database construction, and data-driven discovery. However, critical experimental details are often distributed across text, tables, figures, captions, and surrounding discussion, making them difficult to recover using conventional text-only extraction. Existing LLM-based and multimodal RAG pipelines typically rely on full-document context or coarse page-level retrieval, introducing substantial irrelevant evidence and high textual and visual token costs. We propose GERF, a Graph-based Evidence Retrieval Framework for token-efficient, schema-guided multimodal scientific IE. GERF represents each article as a heterogeneous evidence graph that connects schema fields, text chunks, figures, and figure-derived content through semantic and structural relations. Using schema fields as retrieval anchors, GERF combines direct semantic retrieval, Random Walk with Restart, and null-aware evidence expansion to construct compact, field-specific multimodal evidence packages. Visual interpretation is applied only to graph-selected figures, avoiding indiscriminate processing of the entire document. We evaluate GERF from two complementary perspectives: evidence retrieval quality and pipeline-level input-token consumption. On the expert-annotated SOFC-Exp corpus, GERF retrieves gold-supported evidence for 94.55% of the evaluated field instances, providing broad field-level evidence coverage for downstream extraction. In the token comparison, GERF reduces average input-token usage by 73.40% relative to full-context processing and uses fewer tokens than the evaluated page-level pipelines.
authors: Yiyu Qian (Cornell University), Xing Wu (Shanghai University)
bullets: Targets experimental details distributed across text, tables, figures, captions, and discussion—beyond the reach of text-only extraction.
Builds a heterogeneous graph linking schema fields, text chunks, figures, and figure-derived content.
Combines semantic retrieval, Random Walk with Restart, and null-aware evidence expansion to assemble multimodal evidence packages.
Applies visual interpretation only to graph-selected figures rather than the entire document.
On the SOFC-Exp corpus, retrieves gold-supported evidence for 94.55% of evaluated field instances and reduces average input tokens by 73.40% versus full-context processing.

papers.abstract: Contribution: This study has shown that a shared prompt-refinement procedure, guided by distinct affective and cognitive feedback signals, can improve held-out reference agreement and multi-label classification while reducing affective-generation variability without executor parameter updates. Background: Industry 4.0 has increased demand for personalized technical education across interconnected computing and engineering domains, while prompt sensitivity and generation variability have complicated dependable interpretation of instructional dialogue and learning outcomes. Research Questions: The study has examined whether task-specific feedback can improve affective-reference agreement, generation consistency, and cognitive classification without updating executor parameters. Methodology: A secondary language model has revised executor prompts using executor-output discrepancies against model-generated affective references for four dialogues and annotated Bloom labels for 70 learning outcomes; separate sets of 100 EduTalk conversations and 1,000 outcomes have supported held-out comparisons. Small refinement sets, unvalidated affective references, and absent learner-outcome measures have constrained interpretation. Findings: Affective mean absolute error has decreased from 0.742 to 0.702 and mean generation standard deviation from 0.307 to 0.238, while Bloom micro-F1 has increased from 0.687 to 0.893 and exact-match subset accuracy from 0.418 to 0.636. These findings have supported prompt refinement as a candidate approach for developing adaptive technical instruction, while its effects on workforce learning remain to be established.
authors: Josh Dean, Karan Patel, Gaurangi Raul, Yu-Zheng Lin, Jesus Pacheco, Sicong Shao, Shalaka Satam, Soheil Salehi, Pratik Satam
bullets: Targets dependable interpretation of educational dialogue amid prompt sensitivity and generation variability.
Uses a secondary language model to revise executor prompts from affective-reference discrepancies and Bloom-label feedback.
Held-out results showed lower affective error and variability, alongside higher Bloom micro-F1 and exact-match accuracy.
The study used small refinement sets and unvalidated affective references, with no direct learner-outcome measures.
Effects on workforce learning and adaptive instruction remain unestablished.

papers.abstract: Incremental Vision-Language Object Detection (IVLOD) empowers pre-trained open-vocabulary detectors to continuously learn new visual concepts from sequential tasks without forgetting foundational knowledge. However, existing methods predominantly rely on oracle task identities during inference, severely limiting their open-world practicality. In this paper, we formalize Task-Agnostic IVLOD (TA-IVLOD), a more realistic setting where such priors are unavailable, requiring the model to simultaneously recognize classes from all learned tasks. This unconstrained setting exposes severe performance degradation due to cross-task semantic interference and parameter conflicts. To tackle these challenges, we propose TADA, a novel modular framework. Specifically, TADA introduces Stochastic Prompt Augmentation to mitigate semantic interference via training-time noise injection, and Test-Time Distribution-Aware Fusion to dynamically weight class-specific LoRA experts, effectively resolving parameter conflicts. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms baselines in standard IVLOD and yields substantial improvements in the rigorous TA-IVLOD setting on the ODinW-13 benchmark, while effectively preserving zero-shot generalization on the MS COCO dataset. The code is available at https://github.com/yonghanjiang/TADA.
authors: Yonghan Jiang, Zhengyuan Xie, Wenchu Liu, Linlan Huang, Fei Yang, Xialei Liu
bullets: Introduces Task-Agnostic Incremental Vision-Language Object Detection (TA-IVLOD), where the model must recognize concepts from all learned tasks without oracle task labels.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have shown strong potential for learning complex robotic behaviors from demonstrations. However, learning safe behavior directly from data requires extensive coverage of safety-critical situations, which is often impractical in real-world settings. Test-time safety filters provide an alternative by correcting unsafe actions during deployment, but these interventions can drive the robot into states poorly covered by the training data, thereby degrading task performance. We introduce InteR-VLA, an intervention-robust framework for VLAs that leverages diverse task-completing demonstrations to broaden task-relevant state coverage and maintain competence under safety interventions. By better aligning the training distribution with safety-filtered deployment under the same data budget, our approach mitigates intervention-induced distribution shift while preserving task performance. Real-world experiments across in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings show that InteR-VLA maintains safety, increases Safe Success Rate up to 90% from 0% for nominal policies, and consistently outperforms nominal-data training on both evaluated VLAs.
authors: Tzu-Yuan Huang, Shao-Hsuan Chang, Dai-Jie Wu, Ralf R\"omer, Yung-Hui Li, Stefan Sosnowski, Angela P. Schoellig, Kenneth Marino, Sandra Hirche

Real-world experiments cover in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings across two evaluated VLAs.

papers.abstract: Video verifiers judge whether a candidate answer or trajectory agrees with a video, and are themselves chosen by a score. We show that this score depends on two choices in the test, the type of negative and the judgment interface, strongly enough to reverse conclusions about what a model can do and which verifier to deploy. We separate the two with controlled constructions that have exact truth conditions: endpoint-matched negatives, wrong only in their internal states, and a truth-switch test, in which the same two candidates swap correctness between two videos. Under direct judgment, where the verdict is read from answer scores, models that reject a visibly wrong start fall to near chance against endpoint-matched negatives. When the frames disclose each event, writing out reasoning before the answer lifts three of four models from under 10% to 70-100% on the truth-switch test, and staged inputs trace the direct failure to one step, composing events into states. But when the event must first be found, on human-validated natural video, the same change brings no significant gain under a protocol common to all models and can lower accuracy if one candidate denies that the event occurs. The negative type also changes which verifier is selected: one chosen on event-denial negatives is 8.9 points less accurate against negatives that keep the event and change a detail, the errors a generator mostly makes, and recovers about half as much accuracy when it reranks that generator's answers. A verifier should be evaluated on the errors it will face, and neither a low direct score nor a gain from reasoning should be read as a property of the model alone.
authors: Charles Weng, Zixi Huang
bullets: Endpoint-matched negatives expose failures in composing event-level evidence into internal states, even when the start appears visibly wrong.
Writing reasoning before answering raises performance substantially when all events are disclosed, but not when the event must first be found in natural video.
Verifier rankings change with the negative examples used for evaluation; event-denial negatives may not reflect generator-like detail errors.
Verifier evaluation should match the errors it will encounter in deployment.
Low direct scores and reasoning gains should not be interpreted as intrinsic model properties without controlling the test protocol.

papers.abstract: Beckmann Transport Models (BTM) learn one-step generative maps end-to-end from data, without a teacher, a distillation stage, or pretrained features. We introduce Scalable Beckmann Maps (SBM), which bring to BTM the two ingredients behind the quality of modern multistep generators: classifier-free guidance (CFG) and a training recipe that scales, while keeping sampling at a single network evaluation. CFG combines conditional and unconditional velocity or score predictions, which a Beckmann map does not have. Our guidance rests on one observation: the BTM current is a positive multiple of an autonomous denoising field, to which CFG applies as it does to a velocity. With exact denoisers this gives guided BTM. In practice we substitute the map's own conditional and null predictions for the denoisers, which requires no additional network and introduces a bias that we characterize. We show that the guided update is consistent with a guided conservation equation, and that guidance can move the boundaries between basins, sending more noise to the modes a condition favors. Trained from scratch in the latent of a representation autoencoder, SBM reaches a one-step FID of 1.6 on ImageNet 256x256 without a teacher or a feature loss, outperforming the Improved-MeanFlow baseline with 3.2x fewer FLOPs. In text-to-image generation it reaches a GenEval score of 0.86 with one network evaluation. As a world model, where we train without guidance, the recipe alone outperforms DriftWorld on all five metrics of two robot-manipulation benchmarks, with 1.9-2.8x less training compute and no pretrained auxiliary feature encoder.
authors: Ulrik Unneberg, Shiyi Wang, Lee Cheuk-Kit, Felix Berg, Boris Kozinsky, Yilun Du, Michael S. Albergo, Eric Vanden-Eijnden
bullets: Extends Beckmann Transport Models with guidance by applying classifier-free guidance to their autonomous denoising field.
Uses the model’s conditional and null predictions, requiring no additional network, while characterizing the resulting bias.
Provides a guided conservation-equation interpretation in which guidance shifts basin boundaries toward condition-favored modes.
Achieves 1.6 one-step FID on ImageNet 256×256 and a 0.86 GenEval score for text-to-image generation.
Also improves world-model performance across five metrics on two robot-manipulation benchmarks with lower training compute.

Figure 2 Flow matching, BTM and Equilibrium Matching on the same two-dimensional problem: noise is transported to five data points, whose weights are given in the legend. (a) Flow matching learns a time-dependent velocity; arrows show the field at t = 0.5. Because the velocity changes over time, trajectories can bend sharply and even reverse direction, and this curvature makes the ODE hard to integrate in few steps. (b) BTM assumes an autonomous flow. Its flow lines are fixed and never cross, the endpoint map is constant along each of them, and the separatrices of the map (solid) divide the plane into one basin per data point, each receiving source mass equal to that point’s weight. (c) Equilibrium Matching (Wang and Du, 2025) also learns a time-invariant field, whose magnitude is set by a schedule ct, here ct = (1− t)0.8; the shaded bands are a potential reconstructed from the current, ∆ϕ = ∇ · J . A nonconstant schedule ct can bias the endpoint distribution by shifting the basin boundaries: the separatrices of its map (solid) depart from those of BTM (dotted), and the basins of the two lower modes shrink, so these modes receive too little mass. At ct = 1 the autonomous field is identical to that of BTM.

papers.abstract: Standard autoregressive large language models attend to the growing history of generated tokens, making the key-value (KV) cache a central memory and throughput bottleneck in long-chain reasoning and multi-branch sampling. Yet an important class of reasoning problems is naturally first-order Markovian: the next step depends on a sufficient representation of the current state, rather than on the raw sequence of all earlier steps. We develop a unified design paradigm for Markovian-reasoning specialized large language models. At the cache level, the Markovian state interface transforms history-dependent KV storage into constant-size state transfer with respect to the number of reasoning steps. At the learning level, we reformulate long-chain prediction as independently trainable one-step transition objectives, with explicit state bottlenecks, distillation, invariance, and drift-consistency losses. At the architectural level, we introduce a dual-loop Transformer: an outer loop advances the reasoning state, while an inner recurrent-depth loop allocates adaptive computation to each transition through shared weights and explicit memory tokens or recurrent matrix states. We connect this architecture to a three-region cache, step-relative positions, truncated backpropagation, branch-aware checkpoints, and a transition-centric evaluation protocol. The organizing principle is simple: the optimal reasoning system need not remember everything; it must carry forward exactly what the future needs. This principle opens a path toward specialized reasoning engines whose memory footprint is decoupled from reasoning-chain length.
authors: Haibin Tong, Liangliang Xin, Yamei Zhu, Jiang Yu
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory and throughput bottlenecks in long-chain reasoning and multi-branch sampling.
Uses explicit state bottlenecks and independently trainable one-step transition objectives with distillation, invariance, and drift-consistency losses.
Introduces a dual-loop Transformer: an outer loop advances states, while an inner recurrent loop adaptively computes each transition with shared weights.
Integrates three-region caching, step-relative positions, truncated backpropagation, branch-aware checkpoints, and transition-centric evaluation.
Scope is reasoning tasks where the next step depends on a sufficient Markovian state rather than the full history.

The outer loop advances the reduced state (qt,Mt) across reasoning steps and releases step-local KV, while the inner loop repeatedly applies a shared Transformer core for Rt computation iterations. The transition training objectives shape the same shared core to support state evolution and compact cross-step memory.

Figure 1: Structural KV-cache compression for a Markovian reasoning chain. Conventional autoregressive attention retains the entire sequence of previous reasoning steps. In contrast, a Markovian state-rolling interface retains the fixed context Q, the latest sufficient state zt, and the bounded current-step KV workspace, which is released after each transition. With a fixed-size sufficient-state interface and bounded step length, cross-step memory does not grow with the number of completed steps k.

papers.title: Specialized Large Language Models for Markovian Reasoning: Structural Cache Compression, Transition Pretraining, and Dual-Loop Transformers
papers.tldr: A specialized LLM design treats Markovian reasoning as state transitions, reducing KV-cache growth from sequence-dependent storage to constant-size state transfer.

papers.abstract: In dynamic scenes---football matches, traffic streams, surgery, or assembly---actions unfold at fundamentally different time scales: in football, a kick happens in milliseconds, a possession lasts seconds, and complex events such as a successful pass followed by a goal combine multiple atomic actions over extended durations. Models trained solely on visual data struggle to learn effectively across different time scales, lacking a principled way of reasoning across fine-grained instants and broader intervals. Neither point-wise nor purely interval semantics suffices: the former fragments events into frame-level snapshots lacking overall event identification; the latter treats intervals as atomic truth-values, ignoring state trajectories. We introduce Temporal Logic Tensor Networks (tLTN), a differentiable neuro-symbolic framework addressing this duality via a formal, multi-sorted logic where events and states are structurally interdependent. Extending Interval Logic Tensor Networks (ILTN), tLTN grounds state predicates as fuzzy truth-value paths over time points, while events are first-class entities with learnable trapezoidal fuzzy durations and differentiable Allen-style relations. A compositional semantics fuses static, event-structural, and state-dynamic satisfaction into a single differentiable LTN grounding. Crucially, the modalities constrain each other bidirectionally: the interval layer dictates where point-wise constraints (e.g., Until, Since) are evaluated, restricting them to event-defined spans; conversely, the point-wise layer validates interval relations, rejecting them if underlying state dynamics contradict the relation. Through controlled synthetic examples, we show when single-modality learning fails and how this localization reduces frame-level computational cost on long traces.
authors: Edjard Mota, Artur d'Avila Garcez, Maria Azevedo, Odalisio Neto
bullets: Addresses the limits of frame-level and interval-only temporal semantics in dynamic scenes.
Represents states as fuzzy truth-value paths and events as learnable trapezoidal fuzzy durations.
Uses differentiable Allen-style relations and compositional logic to integrate static, structural, and dynamic constraints.
Constrains point-wise reasoning to event-defined spans while using state dynamics to validate interval relations.
Synthetic examples show failures of single-modality learning and reduced frame-level computation on long traces.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The semantic bridge: the solid curve is a state trajectory (point-wise modality). The dashed trapezoids are fuzzy event extents (interval modality). At t = 4.5, the interval for event B (in green) reaches full membership while the underlying state trajectory is near its minimum, a configuration that interval-only semantics cannot express, since it evaluates properties over intervals as atomic truth values, and that point-wise semantics alone cannot localize, since it has no representation of the interval in which the state’s dip in truth value occurs. Between events B and C (in blue), point-wise constraint evaluation is localized to the event spans rather than the full trace, allowing the system to stop reasoning about what should persist at each time step in the absence of an action.

papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) can transfer agile robot skills from simulation to the real world, but closing the sim-to-real gap by domain randomization requires expert physics knowledge, and simulator calibration from real data typically targets a few hand-picked parameters. Even then, simulators miss real-world effects, and environments reconstructed from onboard perception inherit sensing errors that limit policy improvement. We propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), which uses conditional flow matching to calibrate simulator physical parameters and residual fidelity domains online during deployment. Residual fidelity captures sim-to-real dynamics discrepancies and perception-induced environment uncertainty. NFC operates in a latent space so that realistic environments can be sampled from the inferred posterior for real-to-sim policy fine-tuning. The framework is informative: the pretrained policy is fine-tuned only when an anomaly is detected, sequential NFC seeds its proposal from the simulation-pretrained estimator, and a hallucination policy modulates posterior uncertainty following optimism in the face of uncertainty. NFC attains the most accurate posteriors among established simulation-based inference methods on five robots with up to 39 physical parameters and a 128x128 residual terrain. On a wheeled robot with a broken wheel axle deployed on snow, mud, and wet grass, NFC raises success on rough terrain from 26% to 70% and reduces orientation jerk by 88%. Code and videos will be released upon publication.
authors: Youwei Yu, Lantao Liu
bullets: Addresses sim-to-real gaps caused by imperfect physics, perception errors, and unmodeled dynamics.
Uses conditional flow matching to infer physical parameters and residual fidelity domains in a latent space.
Samples realistic environments from the inferred posterior for real-to-sim policy fine-tuning.
Triggers adaptation only after detected anomalies, with sequential proposals and uncertainty-modulated exploration.
Across five robots, it achieves accurate posterior inference; on a damaged wheeled robot, rough-terrain success increases from 26% to 70% and orientation jerk decreases by 88%.

papers.abstract: A policy that transfers from simulation to a lab robot often fails in the field. Calibrating a simulator from real-world data typically targets only a few hand-picked parameters, and even calibrated simulators fail to capture unmodeled dynamics, while environments reconstructed via onboard perception inherit sensing noise and artifacts. We propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), a framework based on conditional flow matching that infers online, directly from a robot's execution data, both simulator physical parameters and residual fidelity - the remaining dynamics discrepancy and the gap between perceived and true environment geometry. A simulation-trained anomaly detector determines when recalibration or fine-tuning is required using onboard sensory signals alone, while an exploration policy actively modulates posterior uncertainty using optimism in the face of uncertainty. Across five robot platforms with up to 39 calibrated parameters and a 128x128 residual terrain map, NFC achieves the most accurate posterior distributions compared to established simulation-based inference baselines. In physical outdoor experiments with a wheeled robot suffering an axle failure across snow, mud, and wet grass, NFC increases rough-terrain navigation success from 26% to 70% while reducing orientation jerk by 88%.

In outdoor tests with an axle failure, rough-terrain success rose from 26% to 70% and orientation jerk fell by 88%.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for embodied AI, yet their high inference latency and memory footprint remain major barriers to edge deployment. Existing training-free acceleration techniques, such as visual token pruning and action caching, typically rely on static resource allocation. This mismatch with dynamic robotic interactions not only degrades control performance but also causes severe hardware inefficiencies, including fragmented KV-cache layouts and wasted compute on non-critical regions. To address this, we propose FlowPAC, a locality-aware framework that leverages task-aware optical flow as a shared physical signal to jointly optimize visual and action computation. Specifically, we introduce Direction-Aware Trajectory Propagation (DATP) and Locality-Aware Contiguous Token Selection (LACT) to jointly handle visual token dynamics and enforce spatial locality, reducing memory fragmentation and enabling efficient KV-cache compression. This is complemented by Flow-Conditioned Action-Block Refresh (FCAR) for adaptive action computation based on motion dynamics. Extensive closed-loop evaluations on LIBERO demonstrate that FlowPAC achieves a 2.13$\times$ end-to-end speedup over the dense baseline while essentially maintaining the success rate with 30% visual-token retention. These results validate that aligning computation allocation with both physical dynamics and hardware constraints is essential for efficient VLA deployment on edge systems.
authors: Jintao Cheng, Yipu Zhang, Haozhe Wang, Lin Jiang, Jiang Xu, Wei Zhang
bullets: Targets high latency and memory use that hinder VLA deployment on edge devices.
Combines trajectory-aware token propagation, contiguous spatial token selection, and flow-conditioned action-block refresh.
Aligns computation with both scene motion and hardware locality to reduce wasted compute and KV-cache fragmentation.
Closed-loop LIBERO evaluations report a 2.13× end-to-end speedup over dense inference with 30% visual-token retention and essentially unchanged success rate.

papers.abstract: Autoresearch agents, which autonomously design, run, and refine experiments, are accelerating scientific progress, particularly in AI research. However, existing agents rely on harnesses that combine multiple mechanisms, making it difficult to determine how individual components contribute to performance. We systematically study harness design for long-horizon, self-evolving autoresearch agents along two dimensions: context management, which determines what an agent retains from its past attempts, and skill management, which governs how it stores and reuses lessons from those attempts. Across MLE-Bench and KernelBench with gpt-oss-120b, gpt-6-luna, and gpt-6-sol, we isolate the effects of individual harness design choices by evaluating each against a recency-truncation baseline within a shared agent framework. For context management, we find that preserving individually accessible records of past attempts is more effective than maintaining a rolling summary, with context folding performing best across all six settings and improving upon the baseline by up to 19.2%. For skill management, selectively discarding persistently unused lessons is more effective on average than consolidating them or promoting them to standing rules. Building on these findings, we combine context folding and skill deletion in MLEvolver, which achieves a 72.7% medal rate on MLE-Bench Lite and a 94% $\mathrm{fast}_1$ score on KernelBench Level 3, substantially outperforming AIDE and OpenEvolve under the same inference budget. Overall, our study distills design principles for preserving experimental history and curating reusable lessons in autoresearch harnesses, paving the way for agents that turn accumulated experience into sustained progress.
authors: Kelvin Kiu-Wai Tam, Newt Hue-Nam K. Nguyen, Tianshi Zheng, Yunxiang Mo, Weihan Li, Zhongwei Xie, Chiu Yeung Tang, Jui-Yu Ho, Yangqiu Song, Ginny Y. Wong, Simon See

papers.abstract: Surgical triplet recognition requires identifying which instrument performs which action on which anatomical target, and following these interactions as they unfold over time. The task is challenging because several triplets can occur at once, their components span very different durations, and the evidence for an interaction is rarely complete in a single frame. We introduce STRIDE, a post-hoc temporal readout that adds temporal context to any trained recogniser. It averages the recogniser's features and logits over a few fixed temporal windows and combines them with the current frame through ridge regression, solved in closed form on a CPU. Applied as a plug-and-play readout to nine existing methods, STRIDE improves $AP_{IVT}$ in 24 of 27 method-dataset pairs, by up to 7.4 points. Moreover, we propose a simple pipeline consisting of an adapted foundation vision encoder with a linear classifier and STRIDE. Across thirteen encoders, STRIDE improves 37 of 39 encoder-dataset pairs by up to 7.2 points. STRIDE reduces false alarms by 41%, at the cost of a slower response at interaction boundaries. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
authors: Lemar Abdi, Amaan Valiuddin, Fida Mohammad Thoker, Karen Sanchez, Bernard Ghanem, Fons van der Sommen

With a foundation vision encoder and linear classifier, improves 37 of 39 encoder–dataset pairs by up to 7.2 points.
Reduces false alarms by 41%, but responds more slowly at interaction boundaries.

papers.abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) have expanded their role in high-value productivity tasks, including financial analysis and modeling, while enabling models to play an increasingly active role in their own improvement. This motivates two complementary lines of inquiry: can financial modeling capabilities provide a foundation for model self-evolution, and can self-evolution, in turn, advance financial capabilities? We introduce FinEvo, a self-evolution framework that integrates autonomous experience construction with financial capability improvement. FinEvo prepares financial models, iteratively evolves challenges through self-play, and learns from the resulting interactions using executable rewards, relying on the same model throughout. An end-to-end execution with Qwen3.6-27B shows that solving feedback supports both increasing reasoning demands and identifying specification issues that executable checks can miss. Learning from these experiences raises whole-task success from 22.73 to 29.09 on held-out within-source tasks and from 13.13 to 19.19 on SpreadsheetBench 2 Financial. Comparable gains across task sources and evaluation settings, together with improvement on a task category absent from training, suggest that FinEvo strengthens underlying financial modeling capabilities shared across tasks. These findings support self-evolution as a path toward broader financial competence, advancing the empirical exploration of recursive self-improvement (RSI) in professional domains. Code is available at https://github.com/pcj-sudo/FinEvo.
authors: Chengjun Pan, Shichun Liu, Zekai Zhou, Shihan Dou, Jiahang Lin, Chengsong Huang, Dingwei Zhu, Tao Gui

papers.abstract: Memory benchmarks built on question answering tell an agent which fact to recall. Workplace requests often leave that need implicit: to post an update in the team's channel, an agent must work out which channel from earlier interactions and use it in a tool call. We evaluate Memanto, a memory agent that ranks memories with an information-theoretic relevance score, on DolphinBench, which tests memory through 600 simulated workplace tasks, each validated as requiring memory. Running in the Hermes agent harness with GPT-6-Luna and at most 6 iterations per conversation, Memanto completes 503 tasks (83.83%). The strongest configuration reported by the benchmark's authors, Mem0 with GPT-5.6-Luna and up to 60 iterations, completes 424 (70.67%). Memanto's run also has the lowest total cost ($10.86, against $61.48 for the cheapest reported run) and the shortest median task latency (15.32s). Grading uses the benchmark's own judge, but the agent model differs, so these results compare complete systems. The memory system affects both whether an agent completes such tasks and what completion costs.
authors: Suleman Khan, Rasa Rahnema, Tara Khani, Majid Fekri, Fattane Zarrinkalam
bullets: DolphinBench evaluates implicit memory use in 600 simulated workplace tasks requiring agents to infer facts for tool calls.
Memanto ranks memories using an information-theoretic relevance score.
In the Hermes harness with GPT-6-Luna and up to 6 iterations, it completes 503 tasks.
The benchmark authors’ strongest reported Mem0 configuration completes 424 tasks (70.67%), but uses a different agent model and iteration limit.
Memanto costs $10.86 in total and has a 15.32-second median latency; results use the benchmark’s own judge.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) represent videos as thousands of visual tokens, creating a large key-value cache whose memory grows with video length. At the same time, small VLMs that fit on limited hardware understand video far worse than large models. Existing compression methods shorten visual tokens into a brief prompt to save memory, yet the small model still processes them through fixed weights and cannot close this capability gap. To address both challenges, we introduce Video-as-Weights (VaW), which compiles a video once without seeing any question into the parametric and token memory of a frozen interpreter VLM. Specifically, a compiler VLM watches the video, and a single weight decoder jointly generates the interpreter's LoRA weights and optional prefix tokens from every compiler layer, enabling both same-model compilation and strong-to-weak transfer across model sizes and depths. Across six video QA benchmarks, a 0.8B interpreter beats full in-context reading by 1.7 points when compiled by itself and by 4.3 points with a 9B compiler, reducing context from up to 8,192 visual tokens to 64 prefix tokens while using 5.5x less memory than the video's key-value cache. Generated weights add 3.9 points over token compression alone, and all-layer decoding outperforms layer-wise generation by 2.9 points. Mechanistic analysis shows that with prefix tokens, the weights mainly alter attention queries and MLP down projections to guide retrieval and store a baseline summary, whereas without tokens, they shift to attention output projections to write video content directly into the residual stream.
authors: Wentao Zhang, Ian Miao, Chen Qu, Bill Bi, Donna Schut, Yuntian Deng, Yale Song
bullets: Addresses video VLMs’ growing key-value memory and the capability gap of small models.
A compiler VLM processes the video once and a decoder generates interpreter LoRA weights plus optional prefix tokens, without seeing questions.
Across six video QA benchmarks, a 0.8B interpreter improved over full in-context reading by 1.7 points alone and 4.3 points with a 9B compiler.
Compression reduces up to 8,192 visual tokens to 64 prefix tokens and uses 5.5× less memory than the video’s key-value cache.
Generated weights add 3.9 points over token compression alone; their roles differ depending on whether prefix tokens are used.

papers.selection_reason: Compiles video into LoRA weights and prefix tokens for a frozen VLM, combining video understanding, memory efficiency, and inference-time adaptation.
papers.title: Video-as-Weights: Compiling a Video Once into Parametric and Token Memory
papers.tldr: Video-as-Weights compiles a video into LoRA weights and a few prefix tokens, enabling small VLMs to answer questions with far less memory while benefiting from larger models.

papers.abstract: Multimodal foundation models can play video games well when the game waits for them, but often fail when it keeps running. We find that much of this gap lies in the harness, which decides what the model sees, what it remembers, and how its outputs become actions over time. Existing harnesses such as VISTA improve the first two, yet turn each model call into at most one action, so the agent acts only as often as its model thinks. We introduce AutoPILOT, which changes the third: in each model call, the model can send a primitive action, start an open-loop macro, or write a closed-loop controller that keeps playing from the screen without further model calls until it hands control back. To evaluate agents in real-time games, we build AFK-Bench, 120 diverse browser games grouped by how they respond to inaction and playable in real time or with the clock paused. With GPT-6.1 Sol under the same budgets, AutoPILOT reaches 68.6% real-time success against 38.3% for VISTA, and on GameWorld it keeps 80.0% in real time while VISTA drops from 84.1% to 42.9%. Its gains hold across models, and it reaches VISTA's final success rate at a fifth of its API cost. Our results suggest that how a harness turns model outputs into actions over time is a central yet underexplored part of agent design, and we hope AutoPILOT and AFK-Bench will serve as a foundation for agents in a world that does not wait.
authors: Mark Zhao, Pengcheng Wang, Rui Yang, Jiarui Yao, Xirui Jiang, Yuxi Chen, Bingxuan Li, Hanyang Chen, Ke Yang, Manling Li, Tong Zhang, Huan Zhang

Results across models suggest that converting model outputs into temporally extended actions is a central part of agent design.

papers.selection_reason: Presents AutoPILOT, a visual agent harness that enables models to generate actions, open-loop macros, and closed-loop controllers within a single call, significantly improving real-time performance in games.
papers.title: AutoPILOT: A Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay
papers.tldr: AutoPILOT improves multimodal game-playing agents in real-time settings by letting each model call produce sustained, screen-based controllers rather than only one action.

papers.abstract: Coding agents can translate 3D measurements into CAD geometry, but reconstructing engineering models for the built environment demands semantic interpretation and consistent construction constraints beyond surface fitting. We formulate scene-level Scan-to-BIM (Building Information Modeling) as an agentic 3D coding task and introduce S2Bench, comprising public and proprietary scans of 128 real-world scenes across five domains, paired with expert-curated reference models spanning diverse spatial scales. A shared framework lets agents measure scans in Python, build class-labeled components in a live CAD/BIM kernel, and iteratively refine their code. We also propose parallel asynchronous collaboration, where a lead delegates versioned tasks, continues modeling while workers execute, and integrates revision-bound proposals. Evaluating five agents and a collaborative team across 1,028 reconstructions shows that scan-to-model residuals directly guide geometric repair, whereas inferring semantic classes and construction relations requires joint geometric, visual, and engineering reasoning that agents struggle to ground and verify. Consequently, the leading agent fits scan geometry closely ($96\%$ coverage within $5\,\text{cm}$) yet reaches only $63\%$ mIoU, and no agent passes all engineering checks on more than $38\%$ of scenes. Coverage and engineering conformance drop with scene scale, whereas running a smaller model as a team improves all three axes with greater coverage gains on larger scenes. The project page is available at https://tumcms.github.io/S2Bench.github.io/
authors: Changyu Du, Stavros Nousias, Syed Salman Ahmed, Kai Dietmair, Mohammad Alrabab'h, Andr\'e Borrmann
bullets: Introduces 1,028 reconstructions across 128 real-world scenes, five domains, and varied spatial scales, using expert-curated BIM references.
Agents measure scans with Python, create labeled components in a live CAD/BIM kernel, and iteratively refine reconstruction code.
Parallel asynchronous collaboration enables a lead agent to delegate, model concurrently, and integrate versioned worker proposals.
The leading agent achieves 96% scan coverage within 5 cm but only 63% semantic mIoU; no agent passes all engineering checks on over 38% of scenes.
Larger scenes reduce coverage and engineering conformance, while smaller-model teams improve performance, especially on larger scenes.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces S2Bench, a benchmark for agentic 3D reconstruction in the built environment, evaluating coding agents on scan-to-BIM tasks.
papers.title: From Point Clouds to Engineering Models: Benchmarking Agentic 3D Reconstruction in the Built Environment

papers.abstract: Query-based 4D reconstruction models such as D4RT encode a video once into a global scene representation and obtain outputs by decoding independent point queries. However, inference is often influenced by dense outputs and long videos. Although D4RT separates encoding from decoding, a dense output still requires one decoder query for every pixel of every frame, and a long video is still encoded as many overlapping segments. In this work, we analyze the inference cost of D4RT and show that a large part of it is redundant. In particular, we find that the later decoder blocks attend to a small set of tokens shared by all queries. Based on these findings, we propose FastD4RT, a training-free framework that accelerates D4RT. By exploiting the smoothness of the outputs over time and across pixels, FastD4RT encodes and decodes only at sparse anchors and recovers the remaining outputs via interpolation. It decodes the remaining queries against a shared token set selected once per segment. We further characterize the errors introduced by both components. Experimental results show that FastD4RT accelerates D4RT by about 5 times on average across all its tasks with competitive accuracy, and further improves accuracy on long videos. Our code is available at https://github.com/Lycheemeng/fastd4rt.
authors: Meng Bi, Yili Jin, Kaiyuan Hu, Xize Duan, Jiaxin Huang, Hong Huang, Xue Liu
bullets: Targets redundant computation from dense pixel-frame queries and overlapping long-video segments in D4RT.
Uses sparse spatial-temporal anchors and interpolation to recover remaining outputs.
Decodes queries against a shared token set selected once per video segment.
Analyzes the errors introduced by sparse interpolation and shared-token decoding.
Reports competitive accuracy across D4RT tasks and improved accuracy on long videos.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview of FastD4RT. Given a video, FastD4RT encodes only sparse anchor frames, so that a long video is split into fewer segments. For each segment, a small set of calibration queries selects a shared token set once. Each task then issues queries only at sparse anchors, which attend to all tokens in the early decoder blocks and only to the shared tokens in the later blocks. Finally, the remaining outputs are recovered by interpolation, and adjacent segments are aligned.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free acceleration via sparse anchor decoding and shared token selection is a token-level efficiency method.
papers.title: FastD4RT: Training-Free Acceleration of Dynamic 4D Reconstruction and Tracking
papers.tldr: FastD4RT speeds up D4RT about 5× without retraining by exploiting temporal and spatial smoothness plus shared decoder tokens.

papers.abstract: Accurate road surface reconstruction is essential for autonomous-driving mapping and simulation, but existing methods trade reconstruction quality for cross-scene inference. Optimization-based methods recover detailed surfaces through costly per-scene optimization, while feed-forward methods lack road-specific constraints and often produce large elevation errors. We propose \textbf{BReD}, a feed-forward framework for reconstructing road elevation, appearance, and semantics from calibrated six-camera sequences. BReD first estimates coarse elevation through LiDAR-supervised depth learning and BEV lifting, using only cameras at inference. A lightweight BEV residual diffusion model then conditions elevation refinement on a camera-derived depth--elevation discrepancy and elevation-aware image features. Diffusion-indexed perturbations expose the model to different discrepancy corruption levels during training, while inference performs one deterministic refinement from the clean discrepancy. The refined elevations are temporally aggregated to anchor road-aligned Gaussians, whose attributes are predicted by a geometry-prior-guided decoder without test-time optimization. On four held-out nuScenes scenes, BReD achieves 7.34 cm elevation RMSE and 90.92\% semantic mIoU, compared with 14.43 cm for RoGS without test-time LiDAR and 8.88 cm for its test-time-LiDAR-assisted variant; both RoGS variants require per-scene optimization.
authors: Baizhi Wang
bullets: Targets the trade-off between high-quality optimization-based reconstruction and weak cross-scene generalization in feed-forward methods.
Estimates coarse road elevation via LiDAR-supervised depth learning and BEV lifting, using only calibrated six-camera sequences at inference.
Refines elevation with a lightweight BEV residual diffusion model conditioned on depth–elevation discrepancies and elevation-aware image features.
Aggregates refined elevations into road-aligned Gaussians and predicts their attributes with a geometry-prior-guided decoder.
On four held-out nuScenes scenes, achieves 7.34 cm elevation RMSE and 90.92% semantic mIoU, without test-time optimization or LiDAR.

figures.caption: Figure 1. BReD overview. (a) BEVDepth* predicts frame-wise coarse elevation using LiDAR depth supervision during training and camera-predicted depth at inference. (b) ReD* combines depth–elevation discrepancy, BEV context, and elevation-aware image features for single-step residual denoising. (c) Refined elevations are temporally aggregated, and FFGS predicts road-Gaussian attributes without test-time optimization. (d) Reconstructed RGB, semantics, and elevation.

Figure 4. Surround-view elevation errors. Results for (a) BReD, (b) RoMe, (c) RoGS w/o LiDAR, and (d) RoGS w/ LiDAR. Colors show signed vertical errors; statistics report RMSE and valid counts in 5m distance bins.
Figure 6. Progressive elevation evolution. Top: Holistic elevation maps. Bottom: Zoomed-in 12m × 12m ROI. Visually, the surface transitions from zcoarse to zrefined, and ultimately to zfinal.

Figure 2. BEV Residual Diffusion. During training, the cameraderived discrepancy x0 is retained at t = 0 or perturbed at t > 0. A timestep-conditioned ConvGRU predicts a bounded elevation update. Inference uses the clean t = 0 state in one denoising step.
Figure 7. Elevation RMSE versus camera-to-observation XY distance. (a) Stage-wise progression showing error reduction from zcoarse to refined stages. (b) Comparison against state-of-theart baselines.

Figure 3. Extraction of the Multi-Scale Elevation Embedding (fms). Centered around zcoarse, vertical elevation candidates with offsets [−10,−6,−2,+2,+6,+10] cm are projected onto multi-view image planes via World2Cam. Multi-scale features {P2, P3, P4} are bilinearly sampled (BiLinear) and aggregated through an FPN block to produce fms.

Figure 5. Reconstruction at a complex curved intersection. Columns show GT, RoGS w/o LiDAR, and BReD; rows show BEV RGB, semantics, elevation, and elevation residual over the GT support region. Darker residuals indicate higher consistency with GT.

papers.abstract: In NAVSIMv1, the standard benchmark for end-to-end driving, $89.6\%$ of the test scenes lie within 4m of a training scene. We show that this geographic overlap inflates the reported scores. We propose a geographically disjoint split of NAVSIMv1 and an evaluation that compares models trained on either split on the same scenes, which neither has seen in training. All sensor-based models we test, DiffusionDrive, Latent TransFuser, and DrivoR, lose 3.4 to 6.1 PDMS points on these scenes, mainly by leaving the road and coming close to other objects, against 1.5 points for a baseline without sensors. The loss concentrates where a training drive of the original split passed the same place. At all other places, models trained on the original split are no better than those trained on the geographic split. Models trained on the original split predict road geometry that no camera can see. The gap persists when the auxiliary map loss is removed, so the models memorize locations even without being supervised to. On nuScenes, the geographic split cuts SparseDrive's mapping accuracy by $59\%$ and also degrades its planning. Driving scores on logged scenes thus partly measure how well a model remembers the test locations. We release the split to evaluate generalization to new places.
authors: Willi Poh, Kevin R\"osch, Christoph Stiller
bullets: 89.6% of NAVSIMv1 test scenes are within 4 m of a training scene.
A geographically disjoint split evaluates models only on places unseen during training.
Sensor-based models lose 3.4–6.1 PDMS points on disjoint scenes, mainly due to road departures and near-collisions.
The performance gap is concentrated where the original training data passed the same locations; elsewhere, the splits perform similarly.
Models infer unseen road geometry and retain location memorization even without auxiliary map supervision; similar degradation appears for SparseDrive on nuScenes.

papers.selection_reason: Exposes geographic overfitting in end-to-end driving benchmarks, directly relevant to learned navigation and planning.
papers.title: Don't Test Where You Trained: Geographic Overlap Inflates End-to-End Driving Scores
papers.tldr: Geographic overlap between training and test scenes substantially inflates end-to-end driving scores by enabling models to memorize locations rather than generalize to new places.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in expert domains face a trade-off between agentic tool use, which externalizes expertise behind brittle multi-turn runtimes, and end-to-end specialization, which internalizes expertise only implicitly at task-level granularity. We propose internalized meta-capabilities: atomic, parametrically internalized, and composable reasoning units that an LLM can select and combine within a single chain-of-thought (CoT). We instantiate this idea as Med-Agentic for medical visual diagnosis, where the model emits a capability-tagged structured CoT in one forward pass, turning capability invocation into tagged token generation rather than external tool calls. For training, Med-OPD performs multi-teacher on-policy distillation with token-level dual-factor teacher routing conditioned on both the image and the active capability tag, strictly generalizing per-prompt teacher routing. We show that this routing gives an unbiased estimator of the same expected teacher-KL gradient. Across public medical imaging datasets spanning nine anatomies and eight modalities, Med-Agentic consistently improves in-distribution and out-of-distribution diagnostic accuracy over the strong competitors.
authors: Yucheng Zhou, Junwei Sheng, Jianbing Shen
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between brittle external tool use and implicit end-to-end specialization in medical LLMs.
Represents atomic, composable reasoning capabilities that the model selects through tagged token generation.
Uses Med-OPD, a multi-teacher on-policy distillation method with image- and capability-conditioned token-level teacher routing.
Evaluated across public datasets covering nine anatomies and eight imaging modalities.
Reports consistent in-distribution and out-of-distribution accuracy gains over strong competitors.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a method for internalizing agentic tool use into a single-pass CoT for multimodal medical visual diagnosis.
papers.title: Med-Agentic: Distilling Agentic Medical Reasoning with Internalized Meta-Capabilities
papers.tldr: Med-Agentic internalizes modular medical reasoning capabilities into a single-pass, capability-tagged chain of thought, improving diagnostic accuracy across diverse imaging settings.

papers.abstract: Aging is characterized by continuously evolving health states, yet most existing prediction models focus on static health risk at isolated time points rather than explicitly modelling how health trajectories unfold over time. We developed a health world model based on the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture to represent evolving health states and simulate future trajectories under specified actions. The model combines a state encoder, an action- and context-conditioned predictor, a stop-gradient target encoder, and clinical outcome heads. We trained the model on the US Health and Retirement Study (HRS) and evaluated it without refitting in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS). Open-loop evaluation assessed discrimination and calibration for mortality and worsening of activities of daily living (ADL) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL). In the held-out HRS test set, the areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) for mortality, ADL worsening, and IADL worsening were 0.89, 0.93, and 0.93 at the first horizon and 0.84, 0.84, and 0.85 at the fifth horizon, respectively. Predicted risks stratified subsequent outcomes across horizons. Across the evaluated horizons, mortality AUROC ranged from 0.867 to 0.881 in ELSA and from 0.796 to 0.801 in CHARLS. Simulated trajectories preserved the expected risk ordering across predefined action regimes. In counterfactual simulations, changes in lifestyle actions shifted predicted risks in directions consistent with observed associations. The model provides a framework for longitudinal risk prediction and action-conditioned simulation in older adults.
authors: Jingyi Wu, Chenghua Guo, Qianlin Zuo, Pengfei Li, Luxia Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of static, single-time-point risk models by representing longitudinal health-state evolution.
Uses a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with state encoding, action/context-conditioned prediction, target encoding, and clinical outcome heads.
Trained on the US Health and Retirement Study and evaluated without refitting in English and Chinese aging cohorts.
Showed strong discrimination for mortality and ADL/IADL worsening in HRS, with meaningful risk stratification across future horizons and cross-cohort performance.
Action-conditioned and counterfactual simulations preserved expected risk ordering and produced lifestyle-related risk shifts consistent with observed associations.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Study overview. A, World model framework. The overall architecture designed for longitudinal health-trajectory prediction. B, Development and validation pipeline. Model training on the internal HRS cohort and external evaluation on two diverse populations (ELSA and CHARLS), assessing openloop prediction and simulations under static and counterfactual actions. C, Clinical application case study. Demonstration of clinical decision support across four steps: health state representation, trajectory forecasting, counterfactual intervention simulation, and personalized health recommendations. CHARLS, China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study; ELSA, English Longitudinal Study of Ageing; HRS, Health and Retirement Study.

Figure 5. Open-loop validation of simulated age-standardized mortality risk under static and counterfactual light-activity-frequency exposure in HRS, ELSA and CHARLS. The world model was trained on HRS and evaluated by open-loop simulation on held-out HRS individuals (A, B) and, without refitting, on the external ELSA (C, D) and CHARLS (E, F) cohorts. In the left column (A, C, E), individuals are stratified into three static, baseline-fixed light-activity-frequency regimes, defined from activity-frequency codes recorded at both of the first two waves; observed age-standardized risk (dashed lines, circles) is compared with world model-simulated risk (solid lines, dots) within each regime. In the right column (B, D, F), only individuals in the low regime at baseline are retained and further split into three groups by their empirically realized activity status at horizon 2: remained in the low regime, transitioned to the mid regime, and transitioned to the high regime; the world model rollout is counterfactually forced to switch to the corresponding regime at horizon 2, so that simulated and observed risk are compared under the same realized transition. ADL, activities of daily living; AUROC, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; HRS, Health and Retirement Study; IADL, instrumental activities of daily living; MLP, multi-layer perceptron; WM, world model.

papers.abstract: Repeatedly accessing the full key--value (KV) cache is a major bottleneck in long-context language model decoding. We find that small query-specific subsets can accurately approximate full attention, yet their union covers nearly the entire cache, motivating query-adaptive access for the KV cache. A natural approach is to split the KV cache into clusters, using compact representatives for clusters that incur negligible error while expanding the rest to their original KV entries. We derive a selection criterion from an upper bound on attention-output error, which reveals two complementary factors governing the error: importance measures the impact of a cluster, while distortion measures how faithfully the cluster can be represented. Based on this criterion, we propose RefineKV, a decoding-time query-adaptive KV compression method. Experiments on two models and three benchmarks demonstrate that RefineKV retains near-full-attention quality while achieving up to 7.6x speedup in the attention phase and 1.66x faster decoding, establishing a new quality-latency Pareto frontier.
authors: Kewei Lian, Jiayi Zhai, Anji Liu
bullets: Full KV-cache access is a major long-context decoding bottleneck, and query-specific relevant subsets can be much smaller than the full cache.
The method clusters KV entries and represents low-error clusters with compact summaries while expanding higher-error clusters to their original entries.
An attention-output error bound guides selection using two factors: cluster importance and representation distortion.
Across two models and three benchmarks, RefineKV achieves up to 7.6× attention-phase speedup and 1.66× faster decoding while retaining near-full-attention quality.
The approach targets decoding-time KV compression and its reported evaluation covers the stated models and benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Quality-latency trade-off of REFINEKV and existing KV-cache compression baselines. Experiments are evaluated across two models (Llama-3.1 and Qwen-2.5) on three longcontext benchmarks (LongBench, RULER, and HELMET), with results averaged across all tasks. We present a conservative threshold τ = 0.01, which matches full attention performance across all settings while achieving up to 1.56× decode speedup as measured by Time Per Output Token (TPOT). Our method extends the quality–latency Pareto frontier.

Figure 3: REFINEKV Pipeline. Prefill phase: The KV cache is partitioned into contiguous clusters, and a representative key-value pair together with auxiliary metadata is computed for each cluster. Decode phase: Each query qt uses the cached summaries to calculate risk score RC . Clusters with RC > τ are expanded, while clusters with RC ≤ τ retain only their representatives. The resulting mixed KV sequence is used to compute the output ot. The color depth of each block indicates attention score.

Figure 2: Left: Cluster selection is jointly determined by importance and distortion. Each point represents a cluster positioned by its global importance p̂C and local distortion δboundC . Background color encodes the risk score RC , with the dashed line denoting the decision boundary at RC = τ . The tilted boundary captures their trade-off: important clusters tolerate only small local distortion, whereas low-importance clusters can tolerate larger distortion. Point colors indicate the error incurred on approximating cluster. Three cases show the within-cluster attention-score patterns. Right: Risk score RC strongly correlated with approximation error. These figures illustrate the correlation between Risk Score and cluster approximation error ∥oC − ôC∥2, where oC and ôC denote original output and approximate output for cluster C.

Figure 1: Left: Each query needs only a small KV subset, but together these subsets cover nearly the entire cache. For each query, we select the highest-weight KV entries needed to retain p% of its total attention weight. The figure compares sizes of these per-query subsets and their union across queries, alongside the resulting attention output error. At roughly 10% output error, each query needs only a small subset of the cache, yet their union covers most KV entries. Right: Queryadaptive methods surpass query-independent methods. Oracle query-adaptive top-k attention achieves a markedly better perplexity–access trade-off than representative eviction baselines. papers.abstract: Answering questions over days or weeks of video requires searching for scattered clues across long timelines. Existing video agents rely on complex memory graphs and fixed retrieval pipelines, which restrict how the agent can search. We propose VideoJSON, a minimal harness for ultra-long video understanding that keeps the memory simple and lets a coding agent write its own search programs. During indexing, a vision-language model turns each minute of video into a single JSON record containing a dense caption and structured fields such as events, entities, places, and speech transcripts. At query time, the agent writes Python or Bash programs in a sandboxed container to filter, link, and read these records over multiple steps, without task-specific training or raw video access. On four ultra-long video benchmarks, VideoJSON with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash outperforms MAGIC-Video by 7.0, 20.0, and 24.75 points on EgoLifeQA, Ego-R1-Bench, and MM-Lifelong Week, and beats the best prior EgoMemReason score by 12.6 points. Across four policy models of increasing capability, VideoJSON's average score rises by up to 11.58 points over the weakest model, compared with at most 5.50 points for MAGIC-Video. Ablations show that both agentic code search and the structured JSON records drive these gains, while adding hourly summaries, extra tools, or video access changes the average score by less than 1.5 points. In addition, fine-tuning Qwen-3.5-Flash on 64 VideoJSON trajectories from an unrelated 100-hour livestream improves its MM-Lifelong scores by up to 8.25 points. Code will be open-sourced after publication.
authors: Wenqi Marshall Guo, Kuan-Hao Huang, Junda Chen, Hao Zhang
bullets: Targets questions requiring scattered evidence across days or weeks of video.
Indexes each video minute as one JSON record with captions, events, entities, places, and transcripts.
Lets a sandboxed coding agent iteratively filter, link, and read records without task-specific training or raw-video access.
Outperforms prior systems across four ultra-long-video benchmarks, with gains reported up to 24.75 points over MAGIC-Video and 12.6 points over EgoMemReason.
Ablations attribute gains mainly to agentic code search and structured records; fine-tuning on 64 unrelated trajectories further improves one benchmark by up to 8.25 points.

papers.abstract: Language model agents are increasingly asked to run ongoing multi-day operations rather than finish isolated single-turn tasks. In daily operations, today's choices reshape later observations and cash constraints because empty shelves hide lost walk-in demand, short-shipped customers quietly shrink future orders weeks later, and emergency buying drains working capital. We introduce SMB Bench, a calibrated 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and an 859-run frontier trace dataset, to ask what experience and learning signal make an agent better at noticing, attributing, and acting on the delayed consequences of its own decisions in unseen businesses. Across 16 frontier models, only 3 outperform a fixed buying rule; models often record a relevant diagnosis in their notes without changing later purchases in time, showing that diagnosing a problem, changing behavior, and improving a business are separate achievements. To study how experience improves those failures in an open model (Qwen3.8-27B), we used training-business records to identify operational rules and archived frontier quarters as starting states to continue from rather than transcripts to copy. On an unseen test business under identical evaluation instructions, the trained policy followed customer-protection commitments more consistently and reduced severe-loss quarters, while the additional profit benefit remained uncertain. Carrying those commitments through the quarter exposed the cost of fulfilling them, as early-quarter stocking habits left the buyer relying on emergency supply and a deteriorating supplier. The results separate recognizing a delayed effect, acting on it consistently, and coordinating surrounding decisions so that the response improves profit. SMB Bench connects these observations to a learning method by turning archived decisions and their consequences into reusable training experience.
authors: Shardul Bansal, Seth Schilbe, Jarrod Barnes
bullets: Problem: Multi-day business decisions reshape future demand, inventory, supplier reliability, and cash flow through delayed consequences.
Method: A 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and 859 frontier-agent traces evaluates recognition, action, and business outcomes.
Finding: Across 16 frontier models, only 3 beat a fixed buying rule; diagnosis, timely behavioral change, and profitability are distinct capabilities.
Training: An open model was trained from operational rules and archived decision consequences, rather than copied transcripts, then tested on an unseen business.
Scope/limitation: Training improved consistency with customer-protection commitments and reduced severe-loss quarters, but profit gains remained uncertain and introduced emergency-supply costs.

papers.abstract: Interactive long-video generation lets users build a story through successive prompts and reuse earlier characters and settings under new instructions. Existing memory methods retain past content, yet they often fail at precise selective recall, returning the wrong appearance of a person, mixing different people, or keeping an unrequested background. Based on our analysis of memory form and retrieval, we introduce an object-aware key--value (KV) memory framework for a frozen autoregressive diffusion generator. It keeps the original KV of tracked object regions, selects background KV outside them by attention-scores, and links each memory with a readable record of its source scene and observed appearance. An LLM selects the requested records, and a memory integrator supplies their KV for generation under the current prompt. We also introduce a six-scene evaluation that tests selective attribute modification, time-specific appearance recall, and multi-object composition, in which each person's requested past appearance changes across requests. Experiments show that our framework more reliably preserves each person's identity while reproducing their requested past appearance than existing memory methods, under both explicit scene references and natural-language cues.
authors: Hyunwook Kang, Junoh Park, Hyunggyu Lim, Taesup Kim
bullets: Targets failures in existing memory methods, including wrong appearances, identity mixing, and unrequested background retention.
Stores tracked-object KV features, selectively retains background KV using attention scores, and attaches readable scene/appearance records.
Uses an LLM to select requested memories, then integrates their KV into a frozen autoregressive diffusion generator.
Introduces a six-scene evaluation covering selective attribute edits, time-specific appearance recall, and multi-object composition.
More reliably preserves identities and requested past appearances under explicit references and natural-language cues than existing memory methods.
