papers.abstract: Camera-conditioned video world models aim to generate 3D-consistent videos from a single image along specified camera trajectories. However, set-union updates in latent spatial memory leave repeated observations unconsolidated, while frontmost-only readout limits simultaneous access to stored evidence at different depths. To address these limitations, we present ENGRAM, a latent spatial memory framework combining reliability-weighted latent fusion and occlusion-aware layered readout. Specifically, recursive fusion integrates geometrically and visually compatible observations in a channel-normalized latent space, consolidating repeated evidence into a shared scene representation. Layered readout exposes multiple depth-ordered latent candidates with their reliability and availability at each target cell. This gives the generator access to information from multiple surfaces as visibility changes. Explicit camera rays provide viewpoint information independently of memory coverage, while geometric consistency constraints guide memory updates. Memory retrieval uses a single projection at latent resolution, avoiding intermediate RGB rendering and VAE re-encoding. We adapt a pretrained video generator using only 256 training scenes. On 100 RealEstate10K test scenes, ENGRAM improves novel-view-synthesis and closed-loop PSNRs over Spatia by 0.82 and 4.48 dB, respectively. On a 200-case WorldScore evaluation subset, it achieves an average score of 67.78, exceeding Spatia by 3.31 points. Project page: https://wchkoutian.github.io/engram-website/.
authors: Chenhao Wu, Zhaolong Su, Yang Liu, Tianrui Su, Yingguang Yang, Shang Luo, Yancheng Chen, Chongyang Zhang, Hao Zheng, Kefu Xu, Congjing Ran, Bin Chong
bullets: Addresses unconsolidated set-union memory updates and frontmost-only readout limitations.
Uses reliability-weighted recursive latent fusion for geometrically and visually compatible observations.
Provides occlusion-aware, depth-ordered latent candidates with reliability and availability information.
Uses explicit camera rays and geometric consistency constraints, with single-projection latent-resolution retrieval.
With 256 training scenes, improves PSNR and WorldScore over Spatia on the reported RealEstate10K and WorldScore evaluations.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon image animation must keep the scene fixed while natural material (e.g., water, smoke, or fire) continues to move. Autoregressive video generators read recent frames for temporal continuity, but this history also carries accumulated appearance errors, and sparsifying it disrupts motion. We introduce SceneTether, a training-free attention-read policy that keeps where attention reads recent memory but changes what appearance that memory returns. SceneTether keeps every key of the newest latent, blends its low-activity values toward co-located source-image values, and leaves high-activity values untouched so motion can evolve; an activity map estimated from the first generated latents and then frozen decides where to blend. It adds no denoising evaluations and leaves the cache-update rule unchanged. On a Causal Forcing++ generator, SceneTether raises source-support PSNR by 5.15 dB over its framewise Echo host across two seeds with 1.5x its late activity, and by 7.31 dB over spatial Echo-Forcing on a preselected four-minute subset. At equal recent-memory coverage, value anchoring alone adds 8.14 dB. A post-hoc pixel composite with the same map matches static fidelity but retains nearly twice the moving-region color drift, and viewers in a small blinded study preferred SceneTether for its natural scene and motion preservation. bullets: Targets accumulated appearance drift in static scene regions without disrupting evolving materials such as water, smoke, or fire.

Freezes an activity map estimated from early generated latents; adds no denoising evaluations and does not alter cache updates.
Improves source-support PSNR over framewise and spatial Echo baselines, with additional gains from value anchoring alone.
A small blinded study favored SceneTether for preserving natural scene appearance and motion; evaluation covers two seeds and a preselected four-minute subset.

papers.title: SceneTether: Activity-Gated Value Anchoring for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Image Animation

papers.abstract: Cities are sensed by many platforms at once: on-board cameras, LiDAR and radar on autonomous vehicles, roadside units at intersections, drones and satellites overhead, and the GNSS traces of millions of trips. Yet most learned representations are built for one platform, one city, and one task. We survey this fragmented landscape through a single lens, the Urban State Representation (USR): a georeferenced, layered, time-varying, uncertainty-aware state that any sensing platform can write to and any downstream task can read from. We (i) formalize USR and five desiderata for it, and relate it to bird's-eye-view (BEV) features, occupancy, vectorized maps, neural fields and 3D Gaussians, scene graphs, road-network graphs, language tokens, and world-model latents; (ii) organize sensing platforms, cross-view (ground-aerial) matching, fusion operators, 3D geometric foundation models, end-to-end and vision-language-action models, and generative world models and data engines in one taxonomy that spans sensors to decisions; (iii) compile 26 urban datasets and simulators across ego, cooperative (V2X), aerial, trajectory, and language settings, with a metric glossary, a cross-benchmark results snapshot, a trend analysis, and a platform-coverage gap analysis; and (iv) review applications and propose, as an outlook, USR-5, a five-test protocol with explicit references and one aggregate score for measuring whether a state is shared, together with a research agenda of six open problems covering cross-city and cross-sensor transfer, uncertainty, efficiency, sim-to-real evaluation, and governance. This survey is an entry point for computer vision, autonomous driving, transportation, and urban computing researchers; the paper list, datasets, and USR-5 code are at https://github.com/binayksingh/Awesome-Urban-State-Representation.
authors: Binay Kumar Singh, Niels Da Vitoria Lobo
bullets: Formalizes USR and five desiderata, relating it to representations including BEV features, occupancy, maps, neural fields, scene graphs, language tokens, and world-model latents.
Provides a sensor-to-decision taxonomy covering sensing platforms, cross-view matching, fusion, geometric foundation models, end-to-end and vision-language-action models, and generative world models.
Compiles 26 urban datasets and simulators spanning ego, V2X, aerial, trajectory, and language settings, alongside metrics, benchmark results, trends, and coverage gaps.
Introduces USR-5, a proposed five-test protocol and aggregate score for evaluating whether representations are genuinely shared across platforms and tasks.
Highlights open problems in cross-city and cross-sensor transfer, uncertainty, efficiency, sim-to-real evaluation, and governance.

papers.title: Urban State Representation for Autonomous Mobility: A Survey of Multimodal Perception, Architectures, Datasets, and Benchmarks

papers.abstract: Anticipating the future behavior of surrounding objects is key for the safe and efficient navigation of autonomous vehicles. State-of-the-art Transformer-based interaction-aware trajectory prediction models are typically trained and evaluated on large-scale, highly curated datasets obtained by filtering any object detection and tracking noise through extensive offline post-processing. However, in real-world deployments, the detected objects' state (position, heading, and speed) estimates are inherently affected by sensing and localization uncertainties. These uncertainties can be even higher for connected and automated vehicles receiving information from other road users through Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communications. In this paper, we first investigate the sensitivity of five state-of-the-art Transformer-based interaction-aware trajectory prediction models to realistic noisy object state estimates. Numerical results show that prediction accuracy degrades by up to a 6x factor as the noise level increases, highlighting the models' sensitivity to the mismatch between the noise conditions encountered during training and those experienced at deployment. We then show that retraining models on a more realistic noise-augmented dataset is a more effective strategy to mitigate the impact of noisy object state estimates on trajectory prediction accuracy than using denoising modules at the input. Retrained models limit the prediction accuracy degradation below a 1.5x factor. The noise-augmented dataset is openly released to support further research.
authors: Shahab Salehi, Luca Lusvarghi, Miguel Sepulcre, Javier Gozalvez
bullets: Evaluates five interaction-aware Transformer trajectory prediction models under noisy position, heading, and speed estimates.
Prediction accuracy can degrade by up to 6× as noise increases, exposing a deployment–training mismatch.
Retraining on realistic noise-augmented data is more effective than adding input denoising modules.
Noise-augmented retraining limits degradation to below 1.5×.
The augmented dataset is released openly for further research.

papers.abstract: 3D vision-language models (3D VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in 3D scene understanding and spatial reasoning. However, their reliance on multi-view inputs produces long visual token sequences, imposing substantial computational overhead during inference. Existing pruning methods often rely on token salience or feature diversity as proxies for representativeness, without explicitly modeling the representation gap between the original token set and the retained subset, thereby leading to suboptimal representation of the original scene. In this paper, we propose ReMiC, a training-free, representation-driven token pruning framework based on minimax hierarchical clustering. ReMiC treats retained tokens as prototypes for the original observations, formulating pruning as minimizing the maximum representation error under a fixed token budget. Local prototype initialization allocates tokens according to regional representation needs, while global prototype refinement updates the selected prototypes using cross-region information to further reduce the maximum representation error. Extensive experiments conducted on three representative 3D VLMs across five 3D scene understanding benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of our method. Notably, by retaining only 10% of visual tokens, ReMiC preserves 93.2% of the performance of Video-3D LLM and achieves a $2.04\times$ faster inference speed.
authors: Bangfeng Yan, Chaoning Zhang, Yuanhao Liu, Pengcheng Zheng, Mengyuan Li, Wei Dong, Sheng Zheng, Yang Yang
bullets: Targets the long visual token sequences created by multi-view 3D inputs.
Formulates pruning as minimizing the maximum representation error under a fixed token budget.
Uses local prototype initialization followed by global cross-region refinement via minimax hierarchical clustering.
Evaluated across three 3D VLMs and five 3D scene-understanding benchmarks.
With 10% of visual tokens retained, preserves 93.2% of Video-3D LLM performance and delivers 2.04× faster inference.

In Stage 1, local prototype initialization builds a minimax tree within each spatial region and jointly cuts the trees under a shared token budget to select initial prototypes. In Stage 2, global prototype refinement reassigns all original tokens to their nearest prototypes across regions and reselects a prototype for each cluster.

papers.title: ReMiC: Representation-Driven Token Pruning for 3D VLMs via Minimax Hierarchical Clustering
papers.tldr: ReMiC is a training-free token-pruning method that preserves 3D VLM performance while reducing inference cost by selecting representative visual tokens.

papers.abstract: Operating in the physical world requires reasoning beyond what cameras directly capture. In a city, radio signals are invisible to the lens, yet their strength is governed by the buildings and streets an image does show. Given only these visible structures, can vision-language models (VLMs) infer the invisible radio field they shape? Probing true physical reasoning requires exact fields in real cities, alongside controlled interventions where a single physical factor changes. We build a label-free engine that turns any coordinate on Earth into a ray-traceable city, simulates matched single-factor counterfactuals, and computes every answer exactly. This yields RadioVISTA, a benchmark and training dataset for visual reasoning about invisible fields. Physically, a radio field is the sum of its propagation paths, yet across six continents we uncover a striking field-path dissociation: frontier VLMs accurately judge where a field is strong, but fail to tell whether a single direct or one-wall path exists. Open models fail even earlier at reading the field itself, and are systematically wrong, scoring below random guessing even when credited for any of four attempts. On unseen cities, fine-tuning brings a 9B open model close to frontier proprietary models on fields, yet neither supervised nor reinforcement fine-tuning improves path tracing. Supervising only final answers teaches models to approximate the field, yet leaves single-path geometry out of reach.
authors: Yiyang Zhu, Xin Li, Guangyuan Liu, Ziheng Liu, Jiayi Zhang, Chau Yuen
bullets: Creates a label-free benchmark and training dataset using ray-traced cities, exact fields, and matched single-factor counterfactuals.
Evaluates both field-level prediction and fine-grained reasoning about direct or one-wall paths across six continents.
Frontier VLMs judge field strength well but fail at identifying whether individual paths exist; open models often fail at field prediction itself.
Fine-tuning a 9B open model improves field inference on unseen cities but does not improve path tracing.
Results suggest that learning final field answers does not produce the underlying single-path geometric reasoning.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Can vision-language models infer an invisible radio field from the visible scene? Can VLMs “see the invisible” from visual cues alone, and where does their physical reasoning break down? We investigate this with RadioVISTA, which converts any coordinate into a ray-traceable city (1), perturbs one physical factor at a time (2), compiles the resulting fields into a physics exam with simulated ground truth (3) and probes what VLMs perceive and learn (bottom).

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a road-scene segmenter for rain and nighttime driving can introduce errors on normal daytime images. With few labeled normal images for calibration, a whole-image risk check may reject changes that would pass if adopted locally. Risk-Controlled Adoption of Label Changes (RALC) selects local changes from a fixed model update, using confidence differences and an image score to form nested candidates. On each normal calibration image, RALC measures how many more errors each candidate makes than the original model, assigning zero loss when errors stay the same or fall. At test time, each replacement can add at most one error, so the replacement count bounds the net increase without test labels. RALC combines this candidate-dependent bound with recorded calibration losses to select the largest set that passes the risk check. If the models and adoption rules are fixed before calibration and normal calibration and test images are exchangeable, the expected per-image loss stays within budget. On held-out BDD100K, we evaluated three weight-interpolated updates with 10 additional normal images per calibration draw. At a common fixed budget, adverse-scene mIoU was 1.89--3.19 percentage points higher with RALC than with whole-image adoption, while measured mean normal loss was also higher. After matching this loss post hoc at 1,000 pixels per image, RALC still led by 1.135--2.428 points. Selecting changes in $8\times8$-pixel cells recovered 93--98% of this advantage. With 250 calibration images at the original budget, both rules adopted all three updates in full.
authors: Shize Yin
bullets: Addresses errors caused by adapting road-scene segmenters to rain/night conditions while preserving normal daytime performance.
Selects nested local label changes using confidence differences and image scores from a fixed model update.
Uses few normal calibration images to bound the possible test-time increase in errors without test labels.
On held-out BDD100K, RALC improved adverse-scene mIoU by 1.89–3.19 points at a common budget, though normal-image loss was higher.
Cell-based selection retained 93–98% of the advantage; with 250 calibration images, both methods adopted all tested updates fully.

papers.abstract: A cross-modal routing module can improve over its backbone while its transport plan accounts for no demonstrable part of that improvement. In ABVnet with DFEW, Sinkhorn cross-modal routing (SCR) exceeds the retrained baseline by 0.87 unweighted average recall (UAR) points, a resolved difference, yet sits 0.17 points above an individually trained, parameter-matched pooled variant, an unresolved difference that establishes no equivalence; under the development protocol the comparison with the baseline reverses. Separating the two needs comparisons a module-against-backbone test cannot supply: parameter-matched variants changing only the plan rule, and interventions replacing the plan without retraining. The evaluation covers MMA-DFER and ABVnet on DFEW and MAFW, and MMA-DFER on CREMA-D, with a single training run per configuration and paired fold intervals. ABVnet with DFEW motivated the follow-up after the broader results were available. Replacing the plan everywhere with a uniform one reduces UAR by 0.72, whereas permuting its rows gives an unresolved difference of -0.20 UAR points; permutation is less damaging by 0.51 UAR points, a resolved contrast. Replacing the plan with the product of its own marginals, preserving both marginals and removing only frame-specific mixtures, reduces UAR by 0.70. These reductions concern reliance at inference; attribution of the module gain to the transport plan remains unestablished. Under the 1.5 fold-dependence widening, the baseline gain remains resolved, whereas the replacement reductions and the paired contrast are unresolved.
authors: Vu Nhat Minh Pham, Cong Khanh Nguyen, Minh Tuan Le, Van Thong Huynh
bullets: SCR improves over the retrained backbone by 0.87 UAR points in ABVnet on DFEW under one protocol, but this gain reverses under the development protocol.
A parameter-matched pooled comparison and plan-replacement interventions are needed to separate module effects from transport-plan effects.
Replacing the learned plan with a uniform plan or its marginal-product approximation reduces UAR, indicating inference-time reliance on frame-specific routing.
Row permutation is less damaging than uniform replacement, but the corresponding comparisons are unresolved under wider fold-dependence intervals.
Results cover MMA-DFER and ABVnet across DFEW, MAFW, and CREMA-D, with one training run per configuration.

papers.abstract: Reliable vision systems should connect numerical claims to visible evidence. In visual measurement, this requires mapping candidate values to image-specific physical states. StateBind-200 augments 200 real images with human-refined local geometry and matched Numeric, Calibrated, and Physicalized interfaces. Across a 128-image held-out evaluation and 6,696 controlled calls, physicalizing identical candidates raises three-model majority accuracy from 75.54% to 91.13%, a source-image-balanced gain of +15.30 points. Calibration and additional reasoning leave most of the gap intact; target localization can succeed despite incorrect value-lattice binding, with a larger burden for two-endpoint ruler spans. An independent 40-image geometry audit yields a 0.08-tick median target discrepancy and preserves the main effect under disagreement sensitivity. We further propose Factorial StateBind, a training-free selective verifier. Two VLMs propose target and lattice components, an independent VLM validates their evidence, and valid combinations are resolved deterministically. A precision mode selected on 69 development images combines component validity, four-way agreement, and state separation. Applied unchanged to held-out evaluation, this high-precision evidence gate reaches 91.67% candidate precision across 36/128 images (28.12%) and 9.68% of ordered cells. The results identify instance-specific symbol-to-state binding as a distinct reliability bottleneck and provide an interpretable evidence gate for numerical visual claims.
authors: Qing Mu, Jiani Zheng
bullets: Introduces StateBind-200: 200 real images with refined local geometry and matched Numeric, Calibrated, and Physicalized interfaces.
Physicalizing identical candidates raises three-model majority accuracy from 75.54% to 91.13%, a +15.30-point source-image-balanced gain.
Calibration and extra reasoning do not close the remaining gap; localization can succeed while value-lattice binding fails, especially for two-endpoint ruler spans.
Proposes Factorial StateBind, a training-free verifier that independently checks target and lattice evidence before deterministic resolution.
Its high-precision mode achieves 91.67% candidate precision on 36/128 held-out images, covering 28.12% of images and 9.68% of ordered cells.

Fig. 4. Factorial StateBind. Qwen validates Doubao (𝐷) and Gemini (𝐺) target–lattice proposals. Projected schematic grids show four recombinations: shading marks cross-source pairs; brackets show target-to-B residuals. Precision mode requires four valid agreeing pairs and at least four-tick candidate separation. Source: MeasureBench [15], CC BY-SA 4.0; cropped and annotated by the authors.

Fig. 2. Matched interface comparison. Left: call accuracy for the three interfaces. Right: sourceimage-balanced Physicalized-minus-Numeric effects with 95% source-image bootstrap intervals. Calibration remains near Numeric, while physicalizing candidate states produces a consistent gain.

Aggregate target and lattice errors show the same separation, and Physicalized gains are larger for two-endpoint ruler spans than for single-state tasks. papers.selection_reason: Exposes symbol-to-state binding gaps in visual measurement with geometry-aware evaluation and a verifier; directly fits spatial intelligence and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: StateBind: Exposing the Symbol-to-State Binding Gap in Visual Measurement
papers.tldr: StateBind shows that reliable visual measurement depends on binding numerical candidates to image-specific physical states, and that explicit physicalization plus evidence verification substantially improves accuracy.

papers.abstract: As vision-language models enter remote smartphone trade-in, sellers already upload six views and a diagnostic screen, which makes it easy to treat the human quote as a step a model can take over. A model may mark a crack or read the screen, yet the quote is a staff form: appearance fill stays near 0.25, and the closed models that score a little higher do so only on the orders they answer, so human appraisal remains necessary. Two obstacles stand in the way. (1) Single-view defect sets and attribute benchmarks do not score an order-level form under a fixed input contract, so a box or a leaked field can be mistaken for a finished quote. (2) The unread half of the form is the staff fields, and a model left to emit boxes or captions does not learn them. We present PhoneQC, a 335-order iPhone-heavy cut that ranks systems by a 0 to 100 form score (Score100) only inside matched protocols (images alone; images plus a detector sidecar), with a declared upper bound that is not ranked as a peer. As a case study on that board, field-only LoRA freezes the backbone, adapts attention projections, and supervises staff fields while leaving the defect list empty; the adapter sees the same images as the zero-shot model. On image-only T1 the 3B model rises from 26.6 to 33.3 at coverage 0.928; without the empty-blocker item the open ranking still favors the adapter, while the remaining gap to a person stays large on this cut.
authors: Zihan Deng, Xinpei Lin, Du Tiantian, Lequan Yu
bullets: Evaluates order-level quotes from six phone views plus a diagnostic screen, rather than isolated defects or attributes.
Uses Score100 from 0–100 within matched protocols: images only or images with detector sidecar; a declared upper bound is not ranked as a peer.
Introduces field-only LoRA, which adapts attention projections to predict staff fields while leaving the defect list empty.
On image-only T1, the 3B model improves from 26.6 to 33.3 at 0.928 coverage; the remaining gap to human performance is large.
Scope: results are reported on a 335-order, iPhone-heavy cut, and model answering coverage affects comparisons.

papers.abstract: Agentic text-to-image systems wrap generators in loops of planning, routing, verification and refinement, and report large gains on compositional benchmarks, almost always relative to a single sample. We ask how much of the gain survives against Single-tool Rejection Retry (\ours): the strongest generator already in the system's pool, an off-the-shelf verifier, and retries that stop at the first accepted image under the system's own budget. Auditing four recent systems with official evaluators, we find that on GenEval SRR matches the accuracy of OctoT2I (0.962 vs.\ 0.96), recovers 63 to 90% of the gain of GEMS depending on the verifier, and exceeds GenPilot by 12 points with 2.3 generations per image; the effect persists with generators not tuned to the benchmark and on T2I-CompBench++. A closed-form analysis predicts the accuracy of SRR at every budget and shows that its gain is capped by the verifier's likelihood ratio. The same analysis also exposes genuine agentic gains: on GenEval 2, even the best of five samples chosen by the evaluator stays 15 points below the score GEMS reports (12 at the upper end of its 95% interval). We prove a ceiling on the accuracy that routing across generators can add, bracket it between one and three points on OctoT2I's own pool, and show that what OctoT2I's routing buys is compute (about 2.5 less than SRR at equal accuracy), not accuracy. In our offline distillation experiments selected samples teach the generator no more than random ones, which a short information argument explains. We end with a reporting checklist for agentic generation papers.
authors: Jian Xu, Delu Zeng, Qibin Zhao
bullets: Single-tool Rejection Retry (SRR) repeatedly samples the strongest available generator and stops when an evaluator accepts an image.
SRR matches OctoT2I on GenEval and recovers 63–90% of GEMS’s gain, depending on the verifier; it also outperforms GenPilot and generalizes to other generators and T2I-CompBench++.
The analysis predicts SRR’s accuracy across budgets and shows its improvement is limited by the verifier’s likelihood ratio.
Some agency remains: on GenEval 2, GEMS exceeds the best-of-five evaluator-selected samples by 12–15 points.
Routing mainly reduces compute rather than improving accuracy for OctoT2I; selected samples also provide no more distillation benefit than random samples.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes agentic text-to-image systems and separates retry/selection gains from genuine agency; transferable to evaluation of multimodal generation systems.
papers.title: Is It the Agent or the Retry? Separating Selection from Agency in Text-to-Image Generation
papers.tldr: Much of the reported advantage of agentic text-to-image systems can be reproduced by retrying a strong generator with a verifier, though some genuine gains remain.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers (vDiTs) have become the main backbone for video generation. The quadratic cost of self-attention limits their efficiency at high resolutions and long durations. Existing sparse attention methods often rely on preserving high attention weights. However, these criteria do not fully capture the fidelity of the final value-weighted output, whose error depends jointly on changes to the attention numerator and the softmax denominator. We propose NOVA, a coarse-to-fine sparse attention framework that first approximates the full normalized output using size-weighted key/value centroids. Building on this estimate, we construct a residual proxy that accounts for coupled numerator-denominator errors by centering value contributions around the estimated output. This proxy guides the selection of query-key blocks for refinement under a predefined block budget for each query cluster. Selected blocks are evaluated through exact token-level computation, while the remaining blocks contribute through their centroids under a shared softmax normalization. On five vDiTs, NOVA achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among sparse attention methods, improving PSNR by up to 1.55\,dB over the strongest baseline, while delivering up to 1.82$\times$ end-to-end speedup on an H100 GPU.
authors: Wenxuan Miao, Haosong Liu, Aiyue Chen, Yiwu Yao, Zihan Liu, Anbang Wu, Yiming Gan, Jingwen Leng, Minyi Guo, Yu Feng
bullets: Targets the quadratic self-attention cost of high-resolution and long-duration video generation.
Uses size-weighted key/value centroids to estimate full normalized attention outputs coarsely.
Builds a residual proxy that captures coupled softmax numerator and denominator errors.
Refines selected query-key blocks exactly while approximating the rest with centroids under shared normalization.
Across five vDiTs, reports the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among compared sparse-attention methods, with up to 1.55 dB PSNR improvement.

papers.abstract: In open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) of remote-sensing imagery, class-name prompts can miss objects with varied appearances, while richer descriptions can activate competing classes. We propose Response-Oriented Prompt Selection for SAM 3 (ROSE-SAM3), a training-free framework that selects descriptions using frozen SAM 3 responses on unlabeled target-domain images. We screen candidate descriptions for coverage beyond the native prompts while protecting reliable native class responses, retaining candidates that pass these checks on at least four of five image folds. An offline directed acyclic graph (DAG) search then evaluates candidate combinations and builds a compact PromptBank for each class. Each bank retains the native prompts and adds selected descriptions, which we call residual prompts. At inference, the bank is fixed, and Semantic-Instance Cooperative Head (SICH) uses instance evidence to refine semantic responses before assigning pixel labels. We also introduce RS-OVSS-C to evaluate robustness under six image corruption families across eight remote-sensing datasets, preserving their class vocabularies and reference labels. ROSE-SAM3 achieves 57.3% mean mIoU across eight clean benchmarks and 54.7% on RS-OVSS-C, achieving state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/YanghuiSong/ROSE-SAM3.
authors: Yanghui Song, Chengfu Yang, Yongpeng Wen, Zhanxuan Hu, Wei Lu, Qi Ming, Nanqing Liu, Heng-Chao Li
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between fixed class-name prompts and varied object appearances, while avoiding descriptions that trigger competing classes.
Uses frozen SAM 3 responses on unlabeled target-domain images to screen candidate descriptions, then applies offline DAG search to build compact per-class PromptBanks.
Retains native prompts and adds selected residual prompts; SICH further refines semantic responses using instance evidence at inference.
Introduces RS-OVSS-C, a corruption-robustness benchmark spanning six corruption families and eight remote-sensing datasets.
Reports 57.3% mean mIoU on eight clean benchmarks and 54.7% on RS-OVSS-C, with state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is commonly optimized with multiple reconstruction losses, which naturally forms a multi-objective optimization problem. This issue becomes more pronounced when perceptual losses are introduced to improve visual quality, as different objectives may impose competing update directions on Gaussian primitives and make it difficult to simultaneously improve fidelity, perceptual quality, and representation efficiency. Based on this view, we reformulate 3DGS training as a multi-objective optimization problem and derive selective conflict-aware position updates that reduce interference between competing objectives while preserving the contribution of each loss. We further observe that gradient conflicts persist throughout training and are most severe in Gaussian position parameters, indicating that objective conflict is closely tied to geometry optimization. We therefore treat position-gradient conflict as a geometry-aware signal to guide densification and pruning. Experiments show that our method achieves better rendering performance while improving representation compactness and rendering efficiency over existing 3DGS variants.
authors: Chenhao Zhang, Fengze Zhang, Fengqing Zhu
bullets: Reframes 3D Gaussian Splatting training with multiple reconstruction and perceptual losses as a multi-objective optimization problem.
Applies selective conflict-aware position updates to reduce interference while retaining each loss’s contribution.
Finds that conflicts persist during training and are strongest in Gaussian position parameters.
Uses position-gradient conflict to guide Gaussian densification and pruning.
Reports better rendering performance, greater representation compactness, and improved rendering efficiency over existing 3DGS variants.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains video agents to locate sparse evidence for long-video question answering through structured memory retrieval and temporal re-observation. This training, however, faces a long-tail modality distribution in the data. In our source pool, text-heavy questions account for 58% of samples, compared with 15% graph-heavy, 17% visual-heavy, and 10% time-range questions. Fixed-distribution RL therefore allocates fewer rollouts to underperforming question types. Reweighting these types could increase their sampling frequency but repeatedly reuses the same finite banks of original questions. To solve this problem, we introduce VideoGym, a curriculum-based RL environment that jointly constructs video-grounded training tasks and allocates rollouts among them. Within the environment, a memory-augmented VideoAgent is trained to coordinate retrieval from text, graph, and visual memories with temporal re-observation. Across episodes, VideoGym adapts VideoAgent's training distribution online: it casts per-period sample selection as an adversarial bandit over (modality, mode) arms and applies the EXP3 update to shift sampling toward arms with low answer accuracy. To supply the augmented-mode arms, a TaskGenerator-Verifier pipeline produces harder variants of existing questions that remain answerable within the same video. Across five long-video benchmarks, VideoGym lifts RL accuracy from 60.4% to 64.8% on average and by up to 10.5 pp on underrepresented graph-heavy questions with 3.3x sample efficiency. Together, these results show that task expansion and adaptive allocation can improve video agent learning from limited, imbalanced training data.
authors: Jing Wang, Yi Ke Yun, Yifeng Yao, Huishuai Zhang, Dongyan Zhao, Tao Wang
bullets: Addresses imbalanced training data, where text-heavy questions dominate and graph-, visual-, and time-range questions are less frequent.
Uses a curriculum-based RL environment with a memory-augmented VideoAgent for text, graph, and visual retrieval plus temporal re-observation.
Models task selection as an adversarial bandit over modality and task-mode arms, using EXP3 to favor low-accuracy areas.
Generates harder but answerable question variants through a TaskGenerator-Verifier pipeline.
Across five benchmarks, average RL accuracy rises from 60.4% to 64.8%; graph-heavy questions improve by up to 10.5 percentage points with 3.3× sample efficiency.

papers.abstract: Thinking at length before answering is expected to strengthen the visual reasoning of vision-language models (VLMs), yet hybrid VLMs often get lost in thought: their thoughts loop or exhaust the budget without an answer, so thinking can score below answering directly. Existing early-exit methods watch a thought for the moment its answer is ready and force the answer out of it, but in a hybrid VLM that moment often never comes. We find that the remedy is not to stop a failing thought earlier, but to stop taking its answer: once a thought is given up, the model's own direct answers decide. Based on this, we propose **YOTO (You Only Think Once)**, a method that answers first and thinks at most once. YOTO draws direct answers until a probe-weighted vote settles; only an unsettled problem receives a single thought, which a failure head on the hidden state monitors and stops as soon as it predicts failure, handing the problem back to direct answers. At a matched 20k-token budget, YOTO is up to 5.9 points more accurate than the strongest early-exit baseline, using one failure-head threshold across model sizes. Keeping the released weights frozen, it adds only two linear probes. On the full MathVision benchmark, YOTO improves Qwen3.5-2B from 40.1% to 57.3% and Qwen3.5-4B from 68.3% to 73.7%, above the 72.8% that Qwen3.5-9B, a model more than twice its size, reaches with thinking. Its gains carry over to five further benchmarks and a second model family. These results suggest that hybrid VLMs reason better by answering first and thinking once than by thinking longer.
authors: Tianyi Tan, Wentao Wang, Xiaohan Li, Zining Ren, Siyuan Li, Xutao Mao, Rui Qian, Luoxi Zhang, Shiwen Ni
bullets: Hybrid VLMs can loop or exhaust their thinking budget, making extended reasoning worse than direct answering.
YOTO uses probe-weighted voting among direct answers and invokes one thought only when answers remain unsettled.
A failure head monitors the thought and returns to direct answers when failure is predicted.
With frozen model weights and two linear probes, YOTO gains up to 5.9 accuracy points over the strongest early-exit baseline at a matched 20k-token budget.
On MathVision, it raises Qwen3.5-2B from 40.1% to 57.3% and Qwen3.5-4B from 68.3% to 73.7%, with gains transferring across additional benchmarks and a second model family.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video generators differ by two orders of magnitude in price, and a cheap configuration of a strong model is often good enough for a prompt. Routing prompts across such arms (model x sampling configuration) should buy quality at fixed budget, but no dataset supports studying it: public video-preference sets contain only closed models, one configuration each. We release VidRouteBench: 16 arms from 7 open families spanning 121x in measured cost ($0.0025-$0.298 per clip), 27,110 clips (1,421 A800-hours) over 1,625 grouped prompts, a quality score frozen after calibration against human preferences (68.7% CV accuracy vs 66.2% for the best single scorer), per-clip scores on 9 identifiable quality dimensions, repeated seeds, an encrypted test split, and a sealed newest family for cold start. The evaluator compares a router against the best prompt-agnostic mixture of arms, not the best single arm. Per-prompt specialisation here is real and predictable (oracle gap 0.642, 47% reproducible across seeds, prompt-arm interaction F=4.47 at p=1.6e-63), unlike LLM-routing arms, where the same pipeline finds none. We then propose OPMU (one probe, many utilities): label a new arm on K probe prompts, predict its 9 dimensions once, and serve any scenario utility by scalarising afterwards. Over 215 utility directions OPMU Pareto-dominates the prompt-agnostic baseline for 94% of directions versus 90% for per-scenario routers, with no per-scenario retraining. Three baselines fail instructively: bag-of-words features lose almost all routing gain in the low-data regime (0.009 vs 0.168); crediting a new arm with its probe average is harmful (-3.32 recovery) although it is the strong baseline on RewardBench-style arms (0.786); Chebyshev scalarisation does not help, our cost-utility front being convex.
authors: Dayu Wang
bullets: Introduces 16 arms from 7 open model families, spanning 121× in measured generation cost and 27,110 clips across 1,625 grouped prompts.
Provides calibrated quality evaluation across 9 dimensions, repeated seeds, encrypted testing, and a sealed newest family for cold-start evaluation.
Shows prompt-specific arm selection is substantial and reproducible, motivating comparison with the best prompt-agnostic mixture rather than the best single arm.
Proposes OPMU: probe a new arm once, predict its quality dimensions, then scalarise for different utility scenarios without retraining.
OPMU Pareto-dominates the prompt-agnostic baseline for 94% of 215 utility directions; simple bag-of-words and probe-average baselines perform poorly in this setting.

papers.abstract: Two centuries ago, an early cinema-like theater called the Diorama could already control its scenes at will. Today's video generation models produce videos of near-cinematic quality, yet they still lack this controllability. This limitation stems from the inherent semantic gap between text and pixels, since a prompt can describe a video only coarsely and leaves its details and relations beyond control. We bring this ability to video generation with Causal Dioramas, modules that decompose a video into a concept graph of variables that can be intervened on individually. Each instruction is translated into an intervention on the concept graph, modifying the specified concepts and their dependents. A connector then conveys this intervention to the video generator, which reuses the original noise to produce a counterfactual video while preserving all other content. Building on Causal Dioramas, we develop a unified framework for controllable generation, counterfactual revision of generated videos and editing of real videos. We outperform both open-source and commercial models in controllability on T2V-CompBench, CoVEBench and OpenVE-Bench.
authors: Yifan Shen, Xinyi Yang, Peiyuan Zhu, Yichang Jian, Jinyuan Hu, Xilin He, Fengming Zhu, Guangyi Chen, Kun Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limited detail and relational control of text-to-video prompts caused by the semantic gap between text and pixels.
Decomposes videos into concept graphs whose variables can be individually intervened on, including their dependents.
Translates instructions into graph interventions and uses a connector to guide the video generator with reused noise for counterfactual outputs.
Supports unified text-to-video generation, revision of generated videos, and editing of real videos.
Reports better controllability than open-source and commercial models on T2V-CompBench, CoVEBench, and OpenVE-Bench.

papers.abstract: Video large language models (video LLMs) answer a wide range of questions about real videos, yet they remain weak at fine-grained motion such as whether an object speeds up or slows down. Existing methods train these models on synthetic motion clips, on order pretext tasks such as reordering shuffled clips, or with rewards that compare ordered and perturbed frames. None of them requires that the label be unrecoverable from the frames once their order is discarded, so a model can fit such data from static cues without learning to use frame order. We propose ORDO, a framework that builds this requirement into the training data. We define order-necessary supervision as data in which the unordered set of frames has the same distribution under competing labels, and we realise it for motion attributes with three constructions, time-reversal pairing, matched spatial extent and uniform interval coverage. A procedural curriculum of six motion primitives instantiates these constructions, and low-rank adapters of the language model are trained on it with an answer-level objective and self-distillation replay on real videos. With 4,000 synthetic clips, ORDO raises the mean accuracy over four motion benchmarks by +7.6, +4.9 and +5.1 points on Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3-VL-8B and Molmo2-8B, while the same training with shuffled frames changes it by less than one point. Code and generator will be made publicly available.
authors: Jiaye Luan, Chaoning Zhang, Pengcheng Zheng, Dongshen Han, Sheng Zheng, Ping Guo, Caiyan Qin, Yang Du, Yang Yang
bullets: Targets failures on motion attributes such as speeding up or slowing down, which models may otherwise solve using static visual cues.
Constructs order-necessary supervision through time-reversal pairs, matched spatial extent, and uniform interval coverage.
Uses six procedural motion primitives, low-rank adaptation, answer-level training, and self-distillation replay on real videos.
Training on 4,000 synthetic clips improves mean accuracy across four motion benchmarks by 7.6, 4.9, and 5.1 points for three video LLMs.
Shuffled-frame training yields less than one point of change, supporting the importance of order-dependent supervision.

papers.abstract: Long videos spanning tens of minutes to hours far exceed the context window of today's vision-language models, and the standard remedy of sparse uniform frame sampling discards exactly the fine-grained evidence that specific questions depend on. Existing video agents explore on demand but re-explore from scratch for every question and discard their exploration state once an answer is produced, so per-question cost scales with video length. Hierarchical-memory methods instead fix the scope of each depth in advance and deepen along a pre-committed pyramid rather than toward the question. We observe that a video's coarse structure (where its scenes and topics begin and end) is question-independent, whereas which part a question must zoom into, and how deep, is question-dependent. We propose VTree, which builds a coarse hierarchical memory tree over a video once and then, for each question, grows branches only where that question needs depth. The growth is globally routed so any part of the timeline is reachable, sufficiency-gated so drilling stops when the evidence suffices, and query-conditioned so a branch unfolds into the sub-intervals that answer \emph{this} question. Crucially, every expansion is written back into the video memory, allowing later questions to reuse previously discovered structure and evidence without repeating the corresponding expansion process. Across five long-video understanding benchmarks, VTree consistently improves the accuracy of diverse vision-language backbones while substantially reducing the context length and execution time required for each question.
authors: Xiaoyu Ma, Lianyu Hu, Zixuan Hu, Zhizhen Wu, Zeqin Liao, Shengqian Qin, Yang Liu
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of uniform sampling and agents that re-explore long videos independently for every question.
Separates question-independent coarse video structure from question-dependent evidence and required zoom depth.
Uses globally routed, sufficiency-gated, query-conditioned branch growth to locate relevant fine-grained content.
Writes each expansion back to memory so later questions can reuse discovered structure and evidence.
Improves accuracy across five long-video benchmarks while reducing per-question context length and execution time.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of VTree. (1) Build phase: a question-independent level-1 event skeleton is constructed once per video. (2) Growth phase: for each question, the controller routes over the updated level-1 nodes, reuses stored descendants, and expands an unexplored leaf only when finer evidence is needed. Newly acquired information is propagated bottom-up. (3) Persistent memory: the refined hierarchy is retained across questions for subsequent reuse.
Figure 3: Qualitative examples of the Route–Check–Expand process. VTree routes to a relevant branch, checks evidence sufficiency, and expands the branch only when finer detail is required.

Figure 1: VTree raises accuracy while sharply cutting perquestion cost. Across three backbones (Qwen3-VL, Gemini2.5-Flash, Gemini-3.5-Flash) on LVBench: (a) Accuracy & context—VTree (green) outperforms feeding the video endto-end (purple) while reading 11–14× shorter context per question; (b) Execution time—VTree answers 5.6–7.2× faster in wall-clock time. Rather than ingesting the whole timeline, VTree grows its memory tree toward each question and reads only the branches the answer needs.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Egocentric Human Activity Recognition (Ego-HAR) leverages complementary cues from first-person vision (V) and inertial sensor data (S) to recognize daily activities, where video mainly captures appearance and object-related context while inertial signals capture motion cues that video may miss. However, existing pre-training methods typically supervise the fused representation with a single joint objective, which may underemphasize the complementarity between the two modalities and limit the model's ability to learn from distinct modality-oriented signals. To address this issue, we propose Multimodal Dual Representation Reconstruction (MDR2), a teacher-guided pre-training framework in which frozen, label-informed video and inertial teachers each provide dense, modality-specific targets to a multimodal student trained on temporally sparse inputs. On the EvIs-Kitchen dataset, MDR2 improves noun/verb F1-macro over the supervised M-Baseline by 9.20/6.17 points at K=4 video key frames and by 1.21/1.82 points at K=32. These results show that MDR2 consistently achieves higher mean recognition performance across the evaluated video-observation settings under the unified backbone setting, with more pronounced gains under sparse inputs.
authors: Yuzhe Hao, Ikuro Sato, Rei Kawakami, Koichi Shinoda
bullets: Targets the limitation of single-objective pre-training, which can underuse differences between video and inertial modalities.
Uses frozen, label-informed video and inertial teachers to provide dense modality-specific targets.
Trains a multimodal student from temporally sparse inputs through dual representation reconstruction.
On EvIs-Kitchen, improves noun/verb F1-macro over supervised M-Baseline by 9.20/6.17 points at 4 frames and 1.21/1.82 points at 32 frames.
Reports larger gains under sparse video observation settings within the evaluated unified-backbone setup.

papers.abstract: Convolutional networks for optical flow typically adopt progressively deeper pyramidal encoders under the assumption that larger receptive fields improve motion estimation. For particle image velocimetry (PIV), however, tracer-particle displacement between frames is bounded by the acquisition geometry, allowing network depth to be derived from the physically admissible displacement rather than inherited from general-purpose architectures. Using a layer-by-layer analysis of spatial-support growth, we derive its explicit upper bound and show that deeper architectures substantially exceed the support required for PIV, compromising training stability, spatial resolution under particle loss, and inference efficiency. Based on this analysis, we develop LIMA3, a lightweight pyramidal displacement estimator with 589,000 trainable parameters. Across synthetic and experimental benchmarks, LIMA3 matches the accuracy of established learned and classical methods with at least an order of magnitude less memory and substantially higher throughput, while retaining the physically expected coarsening of spatial resolution as tracer information is lost. Its linear memory scaling enables megapixel processing within embedded memory budgets, such that LIMA3 can reach over 900 image pairs per second at $640\times480$~pixel on an RTX 5090 and 99 image pairs per second on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. The spatial-support analysis provides a transferable design principle for compact optical-flow architectures and bounded-window attention, offering an alternative to compressing oversized general-purpose networks and enabling efficient operation alongside image acquisition.
authors: Claudio Mucignat, Kamila Zdybal, Ivan Lunati
bullets: PIV displacement limits allow the required spatial support—and thus network depth—to be derived from acquisition geometry.
The analysis shows conventional deeper pyramidal networks exceed PIV’s needs, potentially harming stability, resolution under particle loss, and efficiency.
LIMA3 is a 589,000-parameter lightweight pyramidal displacement estimator designed around these physical constraints.
It matches established learned and classical methods across synthetic and experimental benchmarks while using at least an order of magnitude less memory and achieving high throughput.
The design supports megapixel processing on embedded hardware and offers a transferable principle for compact optical-flow and bounded-window-attention architectures.

papers.abstract: The usefulness of an in-context demonstration for a vision-language model (VLM) depends on both the query image and the task posed about it. We study whether the frozen target VLM's own decoder states, read before answer generation, can select such demonstrations. BehaviorICL represents each image and task by a task-conditioned processing signature, the hidden states at the final input position across all decoder layers. Its training-free variant, BehaviorICL-Raw, averages cosine similarities between corresponding layer states and passes the retrieved examples with their reference answers to the same VLM. When the same NICO++ images are asked about their object or their context, Raw retrieves largely different demonstrations for the two questions and outperforms an image retriever given task-matched demonstrations on both VLMs. Across two VLMs and eight classification and visual question answering datasets, Raw gives the highest average accuracy among training-free retrievers on both VLMs and exceeds RICES with a CLIP ViT-L/14 encoder by 3.83 points on Qwen and 1.85 on InternVL. A lightweight shared projection, BehaviorICL-Proj, brings further gains on classification. Analyses of extraction text, decoder depth and bank answers help explain these gains, and attention analysis describes how the task text shifts attention at the extraction position toward the classified object. These results support the target VLM's internal states as a practical basis for visual in-context learning.
authors: Chenyang Wang, Jiamo Hu, Chengrui Wu, Lingyue Chen, Jianguo Chen, Xun Xu, Xulei Yang
bullets: Demonstration usefulness depends on both the query image and the task, so retrieval should be task-aware.
BehaviorICL represents each image–task pair using hidden states at the final input position across decoder layers.
Its training-free Raw variant retrieves examples by averaging layerwise cosine similarities and supplies them with reference answers to the same frozen VLM.

Across two VLMs and eight classification/VQA datasets, Raw achieved the best average accuracy among training-free retrievers, outperforming CLIP-based RICES by 3.83 points on Qwen and 1.85 on InternVL.
A lightweight projection variant further improved classification; analyses link gains to task text, decoder depth, bank answers, and attention shifts.

papers.abstract: Violence in films and streaming media remains a concern for audience protection and creates substantial workload for manual content classification. Existing violence-detection methods often rely on limited modalities or short video clips, making it difficult to capture complementary evidence and localise violent events in long, untrimmed videos. In this study, we develop a framework for multimodal video understanding that classifies violence severity, predicts multiple violence types, and locates violent events in time. We combine temporally aligned visual and audio features extracted using pretrained encoders through attention-based adaptive fusion, followed by Transformer-based temporal modelling. Our framework supports three complementary tasks: video-level violence-severity classification, multi-label violence-type prediction, and temporal localisation of violent events. We evaluate the framework on the XD-Violence benchmark and examine its cross-domain performance using AIRTLab. On XD-Violence, our multimodal model achieves 93.27\% severity-classification accuracy and a micro-F1 score of 88.60\% for multi-label violence-type prediction, outperforming the corresponding unimodal configurations. We achieve a mean temporal intersection-over-union (tIoU) of 0.5075 for temporal localisation. Our cross-domain experiments reveal performance degradation under different recording conditions, while our movie case studies demonstrate the framework's potential to retrieve potentially violent scenes for further review. Our results highlight the practical value of multimodal intelligent systems in supporting human reviewers with the identification, classification, and temporal retrieval of violent content in films and streaming media.
authors: Jiaqian Li, Rohitash Chandra
bullets: Addresses the limitations of single-modality methods and short-clip analysis for violence understanding in untrimmed videos.
Fuses temporally aligned visual and audio features with attention-based adaptive fusion, then models time using a Transformer.
Performs severity classification, multi-label violence-type prediction, and temporal localisation of violent events.
On XD-Violence, achieves 93.27% severity accuracy, 88.60% micro-F1 for violence types, and 0.5075 mean tIoU for localisation.
Cross-domain performance degrades under different recording conditions; movie case studies indicate practical retrieval potential.

papers.abstract: We study the compression of the 48 feed-forward network (FFN) matrices of the Vision Transformer ViT-L/16 to 2--8 bits with four schemes: a per-token grid, a fixed Gaussian Lloyd--Max table, a table fitted to the matrix, and a random-sign Hadamard rotation followed by the fixed table. We evaluate on 50,000 images. At 4 bits the top-1 accuracy of the four schemes lies within 0.8 points of the float32 model, while the agreement with its predictions ranges from 98.4\% to 94.4\%. We use the angular error between the compressed and the float32 residual stream, followed through the blocks, as a portable measure that ranks the schemes as the final classification does and shows where the ranking is built: with rotation the angle grows close to the square root of the number of blocks, the signature of independently accumulating errors, while the other schemes are amplified in the later blocks. The same measure shows that a scheme that is better on one block in isolation can be worse in the whole network. To address this inconsistency we introduce an angular measure of the spectrum of the output of a block, which in isolation orders the schemes as the whole network does where they diverge most. We support these observations with real samples and with statistically generated ones. The scope is one model, the FFN weights only, and float evaluation of compressed weights; no speed-up is claimed. The error measures and the sample generation, however, can be applied to other models and precisions.
authors: Paolo D'Alberto
bullets: Studies compressing all 48 ViT-L/16 FFN matrices to 2–8 bits using four quantization schemes.
At 4 bits, all schemes remain within 0.8 top-1 accuracy points of the float32 model, with 94.4–98.4% prediction agreement.
Angular error in the residual stream ranks schemes similarly to final classification and reveals where errors accumulate across blocks.
Rotation produces near-independent error growth, while other schemes experience stronger amplification in later blocks.
An angular measure of block-output spectra resolves cases where isolated block performance conflicts with whole-network behavior.

papers.abstract: Most of what matters in a day is spoken and written down nowhere: a dosing interval named at a clinic, a deadline moved in passing, the place a document was set down. Such information is consequential because it is operational, and fragile because it arrives during divided attention -- the moment its importance becomes clear is rarely the moment it was said. For people living with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease or age-related episodic memory decline, that gap bounds independent living. Conventional aids close it poorly: notes, reminders and calendars require the user to notice, interrupt and transcribe, adding extraneous cognitive load exactly where attention is already committed. We present REMORA, a voice-first memory assistant that converts consented speech into structured, auditable memory records. REMORA transcribes and diarizes captured audio, extracts memory candidates -- tasks, appointments, names, instructions, object locations -- each retaining provenance into the conversation it came from, and holds records, embeddings and relationships in a single relational system of record. Recall combines lexical, semantic, relational and recency signals, since no one signal covers the ways people interrogate their own past, and reaches the user either through an explicit query or through a confidence-gated cue that stays silent unless it is likely to help. Generation is bound by a grounding contract: only retrieved evidence may be used, and absent a supporting memory REMORA abstains rather than confabulates, because a fluent invention about one's own past will be acted upon as fact. A requirements survey and a pilot study with memory-loss users indicate that conversational forgetting extends well beyond clinical populations, that grounded and concise recall is feasible in controlled settings, and that privacy, rather than accuracy, is the binding constraint on adoption.
authors: Bilal Jawaid, Muhammad Maaz Uddin, Osama Farooqi, Saadia Karim
bullets: Addresses the cognitive burden of manually recording tasks, appointments, instructions, and object locations, especially for people with memory decline.
Transcribes and diarizes consented speech, extracts structured memory candidates, and preserves provenance in a relational system of record.
Combines lexical, semantic, relational, and recency signals for explicit search and confidence-gated proactive cues.
Uses a grounding contract: responses rely only on retrieved evidence and abstain when no supporting memory exists.
A requirements survey and pilot suggest grounded recall is feasible, while privacy is the main adoption constraint.

figures.caption: Figure 2: REMORA system overview. A recall need arises away from the moment of capture and is expressed as a short voice or text query. The unified memory pipeline transcribes and segments captured speech, attributes segments to speakers and extracts memory candidates, stores each as a record carrying provenance, and answers from retrieved records only. Retrieval combines four signals over a single relational system of record, and the answer is returned with the segment it came from.

Figure 1: A representative recall episode. (1) A request is made in conversation and captured with the speaker’s consent. (2) The detail is needed hours later, at the moment it has been forgotten. (3) The user asks for it in a single short question rather than searching for a note. (4) REMORA answers from the stored record and returns the conversation and time the answer came from, so the user can check it against the moment it was spoken.
Figure 3: Survey responses (n = 50): frequency of forgetting conversational detail, problems caused by it, acceptance of consent-based listening, and level of privacy concern.
Figure 4: Situations in which participants expected REMORA to be most useful (n = 50).

Figure 5: Composition of transcription error by acoustic condition. Each bar is segmented into substitutions, deletions and insertions, and labelled with total word error rate. Deletions remain below 0.4% in every condition: the recogniser does not fall silent as conditions worsen, it substitutes. The code-switched condition is omitted here because at 77.36% it is off-scale and, as table 8 notes, reflects a script mismatch rather than a comparable recognition result.

Figure 6: Capture and recall. (a) Capture offers focused recording of a conversation and a passive monitor that keeps a rolling buffer for trigger detection; the Session active banner is persistent, which is the visible-state half of G4. (b) When a session ends, REMORA produces a session summary organised by decisions, commitments and entities, giving the user a reviewable account of what was retained. (c) Recall accepts a typed or spoken question and exposes the retrieval mode explicitly—Hybrid, Keyword or Semantic—so that the signals combined in eq. (3) can also be exercised in isolation.

Figure 7: Stored memory and its provenance. (d) Extracted records are listed with their tags and with per-record controls for editing, viewing revision history, and removal, satisfying the review-and-correct requirement of G4. (e) The verbatim transcript is retained alongside the extracted records rather than discarded, which is what allows an answer to be traced to the source segment xi of eq. (1) rather than only to a summary. (f) Entities and relationships extracted from memories are searchable as a graph, which is the relational signal C of eq. (3); trigger candidates are the inferred memory needs that assisted recall evaluates against the gates of section 5.3.

papers.abstract: Co-creating layouts such as websites and slides is a useful testbed for evaluating multi-turn instruction following of LLM systems. Since an intended layout's appearance cannot be well expressed in a single turn, the user must wait for the LLM to generate a layout then iteratively refine it with the LLM over multiple turns. We present a small-scale, exploratory (n=6) study of this multi-turn process to compare the differences of human-AI and AI-AI teams on the same layout-generation task. Given a reference wire-frame layout, a participant or a language model 'speaker' issues natural-language instructions to a fixed 'listener' LLM over multiple turns until the speaker is satisfied. Rather than an LLM as the judge, we fit a scoring function over geometric layout features using curated human preference data (n=19). We find that LLMs tend to encode the entire layout in the first turn, while humans iterate over many turns on average, writing much shorter instructions. We also find that human-AI teams consistently scored lower than AI-AI teams. This gap is driven by a limiter of human participants in specifying precise sizes and positions (e.g. 42 pixels to the right). Humans perform almost at par with language models on other features like ordering the elements into nested structures. We then perform interventions on the speaker LLMs to make them more human-like, and find it difficult. This raises the challenge of using LLMs as user models to evaluate multi-turn co-creation tasks.
authors: Rajvir Singh Naginder Singh Virdi, Yewen Pu
bullets: Compares human-AI and AI-AI teams refining the same wireframe layout through natural-language, multi-turn instructions.
Uses a learned scoring function based on geometric layout features and human preference data rather than an LLM judge.
LLMs typically encode the full layout in the first turn, while humans use more turns with shorter instructions.
Human performance is especially weaker for specifying exact sizes and positions, but is nearly comparable for nested element ordering.
Interventions to make speaker LLMs behave more like humans were difficult, challenging their use as user models.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can display sycophancy, a tendency to excessively praise, agree with, or validate a user. Existing studies have tested LLMs for sycophancy primarily through application programming interfaces (APIs) rather than the consumer user interfaces (UIs) through which the public commonly interacts with LLMs. Access mode (API vs. UI) may affect observed sycophancy rates. However, it remains unknown to what extent prominent models show API-UI differences in social sycophancy, which includes behaviors potentially more likely in UIs (e.g., softening warranted criticism). We tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek through both APIs and UIs on four dimensions of social sycophancy. Across models, UI access was generally associated with greater social sycophancy, with odds ratios up to 7.56 (95% CI [6.22, 9.20]). However, UI-API differences varied significantly across models for all sycophancy dimensions, including a pronounced reversal for DeepSeek moral sycophancy (43% UI vs. 82.3% API). Overall, our results suggest that API-based LLM evaluations may underestimate the prevalence of sycophancy in corresponding consumer-facing systems, making access conditions consequential for the external validity of LLM evaluation. To facilitate research on access-mode effects, we release 57,000 model responses and SycoUI, a browser-automation pipeline for standardized cross-interface LLM evaluation.

papers.abstract: Deploying large language models on commodity CPUs is often constrained not only by computational throughput but also by the resident memory required to execute quantized models within fixed system budgets. We present MemVanta, an experimental C++20 inference runtime for quantized GGUF language models that treats memory residency as a first-class systems objective. MemVanta combines memory-mapped model access, bounded tensor caching, quantized execution paths, paged key-value state, and explicit memory-pressure validation. We evaluate MemVanta against a pinned llama.cpp baseline using the same OpenLLaMA 7B v2 Q4_0 GGUF under CPU-only execution. Across five measured runs following warm-up, MemVanta records a peak resident set size of 3,983,412 KiB compared with 7,586,960 KiB for llama.cpp, corresponding to a 47.50 percent reduction in peak RSS. This memory reduction involves a substantial throughput trade-off: MemVanta achieves 3.15 +/- 0.04 tokens/s for prompt processing and 1.52 +/- 0.02 tokens/s for token generation, compared with 45.82 +/- 0.96 and 7.76 +/- 0.09 tokens/s, respectively, for llama.cpp. In a separate Linux cgroup-v2 experiment with swap disabled, MemVanta completes execution at a tested 3584 MiB memory ceiling, while llama.cpp is OOM-killed at that ceiling and first succeeds at the tested 3840 MiB level. These results position MemVanta as a memory-efficiency research prototype rather than a throughput competitor. We analyze the architectural mechanisms underlying this trade-off and discuss reproducibility, correctness, limitations, and opportunities for memory-constrained CPU and edge inference.

papers.abstract: Simulation-based evaluation of embodied models requires calibrated interactions, diverse tasks, and explicit execution constraints. We present RoboColiseum, a platform combining system identification, composable physics and rendering, and multidimensional benchmarking. Recorded-command replay characterizes robot dynamics and object interactions, while a shared interface connects rigid and deformable simulation to rendering. Across 22 paired real--simulation robot--task configurations, task scores have a reported Pearson correlation of 0.9686. Eight evaluation tracks span instruction following, spatial reasoning, general manipulation, robustness, dexterous manipulation, precision manipulation, whole-body coordination, and execution across robot embodiments. Budget-aware scoring combines task progress, resource use, and completion rewards. We report 12 selected Season~I policies and all 11 systems on the public Season~II leaderboard, comprising eight Agent systems and three VLA policies. Agent2Act connects language models to robot-control execution; the VLA study uses mixed-task supervised fine-tuning. The results reveal substantial variation across tracks within each evaluation category. RoboColiseum connects simulation development with capability-oriented evaluation and provides a foundation for extending robot interactions and model assessment.

papers.abstract: Current leading video generation models can synthesize highly realistic videos, while still frequently violating physical and logical constraints in multi-step reasoning and planning, even after training with large-scale reasoning data or existing diffusion RL methods. We attribute these failures to the conventional video training paradigm, which treats a solution as a fixed-length clip rather than a chain of decisions. We present ViDecide, a decision-centric framework that trains video diffusion models to predict state transitions causally and decide when to stop, with a decision-focused training schedule. We further propose Corrective Fine-tuning (CFT), which corrects failed decisions by mapping their noise to the model's own successful continuations, achieving stable improvement without policy-gradient optimization. Across abstract games, planning tasks, and a new benchmark of multi-step robot planning, ViDecide achieves an average strict success rate of 83.8%, far above 23.3% for standard fine-tuning and 67.8% for the strongest prior method, and generalizes to larger puzzles and unseen layouts. Our framework therefore unlocks greater potential for video generation models as reliable reasoners and planners in the visual world. Project page: https://kevin-thu.github.io/ViDecide.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures activate only a subset of experts for each token, allowing large language models (LLMs) to scale parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation per token. However, intermediate data movement and uneven expert loads limit the efficiency of MoE inference on TPUs. To address these bottlenecks, we introduce Fuse-All MoE, a TPU kernel design that jointly optimizes expert computation, output communication, and load balancing. The kernel fuses token collection, expert projections, gated activation, and output writes, retaining expert computation intermediates on chip. Fixed token-slot destinations allow scheduling and expert placement to change while preserving routing semantics. In prefill-decode (PD) disaggregated serving, Fuse-All MoE balances EP16 prefill workloads through scheduling and expert redistribution, while symmetric EP8TP2 shares active expert computation between the two TensorCore devices within each chip during decode. Our experiments show that Fuse-All MoE reduces kernel runtime for a measured skewed EP16 prefill workload from 2.3x to 1.09x the same fixed reference time for a balanced workload. Across 32-512 decode tokens, symmetric EP8TP2 reduces kernel latency by up to 21.3% relative to fused EP16. With accompanying serving stack optimizations, the integrated system improves serving throughput by up to 34.5% over the Megablox EP16 baseline.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate responses longer than necessary, increasing inference latency and computational cost. While prompting can encourage conciseness, controlling output length without compromising response completeness remains challenging. Aggressive early stopping can reduce generation costs but risks terminating responses prematurely. We introduce MinimalLM, a training-free framework for reliable verbosity control that combines uncertainty-aware, length-dependent stop-token adjustment with structural completeness guardrails. MinimalLM separates the decision of when to stop from whether stopping is structurally appropriate, coordinating response-level instructions, decoding-time intervention, and completion checks without modifying model parameters or requiring auxiliary models. We evaluate MinimalLM across three open-source LLMs and 330 questions, producing 5,940 responses across baseline and ablation configurations. MinimalLM reduces generated tokens by 47.6%, accelerates individual responses by 19-68%, and eliminates structurally truncated outputs in the primary evaluation. Despite substantial token savings, it achieves an average quality score of 8.04/10, compared with 8.42/10 for unmodified models and 6.46/10 for length-matched truncation. Evaluations across diverse subject domains (such as healthcare, programming, law, and science) demonstrate robust efficiency gains, while ablations establish the complementary roles of decoding control and completeness constraints. Our findings highlight that efficient generation requires more than producing fewer tokens: it requires controlling when generation ends while preserving response integrity. MinimalLM offers a lightweight, training-free approach toward this goal.

papers.abstract: Dynamic and continuously evolving environments present significant challenges for robotic mapping and scene understanding, particularly on construction sites where moving agents, temporary obstacles, and persistent structural changes coexist. While dynamic and long-term SLAM methods can detect motion and environmental changes, their outputs are predominantly metric representations that provide limited structure for higher-level spatial and temporal reasoning. This paper presents a LiDAR-based real-time temporal construction scene graph (T-ConSG) that jointly represents free-space regions, static objects, dynamic objects, and environmental events with spatial-relational and event-participation edges. The proposed framework incrementally constructs the graph from LiDAR-derived geometric evidence, maintaining persistent free-space and static-object information while tracking dynamic objects. Changes in accumulated spatial evidence are further represented as explicit installation and removal events, allowing the graph to capture both transient dynamics and persistent environmental evolution. We demonstrate the proposed representation through three complementary application studies: dynamics-aware navigation in a bricklaying testbed, construction progress monitoring on the ConSLAM dataset, and online change detection in a simulated construction environment. The results demonstrate that the proposed T-ConSG provides a unified representation for organizing spatial and temporal information and supports robotic reasoning across environments containing both short-term dynamics and persistent changes.
