papers.abstract: Goal-conditioned manipulation policies are steered by a goal image, a picture of the desired post-manipulation scene synthesized from the current observation and a language instruction. The prevailing assumption is that better image-editing quality yields better goals, so goal generators are built and compared using general image-editing metrics. We show this assumption is false. Across two independent goal-conditioned policies on CALVIN, the image editors that top aggregate editing-quality leaderboards (Gemini 3 Pro Image and GPT Image 1.5) produce worse control targets than our proposed far smaller finetuned open models, and the gap widens sharply for the multi-step (long-horizon) tasks robots actually face. A per-dimension analysis explains why. Downstream policy success is governed almost entirely by manipulation adherence (selecting the right object and the right final state; Spearman $ρ\approx 0.9$ with success), while photorealism and aesthetic fidelity, precisely where large proprietary editors excel, are uncorrelated with success ($ρ\approx 0$). This dissociation holds on both CALVIN and the real-world-aligned SIMPLER-Bridge benchmark. We then present SGE-Goal, a spatially-grounded decomposed editing framework that predicts initial and final 2D edit-region masks before goal-image synthesis. SGE-Goal turns open base models (FLUX.1 Kontext, FLUX.2 klein) into the strongest goal generators we evaluate on CALVIN, and second only to Gemini 3 Pro Image on SIMPLER-Bridge. Base models fine-tuned with SGE-Goal also hold up under chaining far better than the best proprietary editor, sustaining roughly seven times the success rate at the longest (five-step) chains. We release code, datasets, checkpoints, and a human-aligned diagnostic evaluator. Our results argue that goal generators must be selected by downstream utility, not by editing-quality leaderboards.
authors: Riddhi Chatterjee
Ritish Shrirao
Kushagra Mehrotra
Viswanath Gopalakrishnan
bullets: Image-editing leaderboard performance does not predict the usefulness of generated control targets.
Manipulation adherence—choosing the correct object and final state—strongly correlates with policy success, while photorealism and aesthetics do not.
SGE-Goal predicts initial and final 2D edit-region masks before synthesizing the goal image.
On CALVIN and SIMPLER-Bridge, SGE-Goal makes smaller open models highly effective goal generators and improves robustness to chained tasks.
The work releases code, datasets, checkpoints, and a human-aligned diagnostic evaluator.

papers.selection_reason: Shows goal-image synthesis for goal-conditioned robotic manipulation must be optimized for downstream control utility, with a spatially-grounded editing framework.
papers.title: Goal Images Are Control Targets: Spatially-Grounded Goal-Image Synthesis for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: For robotic manipulation, goal images should be optimized for spatially correct actions—not visual editing quality—and SGE-Goal improves long-horizon control by grounding edits in predicted regions.

papers.abstract: Local learning algorithms can reshape resource requirements of artificial intelligence. The memory bottleneck of standard end-to-end backpropagation lies in the need to store all network activations until the loss gradient has been propagated back through. Local learning avoids this, but typically at a cost in accuracy. We study how to achieve accurate and memory efficient local learning in transformers. For each transformer block, we train a local proxy network to predict the global network output via distillation. Gradients can be independently propagated through this local proxy while estimating well the backpropagation gradients. In theory, this approach is exact for deep linear networks; in non-linear residual models, the gradient error can be bounded when using the appropriate residual proxy. We verify this numerically and demonstrate that optimizing the distillation loss improves gradient estimation. Evaluating the performance of proxy propagation on CIFAR-100 in vision transformers, we find that it achieves a better accuracy/memory trade-off compared to other local algorithms. Finally, we show that the method is further relevant for fine-tuning large language models on a small memory budget. Our method trains faster and achieves higher performance than memory-efficient zeroth-order learning algorithms with comparable memory cost.
authors: Wu S. Zihan
Brian A. Yuan
Guillaume Bellec
bullets: Addresses the activation-memory bottleneck of standard backpropagation and the accuracy loss of typical local-learning methods.
Trains a local proxy for each transformer block to distill the global network output and estimate backpropagation gradients independently.
Provides exactness guarantees for deep linear networks and bounded gradient error for suitable nonlinear residual proxies.
Experiments show improved gradient estimation, a better accuracy–memory trade-off on CIFAR-100 vision transformers, and stronger, faster fine-tuning than comparable zeroth-order methods.
The approach is demonstrated for vision transformers and memory-constrained large-language-model fine-tuning.

papers.title: Local proxies for memory-efficient training
papers.tldr: Local proxy networks enable accurate, memory-efficient local training of transformers without storing all activations for end-to-end backpropagation.

papers.abstract: Reducing memory use in large language model (LLM) training is an ongoing challenge. Activation checkpointing saves memory by recomputation, while lossy compression changes the stored activations. The reemergence of sparse $\relu$ and $\relu^2$ activations creates a third opportunity: losslessly compressing the activation cache itself. We present BitSparse, a GPU-resident lossless compression format for sparse activations. Compression and reconstruction run in custom Triton kernels fused into an autograd function, shrinking the activation cache while recovering it exactly for the backward pass. Bfloat16 (BF16) and FP8 activations are supported. Optional sign-bit packing further increases compression up to close to the theoretical limit. We analyze its compression ratio and compare it to the theoretical optimum. BitSparse lowers per-token VRAM by 31\% and 30\% Modded-NanoGPT and Nemotron-H respectively, with overheads of no more than 1\% at practical sequence lengths. Additionally, a new preallocated buffer system avoids host synchronization during training when variable size tensors are allocated.
authors: Max Zhu
Bohang Sun
Pietro Lio
Jialin Yu
bullets: Targets activation-cache memory, complementing checkpointing and lossy compression.
Uses custom Triton kernels fused with autograd for GPU-resident compression and exact reconstruction.
Supports BF16 and FP8 activations, with optional sign-bit packing for higher compression.
Reduces per-token VRAM by 31% in Modded-NanoGPT and 30% in Nemotron-H, with up to 1% overhead at practical sequence lengths.
Introduces preallocated buffers to avoid host synchronization for variable-size tensors.

papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) reduce or eliminate the need for large labelled datasets by enforcing governing equations during training. Physics-informed Deep Operator Networks (PI-DeepONets) extend this approach to learning solution operators, enabling rapid prediction across families of problems. Despite these advantages, we show that their application to higher-dimensional problems remains limited by the computational cost of training. To address this issue, we propose a modified PI-DeepONet architecture that reduces this cost by removing redundancy in how the Branch network processes input functions across collocation points. The proposed formulation is mathematically equivalent to the original architecture but reduces input tensor sizes and the number of Branch network evaluations. We analyse the computational complexity of both architectures and derive theoretical scaling laws for training time with respect to the number of collocation points and input functions. The proposed architecture is evaluated on 1D, 2D, and 3D linear advection problems. In all cases, it achieves comparable predictive accuracy to the original PI-DeepONet while consistently reducing training time. In 2D experiments, a maximum speed-up of $3.75\times$ is observed, with empirical training-time scaling agreeing with the predicted linear dependence on collocation points and input functions. Furthermore, training a 3D model on an NVIDIA A100 GPU is only feasible using the proposed architecture, as the original formulation exceeds memory limits. These results demonstrate that careful consideration of how PI-DeepONets are implemented can yield substantial gains, enhancing the practical performance of PI-DeepONets and enabling their application to otherwise intractable physics-informed learning problems.
authors: Nahum Banks
Gustavo A. M. de Almeida
Sergio Maldonado
bullets: Reduces redundancy by processing each input function once across collocation points rather than repeatedly in the Branch network.
Mathematically equivalent reformulation lowers input tensor sizes and the number of Branch-network evaluations.
Validated on 1D, 2D, and 3D linear advection problems with comparable predictive accuracy and consistently shorter training times.
Achieves up to 3.75× speed-up in 2D; a 3D model fits on an NVIDIA A100 only with the proposed architecture.
Empirical training-time scaling matches the predicted linear dependence on collocation points and input functions.

papers.abstract: Knowing the layout of the physical world matters for many applications, yet the sensors we rely on for it (e.g., cameras and LiDAR) can fail in darkness, in adverse weather, or behind walls. Wireless signals do not face these limitations: every link between a base station and a user is shaped by the buildings it passes, reflects from, or is blocked by, leaving information about the surrounding scene embedded in the wireless channel measured at the endpoints. However, mapping channel measurements to the environment is a severely ill-posed problem: a measurement records only the structures that interact with the transmitted electromagnetic waves along its propagation paths, and even these observations can often be explained by multiple plausible scenes. We therefore formulate wireless scene reconstruction as posterior inference and develop a hierarchical framework with two complementary stages to approach this problem. A wireless foundation model, pretrained to respect propagation physics, transforms each channel measurement into a representation of the scene structure that shaped the observation. A diffusion model then jointly integrates representations from multiple measurements to model and sample the posterior over building occupancy, with consensus over samples producing the final reconstruction. We demonstrate that the framework can accurately recover building footprints from wireless channel measurements alone and show that its performance depends critically on both design components: physics-grounded representations expose scene-relevant information, while joint posterior inference coherently integrates complementary observations.
authors: Vahid Yazdnian
Yasaman Ghasempour
bullets: Addresses the ill-posed problem of inferring scene geometry from partial, ambiguous wireless propagation observations.
Uses a physics-grounded wireless foundation model to encode each channel measurement into scene-structure representations.
Applies diffusion-based posterior inference to jointly combine multiple measurements and sample plausible building occupancies.
Produces final reconstructions through consensus across posterior samples.
Demonstrates accurate recovery of building footprints from wireless measurements alone; both stages are critical to performance.

papers.abstract: Weather prediction is undergoing an important shift, with data-driven AI models outperforming leading numerical weather prediction systems on average at a fraction of the computational cost. Yet, whether this success extends to extreme events remains contested. Earlier evaluations have exposed important shortcomings, but have largely focused on deterministic models and metrics, leaving the capabilities of the latest probabilistic models less understood. We conduct an extensive benchmark of tropical cyclone forecasting, comparing GenCast, FourCastNet 3, and FGN with ECMWF's operational physics-based ensemble, IFS-ENS. We develop a suite of probabilistic metrics and diagnostic analyses to assess cyclone tracking, intensity biases, uncertainty, and the wind-pressure relationship that characterizes storm structure. We find that, despite remaining limitations in intensity and ensemble spread, leading AI models substantially outperform IFS-ENS in cyclone tracking: FGN achieves better probabilistic location scores for 90% of evaluated storms in 2025. Further analyses reveal model-specific failure modes and suggest a lingering influence of pretraining data, pointing to opportunities for targeted improvement. Nonetheless, these results suggest that AI models are capable of capturing physical relationships that remain predictive well beyond typical weather conditions, motivating further investigation into how these capabilities emerge and how to strengthen them.
authors: Nathan Chalumeau
Xavier Renard
Remi Meynadier
Hugo Rakotoarimanga
Marcin Detyniecki
Emmanuel de Bezenac
bullets: Benchmarks GenCast, FourCastNet 3, and FGN against ECMWF’s IFS-ENS.
Introduces probabilistic metrics and diagnostics for tracking, intensity bias, uncertainty, and wind–pressure structure.
AI models substantially outperform IFS-ENS on cyclone tracking; FGN has better probabilistic location scores for 90% of evaluated storms in 2025.
Models retain limitations in intensity forecasts and ensemble spread, with distinct failure modes.
Findings suggest AI models capture physical relationships relevant to extreme weather, while pretraining data may influence errors.

The shaded area is a model’s additional reduction in the cyclone region. FGN leads GenCast in both domains, and both improve more on IFS-ENS in the cyclone region than globally, though GenCast’s global CRPS is above IFS-ENS’s at the first lead. Right: bias of the ensemble-mean maximum 10m wind speed, averaged across storms per lead and normalized by HRES-fc0’s mean maximum wind (19.5 m/s), with ERA5 for comparison. FGN and GenCast have similar negative peak-wind biases at short and intermediate leads despite their different CRPS.

Figure 7: Stability of the model comparison across subgroups (2021–2023). Track NLL (top row) and cyclone-local CRPS (bottom row) for GenCast, IFS-ENS and FCN3, averaged within subgroups defined by Saffir–Simpson category (left), ocean basin (center) and year (right); n gives the subgroup size. The NLL uses the 106 retained storms and the CRPS all 125, hence the different subgroup sizes. The three models move together across nearly all subgroups.

Figure 2: Typhoon Bualoi (2025). FGN (red) and IFS-ENS (blue) forecasts at four lead times: dots are individual members, contours are their density, and black dots are the observed IBTrACS positions along the track (grey line). IFS-ENS’s members separate into distinct clusters at intermediate leads, which an ensemble mean cannot represent.

Left: reduction of GenCast’s summed normalized fair-CRPS relative to FCN3’s, 100 (1− CRPSGenCast/CRPSFCN3), in cyclone regions (solid) and globally (dashed); positive favors GenCast. The shaded area is GenCast’s additional reduction in the cyclone region: 3–5% from 24–220 h, versus about 1% globally. Right: bias of the ensemble-mean maximum 10m wind speed, averaged across storms per lead and normalized by ERA5’s mean maximum wind (16.6 m/s). GenCast underestimates peak winds at short and intermediate leads despite its better local CRPS.

As in Figure 7, for FGN, IFS-ENS and operational GenCast, at the same scale; subgroups are defined by Saffir–Simpson category (left) and ocean basin (right). The NLL uses the 41 retained storms and the CRPS all 53. Some basins contain very few storms, down to n=1, which explains the larger gaps there.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates AI weather models as predictors of extreme environment dynamics, relevant to world models.
papers.title: Can AI Forecast the Extremes? Evaluating Probabilistic Weather Models on Tropical Cyclones
papers.tldr: Leading probabilistic AI weather models forecast tropical cyclone tracks better than ECMWF’s operational ensemble, but still struggle with storm intensity and uncertainty calibration.
